context_blocks.text: A nondeterministic reachability algorithm can guess the next vertex of a path, checking each edge as it goes. It needs only a current vertex and a step counter, so logarithmic memory suffices. The difficulty is that a graph can offer many successful sequences of guesses. An unambiguous algorithm must retain the ability to recognize a path while allowing only one successful computation.

This restriction is weaker than determinism. The machine may still branch many times and have many rejecting computations. On a reachable graph, only one complete branch may accept. Consequently, \(\mathrm{NL}=UL\) would explain something about the source of nondeterministic power without establishing \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\). A proof that \(\mathrm{NL}\ne UL\) would, however, also separate deterministic and nondeterministic logspace, since \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq UL\subseteq \mathrm{NL}\).

One approach is to assign positive integer weights to edges so that every reachable ordered pair has a unique minimum-weight path. Reinhardt and Allender show how such min-isolating weights support an unambiguous reachability algorithm. If the weights are polynomially bounded and can be generated in deterministic logspace from the graph, the resulting memory use remains logarithmic. Randomly choosing suitable weights can give isolation, but does not provide a uniform deterministic construction.

Reinhardt and Allender also prove NL/poly=UL/poly. Here a polynomial-length advice string may depend on the input length and be shared by every input of that length, without any requirement that the string be generated efficiently. This is evidence that isolation is possible in a broad nonuniform sense. Removing the advice is essential to the ordinary \(\mathrm{NL}=UL\) question.

The strongest checked unconditional general simulation uses more than logarithmic memory. Van Melkebeek and Prakriya give an unambiguous polynomial-time simulation of NL using \(O((\log  N)^{3/2})\) space. Their work reduces the randomness and weight-description costs of isolation. The remaining square-root-of-logarithm factor is small numerically, but it is an unbounded factor in the resource defining the target class.

The inherited 2025 paper by Doron, Pyne, Tell and Williams develops new hardness-versus-randomness tools for isolation. Its main conditional unambiguity theorem concerns the linear-space analogue \(\mathrm{NSPACE}[n]\subseteq\)USPACE\([O(n)]\), under uniform circuit lower bounds with specified oracle access. The March 2026 Pyne–Tell survey gives a refined version. These assumptions are unproved, and the linear-space conclusion should not be reported as an unconditional logspace equality.

A February 2026 revision by Arvind, Chakraborty and Datta gives reachability algorithms in a catalytic model with UL oracle access. Catalytic computation permits extra memory initially containing arbitrary data, provided that the data are restored at the end. This is an interesting way to use storage, but it supplies resources absent from a plain UL machine. The headline about derandomizing isolation therefore does not resolve this card.

Hoza proves a new limitation in July 2026. Suppose one weight assignment must work for every layered graph of given width w and length \(\ell\), without examining which edges are actually present. Such an oblivious min-isolating assignment requires weights of magnitude \(2^{\Omega (\log  w\cdot \log  \ell )}\), so polynomially bounded universal weights cannot solve the general problem by this route. This restriction does not cover assignments that depend on the actual graph or other unambiguous algorithms.

A solution would determine whether many successful paths are ever intrinsically necessary when computation has only logarithmic memory. It would also clarify how much information must be retained to select a unique witness from a large implicitly represented family. The challenge is not to name a canonical path mathematically, but to recognize one with the required uniqueness guarantee and very little working storage.

cards.title: L versus NL
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine A and an absolute constant C such that, for every directed graph G on vertices \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and every s,t, A decides whether t is reachable from s while using at most $C\log_2(n+2)$ work-tape cells? G is supplied explicitly as a read-only adjacency matrix, together with s and t. The machine must halt and be correct on every input. This is equivalent to \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\).
cards.definitions: The graph may have self-loops; reachability allows a path of length zero, so \(s=t\) is a yes instance. Input access is two-way and read-only. Work tapes have a fixed finite alphabet; visited work-tape cells, including all counters and stored vertex identifiers, count toward space. The finite control and read-only input cells do not. There is no advice, random tape, oracle, writable copy of the input, or external storage. L is deterministic \(O(\log  N)\) work space on binary inputs of bit length N. NL uses the same space bound with nondeterministic transitions and accepts exactly when some computation branch accepts; all branches can be clocked to halt within polynomial time. Since the matrix encoding has \(N=Theta(n^{2})\) bits, \(O(\log  N)=O(\log  n)\). A halting deterministic machine with this space bound automatically runs in polynomial time: it cannot repeat a complete configuration.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an always-correct deterministic logarithmic-space reachability algorithm for all directed graphs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. By NL-completeness under deterministic logspace reductions, either direction settles L versus NL. An algorithm for undirected graphs, a nondeterministic algorithm, or an algorithm using a larger power of log n does not answer the stated question.
cards.why: Directed reachability is the canonical model of exploring possible computational states. Its space complexity determines whether nondeterministic logarithmic memory can be replaced by deterministic logarithmic memory, with consequences for low-memory graph algorithms and complexity theory.

importance.reason: A central space-complexity separation expressed by a basic graph problem. The contrast with solved undirected reachability isolates a fundamental role of edge direction and nondeterminism.

progress.text: Savitch proves that nondeterministic space s can be simulated deterministically in \(O(s^{2})\) space, for s at least logarithmic. Directed reachability consequently has an \(O(\log ^{2} n)\)-space algorithm.

Immerman and Szelepcsényi independently establish closure of nondeterministic space under complementation. In particular \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\), so both reachability and nonreachability admit nondeterministic logspace algorithms.
Reingold obtains deterministic logarithmic space for undirected connectivity, published at STOC 2005 and subsequently in JACM. Arbitrary directed graphs are outside that theorem.

Doron, Pyne, Tell, and Williams give two algorithms such that, on each directed graph, at least one succeeds: deterministic polynomial-time, polylogarithmic-space transitive closure, or nondeterministic logarithmic-space random-walk estimation. This per-graph alternative does not give the first algorithm on every graph or reduce its space to \(O(\log  n)\).

Bhadra and Tewari show NL-hardness even for directed graphs whose edges can be partitioned into two forests of directed paths of length at most two, including when the partition is supplied. Such a simple decomposition therefore does not make the general logspace obstacle disappear.

context_blocks.text: A graph search usually remembers which vertices it has visited. With only logarithmic space, it can store a constant number of vertex names and counters, but cannot keep a separate visited bit for every vertex. The input may be rescanned as often as necessary. The challenge is to organize those repeated scans so that arbitrary directed paths can be detected without retaining a large search frontier.

Nondeterminism gives a simple logarithmic-space procedure: keep the current vertex and a length counter, guess the next edge, and accept if t is reached within \(n- 1\) edges. Any reachable target has a simple path within that bound. For a general nondeterministic logspace computation, vertices can instead represent machine configurations. An accepting computation becomes a directed path, explaining why this graph problem captures the whole class NL.

Savitch’s algorithm recursively asks whether a path can pass through a candidate midpoint. It saves space by recomputing subproblems, but a logarithmic recursion depth with logarithmic information per level uses \(O(\log ^{2} n)\) space. Its running time is quasipolynomial. Reducing the storage to a single logarithmic factor would also force polynomial time in the stated machine model.

For undirected graphs, Reingold already achieved the logarithmic target. Edge direction is therefore a substantive part of this card. Likewise, \(\mathrm{NL}=\mathrm{coNL}\) shows that nonreachability has a nondeterministic logspace procedure; it does not remove nondeterminism. Recent connections with random-walk estimation make the landscape richer, while leaving the same deterministic directed question.

cards.title: Sliding-scale PCP conjecture
cards.formal: Do constants \(a,b,c>0\) and \(q\ge 1\) exist such that 3-SAT has a verifier using at most a \(\log _{2}(N+2)\) random bits and q queries to a proof of at most \((N+2)^{b}\) symbols over an alphabet of size at most \((N+2)^{b}\), with perfect completeness and soundness at most \((N+2)^{- c}\)?
cards.definitions: N is the bit length of an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula. A uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier receives the input, a uniform random bit string and oracle access to a fixed proof string. It reads at most q alphabet symbols, each encoded with \(O(\log  N)\) bits, and accepts or rejects. Queries may be adaptive. On a satisfiable formula some proof is always accepted; on an unsatisfiable formula every proof has acceptance probability at most \((N+2)^{- c}\). Polynomial bounds and all constants are universal. No cryptographic soundness assumption or interaction is allowed.

context_blocks.text: The PCP theorem achieves constant error with a constant number of queries. Driving soundness down to an inverse polynomial while retaining a constant number of queries would give substantially stronger verification and constraint-satisfaction gaps.

Dinur, Harsha and Kindler obtain inverse-polynomial error with polyloglogarithmically many queries. Their paper explicitly names the constant-query polynomial-alphabet endpoint as the sliding-scale conjecture in this regime. cards.definitions: Inputs are finite tuples \(x\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}\), with input size n. A machine has a finite program and finitely many fixed real constants. cards.title: \(\exists\mathbb{R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}\)

cards.definitions: Let ETR be the following language of finite binary strings. cards.title: DNF versus d-DNNF succinctness
cards.formal: Is the following nonuniform size separation true? For every \(C\geq1\), integer \(k\geq1\) and \(N\geq1\), there is a DNF formula \(F\) of size \(s\geq N\) such that every d-DNNF circuit computing exactly the same Boolean function on the same input variables has size greater than \(C(s+1)^{k}\). Equivalently, is there no single polynomial bound on the size of a d-DNNF representation of an arbitrary DNF? No efficient construction or conversion algorithm is required on either side of this size comparison.
cards.why: The question measures an inherent space cost of making overlapping explanations disjoint while retaining decomposable structure. It determines whether the simplest compact disjunctive representation can always remain compact in a form suited to exact counting, independently of how difficult that form is to find.

Determinism requires disjoint alternatives, while decomposability requires conjunctions to separate their variables.

The question is about the existence of compact equivalent circuits, so hardness of efficiently finding a conversion or a separation for unrestricted DNNFs does not by itself answer this more specific size comparison.

cards.definitions: Inputs are Boolean variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\). A literal is \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\). A DNF is a finite disjunction of terms, each a conjunction of distinct literals with no contradictory pair; the empty conjunction is true and the empty disjunction false. Its size is one plus its number of terms and literal occurrences. An NNF circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output, leaves labeled by literals or the constants zero and one, and internal AND and OR gates of arbitrary finite fan-in. It may share subcircuits and have unrestricted depth. Its size is its total number of vertices and edges. The variable set of a gate comprises variables labeling leaves that reach it. Decomposability means that the variable sets of different children of every AND gate are pairwise disjoint. Determinism means that, for every OR gate and every assignment to the union of its children’s variable sets, at most one child evaluates to one. A d-DNNF satisfies both conditions. Equivalent circuits agree for every input assignment, with no error or auxiliary existentially quantified variables. There is no common variable order, tree-structured decomposition, restriction to decision gates, or uniformity requirement. Polynomial comparisons use the DNF representation size, including all literal occurrences; ordinary explicit gate/edge encodings give the same polynomial-versus-superpolynomial distinction. The family formulation using polynomial-size DNFs in the number of inputs is equivalent after permitting unused input variables as padding.

context_blocks.text: Decomposability separates the variable sets of conjunctions, while determinism makes the alternatives at each disjunction disjoint. These restrictions support exact model counting in time polynomial in the representation size. A DNF already satisfies decomposability after inconsistent terms are removed, but its terms need not be disjoint.

Capelli’s June 2026 habilitation explicitly asks for a superpolynomial d-DNNF lower bound for DNF formulas. The known separation of unrestricted DNNF from d-DNNF uses a broader source representation and therefore does not settle this DNF restriction.

Even if every DNF has a polynomial-size d-DNNF representation, finding one in polynomial time would have additional counting consequences. The source distinguishes this algorithmic conversion issue from the existence of small representations; conditional conversion hardness supplies no unconditional size separation.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified superpolynomial size separation, or refute it by proving that one polynomial bounds the minimum equivalent d-DNNF size for every DNF. A negative answer need not give an efficient converter. A lower bound for decision-DNNF, structured d-DNNF, or a broader DNNF input family does not meet the stated unrestricted-output, DNF-input criterion.

cards.title: CLS versus FP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\)? Equivalently, does a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm solve the following Either-Solution problem: given an End-of-Line instance and an independent Localopt instance, return a valid solution of at least one of them?
cards.definitions:
Every circuit is an explicitly encoded acyclic Boolean circuit with fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}, \mathrm{NOT}\), constants, listed wires and ordered input/output nodes. An End-of-Line instance consists of \(S,\mathrm{P}:\{0,1\}^{n}	o \{0,1\}^{n}, n\ge 1\), satisfying \(\mathrm{P}(0^{n})=0^{n}\) and \(S(0^{n})
e 0^{n}\). An accepted output is a bit string \(v\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) with \(\mathrm{P}(S(v))
e v\), or with both \(v
e 0^{n}\) and \(S(\mathrm{P}(v))
e v\). In particular \(v=0^{n}\) is permitted only for the first condition. A Localopt instance consists of \(T:\{0,1\}^{m}	o \{0,1\}^{m}\) and \(V:\{0,1\}^{m}	o \{0,1\}^{r}\), with \(m,r\ge 1\). Treat V’s output as an unsigned binary integer; an accepted local-search output is w with \(V(T(w))\ge V(w)\). The joint instance contains both independent sets of circuits; n,m,r may differ. A solution is a tag selecting one instance and a string meeting that instance’s condition. On malformed encodings or failure of the two easily checkable End-of-Line conditions, output INVALID; on a valid joint instance INVALID is forbidden. The algorithm must halt within one fixed polynomial in the combined encoded length, including all circuit input/output nodes. It receives no advice, randomness or oracle. Total NP search problems are polynomially bounded input-output relations with polynomial-time verifiable outputs and at least one output for each input. A reduction maps an input to an instance and transforms every valid answer back to a valid original answer, using deterministic polynomial time for both maps. PPAD and PLS are the classes reducing to End-of-Line and Localopt respectively. The source proves that the either-solution problem is complete for their intersection and that CLS=PPAD∩PLS. These equalities give the stated equivalent discrete formulation of \(\mathrm{CLS}\subseteq\mathrm{FP}\); no new smoothness or numerical promise is introduced.

context_blocks.text: CLS captures total search tasks motivated by continuous local improvement. Fearnley, Goldberg, Hollender and Savani proved that it equals PPAD∩PLS, connecting this optimization class to two discrete existence principles.

The equivalent task presented here gives two independent succinct problems and asks for a solution to either one. The known completeness theorem means that an efficient algorithm for this task would solve every problem in CLS. The theorem identifies the class; it does not supply a polynomial-time solution algorithm.

cards.title: Polynomial-size circuits for EXP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\)? More explicitly, does there exist a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\), decidable by one deterministic exponential-time algorithm, whose circuit complexity \(s_L(n)\) satisfies \[\forall C\geq1\;\forall k\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\;\forall N\geq1\;\exists n\geq N:\quad s_L(n)>C(n+1)^{k}?\]
cards.why: This is a central test of whether explicit computation can be proved to require large unrestricted Boolean circuits. Resolving it would cross the gap between uniform time hierarchy theorems and lower bounds that defeat arbitrary nonuniform circuit families.

cards.definitions: \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup_{a\geq1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{a}})\), with the usual multiplicative constants and polynomially equivalent deterministic multitape Turing-machine encodings. The input is an arbitrary binary string and the machine decides membership without a promise, advice or oracle. A Boolean circuit on \(n\) inputs is an acyclic graph using fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, constants, and one output. Its size is the number of noninput gates; replacing this by its explicit gate-and-wire encoding length preserves polynomial size. The quantity \(s_L(n)\) is the minimum such size for exact agreement with membership in \(L\) on all \(n\)-bit strings. Circuit choices for different lengths are arbitrary and need not be computable. The class \(\mathrm{P/poly}\) comprises languages with \(s_L(n)\leq C(n+1)^k\) for all \(n\), for some constants \(C,k\) depending on the language. The quantifiers in the question require one language defeating every polynomial size bound; they do not require a lower bound at every sufficiently large length. The source uses exponential-time notation in a truth-table generation discussion; the card uses the standard union defining EXP. Using \(\mathrm E=\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{O(n)})\) instead gives the equivalent class-containment question by polynomial padding.

context_blocks.text: The deterministic time hierarchy separates polynomial from exponential uniform running time. It does not rule out small circuits chosen independently at each input length, which is the nonuniform issue in this conjecture.

Wigderson states the separation as Conjecture 8.6 in a discussion of explicit hard Boolean functions and pseudorandomness. Counting shows that many truth tables need large circuits, but the conjecture additionally places a hard language in a fixed uniform exponential-time class.

A 2026 preprint by Atserias and Müller proves a consistency result relating bounded arithmetic to \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{P/poly}\). Consistency of the separation with a formal theory is distinct from a proof of the separation itself.

Different hard languages for different fixed exponents, a lower bound for a restricted gate basis, or a consistency theorem alone do not settle the question.

cards.definitions: For \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), \(\mathrm{MAJ}_{n}(x)=1\) if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}x_i\geq\lceil n/2\rceil\). An ACC circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with one output, unbounded-fan-in AND, OR and \(\mathrm{MOD}_m\) gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and constants. A \(\mathrm{MOD}_{m}\) gate outputs one precisely when the sum of its Boolean inputs is divisible by \(m\). Depth is the maximum number of noninput gates on an input-output path, including NOT gates. Size is the number of noninput gates; counting wires instead gives the same polynomial-size class. The modulus, depth and polynomial-size constants are fixed for the whole family and cannot depend on \(n\). Circuits may be chosen separately for every length, without any construction algorithm, uniformity or bound on fan-out. The class \(\mathrm{ACC}^{0}\) is the union of these polynomial-size, constant-depth families over all fixed moduli. Allowing a fixed finite collection of moduli is equivalent, by using their common multiple with a constant-size gate substitution. All assignments must be computed correctly; no probability of error is allowed.

context_blocks.text: Jukna’s Research Problem 12.28 asks whether Majority lies outside ACC⁰. This is a lower bound for one concrete counting function, stronger in explicitness than separating a large uniform complexity class from the circuit class.

Prime-modulus lower bounds and the separation of nondeterministic exponential time from ACC⁰ concern different targets from the full majority question. In particular, results for prime moduli do not cover arbitrary composite moduli such as six.

Pago’s 2026 work proves lower bounds for computing AND using modular gates under syntactic symmetry assumptions. The permitted gate basis, target function and symmetry restriction differ from the unrestricted majority circuits in this card, so that result does not resolve this question.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal lower-bound statement, or refute it by proving the existence of fixed \(m,d,C,k\) and circuits of size at most \(C(n+1)^k\) computing majority for every input length. Refuting one fixed size exponent is insufficient for a positive answer. Results for a prime modulus, a restricted wiring symmetry, uniform circuits alone or a different hard function do not meet the complete criterion.

cards.title: P versus NP intersect coNP
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\)? Equivalently, does there exist a language \(L\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\) with polynomially bounded, polynomial-time verifiable certificates for both membership and nonmembership, but no uniform deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm?
cards.why: This asks whether computational difficulty can persist even when every yes answer and every no answer has a short efficiently checkable proof. It isolates a basic boundary between verification and decision that is finer than the usual one-sided NP condition.

sentences: A language in NP intersect coNP has short efficiently checkable certificates for both yes and no instances.
The question asks whether some such language still lies outside deterministic polynomial time.
Having two kinds of witnesses does not automatically tell an algorithm how to find either one.
The separation would identify difficulty independent of the asymmetric certification typical of NP-complete problems.
The project explores whether efficiently verifiable certainty on both sides can coexist with an intrinsically hard decision process.

cards.definitions: For a binary string \(x\), write \(n=|x|\). Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP}\) means that there are one polynomial \(q\) and two deterministic polynomial-time Boolean verifiers \(V_1,V_0\) such that, for every \(x\), \[x\in L\iff\exists y\in\{0,1\}^{\leq q(n)}:V_1(x,y)=1,\qquad x\notin L\iff\exists z\in\{0,1\}^{\leq q(n)}:V_0(x,z)=1.\] In particular, no input has accepted certificates of both types and every input has an accepted certificate of one type. Verifier time is polynomial in the combined bit length. The class \(\mathrm P\) consists of languages decided on every input by one deterministic multitape Turing machine within \(C(n+1)^k\) steps for fixed constants \(C,k\). The proposed language must defeat every such machine and polynomial bound. Algorithms have no advice, oracle or random bits. This is a total language-class comparison, not a promise problem or a requirement to output certificates. Witness lengths and machines are uniform over all input lengths.

context_blocks.text: A deterministic polynomial-time decision supplies trivial short certificates for either answer, so P is contained in NP ∩ coNP. The conjecture asks whether this containment is strict: efficiently checking either kind of answer need not give a method for deciding which kind exists.

Wigderson states this as Conjecture 3.9. The surrounding discussion uses problems such as linear programming and primality to illustrate that two-sided verification alone is not evidence of a separation; those problems have deterministic polynomial-time algorithms.

A strict separation would imply P ≠ NP, but the P versus NP question alone does not specify whether the intersection is larger than P. Search problems associated with finding certificates introduce another task and are not the language-class comparison asked here.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a language in \((\mathrm{NP}\cap\mathrm{coNP})\setminus\mathrm P\), including both verifiers and an unconditional uniform lower bound, or prove that every language satisfying the two verifier conditions belongs to \(\mathrm P\). An unproved hardness assumption, a promise-problem separation or hardness of finding witnesses alone does not decide this statement.

cards.title: Exponential lower bounds for unrestricted threshold-of-threshold circuits
cards.formal: Does there exist an explicit Boolean function family \((f_n)_{n\geq1}\), in the source’s sense \(\mathrm{NP}\), and constants \(c>0\) and \(n_0\), such that every unrestricted depth-two threshold circuit computing \(f_n\) has at least \(2^{cn}\) gates for every \(n\geq n_0\)?

sentences: A threshold gate decides whether a weighted sum of Boolean inputs reaches a specified threshold.
This question asks for an NP function family requiring exponentially many gates in every two-layer threshold circuit.
All weights are unrestricted real numbers, and size counts gates rather than their weights.

cards.definitions: A threshold gate on Boolean inputs \(z_1,\ldots,z_t\) outputs one if and only if \(\sum_{i=1}^{t}w_i z_i\geq\theta\), where all weights \(w_i\) and the threshold \(\theta\) are arbitrary real numbers of either sign. An unrestricted depth-two threshold circuit on \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\) consists of any finite number \(s\) of such gates applied to the original input bits, followed by one threshold output gate applied to their outputs. Arbitrary fan-in, fan-out and length-dependent weights are permitted; omitted inputs can have weight zero. Its size is \(s+1\), the number of threshold gates, not total weight magnitude or the number of bits encoding weights. Constants and direct input-to-output connections can be represented by additional threshold gates, changing size by at most \(n+1\), which does not alter exponential-size existence. Computation must agree with \(f_n\) on every input, with no approximation. The family is explicit in the definition of Section 1.5.1 of the source: there exist a polynomial \(q\) and a single deterministic polynomial-time verifier \(V\) such that \(f_n(x)=1\) precisely when some binary witness \(y\) with \(|y|\leq q(n)\) satisfies \(V(x,y)=1\). Verifier cost is measured on a standard bit Turing machine. Neither circuit weights nor circuits are required to be uniform or polynomially bounded. The exponential target is interpreted as \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) for all sufficiently large input lengths, with one fixed positive exponent coefficient.

context_blocks.text: Research Problem 11.40 asks for an exponential lower bound for unrestricted depth-two threshold circuits. The preceding discussion obtains strong bounds under restrictions on the weights; dropping such restrictions is the point of the question.

The source explicitly defines “explicit” in Section 1.5.1 through polynomial-time verification, corresponding to NP. Requiring the chosen function to lie in P would add a stronger condition that is not imposed here. Counting the existence of hard truth tables without this uniform verification condition would miss the intended explicit lower bound.

Chen’s 2018 paper describes even superpolynomial unrestricted depth-two threshold lower bounds for NEXP as a major frontier and develops conditional implications. Those implications do not supply the unconditional exponential lower bound for an NP family required by this card.

cards.definitions: An MCSP input is the complete truth table \(t\in \{0,1\}^{2^{n}}\) of a Boolean function on \(n\ge 1\) input bits, in lexicographic order, together with a nonnegative integer size threshold s in binary. It is accepted if some Boolean circuit of size at most s computes that function. Circuits are finite acyclic graphs over binary AND and OR, unary NOT, input variables and constants 0,1, with one designated output and unrestricted sharing. Size counts noninput gates, including constant gates. The total encoded input length counts the truth table, threshold and delimiters. Invalid encodings are rejected. NP-hardness means that for every language L in NP there is a deterministic polynomial-time map r such that \(x\in \mathrm{L}\) iff \(r(x)\in\)MCSP. NP consists of languages accepted by nondeterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. \(\mathrm{EXP}=\bigcup _{k\ge 1}\mathrm{DTIME}(2^{n^{k}}); \mathrm{P}\)/poly consists of languages decided by families of Boolean circuits whose sizes are bounded by a polynomial in input length, with no uniformity condition on their construction. \(\mathrm{EXP}\not\subset \mathrm{P}\)/poly means that some language in EXP has no such polynomial-size circuit family.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the conditional implication or its logical negation in these exact reduction and circuit models. Deriving only \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{ZPP}\) or \(\mathrm{EXP}\ne \mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{P}\)/poly is a weaker consequence. A theorem for a restricted reduction class or for partial, promise or approximate circuit minimization does not prove the stated implication.

cards.title: Hartmanis–Stearns conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(b\ge 2\) and every real \(x\in\)[0,1), if a deterministic multitape Turing machine generates the base-b digits of x in order with a constant bound on the time between successive digits, must x be rational or transcendental?
cards.why: A proof would impose a strong arithmetic restriction on numbers generated at the fastest possible asymptotic output rate. The checked 2024 source also records that the conjecture would rule out linear-time integer multiplication on multitape Turing machines.

cards.definitions: Write \(x=\sum _{n\ge 1}d_{n} b^{- n}\), where \(d_{n}\in \{0,\ldots ,b- 1\}\), using the unique expansion that is not eventually all \(b- 1; a\) terminating expansion continues with zeros. Rational means \(x=p/q\) for integers p,q with \(q\ne 0\). Algebraic means \(\mathrm{P}(x)=0\) for a nonzero polynomial P with integer coefficients; transcendental means not algebraic. A machine has a finite control, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of two-way infinite work tapes, each with one head and initially blank. Each transition reads the symbols under the heads, writes at those cells, changes state and moves each head at most one cell. It may also append one digit to a separate write-only output stream; written digits are irrevocable. It starts with no input and no advice or oracle and runs indefinitely. There must be a constant \(C\ge 1\) such that its first digit appears by step C and, writing \(t_{n}\) for the step at which \(d_{n}\) appears, \(1\le t_{n+1}- t_{n}\le C\) for every \(n\ge 1\). The finite machine and C may depend on the fixed x and b, but not on n. This is the constant-delay, or real-time, convention used by this card. Restricting to [0,1) only removes an integer part, which does not change rationality or transcendence.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for all bases, numbers and machines just defined, or refute it by exhibiting an algebraic irrational x, a base b and a machine with proofs of correct infinite digit generation and a uniform constant delay. A computation of any finite prefix, a slower digit algorithm or a theorem restricted to finite automata does not settle the statement.

context_blocks.title: A steady stream of digits
context_blocks.text: For example, \(1/7=0.142857142857\ldots\) in base 10. A finite machine can cycle through the six-digit block forever with bounded delay. Every rational has an eventually periodic expansion, so rational numbers fit the model. In contrast, \(\sqrt{2}- 1\) is algebraic and irrational: it satisfies \(x^{2}+2x- 1=0\). The conjecture excludes such numbers from all constant-delay generators, even though their digits are computable.

context_blocks.title: The finite description is not the resource bound
context_blocks.text: The same program must produce the entire infinite expansion; it cannot receive a longer precomputed digit table for each requested precision. Work tapes may grow without bound. The restriction is how many elementary steps separate outputs, not a fixed bound on memory. No claim is made that every transcendental number has such a generator.

context_blocks.title: Why sources also say linear time
context_blocks.text: Fischer, Meyer and Rosenberg establish that linear-time and real-time sequence generation coincide for multitape Turing machines. This concerns the existence of a suitable generator; a particular implementation with linear total time need not itself have bounded gaps. The constant-delay wording therefore agrees with the linear-prefix formulation used in the cited Hartmanis–Stearns literature.

context_blocks.title: What the partial results establish
context_blocks.text: Adamczewski, Cassaigne and Le Gonidec exclude algebraic irrationals from several restricted generation models, including a deterministic pushdown transducer supplied with a digit index. Their one-stack theorem is not a theorem about arbitrary multitape generators. The 2024 ICALP paper likewise obtains transcendence for particular word classes and explicitly retains the full conjecture.

context_blocks.title: The input representation matters
context_blocks.text: The 2026 automata result obtains a digit of a quadratic irrational from \(b^{n}\) supplied in a special Ostrowski numeration system. This is additional structured input, whereas the machine in this card starts blank and produces digits indefinitely. The authors do not claim a fast general digit generator, so that result is not a counterexample.

A proof would connect the arithmetic nature of numbers to a stringent computation bound and rule out linear-time integer multiplication.

cards.context:
For example, \(1/7=0.142857142857\ldots\) in base 10. A finite machine can cycle through the six-digit block forever with bounded delay. Every rational has an eventually periodic expansion, so rational numbers fit the model. In contrast, \(\sqrt{2}- 1\) is algebraic and irrational: it satisfies \(x^{2}+2x- 1=0\). The conjecture excludes such numbers from all constant-delay generators, even though their digits are computable.

The same program must produce the entire infinite expansion; it cannot receive a longer precomputed digit table for each requested precision. Work tapes may grow without bound. The restriction is how many elementary steps separate outputs, not a fixed bound on memory. No claim is made that every transcendental number has such a generator.

Fischer, Meyer and Rosenberg establish that linear-time and real-time sequence generation coincide for multitape Turing machines. This concerns the existence of a suitable generator; a particular implementation with linear total time need not itself have bounded gaps. The constant-delay wording therefore agrees with the linear-prefix formulation used in the cited Hartmanis–Stearns literature.

Adamczewski, Cassaigne and Le Gonidec exclude algebraic irrationals from several restricted generation models, including a deterministic pushdown transducer supplied with a digit index. Their one-stack theorem is not a theorem about arbitrary multitape generators. The 2024 ICALP paper likewise obtains transcendence for particular word classes and explicitly retains the full conjecture.

The 2026 automata result obtains a digit of a quadratic irrational from \(b^{n}\) supplied in a special Ostrowski numeration system. This is additional structured input, whereas the machine in this card starts blank and produces digits indefinitely. The authors do not claim a fast general digit generator, so that result is not a counterexample.

cards.title: Linear-size circuits for stable ternary compaction
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant \(C\ge 1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\), the function \(S_{n}:\{0,1,2\}^{n}\to \{0,1,2\}^{n}\) that removes all symbols 2 and appends the same number of 2s on the right, preserving the order of the other symbols, is computed by a Boolean circuit with at most Cn gates in the model below?
cards.definitions: Encode symbols 0,1,2 as 00,01,10 respectively. The circuit has 2n input bits and 2n output bits, with arbitrary fan-out, binary AND and OR gates, unary NOT gates, and optional Boolean constant gates. Size counts all non-input gates, including constants; wires and output designations cost nothing. Correctness is required only on concatenations of the three valid encodings; output on inputs containing 11 is unrestricted. If \(i_{1}<\ldots <i_{m}\) are exactly the indices with \(a_{i}\ne 2\), the required decoded output is \(a_{i_{1}}\ldots a_{i_{m}}\) followed by \(n- m\) copies of 2. In particular, 0s and 1s retain their relative order. The circuit may depend on n; no uniform construction algorithm, depth bound, monotonicity restriction or indivisible-record model is imposed. The constant C is independent of n.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
cards.why: Test linear circuit size for a concrete, sequentially simple function whose stability requirement preserves substantial information.

importance.reason: A specific circuit-size barrier beyond generic lower-bound statements; stable compaction connects elementary data movement with unrestricted Boolean computation.

cards.title: Reversible simulation in polynomial time and linear space simultaneously
cards.formal: Does there exist a computable compiler that takes any deterministic multitape Turing machine M to a reversible multitape machine R such that the following holds? For each M there are constants \(c_{M} \ge  1\) and an integer \(d_{M} \ge  1\) so that, on every input x on which M halts, R halts with the pair \((x,M(x))\), uses at most \(c_{M} S_{M}(x)\) tape cells, and takes at most \(c_{M} T_{M}(x)^{d_{M}}\) steps. R must not halt on an input on which M does not halt. Here \(S_{M}\) counts total storage including input and output, and \(T_{M}\) is at least the input length, as defined below.
cards.definitions: Machines have a finite state set, a fixed finite alphabet containing binary input symbols and a blank, and a fixed finite number of tapes and heads. Each step reads the scanned symbols, writes symbols, and moves each head by at most one cell. The complete configuration includes state, tapes, and head positions. Reversible means the partial one-step function on configurations is injective. The input x is initially present with delimiters on one tape and all other tapes are blank. M has a designated finite binary output on halting. \(S_{M}(x)\) is the number of cells initially occupied or visited on any tape during that run, with a minimum of 1; input and output cells are included. \(T_{M}(x)\) is max(1,|x|,number of transitions). Apply the same storage convention to R. Its output tapes retain x and \(M(x)\), and all auxiliary tapes are blank on termination. The compiler must halt on every finite syntactically valid machine description; its own running time is unrestricted. Simulation here preserves the computed partial function, not every intermediate configuration. The overhead constants may depend on M but not on x.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that such a compiler and bounds exist, or prove that no such compiler can satisfy them for all deterministic machines. Both resource guarantees must hold simultaneously for the same reversible simulation.
cards.why: Reversible computation avoids logical information erasure, but that advantage may require additional memory or time. This question asks whether a general computation can retain its asymptotic storage scale while paying only a polynomial time overhead.

importance.reason: A basic simultaneous-resource question about reversible computation, connecting time-space complexity with the informational cost of computation.

context_blocks.text: Saving the input is necessary when the simulated function is many-to-one: reversible configurations cannot merge different initial inputs into one final configuration. Counting input and output storage prevents free external memory from changing the target.

Known general simulations occupy different parts of the time-space tradeoff. Polynomial-time simulations use more than linear space in general; a simulation with \(O(S)\) space can take exponential time. The requested conjunction does not follow from either result separately.

The compiler formulation makes the simulation uniform across inputs, while allowing machine-dependent constants. It is the polynomial-time, linear-space version requested here, rather than a demand for nearly linear time.

context_blocks.text: \(\mathrm{IP} = \mathrm{PSPACE}\) alone does not guarantee that producing the proof costs only a polynomial in the original computation time.

Interactive proofs separate the effort of checking a computation from the effort of producing a convincing transcript. The usual class equality allows an honest prover to use enormous resources. The target compares the honest prover directly with the original running time T. A prover using a polynomial in T would have controlled overhead even when the verifier has only polynomial time in the input length. Soundness still has to hold against a cheating prover of unlimited power; restricting the honest prover does not weaken the adversary in the definition.

cards.title: Formula versus circuit noise thresholds
cards.formal: For p in [\(0,1/2\)), let \(Reliable(p)\) mean that there exists a constant delta>0 such that for every \(n\ge 1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}->\{0,1\}\), some finite circuit C of the kind below satisfies \(\Pr [C(x)=f(x)]\ge 1/2\)+delta for every input x. Is \(Reliable(p)\) true exactly for \(p<(3-\sqrt{7})/4\)? In particular, is it false at the boundary as well as above it?
cards.definitions: A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input sources \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\), constant sources 0 and 1, gates of fan-in at most two, and one designated output wire. Any Boolean function of a gate's input bits is allowed. Each gate is evaluated once in topological order and independently flips its correct Boolean output with probability exactly p. All outgoing wires from that gate carry the same resulting bit; reuse does not generate fresh independent copies. Inputs, constants, and wires are noiseless. Every computational gate, including the output gate when present, obeys the noise rule; there is no extra noiseless decoder. Fan-out is unrestricted, and different incoming paths may share gates. C may depend on p,n,f but not on x. Its size and construction time are unrestricted. The probability is solely over independent gate failures. Delta may depend on p but is common to all n,f,x. A formula is the restricted case in which computational gates have fan-out at most one, with input variables still allowed to occur repeatedly.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the stated equivalence for the full interval \(0\le p<1/2\), including \(p=(3-\sqrt{7})/4\). A proof or refutation must use the specified independent gate-flip model and a uniform positive correctness advantage across all functions.
cards.why: The problem asks how much unreliable local computation can be tolerated when arbitrary redundancy and reuse are available. It would determine whether sharing intermediate noisy values changes the fundamental threshold already known for formulas.

importance.reason: A sharp reliability boundary for general classical computation, separating the effects of gate errors from circuit size and design effort.

context_blocks.text: The success advantage must be fixed before choosing a function or its number of inputs. Allowing it to shrink with the function would describe a much weaker task. The noisy output itself is read, so the target does not assume an unlimited perfect final computation.

Unger establishes the exact threshold for two-input formulas, extending the earlier NAND-gate result, and conjectures the same threshold for circuits. Shared subcomputations correlate wire values even though the underlying gate failures are independent.

Later work studies asymmetric noise on AND and XOR gates and relates reliability to amplification. Its different gate-specific error assumptions and formula bounds do not settle the common-noise, unrestricted-fan-out proposition here.

progress.text: Unger proves the formula threshold \((3-\sqrt{7})/4\), including impossibility at equality, and states the circuit extension as a conjecture.

cards.title: Closure of d-DNNF under negation
cards.formal: Do a constant \(c>0\) and an integer \(k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every finite variable set X and every d-DNNF circuit C over X of size s, there is a d-DNNF circuit D over X of size at most \(c(s+1)^{k}\) computing the Boolean complement of C on every assignment \(X->\{0,1\}\)? No algorithm for finding D within that bound is required.
cards.definitions: An NNF circuit is a finite rooted directed acyclic graph whose leaves are constants 0,1 or literals x,not-x for x in X, and whose internal nodes are AND or OR gates. Edges run from a gate to its inputs. The variable set of a subcircuit comprises the variables occurring in its reachable literals. Decomposable means that the input subcircuits of every AND gate have pairwise disjoint variable sets. Deterministic means that no assignment to X makes two different inputs of any OR gate both true. A d-DNNF satisfies both properties. Size is the total number of vertices plus edges; fan-in is arbitrary and part of that size. Evaluation has the usual Boolean meaning. No negation gates above leaves, additional variables, or requirement of compatibility with a common variable decomposition tree is allowed. Constants c,k are independent of X and C. The output D may use any decompositions meeting these conditions.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal polynomial size bound, or prove that no constants c,k satisfy it. Algorithmic difficulty of producing a small complement alone does not refute this size-existence statement.
cards.why: Deterministic decomposable circuits represent Boolean solution sets while supporting exact counting. Closure under complement asks whether a compact representation of satisfying assignments necessarily gives a comparably compact representation of nonsatisfying assignments, independently of construction time.

importance.reason: A central representational-closure question in knowledge compilation that separates succinctness from the cost of performing a logical operation.

context_blocks.text: Decomposability prevents conjunctions from sharing variables and determinism prevents disjunctions from sharing satisfying assignments. Negating a circuit syntactically need not preserve both properties.

Structured d-DNNFs additionally respect a variable decomposition tree. The 2024 negative result for that restricted class cannot be transferred automatically to unrestricted d-DNNF, since a complementary circuit here may use other decompositions.

The STACS 2026 discussion retains complementation as an open question. The separate algorithmic question asks for a polynomial-time procedure producing the complement. Such a procedure implies the size bound on this card; the converse is not established. Both targets are retained because an existence theorem would settle a representation barrier without necessarily supplying the algorithmic transformation.
The stronger polynomial-time construction question is retained as TCS-0306. The existence of small complementary circuits does not by itself give an efficient algorithm for constructing them.

cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly encoded 3-CNF formula, as permitted by the source’s SAT convention. To fix a binary representation, encode a literal by a sign bit (0 for \(x_{i}\), 1 for \(\neg x_{i}\)), followed by the positive index i in Elias gamma code: \(\lfloor \log _{2}i\rfloor\) zero bits followed by the ordinary binary representation of i. Consecutive triples of literals are clauses, and the formula is their conjunction. Repeated literals and clauses are allowed, the empty conjunction is true, and malformed strings are rejected. \(\mathrm{SAT}_{n}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) is 1 exactly for strings encoding satisfiable formulas. The parameter n counts all encoding bits, including signs and indices, rather than the number of distinct variables or clauses. This explicit binary-list convention fixes the source’s otherwise implicit SAT representation. A De Morgan formula is a rooted tree with AND and OR gates of fan-in two. Each leaf is an input bit, its negation, or a Boolean constant. Equivalently, unary NOT gates can be used anywhere and then pushed to the leaves without changing the leaf count. Internal computations cannot be shared between two parents. Its size is the number of leaf occurrences, so repeated uses of the same variable are charged separately. All input strings must be answered exactly. A family is LOGTIME-uniform when one deterministic machine, given binary n and a binary position j, returns the requested bit of the description of its n-input formula or circuit in \(O(\log  n)\) time, on a standard multitape Turing machine; positions outside the description return zero. Descriptions are explicit binary netlists: a header gives the number of nodes and the output node, nodes have consecutive binary identifiers and gate-type records, and a list gives each wire’s source, destination and input port, with negation flags when applicable. Each integer field is self-delimited in binary. Input-node records give their input-bit indices or a constant 0 or 1. The family may choose a consistent numbering but must have one such uniform description algorithm for every n. There is no advice and no randomness. Polynomial-size candidate families have polynomial-length descriptions and \(O(\log  n)\)-bit identifiers; the machine’s description and running-time constant are independent of n. The exponent \(\varepsilon\) is chosen once, before quantifying over families and their uniformity machines. A family has \(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) leaves if some constant C bounds its size by \(Cn^{3+\varepsilon}\) for all sufficiently large n. Constants may depend on the family and \(\varepsilon\), but not n. The source writes “requires” such size; the formal statement adopts uniform-class nonmembership, equivalently arbitrarily large failures of each candidate big-O bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that there is a fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) for which every correct LOGTIME-uniform De Morgan formula family has, for every \(C>0\) and every \(N_{0}\), some \(n\ge N_{0}\) with more than \(Cn^{3+\varepsilon}\) leaves. Alternatively, refute this by proving that for every \(\varepsilon >0\) some correct LOGTIME-uniform family has \(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) leaves. The target is exact worst-case computation of SAT, with the stated basis, uniformity and size measure.

context_blocks.text: The object computing SAT receives the bits of a formula and outputs whether some assignment satisfies it. This card asks whether even a uniformly described De Morgan formula must exceed the \(n^{3}\) scale by a fixed positive exponent. context_blocks.title: What is being counted
context_blocks.text: The formula \((a\land b)\lor (a\land c)\) has four leaf occurrences, although it mentions only three variables. This illustrates why a formula-size bound counts uses of inputs, not distinct variable names. The benchmark size is for the formula computing SAT on n encoding bits.

context_blocks.title: Uniformity constrains the whole family
context_blocks.text: A separate small circuit for every input length could contain information chosen independently at each length. LOGTIME-uniformity requires one short-running algorithm to describe all those circuits locally. The input to that description algorithm is the input length and a position in the description, not a particular SAT instance.

context_blocks.title: A fixed exponent, with a stated asymptotic convention
context_blocks.text: The question is whether SAT lies outside the uniform size-\(O(n^{3+\varepsilon})\) class for some fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). Thus every correct uniform family must exceed any constant multiple of that bound at arbitrarily large lengths. This uses the standard class-nonmembership interpretation of the source’s lower-bound question; it does not add an almost-everywhere requirement.

context_blocks.title: Dated progress and its scope
context_blocks.text: The 2016 column records nearly cubic De Morgan formula lower bounds for SAT. Bathie and Williams’s ITCS 2024 paper obtains a depth lower bound of \(3.603 \log _{2} n\) for polylogtime-uniform NAND circuits solving SAT. NAND depth uses a restricted gate basis and a different cost measure; this statement alone does not settle the requested De Morgan leaf-size bound.

cards.title: Subquadratic deterministic simulation of nondeterministic space
cards.formal: For every space-constructible function \(s:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\) with \(s(n)\ge \lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\), is every language in \(\mathrm{NSPACE}(O(s(n)))\) decidable deterministically in \(o(s(n)^{2})\) space? Equivalently, for each such s and each language L accepted by an \(O(s(n))\)-space nondeterministic machine, must there exist one deterministic decider D for L whose maximum workspace \(g_{D}(n)\) on n-bit inputs satisfies \(\lim (n\to \infty ) g_{D}(n)/s(n)^{2}=0\)?
cards.why: Would improve the general memory overhead for eliminating nondeterminism beyond a theorem that has stood since 1970. Even a slowly vanishing improvement would sharpen a basic relationship between deterministic and nondeterministic computation, including the logarithmic-space regime.
cards.status_note: Full source question read and standard space conventions made explicit. cards.definitions: Inputs are binary strings of length n. Machines have a finite control, a two-way read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank work tapes over a fixed finite alphabet. Space is the maximum total number of visited work-tape cells; the read-only input itself is not charged. Machines are uniform, with no advice, random bits, oracle or uncharged auxiliary memory. Nondeterministic machines have finitely many possible next moves, accept exactly when some branch accepts, and halt on every branch; the space bound applies to every branch and every input of length n. \(\mathrm{NSPACE}(O(s(n)))\) denotes languages with such a machine using at most \(C s(n)\) cells for some fixed C and all sufficiently large n. A deterministic decider must halt on every input, with no imposed running-time bound. A function s is space-constructible here if a deterministic machine on \(1^{n}\) can output \(1^{s}(n)\) using \(O(s(n))\) work cells, with output written on a separate write-only tape. The standard at-least-logarithmic space-constructible regime of Savitch’s theorem supplies the source’s implicit parameter convention. The little-o containment means that the decider and its improvement rate may depend on L and s. It does not require a fixed exponent saving \(s^{2- \varepsilon}\) or one common improvement rate for all languages.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed containment for every admitted space bound and every nondeterministic language, with deterministic workspace little-o of \(s(n)^{2}\). Alternatively, refute it by identifying an admitted s and a language in \(\mathrm{NSPACE}(O(s(n)))\) for which no deterministic decider has that little-o space bound. A constant-factor saving in \(s(n)^{2}, a\) simulation of only a special graph family, or a bound that excludes separately supplied catalytic memory does not meet the stated guarantee.

context_blocks.title: What nondeterminism costs in memory
context_blocks.text: A nondeterministic machine can choose among several next moves and accepts if some sequence of choices succeeds. A deterministic simulation must decide the same question without those choices. Savitch’s theorem shows that squaring the workspace is enough, even though the simulation may take much longer.

context_blocks.title: Any vanishing fraction would count
context_blocks.text: If a nondeterministic computation uses about s cells, the target is a deterministic simulation whose memory divided by \(s^{2}\) tends to zero. A bound such as \(s^{2}/\log (s+2)\) would qualify, while \(0.01s^{2}\) would not. These expressions illustrate the meaning of little-o; the question imposes no particular rate of improvement.

context_blocks.title: The logarithmic-space case
context_blocks.text: For \(s(n)\) of order log n, the target becomes deterministic \(o(\log ^{2} n)\) space for every language in nondeterministic logarithmic space. This includes directed reachability: given a directed graph and two vertices, decide whether there is a directed path between them. The full card quantifies over all admitted s and does not restrict inputs to a special graph family.

cards.title: Polynomial-time weighted falsifiability of unambiguous DNFs
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic algorithm, polynomial in the total binary input length, that solves the following problem? The input consists of an unambiguous DNF $F=\bigvee_{j=1}^{m}T_j$ over n Boolean variables, nonnegative integer weights \(w_{1},\ldots ,w_{n}\) encoded in binary, and an integer threshold t encoded in binary. Decide whether there exists $a\in\{0,1\}^n$ such that $F(a)=0$ and $\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_i a_i\ge t$. Each \(T_{j}\) is an explicitly listed conjunction of literals. Unambiguous means that no assignment satisfies two distinct terms simultaneously.
cards.definitions: A literal is either \(x_{i}\) or its negation. A term is true exactly when all its literals are true; the DNF is true when at least one term is true. Contradictory terms can be discarded. For the remaining terms, unambiguity is equivalent to every pair containing opposite literals on some variable, so this promise is itself checkable in polynomial time. Weights are exact integers, with no rounding. The running time must depend polynomially on their bit lengths rather than on their numerical sum. The threshold uses at least, not exactly; a strict-threshold formulation is equivalent by shifting the integer threshold by one. The output is a yes/no answer. A tautology has no falsifying assignment and always gives no, regardless of the threshold.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all such inputs, or prove that the decision problem is not in P. An NP-hardness proof would provide a negative answer conditional on P differing from NP; its assumption must be stated. A pseudopolynomial algorithm, a method only for unweighted assignments, or hardness after changing the comparison to exact equality does not settle the specified question.
cards.why: The problem separates easy counting from optimization on the complement of a simple disjoint representation. It tests whether unambiguity retains its algorithmic value when a compactly encoded additive objective is introduced, and it bears on the power of knowledge-compilation representations under negation.

importance.reason: A focused but structural tractability question connecting unambiguous representations, binary-weight optimization, and complementation. It has a clear gap between polynomial unweighted methods and an unresolved weighted case.

progress.text: Monet formulates the binary-weight optimization problem and records NP membership of its decision version, polynomial-time weighted satisfaction, and a pseudopolynomial dynamic program for falsification.
The Dagstuhl seminar on database representation and provenance presents this exact question by linking to Monet’s formulation. The catalogue’s separate TCS-0485 record comes from that link.

context_blocks.text: Unambiguity makes the satisfying regions disjoint. This is useful for counting: after fixing the literals of one consistent term, every remaining variable is free, and the term’s satisfying assignments can be counted directly. Summing across terms gives the total without any inclusion-exclusion correction. Subtracting that count from \(2^{n}\) decides whether a falsifying assignment exists at all.

The weighted version asks where the complement lies relative to an additive score. Knowing how many points lie outside the DNF does not reveal whether even one of them has a large score. For example, take \(F=(x \mathrm{AND} y) \mathrm{OR} ((\mathrm{NOT} x) \mathrm{AND} z)\), whose two terms are incompatible. With weights 8, 3, and 5, the assignment \((1,0,1)\) falsifies F and has score 13. The all-ones assignment has larger score 16 but satisfies F, so unconstrained maximization does not answer the question.

There is an important asymmetry between maximizing over satisfying and falsifying assignments. To maximize over satisfying assignments, optimize each term separately by setting every unrestricted positive-weight variable to one, then take the best result. To falsify the DNF, every term must fail at once, and choices made to destroy one term can interact with all the others.

Dynamic programming over achievable scores gives a pseudopolynomial algorithm; it becomes polynomial when weights are unary. The missing guarantee is polynomial dependence on binary descriptions of potentially large weights. Amarilli also explains a connection to complementing compiled Boolean representations: efficient complementation into a representation supporting weighted maximization would give an algorithm, while suitable hardness would obstruct that route.

cards.title: Expected linear-time integer sorting for every word length
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform Las Vegas word-RAM algorithm and a constant \(C\) such that, for every \(n\ge2\), every integer word length \(w\ge\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\), and every list \(x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\{0,\ldots,2^w-1\}\), the algorithm outputs the list in nondecreasing order with expected running time at most \(Cn\)?
cards.definitions: The input occupies n words, with one unsigned w-bit key per word; repeated keys are allowed. The output must contain exactly the input multiset in nondecreasing numerical order, with no stability requirement. The machine is sequential and has w-bit data registers and random-access memory. Unit-cost operations are reads and writes, comparisons, branches, addition and subtraction modulo 2ʷ, multiplication of two words with the product returned in two words, quotient and remainder of two words with a nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and left or right shifts by a word-specified amount. Shifted-out bits are discarded, and shifts by at least w return zero. Addresses may use a constant number of words to index polynomially many memory cells; all address computation is charged. An operation can generate one fresh independent uniform w-bit random word. These are the only primitive operations; arbitrary-length arithmetic, a built-in sorting operation and free tables are unavailable. All preprocessing, memory initialization performed by the algorithm, and output writes count. A fixed finite program receives n and w; it may select methods according to their values but has no advice depending on them. Las Vegas means every terminating computation is correct and the algorithm terminates with probability one. Expectation is over the internal random choices for each fixed input. C must be independent of both n and w, including when w grows with n.

context_blocks.text: Integer sorting asks how much of the cost of comparison sorting comes from treating keys as indivisible objects. If only comparisons are allowed, identifying one of n! possible orders needs \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) comparisons in the worst case. Word operations can inspect several bits at once, compute bucket addresses and manipulate packed fields. The comparison decision-tree lower bound therefore does not rule out a linear number of word operations.

The relevant input size is n words, not nw individual bits. Reading one entire word is a unit operation regardless of w, but reading a whole list is still n operations. Conversely, the machine cannot concatenate all n keys into an nw-bit integer and then treat that enormous object as one register. Fixing the register width and the permitted instructions is essential; unrestricted unit-cost arithmetic would answer a different question.

Simple radix sorting already handles \(w=O(\log  n)\). Divide each key into digits of about \(\log _{2}n\) bits, and sort stably by one digit at a time using counting arrays of size \(O(n)\). There are \(O(1+w/\log  n)\) passes, giving \(O(n(1+w/\log  n))\) time. For any fixed polynomial-size universe this is linear. If \(w=(\log  n)^{3/2}\), however, that same argument takes about \(\sqrt{\log  n}\) passes and does not prove the desired bound.

Surprisingly, very large words also admit linear expected time. Belazzougui, Brodal and Nielsen achieve this for \(w=\Omega ((\log  n)^{2} \log  \log  n)\), improving an earlier sufficiently-large-word regime. Their construction replaces full keys by shorter signatures and processes many packed fields with a single word operation. Larger keys bring more possible values, but the larger machine words simultaneously provide more internal parallelism. The difficult range sits between the easy radix regime and the proven large-word regime.

The best general expected upper bound retained in the sources is Han and Thorup’\(s O(n\sqrt{\log  \log  n})\), independent of word length. It is substantially below n log n, but the square-root iterated-log factor still grows without bound. The problem asks whether this remaining overhead can be removed completely. An upper bound with any unbounded overhead factor does not imply the stated linear bound.

Han also gives deterministic \(O(n \log  \log  n)\) sorting with linear space. This is a different guarantee: it bounds every computation without random choices. The present question allows randomization and asks only for an expected linear bound on every input. A deterministic linear-time algorithm would answer it affirmatively, while a lower bound confined to deterministic algorithms would not answer it negatively.

Zero error is explicit because sorting has a convenient final check but not every failure mode is detected by checking adjacent comparisons alone. A proposed randomized procedure must preserve the input multiset as well as produce a sorted sequence. The large-word construction uses a verifiable randomized sorting procedure and repeats when needed to obtain a Las Vegas guarantee. This is different from relying on a typical distribution of input keys: adversarially selected keys are permitted here.

Uniformity also prevents the missing work from being hidden in preprocessing. An enormous lookup table listing answers for all possible word patterns cannot be supplied for free. Any table needed for a particular n and w must be constructed within the expected time budget. Likewise, treating a concrete machine’s 64-bit width as an immutable constant does not address the asymptotic problem, where n and w vary together.

The question is fundamental because sorting supplies order to many other algorithmic tasks: grouping equal identifiers, scanning consecutive values, merging collections and organizing events. An affirmative answer would give a clean linear-time primitive across the whole word-RAM range. A negative answer would explain a basic limitation of word arithmetic that is invisible to ordinary comparison-counting arguments. The 2025 teaching source still explicitly presents the unrestricted linear-time target as open.

cards.title: Sorting \(X + Y\)
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic real-RAM algorithm A and a constant C such that, for every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every \(X=(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}), Y=(y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n})\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}, A\) outputs a permutation \(((i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots ,(i_{n^{2}},j_{n^{2}}))\) of \([n]\times [n]\) satisfying \(x_{i_{r}}+y_{j_{r}}\le x_{i_{r+1}}+y_{j_{r+1}}\) for \(1\le r<n^{2}\), in at most \(Cn^{2}\) unit-cost operations?
cards.why: This is a basic test of whether algebraic dependence among many sortable objects can be exploited with no overhead beyond writing them down. It also makes the distinction between short comparison decision trees and fast uniform algorithms unusually concrete.
cards.status_note: TOPP Problem 41, primary comparison and real-RAM sources, and subsequent-result searches were checked on 11 September 2026. No uniform quadratic-time algorithm or matching impossibility result for the stated real-valued problem was found. The \(2017/2018\) decision-tree result does not settle total time. This is a source review, not an independent proof audit.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu give algorithms combining \(O(n^{2})\) comparisons with \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) total time.
The necklace/convolution paper explicitly retains quadratic-time sorting on the real RAM as open while proving faster algorithms for more limited convolution outputs.
Kane–Lovett–Moran obtain \(O(n \log ^{2} n)\) depth using 8-sparse linear tests. The bound concerns decision-tree queries and excludes output and general computational costs.

cards.definitions: The input consists of n and the 2n exact real numbers in random-access arrays; no sortedness, distinctness, integrality or magnitude bound is promised. All \(n^{2}\) index pairs must occur once in the output, including pairs with equal sums. Ties may appear in any order. A real RAM has exact real registers and cells, supporting copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero reals and comparisons at unit cost. A fixed finite program may use rational constants, with no advice depending on n. It also has integer registers and cells of \(b=d\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed integer \(d\ge 3\) chosen with the algorithm. Integer instructions are copy, comparison, branching, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{b}\), quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and logical shifts; shifts by at least b return zero. Integer addresses access individual real or integer cells, and each read or write costs one operation. Integer-to-real conversion is permitted, but real-to-integer conversion, floor on reals, extraction of their bits and arbitrary-precision integer operations are not primitives. Memory starts empty apart from the input and fixed program constants; all preprocessing, table construction, address computation and output writes are charged. The algorithm must halt correctly on every input and uses no randomness. Constants C and d are independent of n and of the real values. This is the quadratic-time real-RAM version explicitly asked in the cited necklace paper and identified as the main target in TOPP. Indexed multiset output resolves possible equal sums; allowing repeated input entries does not change the target, since repetitions can be grouped by \(O(n \log  n)\) comparison sorting and expanded within the output budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Give one uniform deterministic program with a proof of exact output correctness and the \(O(n^{2})\) worst-case total-time bound for every real input, or prove that no such program exists in the specified model. Equivalently, a negative answer shows that every correct program has unbounded worst-case running-time/\(n^{2}\) ratio. Neither a bound only on the number of comparisons nor an algorithm restricted to bounded integers resolves this claim.

context_blocks.text: The input is small compared with the output. For \(X=(0,3)\) and \(Y=(1,4)\), the four indexed sums are 1,4,4,7. Both occurrences of 4 remain in the sorted output because they come from different pairs. In general there are \(n^{2}\) output entries, but only 2n independent input numbers. This strong dependence is the reason ordinary sorting bounds for \(n^{2}\) unrelated numbers may be wasteful.

If the two input lists are already sorted, the matrix \(M_{ij}=x_{i}+y_{j}\) increases along every row and every column. That information alone does not determine the relative order of every two cells: a later row may contain an entry smaller than an entry in an earlier row. Moreover, sum matrices satisfy additional equalities such as \(M_{ij}+M_{kl}=M_{il}+M_{kj}\). The question concerns the full algebraic structure, not just arbitrary matrices with sorted rows and columns.

Explicitly generating and comparison-sorting all \(n^{2}\) sums takes \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) time. Writing the required output already takes \(\Omega (n^{2})\) operations, so quadratic time would match the output-size lower bound. TOPP identifies removal of the logarithmic factor as the main question. The real-valued input convention avoids assuming a small integer universe, where different operations can change the complexity.

Fredman proved that \(O(n^{2})\) comparisons suffice. A decision tree specifies the next comparison after every possible history of answers and places the sorted order at its leaves. Its depth counts comparisons, but it does not charge for constructing the tree or determining the next comparison from a succinct program. Consequently, a short decision tree does not automatically become an equally fast uniform algorithm.

Lambert and Steiger–Streinu made the comparison savings algorithmic while retaining \(O(n^{2} \log  n)\) total running time. This is a concrete separation between counting tests and charging the bookkeeping that organizes them. The target includes both costs, as well as all preprocessing and output writes.

Kane, Lovett and Moran later obtained \(O(n \log ^{2} n)\) decision-tree depth by allowing tests involving differences of sums; each such linear test uses at most eight input coordinates. Those tests are more expressive than simply comparing two entries of \(X+Y\). The subquadratic depth does not conflict with the quadratic output-size lower bound, because decision-tree depth does not charge for writing the output.

Related convolution problems ask only for a minimum, maximum or median on each antidiagonal of the sum matrix. These requests can have subquadratic algorithms without supplying a complete sorted list of all entries. The necklace-alignment paper explicitly records this distinction and the unresolved quadratic-time real-RAM question.

The importance of the question extends beyond sorting. Pairwise sums describe many ordered geometric events, and TOPP records reductions from this sorting task to polygon-containment and arrangement-ordering problems. A resolution would clarify how much algorithmic work can be saved when a large output is generated from a much smaller collection of numerical parameters.
