cards.definitions: For \(n\ge2\), write \(V=[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A weighted hypergraph \(H=(V,E,w)\) has a set \(E\subseteq\{e\subseteq V:|e|\ge2\}\) and finite nonnegative real weights \(w:E\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). For every \(S\subseteq V\), set \(\operatorname{cut}_H(S)=\sum_{\substack{e\in E:\ e\cap S\ne\varnothing,\\e\cap(V\setminus S)\ne\varnothing}}w(e)\). Thus each crossing hyperedge contributes its weight exactly once, regardless of the number of vertices on either side. Empty and singleton edges are omitted because they cross no cut; repeated edges can be merged by summing weights. The approximating hypergraph \(H'=(V,E',w')\) follows the same rules. Its edge set may contain any subsets of the original vertex set, not necessarily original edges; additional vertices are forbidden. Size is \(|E'|\), rather than the sum of edge cardinalities or a bit-encoding length. The same approximation must hold for all cuts simultaneously, and a zero-valued original cut must remain exactly zero. The empty edge set is allowed. This is an existence question with no construction-time, randomness or rational-weight restriction. The constant \(C\) is independent of dimension, accuracy, hyperedge count, maximum edge size and weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of this universal existence theorem with one constant \(C\), or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every \(C>0\), some permitted \(n,H,\varepsilon\) has no same-vertex weighted hypergraph meeting both the size and all-cut guarantees. A refutation must allow arbitrary nonnegative replacement hyperedges, not just sampled original edges. A size bound retaining an unbounded logarithmic factor does not establish the stated theorem.

context_blocks.text: A sparsifier replaces a large interaction structure by a smaller one while preserving the values needed for later cut computations. The guarantee holds for every partition at once, including a partition chosen after seeing the sparsifier. A separate approximation for one predetermined cut would be much weaker. A hypergraph can contain exponentially many distinct hyperedges on n vertices, so reducing their number to near linear can be a large compression.

The cut convention is important for multiway interactions. A hyperedge \(\{1,2,3,4\}\) of weight one contributes one to both the partition \(\{1\}|\{2,3,4\}\) and the partition \(\{1,2\}|\{3,4\}\). Replacing it by a uniformly weighted clique gives contributions proportional to three and four respectively. Thus the ordinary graph representation does not automatically preserve the hypergraph’s cut function.

The formulation follows the broad source question: the approximating hypergraph may introduce different hyperedges on the same vertices. Requiring only reweighting and deleting original edges is an additional restriction. A construction satisfying that stronger condition also answers the stated existence question, but a lower bound restricted to that condition would not by itself refute it.

Ordinary graphs already admit \(O(n/\varepsilon ^{2})\)-edge sparsifiers. Batson, Spielman and Srivastava prove a spectral guarantee, which implies the required cut inequalities by substituting zero-one indicator vectors. This gives the benchmark without a logarithmic overhead. For hypergraphs, preserving an associated energy on all real vectors is also stronger than preserving cut indicators, and the particular energy definition must be specified before importing a spectral result.

The quadratic-in-n bound quoted in the 2018 problem entry is outdated. Chen, Khanna and Nagda give a randomized polynomial-time construction using \(O(n \log  n/\varepsilon ^{2})\) reweighted original hyperedges. Their result removes the extra dependence on maximum hyperedge size. The remaining log n is unbounded, so it cannot be absorbed into the universal C in this card.

Subsequent sketching and streaming results address how a sparsifier can be represented or maintained with limited memory. A rank-r hyperedge can require r vertex identifiers, so near-linear hyperedge count does not mean near-linear bit storage independent of r. The FOCS 2024 sketch bounds retain logarithmic factors in their near-linear output guarantee.
The ICLR 2026 insertion-only work further improves memory use, but its guarantees also retain logarithmic factors. Its space theorem does not establish the \(Cn/\varepsilon ^{2}\) hyperedge count.

Resolving the target would determine whether hypergraph cuts admit the same upper bound on the number of interactions as graph cuts at each accuracy. It would not automatically remove the cost of describing large hyperedges or reading the original input. Those separate costs explain why stronger data-access and streaming results can coexist with an unresolved existence question.

cards.title: Near-linear-time approximation of reachability diameter
cards.formal: For an unweighted directed graph $G=(V,E)$, define $D(G)=\max\{d_G(u,v):d_G(u,v)<\infty\}$. Is there an absolute constant $C\ge1$ and one randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every input, returns an estimate $D(G)/C\le\widehat D\le D(G)$ with probability at least \(2/3\) in $\widetilde O(n+m)$ worst-case time? Here $n=|V|$, $m=|E|$, words have $\Theta(\log n)$ bits, and self-distances are included, giving \(D(G)=0\) on an edgeless graph. The constant and the hidden logarithmic exponent are independent of G.
cards.why: This asks how quickly an algorithm can summarize the routes that actually exist in a directed network. I include it because it exposes a basic weakness of transferring undirected diameter intuition to directed graphs and provides a concrete benchmark for algorithms based on reachability, sampling, and shortcuts.
cards.definitions: Distances count edges on a shortest directed path. The maximum concerns finite distances only; it is neither the longest simple path nor the maximum of the smaller of the two directional distances. $\widetilde O$ suppresses polylogarithmic factors. This card focuses the broader approximation–time tradeoff on near-linear running time.

progress.text: Theorem 9 gives an $n^{1/2+o(1)}$-approximation in near-linear time. Theorem 7 gives additive error $k$ in $O(nm/k)$ time; these guarantees leave the constant-factor near-linear target unresolved.

Corollary 5 conditionally excludes better-than-two approximation below the Boolean-matrix-multiplication exponent; its combinatorial version excludes truly subcubic combinatorial algorithms under combinatorial BMM. These results do not exclude every constant approximation.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. Open Problem 1 at ESA 2026; the near-linear constant-factor target is a focused part of that broader question.

context_blocks.text: A directed graph need not be strongly connected. Taking the maximum over all ordered pairs then produces infinity as soon as one pair is unreachable, concealing the lengths of the routes that do exist. Reachability diameter discards unreachable pairs. On a one-way path of five vertices it is four, even though most ordered pairs have no directed route.

A familiar undirected idea is to search from an arbitrary vertex and use a farthest vertex as a witness. Directionality breaks its guarantee. Consider a long one-way path and an extra sink reached by an edge from the first path vertex. Searching from that sink sees no other vertex; searching toward it sees only the first path vertex. Both searches reveal a distance of one while the reachability diameter can be arbitrarily large. This is an illustrative counterexample to that particular pivot choice, not a lower bound against every sampling algorithm.

There is also a distinction between additive and multiplicative error. An estimate within $k$ of the truth is useful when $D(G)$ is much larger than $k$, but gives little information when the diameter is small. The question requires a useful relative guarantee on every input, including graphs whose longest finite shortest path has only a few edges.
The 2026 paper makes this a fine-grained algorithmic question and leaves a substantial gap for unweighted graphs. Its strong hardness results for weighted graphs do not settle the unit-weight case.

cards.title: Near-linear output-sensitive Subset Sum
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm and constants \(C>0\), \(b\ge0\) that, given \(n\ge1\) positive integers \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\le t\) and an integer \(t\ge1\), output exactly the distinct values in \(S(X,t)=\{\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}:I\subseteq[n]\}\cap\{0,\ldots,t\}\) in at most \(C(n+|S(X,t)|)(\log(n+t+2))^{b}\) operations?
cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly listed multiset; repeated values are allowed and each index can be selected at most once. The empty subset contributes zero. Output every attainable value once, in any order, with no requirement to list subsets or witnesses. Inputs exceeding the threshold can be discarded when represented in the same word model. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+t+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The word-size constant and all time constants are independent of both \(n\) and \(t\). The target permits polylogarithmic dependence on the numerical threshold, but no linear scan of its universe unless covered by the stated output bound.

context_blocks.text: Subset Sum may have very few attainable values below the threshold even when the threshold is huge. Output-sensitive complexity measures the set that must actually be produced, together with reading the input.
Bringmann and Nakos explicitly ask for near-linear time in the number of attainable sums. Their algorithm gives a four-thirds power dependence on the output size.

Chan derandomizes pseudopolynomial Subset Sum in 2026 and also derandomizes the \(\widetilde O(|S|^{4/3})\) and \(\widetilde O(|S|\sqrt n)\) output-sensitive bounds. Those results do not attain the stated near-linear output-sensitive endpoint.

sentences: An adjacency labeling scheme assigns each vertex a short binary string from which adjacency can be determined using only two labels.
The conjecture asks for logarithmic labels in every hereditary class with at most a factorial times a fixed exponential number of labeled graphs.
Hereditary means closed under induced subgraphs, and is weaker than closure under all subgraphs.
The monotone case is known, and a 2025 follow-up proves logarithmic-cubed labels for all hereditary small classes.
The question isolates when low total information content permits efficient storage in locally decodable vertex descriptions.

cards.definitions: Graphs are finite, undirected and simple. A graph class \(\mathcal C\) is closed under isomorphism; it is hereditary when every induced subgraph of every member also belongs to it. Write \(\mathcal C_n\) for its members with labeled vertex set \([n]\). Small means that there is a constant \(c\geq1\) with \(|\mathcal C_n|\leq n!c^n\) for every \(n\geq1\). A labeling scheme consists of an encoder and a decoder, fixed for the class and all input lengths. The encoder, given an adjacency-matrix encoding of \(G\in\mathcal C_n\), assigns one finite binary label to each vertex. The decoder receives only two labels and returns whether the corresponding distinct vertices are adjacent; it receives no graph description, class-membership oracle, additional table or external value of \(n\). Any size information needed by the decoder must be encoded within the labels. Both are deterministic algorithms, with no imposed time bound; encoding must halt on every graph in the class and decoding must halt on every pair of finite labels. Outside-class encoder behavior is unrestricted. All answers for pairs of vertices of an input member must be exact and simultaneous. Label length is the sole resource being bounded. No polynomial-time recognition of the class is assumed. Monotone, which is a stronger condition, means closed under deletion of both vertices and edges; this question assumes only hereditary closure.

The 2025 follow-up proves \(O((\log n)^3)\)-bit labels for every hereditary small class and logarithmic labels for small weakly sparse classes. Weak sparsity means excluding some fixed complete bipartite graph as a subgraph; that additional restriction is absent in the general conjecture.

sentences: An additive spanner keeps original graph edges while limiting the increase in every pairwise distance.
This card fixes the increase to at most four and asks for the optimal worst-case number of edges.
The target is the complete asymptotic function up to universal constant factors.
The familiar candidate is \(n^{4/3}\), while recent constructions still have exponent \(7/5\) up to logarithmic factors.
This gap is a fundamental unresolved regime of distance compression, and the variable-error linear-size tradeoff has its own card.

cards.definitions: Each original edge has length one. \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the minimum number of edges in a path, with \(d_{G}(u,u)=0\). A spanning subgraph H has the same vertex set and a subset of G’s edges, with unchanged unit lengths. If u,v are disconnected in H put \(d_{H}(u,v)=\infty\), so the requirement forces H to be connected. The lower inequality \(d_{H}(u,v)\ge d_{G}(u,v)\) follows from being a subgraph. Both extrema exist because there are finitely many graphs on a fixed labeled vertex set and \(H=G\) is feasible. The cost is number of retained edges; neither construction time nor weights, shortcuts, missing vertices, terminal subsets or faults are part of the model. New weighted edges would be an emulator and are not allowed. Restricting to connected inputs only removes disconnected bookkeeping; applying a universal bound componentwise recovers its usual all-graph form.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(n)\), constants \(a,A>0\) and \(n_{0}\) such that a \(g(n)\le s_{4}(n)\le A g(n)\) for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}\). Prove a universal existence upper bound and a matching worst-case lower bound. Polynomial exponents alone do not settle this constant-factor target if a growing logarithmic gap remains. This is an asymptotic extremal-size question, not an additive 0.01 estimate of an integer function.

cards.title: Quasipolynomial dependence on vertices for hypergraph isomorphism

cards.why: This asks whether symmetry testing can depend quasipolynomially only on the underlying universe, while remaining polynomial in the amount of set-system data. It matters for hypergraphs with many large edges and for algorithms that encode structural graph information as set systems.

cards.definitions: A hypergraph is a finite pair \((V,\mathcal E)\) with \(V=[n]\) and \(\mathcal E\subseteq2^V\). Empty hyperedges and isolated vertices are allowed; edges have no colors, order, weights or repeated copies. The input lists the vertices and every hyperedge explicitly by its incidence bit vector; vertex counts and list lengths are included in the binary encoding. Input length \(N\) therefore includes all incidences and at least \(n\) symbols. An isomorphism from \((V_1,\mathcal E_1)\) to \((V_2,\mathcal E_2)\) is a bijection \(\pi:V_1\to V_2\) with \(\{\pi(e):e\in\mathcal E_1\}=\mathcal E_2\). The algorithm must decide whether one exists and must be correct on every well-formed input; unequal vertex counts imply rejection. Time is worst-case bit time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine with no advice or oracle. Neither the hyperedge size nor the number of hyperedges is bounded polynomially in \(n\). All constants and exponents are uniform over both parameters. Replacing incidence vectors by explicit incidence lists changes length by at most a polynomial and preserves the requested two-parameter bound.

context_blocks.text: The source distinguishes a quasipolynomial dependence on the number of vertices from a polynomial dependence on the possibly much larger collection of hyperedges. Encoding a hypergraph as a bipartite incidence graph does not automatically give that separation of dependencies.

Wiebking discusses a bound whose exponent on total hypergraph size depends polylogarithmically on the vertex count, and explicitly asks for the stronger bound in which the hyperedge-size exponent is constant. The same open question reappears in the outlook section.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of an algorithm with fixed constants satisfying the displayed two-parameter bound, or prove that no such deterministic uniform algorithm exists. A quasipolynomial bound in the full incidence-graph size, or a polynomial exponent depending on the number of vertices or maximum hyperedge size, does not meet the target.

cards.definitions: The input graph is undirected, without loops or parallel edges, and encoded by an adjacency matrix on the labeled vertex set \([n]\). The planarity promise means it admits a crossing-free embedding in the plane; no embedding is required as input. A proper three-edge-coloring is a function \(\chi:E(G)\to\{1,2,3\}\) assigning different colors to any two distinct edges with a common endpoint. Graphs may be disconnected, have bridges or isolated vertices, and need not be regular. A vertex of degree greater than three forces rejection, but no other special degree pattern or augmentation promise is imposed. Running time is worst-case bit time \(C(n+1)^k\) for fixed constants on a deterministic Turing machine, with no advice, randomness or oracle. The answer must be exact on every planar input. A total-language version may reject nonplanar encodings, since planarity can itself be tested in polynomial time. This card asks for decision, not for a prescribed structural characterization of all colorable graphs.

context_blocks.text: The source poses this as Question 1 and explains why the Four-Color Theorem settles the cubic bridgeless case without settling all subcubic planar graphs. A graph with degree-two vertices need not lie in a planar cubic bridgeless supergraph.

The expanded journal article, published online in November 2025 and appearing in Algorithmica’s 2026 volume, again poses planar three-edge-colorability as an open question. Its recognition results concern specified cubic supergraphs and do not identify that augmentation task with the full coloring decision problem.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm for all planar inputs, or prove that no such algorithm exists. NP-hardness together with a Lean theorem conditional on P ≠ NP establishes conditional intractability and must be labeled as such; it is not by itself an unconditional refutation. Solving only cubic graphs or graphs admitting a particular augmentation is insufficient.

cards.definitions: All graphs are finite, undirected and simple. Subcubic means maximum degree at most three; \(H\) need not be connected. A subdivision of \(H\) is obtained by replacing each edge by a path of positive length, with pairwise disjoint internal vertex sets, none of which contains a vertex of \(H\). An induced subdivision in \(G\) is a set \(W\subseteq V(G)\) such that the induced graph \(G[W]\) is isomorphic to a subdivision of \(H\). Equivalently, choose distinct branch vertices for all vertices of \(H\), including its isolated vertices, and replacement paths with exactly the prescribed edges and no additional edges anywhere among the selected vertices. For each fixed \(H\), the decision problem takes only \(G\), encoded by its binary adjacency matrix, and answers whether such \(W\) exists; no degree, planarity or connectivity promise is made on \(G\). Polynomial time means a deterministic Turing machine with running time \(C_H(|V(G)|+1)^{k_H}\) for constants depending on \(H\), but not on \(G\). An algorithm need not be uniform in the pattern \(H\), which is not part of the input. Planarity means admitting a crossing-free drawing in the plane. The complexity assumption uses the ordinary uniform deterministic and nondeterministic polynomial-time language classes.

context_blocks.text: The source proposes planarity of a fixed subcubic pattern as the complete boundary for tractable induced-subdivision detection. Its assumption P ≠ NP is essential to the stated if-and-only-if claim.

The paper exhibits a fixed subcubic pattern whose induced-subdivision containment problem is NP-complete. This establishes an obstruction within low-degree patterns but does not classify every such pattern. Induced containment additionally forbids unwanted edges between the selected paths, unlike ordinary subdivision containment.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal equivalence under the stated P ≠ NP hypothesis, or a proof of its negation under that hypothesis. A counterexample must identify a fixed subcubic pattern and establish the failure of the corresponding direction. Proving hardness for one nonplanar pattern, or algorithms for only some planar patterns, does not settle the whole conjecture. NP-completeness of every nonplanar case would suffice for that direction but is not silently added as a stronger required conclusion.

notes: Restored the omitted P ≠ NP hypothesis rather than asserting the source equivalence unconditionally.
Defined induced subdivisions including isolated pattern vertices, internal disjointness and all forbidden extra edges; distinguished fixed-pattern complexity from an algorithm uniform in H.
Preserved the source in-P iff planar claim instead of silently strengthening all nonplanar cases to NP-completeness.

cards.definitions: All graphs are finite, undirected and simple, with binary adjacency-matrix encodings. The finite forbidden family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed, not part of the input. Let \(\mathcal C_{\mathcal F}\) contain every graph with no induced subgraph isomorphic to a member of \(\mathcal F\). Its isomorphism task receives two members \(G_1,G_2\) and asks whether there is a vertex bijection preserving adjacency and nonadjacency. Polynomial time means worst-case deterministic bit time bounded by a polynomial in their combined encoding length; the machine and polynomial may depend on \(\mathcal F\). Graph-isomorphism completeness means that there is a deterministic polynomial-time map from any pair of arbitrary simple graphs to a pair in \(\mathcal C_{\mathcal F}\), preserving the YES/NO isomorphism answer. The reverse reduction is the identity. Outputs of the hardness reduction must satisfy the class promise on both YES and NO inputs. Class membership can be checked in polynomial time for fixed finite \(\mathcal F\), so a total-language formulation may reject encodings outside the class. No algorithm deciding which side applies from an input description of \(\mathcal F\) is required. The alternatives need not be disjoint if general graph isomorphism is in P; the conjecture asserts their union covers every finite forbidden family.

context_blocks.text: Schweitzer’s Conjecture 1 asks for a polynomial-time versus general-isomorphism-complete dichotomy for finitely forbidden hereditary classes. Finiteness of the forbidden induced family is essential: the discussion distinguishes conditional intermediate examples requiring infinite descriptions.

The source obtains the dichotomy for all but finitely many two-forbidden-graph cases. A classification by forbidden ordinary subgraphs also does not settle the conjecture, because induced exclusions allow a broader range of structural behavior.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the stated universal dichotomy, or exhibit a fixed finite forbidden family and prove that its restricted isomorphism problem has neither property. A complete proof may use a mathematically specified classification without an effective classifier for forbidden families. A two-pattern theorem alone, a result for ordinary subgraph exclusion, or NP-hardness terminology without the required graph-isomorphism reductions does not settle the target.

notes: Recovered the exact finite-family quantifier and Conjecture 1, rather than conflating it with the paper’s almost-complete two-pattern theorem.

Did not require an effective meta-classifier or assume the two alternatives are disjoint when general graph isomorphism could be in P.

cards.why: The question asks whether rich higher-order cut objectives always have representations using quadratically many original terms, independent of their complexity and value ranges. Such a theorem would provide a general compression guarantee across submodular optimization models.

cards.definitions: A submodular hypergraph \(H=(V,E,(g_e)_{e\in E})\) has a finite vertex set \(V\), \(|V|=n\), a finite set \(E\subseteq2^V\) of hyperedges, and, for each \(e\), a function \(g_e:2^e\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) with \(g_e(\varnothing)=0\). Submodularity means \(g_e(A\cup B)+g_e(A\cap B)\leq g_e(A)+g_e(B)\) for every \(A,B\subseteq e\). Neither symmetry under complementation nor monotonicity, bounded positive-value ratios, integral values or bounded hyperedge rank is assumed; in particular \(g_e(e)\) need not vanish. A cut is any \(S\subseteq V\) and its value is \(F_H(S)=\sum_{e\in E}g_e(S\cap e)\). A reweighted sub-hypergraph chooses \(E'\subseteq E\) and one real scalar \(w_e>0\) for each retained edge, giving \(F_{H'}(S)=\sum_{e\in E'}w_e g_e(S\cap e)\). It must satisfy \((1-\varepsilon)F_H(S)\leq F_{H'}(S)\leq(1+\varepsilon)F_H(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq V\), including exact preservation of zero-valued cuts. Size counts retained hyperedges, not total incidences, splitting-function descriptions or bits. This is an existence theorem: no input-oracle representation, construction time, coefficient bit bound or random failure probability is imposed. The constant \(C\) must be independent of every hypergraph parameter and of \(\varepsilon\).

context_blocks.text: Theorem 1.4 of Kenneth and Krauthgamer gives an \(O(n^3/\varepsilon^2)\) reweighted sparsifier for arbitrary nonnegative submodular splitting functions. Their Conjecture 1.14 asks whether the vertex dependence can be reduced to quadratic, while retaining the stated accuracy dependence and the original splitting functions.

A July 2026 preprint proves a \(\widetilde O(n^2/\varepsilon^4)\) bound when all functions take values in a fixed finite integer range. Its Theorem 1.5 and following discussion explicitly leave arbitrary nonnegative submodular functions outside that result.

An August 2026 preprint reports \(O(n/\varepsilon^2)\) sparsifiers for sums of symmetric submodular functions. Symmetry is an additional promise absent here; it does not cover arbitrary directed or asymmetric splitting costs.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a universal constant and the stated simultaneous reweighted sparsifier bound, or prove its negation. A refutation must rule out every possible universal constant, not just one proposed bound. Bounds with additional logarithmic losses, a worse power of inverse accuracy, restricted splitting functions, or newly invented splitting functions do not establish the conjecture.

notes: Recovered nonnegative submodularity with only the empty-set normalization; did not impose symmetry or zero value on the full hyperedge.
Defined cut values, simultaneous relative approximation, positive per-edge reweighting and hyperedge-count size; no construction-time or bit-complexity claim was added.
Checked the exact July 2026 bounded-range theorem and the August symmetric result, retaining their distinct restrictions and accuracy dependence.

cards.definitions: The input is a finite directed graph \(G=(V,A)\), with \(V=[n]\), no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair, together with a length \(\ell(a)\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\) for each arc and three pairs \((s_i,t_i)\in V^2\), \(i=1,2,3\). Graph incidences and all rational numerators and positive denominators are explicitly encoded in binary. A directed path follows the arcs and has no repeated vertex; a zero-arc path is permitted when its endpoints coincide. Its length is the sum of its arc lengths. The distance \(d_G(s,t)\) is the minimum path length, or infinity when no path exists. A valid answer YES means there are paths \(P_i\) from \(s_i\) to \(t_i\), each of length \(d_G(s_i,t_i)\), with \(V(P_i)\cap V(P_j)=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Disjointness includes all terminals. Repeated terminals across different pairs therefore force NO. Distances are measured in the original graph, not after deleting other paths; minimizing the total length of three disjoint paths is a different condition. Time is worst-case deterministic Turing-machine bit time polynomial in the total encoding length, including lengths. No acyclicity or planarity promise, uniqueness of shortest paths, randomness, advice or oracle is allowed. Strict positivity follows the source preliminaries; allowing zero-length directed cycles is not part of this card.

cards.definitions: For every \(n\geq1\), let \(\mathcal G_n\) be the finite set of simple undirected graphs on \([n]\). Every edge has length one. A spanning subgraph \(H\subseteq G\) has the same vertices, retains only original edges, and must have the same connected components as \(G\). There are no Steiner vertices, shortcut edges or changed edge lengths. Let \[\Delta(G,H)=\max_{u,v:\,d_G(u,v)<\infty}\bigl(d_H(u,v)-d_G(u,v)\bigr),\qquad A_c(n)=\max_{G\in\mathcal G_n}\min_{\substack{H\subseteq G,\ |E(H)|\leq\lfloor cn\rfloor\\ H\text{ preserves components}}}\Delta(G,H).\] Distances count edges. Pairs with \(u=v\) are included, so the maximum is defined and nonnegative even in an edgeless graph. A spanning forest is feasible for \(c\geq1\); thus the quantity is finite. A result up to constant factors supplies a nonnegative function \(a(n,c)\) and, for each fixed \(c\), constants \(0<L_c\leq U_c<\infty\) and \(n_c\) with \(L_c a(n,c)\leq A_c(n)\leq U_c a(n,c)\) for every \(n\geq n_c\). Constants may depend on \(c\), never on \(n\). This measures optimal structural approximation, not the running time for finding a spanner; no algorithmic cost bound is imposed. The explicit coefficient \(c\) makes the source’s unspecified linear-size constant a parameter of the target.

context_blocks.text: The survey’s Section 8.4, item 3, asks how much additive error is unavoidable with \(O(n)\) retained edges. Its dated bounds leave a polynomial gap between what sparse subgraphs can achieve and what some input metrics force.

Bodwin and Hoppenworth subsequently establish an \(\Omega(n^{1/7})\) additive-error lower bound for linear-size spanners, improving the lower bound quoted in the survey. This is a lower bound, not a matching determination.

The later Almost-Optimal Sublinear Additive Spanners abstract reports \(O(n^{0.403})\) additive error with \(\widetilde O(n)\) edges. That edge budget hides logarithmic factors and cannot be substituted for a fixed \(cn\) budget in this question.

cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked asymptotic determination of the defined family, with matching upper and lower bounds up to multiplicative constants for every fixed edge coefficient. The upper bound must cover every input graph and the lower bound must establish matching worst cases under the same edge budget. Determining only an exponent with an unresolved polynomial or logarithmic gap does not meet this precision; a numerical tolerance of 1/100 is not an additive error on asymptotic notation.

cards.definitions: Graphs are finite, undirected, loopless and have no parallel edges. Local complementation at a vertex \(v\) toggles adjacency between each pair of distinct neighbors of \(v\), leaving all other adjacencies unchanged. If \(uv\) is an edge in the current graph, pivoting on \(uv\) means local complementation at \(u\), then \(v\), then \(u\). A vertex-minor is obtained by a finite sequence of local complementations and vertex deletions; a pivot-minor instead permits edge pivots and vertex deletions. A deletion removes the chosen vertex and all its incident edges. Isomorphism is a bijection preserving adjacency in both directions; target vertices have no prescribed locations in the host. The empty target is allowed. For each fixed pair \((\rho,H)\), the algorithm receives only \(G\), encoded by its vertex count and adjacency matrix in binary. There must be constants \(C_{\rho,H},a_{\rho,H}>0\) such that it always returns the correct bit in at most \(C_{\rho,H}(n+1)^{a_{\rho,H}}\) Turing steps on every \(n\)-vertex host. Its program and these constants may depend on the fixed target and relation. No uniform construction from an input \(H\), fixed-parameter bound, containment witness or host-width promise is required. There is no advice depending on the growing host.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the quantified polynomial-time decision algorithms for both relations and every fixed target, or a Lean refutation for some fixed target and relation. A result only for hosts of bounded width or a bound exponential in host size does not meet the assertion. A uniform fixed-parameter algorithm would be sufficient but is not required.

cards.definitions: The graph is finite, undirected and simple, with vertex set \([n]\), \(n\geq2\), and an explicit binary adjacency matrix. The integer \(\lambda\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}\) is part of the input, encoded in binary, and need not be fixed. The available links are exactly \(\binom{V(G)}{2}\setminus E(G)\). An augmentation is any subset \(F\) of these links; its cost is \(|F|\), and no new vertices are permitted. The graph \(G+F\) is \(\lambda\)-vertex-connected if deleting any set of fewer than \(\lambda\) vertices leaves a connected graph. The condition \(\lambda<n\) excludes ambiguous conventions on graphs with too few vertices. The optimum is finite because adding every missing edge produces a complete graph. The algorithm must output the exact minimum integer; equivalently it may decide, for a binary budget \(k\geq0\), whether some augmentation has \(|F|\leq k\). The two tasks are polynomial-time equivalent using the finite \(\binom n2\) budget range. Running time is worst-case bit time bounded by one fixed polynomial in the whole input length, with no exponent or multiplicative nonpolynomial dependence on \(\lambda\). The input graph may have arbitrary initial connectivity; there is no promise that the target increases connectivity by only one.

category_assignment.reason: The proposed dichotomy concerns ordinary polynomial-time versus NP-hard hereditary edge-deletion algorithms.

importance.reason: A broad structural classification across finite-forbidden hereditary graph modification problems, with a uniform conceptual reach beyond individual classes or parameterized bounds.

sentences: The target graph property is specified by a fixed finite list of forbidden induced subgraphs.
An instance asks whether deleting at most a supplied number of edges can achieve that property.
The question is whether every such fixed-family problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-complete.
The finite-list domain is an explicit specialization of the survey’s broader hereditary-class research direction.

cards.definitions: A simple undirected graph has no loops or parallel edges. For \(U\subseteq V\), its induced subgraph contains every edge of \(G\) with both endpoints in \(U\). Graph isomorphism is an adjacency-preserving bijection of vertex sets. The class of \(\mathcal F\)-free graphs consists of all finite graphs with none of the forbidden induced subgraphs; it is hereditary, meaning closed under taking induced subgraphs. Deleting \(S\) retains all vertices and exactly the edges in \(E\setminus S\). Edges cannot be added, vertices cannot be removed, and every deleted edge costs one. The empty graph and the empty forbidden family are permitted. The input graph uses its adjacency matrix on numbered vertices; \(k\) is binary. The family \(\mathcal F\) is fixed before the input varies and is not part of the input to this decision problem. For each fixed family, its finite graph list may be built into the program, and polynomial exponents and constants may depend on it. A language is in \(\mathrm P\) if a deterministic Turing machine decides it in polynomial input length. It is in \(\mathrm{NP}\) if polynomial-size certificates can be checked in polynomial time. A polynomial-time many-one reduction from \(K\) to \(L\) is one deterministic polynomial-time function \(f\) on finite binary strings such that \(x\in K\) iff \(f(x)\in L\). NP-completeness means membership in NP and such a reduction from every NP language. Each problem here is in NP because a deletion set can be checked and all induced copies of the finitely many fixed forbidden graphs can be enumerated in polynomial time. The dichotomy is inclusive; it assumes neither \(\mathrm P=\mathrm{NP}\) nor its negation.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every finite family \(\mathcal F\) satisfies the stated P-or-NP-complete alternative. Alternatively specify one finite family and prove in Lean that its decision problem is neither in P nor NP-complete under the stated reductions. A theorem for a single forbidden graph or a fixed selection of graph classes is insufficient. No separate effective procedure for classifying the family \(\mathcal F\) is imposed by this proposition.

context_blocks.text: The survey describes the absence of a general polynomial-time versus NP-hard classification for hereditary edge deletion. Editorial specialization: this card selects the finite-forbidden-induced-subgraph domain, giving the graph properties a finite description and ensuring that every resulting decision problem is in NP. The source’s broader direction also encompasses hereditary classes without such a finite forbidden list.

There are immediate tractable families. If the only forbidden graph is a single edge, all input edges must be removed. If the forbidden graphs are the three-vertex path and the triangle, every remaining component must be an isolated vertex or an isolated edge: maximizing the retained edges is maximum matching, which is polynomial-time solvable.

Deleting an edge can create a forbidden induced subgraph. For example, removing one edge from a triangle creates an induced three-vertex path. Consequently, eliminating all forbidden copies initially visible in the input need not produce a valid final graph.

The survey contrasts edge deletion with the classical broad hardness theorem for vertex removal into nontrivial hereditary properties. That contrast motivates a structural classification for edge operations; it does not transfer the vertex-removal theorem to the problem defined here.

The 2023 journal version still states the absence of a general edge-removal dichotomy. Its detailed tables also concern parameterized algorithms and kernelization. A bound depending arbitrarily on the deletion budget, or the existence of a polynomial kernel, addresses a different question from ordinary polynomial time in the entire input.

Completing the dichotomy would rule out NP-intermediate behavior inside this finite-description family, even if such behavior exists elsewhere in NP. Proving just that some cases are hard is weaker: every finite forbidden family must fall into one of the stated alternatives.

cards.title: Linear-time exact inversion counting
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm that, for every \(n\ge2\) and every explicitly listed permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), computes \(\operatorname{Inv}(\pi)=|\{(i,j):1\le i<j\le n,\ \pi(i)>\pi(j)\}|\) exactly in \(O(n)\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: The input contains \(n\) and the array \(\pi(1),\ldots,\pi(n)\), promised to contain each integer from one through \(n\) exactly once. The output is the single integer inversion count, between zero and \(n(n-1)/2\). Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Choose \(d\ge3\), so the count fits in a word. All constants are independent of the permutation and \(n\). No randomness is allowed. The values are already ranks, so no conversion from arbitrary ordered keys is required.

context_blocks.text: An inversion counts an out-of-order pair in a ranking. The exact total is also the Kendall tau distance from the identity ordering and the minimum number of adjacent swaps needed to sort the permutation.
Chan and Pătraşcu give an \(O(n\sqrt{\log n})\) exact word-RAM algorithm and a linear-time constant-relative-error approximation. The latter does not compute the exact count.
The input is a permutation of small integers, so sorting those integers itself is already easy. Determining how many pairs were out of order is a separate offline aggregation problem.

The linear exact endpoint is an editorial formulation of the remaining gap. The September 2026 search found no general exact linear algorithm, but the status evidence relies mainly on older primary work and is weaker than for the other additions.

cards.definitions: The input is a finite directed graph with vertex set \([n]\), no loops and at most one arc for each ordered pair of vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. The underlying undirected graph is planar, and a combinatorial planar embedding is supplied. Thus the number of arcs is \(O(n)\). Each arc \(a\) has a finite rational capacity \(u_a\geq0\) and rational cost \(c_a\), and each vertex \(v\) has rational supply \(b_v\), with \(\sum_v b_v=0\). All numerators and positive denominators are encoded in binary; no magnitude bound is imposed. A feasible flow assigns rational \(f_a\) with \(0\leq f_a\leq u_a\) and \(\sum_{a\text{ out of }v} f_a-\sum_{a\text{ into }v}f_a=b_v\) at each vertex. Its cost is \(\sum_a c_a f_a\). Strong polynomiality means a bound polynomial in \(n\) on exact rational arithmetic operations, comparisons and index/memory operations, independent of all numeric bit lengths, together with a polynomial bound in total input bit length on every intermediate number’s encoding length. Arithmetic uses addition, subtraction, multiplication and division by nonzero values. The algorithm has finite uniform code and no advice, randomness or oracle. The little-o improvement means that there is a function \(T(n)\) bounding its operation count on every such \(n\)-vertex input with \(T(n)/(n^{2}\log(n+2))\to0\). The source’s instruction to beat the stated bound is interpreted as an asymptotic little-o improvement, not merely a smaller leading constant. The simple planar-network convention prevents arbitrarily many parallel arcs from hiding an unbounded input size in \(n\).

A 2022 preprint gives a nearly linear algorithm for planar minimum-cost flow with polynomially bounded integer costs and capacities. Those numeric restrictions are material: this result does not by itself answer the strongly polynomial question for arbitrary rational input data.

cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of an algorithm with the exact flow guarantee, little-o operation bound and polynomial intermediate bit lengths, or prove that no such deterministic strongly polynomial algorithm exists. A speedup for bounded numerical data, an approximation algorithm, or a lower leading constant at the same asymptotic order does not answer the stated question.

cards.title: Set-system sparsifiers of size proportional to chain length
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that for every integer \(m\ge 1\), every family \(S\subseteq 2^{[m]}\), every weight vector \(w\in \mathbb{R} \ge 0^{m}\) and every \(0<\varepsilon <1\), there is a reweighting \(\tilde\{w\}\in \mathbb{R} \ge 0^{m}\) with at most \(C\cdot CL(S)/\varepsilon ^{2}\) nonzero coordinates and satisfying \((1- \varepsilon )\sum _{i\in A}w_{i}\le \sum _{i\in A}\tilde\{w\}_{i}\le (1+\varepsilon )\sum _{i\in A}w_{i}\) simultaneously for every \(A\in S\)?
cards.why: Would give a sharp structural bound for simultaneous multiplicative compression of arbitrary weighted set families. It asks whether chain length and squared inverse accuracy fully account for the necessary support, without logarithmic losses.

cards.definitions: Here \([m]=\{1,\ldots ,m\}\), and S is any finite collection of subsets, including possibly the empty collection. The support of w̃ is \(\{i:\tilde\{w\}_{i}>0\}\); coordinates outside it are dropped, while retained coordinates may receive arbitrary nonnegative real weights. No normalization such as \(\sum w_{i}=1\) is imposed. Following the source’s witness definition, a chain of length \(\ell\) consists of distinct coordinates \(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{\ell}\) and distinct sets \(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{\ell}\in S\) with \(a_{i}\in A_{i}\) for every i and \(a_{j}\notin A_{i}\) whenever \(i<j\). \(CL(S)\) is the maximum possible \(\ell\), allowing \(\ell =0\). Equivalently, take the union-closure \(U(S)=\{\bigcup T:T\subseteq S\}\), including the empty union; \(CL(S)\) is the largest number of strict inclusions in an ascending chain starting from \(\varnothing\) in \(U(S)\). Thus \(CL(S)=0\) when S is empty or contains only \(\varnothing\). It is not merely the largest chain in the original family. A \((1\pm \varepsilon )\) sparsifier is a reweighting satisfying the simultaneous inequalities in the statement. Sets of original weight zero must retain weight exactly zero. All data and weights are quantified mathematically; the question places no running-time, oracle-access, randomness or bit-complexity requirement on finding w̃. The same C must work independently of m, S, w and \(\varepsilon\). The source allows \(\varepsilon >0\); values \(\varepsilon \ge 1\) admit the zero reweighting, so restricting the nontrivial question to \(0<\varepsilon <1\) preserves it.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal existence bound with one absolute constant C, or refute it by showing that for every C there are a family, weights and an accuracy parameter for which every multiplicative sparsifier needs more than \(C\cdot CL(S)/\varepsilon ^{2}\) coordinates. Bounds with an additional unbounded logarithmic factor do not meet the conjecture; an efficient construction is not required.

context_blocks.title: Preserve all set weights with fewer coordinates
context_blocks.text: A coordinate can represent an edge, a constraint or a position of a codeword. A sparsifier removes coordinates and compensates by reweighting those it keeps. The same reweighting must preserve every specified set’s weight, including small-weight sets, which makes multiplicative error stronger than a global additive-error allowance.

context_blocks.title: One set can be represented by one weighted coordinate
context_blocks.text: If S contains only the whole nonempty universe, its chain length is one. Placing the entire total weight on any one coordinate preserves that sole set weight exactly. A large universe alone therefore does not force a large sparsifier.

context_blocks.title: Union-closure sees constraints absent from direct containment
context_blocks.text: If S consists of all m singleton sets, the original sets are pairwise incomparable. Their unions nevertheless form a chain of m strict inclusions, so \(CL(S)=m\). With unit original weights and \(\varepsilon <1\), every singleton must retain positive weight; all m coordinates are necessary. This explains why the conjecture uses chain length in the union-closure.

cards.definitions: The input is a directed graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(V=[n], n\ge 2\), no loops or parallel arcs, and distinguished \(s\ne t\). Both opposite arcs between two vertices are allowed. The graph is unweighted; every arc has length one. A simple s-to-t path is a sequence \(v_{0}=s,v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}=t\) of pairwise distinct vertices with \((v_{j- 1},v_{j})\in E\) for \(1\le j\le \ell\), and its length is \(\ell\). If t is reachable from \(s, \operatorname{dist}_{G}(s,t)\) is the minimum length of such a path. If t is unreachable, the instance is a no-instance. The input lists all vertices and arcs using binary vertex labels; N is the full encoding length. Polynomial time means one deterministic multitape Turing machine that decides every instance in at most \(C(N+1)^{a}\) steps for absolute constants C,a. NP-completeness uses deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions; in particular, a hardness proof can give a map from Boolean satisfiability instances to these graph instances that preserves yes/no answers. The decision problem is in NP: an at-most-n-vertex path is a polynomial-size certificate, and reachability distance and the path conditions can be checked in polynomial time. No planarity, acyclicity, connectivity or uniqueness of shortest paths is promised.
cards.answer_criterion: Determine the problem’s complexity in the stated unrestricted directed, unweighted model. A deterministic polynomial-time decision algorithm establishes tractability; a polynomial-time many-one reduction from SAT establishes NP-completeness, since membership in NP is known. The latter excludes a polynomial-time algorithm under \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The question does not assume a \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy in advance; any different established classification must explain the remaining boundary. Bounds only for planar graphs, or hardness when k is variable, do not classify the fixed \(k=1\) problem.

cards.definitions: G is a finite simple connected undirected graph with n numbered vertices and unit length on every edge, encoded by an adjacency matrix and the terminal labels. Take the 2k terminals to be distinct; repeated endpoints across different pairs make vertex-disjointness infeasible, and a pair with \(s_{i}=t_{i}\) uses the zero-edge path at that vertex and can be handled separately. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent. Vertex-disjointness includes endpoints and means \(V(\mathrm{P}_{i})\cap V(\mathrm{P}_{j})=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Pairings are fixed: connecting a source to a different pair’s target is not acceptable. Define OPT as the minimum sum of edge counts over all feasible collections and set OPT=∞ when there is none. The output consists of the k vertex sequences of an optimal collection, or an infeasibility answer. For each fixed k the algorithm is a probabilistic Turing machine, with one finite program handling all n and all inputs for that k, running in at most \(C_{k}(n+1)^{c_{k}}\) steps on every random-bit sequence. Constants \(C_{k},c_{k}\) are independent of n. With probability at least \(2/3\) over its independent fair bits, the full output must be correct, including exact optimality. A deterministic algorithm is included as the zero-error case. The formulation asks for polynomial time for each fixed k and does not demand a uniform procedure generating these programs as k varies. The source compares this target with k-DSP, which requires every \(\mathrm{P}_{i}\) separately to have length \(\operatorname{dist}_{G}(s_{i},t_{i})\). Such a collection, when it exists, has the smallest possible total length; minimum-total-length routing must also handle inputs where disjoint routes exist but no collection of individually shortest routes exists.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish or refute polynomial-time solvability, with the stated bounded-error allowance, for every fixed \(k\ge 3\). A positive answer must output an exactly optimal collection or detect infeasibility on all inputs. A conditional negative answer must state its assumption and imply that no such polynomial-time algorithm exists for at least one fixed k. Hardness only when k grows with n, an FPT lower bound, approximation, or an algorithm restricted to individually shortest paths does not decide this question.

cards.definitions:
In the bottleneck path problem (BP), the input is an explicit directed graph G=(V,E), a source s, a target t and a weight w(e) for every edge. Among all directed s-to-t paths P, output one minimizing max_{e∈P}w(e). Any optimal simple path is acceptable; ties require no prescribed choice. If t is unreachable, report that no path exists. When s=t the empty path is returned, with bottleneck conventionally −∞.

In the bottleneck spanning-tree problem (BST), the input is the same kind of directed weighted graph and a specified root s. Output an out-arborescence T spanning all vertices: s has indegree zero, every other vertex has indegree one in T, and there is a directed path in T from s to every vertex. Minimize max_{e∈T}w(e). If no such tree exists, report this. For a one-vertex graph, the empty tree has value −∞. This objective minimizes the single largest tree-edge weight, not the sum of weights. A tree minimizing that largest weight need not supply an individually optimal bottleneck path to every vertex.

Weights are arbitrary elements of a totally ordered set, such as arbitrary real numbers. They are opaque keys: they may be stored, copied and compared in constant time, but their digits, arithmetic values and integer ranks are not available for computation. Equal weights are allowed. The graph is given by adjacency lists with O(log(n+m+2))-bit vertex and edge indices; ordinary operations on these indices have unit cost. The algorithm is charged for all graph operations, comparisons, random sampling and writing its path or tree, not just the number of comparisons. There is no assumption that the weights are sorted, bounded integers, or machine words supporting bit operations.

The randomization convention is Las Vegas: on every fixed input the answer is exact, termination occurs with probability one, and the expected total work over the algorithm's internal random choices is at most C(n+m) for a universal constant C. This includes feasibility checks and output. A randomized algorithm with a small probability of an incorrect optimum would not meet this convention. For BP, isolated and unreachable vertices can be removed in O(n+m) work. A feasible nontrivial BST instance has m≥n−1. Thus O(n+m) makes the source's O(m) target meaningful also on degenerate explicit inputs without changing its substantive content.

The question asks for this guarantee for both tasks, but their expected-linear-time versions are equivalent through the reductions in Section 4 of the source. These reductions do not establish the corresponding deterministic equivalence: the BST-to-BP reduction uses randomness. The source's separate question about a deterministic O(mβ(m,n)) bound is not the target of this card. Neither all-pairs bottleneck paths nor finding every individual single-source bottleneck value is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give always-correct comparison-based algorithms with expected O(n+m) total work for both directed tasks, or use the source reductions to derive both guarantees from one. Alternatively, rule out such algorithms, stating any assumptions used. An undirected algorithm, a word-RAM algorithm inspecting weight representations, a bound on comparisons alone, or a faster algorithm only for sufficiently dense graphs does not settle the unrestricted target. A deterministic lower bound alone does not rule out the permitted randomized algorithms.

references.authors: Abrishami, Tara; Chudnovsky, Maria; Pilipczuk, Marcin; Rzążewski, Paweł
references.locator: STACS 2024, article 4: graph/weight conventions in Section 1, Theorems 1–2 and Conjecture 10 read. S_{t,t,t} is excluded as an induced subgraph. The proved theorem additionally excludes a fixed biclique as a subgraph.

cards.definitions:
Graphs are finite, undirected and simple. A forest has no cycle. In a nontrivial tree, a leaf has degree one; an isolated vertex is allowed as a component. A tree with at most three leaves is a path or a subdivided claw. A subdivided claw \(S_{a,b,c}\), for integers \(a,b,c\geq1\), consists of three internally disjoint paths of respectively \(a,b,c\) edges sharing one endpoint. That common endpoint has degree three, and the other endpoints are the three leaves.

The graph \(G\) is \(H\)-free if no vertex subset induces a graph isomorphic to \(H\). An induced copy must preserve both edges and nonedges. If \(H\) is disconnected, all its components must occur together with no extra edges between their chosen vertices. Excluding the whole forest is therefore not the same as separately excluding every component.

The input explicitly lists \(G\) and nonnegative integer vertex weights \(w(v)\), encoded in binary. The length \(L\) includes the graph and all weight bits; zero weights and the empty independent set are allowed. An independent set \(I\subseteq V(G)\) contains no pair joined by an edge. Its weight is
\[w(I)=\sum_{v\in I}w(v).\]
The required output is a set \(I\) attaining the largest possible weight, not merely an inclusion-maximal set or an approximation.

The forbidden graph \(H\) is fixed before the input varies. The algorithm, polynomial exponent and multiplicative constant may depend on \(H\). The question does not require one exponent independent of \(H\), or fixed-parameter tractability when \(H\) is treated as a variable input. It asks for ordinary polynomial bit complexity for each fixed class.

There is no bound on the maximum degree, clique size or biclique size of \(G\). No sparsity promise is imposed beyond the forbidden induced forest. Recognition of \(H\)-freeness can be done in polynomial time for fixed \(H\), but the optimization guarantee is required only on that class.

Computing the exact optimum value and outputting an optimum set are polynomial-time equivalent here by the usual self-reduction on induced subgraphs, which remain \(H\)-free. The primary source discusses the full family of forests; the symmetric long claws \(S_{t,t,t}\) are a central subfamily, not an unmentioned restriction of this formulation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove polynomial-time solvability for every fixed forest in the stated family, or refute this assertion for at least one fixed forest. Any complexity assumption used for a negative result must be explicit. A quasipolynomial-time algorithm, an approximation scheme or a theorem requiring bounded degree or a forbidden biclique does not meet the full target.

cards.title: Near-linear-query reconstruction of bounded-degree graphs
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(\Delta\geq2\), is there a randomized exact reconstruction algorithm \(A_{\Delta}\) and constants \(C_{\Delta}>0\), \(k_{\Delta}\geq0\) such that every hidden connected simple unweighted undirected graph \(G\) on \(n\) labeled vertices with maximum degree at most \(\Delta\) can be reconstructed using \[\mathbb E[Q(A_{\Delta},G)]\leq C_{\Delta}\,n(\log(n+2))^{k_{\Delta}}\] queries to an oracle that returns the shortest-path distance between one requested pair of vertices?

source_formulation.text: Thus the open question from [27] of whether general graphs of bounded degree can be reconstructed using \(\widetilde{O}\)\((n)\) distance queries remains open and answering it […]

references.title: A Simple Algorithm for Graph Reconstruction

cards.definitions:
The algorithm is given the entire vertex set, identified with \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and the fixed degree bound. The edge set is hidden. The graph is fixed throughout the execution and is promised connected; no random input distribution is assumed.

A query supplies two named vertices \(u,v\) and receives the integer
\[d_{G}(u,v)=\min\{\text{number of edges on a path from }u\text{ to }v\}.\]
The answer contains no path, intermediate vertices or distances to other destinations. An edge has distance one. Computing all distances from one vertex by querying this oracle costs \(n-1\) queries, rather than one query.

The algorithm may choose each new query using all previous answers and its private random bits. Its output must be exactly the set \(E(G)\) on the given vertex labels. Isomorphism type, an approximate metric, a graph consistent with only some answers, or a sample of edges is insufficient.

The randomized convention is Las Vegas: the output is correct whenever returned, and the procedure terminates with probability one. The query bound is an expectation over its internal randomness for each fixed allowed graph. This is not average-case complexity over randomly generated graphs. Deterministic algorithms also qualify.

The constants may depend on the fixed \(\Delta\), but not on \(n\) or the particular graph. The displayed bound specifies the meaning of \(\widetilde O(n)\): a linear number of vertices times a fixed power of a logarithm. A bound \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\) does not meet it.

Only calls to the distance oracle are charged in this query-complexity question. The algorithm must be an effective finite procedure, but no separate polynomial bound on local computation or memory is imposed. No restriction is placed on the number of adaptive rounds. There is no additional promise of bounded treewidth, treelength, cutwidth or a planar graph.

Simplicity matters because distances cannot reveal edge multiplicities or loops. Connectedness is also part of the source model: allowing a graph with just one hidden edge and otherwise isolated vertices would already force a quadratic search for that edge.
cards.answer_criterion: Give algorithms with the displayed expected-query bound for every fixed degree bound, and prove exact reconstruction on every promised graph, or show that such bounds are impossible for at least one fixed degree bound. A lower bound against the source’s particular algorithm alone does not refute the general question.

cards.title: Spanners matching Thorup–Zwick emulator tradeoffs
cards.formal:
For every fixed integer \(k\ge1\), do there exist constants \(C_{k},D_{k}>0\) such that every finite simple undirected unweighted graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(n=|V|\ge1\), has a spanning subgraph \(H=(V,E_{H})\), \(E_{H}\subseteq E\), satisfying
\[
|E_{H}|\le C_{k}n^{\,1+1/(2^{k+1}-1)}
\]
and, simultaneously for all distinct vertices \(u,v\) in the same connected component of \(G\),
\[
d_{H}(u,v)\le d_{G}(u,v)+D_{k}\,d_{G}(u,v)^{\,1-1/k}?
\]
The constants may depend on \(k\), but not on the graph, its size or the vertex pair. This is the fixed-\(k\) size and distance-error tradeoff achieved by Thorup–Zwick emulators, now required of an actual subgraph.
cards.why: Spanners retain real routes in the original network, while emulators can encode long routes as weighted shortcuts. Matching their size/error tradeoffs would establish that this structural restriction costs only constant factors at every fixed level of sublinear distance accuracy. The later almost-matching theorem makes the exact remaining loss especially concrete.

cards.definitions:
The distance \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the number of edges on a shortest path in \(G\); it is \(+\infty\) if there is no path. A spanning subgraph keeps every vertex and may remove edges, but all retained edges still have unit length. It cannot insert shortcut edges or change weights. Consequently, \(d_{H}(u,v)\ge d_{G}(u,v)\) automatically.

The inequality for finite distances requires \(H\) to connect every pair originally connected in \(G\). Vertices in different components remain disconnected because \(H\subseteq G\). Equal vertices have distance zero in both graphs and need no separate distortion inequality. For distinct connected vertices, \(d_{G}(u,v)\ge1\), so the power is defined even at \(k=1\), where it equals 1.

There is one subgraph \(H\) for the entire graph and fixed \(k\). It must satisfy the bound for every distance scale and every pair simultaneously. The quantifier order is
\[
\forall k\ge1\ \exists C_{k},D_{k}>0\ \forall G\ \exists H\ \forall u,v.
\]
The size bound has no hidden logarithmic factor in \(n\), no \(n^{\delta}\) loss for positive \(\delta\), and no additional accuracy parameter affecting the selected subgraph. Dependence on a growing \(k=k(n)\) is not requested.

For \(k>1\), the allowed additive error is sublinear in the distance because \(d^{1-1/k}/d=d^{-1/k}\) tends to zero. It need not be a constant independent of distance. For example, \(k=2\) asks for \(O(n^{8/7})\) edges with additive error \(O(\sqrt d)\). The \(k=1\) case asks for \(O(n^{4/3})\) edges and constant additive error.

An emulator is a weighted graph on the same vertex set that may contain edges absent from \(G\). A shortcut between \(u,v\) can receive weight \(d_{G}(u,v)\), preserving the prohibition on underestimating original distances. A spanner must instead use only original edges. Replacing shortcuts by their full original paths can increase the number of retained edges and does not automatically preserve the size bound.

The main assertion is existential: it asks for the same structural tradeoff, not a prescribed transformation of a supplied emulator or a specified construction running time. A construction establishing these bounds qualifies. This follows the size/stretch question in the source; bounds on construction time are separate from this target.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence assertion for every fixed integer \(k\), or refute it by showing that for some fixed \(k\) no constants \(C_{k},D_{k}\) work for all graphs. A counterexample to one proposed construction is insufficient. A family with the stated edge exponent plus any fixed positive slack, or different spanners for different accuracy parameters, does not establish the exact target.

cards.title: Maximum reset threshold of synchronizing automata
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 1\), determine \(T(n)=\max\){\(rt(A): A\) is a synchronizing complete deterministic finite automaton with n states and any finite nonempty alphabet}, where \(rt(A)\) is its shortest reset-word length.
cards.definitions: An automaton here is a finite transition system \(A=(Q,\Sigma ,\delta )\), with |\(Q|=n, a\) finite nonempty alphabet \(\Sigma\), and a total function \(\delta :Q\times \Sigma \to Q\). Extend \(\delta\) to words by \(\delta (q,\varepsilon )=q\) and \(\delta (q,wa)=\delta (\delta (q,w),a)\). A word w is a reset word when |\(\{\delta (q,w):q\in Q\}|=1\). The automaton is synchronizing if at least one such word exists; its reset threshold \(rt(A)\) is the minimum number of letters in a reset word. The quantification ranges over every n and every finite alphabet and total transition function satisfying this promise. The common final state need not be specified beforehand. Initial states and accepting states play no role. The empty word handles \(n=1\). No strong-connectivity, binary-alphabet, permutation-letter, or other structural restriction is imposed. Partial automata, nondeterministic transitions, and synchronizing only a prescribed proper subset of Q are different models. The maximum is well-defined: on n labeled states there are only \(n^{n}\) different letter transformations, and duplicate transformations may be removed without changing shortest reset lengths. Thus finitely many transition alphabets suffice. \(T(1)=0\). The target is the integer-valued function of n, not the running time of testing synchronization.
cards.answer_criterion: Specify a real-valued approximation g on the positive integers and prove in Lean that |\(g(n)- (T(n) : \mathbb{R} )|\le 1/100\) for every integer \(n\ge 1\), using the model and target defined here. Certified lower and upper functions \(\ell\)\((n)\le T(n)\le u(n)\) with \(u(n)- \ell (n)\le 1/50\) also qualify via their midpoint. The answer may use unambiguous mathematical expressions or certified bounds; g need not be integer-valued, and no simple exact formula for \(T(n)\) is required. An exact determination also qualifies. A one-sided bound, agreement at finitely many n, or an asymptotic estimate without the stated pointwise error guarantee does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: A central extremal problem in automata theory, with a simple finite-state formulation and a sharp explicit candidate bound. It tests whether local compression and algebraic structure can force globally short control sequences in every synchronizing system.

importance.reason: The flagship quantitative question about synchronizing automata, connecting finite-state control, extremal combinatorics, and linear-algebraic methods.

progress.text: Černý constructs an n-state family with reset threshold exactly \((n- 1)^{2}\), establishing the sharp lower-bound target.
The classical Pin–Frankl compression argument gives a general cubic upper bound; the survey records \((n^{3}- n)/6- 1\) for \(n\ge 4\).
Szykuła combines compression with avoiding words to improve the long-standing leading cubic constant.
Shitov improves that argument to a leading constant approximately 0.1654; the exponent remains three.
Volkov’s updated list records established special classes and their reset-threshold bounds while keeping the general conjecture open.
Zhu reports a proof for the one-cluster subclass in a preprint. This card does not independently certify that proof or extend it to unrestricted automata.

context_blocks.text: This card asks for the worst-case reset-length function with absolute approximation error at most 0.01 for every n. The Černý conjecture predicts \(T(n)=(n- 1)^{2}\). Determining a different function would also answer this card, but merely refuting the conjectured formula would not.

Synchronization asks how to restore a finite system to a known state when its current state is unknown. A fixed input sequence must work simultaneously from every possible starting state; it cannot observe the intermediate state and adapt its next letter. The length bound therefore measures the cost of an open-loop reset, rather than ordinary shortest-path navigation from a known vertex.

The proposed constant is forced by a concrete family. On states \(0,\ldots ,n- 1\), let a cyclically increment the state and let b send \(n- 1\) to 0 while fixing the other states. For \(n\ge 2\), the word \(b(a^{n- 1}b)^{n- 2}\) has length \((n- 1)^{2}\) and resets this automaton. Černý’s construction also proves that no shorter reset word works. This is the known lower bound for \(T(n)\); the Černý conjecture predicts equality for every n.

Knowing that a reset exists is much easier than establishing its sharp maximum length. Pairwise merging gives polynomial criteria for synchronizability, and successive compression of subsets gives general polynomial length bounds. The bottleneck is how much progress one can force as the current set of possible states shrinks. Adding separate worst-case bounds for these stages gives a cubic estimate and can lose information about how the stages interact.

The August 2026 open-problems survey records a general upper bound of approximately \(0.1654n^{3}+o(n^{3})\), due to Shitov’s refinement of Szykuła’s result. The gap is therefore in the exponent as well as the leading constant: the conjecture asks for the exact quadratic bound \((n- 1)^{2}\). Results for restricted transition systems do not establish that bound for all synchronizing automata.

A July 2026 preprint reports the conjectured bound for one-cluster automata: systems having a letter whose functional graph has exactly one directed cycle. Its sharper positive-level estimate uses the cycle length and the distance of off-cycle states from that cycle. This is a claim for a restricted class, and the later general survey still states the unrestricted conjecture as open.

cards.title: Sakoda–Sipser problem
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C,k\ge 1\) exist such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every finite nonempty input alphabet \(\Sigma\) and every two-way nondeterministic finite automaton A over \(\Sigma\) with at most n states, there is a two-way deterministic finite automaton D over the same alphabet with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states satisfying \(\mathrm{L}(D)=\mathrm{L}(A)\)? Equivalence must hold on all finite input words, without a length bound.
cards.definitions: The read-only input tape contains a left endmarker, a word \(w\in \Sigma\)*, and a right endmarker. Each automaton has one head, initially on the left endmarker, a finite set Q of states with a designated initial state and designated halting accepting states. In each nonhalting configuration it uses its current state and the scanned symbol to choose a new state and a head displacement in \(\{- 1,0,+1\}\); moves outside the endmarkers are forbidden. A missing transition rejects that branch. A word is accepted if some finite computation reaches an accepting state. Infinite nonaccepting branches do not count as acceptance. For a deterministic automaton there is at most one available transition in each state-symbol pair, and its unique infinite run, if any, rejects. There is no work tape, rewritable input, second head, stack, counter, randomness or advice. State count includes all control and halting states, but the bound is independent of word length and alphabet size. The target is existence of D for each A; computing D from A is not required to take polynomial time. Standard endmarker and stay-put conventions change these state bounds only by polynomial factors.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of universal constants C,k giving an equivalent 2DFA with at most \(C(n+1)^{k}\) states for every n-state 2NFA, or prove that no such constants exist. In the negative direction, every proposed polynomial bound must fail on some source automaton; all language comparisons concern words of every length.
cards.why: A principal unresolved measure of the succinctness provided by nondeterminism. It isolates the issue in finite-state machines, connects to nonuniform space complexity, and asks whether revisiting read-only data can replace a large internal record of possible computations.

importance.reason: The flagship state-complexity problem for two-way finite automata, open since 1978, with unusually direct connections between finite-state descriptions and logarithmic-space complexity.

progress.text: Sakoda and Sipser formulate the polynomial-state simulation questions and conjecture that nondeterminism cannot always be removed with polynomial cost.
The Geffert–Mereghetti–Pighizzini simulation gives \(n^{O(\log  n)}\) states for unary two-way NFAs. It leaves a polynomial-versus-superpolynomial gap.
Kapoutsis characterizes polynomial-state simulation on short inputs by \(\mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{L}\)/poly, carefully distinguishing input-length restrictions and advice.
Clerici Lorenzini and coauthors obtain a polynomial-size normal form for two-way NFAs accepting letter-bounded languages.
Guillon and coauthors give polynomial-size complementation using self-verifying 1-limited automata, with rewritable annotations; the unrestricted read-only determinization question remains open.

Adeogun and Kapoutsis’ revised preprint establishes a quadratic 2DFA state lower bound for one-way liveness and the resulting NFA-to-2DFA conversion. This does not exclude a polynomial determinization bound.
