cards.title: Tarski’s exponential function problem
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine which, on every first-order sentence \(\varphi\) in the language \(\{0,1,+,- ,\times ,<,\exp\}\), halts and correctly decides whether \(\varphi\) is true in \((R,0,1,+,- ,\times ,<,x\mapsto e^{x})\)?
cards.definitions: Sentences have finite syntax and no free variables. Terms are formed from variables, 0,1, the unary symbols − and exp, and binary + and ×; atomic formulas are equalities or strict inequalities of terms. Formulas use Boolean connectives and first-order quantifiers, all ranging over R. Equality has its usual logical interpretation. Inputs are finite parenthesized strings over a fixed finite alphabet, with variable indices written in binary; any fixed effectively interconvertible syntax encoding gives the same decidability question. No arbitrary real constants or oracles for real numbers are allowed. The symbol exp denotes the standard real exponential function on all of R, not a restricted function or an unspecified solution in another structure. There is no time or space bound beyond termination. A positive resolution must be unconditional, rather than assuming an unresolved transcendence conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.
cards.why: Locate a fundamental decidability boundary beyond polynomial real arithmetic, where exact reasoning interacts with transcendence.

importance.reason: A longstanding central question of real model theory with direct relevance to symbolic reasoning about exponential expressions. The explicit 2026 conditional result confirms continuing specialist interest without settling the unconditional target.

progress.text: Macintyre–Wilkie obtain conditional decidability from Schanuel’s conjecture, as recalled by the 2026 primary source.

context_blocks.text: First-order arithmetic over the real numbers can describe polynomial equalities, inequalities and quantifier alternation. Adding the exponential function permits expressions involving growth and decay that are unavailable in the polynomial language. The target is exact truth of every sentence, including cases in which a numerical approximation alone cannot distinguish equality from a very small nonzero quantity.

The syntax is finite even though the quantified domain is infinite. An algorithm receives a formula such as an existential statement about real solutions; it does not receive an arbitrary real constant as an infinitely long input. Conversely, the card imposes no polynomial running-time demand. An unconditional terminating algorithm of any complexity would answer it affirmatively.

cards.title: Continuous Skolem problem
cards.formal: Is there a Turing algorithm that, given any dimension \(d\ge 1\), rational matrix \(A\in Q^{d\times d}\), and rational column vectors \(b,c\in Q^{d}\), always halts and correctly decides whether \(c^{T}\exp (tA)b=0\) for some real \(t\ge 0\)?
cards.definitions: Every input rational is represented exactly by a signed binary integer numerator and a positive binary integer denominator. The dimension is part of the input and has no fixed upper bound. The matrix exponential is \(\exp (tA)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty} t^{j} A^{j}/j!\), and \(x(t)=\exp (tA)b\) is the unique real solution of \(x' (t)=Ax(t), x(0)=b\). The target is the hyperplane \(\{x:c^{T}x=0\}; c=0\) is allowed and gives an immediate yes instance. Time ranges over all finite nonnegative real numbers, not just rational or integer times. Equality is exact. A zero at \(t=0\) counts, as does a trajectory that is identically in the hyperplane. If the scalar function approaches zero only in the limit \(t\to \infty\), the answer is no unless it also has a finite zero. No promise of diagonalizability, simple eigenvalues, bounded dimension, stability, spectral separation, transverse intersection, or robust distance from the hyperplane is supplied. The requested algorithm is an ordinary finite-input decision procedure without real-number or number-theoretic oracles; no complexity upper bound is prescribed. This card retains the rational-data version; some cited work treats the more general real-algebraic-data version.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an unconditional always-halting decision algorithm for every rational input, or prove that no such Turing algorithm exists. A conditional procedure assuming Schanuel’s conjecture, a solver for a fixed low dimension, a procedure that may run forever on some inputs, or a certified answer only under a nonzero distance promise is partial progress. An undecidability theorem allowing more general coefficients or nonlinear differential equations must be reduced to this rational linear model to refute the proposition.
cards.why: A minimal exact reachability question for continuous linear systems whose decidability remains unresolved, linking algorithmic verification to real analysis, transcendence and effective number theory.

importance.reason: A fundamental boundary for verification of linear differential systems, with a precisely finite rational input and an unrestricted exact reachability target.

references.authors: Piotr Bacik; Toghrul Karimov; Florian Luca; Joris Nieuwveld; Joël Ouaknine; David Purser; James Worrell

cards.status_note: No unconditional decision procedure or undecidability proof for this rational linear model was found through 11 September 2026. Bounded conditional results, low-order recurrence algorithms, approximate/robust verification and nonlinear-system hardness do not settle the unbounded exact question.

context_blocks.text: Linear differential equations have explicit matrix-exponential solutions, yet an explicit formula does not automatically decide whether a trajectory hits an exact target. The scalar output \(c^{T}x(t)\) may combine growth, decay, polynomial factors and oscillations. The matrix and vectors are finite rational data, while the possible hitting time is an unrestricted real number. This makes the question a basic test of what exact verification can decide even for linear continuous dynamics.

Numerical proximity is insufficient. The one-dimensional system \(x' =- x, x(0)=1\) has output \(e^{- t}\), which becomes arbitrarily small but never reaches zero. Conversely, a zero need not be accompanied by a sign change: the polynomial \((t- 1)^{2}\) touches zero and returns to positive values. Such a polynomial is itself an output of a rational nilpotent linear system. A grid search or a sign-change detector can therefore miss the distinction required by the card.

Simple degenerate cases can be removed exactly. The initial-time condition is \(c^{T}b=0\). By the Cayley–Hamilton theorem, the scalar function is identically zero precisely when \(c^{T}A^{j} b=0\) for \(j=0,\ldots ,d- 1\). These are finite rational calculations. Outside that case, analyticity ensures only finitely many zeros in each bounded interval, but neither a uniform numerical precision nor a final time beyond all zeros follows from that finiteness statement.

Spectral decomposition writes the output as a sum of polynomial multiples of exponentials, with conjugate terms combining into real sine and cosine expressions. The imaginary parts of eigenvalues give oscillation frequencies. Repeated eigenvalues can introduce polynomial factors. Competing terms can nearly cancel at very large times, so a proof that the long-term behaviour is simple enough to inspect is a substantive part of an unbounded decision procedure.

Chonev, Ouaknine and Worrell prove decidability of the bounded Continuous Skolem problem assuming Schanuel’s conjecture. That conjecture gives a transcendence-degree lower bound for complex numbers linearly independent over the rationals together with their exponentials. Their algorithm uses it to handle possible tangential zeros. The result does not supply an unconditional bounded-time procedure, and a bounded-time procedure alone does not supply a stopping criterion for checking all \(t\ge 0\).

The same paper reduces certain unbounded spectral cases to the bounded problem, including the case with at most one rationally independent frequency. A separate recurrent-reachability result decides whether a solution of differential order at most seven has infinitely many zeros and gives an effective last-zero bound when it has only finitely many. Combined with the conditional bounded solver, this yields conditional decisions in that low-order regime. Infinite recurrence and existence of even one zero are nevertheless different questions.

The broader algebraic-coefficient formulations reveal a connection with effective Diophantine approximation: handling multiple independent oscillations can entail computing quantities measuring unusually good rational approximations to algebraic numbers. Those implications are evidence of the mathematical obstacles, not undecidability proofs. Their precise dimension thresholds belong to the coefficient model of the cited theorem; this card does not automatically transfer them to the rational-matrix representation fixed above.

Platzer and Qian’s 2025 completeness theorem for compact initial-value problems concerns specified open safety and liveness properties. Its discussion explicitly identifies exact hyperplane reachability as an obstacle to replacing those topological conditions by arbitrary closed targets. A proof system that certifies entry into an open neighbourhood need not decide whether the trajectory touches its central hyperplane. This distinction matters when interpreting advances in numerical verification as progress on exact decision questions.

The July 2026 survey by Bacik and coauthors places the continuous problem alongside discrete recurrence questions, while emphasizing differences in technique. Sampling only integer times gives a sequence but changes the question: for example, a rational rotation system can have output cos t and reach zero at \(\pi /2\). The card asks whether any real hitting time exists, so discrete-time zero testing cannot simply replace the continuous analysis.

cards.definitions: Use atoms \(p_{i}\) and their distinct dual literals \(p_{i}^{\perp}\) for integers \(i\ge 0\). Formulas are finite syntax trees generated by \(A ::= p_{i} | p_{i}^{\perp} | 1 | \perp  | (A\otimes A) |\) (A⅋A) | !A | ?A. A sequent \(\Gamma\) is a finite multiset of formulas; commas denote multiset union, retaining multiplicity. The following rules, read from premises to conclusion, define derivations. Identity has no premises and concludes \(\vdash p_{i},p_{i}^{\perp}\). The unit rule has no premises and concludes \(\vdash 1\). Tensor takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\) and \(\vdash \Delta ,B\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,\Delta ,A\otimes B\). Par takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A,B\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\)⅋B. The other unit rule takes \(\vdash \Gamma\) to \(\vdash \Gamma ,\perp\). Dereliction takes \(\vdash \Gamma ,A\) to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Weakening takes \(\vdash \Gamma\) to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Contraction takes \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A,?A to \(\vdash \Gamma\),?A. Promotion takes \(\vdash\)?\(\Gamma ,A\) to \(\vdash\)?\(\Gamma ,!A\), where every formula in ?\(\Gamma\) has outermost symbol ?. Contexts may be empty, and all displayed formula and context choices are arbitrary subject to these conditions. A derivation is a finite rooted tree whose leaves are the two nullary rules and whose internal nodes are instances of the other rules. There are no further rules; exchange is implicit in multisets. This is the cut-free presentation of classical commutative MELL, whose usual cut rule is admissible. Inputs explicitly list formula trees with constructor delimiters and binary atom indices; malformed strings are rejected. Formulas contain neither additives nor quantifiers, and there is just one pair of exponential modalities ! and ?.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the provable sequents of this calculus form a decidable language, or prove that no algorithm can decide that language. A procedure that terminates only on provable sequents does not establish decidability.

context_blocks.text: Linear logic treats assumptions as resources whose occurrences matter. An ordinary assumption cannot automatically be copied or discarded. For example, the resource-reading of \(p\to p\otimes p\) asks for two copies from one and is unavailable in general; marking the input !p permits reuse. MELL keeps multiplicative composition together with these reuse modalities.

The rules make each proposed finite proof checkable. That does not by itself make provability decidable: searching through larger proofs will eventually find a proof when one exists, but need not terminate when none exists. The question asks for a single procedure that also gives a terminating negative answer.

The restrictions on contraction and promotion are part of the problem. Allowing unrestricted contraction gives a different logic, and adding additive connectives or several interacting subexponential modalities changes the decidability boundary. A published 2015 decidability argument was challenged in Straßburger’s 2019 paper, which identifies gaps and separates MELL from its decidable relevant variant.

Branching vector addition systems describe trees of computations with nonnegative integer resources. Their general reachability problem is inter-reducible with MELL provability. The 2025 result in the original reference establishes decidability for two-dimensional systems, so its dimension restriction cannot be omitted.

Status update: the July 2026 preprint claims decidability of general branching vector addition systems and explicitly states that MELL provability follows. This reaches the full decision question, unlike the earlier low-dimensional result. This card records the claim with uncertain status because its proof has not been independently verified here.

cards.title: Unconditional decidability of exact time-bounded CTMDP reachability
cards.formal: Is there an unconditional terminating algorithm that, for every finite rational-rate continuous-time Markov decision process with an absorbing state \(\mathrm{good}\), rational deadline \(T>0\) and rational threshold vector \(r\), decides whether \[\forall s\in\{1,\ldots,n\},\quad \sup_{\pi\in\Pi_T}\Pr_s^\pi[\text{reach }\mathrm{good}\text{ by time }T]>r_s,\] where \(\Pi_T\) consists of the measurable timed positional policies defined below?
cards.definitions: The input lists a finite state set \(S=\{1,\ldots,n\}\sqcup\{\mathrm{good}\}\), with \(n\ge1\); a nonempty finite action set \(A_{s}\) for each state; nonnegative rational rates \(q(s,a,t)\) for \(t\ne s\); \(T\in\mathbb{Q}_{>0}\); and \(r\in([0,1]\cap\mathbb{Q})^{n}\). Integers and rational numerators/positive denominators are binary encoded. All rates out of good are zero, and the diagonal generator entry is \(q(s,a,s)=- \sum_{t\ne s}q(s,a,t)\). A decision vector d chooses one action \(d(s)\in A_{s}\) at each state. A policy is a Lebesgue-measurable map \(\pi :[0,T]\to \prod _{s} A_{s}\): at elapsed time u in state s the instantaneous generator row is \(q(s,\pi (u)(s),\cdot )\). Actions may change while the process remains in the same state, not only at jumps. Policies are deterministic and may depend on time and current state, with no computability restriction. For a fixed policy and initial state s, its probability law is the finite-state inhomogeneous Markov jump law with this bounded measurable generator. Equivalently its row distribution \(\rho _{s}(u)\) is the unique absolutely continuous solution of \(\rho _{s}(0)=e_{s}\) and \(\rho _{s}' (u)=\rho _{s}(u)Q^{\pi (u)}\) for almost every u. Bounded rates ensure nonexplosion. Since good is absorbing, the probability of reaching it at some time in \([0,T]\) equals \(\rho _{s}(T)_{\mathrm{good}}\). The supremum is taken over all such policies separately for each initial state. This defines the value without an attainment assumption; the source also proves existence of an optimal piecewise-constant timed positional policy. The decision uses strict > in every coordinate, so equality to any threshold requires NO. The algorithm is a deterministic Turing machine that halts with the correct YES/NO result on every valid encoding; there is no requested complexity bound and no number-theoretic oracle or unproved premise. Invalid encodings may be rejected.

cards.definitions: A \(d\)-VASS has a finite nonempty control-state set \(Q\) and a finite transition set \(E\subseteq Q\times\mathbb Z^d\times Q\). A configuration is \((q,x)\in Q\times\mathbb N^d\), where \(\mathbb N\) includes zero. A transition \((q,a,q^{\prime})\) takes \((q,x)\) to \((q^{\prime},x+a)\) exactly when every coordinate of \(x+a\) is nonnegative. There are no zero tests, counter resets, unrestricted signed counters, stacks or fractional updates. An instance gives \(Q,E\) and source and target configurations; reachability asks for a finite transition sequence between them, possibly of length zero. For the target \(d=7\) is fixed, but the control graph, vectors and endpoint configurations are inputs. They are listed explicitly. Every integer magnitude in a displacement or endpoint is unary, with a separate sign where necessary; state identifiers use a finite binary encoding. Let \(e_0(n)=n\) and \(e_{j+1}(n)=2^{e_j(n)}\). An elementary time bound is bounded by \(e_k(n^c+c)\) for fixed nonnegative integer \(k\) and positive integer \(c\). Define \(T(0)=1\), \(T(h+1)=2^{T(h)}\). The class \(\mathrm{TOWER}\) consists of languages decidable by deterministic Turing machines in time \(O(T(f(n)))\) for some elementary-time computable nonnegative integer function \(f\). A many-one reduction from a binary language \(K\) to VASS reachability is a total computable function mapping each input string to a valid VASS instance, preserving yes and no answers. Elementary-time reductions must obey one elementary time bound for each fixed source language. TOWER-hardness quantifies over every language in TOWER; it does not additionally assert that the target problem belongs to TOWER.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of TOWER-hardness in exactly the stated seven-counter, unary-encoded model and reduction convention. Alternatively prove in Lean that this problem is not TOWER-hard under those reductions. An elementary algorithm would imply a negative answer, but the target does not require that stronger conclusion. Results using eight counters or additional signed counters do not establish the required lower bound.

context_blocks.text: The original 2025 question asks whether the known eight-counter hardness can be attained in a lower dimension. This is exactly captured by testing seven counters: a lower-dimensional VASS can be padded with permanently zero counters, without changing reachability.

Czerwiński and Orlikowski prove TOWER-hardness already with eight counters and unary displacement encoding. Their result therefore cannot be explained solely by exponentially succinct binary counter values. The elementary reduction convention is significant for this nonelementary complexity class.

A fixed-height tower, such as a double or triple exponential, is an elementary bound. TOWER allows the tower height itself to grow with the input. Hardness for every fixed-height exponential class does not on its own supply the single TOWER-hardness statement.

The 2026 work on VASS extended with signed integer counters reports the ordinary three-counter reachability problem as elementary and the ordinary TOWER lower bound as known in dimension eight. Its new three-counter hardness counts only the nonnegative counters and permits additional unrestricted integer counters. Those extra counters are absent from the present model.

The number of counters stays fixed but the finite control graph can grow. This differs from fixing the entire VASS and varying only its endpoints. It also differs from requiring a long run in a particular example: a complexity lower bound must reduce every problem in the hardness class.

The source separately discusses geometric dimension, defined using the span of cycle effects. That structural parameter is not substituted for the seven actual nonnegative counters in this card; its associated question remains a distinct direction.

cards.definitions: The input dimension is an integer \(d\geq1\). A \(d\)-dimensional branching vector addition system with states (\(d\)-BVASS) has a finite nonempty state set \(Q\) and finite rules \((S,a,q)\), where \(S\subseteq Q\), \(a\in\mathbb Z^d\) and \(q\in Q\). A configuration \(q(x)\) consists of a state \(q\) and vector \(x\in\mathbb N^d\). A rule with \(S=\{q_1,\ldots,q_k\}\) combines one configuration \(q_i(x_i)\) for each input state into \(q(a+x_1+\cdots+x_k)\), provided all coordinates of this output are nonnegative. All child configurations must themselves have nonnegative coordinates. Input states in one rule are distinct, following the source’s set convention. When \(S\) is empty, the rule supplies the initial configuration \(q(a)\) if \(a\geq0\) coordinatewise. A derivation is a finite rooted tree: each node uses one rule, has exactly its rule’s specified children, and its label is obtained by the preceding sum. Leaves therefore use empty-input rules. A target is reachable if some such tree has that target as root. Derivations may use the same rule any finite number of times; there is no global stock of initial tokens shared between different branches. The number of children and the dimension are unbounded input parameters. States, rules, child-state sets and target are listed explicitly, with signed binary integers for displacement coordinates and binary nonnegative target coordinates. There are no equality or zero tests, resets, counter multiplication, probability or additional acceptance conditions. Decidability means one deterministic Turing machine that halts and answers correctly on every valid finite encoding, with no running-time bound requested.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating algorithm for the stated arbitrary-dimensional finite-tree reachability problem, or prove in Lean that it is undecidable. A dimension-dependent result covering only some fixed dimensions, a coverability algorithm, or a procedure that terminates only on reachable targets does not decide this problem. Finite derivation trees must satisfy every branch and every exact target coordinate.

context_blocks.text: A unary rule follows one computation, while a branching rule combines completed subcomputations by adding their counter vectors. For example, in one dimension, initial rules yielding \(p(2)\) and \(q(3)\) together with a zero-displacement rule from \(\{p,q\}\) to \(r\) derive \(r(5)\). Both child computations are required.

Ordinary VASS are the fragment using only initial and unary rules. Their reachability is decidable. Branching changes paths into finite derivation trees, so ordinary reachability decidability does not automatically extend to the system in this card.

Bizière, Hilaire, Leroux and Sutre prove decidability in dimension two in 2025. They obtain an effectively computable semilinear description of the reachable set: a finite union, for each state, of sets consisting of a base vector plus arbitrary nonnegative integer combinations of finitely many period vectors.

The paper explicitly leaves reachability open in arbitrary dimension. It also cautions that its two-dimensional procedure does not provide a complexity upper bound. Decidability in every input dimension is therefore the main target here, rather than an optimization of the two-dimensional running time.

Reachability requires exactly the requested counter vector. Coverability would allow a vector above it coordinatewise and can discard information crucial to exact reachability. Similarly, a derivation that leaves a branch unresolved is not a valid witness.

Since every finite proposed tree can be checked, positive instances have finite verifiable witnesses. This alone gives no way to halt on every negative instance. The question is precisely whether an always-terminating decision procedure exists.

A unary rule follows one computation, while a branching rule combines completed subcomputations by adding their counter vectors. For example, in one dimension, initial rules yielding \(p(2)\) and \(q(3)\) together with a zero-displacement rule from \(\{p,q\}\) to \(r\) derive \(r(5)\). Both child computations are required.

Ordinary VASS are the fragment using only initial and unary rules. Their reachability is decidable. Branching changes paths into finite derivation trees, so ordinary reachability decidability does not automatically extend to the system in this card.

Bizière, Hilaire, Leroux and Sutre prove decidability in dimension two in 2025. They obtain an effectively computable semilinear description of the reachable set: a finite union, for each state, of sets consisting of a base vector plus arbitrary nonnegative integer combinations of finitely many period vectors.

The paper explicitly leaves reachability open in arbitrary dimension. It also cautions that its two-dimensional procedure does not provide a complexity upper bound. Decidability in every input dimension is therefore the main target here, rather than an optimization of the two-dimensional running time.

Reachability requires exactly the requested counter vector. Coverability would allow a vector above it coordinatewise and can discard information crucial to exact reachability. Similarly, a derivation that leaves a branch unresolved is not a valid witness.

Since every finite proposed tree can be checked, positive instances have finite verifiable witnesses. This alone gives no way to halt on every negative instance. The question is precisely whether an always-terminating decision procedure exists.

cards.formal: For every integer \(d\geq1\) and finite set \(V\subseteq\mathbb Z^d\), does there exist a constant \(C_V\geq1\) such that every reachable pair \(s,t\in\mathbb N^d\) has a run of length at most \(C_V(\|s\|_1+\|t\|_1)\)?
cards.why: The conjecture isolates whether unbounded shortest-run growth is caused by changing the transition system or can already occur within one fixed system. This structural distinction is fundamental for understanding the complexity of reachability when only numerical configurations vary.

cards.definitions: A vector addition system (VAS) is the finite set \(V\) of allowed displacement vectors; there is no control-state graph. Its configurations are vectors in \(\mathbb N^d\), where zero coordinates are allowed. A run from \(s\) to \(t\) is a finite sequence \(c_0=s,c_1,\ldots,c_m=t\) with \(c_i\in\mathbb N^d\) and \(c_i-c_{i-1}\in V\) for all \(1\leq i\leq m\). Its length is the number \(m\) of transitions, not the magnitude of its largest counter. Empty runs of length zero are permitted, so every configuration reaches itself. The norm is \(\|x\|_1=\sum_{j=1}^d |x_j|\). The whole system, including its dimension, number of updates and their integer magnitudes, is fixed before \(C_V\) is chosen. The constant must then work for all source and target vectors in that system. There are no tests except the requirement that updated coordinates remain nonnegative. No algorithm for computing \(C_V\), finding a short run or deciding reachability in a specified time is required. The bound measures numerical endpoint magnitudes, not their binary encoding lengths. Choosing another fixed norm would change only the system-dependent constant. The non-strict inequality includes the zero-to-zero empty run; the source’s strict wording otherwise has an artificial zero-endpoint exception. For positive endpoint norm sums, strict and non-strict versions are equivalent after enlarging \(C_V\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal system-dependent linear witness bound. Alternatively give one explicit finite VAS \(V\) and prove in Lean that for every \(C\geq1\) there are reachable endpoints \(s,t\) for which every run has length greater than \(C(\|s\|_1+\|t\|_1)\). Letting the update system vary with \(C\), using binary bit length instead of endpoint magnitudes, or merely displaying one unnecessarily long run does not refute the proposition.

context_blocks.text: For a one-counter system allowing increments and decrements by one, the shortest run has length \(|s-t|\), which meets the desired bound. The conjecture says that more involved interactions among a fixed finite collection of counters never force a superlinear shortest detour as the endpoints grow.

Jecker’s source formulates a short-witness conjecture, despite the entry’s broad complexity title. The present title and criterion expose that actual mathematical claim. The choice of a non-strict bound simply handles the permitted empty run at zero rather than turning a wording defect into a counterexample.

A fixed system can contain very large displacement constants, and the allowed multiplicative constant may be correspondingly large. Exhibiting a family of larger and larger systems with hard instances would not disprove this conjecture: a counterexample must keep one finite update set for every endpoint pair.

The 2024 fixed-VASS paper discusses Jecker’s conjecture and reports that its lower-bound constructions give no evidence against it. It proves PSPACE-hardness for a fixed five-counter VASS when initial counter values are binary and explains the PSPACE upper-bound implication of the proposed short-path property.

There is no conflict between a path linear in endpoint magnitudes and a high complexity measured in binary digits. A counter value with a short binary encoding can be exponentially larger than that encoding, so writing out such a path may already take exponentially many steps.

A positive answer would constrain how much of the infinite configuration graph is needed to witness each reachable pair once the system is fixed. It would not make all VAS reachability uniformly linear-time, since the constant carries the entire fixed system and the target is existential.

cards.title: Elementary-time reachability for one-dimensional grammar-controlled VAS
cards.formal: Can reachability for one-dimensional grammar-controlled vector addition systems be decided in elementary deterministic time? More explicitly, do there exist fixed integers \(h\geq0\), \(c\geq1\) and one deterministic Turing machine deciding every instance of bit length \(n\) within \(O(e_h(n^c+c))\) steps, where \(e_0(z)=z\) and \(e_{j+1}(z)=2^{e_j(z)}\)?
cards.why: This asks whether one nonnegative counter interacting with context-free control can still be analyzed within a fixed-height exponential time bound. It separates existence of a decision algorithm from a meaningful complexity boundary and tests whether enormous reachable sets force equally enormous decision time.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. General 1-GVAS decidability is established by the later Bizière–Czerwiński paper, superseding the survey’s provisional wording. The selected elementary-time question is explicitly left open there and remains distinguished from the 2026 index-dependent thin-grammar bound. These proof texts were checked for statements and scope, not independently formalized in Lean.

cards.definitions: A one-dimensional grammar-controlled vector addition system (1-GVAS) is a finite context-free grammar with nonterminal set \(N\), distinguished start nonterminal \(S\), and finitely many productions \(X\to\alpha\) with \(X\in N\) and \(\alpha\) a finite sequence of nonterminals and integer terminals. There is no restriction on recursion or on the number of nonterminals occurring in a sentential form. The empty right-hand side is allowed. A terminal word \(a_1\cdots a_m\), with \(a_i\in\mathbb Z\), is generated when a finite sequence of production applications transforms \(S\) into that word. Given starting and target counters \(s,t\in\mathbb N\), the word witnesses reachability if \(s+\sum_{i=1}^j a_i\geq0\) for every \(0\leq j\leq m\), and \(s+\sum_{i=1}^m a_i=t\). The terminal order is the left-to-right order in the generated word, not the order in which productions were expanded. An empty terminal word witnesses exactly \(s=t\), if generated. There is one nonnegative counter, no test for zero except through inability to take a negative update, and no restriction on stack depth implicit in the grammar. The whole grammar, both counters and all production sequences are explicit inputs. Integer terminals use signed binary encodings, and \(s,t\) use binary nonnegative encodings; their digits and every symbol occurrence contribute to input length. The tower height \(h\), polynomial exponent \(c\), hidden multiplicative constant and program must be independent of the grammar and both counters. Correctness concerns exact reachability, not coverability or an approximation of the reachable set.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a deterministic decision algorithm with one fixed elementary time bound for all instances, or prove in Lean that no elementary-time decider exists. A bound whose tower height depends on the input grammar or a theorem only for structurally restricted grammars does not establish the positive answer. The output need only decide reachability; it need not print a potentially enormous derivation.

context_blocks.text: The 2024 survey asks broadly for the complexity of 1-GVAS reachability and at that time describes an unconfirmed decidability argument. Editorial specialization: this card selects the elementary-time boundary, explicitly conjectured in the subsequent complete decidability paper. It does not claim that answering this boundary alone determines the exact complexity class.

The counter constrains prefixes, not just the final sum. A generated word \((-1),1\) has total effect zero but is invalid from counter zero. A word \(1,(-1)\) with the same total effect is valid from zero. A grammar’s ordering constraints and counter nonnegativity therefore interact.

Bizière and Czerwiński’s November 2024 paper proves reachability decidable for general 1-GVAS. It constructs a thin grammar with the same reachability relation. A nonterminal is thin if no derivation from it can produce a sentential form containing two copies of that same nonterminal; a grammar is thin when all its nonterminals are thin.

Theorem 2 and Corollary 3 show that an elementary algorithm for thin grammars would imply an elementary algorithm for all 1-GVAS. Thin grammars are already a subclass, so the elementary-time question has the same yes/no answer in the two settings. This is a preservation theorem for the complexity boundary, not an existing elementary bound.

The February 2026 thin-GVAS preprint improves an upper bound parameterized by its structural index and continues to leave an elementary upper bound open. Since that index can grow with the grammar, its stated fast-growing bound does not supply a fixed-height exponential tower for every input.

The survey illustrates small grammars with extremely large finite reachable sets. Such cardinality alone does not prove a matching lower bound for deciding whether one supplied counter value is reachable. Conversely, merely finding short derivations in a collection of examples does not give a uniform decision algorithm.

cards.title: Shortest runs in 3-D VASS
cards.formal: Is there no single-exponential bound on shortest runs in binary-encoded three-dimensional vector addition systems with states? Precisely, is it true that for every integer \(k\ge 1\), every real \(C>0\) and every \(N_{0}\ge 1\), there is a reachable instance I of encoding length \(N\ge N_{0}\) whose shortest source-to-target run has more than \(2^{C N^{k}}\) transitions?
cards.why: Isolates how much witness complexity three unbounded counters can force. Resolving the single-exponential threshold would clarify the gap between low-dimensional reachability and the much more expensive behavior possible when the number of counters grows.
cards.status_note: Original question and the 2025 explicit binary formulation checked, with subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026. The July 2026 preprint improves the upper bound but does not resolve whether single-exponential shortest runs always suffice. No resolution of that threshold was located; proofs were not independently verified.

progress.text: Czerwiński asks for a three-counter shortest-run lower bound beyond the exponential scale; the upper-bound discussion is historical.
The ICALP paper obtains a triple-exponential shortest-run upper bound and 2-EXPSPACE membership. Section 7 retains the question whether single-exponential runs suffice for binary 3-VASS.

Chen and coauthors state a doubly-exponential shortest-run upper bound and EXPSPACE membership in a new preprint. This review checked the model and theorem statements, not the full proof; the result does not supply the requested super-single-exponential lower bound.

cards.definitions: A three-dimensional vector addition system with states (3-VASS) is a finite set Q of control states and a finite transition set \(T\subseteq Q\times \mathbb{Z} ^{3}\times Q\). A configuration is \((q,u)\) with \(q\in Q\) and \(u\in \mathbb{N} ^{3}\), where \(\mathbb{N}\) includes zero. A transition \((q,a,q' )\) sends \((q,u)\) to \((q' ,u+a)\) only when every coordinate of \(u+a\) is nonnegative. There are no zero tests or counter bounds. A reachability instance I consists of Q,T and two configurations s,t. It is reachable if some finite sequence of enabled transitions sends s to t. Its shortest-run length \(\ell\)\((I)\) is the minimum number of transitions in such a sequence; the empty run is allowed, and \(\ell\)\((I)=0\) when \(s=t\). Unreachable instances are excluded from the quantified claim. N is the bit length of an explicit description: states are numbered, the transition list and the source and target are given explicitly, and all integer coordinates are written in signed binary (nonnegative binary for configurations), with delimiters and state indices included. Usual explicit binary-list encodings differ by polynomial factors, which do not affect existence of a \(2^{N^{O}(1)}\) bound. The dimension is always exactly three, while the number of states, transitions and counter magnitudes may grow. No finite-reachability-set promise or effective construction of the hard instances is required. The single-exponential convention and binary encoding follow the explicit later formulation in Section 7 of the 2025 source.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed unboundedness beyond every \(2^{C N^{k}}\), or refute it by proving that there are fixed \(C>0\) and integer \(k\ge 1\) for which every reachable binary 3-VASS instance I has \(\ell\)\((I)\le 2^{C |I|^{k}}\), after adjusting C to include the finitely many small sizes. A long run alone is insufficient: the lower bound concerns the shortest run between the chosen configurations. Neither a lower bound with a growing number of counters nor the mere existence of many reachable configurations establishes this target.

context_blocks.title: Three counters, infinitely many configurations
context_blocks.text: The control graph is finite, but each counter may become arbitrarily large. A transition can consume tokens from one counter and produce tokens in another, provided it never makes a counter negative. Reachability asks whether a target configuration can be obtained from a given start through legal transitions.

context_blocks.title: Why the binary encoding matters
context_blocks.text: Consider one state and the single transition \((- 1,+1,0)\), from counters \((2^{r},0,0)\) to \((0,2^{r},0)\). Every successful run has exactly \(2^{r}\) steps, although the instance uses only \(O(r)\) bits. This gives exponential length in the input description. The question asks whether shortest runs can exceed every bound \(2^{N^{k}}\), with fixed k, rather than merely whether exponential runs occur.

context_blocks.title: Shortest paths control witness size
context_blocks.text: A reachable target may have many very long runs leading to it. Only the minimum length is relevant here. A single-exponential shortest-run upper bound would allow the binary reachability problem to be decided in polynomial space, as the 2025 source explains. A lower bound on the number or largest size of reachable configurations is a different assertion.

context_blocks.title: The known upper bound has changed
context_blocks.text: The 2019 question mentioned a tower-type upper bound. The ICALP 2025 work gives a triple-exponential bound on shortest runs, and the July 2026 preprint states an improvement to a doubly-exponential bound. These upper bounds do not establish that any shortest run actually needs more than single-exponential length.

cards.title: Relative completeness of Kleene induction for the positive calculus of relations
cards.formal: Is every equation valid in binary relations with union, intersection, composition, converse, constants \(0,1,\top\), and reflexive-transitive closure derivable from all valid closure-free equations in these operations together with the Kleene algebra axioms and induction rules specified below?
cards.why: This asks whether standard induction for iteration remains complete when programs can also be intersected and reversed as binary relations. A positive theorem would give a principled relative proof calculus for graph reachability expressions; a negative result would isolate an additional law of relational iteration.
cards.status_note: The 2018 source poses relative axiomatization as an open direction, and the December 2025 paper continues to distinguish axiomatization questions from its decidable full-signature theory. This card explicitly fixes a closure-free full-signature base and finitary induction rules as the concrete editorial variant. No completeness or incompleteness theorem for that exact system was located in the bounded 13 September 2026 check.

importance.reason: A substantial algebraic completeness question for relational reachability, sharpening the distinction between deciding identities and explaining them through reusable finitary proof principles.

sentences: Expressions denote binary relations using positive operations, converse and finite-path closure.
The target asks whether every relationally valid equation follows from a specified proof system.
That system contains all valid closure-free equations and ordinary left and right Kleene induction.
The closure-free base is an explicit editorial choice that fixes interactions among the operations.
The later EXPSPACE validity algorithm and completeness of smaller fragments do not prove this relative-completeness claim.

cards.definitions: Expressions are finite terms over countably many relation variables using binary operations \(+\) (union), \(\cap\) (intersection), \(\cdot\) (composition), unary converse \((-)^{\circ}\), unary closure \((-)^*\), and constants \(0,1,\top\). On any set \(X\), variables denote arbitrary subsets of \(X\times X\). The constants denote the empty relation, the identity relation and \(X\times X\). Composition is \(R\cdot S=\{(x,z):\exists y\in X,\ (x,y)\in R\text{ and }(y,z)\in S\}\). Converse reverses each ordered pair. Closure is \(R^*=\bigcup_{n\geq0}R^n\), with \(R^0=1\) and \(R^{n+1}=R\cdot R^n\); it contains paths of every finite length, including zero. Complements and tests are absent. An equation is valid if it holds for every set \(X\), finite or infinite, and every assignment of its relation variables. Define \(u\leq v\) as the equation \(u+v=v\). The base axiom scheme consists of every valid equation whose expressions have no occurrence of \((-)^*\); it includes the interactions between union, intersection, converse and the constants. The Kleene algebra axioms make \((+,\cdot,0,1)\) an idempotent semiring: addition is associative, commutative and idempotent with identity zero; multiplication is associative with identity one, distributes over addition on both sides and has absorbing zero. The closure axioms are \(1+xx^*\leq x^*\) and \(1+x^*x\leq x^*\). The left induction rule infers \(x^*y\leq z\) from \(y+xz\leq z\); the right rule infers \(yx^*\leq z\) from \(y+zx\leq z\). Proofs are finite derivations using these schemes and rules, equality reflexivity, symmetry and transitivity, congruence for every operation, and uniform substitution of arbitrary expressions for variables. In particular, closure-bearing expressions may be substituted into closure-free axiom schemes. No other closure axiom, infinitary rule, relational-validity oracle for closure-bearing expressions or auxiliary operation is permitted.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that this specified derivation system proves every relationally valid equation. Alternatively exhibit a valid equation and prove in Lean that it is not derivable in this system, for example using a model of all the axioms that refutes it. Decidability of relational validity alone, or a complete axiomatization of a proper signature fragment, does not establish completeness of these particular rules.

context_blocks.text: The source asks for axiomatizations and suggests adding Kleene algebra axioms to a complete closure-free relational calculus. Editorial specification: this card uses all valid closure-free laws in the full positive signature as the base. This explicitly includes interactions between union and intersection rather than leaving the interface between separate axiom systems ambiguous.

Without the specified base and rules, asking for an axiomatization would be too loose: declaring every valid equation an axiom gives no structural explanation. The target instead asks whether ordinary finitary Kleene induction accounts for all additional identities created by closure once the closure-free theory is available.

Intersection requires the same pair of endpoints to satisfy two relational conditions. It cannot generally be pushed through composition: \(R\cdot(S\cap T)\subseteq (R\cdot S)\cap(R\cdot T)\), but the reverse inclusion can fail because the two right-hand paths may use different intermediate points. Such interactions make relational closure more subtle than independent word-language iteration.

The 2018 paper records complete axiomatizations for important smaller signatures and explains why finite axiomatization of representable allegories is already delicate without closure. The target here deliberately permits an infinite closure-free axiom scheme and asks for relative completeness, rather than promising a finite list of all relational axioms.

Nakamura’s December 2025 journal article proves EXPSPACE-completeness of validity for the full positive signature, including identity, top, converse and closure. Its final discussion still distinguishes axiomatizability from the decision procedure. Thus an effective validity test does not by itself verify the relative proof system specified here.

The same later article cites a finite axiomatization for identity-free Kleene lattices. That result omits operations present in this card. It is retained as a boundary of known completeness results, not generalized to the full signature.

cards.title: Word problem for the S-combinator
cards.formal: Is convertibility of closed S-combinator terms decidable? Let \(\mathcal{T}\) be the least set with \(S\in\mathcal{T}\) and \((uv)\in\mathcal{T}\) whenever \(u,v\in\mathcal{T}\). The sole rewrite rule, applicable inside any term context, is \[(((Sx)y)z)\longrightarrow ((xz)(yz)),\qquad x,y,z\in\mathcal{T}.\] Does there exist a deterministic algorithm that halts on every pair \(p,q\in\mathcal{T}\) and decides whether they are connected by a finite sequence of forward or backward applications of this rule?
cards.why: The S-only fragment retains duplication and nonterminating behavior with just one combinator. Its word problem tests whether symbolic equality becomes decidable after removing the other primitives of combinatory logic, beyond the already-known ability to recognize normalizing terms.
cards.status_note: The original RTA list and the 2023 primary Satellite account leave this convertibility problem open. A bounded later-literature check on 13 September 2026 did not find a decision or undecidability theorem. Normalization results do not resolve this target; no exhaustive present-day certification is claimed.

progress.text: Waldmann proves decidability of whether a closed S-term has a normal form, as recorded in the original list and the later Satellite account.
The Satellite account explicitly retains decidability of interconvertibility as an open question.

sentences: Closed S-terms are finite application trees using only the combinator S.
The rule sends S applied to x, y and z to the application of xz to yz, and can be used inside any subterm.
The word problem asks whether two such trees are connected by finitely many forward or backward rule applications.
Normalization is decidable for this fragment, but the 2023 source still leaves general convertibility open.
A solution supplies a Lean-checked decidability or undecidability proof covering nonnormalizing terms as well.

context_blocks.text: RTA Problem 97, attributed to Barendregt in 1975, asks for this exact word problem on ground terms built solely from S and application. Rule direction can be reversed during conversion, even though operational reduction has a forward direction.

The 2023 Satellite account reports decidability of normalization and of head-reduction termination for this fragment, but explicitly leaves interconvertibility open. It also distinguishes convertibility from equality of certain infinitary semantic trees.

source_consolidations.note: The S-only source distinguishes weak convertibility of closed terms from normalization and head-reduction termination. It also records that equal Berarducci trees need not imply convertibility, so that infinite-tree semantics alone does not decide the retained word problem.

definitions: A term is a finite ordered binary application tree whose leaves are all the one constant \(S\). Application is not associative; by convention \(uvw\) abbreviates \(((uv)w)\). There are no object-language variables, other combinator constants, lambda abstractions, types or infinitary terms. The letters \(x,y,z\) in the rule range over entire closed terms.

A one-hole context is built from a hole \(\square\) by repeatedly forming \((Ct)\) or \((tC)\), where \(t\in\mathcal{T}\) and \(C\) is a one-hole context. Write \(C[t]\) for replacing its hole by \(t\). A forward step is exactly \(C[(((Sx)y)z)]\to C[((xz)(yz))]\). Both appearances of \(z\) on the right are copies of the same finite tree.

Terms \(p,q\) are convertible when there exist \(m\geq0\) and closed terms \(t_0=p,\ldots,t_m=q\) such that, for each \(i<m\), either \(t_i\to t_{i+1}\) or \(t_{i+1}\to t_i\). This is the reflexive, symmetric and transitive closure of the contextual rewrite relation. No extensionality, eta law or identification merely by an infinitary semantic tree is added.

The two input trees are written explicitly, for example using prefix encodings \(\operatorname{enc}(S)=0\) and \(\operatorname{enc}(uv)=1\operatorname{enc}(u)\operatorname{enc}(v)\) with a delimiter between the two trees. A decider is one deterministic Turing machine halting on all valid pairs and outputting yes exactly on convertible pairs; malformed descriptions can be rejected. No time bound and no normalization promise are imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: A complete Lean-checked proof of decidability for all pairs of closed S-terms under this conversion relation, or a Lean-checked proof of undecidability. Deciding whether individual terms have normal forms, deciding only pairs of normalizing terms, or comparing a coarser semantic invariant is insufficient.

Defined finite tree encoding, arbitrary subterm rewriting, bidirectional finite conversion, absence of additional equality axioms, and total decidability without a normalization promise. Preserved the consolidated Satellite source and separated its normalization result from the unresolved word problem.

cards.title: Exact finite-iteration reachability for Bellman operators
cards.formal: Is there an algorithm that, given a finite rational Markov decision process with no end components, its reachability Bellman operator \(\Phi:[0,1]^d\to[0,1]^d\), and rational vectors \(s,t\in[0,1]^d\), decides whether \(\Phi^n(s)=t\) for some integer \(n\geq0\)? The dimension is unbounded and several actions may be available, including several actions tight at the fixed point.
cards.why: Exact attainment is a sharper verification property than convergence of value iteration. Resolving it for Bellman operators would locate how much decidability survives the structured maxima of affine probability updates, beyond the already solved two-dimensional and single-policy cases.
cards.status_note: The 2025 primary paper explicitly leaves arbitrary-dimensional BOR open under its no-end-component promise. A bounded 13 September 2026 later-work check did not locate a resolution. The source’s general-semigroup remark is retained only within its Bellman/product-family setting; general matrix-semigroup undecidability is not treated as a solution.

progress.text: Varonka and Watanabe prove decidability for non-fixed-point targets, comparable starting vectors, unique tight actions and all two-dimensional instances; unrestricted dimension with multiple tight actions remains open.

sentences: The input describes a finite rational Markov decision process and two rational value vectors.
Its Bellman operator updates each coordinate by the best available affine probability expression.
The question asks whether exact iteration reaches the target vector after finitely many steps.
The source assumes no end components but allows several actions tight at the fixed point.
Convergence and the known two-dimensional decision procedure do not settle the general finite-attainment problem.

cards.definitions: A Markov decision process (MDP) has finitely many states, a designated target sink \(g\), and a finite set of available actions at each other state. Sinks have no actions. Each available action \(a\) at state \(i\) has rational probabilities \(p(i,a,j)\geq0\), summing to one over all states \(j\). An end component consists of a nonempty state subset \(U\) and a nonempty choice of available actions at each state in \(U\), such that all their positive-probability successors stay in \(U\), and the directed graph of these chosen positive-probability transitions is strongly connected. The input promise excludes all such end components. Let \(Q=\{1,\ldots,d\}\) consist of the non-target states from which a path of positive-probability transitions to \(g\) exists. Other non-target states have reachability value zero and are omitted from the vector coordinates. For every \(i\in Q\), define \(L_{i,a}(x)=p(i,a,g)+\sum_{j\in Q}p(i,a,j)x_j\) and \(\Phi(x)_i=\max_{a\in\mathrm{Act}(i)}L_{i,a}(x)\). Each such action set is nonempty. The maximum is coordinatewise: different coordinates may attain it at different actions. All probabilities, the explicit transition tables and the vectors \(s,t\) are inputs with binary rational encodings; \(d\) is the number of retained coordinates. Iteration is \(\Phi^0(s)=s\) and \(\Phi^{n+1}(s)=\Phi(\Phi^n(s))\). Equality means equality of every rational coordinate at one finite iteration, without a numerical tolerance. An action is tight at a fixed point \(u\) when \(L_{i,a}(u)=u_i\). The no-end-component promise gives a unique fixed point and convergence of all iterations to it; no uniqueness of tight actions is assumed. A decision procedure is one deterministic Turing machine halting on every valid input; no time bound or bound on the witnessing \(n\) is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating exact reachability algorithm on this entire promised class, or prove in Lean that the decision problem on this class is undecidable. Merely computing or approximating the fixed point, deciding whether a limit equals the target, or solving unrestricted matrix-semigroup reachability does not decide finite-iteration reachability of the specified Bellman operator.

context_blocks.text: Convergence does not imply that an iteration ever attains its limit. For \(\Phi(x)=(x+1)/2\), starting at zero produces \(1-2^{-n}\); the fixed point one is approached forever and never reached at a finite step. This scalar map is a valid reachability Bellman operator for a state that either repeats or reaches the target, each with probability one half.

The source proves decidability in arbitrary dimension when the requested vector differs from the unique fixed point. It also handles a fixed-point target when the starting vector is comparable to it coordinatewise, meaning all coordinates lie on the same side of their respective target values.

In dimension two, the paper resolves the remaining incomparable case as well. Thus the outstanding general question permits higher-dimensional starts with some coordinates above and others below their target values, and permits several tight actions.

If every coordinate has a unique tight action, the local fixed-point dynamics reduce to powers of one rational matrix. Proposition 27 gives a finite bound for testing whether these powers send a difference vector to zero. With multiple tight actions, the maximizing matrix can change during the iteration.

The associated matrices have nonnegative entries and row sums at most one. Their available rows can be chosen independently at each coordinate, forming the source’s product family. The resulting map takes coordinatewise maxima; it does not permit an arbitrary favorable sequence of matrices irrespective of those maxima.

The exclusion of end components is part of the target, not an incidental computational convenience. An MDP transformation preserving the least fixed point need not preserve the exact sequence of iterates from a supplied vector. General piecewise-affine undecidability results therefore require an actual reduction into this promised Bellman class before they could answer the question.

cards.title: Computable one-step normalization for finite confluent term rewriting
cards.formal: Does every finite, full, confluent first-order term-rewriting system \(R\) have a total computable one-step strategy \(F_R\) that reaches a normal form from every term having a normal form? The strategy depends only on the current term, may depend on the whole fixed system \(R\), and must also return a step on terms that have no normal form.
cards.why: This asks whether semantic uniqueness of outcomes guarantees an effective local way to reach an outcome whenever one exists. It isolates the interaction of confluence, finite syntax and memory-free evaluation beyond familiar orthogonal rewriting models.
cards.status_note: The source leaves the first-order formulation open and records the weakly orthogonal result as a special case. A bounded later-work check on 13 September 2026 did not locate a general resolution. The source’s optional extension with bound variables is distinguished from the explicit first-order target here.

progress.text: The source attributes the positive weakly orthogonal case to Kennaway’s work on sequential evaluation strategies.
Kennaway poses the finite full Church–Rosser strategy question in RTALooP.
The source adds Antoy and Middeldorp’s work on sequential reduction strategies as related progress.

importance.reason: A structural normalization question separating confluence from effective one-step evaluation; the existing score is retained while the rationale is made specific to the strategy model.

sentences: The system has finitely many first-order rewrite rules and admits every term over its finite signature.
Confluence makes normal forms unique when they exist.
The question asks for a computable strategy that chooses exactly one available contraction from the current term.
The next-step computation must halt even on terms that never reach a normal form, without retaining an external history.
The strategy must nevertheless normalize every term for which some terminating reduction exists.

cards.definitions: A finite ranked signature \(\Sigma\) is a finite collection of function symbols with specified nonnegative integer arities. Terms are all finite ordered trees built from these symbols and a countably infinite set of variables; a variable is a leaf. “Full” means this entire term set is admitted, without a type, language or reachability restriction. A rule \(\ell\to r\) consists of terms, with \(\ell\) not a variable and every variable of \(r\) occurring in \(\ell\). The system \(R\) has finitely many rules. A substitution replaces variables by finite terms; a context is a term with one designated hole. One step \(C[\ell\sigma]\to_R C[r\sigma]\) contracts a single occurrence of a rule instance at any position. No simultaneous contractions, equations modulo which to match, or variable binding are included. Write \(\to_R^*\) for zero or more steps. Confluence means that whenever \(u\to_R^*v\) and \(u\to_R^*w\), there is \(z\) with \(v\to_R^*z\) and \(w\to_R^*z\); this is equivalent to the Church–Rosser property in the source. A normal form has no outgoing rewrite step. A term has a normal form if it reaches one by finitely many steps. The strategy \(F_R\) is a function on all terms, computable by an ordinary Turing machine from a finite tree encoding with numbered variables. It fixes every normal form and satisfies \(u\to_R F_R(u)\) for every other term, even when a permitted rewrite has identical input and output. It is total: computing the next step halts for every finite term. Normalization requires that for every term \(u\) having a normal form there is \(n\geq0\) such that \(F_R^n(u)\) is a normal form. There is no persistent history input or extra state carried between successive applications of \(F_R\). No time bound is required. The quantifiers are \(\forall R\,\exists F_R\,\forall u\); an algorithm synthesizing \(F_R\) uniformly from \(R\) is not additionally required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every system satisfying the hypotheses admits such a total computable strategy. Alternatively exhibit a finite full confluent first-order system and prove in Lean that every total computable valid one-step strategy fails to normalize at least one term that has a normal form. A partial procedure that waits indefinitely on non-normalizable terms, a strategy with external memory, or a strategy allowed several contractions per output does not meet the stated conditions.

context_blocks.text: Confluence ensures that a term cannot have two different normal forms, but an arbitrary choice of reductions can still run forever. For example, the rules \(f(x)\to a\) and \(b\to b\) form a confluent system; \(f(b)\) has normal form \(a\), while repeatedly contracting its occurrence of \(b\) never reaches it.

A search can eventually discover a reduction to a normal form when one exists. That observation does not immediately produce the required total next-step function: on a term without a normal form, the strategy must still choose and return an available step in finite time.

Kennaway’s question combines finite generation, fullness and Church–Rosser confluence. The source reports counterexamples when these restrictions are dropped. This card selects its first-order term-rewriting formulation; the parenthetical extension to calculi with bound variables is not silently included.

The source records a positive result for weakly orthogonal systems: rules are left-linear, and nonvariable overlaps of rule instances give the same immediate reduct. The general question permits nontrivial overlaps, so that result does not establish the full proposition.

One-step and dependence only on the current term are substantive conditions. A procedure that remembers previously explored branches has a larger input state, while outputting a whole discovered reduction sequence changes the required interface. The question asks whether confluence always suffices under the more restrictive interface.

The RTALooP entry cites the later 1996 work on sequential reduction strategies. The source does not mark the general problem solved. Its historical dates identify the provenance of the question rather than certify the entire subsequent literature.

Confluence ensures that a term cannot have two different normal forms, but an arbitrary choice of reductions can still run forever. For example, the rules \(f(x)\to a\) and \(b\to b\) form a confluent system; \(f(b)\) has normal form \(a\), while repeatedly contracting its occurrence of \(b\) never reaches it.

A search can eventually discover a reduction to a normal form when one exists. That observation does not immediately produce the required total next-step function: on a term without a normal form, the strategy must still choose and return an available step in finite time.

Kennaway’s question combines finite generation, fullness and Church–Rosser confluence. The source reports counterexamples when these restrictions are dropped. sentences: The input is one first-order rewrite rule whose left and right sides each use every variable at most once.
The rule may be applied at any position in any finite term, with ordinary syntactic substitutions.
The question asks whether an algorithm can decide absence of every infinite reduction sequence.
Left-linearity alone and the smaller string-rewriting subclass have different known boundaries.
Recent undecidability for linear-interpretation proof methods must not be confused with linearity of the rule itself.

cards.definitions: A ranked signature \(\Sigma\) consists of finitely many function symbols with specified nonnegative integer arities. Terms are finite ordered trees over \(\Sigma\) and a countably infinite set of variables. A term is linear if each variable occurs at most once in that term; occurrences are counted separately on the two sides of a rule. The left side \(\ell\) must not be a variable and every variable of \(r\) must occur in \(\ell\); variables may be erased, but may not be duplicated on either side or newly introduced on the right. A substitution maps variables to finite terms. A one-step rewrite replaces one occurrence of \(\ell\sigma\) by \(r\sigma\) inside an arbitrary term context, for some substitution \(\sigma\). The same single rule may be used at any position and any number of times. Matching is syntactic; no equations, types, binding operations or restrictions such as innermost-only rewriting are present. Termination means there is no infinite chain \(u_0\to u_1\to u_2\to\cdots\) starting from any finite term, including terms with variables. It is not only existence of one terminating reduction, termination from one designated input, or absence of short cycles. If a rewrite returns the same term, it is still a step and can witness nontermination by repetition. The finite signature, symbol arities, variables and both finite term trees are explicitly encoded and form the algorithm’s input. A decision algorithm is one deterministic Turing machine that halts on every valid input rule and answers the global termination question exactly; no complexity bound is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a terminating decision algorithm for every valid rule linear on both sides, or prove in Lean that this restricted global termination problem is undecidable. A single nonterminating example does not prove undecidability. A decision procedure for string rules, a bounded search for loops, or a test for whether one specific interpretation proves termination does not settle the full proposition.

context_blocks.text: Linearity controls variable repetition, not the number of function symbols. Both \(f(x)\to x\) and \(f(x)\to f(f(x))\) are linear on each side. The first decreases term size at every step and terminates; the second can grow forever. Thus the input class includes both possible answers even with unary function symbols.

Dauchet’s 1991 question explicitly requires both left and right linearity. The source cites undecidability for one rule with only left linearity, so omitting the right-side restriction would replace the open question by a known harder model.

One-rule string rewriting is a special case, represented by unary function symbols with a shared tail variable. Its unresolved termination question is therefore related but does not cover the branching first-order terms admitted here. The source separately discusses confluence, which is another property and is not part of the present target.

The 2024 paper Linear Termination is Undecidable studies whether termination can be certified by linear polynomial interpretations. Here “linear” describes the proof interpretation, whereas this card uses it for occurrence of variables in a rule. The paper’s undecidability result is not a resolution of the question merely because the titles share the word linear.

Indeed, that paper can make the interpretation-existence question undecidable even within systems already known to terminate by another polynomial interpretation. This emphasizes the difference between deciding actual termination and deciding whether a particular proof method succeeds.

Global termination quantifies over every finite term and every choice of redex. A collection of successful test reductions or the absence of a repeated term in bounded exploration does not establish it. Likewise, a rule may fail to terminate by unbounded growth without ever repeating a term.

cards.definitions: A machine has a finite control, a finite tape alphabet with a blank symbol, one unbounded tape initially containing the finite input \(w\), and a head position. Nonhalting control states are probabilistic or nondeterministic. Each has a fixed finite nonempty set of actions. An action is a total finite table indexed by the currently scanned symbol, prescribing a symbol to write, a head move by at most one cell and the next control state. Thus an available action is enabled whenever its origin control state is visited. A probabilistic state also has a fixed rational distribution of strictly positive probabilities over its actions; these choices are sampled independently conditional on the execution history. Deterministic behavior is represented by a single action of probability one. Halting states have no actions. A scheduler is any function from finite execution histories ending at a nondeterministic state to an available action. Histories include the configurations and actions taken. Schedulers are deterministic but need not be computable and may use the entire history. A scheduler is fair from the given initial configuration if, on every infinite execution consistent with it and the probabilistic action supports, every nondeterministic action whose origin state occurs infinitely often is itself taken infinitely often. This is pathwise strong fairness, including individual infinite paths of probability zero. The scheduler induces the usual probability measure on executions, with finite-prefix probabilities given by products of the rational choices. Fair almost-sure termination (FAST) means that every fair scheduler gives probability one to reaching a halting state. It imposes no bound on expected running time. Machine tables, rational probabilities and input words have finite binary encodings. A tree on \(\mathbb N\) is a prefix-closed subset of finite sequences of natural numbers. It is presented by a primitive-recursive membership predicate: a finite expression built from zero, successor and projections using composition and primitive recursion, with a fixed effective encoding of sequences. An infinite branch is a function \(b:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) whose every finite prefix belongs to the tree. Well-foundedness means no such branch exists. Branching is not restricted to two children or any fixed finite bound. The reduction must halt on every valid machine/input pair and output a valid predicate for a prefix-closed tree; no resource bound on the reduction is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a total computable reduction satisfying the displayed equivalence for all machine/input pairs, or prove in Lean that no such reduction exists. Requiring computable schedulers, fairness only with probability one, weak fairness, finite expected time, or finitely branching witness trees changes the problem. Sound proof rules for selected program classes alone do not establish this universal reduction.

context_blocks.text: The source asks both for the recursion-theoretic complexity of FAST and for sound complete reasoning techniques. Editorial specialization: this card selects the coanalytic upper-bound question, expressed concretely as a reduction to tree well-foundedness. It does not present a conjectured upper bound as a theorem or claim that this choice already supplies a Hoare-style proof system.

Fairness rules out indefinitely ignoring an action at a control state revisited infinitely often. It still permits arbitrarily long finite postponements. Requiring this property on every supported infinite execution is stronger than requiring that unfair executions merely have probability zero.

The source reports \(\Pi^1_1\)-completeness for the corresponding non-probabilistic fair-termination problem. Well-foundedness of recursive, arbitrarily branching trees is the standard complete problem at that coanalytic level; the reduction target makes the prospective upper-bound question precise.

Probability-one termination permits exceptional nonterminating executions of probability zero. It is therefore weaker than termination on every path, even though the scheduler’s fairness requirement in this card quantifies over every supported infinite path. These two uses of quantification must not be conflated.

The 2023 positive-almost-sure-termination work proves a \(\Pi^1_1\)-complete classification for a different property: finite expected runtime for each scheduler, without the same fair-scheduler restriction. That theorem does not automatically classify FAST.

The 2026 distributed-algorithm verification paper supplies sound rules combining probabilistic reasoning with weak fairness and applies them to consensus protocols. Those applications are important evidence of useful techniques, but its stated soundness and fairness convention do not prove the universal strong-fairness reduction requested here.

cards.title: P versus NC
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NC}\), where NC consists of decision languages recognized by logspace-uniform Boolean circuit families of polynomial size and polylogarithmic depth? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have such a circuit family?
cards.definitions: P is deterministic polynomial time on ordinary Turing machines. For \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{NC}\) there must be fixed constants c,k,C and a family \((C_{n})_{n}\ge 0\) such that \(C_{n}\) decides membership in L correctly on every n-bit input, has at most \(C(n+2)^{c}\) gates, and has depth at most \(C(\log _{2}(n+2))^{k}\). Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; fan-out is unrestricted and one output bit is designated. Depth is the longest input-to-output gate path. A deterministic \(O(\log (n+2))\)-space transducer given \(1^{n}\) must output the description of \(C_{n}\); its polynomial output bound is part of the size requirement. Constants and the generator may depend on L but not on n. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered Boolean gate DAG, its input-bit values, and an output-gate index; it asks whether that gate evaluates to 1. Its input length n is the entire binary encoding length, and malformed encodings are rejected. No randomization, advice, oracle, or restriction to monotone gates is permitted. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every language in P has a logspace-uniform family of polynomial-size, polylogarithmic-depth circuits, or prove that some language in P has no such family. By the stated completeness result, the affirmative answer is equivalent to Circuit Value belonging to NC, and the negative answer to Circuit Value not belonging to NC. Excluding only one fixed depth exponent, nonuniform monotone circuits, or one evaluation procedure does not establish \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NC}\).
cards.why: This asks whether a feasible computation can require intrinsically many sequential stages even when polynomially many processors are available. It is the central unresolved premise behind P-completeness as an explanation for resistance to parallelization, spanning graph algorithms, simulation, optimization, and language processing.

importance.reason: The foundational tractability question for parallel computation: whether every polynomial-time task admits polylogarithmic dependency depth with polynomial work.

progress.text: Ladner establishes that Circuit Value is logspace complete for P, giving a concrete universal target for efficient parallelization.
Greenlaw, Hoover, and Ruzzo organize the theory of P-completeness and its open P-versus-NC question, including uniform circuit and parallel-machine formulations.
Raz and McKenzie prove monotone \(\mathrm{NC}\ne\)monotone P and a strict monotone NC hierarchy. These results restrict the gates used by the computing circuits.

Cavalar and coauthors prove perfect matching requires monotone circuit size \(2^{n^{\Omega (1)}}\), improving Razborov’s quasipolynomial lower bound. The November 2025 revision appears in STOC 2026; general Boolean circuits are not covered.
