progress.text: The ellipsoid method and early interior-point algorithms establish polynomial-time solvability in the total input bit length. They do not provide a general strongly polynomial operation bound.

Tardos gives an algorithm whose arithmetic count is independent of the right-hand side and objective magnitudes, with remaining dependence on the constraint matrix. Small integer entries in that matrix give important strongly polynomial special cases.

Allamigeon, Gaubert, and Vandame construct LP families forcing exponentially many iterations for the self-concordant-barrier path-following methods covered by their theorem. This restricts a route to solving the problem; it is not an unrestricted LP lower bound.

Dadush, Koh, Natura, Olver, and Végh solve minimum-cost generalized flow and LPs with at most two nonzeros per row or column in strongly polynomial time. Their analysis also controls intermediate bit lengths.

Dadush, Ma, Natura, and Végh improve interior-point bounds in terms of straight-line complexity and give strongly polynomial trust-region subroutines. Straight-line complexity can itself be large, so these are not dimension-only bounds for arbitrary LPs.

Version 10 of Awoniyi’s preprint claims at most \(2(m+n)\) complementary-pivot iterations for general LP. This review has not validated the termination/correctness argument and complete bit-complexity guarantee, and found no independent primary confirmation. The claim is not promoted to an established resolution.

context_blocks.text: Linear programming is already solvable in polynomial time when input length includes the bits used to write its coefficients. The unresolved issue is whether the number of arithmetic decisions can depend only on the number of constraints and variables. Very large capacities, costs, or denominators may require long arithmetic operands, but the question asks whether they must also force more arithmetic steps.

Both requirements in the definition are essential. Bounding the number of steps while allowing intermediate integers with exponentially many bits could hide enormous computation inside single arithmetic operations. Bounding only total bit time gives ordinary polynomial-time linear programming, which is already known. The strongly polynomial target combines a dimension-only operation count with controlled numerical representation.

Combinatorial optimization supplies positive examples. Tardos’s method removes dependence on the magnitudes of the right-hand side and objective, and yields strongly polynomial bounds for suitable small-coefficient constraint matrices. More recently, a strongly polynomial algorithm was obtained when each row, or each column, has at most two nonzero entries. These cases show that large numerical data alone need not force many arithmetic steps.

For unrestricted matrices, an algorithm may need a different way to navigate the feasible region. Long central paths can defeat broad classes of path-following methods, even though other approaches remain possible. A separate status issue is a 2025 preprint, revised in July 2026, claiming a general solution. Its claim is recorded below, but this review has not established its correctness or found independent validation.

cards.title: Exact semidefinite feasibility in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is the following language in P in the ordinary Turing model: all lists of symmetric rational matrices \(A_{0},A_{1},\ldots ,A_{m}\in Q^{n\times n}\) for which there exists a real vector \(x\in R^{m}\) satisfying \(A_{0}+\sum _{i=1}^{m} x_{i} A_{i}\succeq 0\)? Both m and n are unbounded parts of the input, and the algorithm must decide exact nonemptiness in time polynomial in the total binary encoding length.
cards.definitions: Every matrix entry is an explicitly supplied rational number, with signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; all matrices have the same size \(n\ge 1\). A symmetric matrix M is positive semidefinite, written \(M\succeq 0\), when \(z^{T}Mz\ge 0\) for every real vector z, equivalently when all eigenvalues are nonnegative. The unknown x ranges over all real vectors, not just rational vectors. Singular feasible matrices count as YES. There is no strict-feasibility, boundedness, conditioning, rank, or distance-to-infeasibility promise, and no radius or accuracy parameter is supplied. The output is one bit specifying whether any feasible x exists; an explicit feasible point is not required. An affine subspace given by rational linear equations can be parametrized by rational Gaussian elimination, so this is also the rational-affine-subspace intersection formulation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A basic boundary between numerical convex optimization and exact efficient computation. Resolving it would clarify what semidefinite programming can guarantee without hidden regularity or witness-size assumptions, with consequences for optimization relaxations, algebraic certificates and verification.

importance.reason: A foundational complexity gap in a widely used convex optimization model; exact decision remains open despite powerful approximation algorithms, exact duality and symbolic decidability.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The primary literature retains general exact SDP feasibility as an open polynomial-time problem. Ramana’s dual does not establish \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) membership in the Turing model, and recent convex-polynomial optimization results address a different constraint family. This card permits real witnesses, singular feasible points, weak infeasibility and unbounded feasible regions.

context_blocks.text: Semidefinite constraints replace scalar nonnegativity by nonnegativity of a quadratic form in every direction. They include linear inequalities as the diagonal-matrix special case and support powerful relaxations in combinatorial optimization. Approximation algorithms are well developed, but their guarantees require attention to input geometry and numerical precision. De Klerk and Vallentin establish polynomial bit complexity for a short-step interior-point method under appropriate assumptions; their theorem is about controlled approximation, not arbitrary exact feasibility.

The unrestricted problem is decidable. Introduce a real \(n\times n\) matrix Y and impose \(A_{0}+\sum _{i} x_{i} A_{i}=YY^{T}\). These are finitely many polynomial equations of degree at most two, and a real symmetric matrix is positive semidefinite exactly when such a factor exists. General real-algebraic decision procedures therefore apply. Henrion, Naldi and Safey El Din develop more specialized symbolic algorithms, including treatment of degenerate feasible sets. None of this supplies polynomial time when both input dimensions vary.

Exact feasibility can differ even from arbitrarily close approximation. The matrix \(M(t)\) with rows \((0,1)\) and \((1,t)\) has determinant −1, so it is never positive semidefinite. Yet as t tends to positive infinity, its negative eigenvalue \((t- \sqrt{t^{2}+4})/2\) tends to zero. Thus these infeasible matrices approach the positive semidefinite cone arbitrarily closely. A numerical tolerance alone cannot distinguish this situation from a singular feasible matrix.

Rational input also need not admit a rational witness. Consider a block diagonal matrix with blocks \([[x,2],[2,2x]]\) and \([[2,x],[x,1]]\). The first block is positive semidefinite exactly when \(x\ge \sqrt{2}\), and the second when |\(x|\le \sqrt{2}\). The whole matrix is therefore feasible exactly at \(x=\sqrt{2}\). All coefficient matrices are rational, but searching only rational substitutions would miss the solution. This example explains why the domain of the unknowns is part of the formal question.

Even rational feasible points can be enormous. Conditions \(x_{1}\ge 2\) and \([[x_{i+1},x_{i}],[x_{i},1]]\succeq 0\) force \(x_{i+1}\ge x_{i}^{2}\), hence \(x_{k}\ge 2^{2^{k- 1}}\). A block diagonal LMI encodes the chain compactly, while writing its final coordinate in ordinary binary needs exponentially many digits in k. Pataki and Touzov analyze how such growth arises beyond isolated examples, including connections to singularity degree. Large explicit witnesses obstruct a naive search algorithm; they do not prove that deciding existence is hard.

Ramana’s exact dual provides an alternative feasibility system of polynomial description size without regularity assumptions. In the Turing model, it implies that semidefinite feasibility belongs to NP if and only if it belongs to coNP. It does not establish either membership individually. The corresponding \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) theorem over exact real-number machines belongs to a different computational model. This distinction prevents a common overstatement of what SDP duality proves about bit complexity.
Pataki’s October 2025 work gives a new derivation and a fuller description of the feasible set of Ramana’s dual using facial reduction.

A separate STOC 2026 result by Slot, Steurer and Wiedmer obtains small approximate solutions for minimizing convex polynomials over polyhedra. That result concerns polynomial objectives with linear constraints; the authors explicitly contrast it with the large-solution obstacle for semidefinite programs. It does not settle general exact semidefinite feasibility.

cards.title: Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite clutter with the packing property have the max-flow min-cut property? Equivalently, if every deletion/contraction minor satisfies unweighted integral packing–covering equality, must weighted integral packing–covering equality hold for every nonnegative integer weight vector?
cards.definitions:
A clutter C on a finite ground set E is a family of subsets of E, no one properly containing another. In the original instance all members are nonempty; the empty family is allowed. A cover \(T\subseteq E\) meets every member, and \(	au (C)\) is the smallest cover size. A packing is a family of pairwise disjoint members, with maximum size \(
u (C)\). Deleting e removes e from the ground set and discards all members containing e. Contracting e removes it from the ground set and from every member, and retains only inclusion-minimal resulting members. A minor results from any sequence of these operations. The packing property means \(	au (C' )=
u (C' )\) for every minor \(C'\). For the empty family both values are zero; for a minor containing the empty set both are defined as +∞, with the empty member permitted arbitrarily many times in a packing. For \(w\in \mathbb{Z} _{\ge 0}^{E}\), let \(	au _{w}(C)=\min\){\(\sum_{e\in T}w_{e}:T\) covers C}. Let \(
u _{w}(C)\) be the maximum of \(\sum_{F\in C}y_{F}\) over nonnegative integers \(y_{F}\) satisfying \(\Sigma\)_{F∋e}\(y_{F}\le w_{e}\) for every \(e\in E\). Thus a weighted packing may use a member repeatedly, subject to capacities w. The max-flow min-cut property is \(	au _{w}(C)=
u _{w}(C)\) for every such w. The original nonempty-member assumption makes these weighted optima finite.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that the packing property implies \(\tau _{w}=\nu _{w}\) for every finite clutter and every nonnegative integer weight vector, or give a finite clutter and weight vector with the packing property and \(\tau _{w}>\nu _{w}\). A counterexample must verify equality for all minors, not merely for the original unweighted clutter. Finite searches, proofs for a proper subclass, or fractional optimality alone do not resolve the universal statement.

context_blocks.text: Packing and covering often give two descriptions of the same combinatorial optimum. In a clutter, the unweighted equality can fail. Requiring equality after every deletion and contraction removes many such obstructions. The Conforti–Cornuéjols conjecture asks whether this local robustness already guarantees equality for every integer capacity vector.

For a concrete example, take E as the vertices of a bipartite graph and the clutter members as its edges. Covers are vertex covers and packings are matchings. This illustrates the familiar kind of min–max equality that the general conjecture seeks to characterize, without restricting its input to graph edge families.

If A is the member-by-element incidence matrix, the associated linear programs are \(\min  w^{T}x\) subject to \(Ax\ge 1\) and \(x\ge 0\), and \(\max  1^{T}y\) subject to \(A^{T}y\le w\) and \(y\ge 0\). Equality of the two integer optima forces their values to agree with the fractional optimum by weak and strong duality. This is the standard MFMC integrality requirement.

Schrijver’s Survey Question 68 calls the target the assertion that every packing hypergraph is Mengerian. The terminology differs, but its packing property includes all minors and its conclusion includes arbitrary nonnegative integer weights. Checking only the all-ones weight on the original instance would yield a much weaker, insufficient hypothesis.

Abdi and Schwarcz’s July 2026 manuscript calls the statement the replication conjecture and explicitly retains it as open. It reports verification for clutters on at most ten elements and for a specified bounded-degree family of cuboids. These are finite or restricted confirmations, not a proof for arbitrary ground-set size.

The same work gives a finite set of weight vectors sufficient to test the MFMC property of a fixed clutter, with an improved bound on their entries. This makes checking individual instances more effective. The number and size of possible clutters still grow without bound, so instance-wise testability does not prove the universal implication.

cards.why: Identify whether all obstructions to weighted integral packing–covering duality are already visible as unweighted failures in minors, a central issue in integer programming and combinatorial optimization.

importance.reason: A central conjecture connecting minor obstructions, integral linear programming and packing–covering duality. Schrijver treats it as a major survey question, and a July 2026 primary paper develops both theoretical and computational methods around it.

cards.title: Nearly linear-time solution of general sparse linear systems
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge 1\), does there exist a uniform randomized classical algorithm \(A_{c}\) with the following guarantee? Given \(n\ge 2, a\) nonsingular rational \(n\times n\) matrix A with m nonzero entries, a nonzero rational vector b, and an integer \(1\le p\le c\cdot \operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\), output a rational vector x̂ such that ||\(A\hat\{x\}- b||_{2}\le 2^{- p}||b||_{2}\) with probability at least \(2/3\). Each numerator and positive denominator of A and b has at most \(c\cdot \operatorname{ceil}(\log _{2} n)\) binary digits, and the spectral condition number \(\kappa _{2}(A)\) is promised at most \(n^{c}\). The worst-case running time must be \(O_{c}(m \log ^{d_{c}}n)\) for some constant \(d_{c}\) independent of the input.
cards.definitions: The input lists the row index, column index and rational value of each nonzero coefficient, without duplicate positions, together with the n entries of b; hence \(n\le m\le n^{2}\). The Euclidean norm is ||\(v||_{2}=(\sum_{i} v_{i}^{2})^{1/2}\), and \(\kappa _{2}(A)=\sigma _{\mathrm{max}}(A)/\sigma _{\mathrm{min}}(A)\), the ratio of its largest and smallest singular values. Nonsingularity makes the denominator positive. A may be nonsymmetric, indefinite and unrelated to a graph Laplacian. The algorithm need only meet its guarantee on promised inputs; it is not asked to certify the condition-number promise. Computation uses a word RAM with \(\Theta (\log  n)\)-bit words, conventional arithmetic, comparison, bit operations and memory access; all operations on longer numbers, preprocessing, random-bit generation and writing the output are charged. No operation on an arbitrary real number has unit cost. Converting word operations to bit operations changes only polylogarithmic factors. Constants and the fixed program may depend on c, but neither nonuniform advice depending on n nor a supplied inverse or preconditioner is allowed. Here \(\varepsilon =2^{- p}\); this is the polynomial-condition, inverse-polynomial-accuracy regime of the near-input-size target. The output is the full list of n rational coordinates, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator; every output bit is charged. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation.

cards.why: This tests whether sparsity and moderate conditioning suffice for solving linear equations at essentially the cost of reading them. A resolution would clarify the limits of graph-based solvers, preconditioning and numerical subroutines used throughout algorithms and optimization.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. This is an editorial, fully specified near-linear target in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime, not a named positive conjecture. The faster-than-matrix-multiplication problem has already been solved. The August 2026 report discusses broader scalable solvers but does not claim this universal guarantee; the simplicial-Laplacian reduction is not a general running-time lower bound.

context_blocks.text: Solving \(Ax=b\) is a basic operation inside scientific simulation, optimization and data analysis. A sparse input can be read and multiplied by a vector without scanning all \(n^{2}\) matrix positions. The question is whether solving one system can always be comparably inexpensive, up to powers of logarithms. Peng and Vempala frame the general complexity problem around exploiting sparsity while also controlling numerical precision, rather than treating arithmetic on exact real numbers as free.

The target fixes a residual norm because different meanings of approximate solution can conceal different costs. If \(x*=A^{-1}b\), the elementary inequality ||\(\hat\{x\}- x*||_{2}/||x*||_{2}\le \kappa _{2}(A)\cdot ||A\hat\{x\}- b||_{2}/||b||_{2}\) relates residual error to forward error. Thus a tiny residual need not mean an equally tiny solution error. For instance, \(A=diag(1,\delta ), b=(1,\delta )\) and \(\hat\{x\}=(1,0)\) have residual \(\delta\) while the second solution coordinate is wrong by one. The condition promise and requested accuracy make this dependence explicit.

Nearly linear solvers already exist for major structured families. Spielman and Teng establish such algorithms for symmetric diagonally dominant systems using preconditioning and graph structure. Their guarantee is naturally expressed in the matrix energy norm. For positive-definite systems, norm comparisons relate this guarantee to residual accuracy, with conditioning affecting the required tolerance. An arbitrary sparse matrix lacks the diagonal-dominance structure that supports this machinery.

Peng and Vempala’s SODA 2021 result breaks the matrix-multiplication barrier for sufficiently sparse, polynomially conditioned systems. They implement a randomized block Krylov approach using structured factorizations and a numerical-stability analysis. This is why merely asking for a sparse solver faster than matrix multiplication would be an obsolete open question. The stronger near-input-size target remains far beyond that theorem.

Nie improves the required anti-concentration bounds for random Krylov matrices. His STOC 2022 result yields a bound of \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m^{(\omega - 2)/(\omega - 1)}n^{2})\) in the polynomial-conditioning and precision regime. For \(m=\widetilde{O} (n)\), this becomes \(\widetilde{O}\)\((n^{(3\omega - 4)/(\omega - 1)})\). The paper’s numerical exponent 2.2716 uses the matrix-multiplication bound available at that time; it is not a claim about today’s best numerical value of \(\omega\). Either expression remains far above linear for very sparse inputs.

The distinction between a sparse matrix and a structurally easy sparse matrix is sharpened by Ding, Kyng, Probst Gutenberg and Zhang. They reduce general linear equations with polynomially bounded integer coefficients and conditioning to Laplacians of two-dimensional simplicial complexes while preserving sparsity up to logarithmic factors. Consequently, extending graph-Laplacian techniques to those higher-dimensional Laplacians would already have general consequences. This is a completeness reduction, not an unconditional proof that a near-linear solver cannot exist.

The Simons workshop report, revised in August 2026, calls for broader classes of scalably solvable systems and studies the finite-precision behavior of iterative methods. Its benchmark questions are more focused than a universal worst-case solver, and its discussion of preconditioning makes clear that constructing a useful preconditioner is itself part of the computational task. The present card is an explicit editorial formulation of the general complexity target; it is not attributed to a numbered conjecture in that report.

The output requirement also matters. An explicit n-vector is compatible with nearly linear time because a nonsingular \(n\times n\) input has at least n nonzeros. Returning only access to a vector, a few observables, or a quantum state encoding its normalized coordinates changes the task. Conversely, demanding an exact rational solution could introduce much larger output encodings; the specified numerical approximation avoids building that extra requirement into the question.

cards.title: Smale’s seventh problem
cards.formal: Do there exist real constants \(C,K>0\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and one deterministic real-number algorithm \(A\) in the model below such that, for every integer \(N\ge2\), \(A(N)\) outputs distinct points \(x_1,\ldots,x_N\in S^2\) in at most \(KN^k\) operations and satisfies \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\le E_N^{\ast}+C\ln N\)?
cards.why: Connects the complexity of constructing global near-minimizers with discrete potential theory and the conditioning of polynomial-root problems. Its logarithmic total-energy tolerance is much sharper than leading-order equidistribution.
cards.status_note: Rechecked on 13 September 2026. No general deterministic polynomial-time construction with logarithmic total-energy excess was located. The March 2026 finite-cardinality classification and existing distributional energy guarantees do not establish the uniform algorithmic target. This source review did not independently verify the cited proofs.

cards.definitions: Let \(S^2=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:x_1^2+x_2^2+x_3^2=1\}\). For distinct points define \(E_N(x_1,\ldots,x_N)=-\sum_{i\ne j}\ln\|x_i-x_j\|_2\), counting ordered pairs; configurations with collisions have energy \(+\infty\). Let \(E_N^{\ast}\) be the infimum over all \(N\)-tuples on \(S^2\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm and \(\|\cdot\|_2\) is Euclidean distance. Use one deterministic finite real-arithmetic program with a fixed finite list of real constants independent of \(N\). The machine has exact real registers, finite control and tapes; each scalar copy, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero register, sign test, or tape movement costs one operation. It may allocate storage, charging the operations that use it, and has no primitive logarithm, square root, floor, randomness or optimization oracle. The input integer \(N\) is supplied as one exact real value. Output is the explicit list of \(3N\) coordinates, all required to lie exactly on the sphere. Time is polynomial in \(N\), not in \(\log N\); this is a real-number computation model, not a bit-cost model. The energy inequality is a mathematical condition on the output, and the machine need not evaluate that energy.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the existence of one permitted real-arithmetic program and constants \(C,K,k\), independent of \(N\), satisfying both the time and energy guarantees for every integer \(N\ge2\), or prove in Lean that no such program and constants exist. The output must lie exactly on the sphere. Expected energy under a distribution, finitely many solved cardinalities, or a larger asymptotic additive error does not meet this criterion.

references.title: Research reference · www.lebesgue.fr
Mathematical Problems for the Next Century
references.locator: Problem 7; real-number computation model and logarithmic excess energy.

context_blocks.text: Imagine placing mutually repelling particles on a sphere. For this problem, a pair contributes minus the logarithm of its straight-line distance through three-dimensional space. Bringing two points together sends their contribution to positive infinity. Spreading points lowers the energy, but the question asks for a guarantee against the best configuration of the entire collection, rather than against a locally stable arrangement. Exact minimizers are called elliptic Fekete configurations.

For two points the answer is concrete: opposite poles have distance 2, the largest possible distance on the unit sphere, and ordered-pair energy −2 ln 2. For general N an optimum still exists: the sphere is compact, collisions have infinite energy, and some distinct configuration has finite energy. Existence therefore is not the open part. The unresolved requirement is one fixed algorithm with a polynomial operation bound for every N.

The tolerance \(C\ln N\) is an additive error in the total energy. The minimum has leading terms \(E_N^{\ast}=(1/2-\ln2)N^2-(N/2)\ln N+O(N)\). An approximation that only matches these leading terms may still have error proportional to \(N\), much larger than the requested logarithmic excess.

Smale’s original statement counts each unordered pair once. This card counts each pair twice, as in much subsequent literature. Both the optimum and excess energy are doubled, so the existence of a universal logarithmic-error constant is unchanged. The real-arithmetic model also comes from Smale’s formulation: a step manipulates an exact real value. A polynomial number of such steps does not assert polynomial bit complexity, and the output inequality does not give the program a free logarithm or minimization instruction.

The generalized Diamond ensemble supplies configurations for every N with a precisely analyzed expected energy: the two leading terms above plus a specified linear term and an \(O(\sqrt{N} \ln  N)\) remainder. These constructions quantify how well a structured distribution spreads points. That estimate is not a deterministic C ln N excess guarantee relative to the unknown optimum.

Beltrán and Hardy obtain the required logarithmic excess for a low-temperature Coulomb-gas distribution: at inverse temperature N, the mean excess is at most 9 ln N, and excess at most 10 ln N holds with probability at least \(1- \exp (- N \ln  N)\). The theorem analyzes the distribution, while polynomial-time sampling from it remains an additional computational issue. A probabilistic existence statement also differs from the deterministic algorithm asked for here.

Michelen and Yakir prove a central limit theorem for the energy of zeros of a rotationally invariant random polynomial, with fluctuations on the \(\sqrt{N}\) scale. This measures variation around that ensemble’s mean, not error from the global minimum.

Recent exact algebraic work by Armentano and coauthors classifies critical configurations with at most six points, and treats seven points under an antipodal-pair restriction. Such finite classifications do not supply a uniform algorithm for arbitrary N.

The original motivation connects low-energy spherical points, through stereographic projection, to well-conditioned polynomials and the complexity of finding polynomial roots. The energy question has its own stronger output guarantee; progress on polynomial conditioning or on a different Smale problem does not automatically resolve it. It also asks a basic algorithmic question in discrete potential theory: how cheaply can globally near-equilibrium configurations be constructed?

cards.title: Polynomial-time simplex pivot rule
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform deterministic primal-simplex pivot algorithm and a polynomial p such that, for every rational linear program \(\max \{c^{T}x: Ax=b, x\ge 0\}\) with A of full row rank, a finite optimum, and any supplied feasible basis \(B_{0}\), the algorithm reaches a basis whose reduced costs are all nonpositive using at most \(p(\mathrm{L})\) bit operations in total? Here L is the binary input length of A,b,c and \(B_{0}\), and every basis change must be a legal improving simplex pivot as defined below.
cards.definitions:
A has m rows and n columns with \(1\le m\le n\); all rational numerators and positive denominators are explicit binary integers. A basis B is a set of m columns with invertible \(A_{B}\). Its basic solution is \(x_{B}=A_{B}^{-1}b\) and \(x_{j}=0\) for \(j
otin B\), and feasibility means \(x_{B}\ge 0\). An entering column \(j
otin B\) must have reduced cost \(r_{j}=c_{j}- c_{B}^{T}A_{B}^{-1}A_{j}>0\). Put \(a=A_{B}^{-1}A_{j}\). Choose a leaving basic index i attaining \(	heta =\min _{k\in B:a_{k}>0}x_{k}/a_{k}\), and replace i by j in the basis. The finite-optimum promise ensures that this minimum exists for an improving column. Ties may be resolved by the rule; \(	heta =0\) is an allowed degenerate pivot and counts toward the bound. The rule may inspect the whole input and maintain history, with all preprocessing, pivot selection, exact arithmetic, helper computations and memory operations charged to \(p(\mathrm{L})\). It must follow these basis exchanges on the supplied LP from \(B_{0}\): it may not jump to another feasible basis or replace the feasible region by an extended formulation. The required terminal condition \(r_{j}\le 0\) for all \(j
otin B\) certifies optimality. This is the supplied-feasible-basis optimization version; phase-I feasibility construction is not part of this card.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a rule and prove its total polynomial bit complexity for every promised input and initial feasible basis, or prove that no such rule exists. Merely bounding the number of pivots while leaving their selection computationally unbounded is insufficient. A lower bound for a prescribed family of rules, or for nonlinear objectives, does not establish the negative answer for all rules here.
cards.why: A fundamental question about whether local, improving basis exchanges can support efficient global optimization. It would explain a central practical algorithm and sharpen the relationship between polyhedral geometry, degeneracy and algorithmic access to an optimum.

importance.reason: A longstanding foundational problem about one of the most important optimization algorithms; the existence and efficient discovery of short improving basis paths remain unresolved even though LP itself is polynomial-time solvable.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The STACS 2026 and March 2026 primary publications retain the general polynomial simplex question as open. This card fixes deterministic total bit complexity for legal improving primal-simplex pivots from any supplied feasible basis on a finite-optimum rational LP. Strongly polynomial algorithms, nonlinear active-set bounds and distributional performance are distinct formulations.

context_blocks.text: Linear programming already has algorithms with polynomial bit complexity, including ellipsoid and interior-point methods. The unresolved question is whether the same guarantee can be achieved while moving through bases by the simplex method. A pivot rule determines which improving direction to expose next and how to break ties. The STACS 2026 paper on ranking-based rules states that the general question remains open.

There are two obstacles to a polynomial guarantee. First, a short route to an optimal basis must exist under the permitted improving moves. Second, the rule must discover such a route efficiently. Knowing the optimum from another computation does not authorize skipping the route: every intervening basis exchange is still required. Likewise, a short path in the undirected graph of a polyhedron need not be a short path along improving edges.

The bit-complexity requirement is deliberately weaker than strongly polynomial simplex. It permits the running time to depend polynomially on the number of bits in coefficients. A strongly polynomial rule would instead bound its arithmetic work polynomially in m and n, together with appropriate bounds on the sizes of numbers used. Therefore this card does not assert that a positive answer alone settles Smale’s strongly polynomial LP problem or a diameter bound depending only on dimension and number of facets.

Degeneracy means several bases can describe the same vertex. A legal pivot with \(\theta =0\) changes the basis without improving the objective value, so an algorithm can stall even if the geometric route is short. Kukharenko and Sanità’s March 2026 paper bounds a block of consecutive degenerate pivots at a nonoptimal vertex by \(n- m- 1\), given an improving feasible direction. Such a direction can be obtained using an LP solver. This controls local stalling, but does not bound how many different nonoptimal vertices the method must visit.

Positive average-case results are also substantial. Spielman and Teng show polynomial smoothed complexity for a simplex algorithm under random perturbations of the input. Smoothed analysis studies the expected behavior around an arbitrary instance as a function of perturbation size. It helps explain good practical performance, but does not give a deterministic worst-case guarantee on every exact rational instance.

The 2026 ranking-based lower bounds exclude broader families than a single greedy rule. One result covers index-ranking rules with a specified limit on their memory states; another covers memoryless rules using rankings by index, reduced cost and objective improvement. Full access to numerical data and unrestricted polynomially bounded history are allowed in this card, so those lower bounds do not cover every candidate.

A striking neighboring result does exclude every pivot rule for the active-set method with a nonlinear objective. Disser and Mosis first use higher-degree polynomial objectives on the hypercube. Bach and coauthors then obtain the phenomenon for maximizing a convex quadratic function, published at SODA 2026. The direction of optimization matters: this is convex maximization. Their construction does not have a linear objective, and the authors explicitly distinguish it from a general simplex lower bound.

cards.title: Komlós conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal real constant \(C>0\) such that, for all integers \(m,n\ge 1\) and every real matrix \(A\in \mathbb{R} ^{m\times n}\) with \(\sum _{i=1}^{m} A_{ij}^{2}\le 1\) for each column j, there is a vector \(x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}\) satisfying \(\max _{1\le i\le m}|\sum _{j=1}^{n} A_{ij}x_{j}|\le C\)?
cards.definitions: All matrices are finite. Columns may have arbitrary real entries, including negative entries. The sign vector may depend on the entire matrix; C may not depend on the dimensions or entries. This is an existence question, with no algorithmic or input-encoding requirement.

context_blocks.text: Discrepancy measures how accurately a fractional choice can be replaced by signs while controlling many linear constraints simultaneously. Komlós asks whether normalizing every column in Euclidean norm suffices to bound every coordinate of the signed sum by an absolute constant.

The 2025 improvement gives a polylogarithmic bound smaller than the classical square-root-logarithmic bound, but does not reach a constant. Komlós implies the Beck–Fiala conjecture after scaling an incidence matrix; the converse is not known. Both are retained as established landmarks with different hypotheses, rather than as unrelated questions.

cards.title: P-matrix linear complementarity in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, given \(n\ge 1, a\) rational P-matrix \(M\in Q^{n\times n}\) and \(q\in Q^{n}\), outputs rational vectors \(z,w\ge 0\) satisfying \(w=Mz+q\) and \(z^{T}w=0\)?
cards.definitions: A principal submatrix \(M[S,S]\) uses the same nonempty index set \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,n\}\) for rows and columns. M is a P-matrix when \(\det  M[S,S]>0\) for every such S. All matrix and vector entries are explicitly listed as binary signed numerators and positive denominators; N denotes their total bit length including dimensions and separators. The algorithm is a deterministic multitape Turing machine whose running time, including output, is at most one polynomial \(p(N)\) independent of n and the entries. It must terminate within that bound on all syntactically valid rational inputs, but its output is required to satisfy the equations only when M is a P-matrix. No P-matrix recognition or certificate is supplied or required. Inequalities are coordinatewise, and \(z^{T}w=\sum_{i} z_{i} w_{i}\). There is no symmetry, positive-definiteness, sparsity, nondegeneracy or coefficient-size promise beyond rational encoding and the P-matrix condition. A numerical approximation alone is not an output solution.

context_blocks.text: Complementarity combines linear constraints with a discrete choice: in each coordinate, at least one of \(z_{i}\) and \(w_{i}\) must vanish. For example, when M is the identity, a negative entry of q is compensated by a positive z entry, while a positive q entry remains in w. For a general matrix the coordinates interact, so the zero pattern cannot be chosen independently.

The P-matrix condition guarantees exactly one solution for every right-hand side q. This removes failure of existence and ambiguity of the answer, yet does not supply a polynomial-time method to find that answer. The distinction is a central example of total search: a mathematical existence theorem can be much easier to state than a fast algorithmic realization.

Exact rational output is meaningful in the bit model. Once a complementary zero pattern is fixed, the remaining coordinates satisfy a nonsingular rational linear system on a principal submatrix. Determinant bounds give polynomial bit length for the solution. Thus the question does not hide an unavoidable exponentially long output.

Several matrix subclasses admit polynomial algorithms. Results for tridiagonal and Hessenberg P-matrices demonstrate how additional structure can make the problem tractable. Such restrictions are absent from this card. Likewise, a polynomial iteration count involving a condition-dependent parameter does not give a polynomial bound in the full input length without a bound on that parameter.

ETH’s 2025 research report identifies general P-matrix LCP as a major unresolved optimization question and relates it to unique-sink orientations. The current target concerns solving rational LCP instances, not recognizing the P-matrix promise and not solving every abstract orientation problem. It complements the existing cards for linear programming and exact semidefinite feasibility.

cards.title: Beck–Fiala conjecture
cards.formal: Is there a universal \(C>0\) such that, for all integers \(m,n,t\ge 1\) and every \(A\in \{0,1\}^{m\times n}\) having at most t ones in each column, some \(x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}\) satisfies \(\max _{i} |\sum _{j} A_{ij}x_{j}|\le C\sqrt{t}\)?
cards.definitions: The matrix is the incidence matrix of a finite set system: its columns are elements and its rows are sets. Thus each element belongs to at most t sets. Empty sets and unused elements are allowed. The bound is independent of the number of elements and sets. The question asks for existence of a signing, without an algorithmic time requirement.

context_blocks.text: Bounded element frequency is a basic sparsity assumption in rounding problems. The conjecture asks whether its discrepancy cost is proportional to the square root of the frequency even when the system is arbitrarily large.

Recent results prove this scale for substantial ranges of t relative to the size of the system. The full statement includes all frequencies and remains stronger than those range-restricted results. The separate Komlós conjecture implies this statement by rescaling each incidence column.

cards.title: Woodall’s conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite weakly connected loopless directed multigraph D that is not strongly connected, let \(\tau (D)\) be the minimum size of a directed cut. Must D contain \(\tau (D)\) pairwise arc-disjoint dijoins?
cards.definitions:
A directed multigraph has a finite vertex set V and a finite set A of individually distinguished arcs; parallel arcs are allowed and loops are excluded. Weak connectivity means connectivity after forgetting arc directions. Strong connectivity means that every ordered pair of vertices is joined by a directed path. For \(\varnothing 
e U\subsetneq V\), let \(\delta ^{+}(U)\) be the arcs with tail in U and head outside U, and \(\delta ^{-}(U)\) the arcs entering U. A directed cut, or dicut, is \(\delta ^{+}(U)\) with \(\delta ^{-}(U)=\varnothing\). Under the stated graph assumptions the family of dicuts is nonempty and each dicut has positive size, so \(	au (D)=\min \{|\delta ^{+}(U)|:\varnothing 
e U\subsetneq V, \delta ^{-}(U)=\varnothing\}\) is a finite positive integer. A dijoin is a subset \(J\subseteq A\) meeting every dicut. Pairwise arc-disjoint means \(J_{i}\cap J_{j}=\varnothing\) for \(i
e j\). Every arc has unit capacity; no zero-capacity arcs or other weights are included.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of \(\tau (D)\) pairwise disjoint dijoins for every stated D, or give a finite D satisfying the assumptions and prove that its maximum packing is smaller than \(\tau (D)\). Since each dijoin must meet a smallest dicut, \(\tau (D)\) is always an upper bound. An approximation by a constant fraction of \(\tau , a\) fractional packing, or a theorem confined to a proper graph subclass is partial progress.

context_blocks.text: A dijoin selects arcs that collectively intercept every one-way boundary of a digraph. Packing dijoins asks how many separate selections can provide this complete coverage without sharing an arc. The smallest one-way boundary is an immediate bottleneck. Woodall’s conjecture says that this visible bottleneck is the only obstruction.

Schrijver lists this exact min–max equality as Survey Question 34. The adjacent Question 33 asks for a polynomial-time algorithm finding a maximum packing. The equality is the structural target here; no efficient construction is demanded as part of a positive answer.

The absence of weights matters. The stronger Edmonds–Giles statement permits arcs of capacity zero as well as one and is false. Deleting a zero-capacity arc can change which sets are dicuts, so it cannot generally turn a weighted counterexample into an unweighted one. The current formulation avoids that false strengthening.

Cornuéjols, Liu and Ravi prove that at least \(\lfloor \tau /6\rfloor\) disjoint dijoins can be constructed in polynomial time. Their argument connects dijoin packing to nowhere-zero flows in the underlying undirected graph. This supplies a constant-factor guarantee while retaining the exact Woodall equality as open.

Weakly disconnected graphs have a zero-size cut and give a trivial zero-packing case. Strongly connected graphs have no dicuts, making the empty set a vacuous dijoin. Restricting the statement to the nontrivial case fixes the meaning of the minimum and maximum without changing the substantive conjecture.

This belongs to combinatorial optimization through the relation between packing and covering, integrality and constructive approximation. It is distinct from a minimum-cost dijoin problem or from maximum directed cut: those optimize different objects, even though some of the vocabulary overlaps.

cards.title: Log-squared query complexity for fixed-dimensional Tarski
cards.formal: Let \(Q(n,k)\) be the minimum worst-case number of adaptive deterministic value queries needed to find any fixed point of an unknown monotone function $f:[n]^k\to[n]^k$, where \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and monotonicity is with respect to coordinatewise order. A query at x reveals the entire vector \(f(x)\). Is it true that for every integer \(k\ge 1\) there is a constant \(C_{k}\) such that $Q(n,k)\le C_k(1+\log_2 n)^2$ for every \(n\ge 2\)? Arbitrary finite computation between queries is allowed. Constants may depend on k but not on n or f. This asks for an exponent independent of the fixed dimension, not a polynomial bound on \(C_{k}\).
cards.definitions: For x,y in the grid, \(x\le y\) means \(x_{i}\le y_{i}\) for every coordinate i. The oracle is promised to satisfy \(x\le y\) implies \(f(x)\le f(y)\). A valid output is any x with \(f(x)=x\); no minimum or maximum fixed point is required. An adaptive query procedure can choose each query using all earlier queries and answers, and must terminate correctly for every promised oracle. Equivalently, \(Q(n,k)\) is the minimum depth of a finite deterministic oracle decision tree whose leaves output valid fixed points for every monotone function consistent with that leaf. Neither a circuit description nor the table of f is part of the input. Query cost is one per returned vector, and places no restriction on the bit complexity of choosing the next query. The finite product grid is a complete lattice, so a fixed point always exists.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the bound for every fixed k, or show that there is a fixed k for which \(Q(n,k)/(1+\log _{2} n)^{2}\) is unbounded as n grows. A growing factor depending only on k is permitted. A bound whose logarithmic exponent grows with k does not answer yes. A lower bound obtained only by letting k grow with n does not answer no unless it implies failure at some fixed k.
cards.why: This probes the information cost of finding a guaranteed fixed point under monotonicity, a basic organizing principle in algorithms, semantics, and equilibrium computation. The same sharp bound in dimensions two, three, and four makes the dependence on dimension a substantive structural mystery rather than just a loose analysis of one algorithm.

importance.reason: A broad oracle-complexity question about monotone fixed points, with a surprising low-dimensional pattern and connections to equilibrium search. It distinguishes intrinsic information requirements from implementation time.

progress.text: Etessami, Papadimitriou, Rubinstein, and Yannakakis prove an \(Omega(\log ^{2} n)\) lower bound already in two dimensions, including for randomized algorithms; the 2022 seminar records this starting point.
Fearnley, Pálvölgyi, and Savani give an \(O(\log ^{2} n)\)-query algorithm in three dimensions, matching the two-dimensional lower bound.

Brânzei, Phillips, and Recker prove randomized query lower bound \(Omega(k \log ^{2} n / \log  k)\) for \(n,k\ge 2\). For fixed k this remains quadratic in log n, so it does not rule out the card’s target.

Chen, Li, and Yannakakis obtain \(O(\log ^{2} n)\) queries in four dimensions and improve the exponent in every fixed dimension. Section 9 proposes the possibility of a generic dimension-dependent constant times \(\log ^{2} n\).

context_blocks.text: Starting at the bottom of the grid and repeatedly applying f gives a nondecreasing chain until a fixed point is reached. This directly proves existence constructively, but the chain can contain a number of steps proportional to n times the dimension. Since the coordinates need only log n bits to describe, dependence on n can be exponentially larger than dependence on the coordinate description length.

One-dimensional search can exploit order by repeatedly discarding a large interval. In a product order, two points can be incomparable: one coordinate is larger and another smaller. The oracle’s monotonicity then does not directly compare their images. The question asks whether these multidimensional interactions must eventually increase the power of log n, or whether they can be absorbed into a dimension-dependent constant.

The first surprise was that dimensions two and three both have \(Theta(\log ^{2} n)\) query complexity. Chen, Li, and Yannakakis extend this equality to dimension four in their March 2026 preprint. Their more general upper bound is \(O(\log ^{\operatorname{ceil}((k-1)/3)+1} n)\) for fixed k. The concluding discussion explicitly raises a bound of the form \(f(k) \log ^{2} n\), which is the target on this card.

Query complexity and computational efficiency must be separated here. The 2026 algorithm uses expensive intermediate search and counting; its authors leave a time-efficient implementation open. Even a positive answer to this card would only limit how much oracle information is needed. Obtaining a polynomial-time algorithm when both k and log n are input parameters would require additional control of the constants and the work between queries.

cards.title: Constant-factor entrywise \(\ell_1\) rank-\(k\) approximation with variable \(k\)
cards.formal: Do a uniform randomized polynomial-bit-time algorithm \(A\) and an absolute constant \(C\ge1\) exist such that, for every rational matrix \(M\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times n}\) and input integer \(0\le k\le\min(m,n)\), \(A\) returns rational factors \(U\in\mathbb{Q}^{m\times k}\), \(V\in\mathbb{Q}^{k\times n}\) satisfying \[\|M-UV\|_1\le C\operatorname{OPT}_k(M),\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_k(M)=\min_{\substack{B\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}\\\operatorname{rank}(B)\le k}}\|M-B\|_1,\] with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input?
cards.definitions: \(m,n\ge 1\); dimensions, k and each signed rational numerator and positive denominator are explicitly encoded in binary. The input length L counts the whole dense matrix description. \(\|W\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}|W_{ij}|\) is the entrywise norm; rank is matrix rank over \(\mathbb{R}\). The optimum is over all real \(m\times n\) matrices of rank at most k and is attained, since a minimizing sequence can be confined to a bounded closed sublevel set. The output consists of binary rational entries of U and V; for \(k=0\) their product denotes the zero matrix. There is a single polynomial P such that A halts within \(P(L)\) Turing-machine steps on every input and every random tape, including the time to write its factors. Therefore the factors have polynomial total encoded length; no unit-cost exact real arithmetic or implicit algebraic-number oracle is available. The approximation factor C and polynomial exponent are independent of m,n,k and entry magnitudes. The probability is over independent fair algorithm coins for each fixed input. Only the displayed multiplicative error is allowed. In particular, when \(\operatorname{rank}(M)\le k\) and \(\operatorname{OPT}_{k}(M)=0\), success requires exact equality \(UV=M\). When the optimum is positive the output need not be an exact real minimizer: the task asks for rational factors meeting the constant-factor inequality. This is the explicit rational bit-model completion of the imported approximation question, not a claim that optimal real factors are rational or efficiently computable.

context_blocks.text: Entrywise absolute error is a standard robust alternative to squared reconstruction error. Exact rank control and a constant independent of k distinguish the target from bicriteria or rank-dependent guarantees.

The existing TCS-7008 asks for a near-optimal relative approximation and does not resolve the weaker but separately significant constant-factor tractability threshold with growing rank. Known fixed-k schemes permit a polynomial exponent depending on k and therefore do not meet this target.

cards.why: Determine whether robust low-rank compression remains computationally tractable with unrestricted target rank.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof that such an algorithm and absolute factor exist with the stated uniform bit bounds, or a Lean proof of their nonexistence. A factor depending on the rank, a polynomial exponent depending on the rank, output rank above the requested rank, or uncharged exact-real computation does not meet this criterion.

cards.title: Input-sparsity relative spectral low-rank approximation
cards.formal: Is there a randomized algorithm and absolute constants \(C,b>0\) that, for every real \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\), integer \(1\leq k<n\) and rational \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\), returns \(Z\in\mathbb R^{n\times k}\) with orthonormal columns such that \[\|A-ZZ^{\mathsf T}A\|_2\leq(1+\varepsilon)\min_{\operatorname{rank}(B)\leq k}\|A-B\|_2\] with probability at least \(2/3\), using at most \(C\operatorname{nnz}(A)+Cn(k/\varepsilon)^b\) operations?
cards.why: Relative spectral approximation protects every direction of a compressed linear operator, making it useful where a small average error is insufficient. Resolving the question would determine whether this stronger guarantee can share the basic input-reading cost of fast Frobenius approximation, without rank or accuracy multiplying the sparse-data term.

sentences: Spectral low-rank approximation seeks a rank-k representation whose largest directional error is near the best possible.
The source asks for a relative-error guarantee in time equal to reading the nonzero matrix entries plus a term linear in n and polynomial in k over epsilon.

cards.definitions: The matrix is given as a list of its nonzero entries, each with its row index, column index and real value; unspecified entries are zero and index pairs do not repeat. The integer \(\operatorname{nnz}(A)\) is the length of this list. The spectral norm is \(\|D\|_2=\sup_{\|x\|_2=1}\|Dx\|_2\). For singular values \(\sigma_1(A)\geq\cdots\geq\sigma_n(A)\geq0\), the optimum on the right is \(\sigma_{k+1}(A)\). Orthonormality means \(Z^{\mathsf T}Z=I_k\), so \(ZZ^{\mathsf T}\) is an orthogonal projection of rank \(k\). The output is the explicit matrix \(Z\); forming the generally dense product \(ZZ^{\mathsf T}A\) is not required. All real input matrices are included, with no gap, conditioning, spectral-decay, positivity or distributional promise. If \(\operatorname{rank}(A)\leq k\), the required residual is exactly zero on a successful run. The selected arithmetic model is a uniform real RAM with unit-cost addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square root of a nonnegative value, real comparison, and indexed memory access. Registers store exact reals or integer indices; integer indexing arithmetic is charged, and no real-to-integer floor or bit extraction is a free primitive. Independent fair random bits and independent standard normal real samples are available at unit cost. This explicitly adopts the ideal arithmetic and sampling convention used in randomized numerical linear algebra; bit complexity is not the target. The operation bound includes reading the input, all preprocessing, random sampling and writing the output, and must hold on every random run. Only correctness may fail with probability at most one third, separately for each fixed input. A single algorithm and the same constants work for all parameters; \(n\geq2\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm and proofs of its probability guarantee and stated arithmetic running time, or prove that no such algorithm exists in this model. The coefficient of the nonzero-entry term must be an absolute constant: multiplying that term by k, inverse accuracy or logarithms of n misses the target. Frobenius-norm error, additive spectral error, extra output rank, or a bound conditional on a singular-value gap does not establish the displayed claim.

context_blocks.text: Woodruff’s Open Question 1 asks whether the input-sparsity bound for relative Frobenius approximation can also give the relative spectral projection guarantee in Equation (65). The card makes the arithmetic model, success probability and output representation explicit; it retains the square-matrix target.

The Frobenius norm sums squared errors over all entries, whereas the spectral norm controls the largest error in a unit direction. A relative Frobenius guarantee therefore need not provide a relative spectral guarantee when many small singular values contribute to the total tail energy.

The survey presents a spectral approximation based on repeated matrix products, but its dependence on repeated passes and the target rank does not have the requested additive input-sparsity form. Its Frobenius result already achieves that form.

Bakshi, Bhattacharyya, Kannan, Woodruff and Zhou’s 2021 latent-simplex algorithm obtains input-sparsity time under a spectral-mass assumption. Their paper connects removal of that assumption to a breakthrough for spectral low-rank approximation, rather than claiming to solve the unrestricted matrix problem.

A bound of the form input size plus a polynomial in rank and accuracy times n matters especially when a large sparse matrix can be read once but cannot cheaply be multiplied by many vectors. The additive second term also accommodates the n-by-k output. No explicit n-by-n projection is requested.

cards.title: Superlinear randomized query lower bounds for submodular minimization
cards.formal: Let \(R(n)\) be the minimum worst-case number of value-oracle queries needed by a randomized algorithm to find an exact minimizer of every real-valued submodular function on \(n\) elements, with success probability at least \(2/3\). Is \(R(n)=\omega(n)\), meaning \(R(n)/n\to\infty\) as \(n\to\infty\)?

cards.why: Submodular minimization is a central tractable optimization problem, yet its information requirements remain far from its best general algorithms. A superlinear randomized lower bound would establish that even unlimited computation and adaptive random querying cannot reduce exact minimization to a linear amount of oracle information.

sentences: A value oracle answers exact evaluations of an unknown submodular set function.
The randomized algorithm must find a true global minimizer on every input with constant success probability.
The question asks whether the worst-case query requirement grows faster than every constant multiple of the ground-set size.
Neither numeric evaluation cost nor local computation is charged.
Known deterministic and parallel-round lower bounds do not settle this randomized total-query question.

cards.definitions: The ground set is \([n]\), and a function \(F:2^{[n]}\to\mathbb R\) is submodular if \(F(A)+F(B)\geq F(A\cup B)+F(A\cap B)\) for all subsets \(A,B\). No monotonicity, nonnegativity, symmetry or normalization is promised. A query specifies any subset \(S\) and receives its exact real value \(F(S)\). The algorithm may adapt later queries to all previous values and its own random choices. Its final answer is a subset \(S_*\) satisfying \(F(S_*)\leq F(S)\) for every \(S\subseteq[n]\); any minimizer is acceptable, including the empty or full set. For every fixed valid oracle \(F\), the probability of a correct output is at least \(2/3\). In the definition of \(R(n)\), a cost bound \(q\) requires at most \(q\) oracle calls on every input and every outcome of the random choices, not just in expectation. Arbitrary finite local computation and exact operations on the oracle answers are free. The algorithm has no direct access to a formula, table or circuit for \(F\). We use classical randomized query complexity: for each dimension, random coins select a deterministic adaptive query procedure, independently of \(F\); the maps and distributions must define measurable success events. An algorithm may depend on \(n\), so lower bounds also apply to nonuniform choices. The value magnitudes and their bit encodings do not enter the query cost. Exhaustively querying all \(2^n\) subsets shows that \(R(n)\) is finite. A superlinear lower bound means that for each real constant \(C>0\), all sufficiently large \(n\) satisfy \(R(n)>Cn\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked superlinear lower bound in the specified randomized bounded-query model. Alternatively prove the negation of that growth statement: a fixed constant C and infinitely many dimensions admit correct algorithms using at most Cn queries. An O(n)-query algorithm for all dimensions would suffice for a negative answer but is stronger than the logical negation. A deterministic lower bound, a lower bound on parallel rounds, or hardness only for finding a nonempty proper minimizer does not establish the target.

context_blocks.text: The source proves an Ω(n log n) deterministic query lower bound and explicitly asks for a superlinear randomized one. The selected target is any unbounded multiplicative improvement over n, rather than a demand for the same n log n expression.

In the deterministic construction, an adversary can exploit the algorithm’s fixed queries to delay discovery of a hidden set. The paper explains why random subsets can defeat the local obstruction used for that logarithmic factor. Transferring the deterministic proof without a new randomized argument is therefore insufficient.

The paper also proves a nearly linear lower bound on the number of adaptive parallel rounds when each round permits polynomially many queries. This measures how often answers must be used to choose the next batch. It does not imply a superlinear lower bound on the total number of sequentially adaptive queries.

Earlier lower bounds include a linear bound for general minimization and stronger statements for nontrivial minimizers of certain function classes. The requirement to exclude the empty and full sets changes the optimization problem; this card allows both and asks for the usual unconstrained minimum.

Exact oracle values can reveal more than comparisons between candidate subsets. A lower bound in this model must survive that extra information and cannot assume a bounded numeric range unless it constructs hard functions within that range. Conversely, bit complexity of evaluating an oracle is outside the target.

Strongly polynomial query upper bounds do not depend on the range of function values. The source compares algorithms with different amounts of local computation, including exponential local time; the lower-bound target here deliberately imposes no polynomial-time restriction.

cards.title: Limited-memory convex optimization
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors, the deterministic first-order oracle complexity \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)\) of minimizing a globally convex, Euclidean \(1\)-Lipschitz function with a global minimizer in the unit ball, when only \(M\) bits can be retained between queries. sentences: First-order convex optimization learns about an objective through queries returning its value and a subgradient.
The source asks how the number of queries needed for a prescribed accuracy changes when the algorithm has limited working memory.
It highlights methods with strong oracle complexity whose stored geometric information can require quadratic space in dimension.
The question is whether that memory cost is inherent or can be traded away without losing the optimal query rate.
A sharp tradeoff would distinguish information acquired from the oracle from information that must remain available between optimization steps.

cards.definitions: Let \(\mathcal F_d\) contain all convex functions \(f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) such that \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq\|x-y\|_2\) for every \(x,y\), and such that some global minimizer \(x_*\) satisfies \(\|x_*\|_2\leq1\). A subgradient at \(x\) is a vector \(g\) with \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,y-x\rangle\) for every \(y\in\mathbb R^d\). A query at any \(x\in\mathbb R^d\) returns the exact pair \((f(x),g)\) for any valid subgradient; correctness is required for every sequence of such choices. An \(M\)-bit, \(t\)-query algorithm consists of deterministic maps \(\phi_i:\{0,1\}^M\to\mathbb R^d\), \(\psi_i:\{0,1\}^M\times\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d\to\{0,1\}^M\) for \(1\leq i\leq t\), and \(\zeta:\{0,1\}^M\to\mathbb R^d\). Starting with \(s_0=0^M\), it queries \(x_i=\phi_i(s_{i-1})\), receives \((f(x_i),g_i)\), and sets \(s_i=\psi_i(s_{i-1},f(x_i),g_i)\). Its final output is \(\zeta(s_t)\); for \(t=0\) it is \(\zeta(s_0)\). All maps may depend on \(d,M,t,\varepsilon\), but not on the unknown function. They are unrestricted mathematical maps: computing an update can use arbitrary real operations and temporary memory. Only the retained state is limited; there is no runtime, uniformity or computability requirement on these maps. The iteration index is implicit in the maps and is not charged to memory. Define \(R(d,M,t)=\inf_A\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_d,\,(g_i)}[f(\zeta(s_t))-\min_x f(x)]\), and \(T(d,M,\varepsilon)=\min\{t\in\mathbb N_0:R(d,M,t)\leq\varepsilon\}\), with the minimum of the empty set equal to infinity. The infimum over algorithms need not be attained: \(R\leq\varepsilon\) means that for every \(\eta>0\) some algorithm has worst-case error at most \(\varepsilon+\eta\). Queries and outputs are not restricted to the unit ball.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular characterization \(G(d,M,\varepsilon)\in[0,\infty]\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(cG\leq T\leq CG\) throughout the stated domain, for fixed \(c,C>0\). Prove exactly which parameters have infinite complexity. The memory argument and requested accuracy must be those stated, without an unstated constant enlargement of memory or accuracy. Upper bounds must respect the infimum convention. Resolving only optimal-query memory requirements or one accuracy regime is not a characterization of the full tradeoff.

context_blocks.text: This is Question 1 of Woodworth and Srebro’s 2019 contribution, with its preferred constant-factor accuracy selected explicitly. The source also permits a weaker polylogarithmic characterization and poses several subsidiary endpoint questions; those alternatives are not the acceptance criterion here.

The normalization loses no scale parameter: a Lipschitz constant \(L>0\) and a known minimizer radius \(B>0\) replace the accuracy by \(\varepsilon/(LB)\). The formal target retains the source’s global-function model and its bottleneck-memory convention, rather than total machine space.

The source exhibits gradient descent with \(O(\varepsilon^{-2})\) queries and \(O(d\log(1/\varepsilon))\) retained bits, and a discretized center-of-mass method with \(O(d\log(1/\varepsilon))\) queries and \(O(d^2\log^2(1/\varepsilon))\) bits. These are achievable resource pairs; neither states the optimal query rate in every dimension and accuracy regime.

Blanchard, Zhang and Jaillet’s 2023 work establishes a nearly quadratic memory barrier for optimal query complexity in convex minimization over the unit ball. This addresses a source endpoint question, not the complete three-parameter tradeoff. Their separate recursive cutting-plane work gives additional memory-query upper bounds, including a high-accuracy regime.

Menart, Nikolov and Shamir’s July 2026 preprint strengthens deterministic and randomized lower bounds and reports a sharp transition near quadratic memory. Its stated model restricts queries to the feasible unit ball. No transfer of its numerical bounds to the global, unrestricted-query model above is assumed by this card.

A real-valued oracle answer can carry unlimited precision, but retaining it requires encoding it in the next finite state. Conversely, restricting temporary arithmetic would create a different problem. These distinctions are central to what a memory lower bound establishes.

cards.formal: For each fixed \(1\leq p<q\leq\infty\) and \(1<\kappa\leq2\), determine the optimal worst-case error \(\mathcal R_{p,q,\kappa}(n,T)\), up to constant factors, of deterministic algorithms making \(T\) exact first-order queries to minimize a convex function whose gradient is Hölder continuous in the \(\ell_q\) geometry over the unit \(\ell_p\) ball. cards.why: The problem isolates whether the geometry of a constrained model can improve the fundamental convergence rate when smoothness is measured differently. sentences: Smooth convex optimization is often analyzed when the objective's regularity and the feasible region use compatible norms.
The source instead studies settings where these geometries differ, including vector norms and their matrix counterparts.
It asks for the optimal oracle complexity of minimizing such functions using black-box first-order information.

cards.definitions:
For \(1\leq s<\infty\), put \(\|x\|_s=(\sum_{i=1}^n|x_i|^s)^{1/s}\), and put \(\|x\|_\infty=\max_i|x_i|\). Write \(B_p^n=\{x:\|x\|_p\leq1\}\). The conjugate exponent \(q_*\) is defined by \(1/q+1/q_*=1\), with \(1/\infty=0\). Let \(\mathcal F_{q,\kappa}^n\) be the class of all continuously differentiable convex functions \(f:\mathbb R^n	o\mathbb R\) such that \[\|
abla f(x)-
abla f(y)\|_{q_*}\leq\|x-y\|_q^{\kappa-1}\qquad(x,y\in\mathbb R^n).\] There is no bound on the affine part of \(f\), no strong-convexity assumption and no promise of a sparse minimizer. One oracle query at any \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) returns the exact pair \((f(x),
abla f(x))\). A deterministic algorithm chooses each query as a function of the parameters and previous answers, and after at most \(T\) queries outputs \(\widehat x\in B_p^n\). It receives no explicit formula, data matrix, decomposition, proximal oracle or higher derivative. All computation between queries is free and unrestricted; arbitrary deterministic decision maps depending on \(n,T,p,q,\kappa\) are allowed, with no uniformity or bit-precision restriction. Its error is \(f(\widehat x)-\min_{x\in B_p^n}f(x)\). Define \(\mathcal R_{p,q,\kappa}(n,T)=\inf_A\sup_{f\in\mathcal F_{q,\kappa}^n}[f(\widehat x_A(f))-\min_{B_p^n}f]\). Allowing an output outside the ball with error infinity gives the same definition. The minimum of each function exists because the ball is compact. The infimum over algorithms need not be attained. A Hölder bound with constant \(L>0\) and a feasible ball of radius \(R>0\) scales this risk by \(LR^\kappa\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a noncircular rate \(G_{p,q,\kappa}(n,T)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(c_{p,q,\kappa}G\leq\mathcal R\leq C_{p,q,\kappa}G\) over the entire stated domain, with positive constants independent of \(n,T\). The upper bound may be approached arbitrarily closely if the minimax infimum is not attained. Both the query and dimension dependence, including any logarithmic factors needed for constant-factor matching, must be established. A result for one pair of norms or for a stronger oracle alone does not characterize this family.

context_blocks.text: Guzmán’s 2015 Open Problem 1 asks for large-scale minimax rates when the feasible ball and the smoothness norm differ. This card explicitly selects the vector case \(p<q\), where the reported gaps are substantial, and exact value-and-gradient access. The source also discusses matrix Schatten norms and a more general class of local oracles; those are related extensions rather than additional requirements.

When \(p<q\), the unit \(\ell_p\) ball is contained in the unit \(\ell_q\) ball. The source asks whether algorithms can exploit this smaller feasible geometry more effectively than methods analyzed only in the smoothness norm.

For \(p=1,q=2,\kappa=2\), the source compares an accelerated \(O(T^{-2})\) upper bound with a lower bound of order \(T^{-3}\), up to logarithmic factors, in its large-scale regime. These are dated nonmatching bounds, not a claimed present-day formula for the minimax risk.

Convex regression over a norm-constrained predictor class motivates the problem. Access to the complete regression data can supply structure unavailable to a first-order black box, so a faster algorithm for one explicit regression loss does not automatically determine this oracle complexity.

Adil, Bullins, Jambulapati and Sidford’s 2026 work studies stronger norm-dependent proximal oracles that solve a regularized minimization problem in one call. Its accelerated rates and matching span-restricted lower bounds concern that different information model.

The precision requested here concerns asymptotic error rates as the query budget and dimension vary. It is not an additive numerical tolerance on the risk. Constants may depend on the fixed norm and smoothness exponents; dependence on dimension cannot be hidden there.

sentences: Two unknown matroids are accessed only by tests of whether a proposed subset is independent.
The algorithm must output a large set independent in both matroids.
The target is deterministic approximation arbitrarily close to optimum with near-linear query complexity.
The guarantee must cover every common rank, without stronger rank queries or matrix representations.
Randomized near-linear schemes and a deterministic two-thirds approximation are known.

cards.definitions: A matroid on \(V=[n]\) is a family \(\mathcal I\subseteq2^V\) containing the empty set, closed under taking subsets, and satisfying augmentation: if \(X,Y\in\mathcal I\) and \(|X|<|Y|\), some \(e\in Y\setminus X\) has \(X\cup\{e\}\in\mathcal I\). The two unknown families \(\mathcal I_1,\mathcal I_2\) are supplied through separate exact independence oracles. A query specifies an index \(j\in\{1,2\}\) and a subset \(S\subseteq[n]\), and returns one bit indicating whether \(S\in\mathcal I_j\). The total number of calls to both oracles is charged, including repeated calls. Queries may depend on all previous answers. The algorithm knows \(n\) and \(\varepsilon\), but need not be told \(r=\max\{|S|:S\in\mathcal I_1\cap\mathcal I_2\}\), and receives no representation, rank oracle or additional promise. It must output the elements of a feasible common independent set, not merely estimate \(r\). The guarantee must hold for every pair of matroids and every attainable \(0\leq r\leq n\); loops, parallel elements, unequal matroid ranks and rank zero are allowed. Computation between queries is unrestricted but finite, and the algorithm is deterministic and uniform over \(n\) and the binary accuracy parameter. The target measures query complexity rather than arithmetic or bit running time. The constants and exponents in the displayed bound are independent of the matroids, \(n,r\) and \(\varepsilon\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm with the stated feasibility, approximation and query bounds, or prove that no such deterministic approximation scheme exists in this oracle model. A randomized scheme, a nearly linear scheme only when the common rank is a constant fraction of n, or a scheme that uses stronger rank queries does not decide the target.

context_blocks.text: Terao’s 2025 paper explicitly asks whether deterministic near-linear-query approximation can approach one throughout the rank range. Its soft-O convention permits polynomial factors in inverse accuracy and logarithms of n; the displayed bound makes those factors explicit.

For two partition matroids representing the endpoints of a bipartite graph, common independent sets are matchings. General matroids can hide much more information behind each membership bit, so algorithms for explicitly represented graphs alone do not answer the oracle question.

A greedy maximal common independent set gives a one-half approximation with a linear number of independence queries. Terao improves the ratio to two thirds minus an accuracy term with O(n/ε+r log r) queries. This is a fixed approximation threshold, not an arbitrarily accurate scheme.

Blikstad and Tu achieve a near-linear-query randomized approximation scheme. Their work also provides a deterministic strictly linear-query guarantee in the large-common-rank regime for fixed accuracy. These results show why neither randomization nor the quantifier over all ranks can be omitted.

Terao’s 2026 algorithm for linear matroid intersection accesses two explicit matrices and exploits linear-algebraic structure. Its input-sparsity running time is a different resource guarantee and does not yield a deterministic near-linear membership-query algorithm for arbitrary matroids.

Taking ε very small eventually forces an exact answer because the output size is integral. This causes no contradiction with exact-intersection lower bounds: the allowed polynomial dependence on 1/ε may then be large. The interesting approximation regime fixes accuracy while n and the optimum rank vary.

cards.title: Polynomial-time linear convergence for geodesically convex optimization
cards.formal: In the geometric arithmetic model below, is there a deterministic first-order algorithm and absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) that minimize every Lipschitz geodesically convex function on a strongly geodesically convex ball in a complete Riemannian manifold, using at most \(C(d+\zeta)^a\lceil\log(2/\varepsilon)\rceil\) objective-oracle queries and at most \(C(d+\zeta)^b\) additional operations between consecutive queries? Here \(d\) is the manifold dimension, \(\zeta=r\sqrt K/\tanh(r\sqrt K)\), with value one at \(K=0\), and the required additive objective error is \(\varepsilon Lr\). The same polynomial overhead bound applies before the first query and after the last.
cards.why: Euclidean cutting-plane methods show that high accuracy need not require a polynomial number of inverse-accuracy steps. Extending that efficiency to geodesic convexity would provide a general computational foundation for optimization on curved spaces, including matrix geometries used in scaling and statistical models.
cards.status_note: The joint query-and-computation question is open in the 2023 source. A bounded review on 13 September 2026 did not find a resolution for the full geodesically convex class. The computational oracle convention is an explicit editorial specification, not a claim that all manifolds admit efficient finite-precision geometric implementations.
