It also requires polynomial arithmetic work per query, so a powerful but computationally intractable geometric oracle would not suffice.
The source develops an ellipsoid-like approach for constant-curvature spaces and identifies obstacles on more general manifolds.
A solution would extend the efficient precision dependence of Euclidean convex optimization to curved spaces while respecting the cost of manipulating their geometry.

cards.definitions: The input consists of a complete connected smooth \(d\)-dimensional Riemannian manifold \(\mathcal M\), \(d\geq1\), a reference point \(x_0\), a radius \(r>0\), a Lipschitz bound \(L>0\), a sectional-curvature bound \(K\geq0\), and real \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\). All sectional curvatures lie in \([-K,K]\). The distance \(\operatorname{dist}\) is the infimum of lengths of connecting curves in the given Riemannian metric. The closed ball \(D=\{x:\operatorname{dist}(x_0,x)\leq r\}\) is promised strongly geodesically convex: every two points of \(D\) have a unique minimizing geodesic in \(\mathcal M\), and its whole segment lies in \(D\). If \(\gamma\) is such a segment parametrized on \([0,1]\) at constant speed, the unknown function \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) satisfies \(f(\gamma(t))\leq(1-t)f(\gamma(0))+tf(\gamma(1))\), and \(|f(x)-f(y)|\leq L\operatorname{dist}(x,y)\). A function query at \(x\in D\) returns \(f(x)\) exactly and any tangent vector \(g\in T_x\mathcal M\) satisfying \(f(y)\geq f(x)+\langle g,\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\rangle_x\) for every \(y\in D\); correctness is required for every valid sequence of returned subgradients. Here \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\) is the initial velocity at time zero of the unit-time minimizing geodesic from \(x\) to \(y\). Only functions and subgradient oracles meeting these conditions are inputs. The output must be a point \(\widehat x\in D\) with \(f(\widehat x)-\min_D f\leq\varepsilon Lr\). Completeness makes the closed bounded ball compact, so this minimum exists. The algorithm has no access to a formula for \(f\). For computational access to geometry, points and tangent vectors are exact typed objects supplied by a geometric oracle; the input includes an orthonormal basis of \(T_{x_0}\mathcal M\). The available geometric operations are: distance between points; inner product of two vectors in one tangent space; linear combination of such vectors; \(\operatorname{Exp}_x(v)\), the time-one point of the geodesic with initial velocity \(v\); \(\operatorname{Log}_x(y)\) for \(x,y\in D\); and parallel transport of a tangent vector along the explicitly specified geodesic \(t\mapsto\operatorname{Exp}_x(tv)\), \(0\leq t\leq1\). Each such operation is charged \((d+1)^3\) units, irrespective of point or vector magnitude. Object storage and access cost one unit; objects cannot be inspected except by these operations. Exact real scalar addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square root on nonnegative arguments, exponential, logarithm on positive arguments, comparisons and integer indexing operations each cost one unit. There is no floor or extraction of bits from a real register. All computation, including geometric operations, is charged apart from the separately counted function queries. One uniform finite program must work for every admissible manifold, basis, oracle and parameter tuple. There is no randomization, integral oracle, convex-hull oracle or free optimization subroutine.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked algorithm with the required uniform objective accuracy, logarithmic query dependence on inverse accuracy, and polynomial overhead independent of inverse accuracy, or prove that no such algorithm exists in the stated access model. A query bound with an uncomputable geometric step, a theorem only for a particular manifold, or an additional logarithmic factor in the query count does not meet the target. A negative result must allow the full list of geometric primitives provided here.

context_blocks.text: This retains the manifold, curvature, ball and objective quantifiers of the source’s Open Question 1. The source leaves the computational representation of a general manifold implicit. The listed exact geometric primitives and their costs are an explicit editorial choice making its arithmetic-overhead requirement testable. A result in this model is not automatically a polynomial bit-complexity result for an arbitrary encoded metric.

The parameter \(\zeta\) is comparable within universal constants to \(1+r\sqrt K\). It allows dependence on the curvature scale and radius. The source explains that curvature dependence cannot generally be removed, even though logarithmic dependence on inverse accuracy remains the requested target.

The source distinguishes methods with good query complexity but expensive geometric work from subgradient methods with cheap steps but slower precision dependence. Thus proving either resource guarantee separately does not settle the joint question.

For constant-curvature spaces the source gives an ellipsoid-like method with \(O(\zeta d^2\log^2(1/\varepsilon))\) queries and polynomial per-query work. This is a substantial partial result, but its extra logarithm and restricted geometry are both relevant to the full statement.

Positive definite matrices with the affine-invariant Riemannian metric are an important nonconstant-curvature example discussed by the source. Boumal’s textbook gives explicit distance, exponential and logarithmic maps for that geometry. These differ from the log-Euclidean metric, under which a coordinate logarithm makes convexity Euclidean.

Criscitiello and Kim’s 2025 work develops algorithms for horospherical convexity, a stronger geometric notion with additional structure. It does not by itself supply the required method for every geodesically convex objective in this question.

cards.title: Gap-entropy conjecture
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants \(0<c\leq C<\infty\) such that, for every Gaussian best-arm instance \(I\) defined below and every \(0<\delta<1/10\), \[cH(I)\bigl(\log(1/\delta)+\operatorname{Ent}(I)\bigr)\leq L(I,\delta)\leq CH(I)\bigl(\log(1/\delta)+\operatorname{Ent}(I)\bigr)?\] Here \(L\) is the order-oblivious instance-wise optimum over globally correct sampling algorithms, not the performance of one algorithm required to attain the bound on every instance.
cards.why: The conjecture predicts the full instance-sensitive cost of identifying the best alternative, including the cost of learning which gap scales matter. Its entropy term would explain why instances with the same total inverse-square gap can have different exploration costs at fixed confidence.
cards.status_note: A preprint submitted on 9 September 2026 explicitly claims a positive resolution of this exact Gaussian instance-wise conjecture. Its Theorem 1.1 matches the target and its separate uniform-algorithm theorem addresses the related conjecture. This 13 September review has not independently checked the entire proof or located an established validation, so the status is uncertain, not source-open and not certified resolved.

sentences: The arms have independent Gaussian rewards with unit variance and a unique best mean.
The benchmark averages expected sample cost over arm relabelings and takes an infimum over globally correct algorithms.
The conjecture predicts that cost from the total inverse-square gaps and the entropy of their scale distribution.
It differs from asking one algorithm to attain the benchmark on all instances without an adaptation cost.
A 9 September 2026 preprint claims the precise formula; its proof has not been independently certified in this review.

cards.definitions: An instance has \(n\geq2\) independent arms with distributions \(\mathcal N(\mu_i,1)\), unknown means \(\mu_i\in[0,1]\), and a unique largest mean \(\mu_*\) at index \(*\). Each pull of arm \(i\) reveals a fresh independent sample from its distribution. An adaptive sampling algorithm knows \(n\) and \(\delta\), chooses pulls using earlier samples and independent internal randomness, and eventually outputs an arm index. It is \(\delta\)-correct if on every valid instance it stops almost surely and outputs its unique best arm with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Local computation is unrestricted; the resource is total number of pulls, and expectations include sampling noise and algorithmic randomness. Algorithms are measurable so that these probabilities and expectations are defined. Let \(T_A(I)\in[0,\infty]\) be the expected number of pulls. If \(S_n\) is the set of all permutations of arm labels and \(\pi I\) is the corresponding relabeled instance, define \(L(I,\delta)=\inf_A (1/n!)\sum_{\pi\in S_n}T_A(\pi I)\), where the infimum ranges over algorithms correct on every instance of the same Gaussian model. The infimum is taken separately for each \(I,\delta\): an algorithm selected for favorable performance at I must nevertheless remain correct on all other instances. It need not attain the infimum. For each suboptimal arm, set \(\Delta_i=\mu_*-\mu_i\in(0,1]\), and \(H(I)=\sum_{i\ne *}\Delta_i^{-2}\). For integers \(r\geq0\), set \(G_r=\{i\ne *:2^{-(r+1)}<\Delta_i\leq2^{-r}\}\), \(H_r=\sum_{i\in G_r}\Delta_i^{-2}\), and \(p_r=H_r/H(I)\). The gap entropy is \(\operatorname{Ent}(I)=\sum_{r:p_r>0}p_r\log(1/p_r)\), with natural logarithms. Only finitely many groups are nonempty. The constants in the conjecture are independent of n, all means, the number of gap scales and δ.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of both uniform constant-factor bounds, or prove that no such universal pair of constants exists. A result only as δ tends to zero with the instance fixed, only for dyadic gaps or monotone algorithms, or an algorithm with an extra closest-gap term does not by itself prove the displayed claim about L. The recent claimed proof must meet the same mathematical and Lean-checking requirement.

context_blocks.text: This card selects Chen and Li’s Conjecture 3.5, which gives an explicit formula for the instance-wise optimum. Their separate Conjecture 3.2 asks for one algorithm attaining that optimum up to an additive two-arm adaptation term. The two statements are related but are not interchangeable.

Averaging over relabelings prevents an algorithm from gaining an artificial advantage because the best arm was placed at a preferred index. Taking an infimum over globally correct algorithms still permits a different favored sampling schedule for each target instance; it does not allow an algorithm to simply output a known best label without verifying correctness elsewhere.

Gap entropy weights a scale by its share of the inverse-square sampling burden, not by its fraction of arms. It vanishes when all gaps fall in one group and can grow when many scales carry comparable burden. The specified dyadic endpoint convention includes gaps equal to one; changing boundary conventions affects the full proposed complexity by at most constant factors.

Chen, Li and Qiao’s 2017 progress gives a nearly matching algorithmic bound and a lower bound for dyadic-gap instances under a monotonicity condition on algorithms. These restrictions and extra factors are relevant because the conjecture quantifies over all Gaussian instances and all correct algorithms.

A preprint submitted on 9 September 2026 by Aronow, Kallus and Lopatto states the displayed two-sided result as Theorem 1.1. It also states a separate uniform-algorithm theorem with the closest-gap adaptation term. The present review matched their definitions and theorem statements, but has not independently certified the complete proof.

Asymptotic confidence-optimal algorithms study δ tending to zero for a fixed instance, when log(1/δ) eventually dominates its fixed entropy. Such a limit does not determine the uniform cost when gap scales and confidence vary together. This is why the nonasymptotic quantifiers matter.

cards.title: Second-order cone lift dimension of semialgebraic convex hulls
cards.formal: Determine the function \(a(S)\) giving the minimum number of auxiliary real scalar variables in an exact second-order cone representation of \(\operatorname{conv}(S)\), for every semialgebraic set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and every integer \(n\geq1\). Set \(a(S)=\infty\) when no finite such representation exists. For finite values, the benchmark accepts a real approximation within absolute error \(1/100\); infinite values require proof of nonrepresentability.
cards.why: Second-order cone lifts expose nonlinear convex structure through a class of conic constraints with effective optimization methods. Understanding both representability and the minimum added dimension would distinguish intrinsic geometric obstacles from the overhead of particular reformulations, while keeping those questions separate from numerical relaxation quality.
cards.status_note: The general characterization and auxiliary-dimension questions are open directions in the 2018 source. The individual review on 13 September 2026 checked major obstruction and positive-family results through 2025 but found no complete determination of the selected function. No exhaustive present-day openness certification is claimed.

sentences: A semialgebraic set is described by polynomial equalities and inequalities, while its convex hull collects all convex combinations of its points.
The source asks when that convex hull can be represented using second-order cone constraints and auxiliary variables.
It also asks how many additional variables such a representation requires.
Representability is stronger than having a useful numerical relaxation, because the projected feasible region must agree exactly with the desired hull.
A structural answer would identify nonlinear models that can be converted into a tractable conic formulation and quantify the cost of that conversion.

cards.definitions: A semialgebraic set is one defined by a finite Boolean combination of polynomial equalities and strict or non-strict polynomial inequalities with real coefficients. Its convex hull is the set of all finite convex combinations of its points: \(\sum_{i=1}^t\lambda_i s_i\), where \(t\geq1\), \(s_i\in S\), \(\lambda_i\geq0\) and \(\sum_i\lambda_i=1\). The convex hull of the empty set is empty. No closure is taken, and neither compactness nor closedness is assumed. For \(d\geq2\), the Lorentz cone is \(\mathcal L_d=\{(t,z)\in\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{d-1}:t\geq\|z\|_2\}\); also let \(\mathcal L_1=\mathbb R_{\geq0}\). An admissible representation with \(r\in\mathbb N_0\) auxiliary variables has the form \[\operatorname{conv}(S)=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:\exists y\in\mathbb R^r,\ E(x,y)=e,\ F_j(x,y)\in\mathcal L_{d_j}\ (1\leq j\leq N)\},\] where \(N\geq0\), all cone dimensions \(d_j\geq1\) are finite, \(E\) is a real linear map with finitely many rows, \(e\) is a real vector, and each \(F_j\) is a real affine map into \(\mathbb R^{d_j}\). There is no bound on the number or dimensions of the cones, the number of affine equations or coefficient sizes. The number \(r\) counts only the scalar coordinates of \(y\), not the original coordinates of \(x\), the number of constraints or their output dimensions. Let \(a(S)\) be the least such \(r\), or infinity if the set of admissible integers is empty. In particular, zero auxiliary variables are allowed. The domain consists of mathematical sets with their ambient dimension, not particular defining formulas; equivalent descriptions of the same set must give the same answer. Coefficients of both the input descriptions and the lifts may be arbitrary real numbers. This is a characterization problem, not a claim that arbitrary real coefficients have finite machine encodings.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular mathematical description or certified rule for \(a\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof identifying its infinite-value domain and giving a real-valued function \(g\) with \(|g(S)-a(S)|\leq1/100\) whenever \(a(S)<\infty\). A proved interval of width at most \(1/50\) may specify a finite answer through its midpoint. The approximation need not be integer-valued. Upper-bound constructions without matching minimality information, isolated representable families, or merely repeating the defining optimization over lifts are insufficient.

context_blocks.text: Section 5.1 of the 2018 Dagstuhl report asks both when a semialgebraic convex hull has a second-order cone representation and how many extra variables are necessary. The minimum-auxiliary-dimension function combines these into one target. The displayed model is an explicit editorial convention for “extra variables”; it permits all finite Lorentz-cone dimensions and real affine coefficients.

Allowing auxiliary variables can express convex sets that are not intersections of second-order cone constraints in their original coordinates. The number of auxiliary variables differs from conic extension complexity measured by the number of cones, their total dimension, or a semidefinite matrix block size. Those measures cannot silently replace a(S).

Fawzi proves that the cone of positive semidefinite real symmetric three-by-three matrices has no second-order cone representation. Thus even a semialgebraic convex set with a direct semidefinite description can have an infinite value here.

Scheiderer proves that every closed convex semialgebraic subset of the plane is second-order cone representable. This establishes finiteness for that class, but does not on its own give the minimum number of auxiliary variables for each member.

Scheiderer’s 2025 preprint proves representability for compact convex semialgebraic sets with Nash-smooth boundary of strictly positive curvature and for Nash-smooth hyperbolicity cones. These are substantial additional sufficient conditions, not a characterization of every set or its minimum auxiliary dimension.

Exact equality matters even for nonclosed hulls: linear projections of closed conic feasible sets need not be closed. Replacing a convex hull by its closure can therefore change the problem. Since this target leaves constraint counts unrestricted, a small auxiliary dimension alone is not a polynomial runtime guarantee.

cards.title: Deterministic competitive ratio for matching with delays
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(n\to\infty\), the optimal deterministic competitive ratio \(\rho(n)\) for online minimum-cost perfect matching with linear waiting costs on a known \(n\)-point metric. The ratio must depend only on \(n\), uniformly over the number and timing of requests and all distances in the metric.
cards.why: This question measures the unavoidable cost of making irrevocable pairings while deciding how long to wait for future demand. A sharp deterministic ratio would separate the value of randomization from the difficulty of balancing spatial matching cost and elapsed waiting time in general metric spaces.
cards.status_note: The n-parameter deterministic gap is open in the 2020 source. Checks through 13 September 2026 found the major new polylogarithmic m-bound and results for other delay models, but no matching characterization of the stated n-only function. This bounded review does not exhaustively certify current openness.

sentences: Matching with delays pairs arriving requests while charging both the distance between partners and the time each request waits.
The selected question asks for the optimal deterministic competitive ratio as a function of the number of points in a known metric.
The guarantee must hold for any finite even request sequence, with no bound on its length or advance notice of its end.
A SODA 2026 algorithm gives a polylogarithmic ratio in the number of requests, which does not alone determine the ratio uniformly in metric size.
Matching bounds in the metric-size parameter would clarify the value of randomization in balancing spatial cost against waiting.

cards.definitions: A metric on \([n]\) is a symmetric map \(d:[n]^2\to\mathbb R_{\geq0}\) that vanishes exactly on equal points and satisfies the triangle inequality. The algorithm knows the whole metric before requests arrive. An input is any finite sequence of \(m\geq2\) distinctly identified requests, with \(m\) even, locations \(v_i\in[n]\), and arrival times \(0\leq a_1\leq\cdots\leq a_m<\infty\). Repeated locations and simultaneous arrivals are allowed; all requests at a given time are revealed before decisions made at that time. The algorithm does not know \(m\), future arrivals or an end-of-input time. It can irrevocably match two currently unmatched requests \(i,j\) at any real time \(t\geq\max(a_i,a_j)\), paying \(d(v_i,v_j)+(t-a_i)+(t-a_j)\). Every request must eventually be matched at a finite time on every finite even input. There are no colors, capacities or restrictions on the pairs. A deterministic online algorithm is a causal rule: its decisions through time \(t\) depend only on the known metric and requests revealed through \(t\). Computation and memory are unrestricted and uncharged, and decisions may be scheduled between arrivals. The total cost is the sum of all pair costs. The offline optimum, knowing the entire sequence, is \[\operatorname{OPT}(d,\sigma)=\min_{\text{perfect matchings }P}\sum_{\{i,j\}\in P}\bigl(d(v_i,v_j)+|a_i-a_j|\bigr),\] since an offline pair can be matched when its later request arrives. Define \(r(d)=\inf\{C\geq1:\exists A\ \forall\sigma,\ \operatorname{cost}_A(d,\sigma)\leq C\operatorname{OPT}(d,\sigma)\}\), with infinity if no finite ratio is possible, and \(\rho(n)=\sup_{d\text{ on }[n]}r(d)\), for \(n\geq2\). The algorithm in the infimum may depend on the entire metric. This is pure multiplicative competitiveness, with no additive constant; an input of optimum zero must incur zero cost. Infima over algorithms and suprema over metrics need not be attained. For deterministic rules, allowing an adaptive adversary does not change the requirement over all inputs.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a noncircular rate \(G(n)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof of \(cG(n)\leq\rho(n)\leq CG(n)\) for universal positive constants and all sufficiently large \(n\). Upper bounds must hold for every metric and all finite even request sequences; lower bounds must apply to every deterministic online algorithm in the specified model. Use approaching bounds if an extremum is not attained. A ratio depending on the request count, a randomized expected guarantee, or a theorem only for the line or uniform metrics does not determine this function.

context_blocks.text: Azar’s 2020 problem statement asks to close the deterministic competitiveness gap, expressed either through the metric size or through the number of requests. This card explicitly selects the known finite metric and metric-size parameter. Its separately mentioned red-blue matching variant is not part of the target.

The source reports an \(O(n)\) deterministic upper bound and a lower bound of order \(\log n/\log\log n\), the latter holding even against randomized algorithms. It also reports an \(O(\log n)\) randomized upper bound. These are dated source bounds and should not be conflated with a deterministic logarithmic theorem.

Dufay and Wattenhofer’s SODA 2026 result gives a deterministic \(O(\log^5 m)\)-competitive algorithm even when the metric and request count are unknown. It substantially improves the source’s request-count comparison. However, \(m\) can be arbitrarily large at fixed \(n\), so that displayed bound alone gives no uniform polylogarithmic bound in \(n\).

Gan, Sun and Umboh’s September 2026 paper studies general size-dependent delay rates and nonlinear convex waiting costs. Its tight deterministic result for the broader size-dependent model is not a matching lower bound for this fixed linear-per-request delay objective. Its uniform-metric results also have a narrower geometric scope.

Waiting may expose a nearby future partner, but it also accumulates cost on every unmatched request. The metric can have arbitrary scale and aspect ratio, making the information available from future arrivals essential even when computation of a present-day best matching is free.

cards.title: Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for every dimension \(n\ge 1\), every isotropic log-concave probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb{R} ^{n}\), and every locally Lipschitz \(f:\mathbb{R} ^{n}\to \mathbb{R}\) with finite second moment and finite gradient energy, $\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f)\le C\int\|\nabla f(x)\|_2^2\,d\mu(x)$? This is the Poincaré formulation of the Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits conjecture.
cards.definitions: The measure has a Lebesgue density \(\rho =e^{- V}\), where \(V:\mathbb{R} ^{n}\to \mathbb{R} \cup \{+\infty\}\) is convex and \(\int \rho =1\); allowing \(V=+\infty\) includes uniform distributions on full-dimensional convex bodies. Isotropy means \(\int x d\mu (x)=0\) and \(\int xx^{T} d\mu (x)=I_{n}\). Variance is \(\operatorname{Var}_{\mu}(f)=\int (f- \int f d\mu )^{2}d\mu\), and \(\nabla f\) is the almost-everywhere Euclidean gradient. Let \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu )\) be the infimum of constants that make the displayed inequality hold for all the stated f. The requested bound is \(\sup _{n} \sup_{\mu}  C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu )<\infty\), with \(\mu\) ranging over isotropic log-concave measures in \(\mathbb{R} ^{n}\). There is no symmetry, product structure, smoothness, or positive lower curvature bound on V. The universal constant may depend on none of \(n, \mu\), or f. In the isoperimetric convention used by the recent papers, \(\psi_{\mu}\) is the reciprocal Cheeger expansion constant; \(\psi_{\mu} ^{2}\) is comparable to \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu )\) up to universal factors. Thus a bound on \(\psi_{\mu}\) must be squared when expressed as a bound on the Poincaré constant used here.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: KLS links the geometry of high-dimensional convex sets to spectral gaps, concentration, and the efficiency of sampling. It asks whether covariance normalization alone removes every dimension-dependent bottleneck for log-concave measures, making it a central structural question behind continuous randomized algorithms.

importance.reason: A foundational high-dimensional geometry conjecture with substantial consequences for sampling, integration, optimization, and concentration inequalities.

progress.text: Kannan, Lovász, and Simonovits formulate the isoperimetric conjecture in connection with localization and random-walk sampling in convex bodies.
Klartag and Lehec obtain the first polylogarithmic bounds for the KLS isoperimetric constant using stochastic-localization techniques.
Klartag proves \(\psi_{\mu} =O(\sqrt{\log  n})\), equivalently \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu )=O(\log  n)\), through an improved log-concave Lichnerowicz inequality.

Klartag and Lehec settle the thin-shell conjecture. The 23 February 2026 revision controls \(E(\Vert X\Vert _{2}- \sqrt{n})^{2}\) uniformly, a particular radial concentration target rather than the full Poincaré inequality.

Letwin’s preprint reports \(\operatorname{Var}(X^{T}MX)\le 2E\Vert \nabla (X^{T}MX)\Vert _{2}^{2}\) for every symmetric M and isotropic log-concave X, and derives \(\psi _{n}=O((\log  n)^{1/4})\). In this card’s normalization the resulting general-function bound is \(C_{\mathrm{P}}=O(\sqrt{\log  n})\), not \(O((\log  n)^{1/4})\).

cards.status_note: The full KLS conjecture is explicitly open in the primary sources, including Letwin’s July 2026 preprint. Research through 10 September 2026 found no dimension-free general-function resolution. The recent quadratic-form and thin-shell results are not treated as proofs of the full conjecture; the July bound is labeled as a preprint result.

context_blocks.text: The inequality asks whether a function can vary substantially across a log-concave distribution while changing only slowly in the regions where that distribution places mass. Isotropy fixes the scale: each unit-direction linear function already has variance one and gradient energy one. The conjecture says that nonlinear functions cannot create an arbitrarily larger ratio as dimension grows.

The geometric version rules out a hidden bottleneck separating two substantial portions of the measure. For a log-concave density, the conjecture says that the best arbitrary separating set has boundary expansion comparable to an appropriate halfspace cut. Uniform distributions on convex bodies are included, so the question is not confined to smooth, strongly convex potentials where curvature can directly control a spectral gap.

The original algorithmic motivation was sampling by random walks. Poor expansion can trap a local walk in one part of a body for a long time; good expansion bounds its mixing. Sampling then supports volume estimation, integration, and convex optimization. A KLS theorem would improve the geometric ingredient in these analyses, though total algorithmic complexity would still account for access to the body, initialization, and the chosen walk.

Thin-shell concentration concerns the special observable \(\Vert X\Vert _{2}\). Klartag and Lehec’s 2025 result, revised in February 2026, bounds \(E(\Vert X\Vert _{2}- \sqrt{n})^{2}\) by a universal constant. This settles thin-shell concentration and also supports the resolved slicing question, but does not by itself control every test function in the Poincaré inequality. These neighboring geometric conjectures must therefore be tracked separately.

The remaining dimension dependence is small but substantive. Klartag’s 2023 theorem gives \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu )=O(\log  n)\). Letwin’s July 2026 preprint reports a dimension-free inequality for quadratic forms and derives \(\psi_{\mu} =O((\log  n)^{1/4})\), hence \(C_{\mathrm{P}}(\mu )=O(\sqrt{\log  n})\). The latter is a reported preprint improvement, and even that estimate still leaves a growing factor rather than the universal constant required here.

cards.title: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair conjecture
cards.formal: For every fixed finite simple graph H, is there a finite constant \(C_{H}\ge 1\) such that, for every finite connected simple undirected H-minor-free graph G with strictly positive real edge lengths, its shortest-path metric \(d_{G}\) admits a map \(f:V(G)\to \mathbb{R} ^{m}\) into some finite-dimensional \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) space satisfying \(d_{G}(u,v)\le \Vert f(u)- f(v)\Vert _{1}\le C_{H} d_{G}(u,v)\) for all vertices u,v?
cards.definitions: H-minor-free means that deleting vertices and edges and contracting edges of G cannot produce a graph isomorphic to H, after removing loops and duplicate edges. The length of a path is the sum of its edge lengths, and \(d_{G}(u,v)\) is the minimum path length. In \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}, \Vert x- y\Vert _{1}=\sum_{j=1}^{m} |x_{j}- y_{j}|\). The displayed inequalities normalize the embedding to be noncontracting; permitting a common scaling factor gives the same distortion notion. The constant \(C_{H}\) may depend on the excluded graph H, but must be independent of |\(V(G)|\), the edge lengths and their ratio. The target dimension m and the map f may depend on the entire weighted graph and have no computational or dimension bound. This is an existence question for all vertex pairs simultaneously. It concerns undirected shortest-path distances themselves, without a snowflake transformation, average-pair guarantee or restriction to selected terminals.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether excluded graph minors exactly prevent unbounded \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) distortion and multicommodity flow–cut gaps in proper minor-closed graph families.

importance.reason: A central link between graph minor structure, metric embeddings and the quality of the basic sparsest-cut relaxation, already open in the planar case.

progress.text: Gupta–Newman–Rabinovich–Sinclair formulate the conjecture and prove constant bounds for restricted families including series-parallel graphs; FOCS 1999 and Combinatorica 2004.
Lee–Sidiropoulos prove bounded-distortion random-tree embeddings for fixed pathwidth, establishing GNRS for minor-closed families excluding a tree.
Chlamtac–Krauthgamer–Raghavendra give a constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on fixed-treewidth graphs using a stronger LP; this does not bound the ordinary flow–cut gap.
Filtser improves the planar terminal face-cover bound to \(O(\sqrt{\log (\gamma +1)})\); checked July 2024 revision and November 2024 online journal publication.
Mori determines the exact worst-weight distortion of each \(K_{2},_{n}\), approaching \(3/2\) with increasing n.
Chekuri’s updated approximation-algorithms notes still list the planar constant flow–cut-gap question as open, with \(O(\sqrt{\log  n})\) upper bound and no superconstant lower bound.

cards.status_note: The planar constant-distortion case remains explicitly open in the checked May 2026 notes. Restricted-family and face-cover results, including February 2026 exact values for \(K_{2},_{n}\), do not settle arbitrary fixed-minor-free metrics. The inherited fixed-treewidth approximation theorem uses a stronger relaxation and expressly does not prove a flow–cut-gap bound. No general settlement found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: The conjecture asks whether excluding a fixed graph minor removes every large-scale obstruction to representing graph distances as sums of coordinate differences. The graph can have arbitrarily many vertices and very unequal edge lengths. Its topology supplies the restriction, while the conclusion concerns the metric generated by all those lengths. Gupta, Newman, Rabinovich and Sinclair formulate this connection in their work on cuts, trees and \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) embeddings.

The target \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) space is useful because its finite metrics are nonnegative combinations of cut metrics. A cut metric assigns distance one to pairs separated by a chosen vertex subset and zero to other pairs. Coordinates can be decomposed by thresholding their values, producing precisely such cuts. Thus an \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) embedding replaces a complicated distance function by weighted separation tests that are closely connected to graph partitioning.

Trees give a concrete exact example. Root a weighted tree and assign one coordinate to each edge. For that coordinate, give a vertex the edge’s length if it lies below the edge and zero otherwise. Two vertices differ in exactly the coordinates corresponding to their unique connecting path. Their \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) distance therefore equals their original tree distance. Cycles allow competing shortest paths, which makes a common coordinate representation much harder.

The equivalent flow formulation compares two bounds on simultaneous routing. A concurrent flow routes the same fraction of every specified pair’s demand through a capacitated graph, splitting traffic among paths when useful. Every cut bounds that fraction by its available capacity divided by the demand it separates. GNRS predicts that, on any fixed-minor-free family, the best cut bound exceeds the achievable concurrent-flow value by at most a family-dependent constant, for arbitrary nonnegative demands.

Arbitrary demands are essential. Restricting to uniform demand between all vertex pairs gives an easier problem with stronger known results. Likewise, the capacity graph can be minor-free while demand pairs connect vertices in any pattern. Requiring the demands themselves to form a planar graph would change the target. The geometric formulation avoids these auxiliary conventions by requiring distance preservation for every vertex pair.

The planar case remains a central unresolved test. Rao’s general guarantee is \(O(\sqrt{\log  n})\) distortion for n-vertex planar metrics, and Chekuri’s May 2026 lecture notes still list a constant bound as open. No growing lower bound for planar metrics is known in that account. Both a constant upper bound and a superconstant counterexample would therefore represent a substantial change in understanding.

Several restricted families do satisfy constant distortion bounds. The original work handles series-parallel graphs. Lee and Sidiropoulos prove a stronger random-tree embedding result for graphs of any fixed pathwidth k, with distortion depending only on k. Their theorem establishes GNRS for minor-closed families that exclude a tree. Fixed pathwidth is a substantial additional restriction and does not include all graphs of fixed treewidth.

This last distinction exposes a common pitfall in reading algorithmic progress. Chlamtac, Krauthgamer and Raghavendra obtain constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on every fixed-treewidth class using the Sherali–Adams hierarchy. They explicitly explain that their stronger relaxation does not establish a constant gap for the ordinary concurrent-flow LP. Thus the inherited paper is important context and an algorithmic success, but it is not a proof of the bounded-treewidth case of GNRS.

Filtser improves a terminal-sensitive planar bound: when the terminals can be covered by \(\gamma\) faces of a planar drawing, their metric embeds with distortion \(O(\sqrt{\log (\gamma +1)})\). The added one simply handles the single-face case in asymptotic notation. This is constant for fixed \(\gamma\) and recovers the familiar n-dependent bound when all vertices require many faces. The 2024 journal-online publication refines which geometric parameter creates the loss.

There is also recent exact progress inside small planar families. Mori’s February 2026 preprint calculates the worst-over-edge-lengths distortion of \(K_{2},_{n}\) as \((3k- 2)/(2k- 1)\), where \(k=\lceil n/2\rceil\). The values approach \(3/2\). This demonstrates a nontrivial bounded loss in an infinite family, rather than a counterexample with distortion growing without bound. Such examples help test the sharpness and limitations of proposed embedding mechanisms.

A solution would connect a qualitative structural restriction—excluding one fixed minor—to a uniform quantitative statement about all distances and all concurrent-routing instances. It would explain whether the logarithmic losses in current general embedding arguments are unavoidable on these graph families. The question remains meaningful independently of how efficiently the embedding can be constructed.

Their theorem establishes GNRS for minor-closed families that exclude a tree. Fixed pathwidth is a substantial additional restriction and does not include all graphs of fixed treewidth.

This last distinction exposes a common pitfall in reading algorithmic progress. Chlamtac, Krauthgamer and Raghavendra obtain constant-factor sparsest-cut approximation on every fixed-treewidth class using the Sherali–Adams hierarchy. They explicitly explain that their stronger relaxation does not establish a constant gap for the ordinary concurrent-flow LP. Thus the inherited paper is important context and an algorithmic success, but it is not a proof of the bounded-treewidth case of GNRS.

Filtser improves a terminal-sensitive planar bound: when the terminals can be covered by \(\gamma\) faces of a planar drawing, their metric embeds with distortion \(O(\sqrt{\log (\gamma +1)})\). The added one simply handles the single-face case in asymptotic notation. This is constant for fixed \(\gamma\) and recovers the familiar n-dependent bound when all vertices require many faces. The 2024 journal-online publication refines which geometric parameter creates the loss.

There is also recent exact progress inside small planar families. Mori’s February 2026 preprint calculates the worst-over-edge-lengths distortion of \(K_{2},_{n}\) as \((3k- 2)/(2k- 1)\), where \(k=\lceil n/2\rceil\). The values approach \(3/2\). This demonstrates a nontrivial bounded loss in an infinite family, rather than a counterexample with distortion growing without bound. Such examples help test the sharpness and limitations of proposed embedding mechanisms.

A solution would connect a qualitative structural restriction—excluding one fixed minor—to a uniform quantitative statement about all distances and all concurrent-routing instances. It would explain whether the logarithmic losses in current general embedding arguments are unavoidable on these graph families. The question remains meaningful independently of how efficiently the embedding can be constructed.

cards.title: Unknot recognition in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing algorithm and a constant c such that, on every explicit combinatorial knot diagram D of encoding length N, the algorithm decides in \(O((N+1)^{c})\) bit operations whether the represented knot in the 3-sphere is ambient isotopic to the unknot?
cards.definitions: A knot is a tame embedding of one circle into \(S^{3}\); the unknot is the isotopy class of a round circle. Ambient isotopy means a continuous family of homeomorphisms of \(S^{3}\) starting at the identity and carrying one embedded circle to the other at its endpoint. A diagram is a generic projection with transverse double crossings and specified over/under information. Encode it by an explicitly listed connected 4-regular planar multigraph, including loops when needed, its cyclic orders of half-edges at vertices, a distinguished outer face and the overpassing pair of opposite half-edges at each crossing. Tracing the opposite pairs must give one component. A separate constant-size encoding represents the crossing-free circle. The embedding is required to be a valid sphere embedding; malformed encodings may be rejected by polynomial-time combinatorial checks. If the diagram has n crossings, a standard such encoding has \(O(n \log (n+1))\) bits. The complexity parameter is the supplied encoding length N, not the minimum crossing number among equivalent diagrams. The input is explicit rather than a compressed description of an exponentially larger diagram. No disk, simplification sequence, knot invariant, auxiliary advice or promise of triviality is supplied. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether triviality of an explicitly given knot can be decided efficiently, a foundational test of the gap between topological certificates and algorithms.

importance.reason: A central algorithmic topology problem in NP∩coNP; a fresh claimed polynomial-time solution makes precise formulation and validation especially valuable.

cards.status_note: Musick’s 6 September 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time solution. Its correctness has not been independently established in this review, so the card is not labelled either a settled theorem or an unqualified open problem. context_blocks.text: Status requires special care: Chad Musick’s preprint of 6 September 2026 claims a positive answer in Corollary 1. Its route is a polynomial-time construction of a locally minimal bridge presentation using compressed descriptions, followed by an existing characterization of bridge presentations of the unknot. I checked the claim and its main proof dependencies, but have not independently verified the local-minimality argument or compressed-update complexity. The card is therefore marked uncertain pending validation of this fresh claimed resolution.

The underlying task is deceptively simple: determine whether a closed loop can be untangled without cutting it or passing one strand through another. A diagram can contain many crossings that are artifacts of its projection. Looking complicated does not prove knottedness, while repeatedly removing visible twists can get stuck on a diagram that still represents the unknot. The input can be deliberately chosen to frustrate familiar simplification strategies.

The chosen representation makes the computational question independent of numerical geometry. Coordinates, thickness, physical forces and drawing quality do not enter the running time. Cyclic orders record the planar embedding, and the crossing data tell us which strand passes over the other. The task concerns the topology represented by those finite combinatorial data, not the visual complexity of a particular rendering.

Hass, Lagarias and Pippenger prove that unknot recognition belongs to NP using normal-surface techniques. Informally, an unknot bounds an embedded disk, and a suitable disk can be encoded compactly through its intersections with tetrahedra in a triangulation. Large counts are stored in binary. The existence of a polynomial-size verifiable certificate gives an upper bound on nondeterministic complexity, while finding such a certificate may still require substantial search.

Lackenby proves that knottedness also belongs to NP, so unknot recognition lies in coNP as well. This is an unconditional theorem, unlike earlier approaches that required the generalized Riemann hypothesis. It places the problem in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\) and makes ordinary NP-completeness unlikely: an NP-hard language in coNP would imply \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). Membership in both classes does not itself give a polynomial-time decision algorithm.

There is another strong certificate theorem. Lackenby proves that any n-crossing unknot diagram can be reduced to a crossing-free circle using at most \((236n)^{11}\) Reidemeister moves. These are local diagram changes preserving the knot type. The result bounds the length of a successful route; it does not identify which route to choose efficiently. Enumerating a branching collection of polynomial-length routes can still take exponential time.

In 2021, Lackenby announced an algorithm with quasipolynomial running time. The SoCG 2025 source still describes this as an announcement, and the checked author webpage lists talks on it. I retain that attribution rather than presenting a fully checked published proof. Quasipolynomial time, of the form \(\exp ((\log  N)^{O(1)})\), can be much smaller than exponential time while remaining above a fixed polynomial bound.

Practical algorithms illustrate a different kind of progress. He, Sedgwick and Spreer’s SoCG 2025 paper builds knot factorisation machinery around edge-ideal triangulations and normal-surface crushing. Their introduction notes that Regina’s unknot-recognition implementation behaves polynomially in experiments but has an exponential worst-case bound. Strong performance on a census or on difficult examples is useful evidence for implementation design, without controlling every possible input diagram.

Lackenby’s July 2026 preprint gives a new algorithm through incompressible surfaces and hierarchies. For a nontrivial knot, the boundary of its exterior is incompressible; for the unknot it is compressible. This turns knot recognition into a question about surfaces in a 3-manifold. The paper’s Section 9 explicitly leaves key hierarchy-length and surface-complexity parameters unbounded in terms of the input, so it does not establish polynomial running time.

The central challenge is algorithmic control over global topology. A small diagram may hide the disk or decomposition that makes its type evident. Good certificates show that concise explanations exist; an efficient recognizer would show how to decide without searching an uncontrolled space of explanations. Any verified polynomial-time solution, including the new claimed one, would resolve a basic benchmark of computational topology and change how we understand this gap.

cards.title: Polynomial Hirsch conjecture
cards.formal: Do universal constants \(C>0\) and \(k\ge 1\) exist such that every nonempty pointed d-dimensional convex polyhedron with n facets has vertex-edge graph diameter at most \(C(n+d)^{k}\)?
cards.definitions: A polyhedron is an intersection of finitely many closed affine halfspaces over the real numbers. Work in its affine hull, identified with \(R^{d}\), where \(d\ge 1\), and require it to be pointed, meaning that it contains no affine line; this ensures that its vertices are present. Both bounded polyhedra, called polytopes, and unbounded pointed polyhedra are included. The number n counts distinct facets in an irredundant description, rather than repeated input inequalities. The graph \(G(\mathrm{P})\) has one vertex per geometric vertex of P and an undirected edge between u and v precisely when their segment is a bounded one-dimensional face of P. An unbounded ray is not an extra graph vertex or an edge to infinity. Graph distance counts edges, each at unit cost; diameter is the maximum distance between vertices and is zero for a one-vertex polyhedron. The constants C,k must be independent of dimension, facet count, coordinates, coefficient bit length and the choice of polyhedron. Real coordinates are allowed, and no simplicity or nondegeneracy assumption is made. Paths need not improve any objective function, and no algorithm for finding them is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether all polyhedral feasible regions have uniformly short edge routes, a central structural question underlying linear programming.

importance.reason: The surviving fundamental diameter question after the original Hirsch bound failed; it separates geometric existence of short routes from algorithmic navigation and the newly resolved circuit analogue.

progress.text: Kalai–Kleitman establish a quasipolynomial general edge-diameter bound; Todd’s paper records and sharpens the recurrence-based result.
Santos disproves the original linear Hirsch conjecture with a 43-dimensional bounded polytope having 86 facets.
Todd proves the upper bound \((n- d)^{\log _{2}d}\).
Sukegawa’s asymptotic improvement lowers the exponent by \(\log _{2}\log  d\) up to an additive constant, still quasipolynomial.
The ETH geometry notes retain the polynomial problem; Wulf establishes \(\Pi _{2}^{p}\)-hardness of computing diameters even for bipartite perfect-matching polytopes.
Natura’s revised manuscript proves polynomial circuit diameter, including monotone circuit walks; ordinary edge diameter remains open.

context_blocks.text: The feasible region of a linear program is a polyhedron. Its vertices are candidate basic feasible solutions, and its edges describe elementary geometric moves between them. The diameter asks for the largest minimum number of such moves between any two vertices. It is therefore a question about the geometry of feasible solutions before one chooses a particular rule for navigating them.

The facet count is the relevant measure of description size here. A polyhedron described by a modest number of inequalities can have exponentially many vertices, so the trivial bound by the number of vertices is far too large. The d-dimensional cube illustrates the distinction: it has 2d facets and \(2^{d}\) vertices, yet its diameter is only d because one can change differing coordinates one at a time.

Polynomial means a fixed exponent that works in every dimension. An \(n^{d}\) upper bound is polynomial in n when d is held fixed, but does not answer this question. Neither does a bound whose constant grows exponentially with d. The card includes pointed unbounded polyhedra, matching the saved formulation; pointedness removes polyhedra with no vertices, for which a vertex-graph diameter would not express the intended problem.

Hirsch originally proposed the much sharper \(n- d\) bound for bounded polytopes. Santos’s counterexample, announced in 2010 and published in 2012, has dimension 43 and 86 facets, with diameter exceeding 43. This refutes that linear expression, but it remains fully compatible with a bound such as \(Cn^{2}\) or \(Cn^{10}\). The distinction between failure of one attractive formula and failure of every polynomial is the reason a major open question survived.

General upper bounds are quasipolynomial. Kalai and Kleitman’s 1992 argument gave \(n^{2+\log _{2}d}\); Todd improved it in 2014 to \((n- d)^{\log _{2}d}\). For large d, Sukegawa’s later asymptotic refinement has the form \((n- d)^{\log _{2}d- \log _{2}\log  d+O(1)}\). The last exponent still grows with dimension. These are substantial structural bounds, but they do not reach one universal constant exponent.

The conjecture concerns shortest available paths, not the paths a chosen simplex pivot rule happens to take. A rule may visit exponentially many vertices even on a polytope whose graph has small diameter. Conversely, proving that short undirected paths exist would not tell a solver which edge to select efficiently, or ensure a short path that improves a specified linear objective at every step. Polynomial diameter is a geometric ingredient, not by itself a strongly polynomial linear-programming algorithm.

Recent complexity results make the distinction sharper. Wulf’s FOCS 2025 paper proves \(\Pi _{2}^{p}\)-hardness of computing the diameter of bipartite perfect-matching polytopes, and the corresponding decision problem is complete for that class. Such hardness is compatible with a polynomial upper bound on the value of the diameter. A small optimum can be difficult to compute exactly, just as short witnesses can be difficult to find.

Natura’s February 2026 paper proves a polynomial bound for a different geometric distance: circuit diameter. For a standard-form polyhedron \(\{x\in R^{N}:Ax=b,x\ge 0\}\), with A having r rows, the stated bound is \(O(r^{2}\log  r)\), and the construction also supplies monotone circuit walks. Circuit directions are support-minimal dependencies of A; a maximal feasible step in such a direction need not stay on an edge of the current polyhedron.

Every edge step is allowed among the circuit moves, but the converse fails. Consequently, a short circuit walk gives no automatic equally short edge walk: its intermediate points may lie inside higher-dimensional faces. The 2026 theorem settles the circuit analogue of the polynomial conjecture, while its introduction explicitly retains the ordinary combinatorial-diameter problem. The distinction is geometric, not a question of hiding logarithmic factors.

Other positive results exploit extra structure, such as totally unimodular constraint matrices or numerical bounds on subdeterminants. Those assumptions control features absent from the unrestricted statement. Random-polytope and smoothed analyses likewise describe particular distributions or perturbations; a worst-case theorem must include every allowed realization. This is why the model specifies arbitrary coefficients and requires constants independent of their encoding.

A positive resolution would reveal a universal short-route property of all polyhedral feasible regions, despite their potentially enormous vertex sets. A negative resolution would produce polyhedra on which every route between some vertices is intrinsically long. Both outcomes would identify a basic geometric limit underlying pivot-based optimization, independently of the performance of any individual implementation.

cards.title: Planar k-set extremal function
cards.formal: Let \(K_{2}(n,k)\) be the maximum, over sets P of n distinct points in $\mathbb R^2$ with no three collinear, of the number of distinct subsets \(S\subseteq \mathrm{P}\) of size k strictly separable from \(P\setminus S\) by a line. Determine \(K_{2}(n,k)\) up to universal constant factors, uniformly for all integers \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\).
cards.definitions: Strict separation means that there are real a,b,c with \((a,b)\ne (0,0), ax\)+by<c for every \((x,y)\in S\), and ax+by>c for every \((x,y)\in\)\(P\setminus S\). The objects counted are subsets S, not their infinitely many possible separating lines. Coordinates have no bounded-precision, grid, or random-distribution promise. The target is worst-case combinatorial complexity, not the running time of an enumeration algorithm. A matching bound means an asymptotic expression \(F(n,k)\) and absolute constants \(0<c_{0}\le C_{0}<\infty\) such that \(c_{0}F(n,k)\le K_{2}(n,k)\le C_{0}F(n,k)\) throughout the stated range, apart from finitely many n which can be absorbed into the constants. Bounds must cover k that grows with n. Complementation supplies the remaining values \(n/2<k<n; k=0,n\) each have one subset. This card specializes the original all-dimensions problem to the plane.
cards.answer_criterion: Determine a positive function \(F(n,k)\) and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) with \(cF(n,k)\le K_{2}(n,k)\le CF(n,k)\) throughout \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le k\le \lfloor n/2\rfloor\). Prove the universal upper bound and existence of matching point sets for every parameter pair in Lean. No predetermined formula grammar or closed form is required; a mere restatement of the defining extremum is insufficient. This asymptotic-complexity target uses constant-factor precision, not additive 0.01. A fixed-k result or the halving case alone does not determine the whole function.
cards.why: A central unresolved counting problem in computational geometry, it controls the complexity of levels and line-separated ranges. importance.reason: A defining extremal-complexity question for geometric algorithms, already unresolved in the plane and connected to levels, geometric selection, and parametric optimization.

progress.text: Dey proves \(K_{2}(n,k)=O(n k^{1/3})\) for \(1\le k\le n/2\) through a crossing-number argument. The balanced specialization gives an \(O(n^{4/3})\) upper bound.

Tóth constructs planar point sets with \(n \exp (\Omega (\sqrt{\log  k})) k\)-sets for \(n\ge 2k>0\), improving the earlier n log k scale. This remains separated from the upper bound by an unbounded factor when k grows.

Nivasch gives a simpler halving-edge construction improving the constant in the square-root-log exponent. The construction does not produce \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) halving edges for any fixed positive \(\varepsilon\).

The revised Open Problems Project entry still lists the planar asymptotic gap as unresolved. A search through September 2026 did not locate matching general upper and lower bounds.

context_blocks.text: A line can realize only a small fraction of all choices of k points. The question measures the combinatorial capacity of one linear cut at a fixed output size. For example, when \(k=1\) the separable points are the convex-hull vertices, and their maximum number is n. The difficult regime lets k increase with the input size.

Point-line duality translates changes of a separating line into the structure of levels in a line arrangement. A level tracks positions having a specified number of lines below them. These level bounds recur in geometric selection and in analyses of parametric optimization. Dey’s method also yields bounds for related level structures, convex chains, and parametric spanning-tree problems.

For even n, the balanced case is closely tied to halving edges: segments joining two input points whose supporting line leaves \((n- 2)/2\) of the other points on each side. A halving edge is not itself a separating line, since it passes through input points. The correspondence between k-sets and directed \((k- 1)\)-edges gives \(K_{2}(n,n/2)\) equal to twice the maximum number of undirected halving edges.

The known planar upper bound is \(O(n k^{1/3})\), whereas constructions give \(n \exp (\Omega (\sqrt{\log  k}))\) subsets. In the balanced regime the latter grows faster than n times any fixed power of log n, yet slower than \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) for each fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). Thus neither a linear bound nor an ordinary polylogarithmic correction to linear growth can describe the worst case.

Sharper finite-size constructions and improvements to the additive terms of halving-line bounds are useful progress. They do not close the gap in asymptotic growth. Keeping this distinction explicit matters here: an improved upper bound may retain the same \(4/3\) exponent in the balanced case.

cards.title: Lang–Plaut problem
cards.formal: For every integer \(K\geq2\), do there exist a finite integer \(N(K)\geq1\) and a finite real constant \(D(K)\geq1\) such that every \(K\)-doubling subset \(X\) of real Hilbert space admits a map \(F:X\to\mathbb R^{N(K)}\) satisfying \[\|x-y\|_2\leq\|F(x)-F(y)\|_2\leq D(K)\|x-y\|_2\qquad(x,y\in X)?\]
cards.why: The problem asks whether intrinsic local metric dimension completely controls Euclidean dimensional reduction once Hilbert embeddability is available. Its resolution would clarify a central obstruction to finite-dimensional metric representation and the limits of geometry-based compression independent of dataset size.
cards.status_note: Open in the checked Naor–Neiman and Lafforgue–Naor sources. A bounded later-work search on 13 September 2026 did not identify a resolution for the Hilbert case. Results for other Banach spaces or restricted families do not supply one; this is not an exhaustive current-openness certification.

sentences: A doubling metric has uniformly limited local branching: each ball can be covered by a bounded number of smaller balls.
The Lang–Plaut problem considers such a metric when it already sits inside a Hilbert space.
It asks whether the points can be represented in some finite-dimensional Euclidean space while changing all distances by only a bounded factor.
Both dimension and distortion should depend only on the doubling constant.
The issue is whether intrinsic metric simplicity suffices to eliminate an infinite-dimensional ambient representation.

cards.definitions: It suffices to use the real Hilbert space \(\ell_2=\{(x_i)_{i\geq1}:\sum_i x_i^2<\infty\}\), with norm \(\|x\|_2=(\sum_i x_i^2)^{1/2}\). A doubling subset of any Hilbert space is separable and isometrically identifies with a subset of this space. Give \(X\subseteq\ell_2\) the restricted Hilbert distance. It is \(K\)-doubling if, for every \(x\in X\) and \(r>0\), the closed ball \(B_X(x,r)=\{y\in X:\|x-y\|_2\leq r\}\) is covered by at most \(K\) closed balls \(B_X(z,r/2)\) with centers \(z\in X\). No boundedness, closedness, compactness or finiteness of \(X\) is assumed. Empty sets and singletons cause no difficulty. The codomain has its ordinary Euclidean norm. The displayed lower inequality makes the map injective and fixes its arbitrary scale; without that normalization, distortion is the product of the Lipschitz constants of a map and its inverse on its image. The functions \(N,D\) must be chosen before \(X\), and may depend only on \(K\), not on the number of points, diameter, aspect ratio or ambient Hilbert dimension. The embedding may be nonlinear and may be chosen separately for each \(X\). There is no algorithm, continuity beyond the displayed bounds, or prescribed polynomial dependence on \(K\) required. Distances themselves must be preserved within these factors; replacing them by a power smaller than one changes the target.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal statement in Lean, or give a complete Lean-checked refutation with a fixed doubling bound for which no uniform pair of finite dimension and distortion bounds works. Equivalently, the qualitative Lang–Plaut formulation can be settled by proving that every doubling Hilbert subset has some finite-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embedding, or by exhibiting one that has none; the source proves the equivalence with the quantitative formulation. A restriction to linear maps, snowflaked distances, or bounds growing with the number of points does not resolve the question.

context_blocks.text: Naor and Neiman state the Lang–Plaut question in Section 1.1 and justify its quantitative form in Section 4. This card uses that form so the dependence of dimension and distortion is explicit. The original question is attributed there to Lang and Plaut’s Question 2.4.

Every subset of a fixed-dimensional Euclidean space is doubling, with a bound controlled by dimension, and is already a subset of Hilbert space. A positive answer would make these two necessary conditions sufficient for finite-dimensional bi-Lipschitz embeddability.

Naor and Neiman prove that for an arbitrary doubling metric \((X,d)\), every snowflake \((X,d^{1-\eta})\), \(0<\eta<1/2\), embeds into a Euclidean space whose dimension depends only on the doubling constant. The distortion still depends on \(\eta\). Letting \(\eta\) tend to zero therefore does not supply the uniformly controlled embedding asked for here.

Lafforgue and Naor construct, for every \(p>2\), a doubling subset of \(L_p\) that has no bi-Lipschitz embedding into any finite-dimensional Euclidean space. Their theorem explicitly leaves the Hilbert case \(p=2\) open, so replacing Hilbert space by a general Banach space changes the answer.

Usual finite-set dimension reduction allows dimension to grow with the logarithm of the number of points. Here arbitrarily large or infinite sets with the same doubling bound must share a finite target dimension and distortion bound. This is a geometric existence question rather than a request for a faster implementation of a known projection.

cards.title: Decidability of PL four-sphere recognition
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic Turing machine which, on every finite simplicial complex K promised to be a closed combinatorial 4-manifold, halts and decides whether K is piecewise-linearly homeomorphic to the boundary of a 5-simplex?
cards.definitions: A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite family of finite vertex sets closed under taking subsets; its maximal sets are its facets. The input lists all facets with integer vertex labels in binary. K is pure of dimension 4 when all facets have five vertices. The link of a vertex v consists of the faces \(\sigma\) not containing v for which \(\sigma \cup \{v\}\) is a face of K. A closed combinatorial 4-manifold here is a nonempty pure 4-dimensional complex in which each vertex link is a PL 3-sphere; connectedness is not promised. The standard PL d-sphere is the boundary complex of a \((d+1)\)-simplex. Two complexes are PL homeomorphic when they admit finite simplicial subdivisions that are simplicially isomorphic, equivalently when their geometric realizations admit a homeomorphism affine on the simplices of suitable finite subdivisions. A simplicial subdivision triangulates the same realization by smaller simplices contained in the old simplices. Correctness and termination are required on every promised input; no behavior is required on other inputs. There is no time or space bound beyond termination.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. sentences: A weak \(\varepsilon\)-net places auxiliary points so that every convex set containing at least an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of a given point set contains an auxiliary point.
The auxiliary points may lie anywhere in the ambient Euclidean space.
For each fixed dimension, the task is to determine the smallest worst-case net size as \(\varepsilon\) decreases.

Sharp bounds would quantify how economically a finite set can represent its large convex subsets.

cards.definitions: Let \(P\subset\mathbb R^d\) be any nonempty finite set of distinct points, and let \(0<\varepsilon\leq1/2\) be real. A weak \(\varepsilon\)-net is a finite set \(N\subset\mathbb R^d\) such that \(N\cap C\ne\varnothing\) for every convex set \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) satisfying \(|P\cap C|\geq\varepsilon|P|\). A set is convex if it contains the segment joining any two of its points. All convex ranges, including unbounded and lower-dimensional ones, are allowed; no restriction to halfspaces, simplices or a given finite family is made. Equivalently it is enough to hit \(\operatorname{conv}(Q)\) for every \(Q\subseteq P\) with \(|Q|\geq\lceil\varepsilon|P|\rceil\), so using only closed convex ranges gives the same condition. Net points can lie anywhere in \(\mathbb R^d\) and need not belong to \(P\). Put \(w(P,\varepsilon)=\min\{|N|:N\text{ is a weak }\varepsilon\text{-net for }P\}\) and \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\sup_{P\subset\mathbb R^d,\,0<|P|<\infty}w(P,\varepsilon)\). The minimum exists since \(N=P\) is feasible. The supremum ranges over every size and configuration with the same fixed dimension and accuracy; a bound depending on \(|P|\) is not a bound on \(f_d\). The weak-net theorem ensures \(f_d(\varepsilon)<\infty\). There is no general-position, rational-coordinate, uniform-measure-on-space, algorithmic or randomized guarantee in the target: the only measure is the uniform counting measure on the given finite set. The problem measures extremal cardinality, not construction time.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a noncircular rate \(G_d(\varepsilon)\) and a complete Lean-checked proof that for each fixed \(d\geq2\) there are \(c_d,C_d,\varepsilon_d>0\) with \(c_dG_d(\varepsilon)\leq f_d(\varepsilon)\leq C_dG_d(\varepsilon)\) whenever \(0<\varepsilon\leq\varepsilon_d\). Upper bounds must cover all finite configurations; lower bounds must establish configurations requiring the matching order. Constants may depend on dimension but not on accuracy or input size. The exponent alone, bounds missing logarithmic factors, or a solution only for the plane do not characterize the stated family.

context_blocks.text: Rubin’s paper explicitly identifies the true asymptotic behavior of weak-net size in every fixed dimension at least two as an outstanding problem. The cardinality function above is the source’s extremal target, with its counting, rounding and range conventions made explicit.

A strong net is required to choose its points from the input. Allowing auxiliary points is essential for arbitrary convex ranges: arguments for bounded-complexity range families do not automatically supply weak nets for all convex sets.

Bukh, Matoušek and Nivasch prove the general lower bound \(f_d(\varepsilon)=\Omega_d(\varepsilon^{-1}\log^{d-1}(1/\varepsilon))\). In particular, already in the plane a universal bound proportional to \(1/\varepsilon\) is impossible.

Rubin improves the planar upper bound to \(O_\gamma(\varepsilon^{-3/2-\gamma})\) for every fixed \(\gamma>0\). The constant can depend on \(\gamma\); this theorem is not the assertion of an \(O(\varepsilon^{-3/2})\) bound with a uniform constant.

Rubin’s higher-dimensional work, including its December 2023 revision, improves the previously known upper bounds in all fixed dimensions at least three. Those bounds still do not match the lower bound above. Their dependence on dimension does not turn the problem into a joint large-dimension asymptotic question.

The same net must hit all heavy convex ranges simultaneously. Choosing a different auxiliary point after seeing each range would be a different and trivial requirement. This simultaneous coverage is what makes the extremal bound relevant to geometric transversals and sampling.

cards.definitions: A convex polytope is the convex hull of a finite set of real points. Its faces here are its maximal two-dimensional facets, and adjacent facets share an entire polytope edge. Choose a spanning tree of the facet adjacency graph. Make separate copies of all facets and glue only the pairs of matching edges selected by that tree, retaining the edge identifications inherited from \(P\). An edge unfolding is a map of this glued polygonal surface to \(\mathbb R^2\) whose restriction to each copied facet is a Euclidean isometry and whose restrictions agree on glued edges. Require images of the relative interiors of distinct facets to be disjoint. Contacts between boundary points are permitted; cuts may run only along original polytope edges. The glued surface and its image are connected. This is a geometric existence statement with arbitrary real coordinates, not an algorithmic runtime claim.

context_blocks.text: A net lays out the actual faces of a solid in one plane without stretching them. A cube provides familiar examples: its six squares can remain connected along selected edges and spread out without their interiors covering one another. The conjecture asks for such a choice for every convex polytope, regardless of the number, shape or arrangement of its facets.

The connected gluing pattern matters independently of overlap. Keeping a tree of facet adjacencies attaches every face to one planar assembly. It does not guarantee that faces far apart in that tree avoid one another after flattening. The existence question concerns a suitable choice of the whole pattern, not whether every possible net succeeds.

Only original polytope edges are available for cuts. Triangulating a facet and then allowing cuts on the new diagonals, slicing through face interiors, or returning disconnected pieces changes the task. Nonconvex examples without suitable unfoldings likewise do not refute a statement restricted to convex input.

This card retains its explicitly chosen nonoverlap convention: relative interiors of distinct facets must be disjoint, while boundary contacts are allowed. A requirement that the entire unfolded boundary be a simple Jordan curve is an additional condition; no equivalence to that stricter condition is assumed. The distinction is explicit in the unfolding literature.

O’Rourke’s March 2026 preprint still identifies even the general prismatoid case as unresolved. A prismatoid is a convex polytope whose vertices lie in two parallel planes. Its nested special cases concern a restricted geometric arrangement, leaving arbitrary convex polytopes outside their guarantee.

The July 2026 overlap construction finds convex polyhedra with particular edge unfoldings of arbitrarily large overlap thickness. Showing that one choice of cuts overlaps is different from showing that every choice overlaps. The latter universal failure would be needed for a counterexample to the existence question.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that every convex polytope in the stated domain has a spanning tree of facet adjacencies and compatible planar facet isometries with pairwise disjoint relative interiors, or prove a counterexample in Lean: one such polytope for which every permitted gluing tree and planar realization fails. No algorithmic runtime or stricter boundary-injectivity claim is required.

cards.title: Constant-distortion Steiner point removal
cards.formal: Is there an absolute constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for every finite connected undirected graph \(G\) with nonnegative real edge lengths and every terminal set \(K\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|K|\geq2\), there is a reweighted terminal-preserving minor \(H\) with vertex set exactly \(K\) satisfying \[d_G(s,t)\leq d_H(s,t)\leq C\,d_G(s,t)\qquad(s,t\in K)?\]
cards.why: Steiner point removal asks how much of a network’s geometry and topology can survive when only designated terminals remain. A universal constant would establish a strong form of graph compression; an unbounded lower bound would show that the topology of general graphs forces a growing loss even when edge lengths may be redesigned.
cards.status_note: The checked 2024 source settles fixed-minor-free graphs and records logarithmic distortion for general graphs. A bounded review on 13 September 2026 did not find a universal constant for all graphs or a refutation. The solved planar question is not presented as still open.
cards.review_note: Completed individual review against P versus NP on 13 September 2026; see research/card-completion-20260913/reviews.jsonl.

importance.reason: A central distance-preserving graph compression question, now settled for fixed-minor-free families but still demanding a topology-independent constant in general graphs.
