cards.title: NP recognition of closed hyperbolic three-manifolds
cards.formal: Does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time verifier V and a polynomial p such that, for every finite PL-triangulation T of a compact connected three-manifold M, M is closed and admits a hyperbolic metric if and only if there exists a binary certificate w with |\(w|\le p(|T|)\) and \(V(T,w)=1\)?
cards.why: Would show that a global constant-curvature geometry can always be certified using polynomially bounded discrete evidence from an arbitrary triangulation. It would sharpen the complexity of a central geometric recognition problem beyond mere decidability.

cards.definitions: The input consists of t abstract tetrahedra and a finite list of affine face identifications, each encoded by two tetrahedron indices, face indices and a permutation of the face vertices. Unpaired faces are permitted. Identifying these faces produces the quotient space \(M=|T|\). The input is promised to be a PL-triangulation of a compact connected topological three-manifold, possibly with boundary; no orientability or irreducibility promise is imposed. Its encoding length |T| counts all bits in the explicit tetrahedron and face-pairing data, with binary indices. Closed means that M has empty boundary, since compactness is already promised. A hyperbolic metric means a Riemannian metric locally isometric to hyperbolic three-space \(H^{3}\); for example \(H^{3}\) is the upper half-space \(\{(x,y,z)\in \mathbb{R} ^{3}:z>0\}\) with metric \(ds^{2}=(dx^{2}+dy^{2}+dz^{2})/z^{2}\). Equivalently, the metric has constant sectional curvature −1. On closed M it is complete. The abstract tetrahedra in the input are topological data and are not supplied as geometric tetrahedra in that metric. V is one uniform deterministic Turing algorithm without advice or an oracle, and runs in time polynomial in |T|+|w| on all encoded inputs. Correctness is required on every promised manifold triangulation; no particular certificate format or method is prescribed. The polynomial certificate bound and verifier are fixed for the entire problem, not chosen separately for each manifold.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a polynomial certificate bound and a uniform polynomial-time verifier that accepts some bounded-length certificate for every closed hyperbolic input and accepts none for every other promised manifold input. Alternatively, prove that no such bound and verifier exist. A terminating recognition algorithm alone, or certificates for non-hyperbolicity, do not establish this NP membership.

cards.definitions:
A finite metric space consists of a finite set X and a symmetric function d:X×X→[0,∞) with d(x,y)=0 exactly when x=y and d(x,z)≤d(x,y)+d(y,z). Its half-snowflake is the metric space with distance √d(x,y). The square root applies to the original distances, not to the Wasserstein distance or to the dimension. Distances in the base space R³ are the usual Euclidean distances.

The set \(\mathcal P_p(\mathbb R^3)\) consists of Borel probability measures μ on R³ satisfying \(\int\|u\|_2^p\,d\mu(u)<\infty\). A coupling of μ and ν is a probability measure π on R³×R³ with these two marginals. Write Π(μ,ν) for all such couplings. The Wasserstein metric is \(W_p(\mu,\nu)=(\inf_{\pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu)}\int\|u-v\|_2^p\,d\pi(u,v))^{1/p}\). Thus the transport cost uses the pth power of Euclidean distance and takes a pth root after minimizing. Images may be arbitrary measures of finite pth moment; no support-size, equal-mass, rational-coordinate or computability restriction is imposed.

The two-sided inequality means a bi-Lipschitz embedding of distortion at most C_p after a common rescaling s. It forces F to be injective when X has more than one point. Both F and s may depend on p and the entire finite metric. The quantifier order is ∀p>2 ∃C_p<∞ ∀(X,d) ∃F,s; there is no single bound required to work uniformly as p varies, and p=∞ is excluded. This is an existence question, with no algorithmic running-time target.

The source writes c_Y(X,√d)≤D_p, where c_Y is the infimum of the distortions of all embeddings. The infimum need not be attained. Existence of some finite uniform bound in that formulation is equivalent to the displayed formulation: increasing an available finite infimum bound, for example to twice its value, allows actual embeddings for each finite X. The source's stronger suggestion D_p=1 instead means distortion arbitrarily close to one for every finite metric. It must not be silently replaced by a demand for an attained isometric embedding, and neither strengthening is required here.

The already-proved theorem embeds the 1/p-snowflake, with distances d(x,y)^{1/p}, with distortion arbitrarily close to one. When p>2 its exponent is smaller than 1/2, so it does not answer this question. At p=2 it does give the half-snowflake result; that endpoint is background, outside the unresolved range.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniform-in-X finite-distortion assertion for every fixed p>2, or refute it by finding a fixed p>2 for which half-snowflake distortions into this exact target space are unbounded across finite metrics. A single finite metric with distortion greater than one does not refute the claim. cards.definitions:
A finite abstract simplicial complex is a finite collection of nonempty finite vertex sets, called simplices, closed under taking nonempty subsets. A simplex with \(r+1\) vertices has dimension \(r\). The input explicitly lists its simplices, or equivalently its maximal simplices and their vertex labels. The promise is that every simplex has at most three vertices. Edges and triangles need not form a manifold or embed in Euclidean three-space.

An elementary collapse removes a pair \((\sigma,\tau)\) of simplices, where \(\sigma\) is a codimension-one face of \(\tau\) and the only simplex properly containing \(\sigma\) is \(\tau\). An elementary expansion is the inverse: add such a pair so that the result is again a simplicial complex and that pair could be collapsed immediately.

Simple-homotopy equivalence to a point means that a finite sequence of expansions and collapses takes \(K\) to a complex consisting of a single vertex. New vertices may be introduced; intermediate complexes may be larger and have dimension greater than two. There is no prescribed bound on the number of moves, number of vertices or intermediate dimension. Relabeling vertices has no mathematical effect.

For comparison with the topological formulation, the geometric realization \(|K|\) is obtained by gluing an ordinary Euclidean simplex for each face along its common subfaces. It is contractible if its identity map can be continuously deformed to a constant map: there exist \(p\in|K|\) and a continuous
\[H:|K|\times[0,1]\longrightarrow |K|,\qquad H(x,0)=x,\quad H(x,1)=p.\]
For a finite complex, being contractible is equivalent to having the simple-homotopy type of a point, as recalled in the sources.

The algorithm is a single deterministic Turing machine acting on the finite encoding. It must give the correct yes/no answer and terminate on both contractible and noncontractible inputs. No polynomial-time or other running-time bound is required. There is no promise that \(K\) is already contractible or simply connected, and no contraction certificate is supplied.

This is specifically recognition of the simple-homotopy type of a point. The card does not ask to decide equivalence of an arbitrary pair of complexes. It also does not restrict allowed moves to collapses alone, or impose a fixed expansion budget.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of a total decision algorithm for this input class, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A procedure that eventually finds a contraction on yes-instances but may run forever on no-instances is insufficient. A hardness theorem ruling out efficient algorithms does not establish undecidability.

cards.title: Linear-size sample compression
cards.formal: Is there a universal constant C such that every nonempty binary concept class \(H\subseteq \{0,1\}^{X}\) of finite VC dimension \(d\ge 1\) admits a labeled sample compression scheme with kernel bound k and side-information bound b satisfying \(k+b\le Cd\), in the model below? The same compressor and reconstructor must work for every finite H-realizable sample, independently of its size.
cards.definitions: The domain X is an arbitrary set, and a concept \(h\in H\) is a total function \(X\to \{0,1\}\). A finite set \(A\subseteq X\) is shattered if \(\{h|_{A}:h\in H\}=\{0,1\}^{A}; d\) is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A realizable sample is a finite set \(S\subseteq X\times \{0,1\}\) agreeing with some \(h\in H\). A scheme consists of deterministic maps \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\), which may depend on H, and nonnegative integers k,b. For every realizable \(S, \kappa (S)=(T,z)\), where \(T\subseteq S\) is an unordered labeled subset with |\(T|\le k\) and \(z\in \{0,1\}^{b}\). The reconstructor receives only T and z and produces a total predictor \(\rho (T,z):X\to \{0,1\}\) agreeing with every pair in S. It does not receive S, its size, the omitted points, or their indices. The side string has fixed length b; padding shorter strings changes only constant-factor size conventions. Reconstruction need not lie in H, be stable under deleting unused examples, or have any prescribed computational complexity. No probability distribution, efficiency, or measurability condition is part of this combinatorial existence question. Dimension zero is harmless: a nonempty such class has one labeling and needs no stored examples.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.

importance.reason: A longstanding general conjecture asking whether VC dimension controls sample representation up to a constant factor; it reaches far beyond any one learning algorithm or geometric example.

progress.text: The framework of Littlestone and Warmuth led to the conjecture that compression size can be linear in VC dimension; the general conjecture remains explicit in the 2025 survey of reductions.
Moran and Yehudayoff prove a general \(2^{O(d)}\) bound for binary classes. The corrected arXiv v2 is the appropriate preprint; the journal version appeared in JACM in 2016.
Chase and coauthors prove an exponential dimension obstruction to embedding arbitrary VC classes in extremal classes, limiting a major proposed approach without refuting sample compression itself.
Bourneuf and coauthors obtain almost-linear proper compression in treewidth and cliquewidth for graph-ball classes, while retaining the general conjecture as open.

The latest version of arXiv:2603.23561, which had earlier claimed a compression breakthrough and later a no-clash teaching result, is withdrawn. Its authors identify an incorrect proof of Lemma 2. This is not a resolution.

context_blocks.text: The stored object is a small selection of examples that lets a fixed decoding rule recover every training label. It need not identify the unknown target function on points never observed. For example, consider indicators of closed intervals on the real line. Retain the leftmost and rightmost positive examples, or the empty set if there are no positives. Decode to the interval between those retained points, or to the all-zero function in the empty case. Realizability ensures that no negative example lies between the extreme positives. Thus an arbitrarily large sample can be represented by at most two examples.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A real-valued example may itself require arbitrarily many bits to describe; sample compression charges one unit for retaining it. Conversely, permitting an arbitrary uncharged side message would trivialize the problem, because that message could encode the whole sample. The fixed reconstructor and the explicit bound b prevent this loophole. The question concerns the combinatorial information carried by selected observations, rather than ordinary lossless compression of their numerical representations.

Moran and Yehudayoff proved that every finite-VC binary class has a scheme of size \(2^{O(d)}\), settling the earlier existence question. Their argument combines learning with an approximate minimax principle. More precisely, their bound also involves the dual VC dimension: this reverses the roles of domain points and concepts, treating each point as its pattern of membership across the concepts. Since the dual dimension can be exponential in d, that result leaves a substantial quantitative gap. Their corrected 2015 version retains the binary theorem while withdrawing an erroneous multiclass extension.

A studied auxiliary question asks whether each class embeds in an extremal class of comparable VC dimension. Chase and coauthors show that such embeddings can require an exponential increase in dimension. Their COLT 2024 result rules out that general route to a linear bound; it does not show that the original class itself needs exponential compression. A failed intermediate representation is different from a lower bound against every compressor.

The problem also has concrete graph instances. Fix a graph and label sampled vertices according to membership in an unknown metric ball. Bourneuf and coauthors give proper schemes of size \(O(t \log (t+1))\) when the graph has treewidth at most t, and an analogous bound for cliquewidth. Proper means that decoding produces another ball, a stronger requirement than this card imposes. Their April 2026 work supplies structured examples and explicitly leaves the general linear-VC conjecture open.

Attias, Hanneke, and Ramaswami show how binary compression results transfer to multiclass, regression, and robust-learning settings, with additional factors or additional requirements on the binary scheme. Consequently, a solution could have consequences beyond binary prediction, but those transfers have hypotheses. In particular, their Open Problem 28 is about adversarially robust compression; the standard conjecture used here appears in their introduction.

cards.title: Learning parity with noise in polynomial time
cards.formal: For every fixed rational noise rate \(\eta\) with \(0<\eta <1/2\), does there exist a uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, for every n and every secret \(s\in \{0,1\}^{n}\), recovers s with probability at least \(2/3\) from independent samples \((a,\langle a,s\rangle \oplus e)\), where a is uniform in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and e is independently \(Bernoulli(\eta )\)?
cards.definitions: The inner product \(\langle a,s\rangle\) is \(\sum_{i} a_{i} s_{i}\) modulo two, and ⊕ is addition modulo two. The unknown s is fixed throughout an execution. Each requested sample uses a fresh independent uniform vector a and an independent error bit e, with \(\Pr [e=1]=\eta\). The learner knows n and the fixed rate \(\eta\), and receives only classical samples. It cannot choose a, request a noiseless label, identify which labels were corrupted, or make coherent quantum queries. For each fixed \(\eta\) the algorithm and its polynomial bound \(p\eta\) may depend on \(\eta\), but they must be uniform in n, without advice. Every execution uses at most \(p\eta (n)\) bit operations and requests at most \(p\eta (n)\) samples; reading and storing samples is charged. Polynomially many stored bits and repeated access to stored samples are allowed. The success probability is over the example generator and the learner’s random coins, for each fixed s. The desired output is the entire secret vector, not merely a predictor with unspecified advantage. No sparsity promise is imposed on s or on a. The quantifier over fixed rational \(\eta\) does not demand a running-time bound uniform as \(\eta\) approaches \(1/2\) with n.

cards.status_note: The primary literature checked through 11 September 2026 leaves classical polynomial-time learning at fixed constant noise open. The card asks for all fixed rational rates separately, allowing rate-dependent polynomial bounds. context_blocks.text: A parity function is among the simplest algebraic classifiers: choose a hidden subset of coordinates and return their XOR. Without label noise, sufficiently many random examples give linear equations, and Gaussian elimination recovers the secret with high probability. Independent noise changes the task from solving a consistent system to identifying which apparent equations should be trusted. Ordinary elimination mixes error bits along with the equations, so its usual exactness argument no longer applies.

The difficulty is computational rather than a lack of information. For a fixed noise rate below one half, the true secret agrees with a fresh label with probability \(1- \eta\). Every other secret agrees with probability one half under the uniform distribution on inputs. With a sufficiently large constant multiple of n examples, concentration and a union bound over the \(2^{n}\) candidates identify the true secret with high probability. Exhaustively testing those candidates takes exponential time, leaving open whether their search can be avoided.

At \(\eta =1/4\), for example, the correct candidate has expected agreement \(3/4\), while every incorrect parity has expected agreement \(1/2\). A threshold strictly between these values separates them once enough independent samples have been collected. This simple gap explains why a polynomial sample bound alone is not the desired breakthrough. One must locate the exceptional candidate efficiently among exponentially many possibilities.

Writing the sample vectors as rows of a matrix A gives b=As+e over the binary field. The columns of A generate a random linear code, and the task becomes decoding a random noisy codeword. This connection explains the relevance to cryptography. It does not turn a worst-case NP-hardness theorem for decoding arbitrary codes into an average-case hardness theorem for the random distribution used here. Quantifiers over matrices, errors and sample counts have to survive the reduction.

Blum, Kalai and Wasserman give a \(2^{O(n/\log  n)}\)-time algorithm using a comparable subexponential number of examples for constant noise. Combining examples cancels blocks of coordinates, while the analysis controls how the combined noise approaches a fair coin. Their work also separates noise-tolerant learning from the statistical-query framework in an appropriate restricted parity regime. Thus failure of statistical-query methods cannot simply be interpreted as failure of all algorithms with access to individual examples.

Lyubashevsky answers a different sample-efficiency question: subexponential computation is possible using only \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) examples for each fixed \(\varepsilon >0\). The resulting running time is \(2^{O(n/\log  \log  n)}\). This result is directly relevant to a learner that can collect only polynomially many samples, but its time bound is still superpolynomial. Keeping the two resources visible prevents the better exponent of the many-sample algorithm from being quoted as a polynomial-sample guarantee.

There are substantial unconditional lower bounds in restricted resource models. Garg, Kothari, Liu and Raz show that a streaming learner needs either \(\Omega (n^{2}/(1/2- \eta ))\) bits of memory or exponentially many samples, with a strong success-probability guarantee in their theorem. For fixed \(\eta\), the memory alternative is quadratic, which is permitted by the polynomial-time question. This establishes a real storage cost without ruling out a general polynomial-time algorithm.

Aggarwal, Gupta and Zeyong’s May 2026 hardness amplification relates success on a small fraction of instances to success on almost all instances after changing the dimension and noise parameters. Aggarwal and coauthors’ September 8 revision gives low-noise LPN hardness under simultaneous worst-case assumptions concerning decoding a code and distinguishing noisy codewords of its dual. These strengthen the understanding of hardness assumptions; neither is an unconditional proof that this learner cannot exist.

The every-secret guarantee is not an artificial extra obstacle compared with a uniform random secret. A learner can choose a uniform mask r, replace each label b by \(b\oplus \langle a,r\rangle\), learn the masked secret \(s\oplus r\) and remove the mask. The transformed secret is uniform while the noise law is unchanged. The central uncertainty therefore persists even when randomness in the hidden parity itself is supplied for free.

cards.title: Learning Boolean juntas from uniform random examples
cards.formal: Does there exist a uniform randomized algorithm that learns every Boolean k-junta on n variables from independent uniform random labelled examples in time polynomial in \(n, 2^{k}\) and \(1/\varepsilon\), with uniform-distribution error at most \(\varepsilon\) and success probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: For integers \(0\le k\le n, a k\)-junta is a function \(f:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) for which there is an unknown set \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,n\}, |S|\le k\), and an arbitrary Boolean function g on |S| bits such that \(f(x)=g\)(x restricted to S). The learner receives n,k and a positive integer \(t\ge 3\), setting \(\varepsilon =1/t\). Each requested example consists of an independently uniform \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) and its exact, noiseless label \(f(x)\). The learner may request further independent examples, but cannot choose inputs to be labelled or obtain correlated examples. The output is a finite Boolean circuit h on n input bits; it need not itself be a k-junta. With probability at least \(2/3\) over all examples and internal random bits, Pr over a fresh uniform x that \(h(x)\ne f(x)\) is at most \(1/t\). One fixed classical probabilistic Turing machine must run, on every sample and random tape, for at most \((n+2^{k}+t)^{C}\) steps, up to a fixed multiplicative constant, for a universal constant C independent of n,k,t,f. Reading examples, computation and writing the circuit count toward this bound. Restricting \(\varepsilon\) to reciprocal integers is equivalent, up to polynomial factors, to the usual arbitrary-accuracy requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determine whether arbitrary dependence on a small hidden set of variables can be learned efficiently from ordinary observations, separating computational search from sample sufficiency.

importance.reason: A central unresolved task in computational learning theory, isolating feature selection and serving as a prerequisite for efficient learning of general decision trees and DNF formulas.

progress.text: Mossel–O’Donnell–Servedio publish the first constant-factor improvement over the brute-force exponent for learning arbitrary juntas from uniform examples.

Beretta’s revised RANDOM paper distinguishes junta-distribution learning from noiseless function learning and records the continuing computational gap.
Servedio’s survey explicitly retains the uniform-example junta barrier and contrasts it with efficient learning using membership queries.
A new gradient-based learning result uses labelled samples from a lazy random walk; its temporal dependence is outside the independent-example model.

context_blocks.text: A junta is a model of prediction with many irrelevant features. The target may use only a small hidden subset of a very long input, but its behaviour on those relevant features is unrestricted. The goal is accurate prediction on a new uniform input. Identifying the support exactly is not required: variables that affect too little probability mass may be ignored at the requested accuracy.

The allowance of \(2^{k}\) is deliberate. An arbitrary function on the relevant coordinates can have a truth table with \(2^{k}\) entries, so a polynomial dependence on that quantity accommodates the complexity of the target itself. The desired improvement is in locating useful coordinates among n possibilities. For k proportional to log n, the proposed bound would give polynomial-time learning. Brute-force support enumeration has about \(n^{k}\) possibilities and becomes quasipolynomial in that regime.

The sample requirement already fits the target. There are at most \((k+1)n^{k}\cdot 2^{2^{k}}\) juntas on n variables. A union bound shows that \(O((2^{k}+k \log (n+1)+\log (k+1)+1)/\varepsilon )\) independent examples suffice for every consistent hypothesis in this finite class to have error at most \(\varepsilon\), with constant confidence. Such a hypothesis exists because the labels come from a junta. The difficulty is finding it efficiently; enumerating supports and filling their truth tables gives a direct but expensive method.

Mossel, O’Donnell and Servedio obtained the first constant-factor improvement in the exponent of this search. Their algorithm combines structural information about Boolean functions with algebraic computation and learns exactly in approximately \(n^{0.704k}\cdot \operatorname{poly}(n,2^{k})\) time at the matrix-multiplication exponent used in the paper. This is an algorithm for arbitrary juntas from uniform random examples, so it addresses the same access model.

Gregory Valiant subsequently improved the exponent to below 0.6k, with polynomial factors in n and \(2^{k}\), through algorithms for finding correlations and learning sparse parities with noise. His argument combines a noise-robust parity learner with the junta structure used in earlier work. The approximately \(n^{0.6k}\) benchmark is still stated in Servedio’s November 2025 survey. It is a major improvement over exhaustive search, but the exponent on the ambient dimension still grows with k.

Simple correlation screening is insufficient. For example, \(f(x)=x_{1} \mathrm{XOR} x_{2} \mathrm{XOR} x_{3}\) is independent of each individual input bit under the uniform distribution, although all three are relevant. This does not make noiseless parity computationally hard: one can learn an unknown parity by solving linear equations over the two-element field. It explains why a limitation of low-order correlations or statistical queries cannot automatically be converted into a lower bound for every algorithm using actual examples.

Membership queries change the task substantially. They allow the learner to choose an input and ask for its label, making it possible to isolate relevant variables by carefully comparing nearby points. Learning juntas in polynomial time in n and \(2^{k}\) is known with this additional access. Servedio’s survey also notes that monotone juntas admit the desired bound from ordinary uniform examples; arbitrary juntas need not expose their variables through such first-order information.

The phrase “learning junta distributions” describes another problem: recovering a probability mass function that depends on a small coordinate set. Beretta’s RANDOM 2025 paper relates that distribution-learning task to learning sparse parities with noise. Its introduction explicitly distinguishes noiseless Boolean junta learning and reports the existing \(n^{0.6k}\) benchmark. An equivalence for distribution learning is not an unconditional lower bound for the noiseless prediction task here.

Cornacchia, Mikulincer and Mossel show in May 2026 that a suitable neural-network training procedure can learn juntas efficiently from a lazy random walk on the hypercube, with essentially linear sample complexity in ambient dimension for each fixed k. Their loss uses differences between consecutive samples. Even if each sample has a uniform marginal distribution, consecutive samples are correlated; an independent-example oracle does not provide those labelled neighbouring points. This result therefore leaves the present question intact.

The problem is a gateway to learning richer representations. A k-junta has both a decision tree and a DNF representation of size at most \(2^{k}\). Efficient uniform-example learners for those general classes would consequently learn juntas within the requested resource bound. A positive result here would solve a central obstacle, while a negative result for unrestricted learners would explain a computational limitation of feature selection even under a particularly simple input distribution.

Wigderson’s Open Problem 17.9, the source inherited as TCS-0023, concerns the class \(F_{k}\) of functions depending on at most k input bits. The old catalogue title incorrectly described it as growing-size DNF learning. Its challenge is to go beyond constant support size with polynomial-time learning, or justify a hardness assumption. This card retains the precise stronger target \(\operatorname{poly}(n,2^{k},1/\varepsilon )\) for every k. A positive answer supplies polynomial time when \(k=O(\log  n); a\) learner for only one slower-growing support regime need not meet the full target. Conditional hardness allowed as an outcome in the source is also weaker than an unconditional negative answer here. The source record is consolidated as a related milestone, not asserted to be an equivalent formulation; The removed TCS-0023 keeps its reserved ID and deletion reason; its bibliography and weaker milestone are preserved here.

cards.title: Polynomial-time distribution-free PAC learning of DNF
cards.formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every \(n,s\ge 1\), every Boolean function f representable by a DNF with at most s terms on n variables, every distribution D on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\), and all accuracy and confidence parameters \(\varepsilon ,\delta \in (0,1)\), PAC learns f from independent D-distributed labelled examples in time polynomial in \(n,s,1/\varepsilon\) and \(\log (1/\delta )\)? The output may be any efficiently evaluable Boolean hypothesis; membership queries are not allowed.
cards.definitions: A literal is a variable \(x_{i}\) or its negation. A term is a conjunction of literals, and a disjunctive normal form \((\mathrm{DNF})\) is an OR of terms. Terms may have arbitrary width up to n after simplification. The size parameter s bounds the number of terms; counting literal occurrences instead changes polynomial bounds by at most a factor n. The target DNF is unknown: the learner is supplied only n, the upper bound s, and learning parameters. For an exact encoding, supply integers \(t,b\ge 2\) and set \(\varepsilon =1/t\) and \(\delta =2^{- b}\). One fixed probabilistic Turing machine must use at most \(p(n,s,t,b)\) steps for one fixed polynomial p, on every sequence of sample and random outcomes. Each example-oracle request supplies a fresh pair \((x,f(x))\) with x drawn independently from the same arbitrary unknown D; the learner cannot select x. Receiving and reading the n-bit sample counts toward the time bound. Samples are noiseless and realizable by the promised target. The output is an explicitly written deterministic Boolean circuit h on n input bits, not necessarily a DNF. With probability at least \(1- \delta\) over the examples and internal randomness, \(\Pr_{x\text{ drawn from }D}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon\). Writing and evaluating this circuit have polynomial cost. Reciprocal-integer accuracy and dyadic confidence suffice for the usual general parameters by rounding toward stronger guarantees. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.

context_blocks.text: A DNF represents a union of rule-defined regions: an example is accepted when it satisfies at least one conjunction of feature conditions. The task is to infer accurate predictions from observations, without being given those rules. Feldman’s introduction identifies the general distribution-free question before studying more structured input distributions; that introductory question is the source of this catalogue record.

There is no information-theoretic obstacle to using polynomially many examples. There are at most \(3^{n}\) simplified conjunctions, since each variable is absent, positive or negative. Padding a DNF with empty slots bounds the number of candidate formulas by \((3^{n}+1)^{s}\). The finite-class union bound therefore gives \(O((ns+\log (1/\delta ))/\varepsilon )\) samples sufficient for every consistent DNF in this class to generalize. Exhaustively finding such a DNF may still take enormous time. The question asks whether that computational search can be avoided, even by outputting a different representation.

The distinction between a constant and a growing number of terms is essential. The classical \(n^{O(s)}\) algorithm is polynomial for each fixed s, but does not provide a single polynomial in n and s. Servedio’s 2025 survey records the longstanding goal and the subexponential distribution-free upper bound \(2^{\widetilde{O} (n^{1/3} \log  s)}\). For polynomially many terms and fixed learning accuracy, this still leaves a substantial gap to polynomial time.

A distribution-free learner must handle probability concentrated on any subset of the Boolean cube. An argument that a long conjunction rarely holds under independent uniform coordinates need not survive such a distribution. Feldman’s Fourier-based work uses uniform or product structure and, in some settings, additional query access. Its positive results should not be read as a solution from arbitrary-distribution random examples alone.

Allowing hypotheses outside the target class is substantive. A hardness proof for producing another DNF can leave open an efficient learner that outputs a Boolean circuit or a polynomial threshold function. Daniely and Shalev-Shwartz obtain hardness that also covers improper learning, under their assumption about refuting random K-SAT. The assumption is part of that theorem, so it supplies evidence against efficient learning without deciding the unconditional question posed here.

Daniely and Vardi later derive hardness for DNF with a growing number of terms from an assumption about local pseudorandom generators. This gives a second precise route connecting the computational difficulty of learning compact rules to average-case complexity. Neither theorem should be abbreviated to an unconditional assertion that DNF cannot be learned.

The May 2026 Iterative Chow Filtering paper obtains quasipolynomial-time DNF learning under a uniform training distribution in a framework permitting abstention under distribution shift. Those distribution, output and runtime guarantees differ from the present target. This recent result was included in the status check and does not supply the required polynomial-time distribution-free learner.

A positive resolution would also give the learner sought in TCS-6543: every k-junta can be written as a DNF with at most \(2^{k}\) terms, and the uniform distribution is one allowed choice of D. This implication goes from general DNF learning to junta learning; learning juntas alone does not supply an algorithm for general DNF targets. The two cards retain distinct targets. The mislabelled legacy record TCS-0023 is consolidated with the junta card because its actual cited problem concerns growing junta support.

cards.title: Distribution-free learning of two margin halfspaces
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized learner and one polynomial \(p\) with the following guarantee? For every dimension \(d\geq 1\), every \(0<\gamma,\varepsilon<1\), and every distribution \(D\) satisfying the realizability and margin promises below, the learner receives independent labeled examples from \(D\) and, within \(p(d,\lceil1/\gamma\rceil,\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil)\) operations, outputs a hypothesis \(h\) such that \[\Pr_{\text{samples, learner}}\!\left[\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\leq\varepsilon\right]\geq 2/3.\] The hypothesis may be improper, but its evaluation on a new point must also take polynomial time in these parameters. No factorization or other restriction on the example distribution is imposed beyond the stated promises.
cards.why: This asks whether the simplest intersection of linear classification rules remains efficiently learnable from ordinary examples under arbitrary distributions. A positive answer would remove a distributional assumption from a central margin-learning model; a negative answer would establish a computational obstruction even when the learner may use any efficiently evaluable representation.

sentences: The intersection of two halfspaces labels a point positively when both linear inequalities hold.
This question asks whether such labels can be learned in polynomial time from independent examples under any distribution with a margin from both boundaries.
The learner may output a different kind of hypothesis, provided that predictions remain efficient.
The 2025 source proves efficient learning under an extra factorization assumption, while two 2026 preprints report broader bounds that do not by themselves meet this polynomial target.
A resolution would determine whether two linear rules can be learned efficiently without favorable structure in the example distribution.

cards.definitions: The instance distribution is a Borel probability distribution on \(\mathbb R^{d}\times\{-1,+1\}\). There exist unknown unit vectors \(u,v\in\mathbb R^{d}\) and thresholds \(a,b\in\mathbb R\) such that, almost surely, \(\|x\|_{2}\leq1\), \(|\langle u,x\rangle+a|\geq\gamma\), \(|\langle v,x\rangle+b|\geq\gamma\), and \(y=+1\) precisely when both \(\langle u,x\rangle+a\geq0\) and \(\langle v,x\rangle+b\geq0\). In particular the margin promise applies to both defining hyperplanes, including on negatively labeled examples. The learner receives \(d,\gamma,\varepsilon\) and a sample oracle for independent draws from \(D\); it does not receive the unknown vectors, thresholds, a description of \(D\), membership queries or statistical-query oracles. Time is measured in the real-arithmetic model for the continuous-example formulation: a finite uniform program, with rational constants, exact real registers, integer indexing, arithmetic \(+, -, \times, /\) (division only by nonzero values), comparisons and independent fair random bits. Each arithmetic operation, comparison, register access and random bit costs one step; obtaining and reading a sample costs \(d+1\) steps. No operation extracts arbitrarily many bits of a real number in one step. The learner outputs a finite description of a deterministic prediction program together with finitely many stored real parameters; description length, storage, sample count, training time and evaluation time must obey fixed polynomial bounds. All bounds are worst-case over samples and internal randomness; only the accuracy guarantee is probabilistic. This explicitly fixes the arithmetic-cost convention for the source model, rather than asserting a finite-bit running-time theorem for arbitrary-precision real inputs.

context_blocks.text: A single separating hyperplane with a margin is a basic tractable classification model. Intersecting two such regions is already a substantial test of distribution-independent learning: allowing an arbitrary output hypothesis removes the requirement to recover two separating hyperplanes themselves.

Diakonikolas, Ma, Ren and Tzamos obtain an efficient learner when the distribution factors between the span of the two normal vectors and its orthogonal complement. Their general-model discussion on printed page 1473 leaves the distribution-free margin problem unresolved. The factorization promise is an additional assumption, not a consequence of a geometric margin.

A July 2026 revision by Alman, Patel and Servedio reports subexponential-time distribution-free learning for Boolean functions of a fixed number of halfspaces. That running time does not meet the polynomial bound asked here.

A separate July 2026 revision by Patel and Vempala reports a margin-sensitive algorithm for intersections of a variable number of halfspaces. Its abstract does not establish a polynomial-time learner for two halfspaces; its discussion of matching lower bounds cannot be transferred to the fixed-two case without checking their parameter range.

cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified learner-existence statement or its negation in the specified arithmetic and sampling model. A positive answer includes the learner, its hypothesis representation, the polynomial training and evaluation bounds, and its distribution-independent accuracy guarantee. A negative answer must be unconditional for this model; hardness restricted to proper learners, statistical-query learners, a growing number of halfspaces, or an additional complexity assumption does not refute the statement.

cards.title: Learning decision trees from uniform random examples in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized learner which, for all \(n,s\ge 1\) and rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), learns every size-at-most-s Boolean decision tree on n variables from uniform random labeled examples in time \(\operatorname{poly}(n,s,1/\varepsilon )\), with error at most \(\varepsilon\) and success probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: A decision tree has internal nodes querying one input coordinate, two outgoing edges labeled zero and one, and leaves labeled zero or one. Size counts all nodes. Samples are independent uniform \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) labeled by the unknown target f. The learner receives \(n,s,\varepsilon\) and may draw samples but cannot request labels at chosen inputs. It outputs a Boolean circuit h of polynomial size, with \(\Pr_{x\text{ uniform}}[h(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon\) on at least two thirds of runs. All sampling, computation, circuit writing and evaluation costs use classical bit operations; the total worst-case learning time has one polynomial bound.

context_blocks.text: Decision trees are an elementary representation for Boolean classification. Uniform data removes distributional pathologies but still leaves open whether random examples suffice for fully polynomial learning.

Kalai and Teng contrast the unresolved uniform-distribution problem with their positive result for most perturbed product distributions. Chosen-input queries can provide information unavailable from examples alone. The existing proper-learning card allows membership queries and requires a tree output. This target permits improper output but removes that query access.

cards.title: Distribution-free improper learning of two unrestricted halfspaces
cards.formal: Is there a single randomized learner that, for every distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^n\), every target \(f\) expressible as the intersection of two integer-weight halfspaces of total description length at most a supplied bound \(B\), and every rational \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), uses only independent labeled examples from \(D\) to output a Boolean circuit \(H\) with \(\Pr_{x\sim D}[H(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\), in time polynomial in \(n+B+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)\)?
cards.definitions: A halfspace is \(h(x)=1\) exactly when \(\sum_{i} w_{i} x_{i}\ge \theta\), with \(w_i,\theta\in\mathbb{Z}\) in signed binary; equality is positive. The target f is the conjunction of two such predicates. Its description length is the bit length of a list of both weight vectors and thresholds, using self-delimiting binary integers. The learner receives n and B in unary and a rational \(\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon <1/2\) in binary. It is promised that f has at least one such description of length at most B, but receives neither that description nor its weights. An example oracle returns independent pairs \((x,f(x))\) with x sampled from an arbitrary fixed distribution D on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\). The learner receives only these labeled examples and its own independent fair coins. Each oracle call costs at least \(n+1\) steps to receive its bits; all further work is charged in Turing-machine bit steps. Membership queries, advice and descriptions or probability evaluations of D are absent. There must be a fixed polynomial P such that on every random tape the running time, and hence sample count and output length, are bounded by \(P(n+B+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon))\). Output a deterministic Boolean circuit \(H:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) in the explicit \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}/\mathrm{NOT}\) basis. The success condition is \(\Pr_{\mathrm{samples,coins}}[\Pr_{x\sim D}[H(x)\ne f(x)]\le\varepsilon]\ge2/3\), uniformly over \(n,B,\varepsilon ,D\) and every promised f. Circuit evaluation costs polynomial time in its output encoding. The hypothesis need not be an intersection of halfspaces. Encoding an arbitrary deterministic polynomial-time evaluator by its Boolean circuit preserves this unrestricted efficient-output convention.

cards.definitions: Let X be an instance set, Y a label set and \(\varnothing \ne H\subseteq Y^{X} a\) known hypothesis class. On round t an adversary presents \(x_{t}\in X\), the learner chooses a probability distribution \(p_{t}\) on Y, and the adversary then reveals \(y_{t}\in Y\). The learner suffers loss \(1- p_{t}(y_{t})\), the probability of a wrong randomized prediction. It observes the actual label, not just whether its prediction was correct. Its regret is \(\sum_{t=1}^{T}(1- p_{t}(y_{t}))- \min _{h\in H}\sum_{t=1}^{T}1[h(x_{t})\ne y_{t}]\). Let \(R_{T}(H)\) be the infimum over learner strategies of the supremum of this regret over adversarial plays; the adversary may observe \(p_{t}\) before choosing \(y_{t}\). This distribution-valued convention already accounts for prediction randomness. There is no computational-efficiency restriction on a strategy, and it may know T. A depth-d Littlestone tree is a complete binary tree with an instance \(x\in X\) at each internal node and two distinct labels from Y on its two outgoing edges. It is shattered by H if every root-to-leaf path has some \(h\in H\) whose labels on the encountered instances equal all the path’s edge labels. The Littlestone dimension \(\mathrm{L}(H)\) is the greatest shattered depth, or infinity if depths are unbounded. Define \(R(d,T)\) by the supremum in the statement; the bound sought is uniform across all choices of X,Y,H. If \(\mathrm{L}(H)=0\) all hypotheses agree pointwise and zero regret is attainable. The domain \(T\ge d\) avoids the separate saturation regime in which regret is capped by T.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(d,T)\) and constants \(a,A>0\) independent of both parameters, all label sets and all hypothesis classes, and prove a \(g(d,T)\le R(d,T)\le A g(d,T)\) for every integer \(T\ge d\ge 1\). Lower bounds may use families of classes; a worst-case class need not attain the supremum. This is an asymptotic regret target with multiplicative constants, not additive 0.01 error.

cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants \(c_{1},c_{2}>0\) and \(n_{0}\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}\), every \(0<\varepsilon <1/2\) and every one-pass learner recovering a uniformly random \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) from the noisy parity samples defined below, its worst-case memory S and maximum sample count T satisfy \(S\ge c_{1}n^{2}/\varepsilon ^{2}\) or \(T\ge 2^{c_{2}n}\)? cards.definitions: Arithmetic in 𝔽\(_{2}=\{0,1\}\) uses addition and multiplication modulo two; \(\langle a,x\rangle =\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}x_{i}\) mod 2. First choose x uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and hold it fixed. Independently for each t, choose \(a_{t}\) uniformly from \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) and a noise bit \(Z_{t}\) with \(\Pr [Z_{t}=1]=1/2- \varepsilon\); observe \((a_{t},b_{t})\) with \(b_{t}=\langle a_{t},x\rangle +Z_{t}\) mod 2. Noise bits, query vectors and internal learner coins are mutually independent. The learner outputs one estimate x̂; success means \(\hat\{x\}=x\), and its probability averages over x, all observations and internal coins. The learner sees each sample once in order, cannot choose \(a_{t}\) or revisit discarded observations, and has no computational-time restriction. Formally use a branching program with \(T+1\) layers and width at most \(2^{S}\), one start vertex and one outgoing edge for each possible sample at each nonterminal vertex, all going to the next layer. Leaves, possibly in earlier layers, are labelled by estimates in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\). Randomized learners may use fresh coins to choose state updates; retained coins are part of the state. Equivalently, the lower bound may be checked on deterministic nonuniform programs, since a random tape can be fixed to achieve at least the average success under this fixed input distribution without increasing width or length. The program may depend on n and \(\varepsilon\); its transition description, current layer and input sample are not charged as stored data. Memory counts persistent state bits, \(S=\lceil \log _{2}(\operatorname{width})\rceil\), and T is the maximum number of consumed samples, not its expectation. No hypothesis is made about the hardness of LPN in unrestricted computation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the universal bounded-error memory/sample tradeoff with constants uniform in \(\varepsilon\), or refute that asymptotic claim by showing that no such constants can work. A bound \(\Omega (n^{2}/\varepsilon ), a\) result only for constant \(\varepsilon\), or a lower bound in a restricted statistical-query model does not settle the proposed dependence on noise.

cards.title: Proper decision-tree learning in polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a uniform randomized membership-query algorithm that properly learns Boolean decision trees under the uniform distribution in polynomial time? For every \(n,s\geq1\), every integer \(m\geq2\), and every \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) representable by a decision tree with at most \(s\) leaves, the learner is given \(n,s,m\) and oracle access to \(f\). It must output an explicitly represented decision tree \(h\), with probability at least \(2/3\), such that \[2^{-n}|\{x\in\{0,1\}^n:h(x)\ne f(x)\}|\leq1/m.\] Its worst-case running time must be polynomial in \(n,s,m\).
cards.why: The question tests whether efficient prediction can be achieved while retaining a decision-tree representation in a basic, well-specified query model. Its resolution would clarify the computational cost of proper learning beyond sample complexity alone.
cards.status_note: The exact uniform-distribution proper query question is explicit in the 2022 source. Checked later hardness results do not cover this distributional setting. The bounded review through 14 September 2026 found no polynomial-time learner or unconditional impossibility theorem for the stated model.

cards.definitions: A Boolean decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node queries one coordinate \(x_i\), \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\), and its two outgoing edges correspond to values zero and one. Leaves are labelled zero or one; following the input’s path defines the output bit. Size means the number of leaves. Repeated coordinate tests are allowed. The unknown target need only admit a tree with at most \(s\) leaves; that tree is not supplied. A membership query may be any chosen bit string \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) and returns the exact noiseless bit \(f(x)\). The learner is one finite probabilistic multitape Turing program with independent fair random bits, no advice, and no other oracle. Writing the \(n\)-bit query costs ordinary bit steps; reading its returned label costs one. All random-bit generation, computation and output are charged. Its time is bounded by \(K(n+s+m+1)^a\) on every target and every random execution, for constants \(K,a\) independent of parameters. Integers are supplied in binary. The accuracy convention \(\varepsilon=1/m\) specifies the usual inverse-accuracy parameter without an arbitrary real input encoding; existence for these accuracies is equivalent to existence for arbitrary requested positive accuracy by rounding to a smaller reciprocal accuracy. Properness is weak properness: the output must be a decision tree, but need not have at most \(s\) leaves. Its full explicit description, with variable indices, children and leaf bits, must fit the polynomial time bound. The success probability concerns the learner’s randomness; prediction error is measured over a fresh uniform point and the guarantee holds for every promised target.
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete Lean-checked proof that a learner satisfying all these quantifiers exists, or that no such learner exists. The positive direction requires polynomial bit time, a proper explicit tree output and the uniform-distribution error bound with probability at least \(2/3\). A negative result must rule out all randomized learners of this kind, including those allowed polynomial-size trees larger than the target. An improper hypothesis, a random-examples-only result, distribution-free hardness alone, or a conditional obstruction whose assumption is unproved does not settle the stated existence question.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 1 asks for polynomial time in the number of variables, target size and inverse accuracy. The source explicitly distinguishes strict properness, which preserves the target size bound, from weak properness, which merely returns a tree; its question is open even for the latter.

The representation constraint matters: an efficient predictor need not come with a comparably small tree representation. Membership queries also matter because they let the learner choose inputs instead of relying only on the examples that a distribution happens to provide.

The source’s Theorem 2 reports an almost-polynomial proper query learner, with time \(\widetilde O(n^2)(s/\varepsilon)^{O(\log((\log s)/\varepsilon))}\). In the usual polynomial-size, constant-error regime this yields \(n^{O(\log\log n)}\), which still exceeds a fixed polynomial.

Koch, Strassle and Tan prove NP-hardness for distribution-free proper learning with queries in FOCS 2023. Their paper explicitly contrasts that result with the easier uniform-distribution setting. A lower bound obtained from a specially chosen distribution does not rule out this card’s learner.

Their FOCS 2024 coding-theoretic work gives further hardness connections for decision-tree learning. Its discussion distinguishes the remaining uniform-distribution problem from the distributions used in its reductions.

An empirical tree-fitting procedure and its success on a finite collection of datasets are not the universal learning guarantee. The error bound must hold for every small-tree target, even when the target’s structure is unknown and the output tree has a different topology.

cards.title: NP-hardness of improper learning of \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\)
cards.formal: Is there an integer \(a\ge1\) such that, for every integer \(b\ge a\), there are an integer \(r\ge1\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time oracle reduction \(R_b\) which decides SAT with success probability at least \(2/3\) using the following agnostic circuit-learning oracle? A query is a Boolean sampling circuit producing a distribution \(D\) on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\times\{0,1\}\). Every oracle reply must be a circuit \(h\) of size at most \((m+1)^{b}\) satisfying \[L_D(h)\le\min_{g\in\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}((m+1)^{a})}L_D(g)+(m+1)^{-r}.\] The reduction must succeed for every sequence of valid replies. The exponent \(r\), reduction and its running-time polynomial may depend on \(b\), but not on the SAT instance. No cryptographic or unproved complexity assumption is part of the target. This selects the source's agnostic, efficiently samplable-distribution reduction formulation.
cards.why: This asks whether learning general small circuits remains hard when the learner is free to use a different and polynomially larger representation. Establishing such hardness from SAT would connect worst-case NP difficulty with a central general learning task, while the known links to witness encryption expose consequences beyond learning itself.

A June 2026 follow-up gives related conditional hardness, leaving the unconditional target unresolved.

cards.definitions:
A Boolean circuit is an explicitly listed directed acyclic graph with named input wires, constant zero and one wires, fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates, and named output wires. Its size is its number of noninput gates, including constant gates. Gate types and predecessor indices are encoded in binary in topological order; all input and output counts are explicit. Write \(\operatorname{SIZE}_{m}(s)\) for the binary functions on \(m\) input bits computed by one-output circuits with at most \(s\) gates. A language is in \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{poly}\) if its restriction to each input length is computed by a circuit family with polynomial size; those circuits need not be generated uniformly.

A sampling-circuit query has some number \(q\ge0\) of random input bits and \(m+1\) output bits, with \(m\ge1\). Uniform independent bits in \(\{0,1\}^{q}\) induce the joint distribution \(D\); the first \(m\) outputs are the example and the last is its label. Labels may be noisy and need not be realizable by a small circuit. The risk is \(L_D(h)=\Pr_{(x,y)\sim D}[h(x)\ne y]\). The oracle returns the full description of a predictor satisfying the displayed excess-risk guarantee. An answer always exists because the smaller comparator family is finite, contains constant functions, and is included in the allowed output family. The oracle itself has no computational restriction. It may select different valid circuits based on the query history; the reduction must work for all such selections, not only for a favorable learning rule.

The reduction is a randomized multitape Turing machine using independent fair bits. For each fixed \(b\), one polynomial in the SAT input bit length bounds its running time on every random tape and response history, counting construction of all sampling circuits and reading all reply descriptions; oracle computation is uncharged. Queries may be adaptive and may have different \(m,q\). In particular, the entire sampling circuit and every reply must have polynomial encoding length in the reduction's input length. The reduction may inspect hypothesis descriptions and evaluate them; it has no additional oracle or advice. SAT uses an explicit syntax-tree encoding of AND, OR and NOT formulas, with malformed encodings rejected. Probability of a correct SAT answer is over the reduction's coins, for each fixed input and each valid response policy.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such an exponent \(a\) and reductions exist, or a proof of the negation. A positive answer must cover every polynomial output-size exponent \(b\ge a\), allowing the stated dependence of the reduction on \(b\). Hardness only when the predictor is restricted to the target size, or only under an additional cryptographic assumption, does not suffice. A negative answer must rule out the displayed family of reductions, not merely one restricted reduction technique.

Showing hardness only for size-preserving output can therefore leave an efficient improper learner possible. The source defines learning reductions by giving the oracle a sampling circuit for a distribution and receiving a sufficiently accurate hypothesis. This card retains that oracle interface. Sampling distributions are generated by the reduction; the task does not give a practical learner arbitrary target membership queries.

The polynomial target-size exponent is fixed before the allowed output exponent. For each allowed output exponent the reduction may be different. Adaptive randomized Turing reductions are allowed; the card does not impose the additional deterministic, nonadaptive, witness-mapping or honesty conditions used in some of the source’s cryptographic consequences.

The June 2026 paper proves conditional hardness for a related full-support learning problem. It assumes a strong indistinguishability obfuscator and a lower-bound hypothesis for propositional proof systems. cards.title: Proper unlabeled compression of ample classes
cards.formal: Does every nonempty ample concept class \(C\subseteq \{0,1\}\)ᵁ on a finite domain U admit a proper unlabeled sample compression scheme of size at most \(d=\operatorname{VC}(C)\)? Precisely, do there exist maps \(\kappa :RS(C)\to \{A\subseteq U:|A|\le d\}\) and \(\rho :\{A\subseteq U:|A|\le d\}\to C\) such that, for every realizable labeled partial sample \(s, \kappa (s)\subseteq dom(s)\) and \(\rho (\kappa (s))\) agrees with every label in s? The stored object is only an unordered subset of the sample’s input points. The bound is d, not an unspecified multiple of d.
cards.why: Would extend sharp label-free sample compression from maximum classes to the larger class characterized by equality of shattering and strong shattering, clarifying how far the VC dimension controls lossless reconstruction of consistent samples.

cards.definitions: A concept \(c\in C\) is a function \(c:U\to \{0,1\}\). A set \(A\subseteq U\) is shattered by C if \(\{c|_{A}:c\in C\}=\{0,1\}^{A}\). It is strongly shattered if some \(b:U\setminus A\to \{0,1\}\) has the property that, for every \(a:A\to \{0,1\}\), the combined labeling \(a\cup b\) belongs to C. Thus strong shattering requires a full cube of concepts with identical labels outside A. The class is ample when every shattered set is strongly shattered; ample classes are also called lopsided or shattering-extremal. Its VC dimension d is the maximum size of a shattered set. A labeled partial sample is a function \(s:A\to \{0,1\}\) on some \(A\subseteq U\), equivalently a set of pairs \((x,s(x))\) with distinct x. It is realizable if \(s=c|_{A}\) for some \(c\in C; RS(C)\) contains every such sample, including the empty sample. The compressor \(\kappa\) sees the entire labeled sample and may use its labels to choose a subset \(\kappa (s)\) of its domain, of size at most d. It sends only that subset. The reconstructor \(\rho\) receives no labels, ordering, multiplicities, sample size, omitted sample points or auxiliary bits; \(U,C,\kappa\) and \(\rho\) are fixed and shared beforehand. It returns a total concept belonging to C, which must agree with the original entire sample, including omitted labels. This is the proper convention explicitly used in the full source. Requiring \(\rho\) on all subsets of size at most d is equivalent to defining it only on \(Im(\kappa )\), because C is nonempty and unused inputs can be assigned any fixed concept. The existence of \(\kappa ,\rho\) is quantified separately for each finite C; no running-time bound for constructing or evaluating them, distributional assumption or probability of error is part of the statement. For \(d=0 a\) nonempty class has a single concept and the empty compressed set suffices. A maximum class of dimension d has cardinality \(\sum_{j=0}^{d} binomial(|U|,j)\); every maximum class is ample, but the converse need not hold.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the two maps with the stated d-point bound for every finite nonempty ample class, or give an ample class with a proof that no such pair of maps exists. A scheme retaining labels, returning a hypothesis outside C, storing extra information, or exceeding d points does not meet the target. A scheme that handles only full concepts rather than every realizable partial sample is also insufficient. Failure of a proposed corner-peeling construction alone does not refute existence of a compression scheme.

references.title: Optimal Collusion-Free Teaching
references.authors: David Kirkpatrick, Hans U. Simon, Sandra Zilles
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 12; PDF page 12

cards.definitions: A concept \(C\in C\) is a subset of the finite instance set X, identified with its indicator function \(1_{C}:X\to \{0,1\}\). A labeled sample is an unordered subset of \(X\times \{0,1\}\). It is consistent with C if each \((x,y)\) in it has \(y=1_{C}(x)\). A teaching map T assigns a sample \(T(C)\) consistent with C to every concept C in the class. It is non-clashing if, for every distinct \(C,D\in C, T(C)\) is not consistent with D or \(T(D)\) is not consistent with C. Equivalently, some point appearing in either teaching set has different labels under C and D. The condition is pairwise: \(T(C)\) need not by itself distinguish C from every other concept. A positive example has label 1 and a negative example has label 0; both count as one example. The size of T is \(\max _{C\in C}|T(C)|\), and \(NCTD(C)\) is the minimum of that size over all non-clashing teaching maps. The minimum exists because X and C are finite and giving all labels is a valid map. No sample order, extra message or additional side information is part of this definition. A subset \(S\subseteq X\) is shattered by C when \(\{C\cap S:C\in C\}=2\)ˢ. The VC dimension \(\operatorname{VC}(C)\) is the maximum cardinality of a shattered set. For a singleton concept class it is zero, and the empty teaching set works. The statement quantifies over all finite X and nonempty C, including that case; it concerns existence of a map, without an efficiency or encoding-size requirement on constructing it. The positive-only parameter NCTD\(^{+}\) restricts \(T(C)\) to samples with label 1 and can be larger. It is not the parameter in this conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the exact inequality for every finite concept class by establishing existence of a valid map of maximum size at most its VC dimension, or give a finite concept class and a proof that every non-clashing teaching map has larger maximum size. A quadratic bound or even a larger-constant linear bound is insufficient. A separation for positive-only maps, another teaching model, or an algorithmic hardness result for finding maps does not refute this existence statement.

cards.title: Recursive teaching dimension conjecture

importance.basis: Individual statement and primary-source review.

sentences: A finite concept class can be studied through both its VC dimension and its recursive teaching dimension.
VC dimension measures the ability to realize label patterns, while recursive teaching measures how examples can identify concepts through successive elimination.
The question asks whether one universal constant always bounds recursive teaching dimension by that constant times VC dimension.
The same constant must work for every finite class.
The project seeks a direct quantitative link between the complexity of learning from samples and the information needed for structured teaching.

context_blocks.text: Simon’s 2023 Open Problem 3 asks for precisely this universal linear relationship. The earlier Simon–Zilles open-problem paper is retained as provenance from the already consolidated duplicate; there is a single active target.

VC dimension measures how freely a class can realize labels on a chosen set of instances. Teaching instead allows examples tailored to one concept. Recursive teaching measures the hardest easiest-to-teach concept that remains after restricting the candidate class; it is not the maximum ordinary teaching dimension of the original class.

Hu, Wu, Li and Wang prove \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)=O(\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)^2)\). This bounds teaching complexity by VC dimension alone but leaves open whether the dependence can always be linear.
Simon’s 2025 paper verifies the conjecture for graph-induced star classes and graph-induced connected-set classes. These positive results cover rich families but not arbitrary Boolean classes.

Compton, Pabbaraju and Zhivotovskiy give lower bounds for particular greedy teaching-set constructions in 2025. They describe the universal conjecture as unresolved; limitations of those constructions are not counterexamples to the existence of small teaching sets.

The conjecture permits any universal constant, so examples separating the two dimensions by a fixed factor are compatible with it. Its failure would require ratios with no finite upper bound, while an affirmative result would uniformly connect two distinct notions of information needed for learning.

cards.definitions: A concept is a function \(h:X\to\{0,1\}\); repeated copies are not distinct concepts. A set \(S\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(\mathcal C\) if every Boolean labelling of \(S\) is the restriction of some member of \(\mathcal C\). The VC dimension is the largest size of a shattered set, with value zero for the empty class. For a nonempty subclass \(\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C\) and \(h\in\mathcal D\), put \[t(h,\mathcal D)=\min\{|S|:S\subseteq X,\ \forall g\in\mathcal D,\ g|_S=h|_S\Rightarrow g=h\}.\] These are labelled teaching examples: the labels are those assigned by \(h\). The minimum exists, and for a singleton class it is zero. Set \(t_{\min}(\mathcal D)=\min_{h\in\mathcal D}t(h,\mathcal D)\), and define \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)=\max_{\varnothing\ne\mathcal D\subseteq\mathcal C}t_{\min}(\mathcal D)\), with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\varnothing)=0\). Equivalently, repeatedly remove all concepts of minimum teaching-set size from the current class and take the largest such minimum encountered. No computational-efficiency, random-sampling or teacher-algorithm requirement is imposed. Restricting to finite \(X\) loses no instance for finite concept classes on an arbitrary domain: retain one domain point for each distinct vector of labels across the class. This preserves both dimensions and yields a finite domain.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal linear bound for some finite \(K\), or of its negation. A refutation must establish that for every \(K>0\) there is a finite class of positive VC dimension with \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)>K\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)\); one class with \(\operatorname{RTD}>\operatorname{VCdim}\) only rules out constant one. The optimal constant need not be determined. A quadratic upper bound, a result for special concept classes, or a lower bound for one teaching-set construction does not resolve the statement.

VC dimension measures how freely a class can realize labels on a chosen set of instances. Teaching instead allows examples tailored to one concept. Hu, Wu, Li and Wang prove \(\operatorname{RTD}(\mathcal C)=O(\operatorname{VCdim}(\mathcal C)^2)\). This bounds teaching complexity by VC dimension alone but leaves open whether the dependence can always be linear.

Simon’s 2025 paper verifies the conjecture for graph-induced star classes and graph-induced connected-set classes. These positive results cover rich families but not arbitrary Boolean classes.

cards.definitions: A member of Hn,r is a function \(h:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,+1\}\) of the form \(h(x)=+1\) if \(\sum j w_{j}x_{j}\ge \theta\) and \(h(x)=- 1\) otherwise, where \(w\in \mathbb{R} ^{n}\) has at most r nonzero coordinates and \(\theta \in \mathbb{R}\). Different weight representations of the same function define one member. For any probability distribution D on the finite cube and \(0<\gamma <1, SQ-DIM(Hn,r,D,\gamma )\) is the largest integer d for which there are d distinct functions \(h_{1},\ldots ,hd\) in Hn,r satisfying |\(\sum x D(x)h_{i}(x)h_{j}(x)|\le \gamma\) whenever \(i\ne j\). Then \(SQ-DIM(Hn,r,\gamma )\) is the maximum of this integer over all D, without any uniformity, product-distribution or margin promise. These maxima exist because the Boolean function class is finite and each feasible correlation condition is a closed constraint on the finite probability simplex. The constants C,a,b must work simultaneously for all n,r and all distributions. This is exactly the polynomial-versus-superpolynomial parameter question in source Problem 3, with its \(O(1)\) exponents made explicit. It asks for an upper bound on this dimension, not polynomial time to enumerate the functions or evaluate real weights.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound for some fixed C,a,b, or prove its negation: for every choice of such constants there are n,r and a distribution supporting a family larger than \(Cn^{b}\) with pairwise absolute correlations at most \(1/[C(r \log _{2} n)^{a}]\). The target is this source-defined parameter statement, not a guarantee restricted to one distribution or to halfspaces with large margin.

context_blocks.title: Learning with many irrelevant coordinates
context_blocks.text: A sparse halfspace uses at most r of n coordinates, even though the learner does not know which ones matter. context_blocks.title: What a statistical query reveals
context_blocks.text: An SQ learner asks for an approximate expectation of a bounded function \(\varphi (x,h(x))\in [- 1,1]\). A tolerance \(\tau\) allows any answer within \(\tau\) of the true expectation. Smaller tolerance requires more precise information. context_blocks.title: Why nearly uncorrelated functions appear
context_blocks.text: Under the uniform distribution, the one-sparse rules \(2x_{1}- 1\) and \(2x_{2}- 1\) have correlation zero: they agree as often as they disagree. SQ-DIM asks how many candidate halfspaces can be almost uncorrelated at once under the same distribution. It then takes the worst distribution, which need not be uniform.

context_blocks.title: The two polynomial requirements differ

Replacing the latter with a polynomial in r log n would ask for a stronger statement. Allowing inverse-polynomial tolerance in n instead would change the intended attribute-efficiency regime.

cards.title: Improper compression for Gaussian-mixture reconstruction
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized learning procedure with the following guarantee? For all integers \(d\ge1\), \(k>d\) and \(t\ge2\), and every Borel probability distribution \(D\) on the closed Euclidean unit ball \(B_d\), it learns a shared model \(w\) and an encoder–decoder pair \(E_w:B_d\to\{0,1\}^{b}\), \(Q_w:\{0,1\}^{b}\to B_d\) such that, with probability at least \(2/3\), \[\mathbb E_{x\sim D}\|Q_w(E_w(x))-x\|_2^{2}\le\operatorname{OPT}_k(D)+1/t,\qquad \operatorname{OPT}_k(D)=\inf_{\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_k\in B_d}\mathbb E_{x\sim D}\min_{i\in[k]}\|x-\mu_i\|_2^{2}?\] Training, sample count, model storage, encoding and decoding must all be polynomial in \(d,k,t\), while the number of bits per encoded point satisfies \(b\le C(1+\log_2 k+\log_2 t)^{q}\) for universal \(C,q>0\). This is the explicitly normalized, bounded-data version of the source's first reconstruction question, in the overcomplete regime \(k>d\).
cards.why: The task asks whether efficient unsupervised reconstruction can compete with a small optimal codebook while using only a polynomial in the logarithms of its size and accuracy per point. It separates the cost of discovering original mixture parameters from the cost of learning a useful compact representation.
cards.status_note: The first reconstruction question is open in the COLT 2018 source. The bounded-data real-RAM version is an explicit editorial specification, not a verbatim complete model supplied there. cards.definitions:
Here \(B_d=\{x\in\mathbb R^{d}:\sum_{j=1}^{d}x_j^{2}\le1\}\), \([k]=\{1,\ldots,k\}\), and \(\|x\|_2^{2}=\sum_jx_j^{2}\). The comparator is the best set of \(k\) reconstruction centers; repeated centers are allowed. The distribution need not itself be a Gaussian mixture. There is no separation, covariance or minimum cluster-weight promise. Accuracy is additive squared Euclidean reconstruction error in these unit-ball coordinates. The integer \(t\) requests error \(1/t\); all positive accuracy levels are covered by rounding to a smaller reciprocal-integer tolerance.

Fix three finite programs, for training, encoding and decoding. They use a real RAM with rational program constants, exact addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by nonzero values, square roots of nonnegative values, comparisons and indexed memory access, each charged one operation. Integer counters and addresses use logarithmically many bits in \(d+k+t+2\), with a fixed constant factor allowed for each program. There is no floor operation, real-digit extraction, advice, or noncomputable real program constant. Training also has independent fair random bits and a sampling oracle returning independent points from \(D\). One sample request and reading each of its coordinates are charged. There must be one polynomial \(p\), independent of \(D,d,k,t\), bounding training operations, samples, and stored scalar or integer cells, and bounding operations for encoding any one point and decoding any codeword. All executions must halt within these bounds, even on the probability-of-failure event.

Training returns a finite shared parameter vector \(w\) and the integer code length \(b\); the two fixed evaluation programs use \(w,d,k,t,b\). They are deterministic after training. Every codeword has exactly \(b\) bits, with padding allowed. The decoder receives only that codeword and the shared model, and returns a point in \(B_d\). The original point and extra point-dependent information are unavailable to it. Model storage is charged to the polynomial storage bound, not again to each point's code length. Probability of training success is over its samples and random bits; the expectation in the successful guarantee uses a fresh independent point. No restriction to a nearest-center decoder or to \(k\) possible reconstructions is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of the three uniform procedures and universal polynomial and code-length bounds, with the stated error guarantee, or a proof that no such procedures exist in this model. A negative result for a proper Gaussian-parameter estimator or a decoder restricted to exactly \(k\) centers does not refute this improper target. A multiplicative constant greater than one in front of \(\operatorname{OPT}_k(D)\) does not meet the required additive guarantee.
