cards.title: Key agreement from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical two-party key-agreement protocol with negligible disagreement and computationally secret shared keys, against passive probabilistic polynomial-time eavesdroppers, in the plain public-channel model defined below?
cards.definitions: All algorithms are uniform classical probabilistic Turing machines; security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* such that, for every probabilistic polynomial-time I, Pr[\(f(Y)=f(X)\) and |\(Y|=\lambda\)] is negligible in \(\lambda\), where X is uniform in \(\{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) and Y is the single output of \(I(1^{\lambda},f(X))\); probability also includes I’s private coins. A function \(\mu :N\to [0,1]\) is negligible if for every integer \(d\ge 1\) there is \(\lambda _{0}\) such that \(\mu (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- d}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda _{0}\). The protocol consists of two interactive machines A,B with independent private fair coins and total worst-case computation and communication polynomial in \(\lambda\). They exchange classical messages on a noiseless public channel, with no correlated initial secrets, trusted setup, random oracle or quantum communication. At termination each outputs a \(\lambda\)-bit string \(K_{A},K_{B}\). Correctness requires \(\Pr [K_{A}\ne K_{B}]\) to be negligible. Let T be the full public transcript, and let \(U_{\lambda}\) be an independent uniform \(\lambda\)-bit string. For every probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher \(D, |\Pr [D(1^{\lambda},T,K_{A})=1]- \Pr [D(1^{\lambda},T,U_{\lambda})=1]|\) must be negligible, over the honest coins, D’s coins and \(U_{\lambda}\). The eavesdropper observes T but does not alter the messages. The target is the unrelativized existence implication; neither the construction nor its proof is required to treat f as a black box. Both premise and conclusion use the same uniform adversary convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function supplies a computational asymmetry: evaluating it is easy, while recovering a preimage of a random image is hard. Key agreement asks for a different capability. Two parties begin without a common secret and exchange visible messages, yet their final common key must remain hidden from an observer. The question is whether the first kind of asymmetry always suffices for the second.

The security definition concerns the entire transcript. Merely showing that a transcript has many possible explanations is insufficient if an efficient observer can identify the common key. Likewise, keeping each party’s private randomness hidden is weaker than hiding the particular string on which both parties agree. Comparing the actual key with an independent uniform key makes the secrecy requirement explicit.

Impagliazzo and Rudich established a black-box barrier between one-way functions and key agreement. Couteau, Farshim and Mahmoody’s 2021 work studies stronger notions of black-box uselessness and proves results for specified restricted settings. Such results delimit families of constructions; they do not refute the unrestricted existence implication on this card.

The existing TCS-6545 asks for public-key encryption from one-way functions. Public-key encryption would yield a key-agreement protocol by sending a fresh random key under the published encryption key. General interactive key agreement is a separate, weaker desired primitive. A negative conclusion about a restricted encryption construction cannot by itself rule out all interactive protocols.

The classical and passive conventions matter. Quantum key distribution uses an additional communication resource, while protection against an active man-in-the-middle requires an authentication model. Neither is part of this target. The card isolates the foundational question of creating a secret by classical public interaction from the minimal generic computational assumption.

Impagliazzo and Rudich established a black-box barrier between one-way functions and key agreement. Couteau, Farshim and Mahmoody’s 2021 work studies stronger notions of black-box uselessness and proves results for specified restricted settings. Such results delimit families of constructions; they do not refute the unrestricted existence implication on this card.

The existing TCS-6545 asks for public-key encryption from one-way functions. Public-key encryption would yield a key-agreement protocol by sending a fresh random key under the published encryption key. General interactive key agreement is a separate, weaker desired primitive. A negative conclusion about a restricted encryption construction cannot by itself rule out all interactive protocols.

The classical and passive conventions matter. Quantum key distribution uses an additional communication resource, while protection against an active man-in-the-middle requires an authentication model. Neither is part of this target. The card isolates the foundational question of creating a secret by classical public interaction from the minimal generic computational assumption.

cards.title: Oblivious transfer from public-key encryption
cards.formal: In the classical plain model, does the existence of an IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption scheme for bits imply the existence of a polynomial-time 1-out-of-2 bit oblivious-transfer protocol secure against static semi-honest corruption of either party? Both primitives have negligible error and computational security as defined below. The implication may use arbitrary non-black-box techniques and a polynomial number of communication rounds.
cards.definitions: The security parameter is \(\lambda\), supplied in unary. Honest algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time Turing machines; adversarial distinguishers are polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function \(\mu\) is negligible if for every \(c>0, \mu (\lambda )<\lambda ^{- c}\) for all sufficiently large \(\lambda\). Public-key encryption consists of \(KeyGen(1^{\lambda})=(pk,sk), Enc(pk,m;r)\), and \(Dec(sk,c)\), for \(m\in \{0,1\}\); decryption fails with negligible probability over key generation and encryption coins, for each m. IND-CPA means that no such adversary given pk distinguishes \(Enc(pk,0)\) from \(Enc(pk,1)\) with nonnegligible advantage; public encryption is available to it. In OT, sender S has bits \((m_{0},m_{1})\), receiver R has a choice bit c, and R must output \(m_{c}\) except with negligible probability for every input triple; S has no output. The parties follow their prescribed algorithms but keep their entire views, including inputs, random tapes, and messages. There must be uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulators \(Sim_{S}(1^{\lambda},m_{0},m_{1})\) and \(Sim_{R}(1^{\lambda},c,m_{c})\) whose outputs are computationally indistinguishable from the corresponding real views for every sequence of input triples. Thus S learns nothing about c and R learns nothing beyond \((c,m_{c})\). The parties have independent private randomness and exchange classical messages directly. There is no trusted setup, common reference string, random oracle, pre-shared correlated randomness, trusted hardware, or quantum resource.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without a second unproved hardness assumption, or refute that unrelativized implication. A construction may inspect and use the code of the encryption algorithms and use non-black-box security arguments. An oracle separation or a lower bound restricted to black-box reductions is a barrier, not a negative resolution of this question. A construction requiring an additional property of encryption must also derive that property from arbitrary IND-CPA encryption to settle the card.
cards.why: Determines whether the ability to send secrets to a designated receiver already suffices for general private computation between mutually distrustful parties. It is a basic boundary in the hierarchy of cryptographic assumptions, with a longstanding black-box barrier and no known unrestricted implication.

importance.reason: A foundational comparison between ordinary public-key confidentiality and a primitive complete for secure computation; resolving it would change which assumptions suffice for a broad range of protocols.

progress.text: Gertner and coauthors prove an oracle with PKE but no semi-honest OT, and give positive constructions when PKE has specified extra properties. Their oracle separations use uniform adversaries.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No unrestricted classical implication from arbitrary IND-CPA public-key encryption to OT was identified. Known oracle/black-box separations and positive results for rerandomizable or suitably samplable encryption do not settle this formulation. The card fixes semi-honest standalone security with classical communication and no setup.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary encryption protects a message from someone who lacks the secret key. Oblivious transfer must arrange a more selective situation: the receiver can read one of two messages, cannot read the other, and does not disclose which one it selected. This combines privacy for both participants. Merely encrypting both messages under a key generated by the receiver fails, because that receiver can decrypt both ciphertexts. Asking the receiver to reveal which key it can decrypt would instead reveal its choice.

Some encryption schemes offer the missing structure. If a receiver can create two indistinguishable-looking public keys while knowing a decryption key for just one, it can place the decryptable key in position c. The sender encrypts the two messages under the corresponding keys. Such an argument needs a suitable oblivious-sampling property, including security even given the sampler’s retained randomness. Gertner and coauthors identify sufficient properties and also prove an oracle separation between general PKE and even semi-honest OT. Their historical separation uses uniform adversaries.

That result constrains a style of construction, rather than deciding the unrestricted implication. In an oracle argument all algorithms are given access to an additional idealized operation. A construction based on the actual implementation of an encryption scheme may use features that do not survive replacement by an arbitrary oracle. Consequently, the qualifier allowing non-black-box techniques is substantive; removing it would turn the card into a question already addressed by known barriers.

The semi-honest target is already powerful. Haitner, Ishai, Kushilevitz, Lindell, and Petrank show how to transform semi-honest OT into OT secure against malicious parties, and obtain general secure computation without an honest majority. Their result fixes static corruption and standalone security; it does not promise fairness or guaranteed output delivery against a party that aborts. This explains why the basic passive-security implication matters without building stronger composition or fairness requirements into the question.

Progress continues through additional algebraic or sampling structure. Li, Zhang, and Lin construct OT from rerandomizable PKE: anyone with the public key can turn a ciphertext into a fresh encryption of the same plaintext. This avoids their predecessors’ oblivious-sampling requirement but introduces a different hypothesis. Ordinary IND-CPA security alone does not include a public rerandomization algorithm.

A 2026 journal paper by Tanishita and coauthors studies updatable encryption, where update tokens let a third party transform ciphertexts across keys. With specified oblivious-sampling properties, it derives two- or three-round OT. Those theorems refine the boundary for a structured encryption primitive. They do not give a transformation starting with an arbitrary public-key encryption scheme.

A related barrier concerns fair coin tossing. Maji and Wang show limits for protocols using public-key encryption or key agreement as black boxes, whereas OT supports optimally fair constructions. This gives another operational way to see the distinction between ordinary encrypted communication and primitives complete for secure computation. The fairness result has its own model and does not constitute a proof against all non-black-box OT constructions.

cards.title: Collision-resistant hashing from one-way functions
cards.formal: In the ordinary classical computational model, does the existence of a polynomial-time computable one-way function secure against all polynomial-size circuit families imply the existence of a publicly keyed collision-resistant hash family \(H_{k}:\{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\to \{0,1\}^{\lambda}\) secure against all polynomial-size circuit families?
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a deterministic uniformly polynomial-time computable map f on finite binary strings, with output length bounded by a polynomial in the input length, such that for every family of possibly randomized Boolean circuits \(A_{n}\) of size polynomial in n, Pr[\(f(A_{n}(1^{n},f(X)))=f(X)\) and |\(A_{n}(1^{n},f(X))|=n\)] is negligible in n, where X is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\). The same invocation of \(A_{n}\) supplies the candidate preimage in both parts of this event. A function \(\mu\) is negligible if for every \(c>0\) there is \(N_{c}\) such that \(\mu (n)\le n^{-c}\) for all \(n\ge N_{c}\). A hash family consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time key generator \(Gen(1^{\lambda})\) producing a polynomial-length public key k, and a uniform deterministic polynomial-time evaluator \(H(1^{\lambda},k,x)\). For every key in the generator’s support, \(H_{k}\) maps every \(2\lambda\)-bit input to a \(\lambda\)-bit output. Collision resistance means that for every polynomial-size possibly randomized circuit family \(B_{\lambda}\), the probability that \(B_{\lambda}(1^{\lambda},k)\) outputs distinct \(x,x' \in \{0,1\}^{2\lambda}\) with \(H_{k}(x)=H_{k}(x' )\) is negligible in \(\lambda\), over \(k\leftarrow Gen(1^{\lambda})\) and the attacker’s coins. Both messages may be chosen after the attacker sees k. Circuit descriptions may depend on the security parameter, but not on the freshly sampled key. The implication permits arbitrary use of the description of f and arbitrary proof techniques; no random oracle, additional setup assumption, quantum resource, trapdoor, or stronger quantitative hardness assumption is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish the stated existence implication without additional assumptions, or refute it in the ordinary unrelativized model. A positive result may use non-black-box techniques. An oracle world where one-way functions exist but collision-resistant hashing fails proves only a relativizing barrier. Failure of a particular construction, even for a specific one-way function, is also insufficient to refute the existence implication. Producing only target-collision resistance, noncompressing injective functions, or a construction from stronger product-hardness assumptions does not settle the proposition.
cards.why: Determines whether a fundamental compressing cryptographic primitive needs assumptions beyond ordinary one-wayness, while exposing the gap between known black-box barriers and unrestricted constructions.

importance.reason: A central unresolved implication among cryptographic primitives, with consequences for authentication, data commitments and succinct verification.

cards.status_note: No unrestricted implication or refutation was found in the primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. Existing black-box separations do not settle this ordinary-model existence statement. The definitions explicitly use uniform honest algorithms, nonuniform classical adversaries, public fresh keys and factor-two compression.

context_blocks.text: A collision-resistant hash compresses its input while making it computationally difficult to find two distinct messages with the same digest. Collisions must exist by the pigeonhole principle: there are \(2^{2\lambda}\) possible inputs and only \(2^{\lambda}\) outputs. Security is therefore not a claim that collisions never occur, or that a digest uniquely identifies a message. It is a claim about what an efficient adversary can construct after learning the hash key.

A one-way function poses a different challenge. The attacker receives the image of a random input and must find any preimage. An injective one-way function can have no collisions at all, yet it is not a compressing hash. Conversely, a compressing map may have easily found collisions even if some inversion tasks look difficult. The question asks whether the minimal assumption of computationally hard inversion can always supply the more structured difficulty of finding collisions.

The public key matters to the asymptotic definition. If a single compressing function were fixed at each security parameter and security were required against nonuniform circuits, an attacker could hard-code one collision for each parameter. A fresh polynomial-length key prevents that pair from being selected in advance for the actual function used. The key is not secret: the adversary sees it before choosing either colliding message.

Target-collision resistance changes the order of moves. An attacker first commits to one message, then sees a random key and seeks a second message colliding with its committed target. Rompel constructs universal one-way hash functions of this kind from arbitrary one-way functions, as part of the route to secure signatures. That theorem does not give the present game, where both messages are chosen after the key is known. The order difference is small syntactically but central to the unresolved assumption gap.

Simon constructs an oracle setting with one-way permutations but no collision-resistant hash functions in the relevant relativized sense. It rules out building and proving the desired primitive by treating the assumed function purely as an oracle in the separated framework. The theorem does not rule out exploiting a function’s implementation or a proof that fails to relativize. The ordinary mathematical implication in this card therefore remains stronger than the black-box construction question already answered negatively.

Holmgren and Lombardi give a positive route under stronger assumptions about simultaneously inverting independent challenges. Their one-way product functions require quantitative batch hardness beyond ordinary one-wayness. They construct collision-resistant hashing from suitable such functions and connect the missing assumption to unusually strong parallel repetition. This identifies a concrete intermediate target without showing that every ordinary one-way function possesses the required batch security.

The separation also connects hashing to total search problems. Given a circuit for a compressing map, a collision is guaranteed to exist and can be checked efficiently. Folwarczný and coauthors study whether one-way functions can establish hardness for total NP search more generally, extending limitations for a class of single-query reductions. These are restrictions on reductions, not an unconditional proof that collision-resistant families cannot follow from one-wayness by any method.

Applications can sometimes avoid the full primitive. Rothblum’s July 2026 work constructs efficient interactive arguments for bounded-space computations from one-way functions. Communication depends on the space bound times a polynomial in log T and the security parameter, and the security loss depends polynomially on the computation time T. This weakens assumptions for that interactive application; it does not construct a publicly evaluable compressing hash that withstands arbitrary key-dependent collision attempts.

A resolution would clarify the foundations of many protocols that use short commitments to large data. It would either place full collision resistance on the same assumption level as ordinary one-wayness, or demonstrate a separation that survives beyond black-box barriers. The card asks for polynomial security only; requiring near-optimal exponential security or resistance to quantum attacks would introduce additional questions.

cards.title: One-way permutations from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of classical one-way functions secure against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries imply the existence of a classical, efficiently generated family of full-domain one-way permutations with the same security convention?
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a uniformly polynomial-time computable family \(f_{n}:\{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}^{\ell (n)}\), for a polynomially bounded, computable output length \(\ell\), such that for every randomized polynomial-size circuit family \(A_{n}, \Pr [f_{n}(A_{n}(1^{n},f_{n}(X)))=f_{n}(X)]\) is negligible in n for uniform \(X\in \{0,1\}^{n}\); outputs outside \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) fail. A function \(\mu\) is negligible if for every \(c>0, \mu (n)\le n^{-c}\) for all sufficiently large n. A permutation family consists of a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time key generator \(Gen(1^{n})\) and deterministic polynomial-time evaluation \(Eval(1^{n},pk,x)\), with a fixed polynomially bounded, polynomial-time computable integer \(m(n)\ge n\). For every pk in the support of \(Gen(1^{n})\), Eval defines a bijection \(\pi _{pk}:\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\to \{0,1\}^{m(n)}\). For every randomized polynomial-size adversary \(A_{n}, \Pr [\pi _{pk}(A_{n}(1^{n},pk,\pi _{pk}(X)))=\pi _{pk}(X)]\) must be negligible, with \(pk\leftarrow Gen(1^{n})\), independent uniform X and independent adversary coins. Malformed outputs fail. The public key is available to the attacker; no trapdoor is required or given. All security is classical. “Full-domain” fixes the input set to the whole Boolean cube; the valid public-key set need not be all bit strings of its length. The implication is an ordinary existence implication, without restrictions to black-box constructions and without extra assumptions such as obfuscation or subexponential security.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence implication, allowing any mathematical construction or proof technique, or refute that implication in the ordinary computational model. Proving that one-way functions do not exist would make the implication vacuously true. An oracle separation or a theorem excluding a restricted class of reductions is a construction barrier, not a refutation of the unrestricted implication. A permutation family on special sparse domains does not meet the full-domain convention fixed here; an additional trapdoor property would be a stronger positive result.
cards.why: Determine whether basic average-case inversion hardness necessarily supports efficient bijections, a rigid primitive at the foundation of cryptographic constructions.

importance.reason: A longstanding question about the structure obtainable from minimal cryptographic assumptions, with strong construction barriers and a recent full-domain breakthrough under additional assumptions.

The 2025 full-domain trapdoor construction requires subexponential iO and OWF assumptions. Existing oracle and black-box barriers do not settle the unrestricted question. This card explicitly fixes the full-domain keyed convention.

context_blocks.text: A one-way function is easy to evaluate but hard to invert on a random input. It may identify many different inputs and need not cover its output space. A one-way permutation has exactly one preimage for every output in its domain. The extra requirement is structural: nothing is lost mathematically, yet efficiently recovering the uniquely determined input must remain infeasible.

This card fixes the full-domain, public-key family version because the original phrase “one-way permutation” leaves several conventions unspecified. A public key chooses a permutation of an entire Boolean cube; all input strings of that length are valid. A stronger unkeyed formulation asks for a single length-preserving permutation on all bit strings. A more permissive formulation allows key-dependent sparse domains. Results in those settings must be compared with their domain and sampling requirements visible.

Making a computation reversible is not enough. The map \((x,z)\mapsto (x,z \mathrm{XOR} f(x))\) is a bijection for any efficiently computable length-compatible f, but its inverse is obtained by applying exactly the same map. Likewise, simply attaching x to \(f(x)\) makes the output injective while revealing the desired preimage. The construction has to preserve computational difficulty while removing collisions and covering the domain, without publishing the information needed for inversion.

Many other forms of cryptographic structure can be derived from bare one-wayness. Håstad, Impagliazzo, Levin and Luby show that every one-way function yields a pseudorandom generator. It uses a new kind of pseudorandom permutation that supports controlled permutation of its outputs. The valid-key domain therefore depends on the building blocks. The older formal domain-invariance condition constrains both input and key domains. Keeping these two notions separate prevents an erroneous claim that a published barrier has been contradicted.

A negative answer would reveal a structural separation inside foundational cryptographic assumptions. Existing barriers make the problem especially informative: a successful construction from ordinary one-way functions would need to escape the established generic approaches, rather than merely improve their efficiency.

cards.title: Chosen-ciphertext security from ordinary public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key encryption imply the existence of IND-CCA2-secure public-key encryption in the plain model, with classical security against all nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries and no additional computational assumption?
cards.definitions: A public-key encryption scheme has uniform probabilistic polynomial-time algorithms \(Gen(1^{n})\to (pk,sk)\) and \(Enc(pk,m)\to c\) and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm \(Dec(sk,c)\to m\) or ⊥. It supports bit-string messages of any polynomially bounded length. For every polynomial p, the maximum decryption-error probability over messages |\(m|\le p(n)\) is negligible in n, with probability over key generation and honest encryption. In the IND-CPA game an adversary receives pk, chooses equal-length messages \(m_{0},m_{1}\) and state, receives \(c*=Enc(pk,m_{b})\) for an independent uniform bit b, and guesses b. Its advantage is |Pr[guess=b]−\(1/2|\). In the IND-CCA2 game it also has adaptive access to \(Dec(sk,\cdot )\), both before and after choosing the challenge messages and receiving c*. After the challenge, the oracle rejects the exact bit string c*; all other ciphertext queries are allowed. Security requires negligible advantage for every nonuniform probabilistic polynomial-time adversary, allowing any polynomial number of oracle queries. Negligible means eventually smaller than \(n^{-a}\) for every \(a>0\). Each adversary has its own polynomial resource bound, but the scheme is fixed independently of that bound. The plain model has no ideal random oracle, externally supplied common reference string, hardware or trusted setup beyond the recipient generating its own key pair. This is an unrestricted existence implication, not a requirement that a compiler treat the original scheme as a black box.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that an IND-CCA2 scheme with these guarantees exists whenever an IND-CPA scheme exists, or refute that implication in the ordinary computational model. A conversion assuming additional trapdoor functions, suitable proof systems, special pseudorandom generators or ideal random oracles does not by itself suffice. A theorem excluding a restricted class of black-box conversions is a barrier, not a negative answer to the unrestricted implication. Fixed-query bounded CCA2, pre-challenge-only CCA1 and non-malleability without adaptive decryption access are weaker targets.
cards.why: Determine whether public-key confidentiality alone can always be strengthened to resist adaptive decryption attacks, without importing another cryptographic assumption.

importance.reason: A central question about the minimal assumptions for robust public-key encryption, connecting encryption, proof systems, trapdoor structure and generic security transformations.

The revised threshold-encryption work retains additional-model or stronger-security requirements in its CPA-to-CCA transformations.

context_blocks.text: Public-key encryption already allows anyone, including the attacker, to create ciphertexts. Ordinary chosen-plaintext security protects the contents of an honestly generated challenge ciphertext. Chosen-ciphertext security additionally protects it while the attacker submits other ciphertexts for decryption and uses the responses to decide what to ask next. The only forbidden query is the challenge itself, because returning its plaintext would make confidentiality impossible by definition.

A simple modification illustrates the gap between definitions. Start with a secure ordinary scheme, append an unused bit to every ciphertext, and make decryption ignore that bit. The modification preserves chosen-plaintext security. A chosen-ciphertext attacker flips the challenge’s unused bit and submits the resulting different string to the oracle, which returns the challenge plaintext. This proves that a particular CPA scheme need not itself be CCA-secure; it does not rule out building another scheme from its existence.

This is why the question concerns a construction or existence implication. A successful transformation may change the ciphertext format, use many public keys, encode messages, and inspect the original algorithms’ descriptions. It must arrange that responses to every other ciphertext remain harmless. A proof faces the corresponding simulation problem: how can it answer decryption queries while relying only on a challenge from the weaker security game?

The source proposal points to Trevisan’s cryptography project list, which explicitly asks whether CCA security can be derived from CPA security by black-box techniques or by any techniques. Its bibliography juxtaposes partial negative results with positive results for non-malleability. That distinction remains important: an advance for one attack model should not silently be reported as a solution for another.

Gertner, Malkin and Myers give a black-box separation for constructions whose new decryption algorithm never calls the original encryption algorithm. This covers a substantial class of natural attempts. It still leaves constructions that re-encrypt during decryption, and does not cover arbitrary use of the source code. The scope of that restriction is central to the theorem, rather than a technical detail that can be omitted.

Choi, Dachman-Soled, Malkin and Wee construct non-malleable encryption from any semantically secure scheme and extend their approach to bounded chosen-ciphertext attacks. In the bounded version, the permitted number q of decryption queries is fixed before constructing the scheme. Full CCA2 instead asks for one scheme that withstands every polynomial-time attacker, whose query polynomial can be larger than any particular bound built into that scheme.

Another productive route adds a primitive that helps enforce ciphertext validity. Hohenberger, Koppula and Waters prove in CRYPTO 2020 that injective trapdoor functions suffice for CCA-secure public-key encryption, without requiring lossiness or correlated-product security. This removes significant earlier restrictions. An arbitrary encryption scheme is not automatically such a trapdoor function: its decryption need only recover the message, not a unique full input including encryption randomness.

Koppula and Waters obtain generic upgrades using a hinting pseudorandom generator, whose security survives a special kind of auxiliary information. Ordinary pseudorandomness does not state that guarantee. Their construction offers another way to organize the decryption proof, but applying it to arbitrary public-key encryption still requires establishing the additional hinting property from the original assumption.

Matsuda’s PKC 2025 work shows that a publicly verifiable noninteractive batch argument for NP can supply the additional ingredient. The May 2025 revision weakens the required proof-length savings: they need not be strong enough for currently known constructions of noninteractive zero knowledge. This is progress in reducing the extra structure needed for the upgrade. The paper still assumes the batch argument; it does not construct it from arbitrary CPA encryption.

A PKC 2026 paper by Brzuska, Klooß and Woo gives CPA-to-CCA transformations for threshold encryption, where several parties jointly decrypt. Its generic transform from arbitrary CPA-secure threshold encryption uses a random oracle. Its other route has additional requirements, including a stronger semi-malicious CPA notion. The July 2026 revision therefore does not establish the plain-model implication in this card.

Resolving the implication would clarify whether protection against active ciphertext manipulation is an additional foundational assumption or a consequence of ordinary public-key confidentiality. It would also explain why existing general approaches repeatedly need structure beyond the weak starting primitive. The target is a foundational security theorem; it does not ask that the resulting construction be practical or preserve the original scheme’s efficiency.

cards.title: Noninteractive zero knowledge from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of classical one-way functions imply reusable, adaptively secure noninteractive zero-knowledge arguments for circuit satisfiability in the honestly generated common-reference-string model, with computational soundness and computational zero knowledge against nonuniform polynomial-size adversaries?
cards.definitions: A one-way function is a uniformly polynomial-time computable family \(f_{n}\) on uniform n-bit inputs with polynomial-length outputs, such that every nonuniform randomized polynomial-size adversary given \(1^{n}\) and \(f_{n}(X)\) finds any n-bit preimage with negligible probability. Circuit satisfiability has statements x encoding Boolean circuits and witnesses w assigning their inputs, with \(R(x,w)=1\) exactly when the circuit outputs 1. A proposed argument consists of uniform algorithms \(Setup(1^{\lambda},1^{B})\to\)crs, Prove(crs,x,w)→\(\pi\), and Verify(crs,\(x,\pi\))→\(\{0,1\}\); their time and output length are polynomial in \(\lambda +B\), where B bounds statement and witness lengths. Setup is independent of the later statements; its private coins are not published. For every polynomial \(B=B(\lambda )\), completeness error is negligible uniformly over valid \((x,w)\) of length at most B. Adaptive computational soundness means that every nonuniform polynomial-time adversary given crs has negligible probability of outputting an unsatisfiable x and an accepted \(\pi\). Reusable computational zero knowledge means there exist uniform polynomial-time SimSetup and SimProve such that no nonuniform polynomial-time distinguisher separates these experiments: \((i)\) it receives honest crs and can adaptively request Prove(crs,x,w) for polynomially many valid pairs; \((ii)\) it receives simulated crs from SimSetup, and each valid query is answered by SimProve using the simulation trapdoor and x, without receiving w. Both experiments reject invalid queries, and the distinguisher retains arbitrary polynomial-size auxiliary information. All negligible bounds are in \(\lambda\): for each \(a>0\) the error is eventually below \(\lambda ^{-a}\). Only crs is public in the real system, and one proof message is sent for each statement. No random oracle, extra cryptographic assumption, online verifier challenge, proof of knowledge or succinctness requirement is included. Circuit satisfiability covers every NP language through witness-preserving polynomial reductions.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence implication, or refute it in the ordinary computational model. The result may use the code of the one-way function and need not be black-box. A construction adding LWE, an appropriate batch argument, trapdoor hashing, or strong extra complexity assumptions does not suffice unless those ingredients are themselves derived from the same ordinary OWF premise. An interactive proof, a witness-indistinguishable argument, or a single-theorem result without a justified reusable upgrade is not the specified conclusion.
cards.why: Determine whether the minimal assumption supporting basic cryptography is sufficient for reusable, publicly verifiable proofs that reveal no witness and require no online interaction.

importance.reason: A fundamental boundary between interactive and noninteractive zero knowledge, with implications for the assumptions behind privacy-preserving proof systems and cryptographic transformations.

context_blocks.text: An NP witness can be easy to check and sensitive to reveal. For circuit satisfiability, publishing a satisfying assignment gives a verifier complete evidence, but also exposes every bit of that assignment. Zero knowledge asks for convincing evidence whose visible distribution can instead be simulated without the assignment. It formalizes the requirement that verification disclose no additional information beyond the statement’s truth.

The common reference string is an explicit resource. An honest setup algorithm produces public parameters before any statements are selected. After that setup, a prover sends one message that anyone can verify. The setup may retain randomness while generating the string, but that randomness is not handed to users. The simulation trapdoor exists only in the security experiment. This model differs from asking for a noninteractive system with no setup at all.

The card allows computational soundness: a computationally unbounded attacker might find a false accepted proof, but efficient attackers must not. Such a system is called an argument. It also asks for a reusable reference string, with statements chosen after seeing the string and earlier proofs. These choices make the target precise without requiring short proofs or a way to extract a witness from a successful prover.

The classical Goldreich–Micali–Wigderson theorem already supplies interactive zero-knowledge proofs for NP from one-way functions. Interaction gives the verifier a role in challenging what the prover has prepared. The inherited Damgård–Nielsen survey explicitly asks whether one-way functions suffice in the noninteractive setting. That survey discusses a proof-system version with stronger soundness; the argument target here asks for protection only against efficient cheating.

Known positive constructions use more structure. Peikert and Shiehian construct NIZK for NP from ordinary LWE in 2019. Their method builds hash families whose correlation-intractability property supports a sound Fiat–Shamir transformation. The point is a proved property of a specially constructed family, not simply substituting an arbitrary hash function for a verifier’s random challenge. LWE is a sufficient assumption, but it has not thereby been derived from arbitrary one-way functions.

Bradley, Waters and Wu show that an adaptively sound noninteractive batch argument for NP, together with a one-way function, yields NIZK. Their TCC 2024 result also studies how to obtain the needed adaptive soundness from other batch-argument guarantees. The title “Batch Arguments to NIZKs from One-Way Functions” must be read with its starting resource intact: the batch argument is an additional primitive, rather than something their theorem constructs from a bare one-way function.

Branco and coauthors develop a vector-trapdoor-hash approach, with an updated version in March 2026. Their constructions use either LWE or a combination of DDH and LPN assumptions. The initial black-box constructions provide single-theorem zero knowledge, and their multi-theorem upgrade uses cryptography in a non-black-box way. This distinction is compatible with the target here, which allows any construction technique but requires the OWF-only assumption and reusable security.

Chen, Rothblum and Tell pursue a different route through derandomization and strong computational hardness. Their construction combines a subexponentially secure one-way function with an additional complexity assumption and obtains computational soundness against uniform adversaries. It is progress toward avoiding highly structured cryptographic primitives, but the extra hardness and the adversary convention both differ from this card.

Recent results in the reverse direction should not be read as a construction. Chakraborty, Hulett, Khurana and Tomer show in February 2026 that nontrivial NIZK arguments imply one-way functions under the hypothesis that NP is not contained in ioP/poly, even in a broad high-error regime. Their amplification consequences improve existing weak NIZK systems. Neither direction starts with an ordinary OWF alone and produces the desired NIZK system.

Another 2026 result gives succinct zero-knowledge proofs using one-way functions as black boxes. Florentz–Konopnicki and Rothblum’s protocol is interactive: its theorem explicitly bounds a number of public-coin rounds that depends on the relation’s parameters. Its noninteractive commitment component does not make the whole protocol noninteractive. A resolution of this card would isolate exactly how much cryptographic structure is needed to remove that interaction after a single reusable setup.

sentences: Noninteractive zero knowledge lets a prover demonstrate an NP statement with one message without revealing its witness.
This project asks whether one-way functions suffice for reusable, adaptively secure arguments of this kind after an honest common-reference-string setup.
Reusability means that the same public parameters must remain suitable as many statements are selected and proved.
The target uses computational soundness and computational zero knowledge, so both guarantees are formulated against efficient adversaries.
A construction would show that the setup model can support powerful noninteractive privacy guarantees from the basic assumption underlying symmetric cryptography.

cards.context:
An NP witness can be easy to check and sensitive to reveal. For circuit satisfiability, publishing a satisfying assignment gives a verifier complete evidence, but also exposes every bit of that assignment. Zero knowledge asks for convincing evidence whose visible distribution can instead be simulated without the assignment. It formalizes the requirement that verification disclose no additional information beyond the statement’s truth.

The common reference string is an explicit resource. An honest setup algorithm produces public parameters before any statements are selected. After that setup, a prover sends one message that anyone can verify. The setup may retain randomness while generating the string, but that randomness is not handed to users. The simulation trapdoor exists only in the security experiment. This model differs from asking for a noninteractive system with no setup at all.

The card allows computational soundness: a computationally unbounded attacker might find a false accepted proof, but efficient attackers must not. Such a system is called an argument. It also asks for a reusable reference string, with statements chosen after seeing the string and earlier proofs. These choices make the target precise without requiring short proofs or a way to extract a witness from a successful prover.

The classical Goldreich–Micali–Wigderson theorem already supplies interactive zero-knowledge proofs for NP from one-way functions. Interaction gives the verifier a role in challenging what the prover has prepared. The inherited Damgård–Nielsen survey explicitly asks whether one-way functions suffice in the noninteractive setting. That survey discusses a proof-system version with stronger soundness; the argument target here asks for protection only against efficient cheating.

Known positive constructions use more structure. Peikert and Shiehian construct NIZK for NP from ordinary LWE in 2019. Their method builds hash families whose correlation-intractability property supports a sound Fiat–Shamir transformation. The point is a proved property of a specially constructed family, not simply substituting an arbitrary hash function for a verifier’s random challenge. LWE is a sufficient assumption, but it has not thereby been derived from arbitrary one-way functions.

Bradley, Waters and Wu show that an adaptively sound noninteractive batch argument for NP, together with a one-way function, yields NIZK. Their TCC 2024 result also studies how to obtain the needed adaptive soundness from other batch-argument guarantees. The title “Batch Arguments to NIZKs from One-Way Functions” must be read with its starting resource intact: the batch argument is an additional primitive, rather than something their theorem constructs from a bare one-way function.

Branco and coauthors develop a vector-trapdoor-hash approach, with an updated version in March 2026. Their constructions use either LWE or a combination of DDH and LPN assumptions. The initial black-box constructions provide single-theorem zero knowledge, and their multi-theorem upgrade uses cryptography in a non-black-box way. This distinction is compatible with the target here, which allows any construction technique but requires the OWF-only assumption and reusable security.

Chen, Rothblum and Tell pursue a different route through derandomization and strong computational hardness. Their construction combines a subexponentially secure one-way function with an additional complexity assumption and obtains computational soundness against uniform adversaries. It is progress toward avoiding highly structured cryptographic primitives, but the extra hardness and the adversary convention both differ from this card.

Recent results in the reverse direction should not be read as a construction. Chakraborty, Hulett, Khurana and Tomer show in February 2026 that nontrivial NIZK arguments imply one-way functions under the hypothesis that NP is not contained in ioP/poly, even in a broad high-error regime. Their amplification consequences improve existing weak NIZK systems. Neither direction starts with an ordinary OWF alone and produces the desired NIZK system.

Another 2026 result gives succinct zero-knowledge proofs using one-way functions as black boxes. Florentz–Konopnicki and Rothblum’s protocol is interactive: its theorem explicitly bounds a number of public-coin rounds that depends on the relation’s parameters. Its noninteractive commitment component does not make the whole protocol noninteractive. A resolution of this card would isolate exactly how much cryptographic structure is needed to remove that interaction after a single reusable setup.

cards.title: Public-key quantum money from LWE alone
cards.formal: Does quantum hardness of decisional Learning with Errors with the fixed polynomial parameters below imply reusable, unforgeable public-key quantum money in the standard model?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(\lambda\ge2\), let \(q(\lambda)\) be the least prime at least \(\lambda^4\), and let \(\chi_\lambda\) give integer z probability proportional to \(\exp(-\pi z^2/\lambda^2)\). The assumption states that, for every polynomially bounded sample count m, the distributions \((A,As+e\bmod q)\) and \((A,u)\) are computationally indistinguishable: A is uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^{m\times\lambda}\), s is independently uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^\lambda\), the coordinates of e are independent samples from \(\chi_\lambda\), and u is independent uniform in \(\mathbb Z_q^m\). Indistinguishability is against all nonuniform polynomial-size quantum circuit families with classical advice. Advantage is the absolute difference of acceptance probabilities and must be negligible in lambda, meaning eventually less than \(\lambda^{-c}\) for every constant c>0. Quantum circuits use a fixed universal Clifford-plus-T gate set, zero-state ancillas and computational-basis measurements; polynomial-size classical control is allowed. A money scheme consists of uniform quantum polynomial-time algorithms Gen, Mint and Verify. Gen on unary lambda outputs classical keys (pk,sk). Mint(sk) outputs a classical serial string s and a quantum register rho; their lengths are polynomial in lambda. Verify(pk,s,rho) returns an accept/reject bit and a residual note register, without secret information. For every polynomial t, an honestly generated note survives t successive verifications, all accepting, with probability at least one minus a negligible function, over key generation, minting and verification. For every polynomially bounded integer-valued k and every nonuniform polynomial-size quantum adversary with classical advice, give the adversary pk and k independently minted notes under the same key. The probability that it produces k+1 serial/register pairs all accepted by fresh local applications of Verify is negligible; its output registers may be jointly entangled and serials need not be distinct. This also applies to k=0. The construction has no ideal oracle, externally supplied setup, obfuscation assumption, leakage assumption, or additional hardness assumption. The target is the implication from the explicitly stated LWE assumption; a construction with an arbitrary computational reduction qualifies.

context_blocks.text: Public-key quantum money requires anyone holding the classical public key to verify a note while preventing a holder of several notes from creating an additional valid one. Reusability makes verification compatible with repeated transfer.

Known constructions with stronger assumptions and restricted impossibility results leave a gap. iO-based schemes and schemes founded on group-action assumptions do not establish the LWE-only implication specified here.
The 2025 obfuscation barrier applies to a particular black-box interface. It is evidence about a restricted class of constructions, not a refutation of this unrestricted implication.

cards.title: Average-case RSA inversion versus factoring for exponent 65537
cards.formal: For the fixed exponent \(e=65537\) and the balanced-prime ensemble below, does the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time RSA inverter with inverse-polynomial average success imply the existence of a uniform randomized polynomial-time factoring algorithm with inverse-polynomial average success?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 3\) let \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) be the finite set of primes p with \(2^{n- 1}\le p<2^{n}\) and \(\gcd (e,p- 1)=1\). Choose an ordered pair \((p,q)\) uniformly from \(\{(p,q)\in \mathrm{P}_{n}^{2}:p\ne q\}\), and set \(N=pq\). All assertions are for sufficiently large n with at least two such primes. Conditional on N, choose x uniformly from \(\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{*}=\{a\in \{0,\ldots ,N- 1\}:\gcd (a,N)=1\}\), independently of algorithm coins, and set \(y=x^{e}\) mod N. The inverter I receives \((1^{n},N,y)\), in binary except for \(1^{n}\), and must output the unique \(x\in\mathbb{Z}_{N}^{*}\) with that image. Nonnegligible success here means that some integer \(a\ge 1\) and \(n_{0}\) exist such that \(\Pr [I(1^{n},N,y)=x]\ge n^{- a}\) for every \(n\ge n_{0}\). The factoring algorithm F receives \((1^{n},N)\) and succeeds by outputting p or q; require some \(b\ge 1\) and \(n_{1}\) such that \(\Pr [F(1^{n},N)\in \{p,q\}]\ge n^{- b}\) for every \(n\ge n_{1}\). Both machines use independent fair random bits and have worst-case running time bounded by their own fixed polynomials in their input lengths on every random tape. The probabilities average over the stated modulus ensemble as well as x and the coins, with no promise of success separately on each modulus. The assertion is the ordinary existence implication \((\exists I,a,n_{0})\Rightarrow (\exists F,b,n_{1})\). It does not restrict a proof to black-box reductions: a construction of F may use the fixed code of I and count all calls to it in F’s polynomial running time. No independent oracle or advice is supplied.

context_blocks.text: Factoring an RSA modulus gives the private exponent and hence breaks encryption, but the reverse reduction is a longstanding cryptographic question. It would identify whether RSA inversion rests on precisely the factoring assumption or on a potentially weaker computational task.

Boneh’s survey asks about factoring with an RSA inversion oracle. This card retains the imported fixed-exponent average-case specialization and explicitly compares inverse-polynomial average success on its balanced-prime ensemble. The implication permits arbitrary constructions; restricted-model separation results do not refute it.

cards.title: Noninteractive SZK versus SZK
cards.formal: Does NISZK equal SZK? Equivalently, does there exist a uniform deterministic polynomial-time reduction that maps every promised pair of sampling circuits X,Y to a sampling circuit Z, preserving the near/far promises specified below?
cards.definitions: A sampling circuit is a finite acyclic Boolean circuit with AND and OR gates of fan-in two, NOT gates, constants, a specified list of random input bits and an ordered list of output bits. Its description explicitly lists gates and wires in binary. Fresh independent uniform bits are supplied to all random inputs; the output distribution is the resulting distribution on bit strings. X and Y may have different numbers of random inputs but have the same output length. For finite distributions P,Q on the same set, \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(P,Q)=\tfrac12\sum_z|P(z)-Q(z)|\). The source convention for Statistical Difference has YES instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)<1/3\) and NO instances with \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(X,Y)>2/3\). Inputs between these promises impose no correctness obligation. The reduction outputs one circuit Z with \(m\ge 3\) output bits. On every YES input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})<1/m\); on every NO input require \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(Z,U_{m})>1- 1/m\), where \(U_{m}\) is uniform on \(\{0,1\}^{m}\). The reduction runs in a fixed polynomial of the combined encoded input length on every syntactically valid input, including inputs outside the promise; writing Z and all its input/output nodes counts in that time. It receives no advice or sampling oracle. These are the source’s Statistical Difference and Statistical Difference from Uniform promise problems. Their completeness under deterministic polynomial-time many-one reductions makes existence of this reduction equivalent to the original class equality. Thus the complete-problem formulation fixes the question without having to choose a new auxiliary-input or setup convention for protocols.

context_blocks.text: Statistical zero knowledge asks whether a verifier can be convinced while learning only information that a simulator could reproduce. The unresolved equality asks whether interaction adds power when a noninteractive protocol has an honestly sampled public random string.

The same question can be stated entirely in terms of finite sampling circuits. Statistical Difference is complete for SZK, while Statistical Difference from Uniform is complete for NISZK. The requested reduction therefore tests the original class equality with a fully discrete input and output contract.

The source’s complete-problem equivalence identifies these alternatives with equality or inequality of NISZK and SZK. Randomized reductions or computational zero knowledge concern different targets.

cards.title: Fully homomorphic encryption from public-key encryption
cards.formal: Does the existence of IND-CPA-secure public-key bit encryption imply the existence of an IND-CPA-secure, compact, unleveled fully homomorphic bit-encryption scheme for every polynomial-size Boolean circuit, with the algorithms and security convention below?
cards.definitions:
All algorithms are uniform probabilistic Turing machines with worst-case polynomial bit running time in their explicit input lengths; decryption is deterministic. The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. An adversary is a nonuniform family of randomized Boolean circuits of size polynomial in \(\lambda\), including its advice and random-input nodes. All random bits are independent and fair. A function \(
u:\mathbb{N}	o [0,1]\) is negligible when for every positive integer a there exists \(\lambda _{0}\) such that \(
u (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- a}\) for all \(\lambda \ge \lambda _{0}\). Security is quantified separately over every such adversary family, with a negligible bound allowed to depend on the family. u\) such that for every \(\lambda\) and b, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,b))

u(\lambda)\), over key generation and encryption. u _{s}\) such that for every \(\lambda\), every such C of description length and input count at most \(s(\lambda )\), and every \(m\in \{0,1\}^{t}\), independently of the generated keys, \(\Pr[\operatorname{Dec}(sk,\operatorname{Eval}(evk,C,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_1),\ldots,\operatorname{Enc}(pk,m_t)))
e C(m)]\le

cards.title: PZK versus SZK
cards.formal: Does PZK=SZK for classical single-prover interactive proofs of promise problems, with polynomial-time verifiers and simulators, negligible proof error, and zero knowledge against every polynomial-time verifier?
cards.definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((Y,N)\) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings. An interactive proof consists of a computationally unbounded prover P and a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V exchanging polynomially many bits on common input x. There is a negligible function \(\varepsilon\) such that on \(x\in Y\) the honest interaction accepts with probability at least \(1- \varepsilon (|x|)\), and on \(x\in N\) every prover strategy is accepted with probability at most \(\varepsilon (|x|)\). Negligible means smaller than |\(x|^{- d}\) for every fixed \(d>0\) at all sufficiently large lengths. No condition is imposed outside \(Y\cup N\). The view of a verifier consists of its random bits and exchanged messages. SZK requires that for every uniform probabilistic polynomial-time verifier V* there is a uniform probabilistic polynomial-time simulator S* which, on x alone, produces a distribution within negligible total variation distance of the view of \((\mathrm{P},V*)(x)\), for every \(x\in Y\). Total variation distance is one half of the sum of absolute probability differences over possible views. PZK instead permits S* to output a failure symbol ⊥ with probability at most \(1/2\); conditioned on nonfailure, its output distribution must equal that view exactly. Every runtime bound is a strict polynomial bound over all random outcomes, with a polynomial allowed to depend on the fixed verifier or simulator. This is the ordinary input-only simulation convention of the cited definitions, without a shared random string, an oracle, a setup assumption, or a restriction to honest verifiers.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every promise problem admitting the stated statistical proof also admits a perfect one in this model, or exhibit a promise problem in SZK and prove that it has no PZK proof. The protocol may change completely in a positive result. An oracle separation, a failure of one proposed compiler, a perfect-zero-knowledge PCP, or an honest-verifier-only theorem does not resolve this unrelativized class equality.

context_blocks.text: Zero knowledge formalizes the idea that a verifier can reproduce what it sees without receiving help from the prover. Statistical simulation permits a negligible discrepancy between distributions. Perfect simulation requires exact agreement after the allowed failure event. Goldreich’s textbook asks whether this difference changes which statements can be proved.

The failure convention is part of the model. A strict polynomial-time perfect simulator that never fails is a different requirement, often called super-perfect zero knowledge. Allowing an expected polynomial runtime is also a separate definitional issue discussed in the source. Neither convention is silently substituted here.

PZK is contained in SZK: repeat the bounded-failure perfect simulator polynomially many times until it succeeds, and use an arbitrary output if every attempt fails. The remaining probability of failure is negligible, while successful outputs retain the exact distribution. The open direction asks whether negligible simulation error can always be eliminated by some proof system.

Bouland, Chen, Holden, Thaler and Vasudevan construct an oracle relative to which SZK is not contained in PZK. This supplies evidence against equality and rules out a proof that relativizes in the corresponding way. It does not separate the classes in the ordinary model specified here.

Gur, O’Connor and Spooner explicitly retain PZK versus SZK as open in their 2024 paper. Their perfect-zero-knowledge construction is for probabilistically checkable proofs, where a verifier queries a proof oracle. That achievement concerns a different access model from ordinary interactive proofs and leaves this equality unresolved.

The target asks for a class equality, not a quantitative improvement in a particular cryptographic protocol. Its resolution would determine whether exact distributional privacy has an intrinsic expressive cost. TCS-1929 instead concerns zero knowledge for streaming interactive proofs with a memory restriction.

cards.title: Low-noise LPN hardness from Nearest Codeword hardness
cards.formal: Does the following implication hold? If binary Nearest Codeword is not in BPP, then no uniform probabilistic polynomial-time distinguisher D has advantage at least $n^{-c}$, for any fixed $c>0$ and all sufficiently large square n, between $(A,As+e)$ and $(A,u)$. Here $A\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2\times n}$, $s\in\mathbb F_2^n$, and $u\in\mathbb F_2^{n^2}$ are independent uniform random variables, and the coordinates of e are independent Bernoulli variables with rate $1/\sqrt n$. Advantage is the absolute difference of D’s acceptance probabilities in the two experiments.
cards.why: A basic security assumption would obtain an explanation through independently studied hardness. The extra assumption in the new reduction makes the remaining target concrete.

progress.text: The revision gives a reduction for $\eta=n^{-\alpha}$, any constant $\alpha<1$, from simultaneous worst-case hardness of two tasks on a code and its dual. This advances beyond earlier near-half-noise reductions; the single-assumption target remains stronger.

cards.review_note: Editorial specialization of the NCP-only direction in Section 1.2 of the September 2026 revision. It fixes the starting problem, decision-LPN distribution, sample count, noise, uniformity, and asymptotic advantage, replacing the vague phrase natural worst-case problem. The source does not state this exact parameter specialization as a numbered conjecture.

context_blocks.text: LWE has strong connections to worst-case lattice problems. Establishing comparable foundations for LPN at cryptographically useful noise rates is more difficult.

Without noise, enough independent parity equations reveal the secret by linear algebra. Flipping some answers breaks that direct procedure: the learner must cope with equations whose right-hand sides may be wrong. At a low noise rate, most equations remain correct, which makes the precise source of hardness especially important.

A worst-case-to-average-case reduction would start with an arbitrary hard coding instance and turn it into the random samples used by LPN. It must preserve a usable noise regime and show how an LPN solver would solve the original task. Requiring two different coding tasks to be hard simultaneously is a stronger premise than deriving the guarantee from one standard worst-case problem.

cards.definitions: Binary Nearest Codeword receives a binary matrix G, a binary target y with the same number of rows, and an integer t, and asks whether $\min_z\operatorname{wt}(Gz-y)\le t$, with arithmetic over \(F_{2}\) and Hamming weight wt. BPP means a uniform randomized polynomial-time decider correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every instance. The LPN side here is a decision problem with n-squared samples, random secret, and inverse-square-root noise. Restricting n to squares makes the noise parameter an exact rational; this is an explicit specialization of the source’s broader low-noise direction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed complexity-theoretic implication, for example by a reduction turning such an LPN distinguisher into a BPP algorithm for Nearest Codeword, or prove that the implication is false. Invoking simultaneous hardness of an additional problem on the dual code does not establish this implication.

cards.title: One-way functions in \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) from one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of a classical one-way function imply the existence of a classical one-way function computed by a polynomial-time uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) circuit family?
cards.definitions: The security parameter \(\lambda\) is supplied in unary. Algorithms are uniform probabilistic polynomial-time machines; security is against nonuniform polynomial-size classical circuit families. A function \(\nu (\lambda )\) is negligible if for every \(c>0, \nu (\lambda )\le \lambda ^{- c}\) for all sufficiently large \(\lambda\). Probabilities include setup, algorithm and adversary coins. No ideal oracle or additional trusted setup is supplied unless explicitly stated; arbitrary non-black-box implications are allowed. A one-way function is a deterministic polynomial-time map \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* of polynomially bounded, length-dependent output size, such that every allowed inverter on \((1^{n},f(U_{n}))\) finds any n-bit preimage with negligible probability, for uniform \(U_{n}\). A polynomial-time uniform \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) family is generated from \(1^{n}\) in \(\operatorname{poly}(n)\) time, has polynomial size and a universal constant depth, and uses fan-in-two \(\mathrm{AND}/\mathrm{OR}\) and unary NOT gates. Inversion security quantifies over all polynomial-size adversaries, not just shallow ones.

context_blocks.text: Local evaluation and global inversion difficulty are strikingly different requirements. An \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) one-way function has each output bit depend on only a constant number of input bits, while inverting the full output must defeat every polynomial-size adversary.

Known locality transformations start from stronger assumptions such as one-way functions in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}\). Those constructions establish plausible \(\mathrm{NC}^{0}\) cryptography, but they do not derive it from an arbitrary sequentially computable one-way function. The implication therefore asks whether cryptographic hardness can always be made local.

cards.why: Identify whether extreme locality is inherent in minimal cryptographic hardness or requires a stronger assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

cards.title: Exponentially hard weak versus strong one-way functions
cards.formal: Does the existence of an exponentially hard weak one-way function imply the existence of an exponentially hard strong one-way function, in the following nonuniform-adversary, negligible-success formulation? The premise is that there exist a uniform polynomial-time computable length-preserving function \(f\), a real \(a>0\), an integer \(k\ge1\), and \(n_0\), such that \[\operatorname{Inv}_f(C,n)\le1-n^{-k}\] for every \(n\ge n_0\) and every circuit \(C\) with \(n\) inputs, \(n\) outputs and at most \(2^{an}\) gates. The desired conclusion is that there exist another uniform polynomial-time computable length-preserving function \(g\) and a real \(b>0\) such that, for every integer \(d\ge1\), there is \(n_d\) with \[\operatorname{Inv}_g(C,n)\le n^{-d}\] for every \(n\ge n_d\) and every such circuit with at most \(2^{bn}\) gates. The constants and function in the conclusion may depend on those witnessing the premise.
cards.why: Ordinary hardness amplification equates weak and strong one-wayness at polynomial security scales. Preserving hardness exponential in the actual input length would extend that equivalence to a much stronger regime and clarify how fine-grained average-case hardness supports cryptographic security.

sentences: The premise is a polynomial-time function that defeats exponential-size inversion circuits on an inverse-polynomial fraction of inputs.
The question asks whether this already guarantees a function whose inversion success is negligible for exponential-size circuits.
An attacker succeeds by finding any preimage of a challenge sampled from a uniform input.
Ordinary repetition enlarges the input and can lose hardness exponential in the new length.
Security-preserving results for regular functions do not settle the general case, which remains open in a 2025 revision.

cards.definitions:
A length-preserving function is a single map \(f:\{0,1\}^{*}\to\{0,1\}^{*}\) with \(|f(x)|=|x|\), computed by one deterministic multitape Turing machine in at most \(A(n+1)^r\) steps on every input of length \(n\), for some fixed constants \(A,r\). The same convention applies to \(g\). There is no oracle or advice in forward evaluation.

For a circuit \(C:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}^n\), define its inversion success by \[\operatorname{Inv}_f(C,n)=\Pr_{x\leftarrow U_n}\bigl[f(C(f(x)))=f(x)\bigr],\] where \(U_n\) is uniform on all length-\(n\) bit strings. Finding any length-\(n\) preimage counts as success; the output need not equal the originally sampled \(x\). The challenge is sampled by applying \(f\) to a uniform input, not by choosing a uniform element of its image.

Circuits are finite directed acyclic graphs of fan-in-two AND and OR gates, fan-in-one NOT gates and constants, with named inputs and outputs. Size counts noninput gates, including constants; no restriction is placed on fan-out. Real size limits mean their integer floors. Every circuit is allowed independently at each input length, including circuits with information built into their wiring and constants. No uniform procedure for generating the attack circuits is required. Deterministic circuits suffice for the displayed average-success bound: a randomized attack is a distribution over such circuits, and averaging cannot exceed their common bound.

Weakness means a fixed inverse-polynomial fraction of the sampled challenges defeats every allowed attacker. Strongness here means that the maximum success of any allowed attacker is negligible: smaller than every fixed inverse power for sufficiently large lengths. The exponent \(b\) is fixed before \(d\). This explicitly uses negligible success against exponential-size circuits; it does not add a separate exponentially small success requirement. Security is measured against the input length of each function itself, on all sufficiently large lengths. Both functions are length-preserving, following the source's stated convention; arbitrary padding is not assumed to preserve exponential hardness.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of this implication, or a proof of its negation. A positive answer may use an arbitrary construction or existence argument and need not preserve the original security exponent. It must produce a single polynomial-time function with a positive linear exponential attack-size exponent and negligible inversion success. A negative answer must refute the existence implication itself; a barrier for black-box transformations or for a restricted amplification method is insufficient.

context_blocks.text: The reverse implication is immediate: negligible inversion success also leaves an inverse-polynomial fraction of inputs hard. The substantive question is the weak-to-strong direction. It does not ask to prove that one-way functions exist without assumptions.

The usual direct-product amplification evaluates the weak function on many independent blocks. Its enlarged input length can turn exponential security in a block length into only stretched-exponential security in the new length. The 2025 revision explicitly identifies this loss as the unresolved issue.

Security-preserving amplification is known under regularity assumptions: at a fixed input length, every value in the image of a regular function has the same number of preimages. The present premise includes arbitrary functions with unequal fiber sizes, so that special case does not establish the general implication.

The question is about existence of a suitable strong function. It does not demand a black-box reduction, restrict forward computation to constant depth, or require the new function to use the same input length as a single invocation of the old one. Its exponential guarantee is nevertheless measured in its own full input length.

cards.title: Subpolynomial-key perfectly secure three-server DPFs
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed finite Abelian group \(G\), with \(|G|\ge2\), and a uniform three-server distributed point function with perfect correctness, perfect privacy against any one server, and worst-case key length \(\ell(N)=N^{o(1)}\)? For every integer \(N\ge2\), location \(\alpha\in[N]\), and value \(\beta\in G\), key generation must produce three binary keys \((k_0,k_1,k_2)\) such that \[\sum_{i=0}^{2}\operatorname{Eval}_i(k_i,x)=\begin{cases}\beta&x=\alpha,\\0_G&x\ne\alpha\end{cases}\qquad\text{for every }x\in[N]\] with probability one. For each individual \(i\), the distribution of \(k_i\) must be identical for all pairs \((\alpha,\beta)\) with the same \(N\). Every generated key must have at most \(\ell(N)\) bits. The fixed output group may be chosen as part of a positive answer; requiring all output groups is the source's separate question.
cards.why: Distributed point functions compress secret shares of a sparse vector while letting each holder evaluate its share locally. sentences: A distributed point function gives three servers compact shares of a vector supported at one secret location.
Each server can evaluate its own share, and the three outputs must add to the requested point function.
A single key must reveal exactly no information about either the location or the stored value.
The target is a key length smaller than every positive power of the domain size over some fixed nontrivial finite Abelian group.
Known subpolynomial constructions achieve perfect privacy with four servers or statistical privacy with three, a distinction retained in a 2026 survey.

cards.definitions:
Write \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\). A finite Abelian group is a finite set with an associative and commutative addition, identity \(0_G\), and additive inverses. Its elements have fixed binary names, and its addition table is fixed with the scheme. The point function is zero away from one specified input and takes the specified value there. The case \(\beta=0_G\) is included.

A scheme consists of one randomized Turing machine \(\operatorname{Gen}\) and three deterministic Turing machines \(\operatorname{Eval}_i\), all fixed independently of \(N,\alpha,\beta\). The generator receives the binary encodings of \(N,\alpha,\beta\) and produces three finite bit strings. It may use independent fair bits and must halt with probability one. This convention permits exact sampling from a fixed group of odd order by rejection sampling. Each evaluation machine halts on every valid key and domain input and returns one element of \(G\). The key determines \(N\); its encoding, all public corrections, and any parameter descriptions used in evaluation count toward key length. The machines and the fixed group table are public. There is no additional shared random tape, hidden setup, or uncounted data depending on the particular point function.

This card asks for the information-theoretic key-length bound: it imposes no running-time bound beyond these algorithmic termination conditions. Perfect correctness means that the displayed identities hold simultaneously for all domain inputs with probability one over key generation. Perfect privacy means equality of each single key's entire probability distribution, including its length. Consequently even unlimited computation and arbitrarily many evaluations of that key cannot reveal the location or value. Privacy against a coalition of two servers is not required.

The bound is uniform over locations, values, server indices, and all keys having positive probability. Subpolynomial length means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\), some \(N_\varepsilon\) satisfies \(\ell(N)\le N^{\varepsilon}\) for all integers \(N\ge N_\varepsilon\). The same fixed group and algorithms must work for all \(N\). A security parameter is unnecessary because the privacy error is exactly zero.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a scheme exists, or a proof that no such scheme exists. A positive answer must specify the algorithms and prove correctness, equality of all required key distributions, termination, and the asymptotic key-length bound. A negative answer must cover every fixed nontrivial finite Abelian output group. Statistical privacy with arbitrarily small positive error, or a construction using four servers, does not meet this target.

context_blocks.text: The source obtains subpolynomial keys with three servers when privacy has a small statistical error, and with four servers when privacy is perfect for suitable fixed output groups. This question asks whether three servers can also achieve exact privacy.

The requirement hides both the special location and its output value. Ordinary private information retrieval permits a client to reconstruct replies using additional private information; such a protocol is not automatically a distributed point function whose server outputs add directly to the desired value.

The card makes the output-group scope explicit: existence for some fixed nontrivial group. It does not require a bound uniform over growing groups. The later paper extends the groups supported by efficient information-theoretic constructions, but the checked statements use different server counts or permit statistical security.

The 2026 survey continues to distinguish the known four-party perfectly secure construction from the three-party statistically secure one. Its stated literature snapshot is February 2026, even though the arXiv version was submitted in July.
