cards.status_note: No uniform computability theorem or impossibility proof for this finite-dimensional memoryless unassisted capacity found through 11 September 2026. The corrected 2026 paper explicitly leaves the general question open: its quantum-capacity result is QMA-hardness, while its undecidability result concerns a restricted assisted zero-error classical capacity.

context_blocks.text: Capacity is the best rate at which a noisy channel can transmit information reliably after coding over many uses. For quantum transmission, the object being preserved is an arbitrary quantum state, including its entanglement with a reference system. A channel may badly corrupt each individual input and still support a positive asymptotic rate through suitable coding. This card asks whether that optimal rate can always be computed to requested precision at all.

The quantum coding theorem expresses capacity through regularized coherent information: optimize over a block of n uses, divide by n, and take the supremum over every block length. Devetak’s coding theorem gives an operational justification for this expression. It is an exact mathematical characterization, but it involves infinitely many optimization problems. A numerical procedure needs an additional way to know when unexamined block lengths cannot improve the answer by more than \(\varepsilon\).

For each fixed block length, the input dimension is finite and the coherent-information objective can be approximated on the compact space of density matrices. Exhaustive computation can therefore produce successively better certified lower bounds on Q. This can be absurdly expensive and still count as computation here. The obstruction is that increasing lower bounds need not come with a computable certificate of how far they remain below their limit.

Cubitt, Elkouss, Matthews, Ozols, Pérez-García and Strelchuk show that no universal constant number of channel uses suffices even to expose positive coherent information. For every chosen block length, they construct a channel whose optimized coherent information is zero there, but becomes positive at a larger block length. These are different channels as the chosen length changes. The theorem does not rule out an algorithm whose stopping time depends on the channel description and requested precision.

The input convention is important because a quantum channel is described by real and complex numbers. A finite program that supplies certified rational approximations gives an algorithm meaningful access to those numbers without granting exact tests of arbitrary computable-real equality. It also includes ordinary finite circuit descriptions over computable gates. The validity of the channel and approximation program is promised; solving the separate problem of recognizing all valid descriptions is not required.

Leung and Smith prove continuity of unassisted quantum capacity in finite output dimension, with an explicit bound in terms of channel distance and dimension. Thus small errors in specifying a fixed-dimensional channel change its capacity by a controlled amount. This prevents a simple discontinuity argument from settling this approximation question. Continuity controls perturbations of the channel, while the missing stopping rule concerns convergence over code block lengths.

The 2025 review Undecidability in Physics distinguishes this question from established undecidability results for other information-theoretic quantities. Channels with memory can carry an evolving hidden state across uses; that is different from repeating \(\Phi\) independently. Zero-error capacities demand perfect distinguishability at finite stages, unlike an error that tends to zero under asymptotic coding. Neither change can be imported silently into the present problem.

Bhattacharyya, Mehta and Zhao prove in 2026 that approximating quantum capacity is QMA-hard for channels specified succinctly by circuits. Their promise distinguishes capacity at least \(3/4\) from capacity at most \(1/4\), even for degradable channels. This is strong evidence against efficient computation, but it leaves unrestricted computability untouched: a QMA-hard problem can still have an exhaustive terminating algorithm. Circuit size also differs substantially from the length of a fully expanded channel matrix.

Their corrected March 2026 version proves undecidability for a separate restricted capacity: one-shot, entanglement-assisted, zero-error classical communication through a classical-to-quantum channel, with maximally entangled assistance and projective decoding measurements. Those restrictions are part of the theorem. The paper explicitly says it does not resolve general quantum-capacity computability. Its revision history records a correction to the earlier treatment of the assisted zero-error result.

It is also necessary to separate approximation from deciding whether the answer is exactly zero. Even when a nonnegative real quantity is computable to arbitrary error, every finite approximation can leave open whether it is zero or merely very small. Conversely, identifying some zero-capacity families does not provide approximations for every channel. The requested output and tolerance make this card an unambiguous uniform approximation problem.

A positive resolution would supply a general certification procedure for quantum communication rates, however slow. A negative resolution would show that no universal procedure can always certify the optimal rate to a chosen tolerance, despite finite input and output dimensions and independent repeated noise. Either outcome would clarify whether regularized formulas describe quantities that are algorithmically accessible or can exceed the reach of computation.

sentences: Quantum channel capacity describes the best asymptotic rate for transmitting quantum information through a noisy channel.
This problem asks whether that number can always be approximated by an algorithm from an effective finite description of the channel.
The algorithm may be slow, but it must halt and meet any requested rational accuracy.
Optimizations involving arbitrarily many channel uses make the asymptotic definition harder to turn into a guaranteed finite computation.
Establishing computability or an obstruction would separate the existence of an operational communication rate from our ability to calculate it even in principle.

cards.context:
Capacity is the best rate at which a noisy channel can transmit information reliably after coding over many uses. For quantum transmission, the object being preserved is an arbitrary quantum state, including its entanglement with a reference system. A channel may badly corrupt each individual input and still support a positive asymptotic rate through suitable coding. This card asks whether that optimal rate can always be computed to requested precision at all.

The quantum coding theorem expresses capacity through regularized coherent information: optimize over a block of n uses, divide by n, and take the supremum over every block length. Devetak’s coding theorem gives an operational justification for this expression. It is an exact mathematical characterization, but it involves infinitely many optimization problems. A numerical procedure needs an additional way to know when unexamined block lengths cannot improve the answer by more than \(\varepsilon\).

For each fixed block length, the input dimension is finite and the coherent-information objective can be approximated on the compact space of density matrices. Exhaustive computation can therefore produce successively better certified lower bounds on Q. This can be absurdly expensive and still count as computation here. The obstruction is that increasing lower bounds need not come with a computable certificate of how far they remain below their limit.

Cubitt, Elkouss, Matthews, Ozols, Pérez-García and Strelchuk show that no universal constant number of channel uses suffices even to expose positive coherent information. For every chosen block length, they construct a channel whose optimized coherent information is zero there, but becomes positive at a larger block length. These are different channels as the chosen length changes. The theorem does not rule out an algorithm whose stopping time depends on the channel description and requested precision.

The input convention is important because a quantum channel is described by real and complex numbers. A finite program that supplies certified rational approximations gives an algorithm meaningful access to those numbers without granting exact tests of arbitrary computable-real equality. It also includes ordinary finite circuit descriptions over computable gates. The validity of the channel and approximation program is promised; solving the separate problem of recognizing all valid descriptions is not required.

Leung and Smith prove continuity of unassisted quantum capacity in finite output dimension, with an explicit bound in terms of channel distance and dimension. Thus small errors in specifying a fixed-dimensional channel change its capacity by a controlled amount. This prevents a simple discontinuity argument from settling this approximation question. Continuity controls perturbations of the channel, while the missing stopping rule concerns convergence over code block lengths.

The 2025 review Undecidability in Physics distinguishes this question from established undecidability results for other information-theoretic quantities. Channels with memory can carry an evolving hidden state across uses; that is different from repeating \(\Phi\) independently. Zero-error capacities demand perfect distinguishability at finite stages, unlike an error that tends to zero under asymptotic coding. Neither change can be imported silently into the present problem.

Bhattacharyya, Mehta and Zhao prove in 2026 that approximating quantum capacity is QMA-hard for channels specified succinctly by circuits. Their promise distinguishes capacity at least \(3/4\) from capacity at most \(1/4\), even for degradable channels. This is strong evidence against efficient computation, but it leaves unrestricted computability untouched: a QMA-hard problem can still have an exhaustive terminating algorithm. Circuit size also differs substantially from the length of a fully expanded channel matrix.

Their corrected March 2026 version proves undecidability for a separate restricted capacity: one-shot, entanglement-assisted, zero-error classical communication through a classical-to-quantum channel, with maximally entangled assistance and projective decoding measurements. Those restrictions are part of the theorem. The paper explicitly says it does not resolve general quantum-capacity computability. Its revision history records a correction to the earlier treatment of the assisted zero-error result.

It is also necessary to separate approximation from deciding whether the answer is exactly zero. Even when a nonnegative real quantity is computable to arbitrary error, every finite approximation can leave open whether it is zero or merely very small. Conversely, identifying some zero-capacity families does not provide approximations for every channel. The requested output and tolerance make this card an unambiguous uniform approximation problem.

A positive resolution would supply a general certification procedure for quantum communication rates, however slow. A negative resolution would show that no universal procedure can always certify the optimal rate to a chosen tolerance, despite finite input and output dimensions and independent repeated noise. Either outcome would clarify whether regularized formulas describe quantities that are algorithmically accessible or can exceed the reach of computation.

cards.title: Dihedral hidden subgroup problem in BQP
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform bounded-error quantum algorithm and constants \(C,c>0\) such that, for every \(N\ge 2\) and every oracle f hiding a subgroup H of \(D_{N}\), the algorithm outputs generators of H with probability at least \(2/3\) using at most \(C(\lceil \log _{2}N\rceil +\ell +2)^{c}\) total operations, where \(\ell\) is the bit length of an oracle value?
cards.definitions: The dihedral group \(D_{N}\) has 2N elements represented as pairs \((x,b)\) with \(x\in \mathbb{Z} /N\mathbb{Z}\) and \(b\in \{0,1\}\), and multiplication \((x,b)(y,d)\)=(\(x+(- 1)^{b}y\) mod \(N,b+d\) mod 2). Its identity is \((0,0)\). The classical input is N in binary and the positive integer \(\ell\) specifying the output-register width. An arbitrary subgroup \(H\le D_{N}\) is hidden by \(f:D_{N}\to \{0,1\}^{\ell}\) when \(f(g)=f(g' )\) if and only if \(gH=g' H\), equivalently \(g^{- 1}g' \in H\). Thus distinct left cosets have distinct labels, whose bit patterns carry no promised structure. Quantum access is the reversible XOR oracle \(U_{f}|g,z\rangle =|g,z\oplus f(g)\rangle\), usable on superpositions; it acts as the identity on invalid group encodings. Each call costs one oracle operation. Count all other elementary quantum gates, measurements and classical bit operations as well, using a fixed universal gate set such as Clifford+T. Uniformity requires an effective polynomial-time classical controller, with no advice depending on N, H or f. There is no input truth table for f and no additional subset-sum, state-preparation or memory-access oracle. The output is a finite list of encoded group elements whose generated subgroup equals H; the empty list is allowed for \(H=\{1\}\). The success probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness and measurements, for every legal hiding function separately. The displayed bound is a worst-case bound on total work, not merely query count or parallel depth. When \(\ell\) is polynomial in log N, as in the usual oracle model, the target is polynomial time in log N.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct and prove correct a quantum algorithm with the stated uniform polynomial total-work guarantee, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A polynomial number of oracle queries with superpolynomial postprocessing, a speedup using uncounted parallel hardware, or an algorithm requiring an additional subset-sum oracle does not suffice. Failure of one family of measurements or sieves is not a negative solution for all quantum algorithms.
cards.why: A central test for quantum algorithms beyond abelian Fourier sampling. The information can be acquired with few queries, but extracting the subgroup efficiently remains a fundamental computational challenge with lattice-related consequences under the appropriate reductions.

importance.reason: A basic nonabelian hidden-structure problem with a long-standing gap between polynomial information requirements and subexponential known algorithms.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No verified polynomial-time solution is recorded. Simon’s August 2026 coset-algorithm claim is disputed: the September 1 Gupte–Ragavan–Zhandry response proves failure of the proposed template, and Guo–Yang identify an unsupported independence hypothesis. The review checked these primary statements without independently rerunning the Lean development. The 2022 Moore–Young claim was explicitly withdrawn.

context_blocks.text: Hidden subgroup problems ask a quantum algorithm to recover symmetry from equality patterns in a function. In an abelian group, Fourier sampling can turn those patterns into usable constraints, providing the framework for familiar quantum period-finding algorithms. The dihedral group adds a reflection to a cyclic rotation group and is among the simplest noncommutative settings in which the general polynomial-time method remains unresolved.

A representative hard case has \(H=H_{s}=\{(0,0),(s,1)\}\), with an unknown \(s\in \mathbb{Z} /N\mathbb{Z}\). The hiding promise says \(f(x,0)=f(x+s,1)\), and each restriction to \(b=0\) or \(b=1\) is injective. Recovering the subgroup is therefore recovering a cyclic hidden shift. The unrestricted subgroup problem reduces to this reflection case after handling its rotational part; the inherited Kuperberg paper uses the hidden-shift formulation for its main algorithm.

A coherent oracle query followed by discarding the function value yields a coset state. In the reflection case it has the form \((|0,x\rangle +|1,x+s\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\) for an unknown random x. Fourier transformation of the cyclic coordinate produces a known random label k and a qubit with relative phase exp(\(2\pi\)iks/N). The phase contains information about s, but measuring that qubit does not simply reveal the modular product ks as a classical number.

This is already enough information in a statistical sense: polynomially many queries suffice if computationally expensive processing is allowed. The main obstacle is implementing an effective collective extraction of the hidden shift with polynomial total work. A bound on oracle calls therefore cannot be substituted for a bound on running time. The card deliberately counts both quantum gates and classical postprocessing.

Kuperberg’s first sieve gives time and query complexity \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  N})}\). It repeatedly combines phase states so that their labels become more useful for recovering the shift. This is a substantial speedup over generic classical approaches, yet it is superpolynomial in the input length \(n\approx \log  N\): the target here is \(n^{O(1)}\), not \(2^{O(\sqrt{n})}\).

The resource picture improved further. Regev obtains subexponential time with polynomial space, at a larger exponent involving \(\sqrt{\log  N \log  \log  N}\). Kuperberg’s later collimation sieve restores \(\exp (O(\sqrt{\log  N}))\) time while using only \(O(\log  N)\) quantum space, although classical storage remains subexponential. Small quantum memory and polynomial overall running time are different achievements.

The lattice connection is important but needs its access-model qualification. Regev reduces a unique-shortest-vector problem to solving dihedral coset samples. Thus a polynomial algorithm that works from those samples would have consequences for lattice algorithms. An arbitrary hiding-function oracle provides a different interface, so one should not silently claim that every conceivable oracle-HSP algorithm automatically implements the coset solver required by that reduction.

An older positive claim remains visible in search results. Moore and Young’s February 2022 preprint claimed polynomial time for dihedral groups of power-of-two size, but was withdrawn on February 23. The withdrawal states that Lemma 4.3 is wrong and that the main algorithm needs the states asserted by that lemma. It is retained here as a documented withdrawn attempt, not a known algorithm.

A much more recent claim requires a separate status entry. Daniel Simon’s August 2026 preprint claims a polynomial-time dihedral coset algorithm, replacing a subset-sum step with a different erasure procedure. Its latest listed revision is August 17 and acknowledges a correction to the analysis as well as a new critical response. A valid coset algorithm of the claimed generality would settle the reflection case, making this directly relevant to the present question.

Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised September 1, gives an information-theoretic obstruction to the proposed algorithm. They show that its use of only a truncated portion of the classical Fourier labels leaves negligible advantage in guessing the secret’s least-significant bit. Their theorem covers a broader template containing the proposed procedure; it does not exclude all algorithms for the dihedral problem. The authors also supply a Lean formalization. This catalogue review checked the primary statements and repository description, but did not independently rerun that formalization.

Guo and Yang independently analyze the supporting lemmas. Their August 17 paper proves corrected statements while identifying a remaining independence assumption that the proposed choice of a partition does not supply. They explicitly conclude that establishing those lemmas does not establish correctness of the algorithm. The card therefore flags the recent claim as disputed rather than presenting polynomial time as established.

Positive results elsewhere among nonabelian groups continue to refine the boundary. Morales’ August 2026 algorithm handles certain scalar-action semidirect products with bounded generator rank and exponent-to-prime ratio polylogarithmic in group size, and another family with modular subgroup structure. For the ordinary dihedral family, the relevant ratio would be \(N/2\), which does not meet that condition as N grows. These structural advances leave the unrestricted dihedral target intact.

A solution would identify a new way to convert nonabelian quantum information into efficiently recoverable classical structure. A negative result would be equally consequential because polynomial query complexity is already available: it would isolate a genuine computational obstruction in processing the information. The significance comes from that algorithmic boundary, alongside the precise reductions to coset and lattice problems.

cards.title: Graph isomorphism in BQP
cards.formal: Is \(GI\in \mathrm{BQP}\)? Equivalently, does a uniform quantum algorithm decide, on every pair of finite simple graphs on n vertices given by their adjacency matrices, whether they are isomorphic, with error probability at most \(1/3\) and worst-case total running time \(n^{O(1)}\)?
cards.definitions: A graph is finite, undirected, loopless and has no parallel edges. For equally sized vertex sets \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\), an isomorphism from G to H is a bijection \(\pi :[n]\to [n]\) satisfying \(\{u,v\}\in E(G)\) if and only if \(\{\pi (u),\pi (v)\}\in E(H)\) for every \(u\ne v\). The input consists of the two explicitly written binary adjacency matrices; unequal vertex counts are rejected immediately and empty graphs are handled trivially. There are no promises of rigidity, bounded degree, typicality, or a particular input distribution. BQP means a polynomial-time uniform family of quantum circuits over a fixed universal gate set such as Clifford+T, acting on computational-basis encodings of the classical input and initialized ancillas, with a measured output bit. There must be fixed constants C,c such that all gates, measurements and classical control can be implemented within \(C(n+2)^{c}\) total elementary operations. The algorithm accepts each isomorphic pair with probability at least \(2/3\) and each nonisomorphic pair with probability at most \(1/3\). It receives no nonuniform advice, witness, graph-orbit state, isomorphism oracle or uncounted memory-preparation service. The target is the decision problem for an ordinary vertex permutation; it is not the distinct relation called quantum graph isomorphism in nonlocal-game theory.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove membership by giving a correct uniform quantum algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial total cost, or prove \(GI\notin \mathrm{BQP}\). A classical polynomial-time algorithm would also answer yes. A separation for a specified Fourier-sampling or sieve model is not a negative answer for unrestricted BQP; an invariant that distinguishes only some nonisomorphic pairs is not a complete positive answer.
cards.why: A canonical test of whether quantum computation can efficiently recognize equivalence of explicit combinatorial structures, beyond the algebraic problems already handled by standard period finding.

importance.reason: A central quantum-algorithm target linking graph algorithms, permutation groups and the computational use of entangled states.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No uniform polynomial-time quantum algorithm for ordinary graph isomorphism, or proof of \(GI\notin \mathrm{BQP}\), was found in the checked primary sources. The 2026 correlation tests, state-isomorphism classifications and NPA hierarchy results do not settle this question.

context_blocks.text: Graph isomorphism asks whether two descriptions encode the same finite relational structure after renaming the vertices. It is an exact equivalence problem, rather than a search for approximately similar networks. A proposed permutation is easy to verify by comparing all adjacency entries, but finding a successful permutation or ruling out every permutation can require reasoning about highly symmetric graphs.

Elementary invariants help without settling the problem. For instance, a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices, six edges and degree two at every vertex, but cannot be isomorphic because one is connected and the other is not. More elaborate invariants must likewise be assessed by whether they distinguish every required pair, not just by how well they perform on a test set.

Aaronson’s 2005 challenge list identifies graph isomorphism among the natural targets for quantum algorithms beyond Shor and Grover. The formulation on this card turns that broad research motivation into one exact complexity-class membership question. It imposes no particular algorithmic approach and permits a classical algorithm as a special case of a quantum one.

Babai’s classical breakthrough gives a quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with bound \(\exp ((\log  n)^{O(1)})\). The original argument required a correction in January 2017, after which the quasipolynomial claim was restored. This is the relevant general classical benchmark, rather than brute-force examination of n! permutations. Quasipolynomial time is still larger than the polynomial bound asked for here.

One tempting quantum approach uses the action of permutations on graphs. The state that is a uniform superposition over all distinct labeled copies of G would be identical for isomorphic graphs and orthogonal for nonisomorphic ones. If such states could always be prepared efficiently, an overlap test would help. The state-preparation step is the difficulty: preparing a superposition of pairs |\(\pi \rangle |\pi G\rangle\) is easy, but coherently removing the permutation register does not follow from that construction. Simply discarding the register gives a mixed state, not the desired pure superposition.

The established hidden-subgroup approach makes this difficulty precise in another form. Graph isomorphism can be reduced to finding hidden symmetry in permutation groups, and the standard procedure generates quantum coset states. Hallgren, Roetteler and Sen, independently of Moore and Russell and later in joint work, prove that measurements on too few such states reveal insufficient information in the relevant hard cases. Their bound requires joint access to \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) states to obtain useful information.

That lower bound is a restriction on information extraction in a particular representation. The number of required states is itself polynomial. It does not say that every measurement on that many states needs superpolynomial computation, and it does not forbid an algorithm that uses the explicit input graphs in a different way. A negative solution to \(GI\in \mathrm{BQP}\) would have to rule out those broader possibilities as well.

The inherited quantum-inspired reference has a substantive June 2026 revision. Maxwell, van den Hoven and Renema analyze correlations in Gaussian boson samplers and derive a classical test for a necessary condition of graph isomorphism. At restricted correlation order it can certify that some graph pairs are different. At the maximum order their condition becomes sufficient, but their method is no longer efficient. The authors explicitly separate these two regimes.

This illustrates why a photonic sampling procedure is not automatically a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all graphs. One must account for how many samples or correlations are required to distinguish a worst-case pair, how accurately they must be estimated, and the classical work used to interpret them. Efficiently generating individual samples does not by itself establish a uniform bound for the complete decision task.

May 2026 work by Gheorghiu, Jacobs, Mehraban and Motamedi studies isomorphism of quantum states under group actions. They show, among other results, that a Clifford-group state problem is at least as hard as ordinary graph isomorphism, while a Pauli-group variant is BQP-complete. The direction and the group matter: the BQP algorithm for the Pauli problem is not thereby an algorithm for the GI-hard Clifford problem.

A further naming distinction appears in the 2026 paper on the NPA hierarchy by Kar, Roberson, Seppelt and Zeman. It studies a quantum isomorphism relation and its noncommutative semidefinite relaxations, with polynomial-time algorithms at each fixed level. Those statements concern a different relation on graphs and fixed relaxations; they do not establish a quantum algorithm deciding whether an ordinary vertex bijection exists.

A positive answer would enlarge the collection of important exact structure problems known to admit efficient quantum algorithms, unless a classical polynomial algorithm arrived at the same time. A negative answer would be exceptionally strong: GI has efficiently verifiable permutation witnesses and hence belongs to NP, so \(GI\notin \mathrm{BQP}\) would in particular imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The question is fundamental on both sides, independently of any particular physical implementation.

sentences: Two graphs are isomorphic when a relabeling of vertices preserves every edge.
This question asks whether a quantum algorithm can decide that equivalence in polynomial time for every pair of explicitly given graphs.
The algorithm must include all processing costs and achieve bounded error, rather than merely extract a small amount of information from an oracle.
Symmetry makes graph isomorphism a natural testing ground for quantum methods, but quantum access to related group structure is not itself a complete algorithm.
A resolution would clarify whether quantum computation can efficiently handle this central classification problem.

cards.context:
Graph isomorphism asks whether two descriptions encode the same finite relational structure after renaming the vertices. It is an exact equivalence problem, rather than a search for approximately similar networks. A proposed permutation is easy to verify by comparing all adjacency entries, but finding a successful permutation or ruling out every permutation can require reasoning about highly symmetric graphs.

Elementary invariants help without settling the problem. For instance, a six-cycle and two disjoint triangles both have six vertices, six edges and degree two at every vertex, but cannot be isomorphic because one is connected and the other is not. More elaborate invariants must likewise be assessed by whether they distinguish every required pair, not just by how well they perform on a test set.

Aaronson’s 2005 challenge list identifies graph isomorphism among the natural targets for quantum algorithms beyond Shor and Grover. The formulation on this card turns that broad research motivation into one exact complexity-class membership question. It imposes no particular algorithmic approach and permits a classical algorithm as a special case of a quantum one.

Babai’s classical breakthrough gives a quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with bound \(\exp ((\log  n)^{O(1)})\). The original argument required a correction in January 2017, after which the quasipolynomial claim was restored. This is the relevant general classical benchmark, rather than brute-force examination of n! permutations. Quasipolynomial time is still larger than the polynomial bound asked for here.

One tempting quantum approach uses the action of permutations on graphs. The state that is a uniform superposition over all distinct labeled copies of G would be identical for isomorphic graphs and orthogonal for nonisomorphic ones. If such states could always be prepared efficiently, an overlap test would help. The state-preparation step is the difficulty: preparing a superposition of pairs |\(\pi \rangle |\pi G\rangle\) is easy, but coherently removing the permutation register does not follow from that construction. Simply discarding the register gives a mixed state, not the desired pure superposition.

The established hidden-subgroup approach makes this difficulty precise in another form. Graph isomorphism can be reduced to finding hidden symmetry in permutation groups, and the standard procedure generates quantum coset states. Hallgren, Roetteler and Sen, independently of Moore and Russell and later in joint work, prove that measurements on too few such states reveal insufficient information in the relevant hard cases. Their bound requires joint access to \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) states to obtain useful information.

That lower bound is a restriction on information extraction in a particular representation. The number of required states is itself polynomial. It does not say that every measurement on that many states needs superpolynomial computation, and it does not forbid an algorithm that uses the explicit input graphs in a different way. A negative solution to \(GI\in \mathrm{BQP}\) would have to rule out those broader possibilities as well.

The inherited quantum-inspired reference has a substantive June 2026 revision. Maxwell, van den Hoven and Renema analyze correlations in Gaussian boson samplers and derive a classical test for a necessary condition of graph isomorphism. At restricted correlation order it can certify that some graph pairs are different. At the maximum order their condition becomes sufficient, but their method is no longer efficient. The authors explicitly separate these two regimes.

This illustrates why a photonic sampling procedure is not automatically a polynomial-time decision algorithm for all graphs. One must account for how many samples or correlations are required to distinguish a worst-case pair, how accurately they must be estimated, and the classical work used to interpret them. Efficiently generating individual samples does not by itself establish a uniform bound for the complete decision task.

May 2026 work by Gheorghiu, Jacobs, Mehraban and Motamedi studies isomorphism of quantum states under group actions. They show, among other results, that a Clifford-group state problem is at least as hard as ordinary graph isomorphism, while a Pauli-group variant is BQP-complete. The direction and the group matter: the BQP algorithm for the Pauli problem is not thereby an algorithm for the GI-hard Clifford problem.

A further naming distinction appears in the 2026 paper on the NPA hierarchy by Kar, Roberson, Seppelt and Zeman. It studies a quantum isomorphism relation and its noncommutative semidefinite relaxations, with polynomial-time algorithms at each fixed level. Those statements concern a different relation on graphs and fixed relaxations; they do not establish a quantum algorithm deciding whether an ordinary vertex bijection exists.

A positive answer would enlarge the collection of important exact structure problems known to admit efficient quantum algorithms, unless a classical polynomial algorithm arrived at the same time. A negative answer would be exceptionally strong: GI has efficiently verifiable permutation witnesses and hence belongs to NP, so \(GI\notin \mathrm{BQP}\) would in particular imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). The question is fundamental on both sides, independently of any particular physical implementation.

cards.title: Bell nonlocality from finitely many copies of every entangled state
cards.formal: For every entangled finite-dimensional bipartite state \(\rho\), do finitely many copies \(\rho ^{\otimes}k\) and local filters suffice to produce correlations violating a Bell inequality, without an auxiliary entangled state?
cards.definitions: A state is a positive semidefinite trace-one operator on \(H_{A}\otimes H_{B}\). It is entangled when it is not a convex combination of product states. Local filters are trace-nonincreasing completely positive maps \(F_{A},F_{B}\) applied to the respective k-fold systems before measurement questions are selected; the joint success probability must be positive. Normalize the successful filtered state. Each party then chooses a local measurement from a finite set of positive-operator-valued measurements. The resulting conditional distribution p(a,b|x,y) is Bell-nonlocal when it has no representation \(\sum_{\lambda} q_{\lambda} p_{A}(a|x,\lambda )p_{B}(b|y,\lambda )\), with nonnegative \(q_{\lambda}\) summing to one. Such a representation is precisely a local hidden-variable model for finite questions and answers. Local ancillary states and shared randomness are allowed, but no additional shared entangled state is supplied.

context_blocks.text: Entanglement and observable Bell nonlocality are related but distinct resources. This question asks whether repeated access to the same entanglement always reveals nonlocal behavior after local preprocessing.

Liang, Masanes and Rosset prove an activation result using a suitable auxiliary state. That resource is stronger than additional copies of the given state and is expressly excluded here. Direct one-copy Bell tests also do not settle the finite-copy filtered target.

cards.why: Determine whether every bipartite entangled state has an intrinsic finite-copy nonlocal manifestation.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

cards.title: Maximum randomized-versus-quantum gap for total functions
cards.formal: Determine the optimal polynomial separation exponent \[\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}=\inf\bigl\{a\ge0:\exists C>0\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall\text{ nonconstant }f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\},\ R(f)\le C\,Q(f)^a\bigr\}.\] Here \(R(f)\) and \(Q(f)\) are randomized and quantum bit-query complexities with worst-case error at most \(1/3\). The constant \(C\) must be independent of both \(n\) and \(f\). The known range is \(3\le\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\le4\). This card makes the source's maximum-gap question precise at the level of its polynomial exponent; logarithmic factors are not part of this numerical target.
cards.why: This quantifies the greatest possible quantum query advantage when an algorithm must handle every input, without a promise. It tests a basic limitation on quantum speedups and distinguishes the role of classical randomization from that of deterministic computation.
cards.status_note: Open in Aaronson’s 2021 survey. The near-cubic lower-bound family and universal quartic bound were checked in their primary papers on 2026-09-14. A bounded later-work search found no resolution of the displayed exponent; the September 2026 paper Quantum Query Advantage Requires Space concerns an additional workspace restriction and does not close this gap.

sentences: The question asks for the largest polynomial quantum query advantage over randomized algorithms on total Boolean functions.
Both models must answer correctly with probability at least two thirds on every input.
Only queries to input bits are counted, with other computation and workspace unrestricted.
Known results put the optimal separation exponent between three and four.
The target is to certify that exponent within one hundredth, without resolving finer logarithmic factors.

cards.definitions:
A total Boolean function assigns one output bit to every length-\(n\) bit string, with no promise restricting the inputs. Nonconstant means that both output values occur. A deterministic decision tree adaptively chooses an input coordinate, receives its bit, and ultimately outputs a bit. Its depth is the maximum number of queries on a root-to-leaf path. A randomized query algorithm is a probability distribution over deterministic trees of depth at most \(T\). It must output \(f(x)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for each fixed input \(x\). The least possible \(T\) is \(R(f)\); unlimited computation and storage between queries are free.

For an input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a quantum bit query is the unitary \(O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle\), where \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(z\) is a work register, \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two, and the dummy coordinate has \(x_0=0\). A \(T\)-query algorithm starts in a fixed state, alternates at most \(T\) calls to this oracle with input-independent unitary operations on a finite-dimensional workspace, and finally measures a designated output bit. Arbitrary finite workspace and unitary matrices are allowed. Only oracle calls are charged; all other computation is free. Intermediate measurements and classical random choices can equivalently be included by storing their outcomes coherently. Algorithms may depend on the function and input length, but their operations cannot depend on the unknown input except through oracle calls. No uniform circuit-generation or time bound is imposed. Write \(Q(f)\) for the least integer \(T\) that achieves error at most \(1/3\) on every input in the domain of \(f\). The query bound is a worst-case bound, not an expected number of calls.

Both complexities are positive integers for nonconstant functions and at most \(n\). The infimum takes all real nonnegative exponents with a universal multiplicative bound. An exponent at the infimum need not itself admit such a bound: logarithmic factors may prevent attainment. Removing constant functions avoids zero-complexity conventions. The approximation tolerance for \(\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}\) concerns the exponent itself, not a relative approximation to a query count.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a_*\) and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(|a_*-\alpha_{\mathrm{RQ}}|\le1/100\). A certified interval of width at most \(1/50\) suffices via its midpoint. It must control the universal upper bound and the existence of sufficiently large separations to certify this accuracy; merely improving one currently known bound does not suffice. The benchmark does not require resolving logarithmic factors or proving that the infimum exponent is attained.

context_blocks.text: Quantum algorithms can exploit a special promise to obtain enormous advantages over randomized algorithms. Total functions remove that freedom. Every input string must have a specified correct answer, so both the quantum algorithm and its classical competitors must handle adversarial inputs.

The quartic upper bound follows from \(R(f)\le D(f)=O(Q(f)^4)\), where \(D(f)\) is deterministic decision-tree depth. A matching separation between deterministic and quantum queries does not automatically give a matching separation against randomized algorithms.

The near-cubic lower-bound family comes from stronger promise-problem separations combined with a construction turning them into total functions. This establishes an exponent of at least three; it does not supply a quartic randomized separation.

The exponent formulation intentionally ignores subpolynomial factors. For example, an additional logarithmic factor in a universal cubic bound would still be compatible with exponent three. Establishing the exact bound with exponent three and no extra factor is a finer question.

context_blocks.text: Advice is not a witness chosen for an individual input. It is one nonuniform information resource shared by an entire input-length class.

For a fixed input length, the advice must support all inputs of that length. It cannot be tailored after seeing the particular instance. This makes it different from a witness, which is chosen to establish a claim about one input. A fresh copy of the same quantum advice state can be supplied for each computation.

The possible advantage is not that a measurement reveals an arbitrary amount of classical information from a few qubits. Instead, the algorithm might use the input to choose which computation to perform with the advice. The open question is whether polynomial-length classical advice can always support an equally effective computation for every input.

cards.answer_criterion: Prove that polynomial classical advice suffices for every language decidable with polynomial quantum advice, or prove a separation of the two unrelativized advice classes.

cards.title: Quantum query complexity versus bounded approximate degree
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal multiplicative constants, the extremal function \[M(n,d)=\max\bigl\{Q(f):\varnothing\ne D\subseteq\{0,1\}^n,\ f:D\to\{0,1\},\ \operatorname{bdeg}_{1/3}(f)\le d\bigr\}\] for all integers \(n\ge1\) and \(1\le d\le n\). The bounded approximate degree \(\operatorname{bdeg}_{1/3}(f)\) is the least total degree of a real polynomial \(p\) satisfying \[|p(x)-f(x)|\le1/3\quad(x\in D),\qquad 0\le p(x)\le1\quad(x\in\{0,1\}^n).\] The query measure \(Q\) has worst-case error at most \(1/3\). This makes the source's largest-gap question a two-parameter extremal query bound. The source's additional question of whether an exponential gap exists was answered affirmatively in 2023.
cards.why: Bounded approximate degree is the main numerical object behind the polynomial method for quantum query lower bounds. Determining its worst possible discrepancy from actual quantum query complexity would quantify how much algorithmic difficulty this method can miss under promises.
cards.status_note: The exponential-separation part of the 2021 question was resolved by Ambainis and Belovs at CCC 2023. The card retains the broader maximum-gap target as the explicit extremal curve M(n,d). The source, published separation and 2024 follow-up were checked on 2026-09-14; their checked theorems do not determine this curve, and a bounded later-work search found no complete characterization.

sentences: The question compares quantum query complexity with polynomials that approximate a promised Boolean function.
The polynomial must remain between zero and one even on inputs outside the promise.
The target is the largest quantum query complexity possible at each input length and bounded-degree budget.
A 2023 theorem already proves that the gap can be exponential, so that subquestion is no longer open.

cards.definitions:
A partial Boolean function has a nonempty promise domain \(D\) of valid inputs, with one prescribed output bit for each valid input. An algorithm knows the function and promise but receives the actual input only through its bit oracle. Correctness is required on \(D\). Its fixed query budget applies on every input, including inputs outside the promise, where the output bit may be arbitrary.

For an input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), a quantum bit query is the unitary \(O_x|i,b,z\rangle=|i,b\mathbin{\oplus}x_i,z\rangle\), where \(i\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), \(b\in\{0,1\}\), \(z\) is a work register, \(\oplus\) denotes addition modulo two, and the dummy coordinate has \(x_0=0\). A \(T\)-query algorithm starts in a fixed state, alternates at most \(T\) calls to this oracle with input-independent unitary operations on a finite-dimensional workspace, and finally measures a designated output bit. Arbitrary finite workspace and unitary matrices are allowed. Only oracle calls are charged; all other computation is free. Intermediate measurements and classical random choices can equivalently be included by storing their outcomes coherently. Algorithms may depend on the function and input length, but their operations cannot depend on the unknown input except through oracle calls. No uniform circuit-generation or time bound is imposed. Write \(Q(f)\) for the least integer \(T\) that achieves error at most \(1/3\) on every input in the domain of \(f\). The query bound is a worst-case bound, not an expected number of calls.

A real polynomial is a finite linear combination of monomials in \(n\) real variables; its total degree is the largest sum of variable exponents in a monomial with nonzero coefficient. Multilinear polynomials suffice because \(x_i^j=x_i\) on Boolean inputs for \(j\ge1\). Their real coefficients have no bit-length or computability restriction. Boundedness is imposed only on the entire Boolean cube, not on all of \(\mathbb R^n\), and includes inputs outside the promise. Every partial Boolean function has a bounded exact representing polynomial of degree at most \(n\): extend its values to a total Boolean function and interpolate.

There are finitely many partial Boolean functions on a fixed cube, so the displayed maximum is over a finite set. It is nonempty and satisfies \(1\le M(n,d)\le n\) on the stated domain, using a single input-bit function for the lower bound and reading all bits for the upper bound. The parameter \(n\) counts individual Boolean oracle bits. A symbol from a larger alphabet is not available in one query. Neither the promise nor the polynomial is supplied as an additional input-dependent oracle.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified positive function \(H(n,d)\), universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of \(cH(n,d)\le M(n,d)\le CH(n,d)\) throughout the stated integer domain. The answer must identify the asymptotic dependence on \(n,d\), not merely rename the defining optimization over functions or algorithms. Both a universal upper bound and matching worst-case examples are required. Exponential separation alone is already known and does not settle this full extremal target.

context_blocks.text: A \(T\)-query quantum algorithm has an acceptance probability that is a polynomial of degree at most \(2T\), bounded between zero and one on every Boolean input. Hence bounded approximate degree is always at most twice quantum query complexity. The question asks how far the converse can fail.

The promise does not remove the full-cube boundedness condition. Omitting that condition changes the measure and permits simple examples with artificially low degree. For total Boolean functions the two measures are polynomially related, but promises permit much larger separations.

Ambainis and Belovs give Boolean promise functions on \(n\) bits with bounded exact polynomial degree \(O(\log n)\) and quantum query complexity at least \(n^{1/3}\) up to logarithmic losses along their family. Bounded exact degree also upper-bounds bounded approximate degree, so this answers the exponential-gap subquestion.

The 2024 paper reproves such a partial-function separation through total search problems and strengthens the polynomial measure in additional results. These results establish large gaps, but the checked theorems do not determine the full extremal dependence on the input length and degree budget.

sentences: QAOA is a widely studied quantum optimization ansatz using alternating objective and mixing operations.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 2\) let \(J_{ij}, 1\le i<j\le n\), be independent real normal random variables of mean 0 and variance 1. On \((\mathbb{C} ^{2})^{\otimes n}\), let \(Z_{i}\) and \(X_{i}\) act on the i-th qubit by the Pauli matrices \(Z=diag(1,- 1)\) and X with off-diagonal entries 1 and diagonal entries 0. Put \(H_{J}=n^{- 1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}Z_{i} Z_{j}\) and \(B_{n}=\sum_{i} X_{i}\). Let |+⟩=\((|0\rangle +|1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\). For integer depth \(p\ge 1\) and fixed real angle vectors \(\gamma ,\beta \in \mathbb{R} ^{p}\), define |\(\psi _{p,J}\rangle =e^{- i\beta _{p} B_{n}}e^{- i\gamma _{p} H_{J}}\cdots e^{- i\beta _{1} B_{n}}e^{- i\gamma _{1} H_{J}}|+\rangle ^{\otimes n}\). Matrix exponentials have their usual convergent-series meaning; states have unit norm. Expectation is over J. The n limit exists for each fixed p and angles as established for this model in the source. Angles may depend on p but are fixed independently of n and J. First take the infinite-n ensemble limit for fixed angles, then optimize those angles, then take the supremum over finite depths. Supremum need not be attained. Identity layers imply that the optimized depth values are nondecreasing. They are bounded by \(\Pi *=\lim _{n\to \infty} E_{J}[\max _{z\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}} n^{- 1/2}\sum_{i<j}J_{ij}z_{i} z_{j}]/n\), the finite Parisi ground-state value in this normalization. Maximization, rather than minimization, fixes the sign convention.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous value a and a Lean proof that |\(a- A|\le 1/100\), or certified lower and upper bounds of width at most \(1/50\) with the midpoint as answer. Exact determination also qualifies. Merely restating the defining supremum, reporting floating-point optimization at finitely many depths, or interchanging depth and instance-size limits is insufficient. Equality with \(\Pi\)* is a stronger possible answer, not assumed by the target.

cards.definitions: Write \([d]=\{1,\ldots ,d\}, u_{d}(i)=1/d\) and \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,u_{d})=(1/2)\sum_{i}|p_{i}- 1/d|\). The algorithm receives d and \(\varepsilon\) and oracle access to a unitary \(U_{p}\) satisfying \(U_{p}|0^{k}\rangle =\sum_{i}\sqrt{p_{i}}|i\rangle |\psi _{i}\rangle\), where each garbage state |\(\psi _{i}\rangle\) is normalized. The extension of \(U_{p}\) away from |\(0^{k}\rangle\) and its garbage states are arbitrary; the tester must work for every valid oracle satisfying the promise. A query is one application of \(U_{p}, U_{p}\dagger\) or controlled-\(U_{p}\); intervening quantum operations, ancillas and measurements are unrestricted and do not count toward query complexity. The code is used as a black box: the tester does not get a classical description to inspect for free. Let \(Q(d,\varepsilon )\) be the minimum worst-case number of such queries among testers whose probability of the correct yes/no output is at least 0.99 for every oracle with \(p=u_{d}\) or \(d_{\mathrm{TV}}(p,u_{d})>\varepsilon\), taking the worst case over allowed oracle-register sizes. No guarantee is required in the intermediate gap.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(d,\varepsilon )\) and absolute constants \(a,A>0\) such that a \(g(d,\varepsilon )\le Q(d,\varepsilon )\le A g(d,\varepsilon )\) throughout the stated domain. Prove both bounds uniformly over its two parameters and all valid oracle implementations. A formula or certified evaluation rule may specify g; merely renaming Q is insufficient. This is an asymptotic query bound up to multiplicative constants, not pointwise additive 0.01 accuracy.

context_blocks.title: Running a sampler backwards is extra information
context_blocks.text: Ordinary sample access reveals only independent outcomes. Coherent access to a sampler and its inverse permits interference between executions. context_blocks.title: The upper bound has two regimes

context_blocks.title: A stronger variant fixes a special oracle structure

The authors also conjecture the same lower bound even with this structure available, in the worst case over m and x. This is a stronger claim than the arbitrary-synthesizer target selected here; fixed small m can cap the cost through reading the entire string.

cards.title: \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) versus \(\mathrm{BQEXP}\)
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{BQEXP}\)? In promise-problem terms, does every pair \(\Pi=(Y,N)\) of disjoint sets of binary strings that has a polynomial-time quantum verifier with two unentangled polynomial-size proofs also admit a uniform quantum algorithm running in time \(2^{p(n)}\), for some polynomial \(p\), with error at most \(1/3\) on every promised input? The algorithm receives no proofs. The polynomial may depend on \(\Pi\) and its verifier, but not on the individual input of length \(n\).
cards.why: Unentangled quantum proofs add a nonconvex constraint to quantum verification. An exponential-time quantum simulation would place a meaningful algorithmic limit on this model and clarify whether its power can be explained without nondeterministic exponential-time witness search.
cards.status_note: The source explicitly asks this inclusion in January 2026. Primary definitions and the NEXP upper bound were checked together with July 2026 hierarchy and stoquastic results on 2026-09-14. None of those checked results supplies a BQEXP simulation for general QMA(2); this is a bounded literature check.

Liu and Wu’s revised manuscript gives upper bounds for restricted stoquastic unentangled verification; it distinguishes that setting from general QMA(2).

sentences: The question asks whether every problem with two unentangled quantum proofs can be decided in quantum exponential time without proofs.
The verifier is polynomial-time and may process both proofs jointly, but the proofs must initially be a product state.
The deciding algorithm must be uniform and have bounded error on every promised input.
The standard upper bound uses nondeterministic exponential time, which does not give the requested algorithm.
Recent quantified and stoquastic results concern different upper-bound models and leave this inclusion unresolved.

cards.definitions:
A promise problem specifies yes-inputs \(Y\) and no-inputs \(N\); on inputs outside \(Y\cup N\), a deciding algorithm has no correctness requirement but must still obey its resource bound. A qubit has state space \(\mathbb C^2\). A pure state on \(w\) qubits is a unit vector in \(\mathbb C^{2^w}\). Two unentangled proofs have the tensor-product form \(|\psi\rangle\otimes|\phi\rangle\), where each vector describes at most \(w(n)\) qubits for some polynomial \(w\). Arbitrary entanglement within either proof is allowed, but entanglement between the proofs is excluded.

Membership in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) means that one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine, on input \(x\), generates a quantum circuit \(V_x\) of polynomial size. The circuit takes the two proof registers and zero-initialized work qubits, and finally measures an output bit. Write \(a_x(\psi,\phi)\) for its acceptance probability. Its guarantees are \[x\in Y\ \Longrightarrow\ \exists\psi,\phi:\ a_x(\psi,\phi)\ge2/3,\qquad x\in N\ \Longrightarrow\ \forall\psi,\phi:\ a_x(\psi,\phi)\le1/3.\] The two proofs are sent once; there is no later interaction. The same definition results if mixed product states or convex mixtures of product states are permitted, by linearity of acceptance probability. The verifier need not certify that an arbitrarily supplied entangled pair is a product: unentanglement is the proof model's assumption.

Use the fixed finite gate set consisting of Hadamard \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), its inverse, and controlled NOT, acting on named wires. Circuit size counts every gate; every initialized or proof qubit counts toward the relevant qubit bound. Uniform generation outputs the full gate and wire list.

Membership in \(\mathrm{BQEXP}\) means that one deterministic circuit generator, on input \(x\) of length \(n\), runs in at most \(2^{p(n)}\) steps and outputs a circuit with at most \(2^{p(n)}\) gates and qubits, using the same finite gate set. The circuit begins with zero-initialized qubits, receives no proof or advice, and accepts yes-inputs with probability at least \(2/3\) and no-inputs with probability at most \(1/3\). Classical dependence on \(x\) is through the generator. Polynomial overheads in the generator and circuit can be absorbed into \(p\). No oracle or postselection is available. Probability in both models is ordinary quantum measurement probability.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion, or of its negation. Inclusion requires a bounded-error, uniform exponential-time quantum decision procedure for every problem satisfying the stated two-proof verification definition. Separation requires a promise problem in \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\) with no such decision procedure. Simulations only for restricted verifiers, shorter proofs, or a different completeness-soundness gap do not suffice.

context_blocks.text: Classically, two existential witnesses can simply be concatenated. In this quantum model, allowing an arbitrary joint state would remove the product restriction and give the ordinary single-proof model. That restriction is therefore part of the computational resource, rather than an incidental communication detail.

A known upper bound is \(\mathrm{QMA}(2)\subseteq\mathrm{NEXP}\), where \(\mathrm{NEXP}\) allows nondeterministic time \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\). Guessing sufficiently accurate classical descriptions of the two states and verifying them explains this bound. Enumerating all such descriptions is much more expensive, so this does not give a deterministic or quantum exponential-time algorithm.

The 2026 hierarchy result gives a structural upper bound using competing quantifiers over pure quantum states. Its stated containments still end at nondeterministic exponential time. An existential/universal characterization does not itself implement a bounded-error quantum decision procedure.

The July 2026 work obtains exponential-time algorithms for a stoquastic restriction, designed to remove destructive interference. Its verifier restrictions are substantive, so those algorithms do not yield the requested simulation for general quantum verifiers.

cards.title: Strong quantum IOPs with polynomial communication
cards.formal: Does every QMA promise problem admit a constant-round strong quantum interactive oracle proof with a uniform polynomial-time verifier, total prover-message length polynomial in the input length n, total query complexity \(O(1)\), completeness at least \(2/3\), and soundness at most \(1/3\)? The strong access model is defined below. The prover may be computationally unbounded, and soundness quantifies over all prover strategies.
cards.why: The problem isolates the communication price of an extremely limited quantum verifier. A positive result would eliminate the exponential communication in the present strong construction.

progress.text: The general qIOP has polynomial communication but uses a polynomial private quantum resource. The strong construction operates on constantly many qubits but communicates $\exp(\operatorname{poly}(n))$ qubits. Question 1.9 asks for polynomial communication.

references.locator: Definitions 1.1–1.2; Theorems 1.5, 1.7; Question 1.9

cards.review_note: The statement and listed results were individually checked against the cited sources. New proofs were not independently verified. The assessment of importance is editorial.

context_blocks.text: A quantum proof can be much larger than the portion a verifier actually inspects. An interactive oracle proof lets a prover supply such messages over several rounds, with the verifier charged for the qubits it touches. Communication volume and access complexity are therefore different resources.

The strong model requires the verifier to hand each received quantum message back in full and forbids sending an additional quantum message of its own. It still has private workspace. Returning a message does not mean undoing the measurement or channel applied to the queried qubits; the resulting state can be returned.

For example, a protocol might inspect only two qubits from an enormous register. That has constant query complexity but still transmits the enormous register. Conversely, allowing the verifier to retain part of a received message changes the protocol model even if the amount of communication is small.

The existing constructions meet different combinations of the desired bounds: general qIOPs have polynomial communication, while the strong construction has exponential communication. The question asks for polynomial communication in the strong model itself. The constant-round requirement and constant total query budget must hold together.

cards.definitions: In each round the prover supplies a quantum register W. The verifier chooses queried positions through a measurement and applies a quantum channel only to those qubits and its private register; query cost counts accessed message qubits, summed over rounds. It returns the entire W register, may send additional classical information, and sends no additional quantum register. It can retain its own private workspace, but cannot retain any part of a prover-message register. The parties have no initial shared entanglement. Total prover-message length counts the full incoming registers, not only queried qubits. This restates the strong model of Definitions 5.1–5.2 and 5.13–5.15.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a protocol for every QMA promise problem, or prove that at least one QMA promise problem has no protocol meeting all these bounds. Polynomial communication in the weaker general qIOP model does not suffice.

importance.reason: Tests how far succinct interactive verification can extend to quantum proofs with explicit communication restrictions; affects a broad proof-system design space.

cards.title: Oracle separation of BQP from IP
cards.formal: Does there exist a classical Boolean oracle A and a language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* such that \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) but \(\mathrm{L}\notin \mathrm{IP}^{A}\)?
cards.why: Determines whether classical single-prover verification of efficient quantum computations survives arbitrary oracle access. The distinction is sharper than a quantum speedup over direct classical computation: even an unrestricted interactive helper must fail in the separating world.
cards.status_note: Source Problems 7–8 and the April 2026 paper checked; subsequent-work searches through 11 September 2026 located no resolution of the stated oracle question. The MIP containment changes the prover model and is recorded as preprint progress. This is a formulation and source review, not an exhaustive literature or proof audit.

progress.text: Aaronson states the oracle separation as Problem 7 and defines the distinction between IP and its efficient-quantum-honest-prover variant.

The preprint A Relativizing MIP for BQP states containment in classical MIP for every classical oracle and explicitly leaves the single-prover oracle separation open. The introduction also identifies efficient-honest-prover verification as an open issue. This review checked the statements and model, not the full proofs.

references.title: Open Problems Related to Quantum Query Complexity
references.locator: Problem 7

cards.definitions: An oracle is an arbitrary fixed Boolean function \(A:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\); it need not be computable. All languages are subsets of \(\{0,1\}\)*, and n is the input length. A classical oracle call supplies one string z and returns \(A(z)\). Quantum access uses the unitary |\(z,b\rangle \mapsto |z,b\oplus A(z)\rangle\), extended linearly to superpositions of strings of a given length. Query registers and the work required to prepare them count toward the computation bound. No quantum-valued oracle, advice string or promise on inputs is supplied. \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) consists of languages decided by one uniform quantum algorithm with polynomial total running time, oracle calls and qubits. On every yes input it accepts with probability at least \(2/3\), and on every no input with probability at most \(1/3\). One standard machine convention uses Hadamard \(H=(1/\sqrt{2})[[1,1],[1,- 1]], T=diag(1,e^{i\pi /4})\) and CNOT |\(a,b\rangle \mapsto |a,a\oplus b\rangle\) gates, zero-initialized auxiliary qubits, computational-basis measurements and polynomial-time classical control. Circuit descriptions are generated uniformly in polynomial time; there is no nonuniform advice. Probabilities are over measurements and any internal random bits. An \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\) protocol has one classical probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and one prover, exchanging only classical bit strings. The verifier has private fair random bits and classical access to A. Its total computation, random bits, communication and number of rounds are bounded by a polynomial in n, with no predetermined universal degree. Completeness requires one honest prover strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least \(2/3\) on every yes input. Soundness requires acceptance probability at most \(1/3\) on every no input against every prover strategy, including computationally unbounded strategies. The prover knows the common input and oracle but not the verifier’s unrevealed private coins; its messages can depend on its conversation history. There is no trusted setup or shared entanglement. Prover efficiency is unrestricted in \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\). Probabilities include verifier randomness and any randomness or measurements of the prover.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of one oracle A and language L with the stated separation, ruling out every polynomial-time classical interactive proof for L relative to A. Alternatively, prove \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{IP}^{A}\) for every classical Boolean oracle A. A lower bound for a fixed round limit does not by itself exclude all polynomial-round protocols.

context_blocks.title: Can a classical verifier trust a quantum computation?
context_blocks.text: A quantum computer might efficiently decide a language while a classical computer cannot directly reproduce its calculation. An interactive proof lets the verifier ask questions and test the answers. This card asks whether even an all-powerful helper can always make the quantum answer classically checkable when both sides must use a supplied oracle through its query interface.

context_blocks.title: The same function, different query access
context_blocks.text: The quantum computation may query a superposition, whereas the verifier queries one ordinary string at a time. The oracle function itself is identical for both. Some oracle languages are easy for both: for \(\mathrm{L}=\{x:A(x)=1\}\), the verifier simply queries x. The question requires a language whose quantum computation cannot be certified by the stated interaction.

context_blocks.title: Two distinct single-prover questions
context_blocks.text: For every oracle, \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) and \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{IP}^{A}\) by definition. An oracle separation of BQP from unrestricted-prover IP therefore also separates BQP from \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}\). The efficient-honest-prover separation is a weaker demand: an unrestricted prover might still verify that language. The two cards record this implication without identifying the targets.

context_blocks.title: Unbounded cheating is part of the guarantee
context_blocks.text: The prover can lie in any computationally possible way, even with unlimited computation. Restricting only a dishonest prover to efficient strategies would instead describe a computationally sound argument. Cryptographic verification protocols with that guarantee do not establish the information-theoretic IP containment requested here.

context_blocks.title: What the 2026 multiple-prover result changes
context_blocks.text: Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi state \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\subseteq MIP^{A}\) for every classical oracle. MIP permits several separated provers who cannot communicate during the protocol; the stated result uses classical provers without shared entanglement. The source still identifies the single-prover oracle question as open and does not supply a polynomial-time quantum honest prover for its MIP result.

cards.title: Quantum query–space tradeoffs for collisions and distinctness
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal multiplicative constants, the functions \(T_b(n,m,S)\) for \(b\in\{\mathrm{collision},\mathrm{distinctness}\}\): the minimum worst-case number of quantum queries needed by an algorithm with at most \(S\) qubits of total retained memory to solve the specified decision problem with error at most \(1/3\). The input is an oracle for \(f:[n]\to[m]\). In the collision problem, \(n\) is even and \(f\) is promised to be either injective or exactly two-to-one; distinguish these cases. In element distinctness there is no promise; decide whether \(f\) is injective. The full parameter domain is \(m\ge n\ge2\) and \(S\ge4(\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil+\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil)+10\), with integer parameters. This card selects the source's total-memory tradeoff, allowing all retained memory to be quantum; separating classical and quantum memory budgets is a further variant.
cards.why: Quantum collision and distinctness algorithms gain speed while retaining substantial information about queried values. Their optimal time/space tradeoffs would quantify how much memory is necessary for those advantages and develop lower-bound methods for problems whose output contains only one bit.
cards.status_note: Open in the 2021 source. Checked on 2026-09-14: the February 2026 work concerns nested collision finding; the September 2026 preprint gives claimed search bounds under label symmetry and explicitly leaves removal of symmetry open. Neither checked statement settles the unrestricted, worst-case decision tradeoff formulated here. The total-memory convention is explicit.

progress.text: Aaronson lists the two query/space tradeoffs as open, distinguishing them from the already established unrestricted-query complexities.
Hao, Huang and Liu give space-sensitive lower bounds for nested collision finding, addressing a related short-output barrier.

Magniez and Zur post claimed tight search tradeoffs under label symmetry and explicitly retain the unrestricted-algorithm question. These are restricted-model progress, not a resolution of the displayed decision curves.

importance.reason: Characterizes simultaneous time and memory limits for basic quantum collision tasks, beyond query complexity alone.

sentences: The question asks for the optimal quantum query cost of collision testing and element distinctness at every allowed memory budget.
The oracle returns an output symbol, and the algorithm must decide the answer with bounded worst-case error.
All retained storage counts, including classical tables and query registers.
Recent lower bounds concern nested collision tasks or search algorithms restricted by label symmetry.
The target remains matching upper and lower bounds for unrestricted algorithms solving the two decision problems.

cards.definitions:
The notation \([r]\) means \(\{1,\ldots,r\}\). Injective means that distinct inputs have distinct outputs. Exactly two-to-one means that every value in the image has exactly two preimages; unused output values have none. The required output is one bit, not a pair of colliding indices.

Let \(a=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil\) and \(v=\lceil\log_2(m+1)\rceil\). A query maps \(|i,y,z\rangle\) to \(|i,y\mathbin{\oplus}\operatorname{enc}(f(i)),z\rangle\), with \(a\) address qubits, \(v\) answer qubits and a remaining work register. Here \(\operatorname{enc}\) is the length-\(v\) binary encoding and \(\oplus\) is bitwise addition modulo two. For address zero or an address larger than \(n\), use the all-zero answer. One call returns one entire output symbol and costs one query. The address and answer registers are included in \(S\).

An algorithm begins with an input-independent state on at most \(S\) qubits, alternates a fixed finite sequence of input-independent quantum channels with oracle calls, and ends with a two-outcome measurement. A density matrix describes its state. An allowed intervening channel has the form \(\rho\mapsto\sum_j K_j\rho K_j^\dagger\), where the finitely many matrices satisfy \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I\); it maps the retained memory back into the same bounded space. This allows measurement, randomization and resetting memory. Discarded information cannot be retrieved later. Any measurement outcomes, classical work bits, or tables that remain accessible must occupy the counted memory. Input-dependent classical control is therefore also stored in that memory. There is no external input-dependent advice, second oracle, or uncounted read/write storage.

The channels and measurement may depend on \(b,n,m,S\), but not on \(f\). Their descriptions and the input-independent instruction index are not workspace, and no uniformity, gate-count or computation-time restriction is imposed between queries. Arbitrary computation on the stored memory, including coherent access to stored tables, is free. All oracle calls count, including preprocessing and calls on branches later discarded. The finite query budget is worst-case, and correctness must hold on every valid oracle, with probability at least \(2/3\). The stated space floor allows elementary repeated scans, so both minima are finite; no upper limit on \(S\) is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply positive functions \(H_b(n,m,S)\), universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\), and a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that \(cH_b(n,m,S)\le T_b(n,m,S)\le CH_b(n,m,S)\) for both tasks throughout their parameter domains. Both algorithms and matching lower bounds must respect the stated memory budget; an unrecorded increase in space is not allowed. The functions must describe the asymptotic dependence on the parameters, not simply repeat the optimization defining \(T_b\). Bounds for collision search, random inputs, or label-symmetric algorithms alone do not establish the required worst-case decision tradeoffs.

context_blocks.text: Without a restrictive memory budget, the familiar quantum query scales are \(n^{1/3}\) for the collision promise and \(n^{2/3}\) for element distinctness in their standard parameter regimes. Their optimality as query bounds does not determine the memory needed to attain them.

A classical table that can be queried coherently still occupies memory in this formulation. Counting its bits prevents a large external table from making a small-qubit algorithm appear to use little total storage. The separate question of which part of the storage must preserve quantum coherence is not resolved by a total-space bound.

The February 2026 work establishes memory lower bounds for a nested collision task with short output. Its input uses an additional oracle and a different success condition, so its lower bounds are not automatically the tradeoffs for either decision problem defined here.

The September 2026 preprint claims tight bounds for collision search and element-distinctness search under a label-symmetry restriction. Its Section 1.4 explicitly leaves removal of that restriction open. Permuting labels to symmetrize an arbitrary algorithm may require additional memory, which prevents treating symmetry as free.
