cards.title: Constant-round quantum refereed games versus \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\)
cards.formal: Does \(\mathrm{QRG}_{\mathrm{const}}\subseteq\mathrm{PSPACE}\)? For every promise problem \(\Pi=(Y,N)\) admitting a quantum refereed game with a uniform polynomial-time verifier, two competing provers and some fixed constant \(k\) of interaction cycles, must there be a deterministic algorithm deciding \(\Pi\) using polynomial space? For \(x\in Y\), a yes-prover must have a strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least \(2/3\) against every no-prover strategy. For \(x\in N\), a no-prover must have a strategy that makes it reject with probability at least \(2/3\) against every yes-prover strategy. The constant \(k\) and the polynomial bounds may depend on the problem and verifier, but not on input length.
cards.why: These games combine efficient quantum verification with competition between two powerful provers who have different information. Locating constant-length games would clarify whether repeated alternation of private interaction can increase computational power beyond polynomial space, even when only a few exchanges are allowed.
cards.status_note: The July 2026 source asks the general constant-round question. The primary game definitions, polynomial-length EXP characterization and bounded-turn PSPACE results were checked on 2026-09-14, with a bounded later-work search. The one-switch/DQIP result does not settle arbitrary constant interleaving, and no full resolution was identified.

Gutoski and Watrous characterize polynomial-length quantum refereed games by EXP.
Gutoski and Wu prove DQIP = QRG(2) = PSPACE for their specified one-switch interaction pattern and leave more general bounded-turn games outside that characterization.
The source problem list reiterates the question for a general constant number of rounds.

sentences: A quantum refereed game has two competing provers trying to make an efficient verifier accept or reject.
The provers exchange private quantum messages with the verifier and may keep private memory.
The question asks whether every game with a constant number of interaction cycles can be simulated in deterministic polynomial space.
Polynomial-space simulations are known for specific patterns in which interaction switches from one prover to the other only once.
Polynomially many general rounds capture exponential time, leaving the full constant-round boundary open.

cards.definitions:
A promise problem is a pair of disjoint sets \(Y,N\subseteq\{0,1\}^{*}\); no answer is prescribed outside their union. Both provers know the classical input \(x\) and the verifier's complete specification. The yes-prover seeks acceptance and the no-prover seeks rejection. They cannot communicate directly and do not initially share an entangled state or correlated private randomness. Each may retain private quantum memory throughout the interaction, use randomness, and perform arbitrary finite-dimensional quantum operations without a time or memory bound.

The verifier is generated from \(x\), of length \(n\), by one deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine. Its total gate count, workspace, and total communicated qubits are polynomial in \(n\). It starts with zero-initialized registers. In each of at most \(k\) cycles, it applies a quantum circuit, sends one message register privately to each prover, and receives both response registers. Each prover acts only on its current message and its own retained private memory. The verifier then proceeds to the next cycle or its final two-outcome measurement. Messages to the two provers may be entangled through the verifier's preparation; this is part of the specified protocol. Empty messages are allowed. Sequential exchanges can be scheduled in separate cycles, so allowing every fixed \(k\) includes any constant-length message pattern. The verifier never gives a prover access to the other prover's private channel unless its own prescribed operations deliberately convey information from it.

Use a fixed universal finite gate set: Hadamard maps \(|0\rangle\) to \((|0\rangle+|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\) and \(|1\rangle\) to \((|0\rangle-|1\rangle)/\sqrt2\); \(T\) multiplies \(|1\rangle\) by \(e^{i\pi/4}\) and fixes \(|0\rangle\); include \(T^{-1}\) and controlled NOT. The verifier's measurements, randomness and adaptive choices may be implemented coherently with polynomially many ancillary qubits. Prover operations are unrestricted quantum channels, expressible as \(\rho\mapsto\sum_j K_j\rho K_j^\dagger\) with \(\sum_j K_j^\dagger K_j=I\), on their message and private registers. Initial private states can be prepared by those channels. All winning probabilities are over the resulting quantum measurement outcomes and private randomization. Each winning strategy may depend on \(x\), but must work against every opposing strategy on that input.

The class \(\mathrm{PSPACE}\) consists here of promise problems decided by a deterministic multitape Turing machine with a read-only input tape and at most \(C(n+1)^r\) work-tape cells for fixed constants \(C,r\). It must halt on all inputs and give the correct answer on \(Y\cup N\). It has no oracle or advice. The simulator need only decide which side can force a win; it need not output either prover's strategy.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the inclusion, or of its negation. An inclusion proof must cover every fixed constant number of interaction cycles and every polynomial-time uniform verifier in the stated private-message model. A negative proof must exhibit a promise problem in this class with no deterministic polynomial-space decision algorithm. An exponential-time simulation, or a polynomial-space simulation only for one exchange pattern, does not suffice.

context_blocks.text: The winning-strategy requirements contain opposite quantifier orders on yes- and no-inputs. A prover must force its preferred outcome against all opposing strategies. This is different from two cooperating proof providers or a verifier receiving two unentangled existential witnesses.

Gutoski and Wu prove a polynomial-space simulation when all interaction with one prover is completed before interaction with the other begins. This includes their class QRG(2). Their result does not cover arbitrary repeated interleaving of the two private conversations.

Different papers count individual messages, turns and full send/receive rounds differently. This card fixes a complete interaction cycle explicitly. Since it asks about every constant cycle count, a constant change of counting convention does not change its scope.

With polynomially many messages, quantum refereed games capture \(\mathrm{EXP}\), deterministic time \(2^{\mathrm{poly}(n)}\). This gives an upper bound for constant-length games, but it does not supply a polynomial-space simulation. The constant-length question remains meaningful even for classical messages.

cards.title: Black-box unitary synthesis
cards.formal: Is there one polynomial-time uniform family of polynomial-size quantum oracle circuits \(\{A_n\}_{n\ge1}\) such that, for every \(n\)-qubit unitary matrix \(U\), some Boolean function \(f_U:\{0,1\}^{m(n)}\to\{0,1\}\) makes the channel implemented by \(A_n^{f_U}\) approximate \(\rho\mapsto U\rho U^\dagger\) within diamond distance \(1/10\)? The oracle input length \(m(n)\), total number of qubits, number of ordinary gates, and number of oracle calls must all be bounded by one fixed polynomial in \(n\). The circuit family is chosen before \(U\); only the Boolean oracle may depend on \(U\). This is the fixed-constant-error version of black-box unitary synthesis.
cards.why: The question asks whether implementing arbitrary quantum transformations can be reduced efficiently to evaluating Boolean functions. A negative answer would establish a black-box obstruction to explaining all quantum transformation complexity through classical function computation, a central issue for unitary complexity and quantum cryptography.
cards.status_note: The source question is retained in Rosenthal’s May 2026 revision and the July 2026 Dong–Lombardi–Ma paper. Checked on 2026-09-14. Their bounds concern exponential-time upper bounds or restricted-query lower bounds, not a resolution of the displayed general polynomial-time, constant-diamond-error formulation.

sentences: The problem asks whether every quantum unitary can be implemented efficiently using an appropriately chosen Boolean oracle.
One fixed circuit family must work for all unitaries, with the desired unitary encoded only in the oracle.
The implementation must work on arbitrary inputs, including states entangled with an untouched reference.
Both total computation and coherent oracle access must remain polynomial in the number of input qubits.
Known exponential-time implementations and restricted-query lower bounds leave the general question unresolved.

cards.definitions:
An \(n\)-qubit system has state space \(\mathbb C^{2^n}\). A unitary matrix satisfies \(U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I\), where \(\dagger\) denotes conjugate transpose. A density matrix is a positive semidefinite matrix with trace one and describes a possibly mixed quantum state.

Each circuit receives an arbitrary \(n\)-qubit input, initializes all additional qubits to zero, and outputs a specified \(n\)-qubit register. Other registers are discarded, inducing a quantum channel \(\Phi_{A_n^{f_U}}\). The ordinary gate set is Hadamard \(H=2^{-1/2}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), the phase gate \(T=\operatorname{diag}(1,e^{i\pi/4})\), its inverse, and controlled NOT. Gates may act on any named wires. One oracle call applies \(|z,b\rangle\mapsto|z,b\mathbin{\oplus}f_U(z)\rangle\) to the address and answer registers, including on superpositions; \(\oplus\) is addition modulo two. All calls use the same fixed Boolean function. Oracle inputs and answer registers count toward the qubit bound. The oracle's own computation is uncharged, but every ordinary gate and each oracle call counts toward circuit size. General adaptive quantum computation is allowed through its equivalent coherent circuit representation with polynomially many ancillas.

Uniformity means that a single deterministic Turing machine, on input \(1^n\), outputs the complete gate and wire list in time polynomial in \(n\). It receives no description of \(U\). The oracle function may be arbitrary, and no efficient procedure for computing it or deriving it from \(U\) is required. No additional quantum advice, input-dependent initial ancilla, postselection, or other oracle is available.

For channels with \(n\)-qubit input and output, define their diamond distance by \[D_\diamond(\Phi,\Psi)=\tfrac12\sup_{\rho}\|((\Phi-\Psi)\otimes\operatorname{id}_R)(\rho)\|_1,\] where \(R\) is an untouched \(n\)-qubit reference register and the supremum ranges over density matrices on input and reference together. The trace norm is \(\|M\|_1=\operatorname{Tr}\sqrt{M^\dagger M}\). The desired inequality holds for every input, including one entangled with the reference. The constant \(1/10\) is the allowed channel-approximation error, not an acceptance-probability or heralded-success condition. Global phases of \(U\) are irrelevant to its channel.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof that such a universal efficient oracle-circuit family exists, or a proof of its negation. A positive proof must supply the uniform circuit family and show the existence of a suitable Boolean oracle for every unitary while meeting all resource and diamond-distance bounds. A negative proof must rule out polynomially many sequential oracle calls with polynomial total computation. A lower bound restricted to one query, parallel queries, or a prescribed oracle encoding does not suffice.

context_blocks.text: Preparing a chosen state starts from a known blank input. Unitary synthesis must act correctly on an unknown state and preserve its coherent relationships with any external system. Preparing each output column of a matrix separately does not by itself implement the unitary on an arbitrary superposition.

The Boolean oracle is allowed to encode the desired transformation without a computational restriction. The difficulty lies in extracting and using that information through short coherent queries within polynomial total computation. Counting the number of possible ordinary circuits therefore does not alone refute this model.

Rosenthal gives an oracle implementation using time \(\widetilde O(2^{n/2})\), with exponentially small approximation error. This improves a more direct exponential construction but remains far above polynomial time. His matching lower bound is for a particular column-construction interface, not every possible Boolean oracle.

Lombardi, Ma and Wright rule out general one-query synthesis and the corresponding polynomial parallel-query setting with efficient resources. The July 2026 follow-up studies one-query separations for more structured unitary families. These results leave unrestricted polynomially many sequential queries as a different question.

cards.title: Oracle separation of BQP from efficient-prover interactive proofs
cards.formal: Does there exist a classical Boolean oracle A and a language \(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* such that \(\mathrm{L}\in \mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) but \(\mathrm{L}\notin \mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\), where \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\) requires a polynomial-time quantum honest prover and classical interaction with a polynomial-time classical verifier?
cards.why: Distinguishes the existence of a classical interactive proof from the ability of an efficient quantum device to carry out its honest strategy. It tests whether verification can match the computational resources of the device while retaining soundness against all cheating provers.

The verifier and honest prover access the same classical oracle, with quantum queries available only to the quantum computation.

cards.definitions: An oracle is an arbitrary fixed Boolean function \(A:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\); it need not be computable. All languages are subsets of \(\{0,1\}\)*, and n is the input length. A classical oracle call supplies one string z and returns \(A(z)\). Quantum access uses the unitary |\(z,b\rangle \mapsto |z,b\oplus A(z)\rangle\), extended linearly to superpositions of strings of a given length. Query registers and the work required to prepare them count toward the computation bound. No quantum-valued oracle, advice string or promise on inputs is supplied. \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) consists of languages decided by one uniform quantum algorithm with polynomial total running time, oracle calls and qubits. On every yes input it accepts with probability at least \(2/3\), and on every no input with probability at most \(1/3\). One standard machine convention uses Hadamard \(H=(1/\sqrt{2})[[1,1],[1,- 1]], T=diag(1,e^{i\pi /4})\) and CNOT |\(a,b\rangle \mapsto |a,a\oplus b\rangle\) gates, zero-initialized auxiliary qubits, computational-basis measurements and polynomial-time classical control. Circuit descriptions are generated uniformly in polynomial time; there is no nonuniform advice. Probabilities are over measurements and any internal random bits. An \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\) protocol has one classical probabilistic polynomial-time verifier and one prover, exchanging only classical bit strings. The verifier has private fair random bits and classical access to A. Its total computation, random bits, communication and number of rounds are bounded by a polynomial in n, with no predetermined universal degree. Completeness requires one honest prover strategy that makes the verifier accept with probability at least \(2/3\) on every yes input. Soundness requires acceptance probability at most \(1/3\) on every no input against every prover strategy, including computationally unbounded strategies. The prover knows the common input and oracle but not the verifier’s unrevealed private coins; its messages can depend on its conversation history. There is no trusted setup or shared entanglement. Prover efficiency is unrestricted in \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\). Probabilities include verifier randomness and any randomness or measurements of the prover. \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\) is the subclass of \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) whose languages admit such an \(\mathrm{IP}^{A}\) protocol with one uniform quantum polynomial-time oracle algorithm as the honest prover. Its total local work and oracle queries across all rounds are polynomial in n, under the same quantum access convention as \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\). Only the honest prover is restricted: soundness still quantifies over all computationally unbounded cheating strategies. Polynomial bounds and machines may depend on A and the language, but must work for all input lengths; they cannot depend on the particular input through advice.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the existence of one oracle A and \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) language L for which no classical interactive proof has an honest quantum polynomial-time oracle prover. Alternatively, prove \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}=\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\) for every classical Boolean oracle A. All negative instances must rule out arbitrary polynomial bounds on rounds and honest-prover work, and the positive alternative must retain soundness against unbounded cheating provers.

context_blocks.title: Can a classical verifier trust a quantum computation?
context_blocks.text: A proof of a quantum answer is useful for verification by a classical computer only if the honest quantum device can actually provide it. An interactive proof with an unrestricted prover does not guarantee this. This card asks whether some oracle world separates efficient quantum computation from verification with an efficient quantum honest prover.

context_blocks.title: The same function, different query access
context_blocks.text: The quantum computation may query a superposition, whereas the verifier queries one ordinary string at a time. The oracle function itself is identical for both. Some oracle languages are easy for both: for \(\mathrm{L}=\{x:A(x)=1\}\), the verifier simply queries x. The question requires a language whose quantum computation cannot be certified by the stated interaction.

context_blocks.title: Two distinct single-prover questions
context_blocks.text: For every oracle, \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}^{A}\) and \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}^{A}\subseteq \mathrm{IP}^{A}\) by definition. An oracle separation of BQP from unrestricted-prover IP therefore also separates BQP from \(\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{BQP}}\). The efficient-honest-prover separation is a weaker demand: an unrestricted prover might still verify that language. The two cards record this implication without identifying the targets.

context_blocks.title: Unbounded cheating is part of the guarantee
context_blocks.text: The prover can lie in any computationally possible way, even with unlimited computation. Restricting only a dishonest prover to efficient strategies would instead describe a computationally sound argument. Cryptographic verification protocols with that guarantee do not establish the information-theoretic IP containment requested here.

context_blocks.title: What the 2026 multiple-prover result changes
context_blocks.text: Aaronson, Natarajan, Tal and Villányi state \(\mathrm{BQP}^{A}\subseteq MIP^{A}\) for every classical oracle. MIP permits several separated provers who cannot communicate during the protocol; the stated result uses classical provers without shared entanglement. The source still identifies the single-prover oracle question as open and does not supply a polynomial-time quantum honest prover for its MIP result.

cards.title: Exact quantum fanout in constant depth with unrestricted circuit size
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer d such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), some finite QAC circuit of depth at most d exactly implements FANOUT\(_{n}\) on one control qubit and n target qubits, allowing arbitrarily many clean ancillas and no size bound?
cards.why: Determines whether unbounded-arity quantum AND operations and one-qubit gates can express coherent fanout in bounded depth at any finite size. It isolates a basic limitation of shallow unitary computation that cannot be explained solely by insufficient circuit width.

cards.definitions: For bits \(s,x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\in \{0,1\}\), FANOUT\(_{n}|s,x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\rangle =|s,s\oplus x_{1},\ldots ,s\oplus x_{n}\rangle\), extended linearly to all states; ⊕ is addition modulo two. A permitted circuit acts on \(n+1+a(n)\) qubits for some finite \(a(n)\ge 0\). Its gates are arbitrary one-qubit unitary matrices over \(\mathbb{C}\) and generalized Toffoli gates: for any \(k\ge 1\) distinct controls and a distinct target, |\(z_{1},\ldots ,z_{k},t\rangle\) maps to |\(z_{1},\ldots ,z_{k},t\oplus (z_{1}\cdots z_{k})\rangle\). Each layer contains gates on disjoint sets of qubits, and depth is the number of layers. Gates may connect any qubits; fanout gates, measurements, postselection and classical feed-forward are not additional primitives. Exact implementation means that for some global phase \(e^{i\varphi _{n}}\), independent of the input state \(\psi , C_{n}(|\psi \rangle \otimes |0\rangle ^{\otimes}a(n))=e^{i\varphi _{n}}\)(FANOUT\(_{n}|\psi \rangle\))⊗|\(0\rangle ^{\otimes}a(n)\) for every unit vector \(\psi\) in \((\mathbb{C} ^{2})^{\otimes}(n+1)\). The ancillas must return to zero, as in the source’s implementation definition. Gate count, ancilla count and gate arities may grow arbitrarily with n but must be finite at each n. The family is nonuniform: there is no required circuit-generation algorithm or finite gate alphabet. The one depth bound d must work for all n. QAC0 usually adds a polynomial-size bound; this question explicitly drops it.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct an exact clean-ancilla implementation with a depth bound independent of n, or prove that no such bound exists even when size, ancilla count and Toffoli arity are unrestricted. An approximation with arbitrarily small nonzero error, a lower bound only for polynomial-size circuits, or a bound for one fixed small depth does not settle this formulation.

context_blocks.title: Fanout is a coherent controlled operation
context_blocks.text: On a basis input, the control flips every target when it is one and leaves them unchanged when it is zero. The same circuit must act correctly on superpositions, including inputs entangled with other systems. Agreement only on measured classical outputs would be weaker.

context_blocks.title: This operation does not clone an arbitrary quantum state
context_blocks.text: For example, applying two-target fanout to |+⟩|\(00\rangle\) yields \((|000\rangle +|111\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\). It does not yield three independent copies of |+⟩. The target is therefore compatible with the distinction between coherent basis fanout and cloning.

context_blocks.title: Only depth is restricted
context_blocks.text: A Toffoli gate may inspect many controls in one layer, but a qubit cannot participate in several gates in that same layer. The question permits enormous circuits and arbitrarily many zero-initialized ancillas. A negative answer would therefore be a structural limitation of constant depth, beyond ordinary polynomial-size lower bounds.

context_blocks.title: Exactness remains separate from approximation

Its known parity/fanout equivalence and later 2026 equivalence results connect the task to other shallow quantum operations, but do not constitute the exact implementation or impossibility theorem requested here.

cards.title: Quantum games PCP with efficient honest provers and short messages
cards.formal: Does every promise problem \(\mathrm{L}=(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}},\mathrm{L}_{no})\) in QMA admit a one-round entangled multiprover proof with a uniform classical polynomial-time verifier, a constant number r of provers and polylogarithmic-length classical questions and answers, such that: \((i)\) on every \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some polynomial-size quantum witness permits uniform quantum polynomial-time preparation and local execution of an honest strategy accepted with probability at least \(2/3\); and \((ii)\) on every \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{no}\), every entangled strategy, with no computational bound on the dishonest provers, is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\)?
cards.why: Would connect efficient verification of quantum witnesses to succinct classical interaction with entangled provers. The honest-prover requirement preserves the computational meaning of the witness, which unrestricted entangled proof-system containments do not ensure.
cards.status_note: The full CCC 2026 question and the 2024 status note were checked, with subsequent searches through 11 September 2026. No matching efficient-prover protocol or impossibility theorem was located. The stronger logarithmic-question/constant-answer conjecture is distinguished explicitly.

cards.definitions: Write \(n=|x|\). QMA consists of promise problems whose YES instances have polynomial-qubit quantum witnesses accepted by a uniform polynomial-time quantum verifier with probability at least \(2/3\), while every witness on a NO instance is accepted with probability at most \(1/3\). In the requested game, a classical verifier samples correlated questions, sends one to each of r noncommunicating provers, receives one classical answer from each, and decides acceptance in polynomial time. The provers may share entanglement prepared before the questions arrive. For each L, r and an exponent a are fixed independently of n, and every individual message has at most \(O((\log (n+2))^{a})\) bits. Honest efficiency includes a uniform quantum polynomial-time setup algorithm which, given x and polynomially many copies of a polynomial-qubit state \(\psi _{x}\), prepares the shared state, followed by uniform quantum polynomial-time local response algorithms. The state \(\psi _{x}\) is an existential witness depending on x, not a supplied circuit for preparing it. Soundness quantifies over arbitrary local quantum strategies with arbitrary finite-dimensional shared entanglement; only communication after separation is forbidden. There is no promise on inputs outside \(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}}\cup \mathrm{L}_{no}\). The fixed gap can be amplified by a constant number of repetitions without changing the polylogarithmic communication scale. The question imposes no logarithmic bound on the verifier’s total random bits and no additional cryptographic assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct the stated protocol for every QMA promise problem, proving both witness-assisted honest efficiency and soundness against unrestricted entangled provers; or prove that at least one QMA promise problem has no such protocol. A protocol with polynomial-length answers, or one whose honest entanglement cannot be prepared efficiently from a polynomial witness, does not meet this target.

cards.definitions: A promise problem is a pair \((\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}},\mathrm{L}_{no})\) of disjoint sets of finite binary strings, with no required answer outside their union. Membership in \(StoqMA(a,b)\) means there is a deterministic polynomial-time procedure which, given x of length n, produces a verification circuit \(V_{x}\) on \(m(n)+r(n)+s(n)\) qubits, all counts polynomially bounded in n. Its initial state is |\(w\rangle \otimes |0\rangle ^{\otimes r}\otimes |+\rangle ^{\otimes s}\), where |+⟩=\((|0\rangle +|1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\) and the m-qubit witness has norm one. The circuit uses only classical reversible gates: NOT flips a bit, CNOT flips its target if its control is one, and Toffoli flips its target if both controls are one. These gates act linearly on computational-basis states. There are no intermediate measurements or arbitrary quantum gates. At the end a designated output qubit is measured in the \(\{|+\rangle ,|- \rangle\}\) basis, with |−⟩=\((|0\rangle - |1\rangle )/\sqrt{2}\), and outcome + means acceptance. Its acceptance probability is the squared norm after projection onto |+⟩ on that qubit. If \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{yes}}\), some witness with real nonnegative computational-basis amplitudes must be accepted with probability at least \(a(n)\). If \(x\in \mathrm{L}_{no}\), every normalized witness, including arbitrary complex amplitudes, must be accepted with probability at most \(b(n)\). The source proves that a maximizing witness can be chosen nonnegative. Efficient threshold computability is understood in the standard precision sense: their values can be approximated within \(2^{- t}\) in time polynomial in \(n+t\). The inverse-polynomial gap permits this conventional representation. Class containment quantifies over promise problems and asserts existence of new uniform verifiers; it does not demand a blackbox compiler acting on an arbitrary verifier description. Polynomial bounds of the new verifier may depend on the original verifier, q and \(\ell\). Soundness approaches \(1/2\) from above, not zero; the requested improvement is relative to the stoquastic acceptance baseline.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the containment for every admissible a,b and \(\ell\), or refute this universally quantified amplification statement. A positive answer must achieve both exponentially small completeness error and exponentially small excess soundness above \(1/2\) while retaining the allowed gates, initial ancillas and final measurement. Soundness-only repetition, perfect-completeness special cases, extra destructive-interference gates, or additional unentangled provers do not establish the claim.

sentences: A fixed two-qubit interaction generates circuits by evolving selected ordered pairs for specified times.
Every circuit begins in a computational-basis state and ends with computational-basis measurement.

cards.definitions: The matrix \(H=H^*\) is fixed, not part of a circuit input. Its entries are algebraic complex numbers, specified by finite integer-polynomial and isolating-region descriptions that may be hardcoded into an algorithm depending on \(H\). A circuit has \(N\ge1\) qubits initialized to an explicitly supplied computational-basis string \(b\in\{0,1\}^N\). Each gate chooses an ordered pair of distinct qubits and applies \(\exp(-itH)\) on that pair for a signed rational time \(t\); negative times give exact inverse evolution. There are no free single-qubit gates or intermediate measurements. At the end all qubits are measured in the computational basis, defining a probability distribution \(p_C\) on \(\{0,1\}^N\). The input explicitly lists the initial bits, gate sequence, ordered wire indices and rational numerators and positive denominators in binary. It also includes a unary integer \(B\ge1\) with \(|t|\le B\) for every gate. Let \(L\) be the full bit encoding length. This charges enough description length for polynomial physical evolution time, as required by the source model. The simulation branch requires a single uniform randomized Turing machine for this fixed \(H\), taking \(C\) and a binary rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), that halts on every random tape within a fixed polynomial in \(L+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)\) and outputs a string with distribution \(s_C\) satisfying \(\tfrac12\sum_z|s_C(z)-p_C(z)|\le\varepsilon\). It uses independent fair coins and no oracle or advice. Define \(\operatorname{Post}(H)\) as follows. For a language \(K\subseteq\{0,1\}^*\), a uniform deterministic polynomial-time compiler maps each input \(x\) to such a circuit \(C_x\), a designated output bit, and a disjoint list of postselection bits with prescribed values. There is a polynomial \(p\) such that the prescribed event has probability at least \(2^{-p(|x|)}\) on every input. Conditional on it, the output is 1 with probability at least \(2/3\) for \(x\in K\) and at most \(1/3\) otherwise. Circuit descriptions, including the unary time bound, have polynomial length in \(|x|\). The postselection list and values may depend on the input through the compiler. PP consists of languages for which a uniform polynomial-time fair-coin Turing machine accepts with probability strictly greater than \(1/2\) on members and at most \(1/2\) on nonmembers. The second branch is the source’s postselected-computation criterion expressed via PP; the algebraic-entry, accuracy and exponentially bounded postselection conventions are explicit editorial choices. The alternatives need not be disjoint. No commutativity promise is imposed on \(H\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a Lean proof of the disjunction for every allowed fixed interaction, or a Lean counterexample interaction for which both branches fail. The proof must use the supplied finite-precision sampling and uniform postselection conventions. A classification with free local gates, arbitrary analog reductions, a commutativity promise or a different sampling error does not automatically settle this variant.

cards.title: Martin’s conjecture
cards.formal: Assume \(ZF+DC+AD\). Do both assertions hold? \((I)\) Every Turing-invariant function \(f:2^{\omega}\to 2^{\omega}\) is either constant in Turing degree on a cone or satisfies \(x\le _{T} f(x)\) on a cone. \((II)\) Cone-wise Turing reducibility prewellorders all such functions that are above the identity on a cone, and the pointwise jump \(f'\) has rank exactly \(\operatorname{rank}(f)+1\) in this prewellorder.
cards.definitions: A real \(x\in 2^{\omega}\) is an infinite binary sequence, identified with a subset of the natural numbers. Write \(x\le _{T} y\) if an oracle Turing machine with oracle y computes x, and \(x\equiv _{T} y\) for mutual reducibility. A function f is Turing-invariant when \(x\equiv _{T} y\) implies \(f(x)\equiv _{T} f(y)\). A cone above a real a is \(\{x:a\le _{T} x\}\). Being constant on a cone means \(\exists a,b \forall x\ge _{T} a, f(x)\equiv _{T} b\); the output sequences need not be literally equal. Define \(f\le _{M} g\) by \(\exists a \forall x\ge _{T} a, f(x)\le _{T} g(x)\), and \(f\equiv _{M} g\) by mutual \(\le _{M}\). Let F be the set of all Turing-invariant f for which \(id\le _{M} f\), where \(id(x)=x\). The prewellorder assertion says that \(\le _{M}\) is total on F and its quotient by ≡_M is well-ordered. The rank of f is the ordinal order type of the quotient classes strictly preceding \([f]\). The jump of a real y is \(y'\)={e: the e-th oracle program with oracle y halts on input e}; \(f' (x)=f(x)'\). ZF is Zermelo–Fraenkel set theory without the axiom of choice. DC is dependent choice: every serial binary relation on a nonempty set admits an infinite successive chain. AD says every infinite game in which two players alternately choose natural numbers, with an arbitrary specified set of winning sequences, is determined. Functions are not assumed computable, Borel, order-preserving, or uniformly Turing-invariant. Cone bases may depend on the functions being compared.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central structural problem in computability theory: whether invariance alone, under determinacy, forces nontrivial operations on computational degrees into a well-ordered hierarchy. It connects relative computability, definability, descriptive set theory, and analogies with hierarchies of proof-theoretic strength.

importance.reason: A flagship conjecture about the global structure of Turing degrees and the classification of invariant computational operations.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in Walsh’s March 2026 survey; checked through 10 September 2026. The saved draft’s already-settled regressive subcase has been replaced by the full quantified Part I, together with Part II. Determinacy, degree-wise constancy, and restrictions in the partial results are stated explicitly.

context_blocks.text: The Turing degrees form a complicated partial order, with many incomparable and specially constructed degrees. Yet operations arising naturally by relativizing mathematical definitions often produce a much more organized hierarchy. Martin’s conjecture attempts to make that phenomenon precise through invariance under Turing equivalence and comparison on cones, rather than through an undefined requirement that a construction be “natural.”

The two parts have different jobs. Part I rules out a function that remains nonconstant on every cone but never uniformly reaches the input degree on any cone. Part II concerns functions already above the identity. It asserts comparability and well-foundedness of their cone-equivalence classes, and says that taking an oracle halting problem moves exactly one level up, leaving no intervening class.

Cone-wise comparison ignores behaviour below a fixed computational base. This is meaningful under determinacy: every Turing-invariant set either contains a cone or is disjoint from one, giving Martin’s zero-one measure on degree-invariant sets. Thus “almost everywhere” in the literature means on a cone, not outside a null set for ordinary Lebesgue measure on binary sequences.

Restricting to functions below the identity gives a strictly narrower case with a known theorem: Slaman and Steel show that a Turing-invariant function satisfying \(f(x)\le _{T} x\) on a cone must be constant there or equivalent to the identity on a smaller cone. The unresolved Part I quantifies over all invariant functions, including ones not initially comparable with the identity.

Uniform invariance is another substantial restriction. It requires a single map that turns indices witnessing \(x\equiv _{T} y\) into indices witnessing \(f(x)\equiv _{T} f(y)\), independently of the actual reals. Steel and Slaman–Steel establish the conjecture for this subclass. Merely preserving equivalence classes, as the question requires, does not supply that uniform map.

Lutz and Siskind prove Part I for all order-preserving functions and more generally for measure-preserving invariant functions. Here measure-preserving means that for every fixed degree a there is a cone on which \(f(x)\) computes a. Their theorem supplies major new cases.
The March 2026 survey by Walsh still presents the full conjecture as open and keeps the Borel restriction on the earlier Part II result for order-preserving functions.

cards.title: Kolmogorov–Loveland randomness versus Martin-Löf randomness
cards.formal: Is every Kolmogorov–Loveland random infinite binary sequence Martin-Löf random with respect to the fair-coin product measure?
cards.definitions: Work in Cantor space \(2^{N}\), with coordinates numbered \(0,1,\ldots\) and fair-coin product measure \(\mu\). For a finite binary string \(\sigma\), the cylinder \([\sigma ]\)={\(X:\sigma\) is a prefix of X} has measure \(2^{- |\sigma |}\). A Martin-Löf test is a sequence \((U_{k})_{k\ge 1}\) of open sets obtained by one algorithm enumerating pairs \((k,\sigma )\), with \(U_{k}\) equal to the union of its enumerated cylinders for index k and \(\mu (U_{k})\le 2^{- k}\). A sequence X is Martin-Löf random if for every such test \(X\notin \bigcap _{k} U_{k}\). A Kolmogorov–Loveland betting strategy starts with capital 1. From the finite history h of bits already revealed, a partial computable procedure outputs a previously unqueried coordinate j and a rational multiplier \(q\in [0,2]\), before seeing \(X(j)\). The selected coordinates can be reconstructed from the earlier history and the same procedure; no coordinate may be selected twice along any run. After \(X(j)\) is revealed, the capital is multiplied by q if the bit is 0 and by \(2- q\) if it is 1, and that bit is appended to h. Thus each bet preserves expected capital under a fresh unbiased bit and cannot create debt. \(q=1\) allows reading a bit without risking capital. The next coordinate may depend on all revealed values and need not exceed previous coordinates. If the procedure fails to produce its next action, no further capital is earned. There are no oracle, running-time or space allowances beyond ordinary partial computability. A strategy succeeds on X if its capital at completed bets has unbounded supremum. X is Kolmogorov–Loveland random if every such strategy has bounded capital on X; the bound may depend on both X and the strategy. Rational multipliers suffice for the standard notion, and allowing partial rather than total computable strategies does not change the resulting class.

cards.status_note: The revised 2025 primary paper and its journal version explicitly retain KLR=MLR as a major open problem. Its finite-family/open-set obstruction is not a separating infinite sequence. No later resolution found through 11 September 2026. The formulation fixes fair-coin measure, fresh adaptive coordinates, rational fair bets, partial computability and unbounded-capital success.

context_blocks.text: These are two ways to say that an individual infinite sequence behaves randomly. Martin-Löf tests describe effectively recognizable events of arbitrarily small probability, and a sequence is nonrandom if one test catches it at every level. The betting definition instead asks whether an algorithm can turn knowledge of selected bits into unbounded profit. It measures mathematical unpredictability of a whole sequence, rather than a statistical confidence score assigned to a finite data sample.

The betting order is adaptive. A strategy may inspect a faraway coordinate before deciding which earlier, still unseen coordinate to bet on. It may also read a coordinate with a zero wager to gather information. It cannot bet on a bit already revealed, since that would permit guaranteed profit even from a fair-coin sequence. Its choice of the next position must be computed using only the information it has actually observed.

The known implication from Martin-Löf randomness follows from the fairness of the bets. For a fixed strategy starting with capital one, the set of sequences on which capital ever reaches a threshold R has measure at most \(1/R\). Reaching a threshold is witnessed after finitely many completed actions and can be effectively enumerated. Taking increasing thresholds produces a Martin-Löf test covering the sequences on which this strategy succeeds. The unresolved direction would convert every effective failure of randomness into success of some permitted gambler.

Choosing the query order in advance is insufficient. Kastermans and Lempp show that randomness against computable injective query orders is weaker than Martin-Löf randomness; they also establish the separation for computable permutation orders. The full Kolmogorov–Loveland definition permits choices that depend on observed bit values. Consequently their separating sequences do not establish the separation requested here.

Merkle, Miller, Nies, Reimann and Stephan prove that Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequences have arbitrarily dense subsequences that are Martin-Löf random. A key splitting result says that when a computable set of coordinates and its complement are both infinite, at least one of the two resulting subsequences is Martin-Löf random. This places the notion close to Martin-Löf randomness, but the randomness of a subsequence does not by itself imply randomness of the original interleaving.

Generalized betting games use a different query model. Generalized betting games may split a current set of possible sequences into computably described pieces, instead of querying exactly one fresh bit. Petrović’s 2021 paper gives a pair of strategies in a generalized half-betting model that together succeed on every non-Martin-Löf-random sequence. The greater freedom of the query is part of that theorem, so it does not directly give two Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies.

Petrović’s 2025 result identifies a limitation of a method used for those more flexible games. Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies do not admit the same finite-family guarantee of uniformly forcing large capital on every sequence in a sufficiently small effective open set. The paper constructs small open sets containing sequences on which the relevant capital bounds are not exceeded. This is a barrier to that style of quantitative coverage argument.

The remaining quantifier matters: finding a suitable sequence inside each of arbitrarily small open sets need not produce one sequence lying in every level of a single Martin-Löf test. Likewise, excluding one fixed finite family of gamblers does not exclude a strategy chosen separately for each nonrandom sequence. The 2025 paper explicitly keeps the equivalence question open.

A positive answer would show that the ability to choose unseen coordinates adaptively compensates for the restrictions of an ordinary computable betting procedure. A negative answer would exhibit effective statistical nonrandomness that escapes every such procedure. Either outcome would resolve a basic mismatch between two precise definitions of randomness and sharpen our understanding of what information an adaptive algorithm can extract from an infinite object.

Kastermans and Lempp show that randomness against computable injective query orders is weaker than Martin-Löf randomness; they also establish the separation for computable permutation orders. The full Kolmogorov–Loveland definition permits choices that depend on observed bit values. Consequently their separating sequences do not establish the separation requested here.

Merkle, Miller, Nies, Reimann and Stephan prove that Kolmogorov–Loveland random sequences have arbitrarily dense subsequences that are Martin-Löf random. A key splitting result says that when a computable set of coordinates and its complement are both infinite, at least one of the two resulting subsequences is Martin-Löf random. This places the notion close to Martin-Löf randomness, but the randomness of a subsequence does not by itself imply randomness of the original interleaving.

Generalized betting games use a different query model. Generalized betting games may split a current set of possible sequences into computably described pieces, instead of querying exactly one fresh bit. Petrović’s 2021 paper gives a pair of strategies in a generalized half-betting model that together succeed on every non-Martin-Löf-random sequence. The greater freedom of the query is part of that theorem, so it does not directly give two Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies.

Petrović’s 2025 result identifies a limitation of a method used for those more flexible games. Kolmogorov–Loveland strategies do not admit the same finite-family guarantee of uniformly forcing large capital on every sequence in a sufficiently small effective open set. The paper constructs small open sets containing sequences on which the relevant capital bounds are not exceeded. This is a barrier to that style of quantitative coverage argument.

The remaining quantifier matters: finding a suitable sequence inside each of arbitrarily small open sets need not produce one sequence lying in every level of a single Martin-Löf test. Likewise, excluding one fixed finite family of gamblers does not exclude a strategy chosen separately for each nonrandom sequence. The 2025 paper explicitly keeps the equivalence question open.

A positive answer would show that the ability to choose unseen coordinates adaptively compensates for the restrictions of an ordinary computable betting procedure. A negative answer would exhibit effective statistical nonrandomness that escapes every such procedure. Either outcome would resolve a basic mismatch between two precise definitions of randomness and sharpen our understanding of what information an adaptive algorithm can extract from an infinite object.

benchmark_focus.reason: A defining open question linking computability, adaptive information access, fair betting and effective null tests; a resolution would settle the relationship between two foundational randomness notions.

cards.title: Rigidity of the Turing degrees
cards.formal: Is every order automorphism of the partial order \((D_{t},\le _{t})\) of all Turing degrees the identity? Equivalently, does every bijection \(\pi :D_{t}\to D_{t}\) satisfying \(a\le _{t}b\) if and only if \(\pi (a)\le _{t}\pi (b)\), for all \(a,b\in D_{t}\), also satisfy \(\pi (a)=a\) for every \(a\in D_{t}\)?
cards.definitions: For sets \(A,B\subseteq \mathbb{N} , A\le _{t}B\) means that an oracle Turing machine with membership-query access to B halts on every natural-number input and decides membership in A. There is no time or space bound. \(A\equiv _{t}B\) means \(A\le _{t}B\) and \(B\le _{t}A\). The Turing degree \([A]\) is the equivalence class of A under ≡\(_{t}\), and \(D_{t}\) is the quotient of all subsets of \(\mathbb{N}\) by this equivalence. The relation \([A]\le _{t}[B]\) is independent of the chosen representatives and is a partial order. An automorphism is any set-theoretic bijection of \(D_{t}\) preserving and reflecting this order. It is not assumed computable, definable, continuous, measure-preserving or induced by one operation on representatives. The domain includes all degrees, not only degrees of computably enumerable sets or degrees below a fixed bound. The question is interpreted for the actual degree structure in ordinary set theory, for example ZFC.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that every such bijection fixes every degree, or prove the existence of one order automorphism and one degree that it moves. An automorphism of a proper substructure, a non-surjective order embedding, or a permutation of subsets that fails to descend to degrees is not a counterexample. Rigidity of one cone or of a restricted class of induced automorphisms is only a partial positive result. An independence result should specify the axiomatic base and would settle provability relative to that base rather than assert either mathematical answer.
cards.why: A central structural question about relative computability: whether the ordering of computational power has any nontrivial global symmetry. It tests how much mathematical information is recoverable from reducibility alone.

importance.reason: A defining open problem of degree theory, closely tied to the intrinsic definability of computational structure and constrained by deep but incomplete rigidity theorems.

progress.text: Cone-rigidity results culminate in Slaman–Woodin’s theorem that all degrees above \(0''\) are fixed; the full structure remains outside this conclusion.
Shore–Slaman prove that the Turing jump is definable from the order, so every automorphism preserves it.
Slaman’s published survey presents the countability of the automorphism group, rigidity above \(0''\) and the unresolved general question.
Kjos-Hanssen excludes nontrivial automorphisms induced by integer permutations and certain measure-preserving homeomorphisms; the journal paper appears in 2018.

cards.status_note: Literature search checked through 10 September 2026. The checked primary sources explicitly retain general rigidity as open; no later verified resolution was located. The last substantive result documented here is the 2018 journal article, not a claimed 2026 advance. The historical Cooper announcement is distinguished from an independently verified solution.

context_blocks.text: Turing degrees classify decision problems by what can be computed from an oracle for them. Different encodings that compute one another become one point, and the order records comparative computational power. The rigidity question asks whether this order has any genuine symmetry: could all degrees be consistently relabeled, changing at least one degree while preserving every reducibility comparison? A positive answer would make the entire relative-computability structure intrinsically asymmetric.

Elementary examples illustrate what is already forced. The degree 0 of computable sets is the unique least element and therefore cannot move. The join of \([A]\) and \([B]\) is represented by \(A\oplus B\), which stores A on even positions and B on odd positions; because it is the least upper bound, every order automorphism preserves joins as well. These observations do not identify arbitrary degrees, whose patterns of predecessors and successors are far more complicated.

The Turing jump sends \([A]\) to the degree of the halting problem for machines equipped with oracle A. Shore and Slaman prove that this operation is first-order definable using the degree order alone. Consequently every automorphism commutes with the jump, and fixes \(0' , 0''\) and all finite iterates starting from 0. This is a major restriction, but commuting with an operation does not by itself force a map to fix every argument.

Slaman and Woodin prove that every automorphism fixes every degree above \(0''\). Their analysis also shows that the automorphism group is at most countable, despite the continuum-sized underlying degree structure. The unresolved region is the complement of that upper cone. It includes degrees incomparable with \(0''\), not just degrees strictly below it. Thus describing the remaining question as only the interval below \(0''\) would omit part of the problem.

One possible way to construct an automorphism would be to permute the natural-number coordinates of every oracle set. Kjos-Hanssen rules this out: if one permutation of \(\mathbb{N}\) induces an order automorphism on all Turing degrees, the induced automorphism is trivial, and the permutation itself must be computable. His result also treats homeomorphisms of Cantor space preserving all Bernoulli product measures. The full question imposes none of these representation or measure restrictions.

Rigidity must also be distinguished from defining every single degree by a first-order formula without parameters. There are only countably many such formulas but uncountably many degrees, so the latter is impossible. A rigid infinite structure can contain elements that are not individually definable: absence of global symmetries is weaker than having a separate finite logical description of each element.

The historical literature includes an announced nontrivial automorphism by Cooper in 1999. Slaman’s survey explicitly reports that its construction had not been independently verified and continues to treat rigidity as open. Kjos-Hanssen’s later journal article likewise states the general question as open. These cards follow the established partial-result literature; an old announcement alone is not treated as a resolution.

This is a foundational computability question rather than an efficient-algorithm problem. Its significance is whether relative computability already determines its own global structure, or whether the degree order admits hidden symmetries that are invisible to all reducibility comparisons.

cards.title: Busy Beaver \(\mathrm{BB}(6)\)
cards.formal: Determine the exact value of $BB(6)=S(6)$ by specifying a machine $M_*\in\mathcal{M}_6$ that halts on the blank tape and proving that $T(M)\le T(M_*)$ for every $M\in\mathcal{M}_6$ that halts on the blank tape. Here $\mathcal{M}_6$ is the class of deterministic Turing machines with six nonhalting states, two tape symbols and one initially all-zero, bi-infinite tape, as defined below, and $T(M)$ counts transitions up to and including the first entry into the separate halting state. The answer is then $BB(6)=T(M_*)$; the witness runtime is an exact description of the value.
cards.definitions: The states are A, B, C, D, E, F and a separate halting state Z; Z is not one of the six states being counted. Tape cells are indexed by the integers and contain 0 or 1. Initially every cell contains 0, the head is at cell 0, and the state is A. For each nonhalting state and scanned symbol, the transition table specifies a symbol to write, a move by exactly one cell left or right, and a next state. Execution stops on entering Z, including that final write-and-move transition in \(T(M)\). Unreachable states are allowed. The finite set of these transition tables is $\mathcal{M}_6$. Here BB is the runtime (maximum-shift) function S, not the function $\Sigma$ that maximizes the number of 1s left on the tape. In the progress note, $2\uparrow\uparrow k$ is a tower of k twos, and $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow 1=2$, $2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow(k+1)=2\uparrow\uparrow(2\uparrow\uparrow\uparrow k)$. For a halting machine \(M, T(M)\) is the least positive integer t at which the execution enters Z. The answer convention never applies T to a nonhalting machine: halting of the proposed witness is a required part of its certificate. Its explicitly specified transition table together with that certificate defines a terminating step-counting computation and hence a unique exact integer, even when evaluating that computation is impractical.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply the complete twelve-entry transition table of a particular machine \(M_\ast\) in the stated class. Provide Lean-checked proofs that (1) \(M_\ast\) halts from the specified blank-tape initial configuration, and (2) every machine M in this class that halts from that initial configuration executes at most \(T(M_\ast)\) transitions. Together these certify \(\mathrm{BB}(6)=T(M_\ast)\) exactly. The runtime of this proved-halting concrete machine is an accepted finite description of the integer; a simple closed form, decimal expansion, separately evaluated integer literal or full execution trace is not required. Specifying a machine without proving its halting and universal maximality, restating the defining maximum over all machines, or giving only an approximate or one-sided bound does not meet this criterion.
cards.why: This is a defining concrete problem in computability: identify the longest finite computation possible in a fixed, exceptionally small universal machine formalism. A proof would advance the boundary of complete mathematical understanding of small programs and test methods for nontermination proofs, recurrence analysis, and formal verification. The significance lies in establishing the exact boundary, not merely constructing a machine with an enormous runtime.

context_blocks.text: Fixing the number of states leaves finitely many machines, so a maximum halting time exists. Nevertheless, enumerating their transition tables does not tell us when to stop waiting for the machines that never halt. The Busy Beaver function packages that obstruction into a sequence of finite integers. Noncomputability of the whole sequence does not prevent individual values from being established.

The five-state case provides a concrete precedent: the bbchallenge collaboration proved \(S(5)=47,176,870\) with the Coq proof assistant. Its proof combines a complete enumeration after symmetry reductions with methods that certify halting or nonhalting. The paper makes precise how a finite search can be accompanied by a universal proof.

Six states introduce obstacles beyond running a larger search. The Antihydra machine has a halting question expressed through an integer recurrence whose parity behavior is still unresolved. A probabilistic heuristic about that behavior is not a proof that the machine runs forever. An exact Busy Beaver bound would also decide its halting behavior in principle, even if the required finite computation were physically infeasible.

The target is the exact six-state runtime maximum. A concrete machine with proved halting and universal maximality specifies that integer through its runtime, without a simple closed form or decimal expansion. Runtime and final tape output are different extremal quantities, and machine conventions matter. Existing catalogue questions about Busy Beaver growth, logical thresholds, or population protocols therefore remain separate problems.

cards.title: Reversal of Hindman’s theorem to the \(\omega\)-jump
cards.formal: Over RCA\(_{0}\), does Hindman’s finite-sums theorem imply ACA\(_{0}^{+}\)? Equivalently, does RCA\(_{0}+HT\) prove that every set X has an \(\omega -th\) Turing jump?
cards.definitions: Work in classical two-sorted second-order arithmetic, with number variables and variables for sets of natural numbers. RCA\(_{0}\) has the usual elementary arithmetic axioms, \(\Sigma ^{0}_{1}\) induction and \(\Delta ^{0}_{1}\) comprehension, allowing set parameters. HT is the assertion that for every integer \(k\ge 1\) and every coloring c of the positive integers into \(\{0,\ldots ,k- 1\}\), there exist an infinite set H of positive integers and a color i such that \(c(\sum_{h\in F}h)=i\) for every nonempty finite subset F of H. Terms in a sum are distinct; there is no fixed upper bound on their number and no additional sparsity requirement on H. For a set X, its Turing jump \(X'\) is {e: the e-th oracle Turing machine with oracle X halts on input e}, using one fixed effective enumeration. The \(\omega\)-jump existence axiom says \(\forall X\exists Y\) [\(Y_{0}=X\) and \(\forall j(Y_{j+1}=Y_{j}' )\)], where \(Y_{j}=\{e:\langle j,e\rangle \in Y\}\) and \(\langle \cdot ,\cdot \rangle\) is a fixed primitive recursive pairing. ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) is RCA\(_{0}\) plus that axiom. The question is formal provability of this implication over the stated base, not truth of Hindman’s theorem in ordinary set theory and not a single-instance computability claim.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the \(\omega\)-jump existence axiom in RCA\(_{0}+HT\), or prove nonimplication by constructing a model of RCA\(_{0}+HT\) in which some set has no coded \(\omega\)-jump. A standard-natural-number model is sufficient for a separation but is not required. A lower bound of ACA\(_{0}\) alone, an upper bound of ACA\(_{0}^{+}\), or a theorem about only bounded-length sums does not decide this implication. A negative answer need not show that HT is equivalent to ACA\(_{0}\); an intermediate strength would also refute the implication.
cards.why: A longstanding gap in the computational and axiomatic strength of a central infinite combinatorial theorem, with a precise target at the \(\omega -th\) Turing jump.

importance.reason: A landmark reverse-mathematical calibration problem connecting finite-sums combinatorics, oracle computation and the hierarchy of set-existence axioms.

progress.text: Blass–Hirst–Simpson establish ACA\(_{0}^{+}\Rightarrow HT\Rightarrow\)ACA\(_{0}\) over RCA\(_{0}\), leaving the reversal in this card open.
Carlucci–Zdanowski characterize ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) using Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large sets; this supplies a comparison principle rather than an HT reversal.
Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski reach the ACA\(_{0}\) lower bound already for sums of at most two elements with four colors; conference precursor 2017, journal version 2020.
Csima and coauthors prove nontrivial computability and reverse-mathematical lower bounds for sums of exactly two elements, a weaker principle than full HT.
Liu–Patey prove new upper bounds and separations for variable-word and unordered Carlson–Simpson principles, without claiming a resolution of HT’s strength.
Le Houérou–Patey obtain a conservation theorem for a one-variable, two-color Carlson–Simpson principle.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No proof or separation for RCA\(_{0}+HT\Rightarrow\)ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) was found in the checked primary literature. The recent variable-word and Carlson–Simpson results have different formulations and do not establish this reversal.

context_blocks.text: Hindman’s theorem says that a finite coloring contains an infinite set whose entire collection of finite sums has one color. This is much more than finding an infinite monochromatic subset: the same color must work for single elements, pairs, triples and every larger finite selection. For parity coloring, the positive even numbers give an immediate example. The theorem must also handle colorings with no such simple arithmetic description.

The combinatorial statement is a theorem, not the unresolved claim on this card. Reverse mathematics asks which set-existence axioms are needed to prove it. One works over a deliberately weak base theory and compares stronger principles by implication. The inherited paper records the classical bounds ACA\(_{0}^{+}\Rightarrow HT\Rightarrow\)ACA\(_{0}\) and identifies closing this gap as a major open problem. This card asks specifically whether the upper implication reverses.

ACA\(_{0}\) allows arithmetic comprehension; equivalently over the base theory, every set has its Turing jump. An individual jump supplies answers to halting questions relative to the given set. Repeating that operation a fixed finite number of times yields increasingly strong information. The \(\omega\)-jump places every finite iterate into the sections of one set. Being able to discuss each fixed finite stage is not the same as having this whole sequence available as a single object.

The distinction is visible in the model consisting of the standard natural numbers together with all arithmetical sets. It is closed under the ordinary Turing jump, since jumping an arithmetical set still yields an arithmetical set. It does not contain the join of all finite jumps of the empty set. Thus ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) demands more set existence than ACA\(_{0}\). Whether Hindman’s theorem already forces that additional existence is the precise issue here.

The computability bounds show why ordinary computable colorings already matter. The account by Csima and coauthors recalls a computable coloring for which every finite-sums solution computes the halting set, and an upper bound placing a solution in the \((\omega +1)-st\) jump of the coloring. These are bounds on information in solutions. Neither identifies the exact reverse-mathematical strength, and noncomputability alone falls far short of an \(\omega\)-jump reversal.

Restricted sum lengths have provided substantial progress without closing the full gap. Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski prove that the version requiring monochromatic singletons and pairs already implies ACA\(_{0}\); four colors suffice without an additional sparsity condition. Their results for sums of exactly \(n\ge 3\) terms use an apartness condition on the binary supports of the chosen integers. These carefully specified variants should not be merged with unrestricted HT.

Even replacing “at most two” by “exactly two” changes the logical picture. Csima and coauthors construct a computable two-color instance of the exactly-two version with no \(\Sigma ^{0}_{2}\) solution and prove a lower bound through diagonally noncomputable functions relative to the halting set. Yet exactly-two sums follow from Ramsey’s theorem for pairs, placing that principle strictly below full HT over the base. This is a useful warning that small wording changes can alter the problem.

There is a separate combinatorial principle known to capture the desired upper level exactly. Carlucci–Zdanowski prove that Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large finite sets is equivalent to ACA\(_{0}^{+}\). A finite set F is exactly large when |\(F|=\min (F)+1\), so its dimension varies with its elements. This yields a potential comparison target: an implication from HT to this precisely defined Ramsey principle would suffice. Its equivalence does not itself supply that missing implication.

Recent results in the neighboring theory of variable words require the same care. Liu–Patey’s June 2026 preprint, revised in July, gives low\(_{2}\) solutions to the Ordered Variable Word theorem for colorings of ordinary words and proves each fixed-dimensional unordered Carlson–Simpson lemma in ACA\(_{0}\). The paper distinguishes these principles from ordered higher-dimensional counterparts and still describes ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) as the weakest known system proving HT. Its new upper bounds should not be transferred to Hindman’s theorem.

Le Houérou–Patey’s July 2026 preprint obtains a conservation result for a one-variable Carlson–Simpson principle with two colors. It controls which arithmetical consequences that particular principle adds to a weak theory. This is a different assertion from constructing the \(\omega\)-jump out of unrestricted finite-sums homogeneity. Together the recent papers sharpen nearby boundaries without answering the implication stated here.

cards.context:
Hindman’s theorem says that a finite coloring contains an infinite set whose entire collection of finite sums has one color. This is much more than finding an infinite monochromatic subset: the same color must work for single elements, pairs, triples and every larger finite selection. For parity coloring, the positive even numbers give an immediate example. The theorem must also handle colorings with no such simple arithmetic description.

The combinatorial statement is a theorem, not the unresolved claim on this card. Reverse mathematics asks which set-existence axioms are needed to prove it. One works over a deliberately weak base theory and compares stronger principles by implication. The inherited paper records the classical bounds ACA\(_{0}^{+}\Rightarrow HT\Rightarrow\)ACA\(_{0}\) and identifies closing this gap as a major open problem. This card asks specifically whether the upper implication reverses.

ACA\(_{0}\) allows arithmetic comprehension; equivalently over the base theory, every set has its Turing jump. An individual jump supplies answers to halting questions relative to the given set. Repeating that operation a fixed finite number of times yields increasingly strong information. The \(\omega\)-jump places every finite iterate into the sections of one set. Being able to discuss each fixed finite stage is not the same as having this whole sequence available as a single object.

The distinction is visible in the model consisting of the standard natural numbers together with all arithmetical sets. It is closed under the ordinary Turing jump, since jumping an arithmetical set still yields an arithmetical set. It does not contain the join of all finite jumps of the empty set. Thus ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) demands more set existence than ACA\(_{0}\). Whether Hindman’s theorem already forces that additional existence is the precise issue here.

The computability bounds show why ordinary computable colorings already matter. The account by Csima and coauthors recalls a computable coloring for which every finite-sums solution computes the halting set, and an upper bound placing a solution in the \((\omega +1)-st\) jump of the coloring. These are bounds on information in solutions. Neither identifies the exact reverse-mathematical strength, and noncomputability alone falls far short of an \(\omega\)-jump reversal.

Restricted sum lengths have provided substantial progress without closing the full gap. Carlucci–Kołodziejczyk–Lepore–Zdanowski prove that the version requiring monochromatic singletons and pairs already implies ACA\(_{0}\); four colors suffice without an additional sparsity condition. Their results for sums of exactly \(n\ge 3\) terms use an apartness condition on the binary supports of the chosen integers. These carefully specified variants should not be merged with unrestricted HT.

Even replacing “at most two” by “exactly two” changes the logical picture. Csima and coauthors construct a computable two-color instance of the exactly-two version with no \(\Sigma ^{0}_{2}\) solution and prove a lower bound through diagonally noncomputable functions relative to the halting set. Yet exactly-two sums follow from Ramsey’s theorem for pairs, placing that principle strictly below full HT over the base. This is a useful warning that small wording changes can alter the problem.

There is a separate combinatorial principle known to capture the desired upper level exactly. Carlucci–Zdanowski prove that Ramsey’s theorem for exactly large finite sets is equivalent to ACA\(_{0}^{+}\). A finite set F is exactly large when |\(F|=\min (F)+1\), so its dimension varies with its elements. This yields a potential comparison target: an implication from HT to this precisely defined Ramsey principle would suffice. Its equivalence does not itself supply that missing implication.

Recent results in the neighboring theory of variable words require the same care. Liu–Patey’s June 2026 preprint, revised in July, gives low\(_{2}\) solutions to the Ordered Variable Word theorem for colorings of ordinary words and proves each fixed-dimensional unordered Carlson–Simpson lemma in ACA\(_{0}\). The paper distinguishes these principles from ordered higher-dimensional counterparts and still describes ACA\(_{0}^{+}\) as the weakest known system proving HT. Its new upper bounds should not be transferred to Hindman’s theorem.

Le Houérou–Patey’s July 2026 preprint obtains a conservation result for a one-variable Carlson–Simpson principle with two colors. It controls which arithmetical consequences that particular principle adds to a weak theory. This is a different assertion from constructing the \(\omega\)-jump out of unrestricted finite-sums homogeneity. Together the recent papers sharpen nearby boundaries without answering the implication stated here.

A positive answer would make a concrete additive-combinatorial theorem a characterization of closure under all finite Turing jumps at once. A negative answer would show that known proofs use more set existence than the theorem itself entails. Either outcome would clarify the information content of an infinite combinatorial search principle, which is the reason for its place in the computability part of this catalogue.

cards.title: Universality of Turing equivalence
cards.formal: For every countable Borel equivalence relation E on a standard Borel space X, does there exist a Borel function \(f:X\to 2^{\mathbb{N}}\) such that x E y if and only if \(f(x)\equiv _{T} f(y)\), for all \(x,y\in X\)?
cards.definitions: The space \(2^{\mathbb{N}}\) consists of all infinite binary sequences, identified with subsets of \(\mathbb{N}\). For \(a,b\in 2^{\mathbb{N}}, a\le _{T} b\) means that some oracle Turing machine with oracle b computes every bit of a and halts on every input coordinate; \(a\equiv _{T} b\) means both \(a\le _{T} b\) and \(b\le _{T} a\). There is no time or space restriction on these computations. A standard Borel space is a set with the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra of some Polish topology. The relation E must be a Borel subset of \(X\times X\) and each equivalence class must be at most countable; X itself may be uncountable. The function f is Borel measurable: inverse images of Borel sets are Borel. It need not be computable, continuous, injective on points, or uniform on indices witnessing equivalence. It must preserve both equivalence and inequivalence on every input pair, not merely almost everywhere for a chosen measure. The quantifiers ask for a separate Borel reduction for each E, without requiring an algorithm that takes a code for E and outputs f. This is the ordinary ZFC formulation of Borel universality.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that Turing equivalence is universal by producing the requisite Borel reductions, or prove it is not by identifying one countable Borel relation that does not reduce to it. Equivalently, settle whether \(E_{\infty}\le _{B}\equiv _{T}\) for a fixed standard universal countable Borel relation \(E_{\infty}\). A negative theorem conditional on a form of Martin’s conjecture must be labeled conditional. Failure of reductions with an additional uniformity or computability requirement is not a negative solution to the unrestricted Borel question.
cards.why: A central bridge between computability and descriptive set theory, asking whether equality of computational power can encode every countable Borel classification problem.

importance.reason: A classical universality question with consequences for Martin’s conjecture and for the distinction between definable and uniform computational encodings.
