context_blocks.text: Two infinite binary sequences have the same Turing degree when each can compute the other. This partitions all possible oracles by their computational power. The universality question asks how complicated that partition is as a classification problem: can every countable Borel pattern of equivalence be represented exactly by equality of Turing degrees? The objects being classified are infinite sequences, not finite machine descriptions.

There are countably many oracle programs. Consequently, for a fixed oracle b, only countably many sequences can be computed from b, and its Turing-equivalence class is countable. The relation is Borel because a claim that an oracle program computes a given sequence can be written using countably many conditions about finite computations. Thus Turing equivalence itself belongs to the class of relations compared on this card.

A Borel reduction is a structured assignment of invariants. If f reduces E to Turing equivalence, the Turing degree of \(f(x)\) is a complete invariant for the E-class of x: equivalent objects receive the same degree, and inequivalent objects receive different degrees. Distinct representatives of one E-class may receive different binary sequences, provided those sequences have the same degree. Injectivity on equivalence classes is essential; injectivity on individual points is not.

It suffices to study a single standard benchmark \(E_{\infty}\). One realization is the orbit relation for the shift action of the free group \(F_{2}\) on \(\{0,1\}^{F_{2}}\): two labelings x,y are equivalent when \(y(h)=x(g^{- 1}h)\) for some group element g and every \(h\in F_{2}\). This countable Borel relation is universal. A reduction of that one relation to Turing equivalence would therefore answer the full universally quantified question.

The inherited Caicedo–Löwe survey records the question as Question 6 in its discussion of Martin’s conjecture. It traces the universality problem to Kechris and distinguishes it from nearby statements about arithmetic equivalence and uniform coding. The source is a 2019 preprint; the later published chapter updates the year in its title. The card retains the exact inherited version and locator.

There are strong positive results for neighboring relations. Slaman and Steel proved that arithmetic equivalence is universal; Marks, Slaman and Steel provide a published proof and discussion. Arithmetic equivalence allows each sequence to be computed from some finite Turing jump of the other, with the finite jump levels depending on the pair. That extra allowance changes which sequences become equivalent.

In the other direction, Marks proved universality of polynomial-time Turing equivalence, as well as polynomial-time many-one equivalence. These compare arbitrary languages over finite strings by resource-bounded oracle reductions. The theorem concerns the entire space of languages, not only decidable languages or languages inside a familiar complexity class. It establishes universality for a finer relation than unrestricted Turing equivalence.

Finer and coarser relations do not give an automatic transfer here. A coding that keeps two outputs inequivalent under polynomial-time reductions may still make them equivalent under unrestricted oracle computation. Once that happens, the reverse implication required of a Borel reduction fails. Preserving the encoding under all additional computations is the missing task; simply reusing the polynomial-time result does not complete it.

There is also a structural obstruction to familiar coding approaches. With Turing equivalence generated in its usual way by oracle-program reductions, it is not uniformly universal. Roughly, uniformity would require indices for computations between encoded outputs to be chosen solely from the indices witnessing the original equivalence, independently of the particular objects. Marks develops this distinction and shows why the choice of generating maps must be specified.

The present problem permits arbitrary Borel reductions, so that uniform obstruction is not the desired nonuniversality theorem. Whether ordinary universality must entail appropriate stronger uniformity properties is itself part of the surrounding theory. A proof that rules out one common coding pattern therefore reveals a methodological barrier without exhausting all Borel encodings.

Martin’s conjecture supplies a competing prediction. Its Borel form implies that Turing equivalence is not universal; in particular, it obstructs reducing two disjoint copies of Turing equivalence into one copy. Conversely, a universality proof would contradict that prediction. The point is a genuine conditional connection between two major structural questions, not an unconditional settlement in either direction.

Day and Marks’ February 2026 revision investigates an older question about writing Turing equivalence as an increasing union whose stages omit certain uniformly computable infinite sequences. A positive answer would imply nonuniform invariant functions and universality of ordinary many-one equivalence. Their consequences remain conditional on that decomposition question, and concern distinctions among degree relations that must not be collapsed into a proof of Turing universality.

Settling the card would tell us whether mutual computability provides a universal language for countable Borel classification, or has a structural limitation absent from some nearby degree notions. Either outcome would matter beyond computability: it would constrain the ways orbit equivalence relations, invariants and definable encodings can interact. The answer criterion is a precise existence theorem for reductions, with no algorithmic-efficiency requirement hidden inside the word “Borel.”

cards.definitions: The input explicitly gives \(m\ge 0\) and all four entries of each \(A_{i}\) as signed binary integers. Entries have no magnitude or sign restriction, and m is part of the input, not a fixed constant. Products use ordinary exact integer matrix multiplication: \((AB)_{r,s}=\sum _{t=1}^{2} A_{r,t}B_{t,s}\). The target \(0_{2}\) is the matrix with all four entries zero. The product length \(\ell\) is finite but unbounded, and generator indices may repeat in any order. Only listed generators can be used; inverses are not supplied automatically. The empty product is excluded, and an empty list is a NO instance. The semigroup generated by the list is the set of all such nonempty products, so mortality means membership of \(0_{2}\) in that set. The machine must return YES exactly for mortal lists and NO otherwise, terminating on both kinds. No running-time or memory bound is imposed beyond finite termination; there is no oracle, numerical tolerance or real-arithmetic primitive.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer gives a uniform decision algorithm with proofs of correctness and termination on every finite input list. A negative answer proves that the stated decision problem is undecidable. A procedure that only certifies particular zero products, a bounded-length decision algorithm, or a lower bound against polynomial time does not settle the target.

context_blocks.title: Can a sequence erase every vector?
context_blocks.text: A product equal to the zero matrix sends every two-dimensional vector to zero at once. The question is whether some finite sequence of the allowed transformations has this effect. It is stronger than sending one specified vector to zero: a matrix can kill that vector while acting nontrivially on others.

context_blocks.title: Two small examples
context_blocks.text: Let \(A=[[1,0],[0,0]]\) and \(B=[[0,0],[1,0]]\). Neither is the zero matrix, but \(AB=0_{2}\), so the list \((A,B)\) is mortal. Reversing the order gives \(BA=B\), showing that order matters. The list containing only A is not mortal, since every positive power of A equals A. Thus the presence of a singular generator by itself does not answer the question.

context_blocks.title: Hardness and undecidability are different claims
context_blocks.text: Bell, Hirvensalo and Potapov established NP-hardness in 2012; their 2024 paper still identifies unrestricted two-dimensional mortality as an open decidability problem. NP-hardness leaves open the possibility of a terminating algorithm with very large running time. Mortality is already undecidable for general finite lists of three-dimensional integer matrices, placing dimension two at a basic boundary.

context_blocks.title: Restricted matrix classes have stronger results
context_blocks.text: Jaax and Kiefer prove NP-completeness when each determinant is either 0 or +1. This gives a decision procedure for that promise and does not cover arbitrary determinants. The 2024 membership theorem concerns generators in \(GL_{2}(\mathbb{Z} )\), whose determinants are ±1; their products are invertible and cannot equal zero. Neither theorem decides mortality when unrestricted singular and nonsingular generators are mixed.

context_blocks.title: Relation to other matrix questions
context_blocks.text: General semigroup membership, discussed in TCS-5921, allows a target matrix supplied as input; mortality fixes that target to zero. A solution of general membership would therefore decide mortality. The April 2026 work on complex matrix embeddings studies different algebraic representation questions and supplies no general resolution of the present integer-matrix target.

cards.definitions: Fix one optimal plain Kolmogorov machine U: an optimal partial computable map from finite binary programs to finite binary strings. \(C(x)\) is the minimum program length with U(program)=x. For \(S=\{i_{1}<\cdots <i_{r}\}\), encode the tuple \(x_{S}\) as \(1^{r}0\) followed, in that order, by the strings \(1^{|x_{i}|}0x_{i}\), and let \(C(x_{S})\) mean the complexity of this encoding. This is a fixed computably decodable encoding. The strings \(b_{i}\) have no prescribed lengths and need not be computable from the \(a_{i}\) by a fixed transformation. Only joint unconditional complexities of all nonempty subtuples are required. The constants may depend on \(k, \lambda\) and U but not on n, the input strings or S. The additive slack is measured in bits. This uses the original length normalization \(O(\log  n)\); it does not silently replace it by the potentially smaller \(O(\log  C(a_{1},\ldots ,a_{k}))\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal statement, or its logical negation with the same quantifier order. Failure of one algorithm for producing b, or failure of obtaining the scaling by conditioning the original strings on an auxiliary string, is not a refutation. The logarithmic slack is part of the proposition, not a numerical-estimation tolerance.

cards.definitions: Fix an optimal plain conditional universal machine U. Define \(C(u|v)=\min\){|\(p|:U(p,v)\) halts with output u}; there is no prefix-free restriction or time bound on programs p. Set \(C(u)=C(u|\varepsilon )\), where \(\varepsilon\) is the empty string. Use the computable, uniquely decodable pairing \(\langle x,y\rangle =1^{|}x|0xy\), and write \(C(x,y)=C(\langle x,y\rangle )\) and \(C(u|x,y)=C(u|\langle x,y\rangle )\). The integer n bounds joint description length, not the bit lengths of x or y; z has no length or complexity bound. The single constant a may depend on U and the fixed encoding, but not on n,x,y,z. Choosing a larger constant absorbs the additive effects of different fixed optimal machines or computable tuple encodings. The auxiliary string \(z'\) may depend on all three strings. No bound on \(C(z' |z)\), and no efficient procedure for finding \(z'\), is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniformly logarithmic bounds for every permitted triple, or refute them by showing that every constant a fails for some n,x,y,z with \(C(x,y)\le n\). An example that only violates a particular small constant does not refute the asymptotic assertion.

cards.title: Superpolynomial Extended Frege lower bounds
cards.formal: Is Extended Frege not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every constants \(C>0\) and \(c\ge 1\), is there a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) whose shortest Extended Frege proof has bit length greater than \(C(|\varphi |+2)^{c}\)? Here |\(\varphi |\) is the bit length of the explicitly written formula.
cards.definitions:
Fix Boolean formulas over \(
eg\) and →, with → interpreted as material implication and variable indices encoded in binary. Use the Frege axiom schemes \(A	o (B	o A), (A	o (B	o C))	o ((A	o B)	o (A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o 
eg A)	o (A	o B)\), together with modus ponens from A and \(A	o B\) to B. An Extended Frege proof of \(\varphi\) may additionally introduce an abbreviation variable e by the two extension axioms \(e	o 	heta\) and \(	heta 	o e\). Here e is fresh, absent from \(\varphi , 	heta\), and every preceding line; \(	heta\) uses original variables of \(\varphi\) and previously introduced extension variables. Extensions are thus acyclic definitions. Other proof lines are axiom instances or applications of modus ponens, and the last line must be \(\varphi\), with no extension variables. Lines may cite and reuse earlier lines arbitrarily: proofs are not required to be trees. Proof size is the full binary encoding length of all explicitly written formulas, extension definitions, and inference references; there is no depth or per-line-size restriction. A tautology is true under every assignment to its variables. This fixed presentation is polynomially equivalent to the usual Extended Frege systems, so changing a standard finite Frege basis does not change polynomial boundedness. context_blocks.text: Extension variables let a proof name a formula once and reuse its name. This can represent shared computations economically, as a Boolean circuit shares intermediate gates. Expanding all abbreviations into formula trees can cause an exponential increase in length, so a lower bound that counts only ordinary Frege proofs does not automatically survive the extension rule.

The question concerns the existence of short certificates, not the time required to discover them. A particular proof search method might take exponential time even though another method could find a short proof; conversely, a proof-size lower bound would constrain every method that outputs an EF derivation. The input length is the final tautology’s actual encoding length, so a lower bound exponential in a smaller hidden parameter may still be only polynomial in the input.

If \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\), every polynomial-time verifiable propositional proof system has hard tautologies, including EF. The converse for this particular system is unknown: showing that EF is inefficient does not rule out a different proof system that gives short certificates for all tautologies. This is why an EF lower bound would be a major advance without automatically constituting a proof of \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\).

cards.title: Frege versus Extended Frege
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(k\ge 1\) such that every Extended Frege proof \(\pi\) of a propositional tautology \(\varphi\) has some ordinary Frege proof \(\rho\) of the same formula with |\(\rho |\le C(|\pi |+2)^{k}\)? Equivalently, if \(sF(\varphi )\) and \(sEF(\varphi )\) are the minimum proof sizes in the two systems, is \(sF(\varphi )\) polynomially bounded in \(sEF(\varphi )\), uniformly over all tautologies?
cards.definitions:
Fix formulas over negation \(
eg\) and material implication →, with binary-encoded variable indices. Ordinary Frege uses the axiom schemes \(A	o (B	o A), (A	o (B	o C))	o ((A	o B)	o (A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o 
eg A)	o (A	o B)\), and modus ponens: infer B from A and \(A	o B\). A proof is a finite sequence ending with \(\varphi\); earlier lines may be cited and reused without restriction. Extended Frege adds acyclic definitions, introducing the pair \(e	o 	heta\) and \(	heta 	o e\), where e is a new variable absent from \(\varphi , 	heta\) and all preceding lines. \(	heta\) may use variables of \(\varphi\) and earlier extension variables. The final formula contains no extension variables. Proof size is the complete binary encoding length of every explicitly written line, definition and inference reference. No formula-depth, proof-depth or tree-shape bound is imposed. These presentations are polynomially equivalent to the usual finite-basis Frege and Extended Frege systems. The target is existence of short translated proofs: it does not require a polynomial-time function that finds \(ho\) from \(\pi\). cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. No polynomial size simulation or superpolynomial separation of unrestricted Frege and EF was found in the primary literature. The newest checked simulation, TR26-166, concerns a restricted algebraic formula system and has quasipolynomial overhead.

context_blocks.text: The extension rule gives reusable names to intermediate computations. If a subformula is used many times, ordinary formula syntax writes out each occurrence; Extended Frege can define it once and refer to its name. A network of such definitions represents a Boolean circuit with shared gates. The rule does not permit a false final theorem: every assignment to the original variables uniquely extends through the definitions, and the conclusion uses only original variables.

Repeated substitution eliminates definitions, but can create exponentially large formula trees. This explains why the obvious simulation is expensive; it does not prove that all ordinary Frege proofs must be expensive. The challenge is to compare the shortest proofs, not one syntactic expansion procedure.

The distinction between proof size and proof-search time is essential. The quantifiers are “for every EF proof there exists a short Frege proof.” They do not supply an algorithm for locating that proof. The stronger notion usually called p-simulation requires a polynomial-time transformation. A size simulation alone can hold even if the available methods for finding the translated proof are much slower.

Buss connects the comparison to finite consistency statements. Frege has polynomial-size proofs of its own partial consistency, meaning the corresponding finite statements that no contradiction has a proof up to a specified length. His theorem characterizes Frege simulation of EF by polynomial-size Frege proofs of the analogous partial consistency statements for EF. This turns a comparison of all proofs into a canonical family of propositional statements; it is not a general proof of the desired simulation.

For example, Aisenberg and coauthors give polynomial-size EF proofs and quasipolynomial-size Frege proofs of propositional Kneser–Lovász coloring principles. That upper bound constrains possible lower bounds for the family, but it does not demonstrate a separation and does not rule out a polynomial Frege upper bound. Quasipolynomial and polynomial must remain distinct in this problem.

Krajíček’s June 2026 paper gives a circuit-rewriting description of EF reasoning. An EF proof of circuit equivalence yields a polynomially long chain of equivalence-preserving rewrites; each rewrite adds at most seven gates and may delete gates. This is a normal-form result about circuit reasoning. The intermediate objects still retain circuit sharing, so it does not turn an arbitrary EF proof into a polynomial-size formula-based Frege proof.

A September 2026 preprint by Chatterjee, Chatterjee, Ghosal and Mukhopadhyay proves a quasipolynomial Frege simulation of a partially commutative formula version of the Ideal Proof System over \(GF(2)\). Variables lie in two groups: they commute across groups but not within a group. The proof formalizes an identity-testing algorithm inside Frege. The restrictions on the algebraic certificates, and the quasipolynomial overhead, both matter; the theorem is not the full EF simulation asked for here.

A negative answer would establish a concrete benefit of reusable definitions for strong propositional reasoning. It would also imply superpolynomial Frege lower bounds, since the final formula is part of every EF proof. By contrast, proving that Frege has some hard tautologies, or assuming \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\), does not automatically separate it from EF: those same tautologies might require equally long EF proofs. The separate question of whether EF itself is polynomially bounded asks about a different comparison.

cards.title: Superpolynomial \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege lower bounds
cards.formal: For every fixed prime p, does there exist a family of propositional tautologies \((\tau _{p,n})_{n\ge 1}\), constructible in time polynomial in n, whose encoded lengths lie between n and \(n^{O}(1)\), such that each \(\tau _{p,n}\) is a DNF and, for every fixed proof-line depth d and every constant \(r>0\), infinitely many n have the following property: every depth-at-most-d Frege proof with \(MOD_{p}\) connectives of \(\tau _{p,n}\) has total encoded size greater than \(n^{r}\)? The proof system and depth convention are specified below; the family may depend on p but not on d or r.
cards.definitions: A tautology evaluates to true on every Boolean assignment. A DNF is a disjunction of conjunctions of literals, with a literal being a variable or its negation. Fix a conventional sound, implicationally complete finite Frege calculus F over constants 0,1 and connectives NOT, AND, OR. A proof is a sequence of formulas, each a substitution instance of an axiom or obtained from earlier lines by a rule of F; earlier lines may be reused arbitrarily. Extend the language and rules as F(\(MOD_{p}\)) in Krajíček §\(5: MOD_{p,j}(A_{1},\ldots ,A_{t})\) is true precisely when the number of true arguments is j modulo p, for \(0\le j<p\). Besides F’s rules with formulas from this language, permit the empty-list axioms \(MOD_{p,0}\)() and \(\mathrm{NOT} MOD_{p,j}\)() for \(j\ne 0\), and all instances of \(MOD_{p,j}(\Gamma ,A) \leftrightarrow\) [(\(MOD_{p,j}(\Gamma ) \mathrm{AND} \mathrm{NOT} A\)) OR (\(MOD_{p,j- 1}(\Gamma ) \mathrm{AND} A\))], with \(j- 1\) taken modulo p and \(\Gamma\) any list of formulas. Constants and variables have depth zero; NOT and MOD increase depth by one, while consecutive ANDs, or consecutive ORs, are flattened and together count as one layer. Every line, including instantiated axioms, obeys the bound d. Proof size counts all symbols and encoded variable indices across all lines, together with rule annotations. Proofs are ordinary Frege proofs, without extension-variable definition axioms; they need not be tree-like or have bounded derivation-graph depth. Standard choices of F give equivalent systems up to polynomial overhead and a constant depth adjustment, immaterial when every fixed d is quantified.
cards.answer_criterion: Exhibit the uniform tautology families and prove the stated superpolynomial proof-size lower bounds, or refute their existence. The tautology condition must itself be established: a formula that has no short proof because it is false is not a hard tautology. A lower bound only for bounded derivation depth, regular proofs, a restricted algebraic subsystem or Boolean circuits alone does not settle this question. A result for one prime is a major partial answer; this single card groups the full fixed-prime frontier rather than duplicating it for each modulus.
cards.why: A central frontier in propositional proof complexity: current methods can handle ordinary bounded-depth reasoning but still cannot establish explicit superpolynomial lower bounds once modular counting is available. The problem tests how circuit lower-bound ideas can constrain entire deductions.

importance.reason: A classical next step beyond the strongest broadly established bounded-depth Frege lower bounds, with direct connections to algebraic proof systems and a persistent gap between circuit and proof complexity.

progress.text: Ajtai establishes superpolynomial bounded-depth Frege lower bounds for the pigeonhole principle; Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo’s 1993 paper gives exponential improvements. These systems lack \(MOD_{p}\) gates.

Efremenko and Itsykson publish amortized-closure lifting and stronger size-versus-derivation-depth results for resolution over parities.
Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret publish their no-short-proof result for candidate DNFs, first posted in September 2025; unconditional tautologicity remains open.
Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov give near-quadratic-depth lifting and a quadratic unconditional size lower bound for parity resolution. These do not settle general modular Frege.
Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret release hard CNF instances for the read-once-oblivious algebraic-branching-program fragment of IPS.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The 2026 primary sources retain modular Frege lower bounds as open. ITCS 2026.99 does not prove that its hard-to-prove candidates are tautologies. ECCC TR26-018 restricts derivation depth or proves a polynomial size bound; TR26-070 treats a restricted algebraic certificate representation. None establishes the fully specified tautology families and unrestricted derivation size lower bounds requested here.

context_blocks.text: Proof complexity measures how long a formal explanation of a tautology must be. A short conclusion can require a much longer sequence of intermediate deductions. Restricting the depth of each intermediate formula limits the expressive power of individual statements while still allowing a long derivation and arbitrary reuse of earlier facts. Modular gates add compact statements about counts modulo p, such as parity when \(p=2\). Krajíček gives the explicit modular axiom presentation used in this card.

The corresponding problem without modular gates has been solved. Ajtai’s work gives superpolynomial lower bounds for the pigeonhole principle in bounded-depth Frege, and Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo strengthen these to exponential bounds. Their argument uses restrictions adapted to the combinatorics of partial matchings. Permitting modular counting defeats the direct extension of that approach: a short parity statement can remain meaningful after many ordinary variables have been fixed.

Circuit complexity provides an analogy but not a solution. Razborov and Smolensky establish lower bounds for constant-depth Boolean circuits with prime modular gates. A proof, however, is a sequence of related formulas, and every tautology itself computes the constant true function. Showing that some nonconstant function requires a large circuit therefore does not directly force long proofs of tautologies. The February 2026 work of Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov explicitly identifies this remaining gap between circuit and proof lower bounds.

Resolution over parities is a much weaker subsystem whose lines are disjunctions of linear equations modulo two. Efremenko and Itsykson’s CCC 2025 work develops amortized closure and strengthens lifting lower bounds for restricted-depth parity-resolution refutations. The restriction there concerns the number of inference steps along a path in the derivation graph. That is different from the constant logical depth of each formula in \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege. A long chain of shallow formulas remains allowed in the present question.

Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov’s February 2026 lifting theorem gives derivation depth \(\Omega (w^{2}/\log  S)\) for size-S parity-resolution proofs when the underlying CNF needs resolution width w. It also gives a pure quadratic size lower bound. These are meaningful advances, but a quadratic bound is polynomial, and a tradeoff requiring sufficiently deep proofs still permits polynomial-size proofs with large derivation depth. Neither gives the superpolynomial unrestricted proof-size target here.

Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret’s ITCS 2026 result studies explicit DNF formulas expressing the difficulty of proving certain algebraic circuit lower bounds. They show that these formulas do not all have polynomial-size \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege proofs. The unresolved point is whether the formulas are tautologies: the theorem leaves open the possibility that some are simply false. They provide a conditional route to tautologicity through hardness of proving properties related to tensor rank. This separates two obligations that a completed lower-bound construction must satisfy.

Algebraic proof systems offer another route, but their representation restrictions matter. Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret’s May 2026 work gives hard CNF instances for a fragment of the Ideal Proof System represented by read-once oblivious algebraic branching programs. It overcomes the obstacle that earlier lower bounds in that line concerned purely algebraic, non-Boolean instances. It does not remove the restricted representation of certificates or establish lower bounds for full modular Frege.

The quantifiers exclude a fixed-degree lower bound such as \(n^{10}\) and require failure of every polynomial size bound at every fixed line depth. They also keep the target formulas short and efficiently constructible, so hardness cannot come from writing an exponentially large conclusion or searching indefinitely for an unnamed formula. Resolving this frontier would extend lower-bound methods to formal reasoning that can perform modular counting, an ability missing from ordinary bounded-depth Frege.

sentences: \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege uses bounded-depth proof formulas that may include modular counting connectives for a fixed prime p.
The saved target asks for explicit polynomial-size DNF tautologies requiring superpolynomial proofs at every fixed formula depth.
Modular gates can retain counting information that ordinary restriction methods erase.
A lower bound would extend the reach of proof complexity beyond the established bounded-depth systems without modular counting.
The reviewed record distinguishes logical depth within proof lines from derivation depth and explains why circuit lower bounds do not automatically imply the requested proof lower bound.

cards.context:
Proof complexity measures how long a formal explanation of a tautology must be. A short conclusion can require a much longer sequence of intermediate deductions. Restricting the depth of each intermediate formula limits the expressive power of individual statements while still allowing a long derivation and arbitrary reuse of earlier facts. Modular gates add compact statements about counts modulo p, such as parity when \(p=2\). Krajíček gives the explicit modular axiom presentation used in this card.

The corresponding problem without modular gates has been solved. Ajtai’s work gives superpolynomial lower bounds for the pigeonhole principle in bounded-depth Frege, and Pitassi, Beame and Impagliazzo strengthen these to exponential bounds. Their argument uses restrictions adapted to the combinatorics of partial matchings. Permitting modular counting defeats the direct extension of that approach: a short parity statement can remain meaningful after many ordinary variables have been fixed.

Circuit complexity provides an analogy but not a solution. Razborov and Smolensky establish lower bounds for constant-depth Boolean circuits with prime modular gates. A proof, however, is a sequence of related formulas, and every tautology itself computes the constant true function. Showing that some nonconstant function requires a large circuit therefore does not directly force long proofs of tautologies. The February 2026 work of Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov explicitly identifies this remaining gap between circuit and proof lower bounds.

Resolution over parities is a much weaker subsystem whose lines are disjunctions of linear equations modulo two. Efremenko and Itsykson’s CCC 2025 work develops amortized closure and strengthens lifting lower bounds for restricted-depth parity-resolution refutations. The restriction there concerns the number of inference steps along a path in the derivation graph. That is different from the constant logical depth of each formula in \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege. A long chain of shallow formulas remains allowed in the present question.

Itsykson, Podolskii and Shekhovtsov’s February 2026 lifting theorem gives derivation depth \(\Omega (w^{2}/\log  S)\) for size-S parity-resolution proofs when the underlying CNF needs resolution width w. It also gives a pure quadratic size lower bound. These are meaningful advances, but a quadratic bound is polynomial, and a tradeoff requiring sufficiently deep proofs still permits polynomial-size proofs with large derivation depth. Neither gives the superpolynomial unrestricted proof-size target here.

Lu, Santhanam and Tzameret’s ITCS 2026 result studies explicit DNF formulas expressing the difficulty of proving certain algebraic circuit lower bounds. They show that these formulas do not all have polynomial-size \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}[p]\)-Frege proofs. The unresolved point is whether the formulas are tautologies: the theorem leaves open the possibility that some are simply false. They provide a conditional route to tautologicity through hardness of proving properties related to tensor rank. This separates two obligations that a completed lower-bound construction must satisfy.

Algebraic proof systems offer another route, but their representation restrictions matter. Hakoniemi, Limaye and Tzameret’s May 2026 work gives hard CNF instances for a fragment of the Ideal Proof System represented by read-once oblivious algebraic branching programs. It overcomes the obstacle that earlier lower bounds in that line concerned purely algebraic, non-Boolean instances. It does not remove the restricted representation of certificates or establish lower bounds for full modular Frege.

The quantifiers exclude a fixed-degree lower bound such as \(n^{10}\) and require failure of every polynomial size bound at every fixed line depth. They also keep the target formulas short and efficiently constructible, so hardness cannot come from writing an exponentially large conclusion or searching indefinitely for an unnamed formula. Resolving this frontier would extend lower-bound methods to formal reasoning that can perform modular counting, an ability missing from ordinary bounded-depth Frege.

cards.title: Superpolynomial lower bounds for unrestricted Frege proofs
cards.formal: Is the Frege proof system not polynomially bounded? Precisely, for every \(C>0\) and \(c\ge 1\), does some propositional tautology \(\varphi\) have shortest Frege proof size \(s_{F}(\varphi )>C(|\varphi |+2)^{c}\)?
cards.definitions:
Use explicitly written Boolean formulas over propositional variables, negation \(
eg\) and material implication →. Fix the axiom schemes \(A	o (B	o A), (A	o (B	o C))	o ((A	o B)	o (A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o 
eg A)	o (A	o B)\), where A,B,C may be replaced uniformly within an instance by any formulas. A proof is a finite sequence of formulas, each either an instance of one of these schemes or inferred from two earlier lines A and \(A	o B\) by modus ponens. Its last line is \(\varphi\). There are no undischarged assumptions and no extension rule introducing abbreviations for other formulas. Previously derived lines may be reused arbitrarily. Intermediate formulas may have arbitrary depth and length; there is no independent cap on a line’s size. Variables not occurring in \(\varphi\) may occur in ordinary axiom instances and inference lines. A tautology is a formula true under every Boolean assignment. Fix a standard binary encoding with variable indices in binary and explicitly encoded connectives, delimiters and inference references. The input size |\(\varphi |\) and the proof size are their full bit lengths, including every repeated formula occurrence. The minimum over all such proofs is \(s_{F}(\varphi )\). Standard finite Frege presentations are polynomially equivalent, so polynomial boundedness is independent of this choice of basis. The question concerns existence of proofs, without a uniform algorithm to generate either the hard tautologies or their shortest proofs.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that no one polynomial bounds the minimum Frege proof size of every tautology, or refute this by proving a universal bound \(s_{F}(\varphi )\le C(|\varphi |+2)^{c}\) for fixed C,c. A fixed-degree lower bound, a lower bound for a restricted subsystem, or hardness of searching for proofs is not a complete affirmative answer. An explicit efficiently generated hard family would be a stronger form of a positive solution, but is not required by the quantified statement.
cards.why: A defining lower-bound problem for formal reasoning. It asks whether an elementary, robust and powerful language of efficiently checkable proofs necessarily fails to certify some short tautologies with polynomial-size derivations.

importance.reason: A central unresolved step in the Cook–Reckhow program, beyond the systems for which current general lower-bound methods succeed.

progress.text: Cook–Reckhow formalize polynomially bounded proof systems and prove robustness of Frege under standard choices of presentation.
Buss proves polynomial-size Frege proofs of the pigeonhole principle, demonstrating why a central resolution lower-bound example does not work here.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No unconditional superpolynomial lower bound for unrestricted Frege proof size was found in the checked primary sources. The April 2026 tree-like result has a line-size cap, the formalization result concerns bounded-depth proofs, and the June 2026 algebraic result does not translate into the required propositional lower bound.

context_blocks.text: Frege systems formalize ordinary propositional deduction with finitely many rule patterns. A proof may introduce a useful intermediate lemma, combine it with other lemmas and reuse it later. Each step is easy to check syntactically. The open question asks whether this familiar form of deduction must sometimes produce certificates whose size exceeds every polynomial in the statement being proved.

The distinction between the size of a statement and the number of its variables matters. A formula on n variables may itself have exponential length in n. An exponential lower bound expressed only in n can therefore be small relative to the actual input. This card compares the complete proof encoding directly with |\(\varphi |\), and counts the sizes of all lines rather than treating a very large intermediate formula as a single unit of cost.

Cook and Reckhow placed these questions in a general theory of efficiently checkable proof systems. There exists some polynomially bounded propositional proof system if and only if \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\). Consequently, \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{coNP}\) would imply a positive answer here. The reverse implication is not established: proving that this particular proof language is inefficient would leave open the possibility that a different language provides short certificates for every tautology.

Short certificates and efficient discovery are separate issues. A failed search through proofs of length at most a million says nothing about all longer proofs, and exponential running time for one search strategy does not establish a lower bound on the shortest proof. Even a universal polynomial size bound would be an existence theorem; it would not by itself supply a polynomial-time algorithm that finds those proofs.

The pigeonhole principle explains why lower bounds for weaker systems have not directly extended to Frege. Its propositional encoding asserts that \(n+1\) pigeons cannot be injected into n holes. Although the familiar encoding requires exponentially large resolution refutations, Buss proved in 1987 that it has polynomial-size Frege proofs. The stronger system can organize counting arguments that clause-by-clause resolution cannot express economically.

Wigderson’s textbook records the unrestricted lower bound as Open Problem 6.10, after surveying systems that already admit strong lower bounds. Frege permits arbitrary Boolean formulas as intermediate assertions. Removing a fixed-depth restriction therefore changes the available reasoning, even if the final tautologies are shallow. A theorem about bounded-depth Frege must control all proofs allowed by its depth bound; it does not control proofs that use deeper intermediate lemmas.

A substantial 2026 result by de Rezende, Engström, Ghannane and Risse gives superpolynomial refutation-length lower bounds for tree-like Frege with bounded line size, including a stronger semantic version. Their explicit families contain formulas for which almost every sampled instance is hard under the prescribed cap. The result is useful because the restricted systems can still efficiently handle several standard combinatorial benchmarks.

The line cap is essential to interpreting that theorem. Without such a cap, ordinary tree-like Frege polynomially simulates general Frege. The usual simulation can enlarge intermediate formulas, however, so it does not preserve the restriction used by the new lower bound. In the semantic setting, sufficiently large lines can even package a whole inconsistent input at once. The paper explicitly explains this obstruction to transferring its theorem to unrestricted Frege.

Davis and Robere’s April 2026 work studies another layer: short proofs of statements asserting that certain bounded-depth proofs must be long. They show that a relatively weak system, \(Res(\log )\), can formalize strong bounded-depth Frege lower bounds in the specified parameter regime. This is progress on the complexity of proving lower bounds themselves, while the underlying lower-bound target retains restrictions on depth and line size.

Alekseev’s June 2026 journal paper gives exponential bit-size lower bounds for a powerful algebraic system with extension variables. It emphasizes that its Binary Value Principle input is not the corresponding translation of a polynomial-size propositional CNF. Thus the algebraic theorem does not establish the propositional Frege lower bound, despite the strength of the algebraic proof system on suitable translations.

Extended Frege is a separate, stronger target elsewhere in the catalogue: it adds variables naming previously written computations. A lower bound for Extended Frege would imply one for Frege, whereas a Frege lower bound need not survive those abbreviations. The present question is already a central obstacle because it asks for a limitation on broad propositional reasoning with unrestricted intermediate formulas and unrestricted reuse of lemmas.

cards.title: Existence of p-optimal proof systems
cards.formal: Does there exist a Cook–Reckhow proof system P for propositional tautologies such that, for every Cook–Reckhow proof system Q for the same tautologies, there is a deterministic polynomial-time translation \(t_{Q}\) satisfying \(\mathrm{P}(t_{Q}(\pi ))=Q(\pi )\) for every finite binary proof string \(\pi\)?
cards.why: Asks whether one efficiently checkable proof formalism can efficiently absorb every other such formalism.

progress.text: Theorem \(2.1(ii)\) relates polynomial simulation of all propositional proof systems to optimal tautology recognition and finite-consistency proof construction; \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) implies this existence.
Q1 explicitly retains (p-)optimality for TAUT as open. New oracle constructions show barriers for relativizing answers even with assumptions about the polynomial hierarchy.
ICALP work on recursive jump operators gives oracle barriers and results for other languages, while retaining the propositional optimality questions.

cards.definitions: Fix an explicit binary syntax for Boolean formulas built from indexed variables, AND, OR and NOT. A tautology evaluates to true under every assignment to its variables; TAUT is the set of encodings of such formulas. A Cook–Reckhow proof system is a total function \(\mathrm{P}:\{0,1\}*\to\)TAUT, computed by one uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine in time polynomial in its input length, whose range is all of TAUT. A string \(\pi\) proves formula F when \(\mathrm{P}(\pi )=F\). Soundness requires every output to be a tautology; completeness requires every tautology to occur as an output. There is no polynomial upper bound on the shortest proof of every formula. In this total-function presentation, strings that would be malformed proofs in a conventional calculus may instead produce a fixed tautology such as \(x_{1}\lor \neg x_{1}\). A simulation translation is total and satisfies the equality on all strings, preserving the exact output formula. Its program, polynomial exponent and constants may depend on Q and P, but not on \(\pi\). The order is \(\exists \mathrm{P} \forall Q \exists t_{Q} \forall \pi\). No algorithm taking an arbitrary program for Q and producing its translator is required. Neither advice, randomization nor an oracle is allowed in the systems or translations. Polynomial translation time also bounds the translated proof length polynomially in |\(\pi |\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that one sound and complete polynomial-time proof system admits the required polynomial-time translations from every other such system, or prove that for every candidate P some sound and complete Q has no such translation. A proof-length comparison without an efficient translation proves only ordinary optimality. Refuting a particular named proof system’s p-optimality does not exclude all systems.

context_blocks.title: One common format for efficiently checked proofs
context_blocks.text: Different proof calculi can establish the same tautology with very different amounts of work. The question asks whether one format can accept a polynomial-time translation of any already-given proof in any other efficiently checkable format. The translator receives the proof; it is not being asked to discover a proof from the formula alone.

context_blocks.title: A simple simulation
context_blocks.text: Suppose Q is a proof system and another system merely adds a leading marker to each Q-proof. Removing the marker translates those proofs back with linear overhead. More generally, any fixed finite collection of sound systems can be combined using a system tag. The question quantifies over every sound polynomial-time system, so combining a predetermined finite list does not finish it.

context_blocks.title: Three distinct notions
context_blocks.text: Ordinary optimality asks only that comparably short proofs exist in the common system. P-optimality additionally asks for efficient translations of the given proofs. Polynomial boundedness instead asks that every tautology have a proof polynomial in the formula’s own length. A p-optimal system could still have very long proofs of some tautologies, so this target does not by itself say \(\mathrm{NP}=\mathrm{coNP}\).

context_blocks.title: Known connections and current limits
context_blocks.text: Krajíček and Pudlák connect p-optimality with a tautology recognizer that is optimal up to polynomial overhead on positive inputs, compared with each other correct recognizer. Their theorem also gives the conditional implication from \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Egidy’s February 2026 paper retains the question as open and proves limitations of relativizing arguments; the oracle supplied to those machines is extra computational power, absent from this card.

context_blocks.title: Later work on improving proof systems
context_blocks.text: The ICALP 2026 paper studies when the absence of an ordinary optimal system entails an effective procedure producing stronger systems. Its oracle and other-language results leave p-optimal propositional proof systems unresolved. Ordinary optimality, a procedure for improving systems, and efficient proof translation are related but separately quantified properties.

sentences: Does one propositional proof system efficiently translate proofs from every other efficiently checkable system?
The translation must preserve the proved formula and run in time polynomial in the given proof length.
Each simulated system may have its own translator and polynomial.
This is stronger than comparing proof lengths alone, and different from requiring short proofs of every tautology.
The 2026 oracle and jump-operator results leave the ordinary, oracle-free existence question open.

cards.title: Complete disjoint NP pairs
cards.formal: Do disjoint languages \(A,B\in \mathrm{NP}\) exist such that, for every disjoint pair \(C,D\in \mathrm{NP}\), there is a deterministic polynomial-time function f with \(f(C)\subseteq A\) and \(f(D)\subseteq B\)?
cards.definitions: All four languages consist of finite binary strings. NP means membership has a polynomial-length certificate checked by a deterministic polynomial-time verifier. Disjoint means \(A\cap B=\varnothing\) and \(C\cap D=\varnothing\). The total function \(f:\{0,1\}*\to \{0,1\}\)* may depend on \((C,D)\); its running-time polynomial need not be universal across pairs. No requirement is imposed on \(f(x)\) when \(x\notin C\cup D\). Completeness uses one function for both sides, not two unrelated reductions.

context_blocks.text: A disjoint NP pair expresses two efficiently certifiable cases that cannot occur together. Complete pairs would provide a universal object for this kind of promise complexity.

Canonical disjoint pairs arise from propositional proof systems, tying the question to proof simulation and finite incompleteness. The existence of a p-optimal proof system would imply a complete pair, but the converse is not asserted. This card asks the pair-completeness question itself.

cards.why: Test the existence of universal promise problems in a class closely connected with proof-system strength and feasible incompleteness.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, with the specified quantifiers, model and guarantees. A conditional theorem settles only that conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

cards.definitions:
A propositional formula uses Boolean variables, negation \(
eg\) and implication →, with the usual truth tables; other connectives are fixed abbreviations. A tautology is true under every Boolean assignment. A literal is a variable or its negation, a clause is a disjunction of literals, and a CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses. The empty clause is false. A Resolution refutation is a finite sequence ending in the empty clause, each line being an input clause or the resolvent \(C\lor D\) of earlier clauses \(C\lor x\) and \(D\lor 
eg x\). Lines can be reused, so the proof is a directed acyclic derivation, not necessarily a tree. Fix Extended Frege as follows: ordinary Frege lines are substitution instances of \(A	o (B	o A), (A	o (B	o C))	o ((A	o B)	o (A	o C))\), and \((
eg B	o 
eg A)	o (A	o B)\), or follow by modus ponens from A and \(A	o B\). One may also introduce an extension axiom \(z\leftrightarrow B\), where z is fresh, does not occur in the target F, and B uses only original variables and previously introduced extension variables. Here \(z\leftrightarrow B\) abbreviates \((z	o B)\land (B	o z)\). The final line is F, containing no extension variables. Formulas, proofs and line references have explicit finite binary encodings; length counts the whole encoding. Standard alternative Frege bases and symbol-count conventions are polynomially equivalent. The input 1ˢ is a unary string, so the permitted time is polynomial in s, not log s. The transformation receives F and s but no EF proof. It must preserve the tautology/unsatisfiability equivalence for every F and every s, even if s is smaller than the shortest proof or F is not a tautology. Only the short-Resolution-refutation guarantee is conditional on an EF proof of length at most s. Resolution is represented by refuting a CNF, while Frege proves a tautology; this explicitly implements the source’s comparison of proof systems over their natural encodings.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove or refute the existence of R,p,q satisfying all these conditions. The requested notion is effective polynomial simulation as in Definition 2.5 of the source. A polynomial procedure that converts a supplied EF proof is an additional, stronger guarantee and is not required. A lower bound on Resolution proofs of the original untransformed formula alone does not refute this claim.

context_blocks.title: Can preprocessing change the proof-size comparison?
context_blocks.text: Resolution is a basic way to certify that a set of clauses is inconsistent. Extended Frege additionally uses named intermediate formulas, allowing compact reuse of complicated expressions. The question asks whether a uniformly efficient transformation of the statement can make Resolution proofs as short, up to a polynomial, as EF proofs.

context_blocks.title: A Resolution step
context_blocks.text: From \(x\lor y\) and \(\neg x\), Resolution derives y. Together with the clause \(\neg y\), it then derives the empty clause and certifies inconsistency. Larger derivations reuse earlier clauses. An extension variable, by contrast, can name a compound formula and be reused wherever that formula is needed.

context_blocks.title: Why the extra input matters
context_blocks.text: The transformation is given a proposed proof-size allowance s. It may spend polynomial time in that allowance, even if the statement itself is short. It must preserve correctness for all allowances, but it needs to guarantee a short output refutation only when an EF proof fits within the allowance. The actual proof is never supplied to it.

context_blocks.title: The known separation answers a different comparison
context_blocks.text: Ordinary polynomial simulation compares proofs of the same statement. Known Resolution lower bounds rule out ordinary simulation of Extended Frege. Effective simulation allows the statement to change through a correctness-preserving transformation, so those lower bounds do not automatically answer this question.

context_blocks.title: A later example of the distinction
context_blocks.text: Buss and Yolcu show that regular Resolution effectively simulates unrestricted Resolution, despite known exponential separations when both systems must use the same formula. Regular Resolution forbids resolving a variable twice along a derivation path. Their result demonstrates that the distinction has mathematical force, but does not provide an effective simulation of EF.

sentences: Resolution refutes inconsistent clauses, while Extended Frege permits named intermediate Boolean formulas.

An answer would clarify whether efficient preprocessing can overcome the proof-size gap between these systems.

cards.definitions:
A literal is \(x_{i}\) or its negation \(
eg x_{i}\). A clause is a disjunction of literals and a CNF F is a finite conjunction of clauses over variables \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\); unsatisfiable means no Boolean assignment satisfies every clause. Resolution derives \(C\lor D\) from \(C\lor x_{i}\) and \(D\lor 
eg x_{i}\), and allows weakening from C to \(C\lor D\); input clauses can be used as axioms. A refutation derives the empty clause. A tree-like proof uses each derived occurrence as a premise at most once, duplicating occurrences when necessary; \(S_{T}(F)\) is the minimum number of leaves, rather than total literal count. A configuration proof starts with no stored clauses and at each step downloads an input clause, erases a stored clause, or adds a resolvent/weakening of clauses currently stored; it ends with the empty clause stored. \(CSpace(F)\) is the minimum, over such proofs with unrestricted length, of the maximum number of simultaneously stored clauses. For PCR fix K and use the polynomial ring \(K[x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n},y_{1},\ldots ,y_{n}]\), where \(y_{i}\) represents \(
eg x_{i}\). A line P means \(\mathrm{P}=0\). Logical axioms are \(z^{2}- z\) for each z among \(x_{i},y_{i}\) and \(x_{i}+y_{i}- 1\). The encoding of a clause is the product of its false-literal indicators: \(x_{i}\) contributes \(y_{i}\) and \(
eg x_{i}\) contributes \(x_{i}\). From P,Q derive \(\alpha \mathrm{P}+ eta Q\) for \(\alpha , eta \in K\); from P derive zP for any literal variable z. A PCR refutation derives 1. Its configurations may download axioms, erase lines or add an inference whose premises are stored. The monomial space of a configuration is the number of distinct formal monomials with nonzero coefficients occurring anywhere in its stored polynomials, counted once across all lines; coefficients and exponents are not separately charged. \(MSpace_{K}(F)\) is the minimum maximum monomial space over all PCR refutations. Every proof is finite and minima concern the specified syntactic systems. The source’s relation \(A\preceq B\) permits \(A(F)\le ((B(F))\log  n)^{O(1)}; \approx\) means both directions. The harmless +1 terms here cover one-leaf or other constant-size cases. No polynomial-length restriction is imposed on the space-minimizing proof.

cards.definitions: Targets are Boolean functions \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) computed by finite acyclic fan-in-two AND/OR and unary NOT circuits with constants and one output. The target description explicitly lists gates and wire indices; its binary length is at most a supplied bound \(s\). A single oracle Turing machine \(A\) receives \(1^n,1^s\) and binary rationals \(0<\varepsilon,\delta<1/2\), and may query \(f(x)\) at any chosen \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Queries may be adaptive and cost the time to write the query plus one step for the answer. The learner has independent fair random coins and no advice, target description or additional oracle. It outputs an explicit deterministic Boolean circuit \(H\) over the same basis. For every permitted input and target it must satisfy \(\Pr_{A\text{ coins}}[2^{-n}|\{x:H(x)\ne f(x)\}|\le\varepsilon]\ge1-\delta\). There is one fixed polynomial \(p\) bounding its time, queries and output length on every random tape by \(p(n+s+\lceil1/\varepsilon\rceil+\lceil\log_2(1/\delta)\rceil+\operatorname{len}(\varepsilon)+\operatorname{len}(\delta))\). The hypothesis need not lie within the target’s size bound; its encoding must obey this output bound. The quantifiers range over every \(n,s\ge1\) and every function with a target description of size at most \(s\). P is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic polynomial-time Turing machines. NP consists of languages with polynomial-length witnesses checked by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time verifier. Equality concerns languages on all binary inputs, not promise classes. The conclusion is deterministic P equals NP even though the learner is randomized. The implication allows arbitrary proofs and use of the fixed learner code; it is not restricted to black-box reductions.

cards.definitions:
A language is a set of finite binary strings. It belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\) if membership has certificates of length polynomial in the string length that a fixed deterministic polynomial-time verifier can check.

A Cook–Reckhow proof system for \(L\) is a total deterministic polynomial-time computable function
\[f:\{0,1\}^{*}\longrightarrow\{0,1\}^{*},\qquad \operatorname{range}(f)=L.\]
The input \(\pi\) is a proof and \(f(\pi)\) is the statement it proves. Thus every output is in \(L\), and every member of \(L\) has some proof. The running time is polynomial in \(|\pi|\), including writing the output. No polynomial bound in the statement length is imposed on the shortest proof. The system is one uniform algorithm, with no nonuniform advice.

For two systems \(f,g\) for the same language, \(f\) simulates \(g\) if there is a polynomial \(p\) such that
\[\forall \pi\in\{0,1\}^{*}\ \exists \sigma\in\{0,1\}^{*}:\quad f(\sigma)=g(\pi),\quad |\sigma|\leq p(|\pi|).\]
The polynomial may depend on the two systems, but not on the individual proof. The system \(f\) is optimal if it simulates every total polynomial-time system \(g\) whose range is exactly \(L\).

Only the existence of these short translated proofs is required. Requiring a polynomial-time algorithm that computes \(\sigma\) from \(\pi\) defines the stronger notion of \(p\)-optimality, which is not the target here. Optimality also does not say that all statements have polynomial-length proofs: the comparison is against competing proof systems, not directly against statement length.

This card selects the existential question explicitly stated on page 2 of the source, making its broad page-3 discussion concrete. It asks for at least one language outside \(\mathrm{NP}\), without requiring arbitrarily high complexity or choosing the tautology language in advance. Such a language is automatically computably enumerable, because it is the range of \(f\); decidability is not an additional requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an unconditional example of a language \(L\notin\mathrm{NP}\) and prove that it has an optimal system under the stated simulation relation, or prove that every language admitting such an optimal system belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\). A conditional existence theorem, an oracle construction, or an example using advice or a weaker simulation relation does not by itself settle this question.

These are limitations on arguments that remain valid relative to arbitrary oracles, rather than a universal negative answer in the ordinary computational model.

cards.definitions:
A CNF formula is an explicit conjunction of clauses over finitely many Boolean variables. Each clause is a disjunction of literals, where a literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(|F|\) be its ordinary binary encoding length, including literal indices and clause boundaries. Variables may be renamed consecutively in polynomial time.

A Resolution derivation is a finite sequence of clauses. Each line is an input clause of \(F\), or follows from two earlier lines by
\[\frac{A\lor x\qquad B\lor\neg x}{A\lor B},\]
where neither \(A\) nor \(B\) contains the pivot variable \(x\). Repeated literals are identified. A refutation ends in the empty clause, which is false under every assignment. Its length is the number of clauses in the sequence. Earlier lines may be reused: this is general directed-acyclic-graph Resolution, with no tree-like or regularity restriction.

The integer \(s\geq1\) is encoded in unary, so the input length is proportional to \(|F|+s\). The short refutation is promised to exist but is not given to the algorithm. Counting total proof symbols instead of clauses changes this polynomial-time question only by polynomial factors, since every clause uses variables of \(F\).

One fixed uniform deterministic algorithm must halt within a fixed polynomial bound on every input. It must output SAT whenever \(F\) is satisfiable, and UNSAT whenever \(F\) has a refutation of length at most \(s\). These cases are disjoint by soundness of Resolution. If \(F\) is unsatisfiable but all its Resolution refutations have length greater than \(s\), either output is allowed. Malformed encodings can be rejected immediately.

No satisfying assignment or refutation has to be output. In particular, the task does not ask whether a refutation of length at most \(s\) exists on every input: an UNSAT output is allowed even when all Resolution refutations are longer. This promise distinction is the decision formulation of weak automatability, corresponding to allowing efficiently checkable proofs in another fixed proof system instead of insisting on Resolution output.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct the stated deterministic polynomial-time separator, or prove that no such separator exists. A conditional obstruction must state its hypothesis explicitly. Hardness of finding a Resolution refutation, estimating its minimum length, or solving unrestricted SAT does not establish hardness of this particular promise separator without a reduction that respects its two promised cases.

The latter side may include unsatisfiable formulas, so it does not give the SAT-versus-short-refutation promise required here.

cards.title: Log-rank conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\) and \(k\ge 1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to \{0,1\}\), on arbitrary nonempty finite sets X,Y, satisfies $D(f)\le C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k$, where \(r(f)\) is the real rank of its \(0/1\) communication matrix and \(D(f)\) is its deterministic communication complexity?
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\) and Bob receives \(y\in Y\). Both know the complete function f and the protocol. They exchange bits interactively; each next transmitted bit is a deterministic function of the sender’s own input and the previous transcript. A binary protocol tree specifies whose turn it is, and every leaf has a Boolean output that must equal \(f(x,y)\) for every input pair reaching it. \(D(f)\) is the minimum, over all such exact protocols, of the maximum number of transmitted bits on an input pair. The number of rounds and the local computation are unrestricted; protocol description length is not charged. The communication matrix \(M_{f}\) has rows X, columns Y, and entry \(f(x,y); r(f)=\operatorname{rank}_{R}(M_{f})\) is ordinary matrix rank over the real numbers. The +2 makes the statement unambiguous for rank zero or one. The same constants C,k must work for all matrix dimensions and all functions. There are no undefined entries, input promises, random bits, quantum messages, approximation errors, or restrictions to one-way protocols. Sign rank and approximate rank are different parameters.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.

importance.reason: A flagship structural conjecture linking deterministic protocols and matrix rank, with many equivalent combinatorial formulations and a large quantitative gap.

progress.text: Lovász and Saks formulate the conjecture relating real rank and deterministic communication; the 2026 equivalent-formulations paper gives the original attribution and related graph versions.
Lovett proves \(D(f)=O(\sqrt{r} \log  r)\), the first general sublinear-in-rank upper bound; the later discrepancy paper explains and improves this step.
Göös, Pitassi, and Watson establish nearly quadratic lower bounds in log-rank, along with separations involving communication partition number.
Sudakov and Tomon improve the universal upper bound to \(O(\sqrt{r})\). The 2023 preprint is published online in 2024 and in Mathematical Programming volume 212 in 2025.

Song reports an explicit lower bound \(\Omega ((\log  r)^{2}/\log  \log  r)\) via alphabet-preserving lifting. The card records this as a preprint refinement, not an independently certified new universal separation record.
The CCC 2026 version of Hambardzumyan–Lovett–Shirley gives the \(O(r \log  r)\) signed-rectangle decomposition and equivalent formulations. It explicitly leaves the general conjecture open.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in the August 2026 CCC version of Hambardzumyan–Lovett–Shirley. Checked through 10 September 2026. The established general upper bound is \(O(\sqrt{r})\); recent fixed-polynomial lower-bound refinements and signed-decomposition equivalences do not settle the conjecture.

context_blocks.text: Matrix rank gives a general lower bound on communication. A protocol using at most d bits has at most \(2^{d}\) leaves, and the inputs reaching each leaf form a rectangle \(A\times B\). Summing the indicator matrices of the output-one rectangles represents \(M_{f}\) as a sum of at most \(2^{d}\) rank-one matrices. Consequently \(\log _{2}r(f)\le D(f)\) when \(r(f)\ge 1\). The conjecture asks whether this algebraic obstruction controls deterministic communication up to a polynomial.

An elementary upper bound goes in the other direction but is much larger. A rank-r Boolean matrix has at most 2ʳ distinct rows: choose r columns that determine every row, and record their Boolean entries. Alice can identify her row with at most r bits, after which Bob can determine the answer and send one output bit. This protocol makes clear why the question concerns the gap between rank and its logarithm.

A low-rank factorization permits arbitrary real coefficients and cancellation. A protocol instead needs a recursively organized partition into monochromatic rectangles. Moving between these kinds of structure is the main difficulty. Lovett used discrepancy to obtain an \(O(\sqrt{r} \log  r)\) communication bound; Sudakov and Tomon remove the logarithmic factor using a stronger discrepancy estimate for sparse matrices. The resulting \(O(\sqrt{r})\) remains far larger than a polynomial in log r.
Lower-bound constructions show that a linear bound in log-rank is too optimistic. Göös, Pitassi, and Watson obtain a nearly quadratic separation through query-to-communication lifting.

Song’s August 2026 preprint revisits the construction without first converting its pointer alphabet to Boolean bits and reports a more precise lower bound \(\Omega ((\log  r)^{2}/\log  \log  r)\). This still has a fixed polynomial exponent and therefore supports no refutation of log-rank.

A recent equivalent formulation isolates the role of cancellation more sharply. Hambardzumyan, Lovett, and Shirley show that a rank-r Boolean matrix is a signed sum of \(O(r \log  r)\) rectangle indicator matrices. The open task can then be expressed as converting such signed decompositions into positive disjoint rectangle decompositions with quasipolynomial growth. This theorem supplies a new formulation, while the needed conversion remains unresolved.

cards.title: Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}, H(f)\le C I(f)\), where \(H(f)\) is the base-two Shannon entropy of its squared Fourier coefficients and \(I(f)\) is its total influence under the uniform distribution, as defined below?
cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). For \(S\subseteq [n]\), let \(\chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with \(\chi _{\varnothing}=1\), and let \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum _{x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}}f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\). Put \(q_{S}=\hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\); Parseval gives \(\sum _{S} q_{S}=1\). Define \(H(f)=\sum _{S} q_{S} \log _{2}(1/q_{S})\), with a zero summand when \(q_{S}=0\). If x is uniform and \(x^{\oplus i}\) differs only by flipping coordinate i, define \(I_{i}(f)=\Pr [f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus i})]\) and \(I(f)=\sum _{i=1}^{n} I_{i}(f)=\sum _{S} |S|q_{S}\). All Boolean functions are quantified, without circuit-size, monotonicity, balance, or efficient-computability assumptions. The same C must work for all dimensions and all functions. Constant functions have \(H(f)=I(f)=0\) and satisfy the non-strict inequality.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central structural conjecture connecting sensitivity to spectral information. Its resolution would sharpen our understanding of Boolean functions and spectral learning, while testing a relation that fails without the Boolean constraint.

importance.reason: A longstanding, broadly consequential conjecture in Boolean function analysis, with direct learning-theory implications and active 2026 progress that still leaves the universal classical inequality open.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The June 2026 primary paper explicitly retains classical FEI as open and proves only specified classes. The August 2026 disproof is of the quantum extension. No classical resolution was found in the checked sources; the formulation uses Shannon entropy, uniform measure and scalar Boolean functions throughout.

context_blocks.text: The Fourier expansion expresses a Boolean rule as a linear combination of parity tests on subsets of its inputs. Squaring the coefficients produces a probability distribution on these subsets. Its entropy measures how dispersed that distribution is; total influence measures the expected size of a subset sampled from it. The conjecture says that the Boolean constraint forces the first quantity to be at most a constant times the second, even though there are exponentially many possible subsets.

This is not a generic fact about probability distributions on subsets. A distribution uniform on the n singleton sets has entropy \(\log _{2} n\) but expected set size one. It is the squared Fourier spectrum of the normalized real function \(g(x)=(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/\sqrt{n}\), which is generally not Boolean. Conversely, a parity of all n inputs has entropy zero and total influence n. These examples explain both why Boolean-valuedness matters and why the proposed inequality has only one direction.

A useful consequence would be spectral concentration: for any \(0<\delta <1\), all but \(\delta\) of the Fourier mass could be captured by at most \(2^{C I(f)/\delta}\) coefficients. This follows by applying Markov’s inequality to the surprisal \(\log _{2}(1/q_{S})\) of a random spectral subset. It supplies a quantitative connection between stability under individual bit flips and approximation by a short linear combination of parities. The dependence on \(\delta\) is essential; the claim is not an accuracy-independent support bound.

O’Donnell, Wright and Zhou establish the conjecture for symmetric Boolean functions and for functions computed by read-once decision trees. Their paper also explains the connection to learning DNF formulas: the conjecture would imply polynomial Fourier concentration for a DNF with polynomially many terms, at each fixed approximation accuracy. This is a structural learning-theory consequence, rather than an assertion that arbitrary Boolean functions become efficiently learnable.

A general bound proved by Han is \(H(f)\le O(I(f)+\sum _{i} I_{i}(f) \log (1/I_{i}(f)))\). The extra term records how influence is distributed across coordinates. It can exceed a constant multiple of \(I(f)\), so this does not settle the conjecture. The December 2025 revision adds an acknowledgement of related earlier work by Keller, Mossel and Schlank. Bounds on min-entropy concern the largest Fourier coefficient alone and must not be substituted for a Shannon-entropy bound.

González, MacManus and Pereyra’s June 2026 revision verifies additional classes, including \(\delta\)-tribes and functions with specified separation properties. Their method splits on selected coordinates and stops at restrictions already satisfying FEI. It also demonstrates failure of a stronger sufficient inequality when the splitting coordinate is chosen badly. Those examples do satisfy FEI when handled with a suitable coordinate, so they expose a limitation of that inductive route rather than a counterexample to the conjecture.

Slote’s August 2026 preprint disproves a quantum analogue using Hermitian unitary operators with flat, very large Pauli expansions. For the constructed degree-d operators, the spectral entropy grows quadratically in d while the influence grows linearly. These are quantum Boolean functions, not scalar maps on the classical Boolean cube. The result makes the distinction between the two settings concrete and does not provide a classical counterexample.

A positive solution would expose a strong restriction on the spectra of every Boolean computation, independently of how that computation is represented. A negative solution would identify Boolean functions whose spectral information greatly exceeds their sensitivity to input changes. Either outcome would clarify a basic link between combinatorial stability, harmonic analysis and the possibility of learning from sparse spectral descriptions.

cards.title: Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C\ge 1\) such that, for all integers \(n\ge 1\) and \(1\le d\le n\) and every real multilinear polynomial f of degree at most d satisfying \(0\le f(x)\le 1\) for every \(x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}\), some coordinate i satisfies \(Inf_{i}(f)\ge (\operatorname{Var}(f)/d)^{C}\)?
cards.definitions: All expectations use the uniform distribution on \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}\). Write \(f(x)=\sum_{S\subseteq [n]} \hat\{f\}(S)\prod _{j\in S}x_{j}\), with \(\hat\{f\}(S)=E_{x}[f(x)\prod _{j\in S}x_{j}]\); degree at most d means \(\hat\{f\}(S)=0\) when |\(S|>d\). Let \(x^{\oplus i}\) be x with just coordinate i negated. Define \(\operatorname{Var}(f)=E[(f- E f)^{2}]=\sum_{S\ne \varnothing}\hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\) and \(Inf_{i}(f)=E[(f(x)- f(x^{\oplus i}))^{2}]/4=\Sigma\)_{S∋i}\(\hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\). This is squared \(\mathrm{L}_{2}\) influence, with the factor \(1/4\) fixed explicitly. The pointwise range restriction holds on the entire cube, not merely with high probability. Coefficients may be arbitrary real numbers; no sparsity, coefficient-size, block structure, Boolean-valued-output or quantum-realizability promise is imposed. C must be independent of n,d,f and its variance. Constant polynomials satisfy the inequality trivially with both sides zero. The one-power notation is a normalized version of a polynomial lower bound in variance and inverse degree; because \(\operatorname{Var}(f)\le 1/4\), fixed positive prefactors can be absorbed by increasing C.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove one universal exponent C works for every admissible polynomial, or show that for every proposed C there is an admissible polynomial of positive variance for which every coordinate has influence smaller than \((\operatorname{Var}(f)/d)^{C}\). Refuting one particular exponent is insufficient to refute existence of some universal exponent. An exponential-in-degree influence bound, a theorem only after randomly fixing coordinates, or a result for a restricted subclass is partial progress.
cards.why: A central structural question about real-valued Boolean-cube functions, with direct consequences for when quantum query algorithms can have large classical simulation costs.

importance.reason: Connects a basic dimension-independent influence bound to almost-everywhere classical simulation of quantum queries, bringing Boolean analysis and quantum complexity together.
