context_blocks.text: A low-degree polynomial contains interactions among only a few variables at a time, yet it may involve a very large number of variables overall. The question asks whether its variation must be detectably concentrated on at least one coordinate. The desired lower bound depends on the interaction degree and on how much the function varies, while having no dependence on the ambient number n of input bits.

Dependence on variance is essential. Consider \(f(x)=1/2+(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/(2n)\). This degree-one polynomial always lies in \([0,1]\), but \(\operatorname{Var}(f)=1/(4n)\) and each coordinate has influence \(1/(4n^{2})\). No positive lower bound depending only on degree could work. The example is consistent with the conjectured polynomial dependence on variance. It also distinguishes an influential coordinate relative to the function’s variation from a coordinate with a constant absolute influence.

The quantum connection comes from acceptance probabilities. A quantum algorithm making t queries to input bits has an acceptance probability represented by a bounded polynomial of degree at most 2t. If the conjecture holds, a classical procedure can repeatedly query an influential coordinate and restrict the polynomial. After sufficiently many such queries, the remaining uncertainty has small variance, allowing its mean to estimate the acceptance probability on most uniformly sampled inputs.

That consequence concerns query complexity. It does not automatically supply polynomial-time classical computation between queries, nor does it promise accurate simulation on every input. A small exceptional set can contain the entire promise domain of a quantum speedup. Also, the influential-variable conjecture is stronger than the simulation statement it implies: not every bounded low-degree polynomial is the acceptance probability of a quantum algorithm with a comparable query budget.

The distinction between bounded real outputs and Boolean outputs is substantial. The conjectured polynomial behavior is known for Boolean-valued functions, but the general real-valued case remains harder. Classical Fourier-analytic techniques yield bounds with exponential dependence on degree. These already force some influence, yet they do not provide the polynomial guarantee needed here.

One productive restriction is complete boundedness. Roughly, this requires the polynomial to remain bounded even when suitable matrix contractions replace scalar inputs, with products taken in a specified order. It is much stronger than being bounded on the scalar Boolean cube. Bansal, Sinha and de Wolf prove influential-variable bounds for completely bounded block-multilinear forms, a class connected to algorithms querying separate input blocks.

Bhattacharya’s random-restriction theorem approaches the unrestricted class differently. Fix most coordinates independently to random signs and leave roughly a \(\log (d)/d\) fraction available. Under a lower bound on the original variance, a non-negligible fraction of restrictions have a polynomially influential remaining variable. The September inequality controls the sum of square roots of influences by the number of blocks times the completely bounded norm. Its extra norm hypothesis is precisely what prevents applying it to every polynomial in this card. The paper explicitly retains the unrestricted conjecture. A historical general proof claim by Keller and Klein is withdrawn because of an error in a key lemma, and is recorded as a withdrawal rather than progress establishing the conjecture.

sentences: A bounded low-degree polynomial on the Boolean cube describes a real-valued function with controlled algebraic complexity.
The Aaronson–Ambainis conjecture asks whether some variable has influence polynomially large in the variance and inverse degree.
It predicts that meaningful variation cannot be distributed too evenly among all coordinates when the degree stays small.
The question matters for understanding when quantum query behavior admits efficient classical simulation.

The reviewed record stresses that results for random restrictions, bounded-round algorithms, or completely bounded norms impose additional structure and do not settle the unrestricted scalar-polynomial statement.

cards.context:
A low-degree polynomial contains interactions among only a few variables at a time, yet it may involve a very large number of variables overall. The question asks whether its variation must be detectably concentrated on at least one coordinate. The desired lower bound depends on the interaction degree and on how much the function varies, while having no dependence on the ambient number n of input bits.

Dependence on variance is essential. Consider \(f(x)=1/2+(x_{1}+\cdots +x_{n})/(2n)\). This degree-one polynomial always lies in \([0,1]\), but \(\operatorname{Var}(f)=1/(4n)\) and each coordinate has influence \(1/(4n^{2})\). No positive lower bound depending only on degree could work. The example is consistent with the conjectured polynomial dependence on variance. It also distinguishes an influential coordinate relative to the function’s variation from a coordinate with a constant absolute influence.

The quantum connection comes from acceptance probabilities. A quantum algorithm making t queries to input bits has an acceptance probability represented by a bounded polynomial of degree at most 2t. If the conjecture holds, a classical procedure can repeatedly query an influential coordinate and restrict the polynomial. After sufficiently many such queries, the remaining uncertainty has small variance, allowing its mean to estimate the acceptance probability on most uniformly sampled inputs.

That consequence concerns query complexity. It does not automatically supply polynomial-time classical computation between queries, nor does it promise accurate simulation on every input. A small exceptional set can contain the entire promise domain of a quantum speedup. Also, the influential-variable conjecture is stronger than the simulation statement it implies: not every bounded low-degree polynomial is the acceptance probability of a quantum algorithm with a comparable query budget.

The distinction between bounded real outputs and Boolean outputs is substantial. The conjectured polynomial behavior is known for Boolean-valued functions, but the general real-valued case remains harder. Classical Fourier-analytic techniques yield bounds with exponential dependence on degree. These already force some influence, yet they do not provide the polynomial guarantee needed here.

One productive restriction is complete boundedness. Roughly, this requires the polynomial to remain bounded even when suitable matrix contractions replace scalar inputs, with products taken in a specified order. It is much stronger than being bounded on the scalar Boolean cube. Bansal, Sinha and de Wolf prove influential-variable bounds for completely bounded block-multilinear forms, a class connected to algorithms querying separate input blocks.

cards.title: Mansour’s conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), integer \(s\ge 2\), Boolean function \(f:\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}\) representable by a DNF with at most s terms, and \(\varepsilon \in\)(\(0,1/2\)], some family \(F\subseteq 2^{[n]}\) satisfies |\(F|\le \lceil s^{C \log _{2}(1/\varepsilon )}\rceil\) and \(\sum_{S\notin F} \hat\{f\}(S)^{2}\le \varepsilon\)?
cards.definitions: A DNF is an OR of conjunctions of literals \(x_{i}=1\) or \(x_{i}=- 1; a\) satisfied formula has value +1 and an unsatisfied formula value −1. Term widths, overlaps, and the number of occurrences of a variable are unrestricted. On the uniform probability space \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}, \chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}, \chi _{\varnothing}=1\), and \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum_{x} f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\). Parseval gives \(\sum_{S} \hat\{f\}(S)^{2}=1\). Thus \(\varepsilon\)-concentration on F means that the polynomial \(g=\sum_{S\in F}\hat\{f\}(S)\chi _{S}\) has \(E[(f- g)^{2}]\le \varepsilon\). The coefficients are ordinary Walsh coefficients, not a basis adapted to a different distribution. The same C must work for all \(n,s,\varepsilon\) and f. This is an existence question about the spectrum; no efficient algorithm for finding F is part of the proposition.
cards.answer_criterion: An affirmative resolution proves the stated bound with one universal C. A negative resolution must show that for every C some admissible \(s,n,\varepsilon\) and DNF require more than \(\lceil s^{C \log _{2}(1/\varepsilon )}\rceil\) coefficients to leave squared Fourier mass at most \(\varepsilon\). A polynomial bound whose exponent has an unspecified dependence on \(\varepsilon\) would settle only the weaker fixed-accuracy form.
cards.why: A fundamental bridge between short logical formulas, sparse spectral representations, and learning with queries. The strong accuracy parameter makes the question a precise test of how much analytic structure small DNF size forces.

importance.reason: A defining conjecture in Boolean function analysis and learning theory, connecting representation size to approximate Fourier sparsity and agnostic learning.

progress.text: Mansour obtains general \(s^{O(\log  \log  s)}\) Fourier concentration for fixed error; the later sources state the full accuracy-dependent bound.
Klivans–Lee–Wan’s final ECCC revision proves the random-DNF result and corrects the read-k theorem. The random model does not cover arbitrary formulas.
O’Donnell–Wright–Zhou explain the weak and strong versions and the weaker accuracy bound implied by FEI.
Lecomte–Tan’s revision improves dependence on the read number and obtains polynomial concentration for a growing range of small read numbers.
Han proves a new Fourier entropy bound with additional individual-influence terms; this is partial progress on the broader FEI direction.
Heidari–Khardon revise generalized-Fourier learning results under Bayesian-network distributions; the setting differs from this uniform spectral conjecture.
González–MacManus–Pereyra extend FEI to further structured classes; no universal DNF concentration theorem is claimed.

cards.status_note: Open in the strong logarithmic-accuracy form stated here, following the inspected primary sources and a later-result search through 11 September 2026. Fixed-error polynomial concentration, restricted DNF models, and generalized-basis learning results do not by themselves settle this formulation.

context_blocks.text: A DNF describes a function as a short list of sufficient conditions for acceptance. Its Fourier expansion describes the same function through parity correlations. Mansour’s question asks whether a short description in the first language forces an approximately short description in the second. The number n of available variables may greatly exceed the number s of terms, yet the proposed number of relevant correlations depends only on s and the permitted error.

The approximation is measured in squared error under uniformly random inputs. It does not require exact agreement everywhere, and the approximating polynomial need not have Boolean outputs. Keeping the largest squared coefficients is the best approximation with that many Walsh characters. Consequently the question is a statement about how rapidly the sorted Fourier mass decays, independent of an algorithm’s ability to identify the important characters.

Sparsity and degree are different resources. A parity involving every variable has just one nonzero Fourier coefficient but has degree n. Conversely, restricting a polynomial to degree d can leave a number of possible coefficients that grows like \(n^{d}\). A theorem saying that high-degree coefficients have little total mass therefore does not by itself give the requested bound, which must avoid such dependence on the ambient dimension.

Even one wide conjunction can have many nonzero coefficients exactly. This does not contradict the conjecture: if the conjunction fixes w distinct coordinates, its satisfying event has probability \(2^{- w}\). Approximating its ±1-valued function by the constant −1 incurs squared error \(4\cdot 2^{- w}\). Rare accepting terms can therefore produce an exactly dense spectrum while contributing very little approximation error. Combining many overlapping terms is where the simple observation stops being sufficient.

There are two common strengths of the named conjecture. The weaker one allows \(s^{K(\varepsilon )}\) coefficients for an arbitrary function K of the error. The stronger one in this saved record asks for \(K(\varepsilon )=O(\log (1/\varepsilon ))\). O’Donnell–Wright–Zhou explicitly distinguish these statements. The card preserves the stronger target instead of treating all polynomial concentration claims as interchangeable.

The connection to Fourier entropy explains that distinction. If the Fourier entropy were \(O(\log  s)\), Markov’s inequality applied to the surprisal \(\log (1/\hat\{f\}(S)^{2})\) would capture all but \(\varepsilon\) of the mass on at most \(s^{O(1/\varepsilon )}\) coefficients. The Fourier Entropy–Influence conjecture, combined with the influence bound for DNF, would supply such an entropy estimate. This implication gives the weaker form, but its exponent does not establish the logarithmic dependence required here.

Mansour’s classical general bound gives \(s^{O(\log  \log  s)}\) coefficients at fixed accuracy. Klivans–Lee–Wan proved polynomial concentration for a specified random-DNF model and for every fixed read number. These are substantial structural results, but randomness in the formula cannot be assumed in a worst-case statement about every DNF. Their final May 2010 revision corrects an earlier issue in the read-number argument.

Lecomte–Tan sharpen the fixed-accuracy general estimate to \(s^{O(\log  \log  k)}\), where k bounds the number of terms containing a variable. Their stronger small-read theorem gives \((s/\varepsilon )^{O(\log (1/\varepsilon ))}\) concentration for read number up to a stated roughly doubly logarithmic range. The explicit \(s/\varepsilon\) base should be retained when comparing accuracy parameters. Their work also explains how control of term covers improves Fourier estimates beyond a single global norm bound.

The learning consequences depend on access to the target. Through the agnostic-learning reduction described by Klivans–Lee–Wan, suitable sparse Fourier approximation yields efficient agnostic learning under the uniform distribution with membership queries, for fixed approximation accuracy. Such queries allow selected input points; they are stronger access than an ordinary stream of independently sampled labeled examples. This conjecture should not be advertised as automatically solving every version of passive DNF learning.

Recent neighboring results retain these distinctions. Han’s 2025 entropy estimate contains an additional sum involving individual influences, rather than the full conjectured constant times total influence. González–MacManus–Pereyra’s June 2026 revision proves FEI for further classes under structural separation conditions. Neither is a universal theorem with the strong DNF accuracy bound in the question.

Heidari–Khardon’s June 2026 revision studies generalized Fourier representations associated with Bayesian networks. Its DNF learning theorem uses membership queries and a restricted distributional model; its agnostic result concerns decision trees. These changes in basis, distribution and target class are mathematically meaningful, but they do not establish concentration of every DNF in the ordinary uniform Walsh basis used here.

cards.title: Maximum influence of polynomial threshold functions
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors jointly for all integers \(n\ge 1\) and \(1\le d\le n, M(n,d)=\max\){\(I(f): f=\operatorname{sign}(p):\{- 1,1\}^{n}\to \{- 1,1\}, \deg (p)\le d\), and p has no zero on the Boolean cube}, using total influence as defined below.
cards.definitions:
A realizing polynomial p is a real polynomial in n variables of total degree at most d, with \(p(x)
e 0\) at every Boolean input. The sign is +1 for positive values and −1 for negative values. Coefficients are unrestricted real numbers; no bound on coefficient magnitude, description length, margin or number of monomials is assumed. One may take p multilinear by reducing \(x_{i}^{2}\) to 1 on the cube. The nonzero convention loses no threshold functions under a fixed sign-at-zero convention, since a sufficiently small constant perturbation preserves all assigned signs. If x is uniform on \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}\), let \(x^{i}\) denote x with coordinate i flipped. Define \(Inf_{i}(f)=\Pr [f(x)
e f(x^{i})]\), pointwise sensitivity \(s_{f}(x)=|\{i:f(x)
e f(x^{i})\}|\), and \(I(f)=\sum_{i} Inf_{i}(f)=E[s_{f}(x)]\). The constants in the requested matching asymptotic bounds must be independent of n,d,f and the realizing polynomial. Constant functions have zero influence; allowing \(d=0\) adds only these trivial cases. The maximum exists because only finitely many Boolean functions occur on a fixed cube; realizing polynomials may have arbitrary real coefficients. The earlier asymptotic Gotsman–Linial question asks for \(M(n,d)=O(d\sqrt{n})\), while an exact symmetric-extremizer conjecture was disproved.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(h(n,d)\) and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) with \(c h(n,d)\le M(n,d)\le C h(n,d)\) for all \(n\ge 1\) and \(1\le d\le n\), and prove both bounds in Lean. This must determine the joint parameter dependence, including saturation at large degree, within constant factors. No particular extremizing Boolean function is prescribed; merely refuting one candidate formula does not determine M.
cards.why: A basic unresolved relation between algebraic threshold complexity and the edge boundary of a Boolean function, central to noise sensitivity, learning and threshold-circuit analysis.

importance.reason: A foundational and quantitatively sharp Boolean-function conjecture whose surviving asymptotic form matters even though the original exact extremizer was disproved.

references.authors: Robin Kothari; Matt Kovacs-Deak; Daochen Wang; Rain Zimin Yang
references.locator: v2, 8 April 2026; §5.2 and Conjecture 2; ECCC TR26-005 revision 1

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The exact symmetric-maximizer conjecture is false, but the universal \(O(d\sqrt{n})\) influence bound remains open in the checked primary literature, including the April 2026 revisions on rational degree and Boolean surface area.

context_blocks.text: The quantitative target is the maximum influence as a function of dimension and degree. The following history concerns the asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture and the separately disproved exact-extremizer claim.

A polynomial threshold function first evaluates a low-degree real polynomial and then keeps only its sign. Linear threshold functions include majority votes and weighted voting rules. Quadratic threshold functions can also include pairwise interactions between inputs. The conjecture asks whether this algebraic simplicity forces the function to change its output relatively rarely along the edges of the Boolean cube.

Total influence counts those changes in an averaged way. If D is the number of undirected cube edges joining opposite outputs, then \(I(f)=2D/2^{n}\). The maximum possible influence of an arbitrary Boolean function is n, achieved by parity. A degree-d bound of \(C d\sqrt{n}\) would sharply restrict the boundary when d is small compared with \(\sqrt{n}\); once \(d\ge \sqrt{n}\), the elementary bound \(I(f)\le n\) already suffices with \(C=1\).

Majority shows why a square root is unavoidable. For odd n, flipping a coordinate changes majority exactly when the other \(n- 1\) coordinates split evenly, giving I(\(MAJ_{n}\))=\(n\cdot \operatorname{binom}(n- 1,(n- 1)/2)/2^{n- 1}\), asymptotic to \(\sqrt{2n/\pi}\). Thus even degree one permits influence growing with dimension. The target is not a constant influence bound for every fixed-degree function.

There is a natural higher-degree candidate: place d parallel threshold hyperplanes between consecutive central Hamming layers, then take the sign of the product of their linear equations. The sign alternates at those layers. When the layers lie near the center, their boundaries together have order \(d\sqrt{n}\). Gotsman and Linial proposed the much stronger assertion that this symmetric construction maximizes influence exactly.

Chapman disproved that exact assertion for most parameter pairs, including quadratic examples in every odd dimension at least five. The paper carefully separates its exact conjecture from Conjecture 1.2, the asymptotic statement discussed here, and leaves the latter open. Its SODA publication was in 2018; the arXiv copy was uploaded in 2021. Neither date turns the disproved exact formulation into a refutation of the remaining asymptotic question.

Products of d linear threshold signs satisfy the desired order by a simple union bound: if the product changes across an edge, at least one factor changes. Summing the factors’ influence bounds gives \(O(d\sqrt{n})\). But a general degree-d polynomial need not factor into d linear forms, and its sign need not admit such a representation. This identifies one tempting argument and the missing structural fact it would need.

Kane proved the near-optimal dimensional estimate \(I(f)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot (\log  n)^{O(d \log  d)}\cdot 2^{O(d^{2} \log  d)}\) for \(d\ge 2\). For each fixed d, this is \(\sqrt{n}\) times a polylogarithmic factor, establishing the correct exponent of n. The extra logarithms can still grow without bound, while the dependence on d is much larger than linear. Removing these losses is exactly what the displayed conjecture demands.

The proof program uses random restrictions and comparisons between Boolean and Gaussian polynomial behavior. Anti-concentration helps ensure that a small perturbation rarely carries the polynomial through zero. Such transfers must deal with coordinates of high influence and with the discrete cube’s concentrated mass. The continuous analogue is informative, but it is not a direct proof for arbitrary Boolean threshold polynomials.

For quadratic functions there are useful structural subcases. Kim, Maldonado and Wellens analyze the graph whose edges indicate nonzero quadratic coefficients and establish asymptotic estimates under restrictions such as low fractional chromatic number or few edges. This connects the influence question to the interaction graph, while leaving general dense quadratic interactions outside those special guarantees.

A 2026 paper by Chang, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proves a polylogarithmic bound, for fixed degree, on Boolean surface area \(BSA(f)=E[\sqrt{s_{f}}(x)]\). The April 27 revision strengthens its original subpolynomial estimate. This is significant new control of boundary geometry, but BSA is a different moment from \(I(f)=E[s_{f}(x)]\). A bound on the expectation of the square root does not directly bound the expectation by its square.

Indeed, pointwise \(s_{f}(x)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot \sqrt{s_{f}}(x)\) yields only \(I(f)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot BSA(f)\). Substituting the new polylogarithmic surface-area bound still leaves a factor depending on log n, with degree-dependent constants. This calculation explains why that recent theorem is compatible with the influence conjecture remaining open, without diminishing its improvement for the different boundary measure.

Kothari, Kovacs-Deak, Wang and Yang’s April 2026 revision on rational degree also restates the influence conjecture and proposes a weaker version using nondeterministic degree. Their theorem resolves a separate polynomial relation between rational and ordinary degree, rather than this threshold-degree inequality. These connections help explain the conjecture’s importance for the relationships among Boolean complexity measures, in addition to its learning and circuit applications.

cards.context:
The quantitative target is the maximum influence as a function of dimension and degree. The following history concerns the asymptotic Gotsman–Linial conjecture and the separately disproved exact-extremizer claim.

A polynomial threshold function first evaluates a low-degree real polynomial and then keeps only its sign. Linear threshold functions include majority votes and weighted voting rules. Quadratic threshold functions can also include pairwise interactions between inputs. The conjecture asks whether this algebraic simplicity forces the function to change its output relatively rarely along the edges of the Boolean cube.

Total influence counts those changes in an averaged way. If D is the number of undirected cube edges joining opposite outputs, then \(I(f)=2D/2^{n}\). The maximum possible influence of an arbitrary Boolean function is n, achieved by parity. A degree-d bound of \(C d\sqrt{n}\) would sharply restrict the boundary when d is small compared with \(\sqrt{n}\); once \(d\ge \sqrt{n}\), the elementary bound \(I(f)\le n\) already suffices with \(C=1\).

Majority shows why a square root is unavoidable. For odd n, flipping a coordinate changes majority exactly when the other \(n- 1\) coordinates split evenly, giving I(\(MAJ_{n}\))=\(n\cdot \operatorname{binom}(n- 1,(n- 1)/2)/2^{n- 1}\), asymptotic to \(\sqrt{2n/\pi}\). Thus even degree one permits influence growing with dimension. The target is not a constant influence bound for every fixed-degree function.

There is a natural higher-degree candidate: place d parallel threshold hyperplanes between consecutive central Hamming layers, then take the sign of the product of their linear equations. The sign alternates at those layers. When the layers lie near the center, their boundaries together have order \(d\sqrt{n}\). Gotsman and Linial proposed the much stronger assertion that this symmetric construction maximizes influence exactly.

Chapman disproved that exact assertion for most parameter pairs, including quadratic examples in every odd dimension at least five. The paper carefully separates its exact conjecture from Conjecture 1.2, the asymptotic statement discussed here, and leaves the latter open. Its SODA publication was in 2018; the arXiv copy was uploaded in 2021. Neither date turns the disproved exact formulation into a refutation of the remaining asymptotic question.

Products of d linear threshold signs satisfy the desired order by a simple union bound: if the product changes across an edge, at least one factor changes. Summing the factors’ influence bounds gives \(O(d\sqrt{n})\). But a general degree-d polynomial need not factor into d linear forms, and its sign need not admit such a representation. This identifies one tempting argument and the missing structural fact it would need.

Kane proved the near-optimal dimensional estimate \(I(f)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot (\log  n)^{O(d \log  d)}\cdot 2^{O(d^{2} \log  d)}\) for \(d\ge 2\). For each fixed d, this is \(\sqrt{n}\) times a polylogarithmic factor, establishing the correct exponent of n. The extra logarithms can still grow without bound, while the dependence on d is much larger than linear. Removing these losses is exactly what the displayed conjecture demands.

The proof program uses random restrictions and comparisons between Boolean and Gaussian polynomial behavior. Anti-concentration helps ensure that a small perturbation rarely carries the polynomial through zero. Such transfers must deal with coordinates of high influence and with the discrete cube’s concentrated mass. The continuous analogue is informative, but it is not a direct proof for arbitrary Boolean threshold polynomials.

For quadratic functions there are useful structural subcases. Kim, Maldonado and Wellens analyze the graph whose edges indicate nonzero quadratic coefficients and establish asymptotic estimates under restrictions such as low fractional chromatic number or few edges. This connects the influence question to the interaction graph, while leaving general dense quadratic interactions outside those special guarantees.

A 2026 paper by Chang, Slote, Volberg and Zhang proves a polylogarithmic bound, for fixed degree, on Boolean surface area \(BSA(f)=E[\sqrt{s_{f}}(x)]\). The April 27 revision strengthens its original subpolynomial estimate. This is significant new control of boundary geometry, but BSA is a different moment from \(I(f)=E[s_{f}(x)]\). A bound on the expectation of the square root does not directly bound the expectation by its square.

Indeed, pointwise \(s_{f}(x)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot \sqrt{s_{f}}(x)\) yields only \(I(f)\le \sqrt{n}\cdot BSA(f)\). Substituting the new polylogarithmic surface-area bound still leaves a factor depending on log n, with degree-dependent constants. This calculation explains why that recent theorem is compatible with the influence conjecture remaining open, without diminishing its improvement for the different boundary measure.

Kothari, Kovacs-Deak, Wang and Yang’s April 2026 revision on rational degree also restates the influence conjecture and proposes a weaker version using nondeterministic degree. Their theorem resolves a separate polynomial relation between rational and ordinary degree, rather than this threshold-degree inequality. These connections help explain the conjecture’s importance for the relationships among Boolean complexity measures, in addition to its learning and circuit applications.

cards.title: Aanderaa–Karp–Rosenberg conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 2\) and every nonconstant function f from the simple undirected graphs on \([n]\) to \(\{0,1\}\) that is invariant under every permutation of \([n]\) and monotone under adding edges, is \(D(f)=n(n- 1)/2\), where \(D(f)\) is its deterministic worst-case adjacency-query complexity?
cards.why: This asks whether every nontrivial monotone graph property can force complete inspection of its adjacency data, even when all computation between queries is free. A resolution would identify an exact limit of adaptive information gathering imposed by graph symmetry.

cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and \(U_{n}=\{\{i,j\}:1\le i<j\le n\}; a\) graph is an arbitrary edge set \(E\subseteq U_{n}\), with no loops, parallel edges or input promises. Nonconstant means that f takes both values 0 and 1. Monotonicity means \(E\subseteq F\) implies \(f(E)\le f(F)\). Invariance means \(f(\pi (E))=f(E)\) for every permutation \(\pi\) of \([n]\), where \(\pi (E)=\{\{\pi (i),\pi (j)\}:\{i,j\}\in E\}\). A deterministic query algorithm is a finite rooted binary decision tree. Each internal node names an unordered pair in \(U_{n}\) and its two outgoing edges correspond to the answer 0 or 1 for absence or presence of that pair; each leaf carries an output bit. Following the answers supplied by E must end with output \(f(E)\) for every \(E\subseteq U_{n}\). The cost on E is the number of internal nodes visited, and \(D(f)\) is the minimum, over all such correct trees, of the maximum cost over E. Repeated queries can be omitted. The tree may depend arbitrarily on n and f; f is the fixed task, not an additional unknown input. Only queries count: computation, storage and the size of the tree are unrestricted, and no uniform procedure for constructing trees across n or f is required. The model is deterministic and exact, with no probability distribution over inputs. Reading every pair gives \(D(f)\le |U_{n}|\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(D(f)=|U_{n}|\) for every n and f satisfying the stated conditions, or refute this universal claim. A finite refutation consists of one n, a completely specified invariant nonconstant monotone f, and a correct decision tree whose depth is at most |\(U_{n}|- 1\). A lower bound only up to a constant factor, or a theorem restricted to particular properties or vertex counts, does not settle the full claim.

context_blocks.text: Imagine receiving a graph behind an interface that answers only whether a chosen pair of vertices is joined. The algorithm can choose its next pair after seeing earlier answers. The conjecture says that, for every qualifying property, even the best such strategy has some input on which it must inspect every possible pair.

For a concrete example, consider the property of having at least one edge. Finding an edge establishes a yes answer immediately. On the empty graph, however, every pair must be inspected: an unexamined pair could hide the only edge. Evasiveness is thus a worst-case requirement; it does not say that every graph forces a complete scan.

The hypotheses specify which questions qualify. A constant answer needs no queries, so it is excluded. Asking whether the particular pair \(\{1,2\}\) is an edge needs one query but depends on vertex labels, so it is excluded by isomorphism invariance. Monotonicity requires a yes answer to survive the addition of edges; connectivity and containing a triangle have this feature, whereas having exactly one edge does not.

Symmetry says that relabeling the graph cannot change the answer. It does not prevent the algorithm from using labels to decide which pair to inspect first. Moreover, the difficult input can depend on the algorithm. These distinctions make the conjecture much stronger than the observation that all edge positions are potentially relevant.

The older quadratic lower-bound question is settled. The remaining target is exact equality with the total number of pairs, including the last possible query. Kahn, Saks and Sturtevant prove this equality whenever n is a prime power, meaning \(n=p^{k}\) for a prime p and an integer \(k\ge 1\). Their result covers every qualifying property at those sizes, but not every integer n.

Aaronson and coauthors establish the optimal universal lower bound of order n for bounded-error quantum queries. Quantum access and a permitted error probability change the model; the theorem does not establish the exact deterministic all-pairs bound.

Elekes and coauthors investigate countably infinite graphs, where versions of the monotone conjecture fail. Their October 2025 revision explicitly states the finite conjecture as open. Infinite-vertex counterexamples do not refute this card.

A June 2026 talk announces a counterexample to a broader topological evasiveness conjecture. That formulation assumes transitivity among the vertices of a simplicial complex; this card requires invariance under every relabeling of an underlying graph. The announcement does not exhibit the latter kind of counterexample, and the associated manuscript is listed as in preparation. It is therefore recorded as related announced work, without treating it as a resolution of this card.

sentences: An algorithm learns an unknown graph by asking whether individual pairs of vertices are edges.
The conjecture asks whether every nonconstant monotone property invariant under vertex relabeling has some input requiring all possible pairs to be queried.
Queries may be adaptive and all computation between them is free.
The example of looking for one edge illustrates how an easy positive instance can coexist with an empty graph that requires a complete scan.

The exact claim is known for prime-power vertex counts, while results about quantum queries, infinite graphs and broader topological symmetry must be distinguished from the full finite deterministic question.

cards.title: Real Grothendieck constant
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Determine the real Grothendieck constant \(K_{G}^{\mathbb R}\), defined as the least universal comparison factor between the vector and sign bilinear optima below.
cards.definitions: For positive integers m,n and a real matrix \(A=(a_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{m\times n}\), define \(S(A)=\max_{\varepsilon\in\{-1,1\}^{m},\,\delta\in\{-1,1\}^{n}}|\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\varepsilon_i\delta_j|\) and \(V(A)=\max_{u_1,\ldots,u_m,v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\mathbb R^{m+n},\,\|u_i\|_2=\|v_j\|_2=1}|\sum_{i=1}^{m}\sum_{j=1}^{n}a_{ij}\langle u_i,v_j\rangle|\). The inner product and norm are Euclidean. Define \(K_{G}^{\mathbb R}=\sup_{m,n\ge1,\,A\ne0}V(A)/S(A)\). The denominator is positive for nonzero A. Grothendieck’s inequality makes the supremum finite. The vector dimension m+n permits every possible Gram matrix of these m+n vectors; this is the unrestricted real constant, with no fixed dimension, complex vectors, computational restriction, or asymptotic input model.

context_blocks.text: The two optima compare a discrete sign assignment with its vector relaxation. The universal loss quantifies a basic limitation of this relaxation across all real bilinear objectives.

The earlier strict improvement over Krivine’s bound disproved a proposed value without determining the constant. A 2026 preprint reports a lower bound of \(6\pi/11\) and a further quantitative upper bound; their separation still exceeds the benchmark tolerance.

cards.why: Determining this constant would settle a foundational quantitative barrier shared by functional analysis, semidefinite optimization and quantum correlations.

cards.title: Polynomial relation between classical and quantum communication
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: For a total Boolean function $F:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}$, let $R^{cc}_{1/3}(F)$ be public-coin randomized communication complexity and $Q^{cc,*}_{1/3}(F)$ quantum communication complexity with unlimited shared entanglement. Is there a universal polynomial $p$ such that $R^{cc}_{1/3}(F)\le p(Q^{cc,*}_{1/3}(F))$ for every total $F$?
cards.why: The problem delineates quantum advantage in a basic distributed model with unrestricted local computation.

progress.text: For $F=f\circ\mathrm{AND}_2$, the source proves $D^{cc}(F)=O((Q^{cc,*}(F))^7\log^2 n)$. The polylogarithmic factor and the restriction to AND-composed functions prevent this from settling the general question.

context_blocks.text: Partial functions can exhibit exponential quantum savings. Requiring correctness on every input pair may fundamentally restrict that advantage.

Alice receives x and Bob receives y. They need to compute a function of both inputs while exchanging as little information as possible. The classical protocol may use randomness, and the quantum protocol may begin with shared entanglement. The cost being compared is the communication, not the complexity of their local computation.

Totality means every pair of legal individual inputs must receive a correct answer, including pairs that a promise problem would exclude. A universal polynomial simulation would limit quantum communication savings across all such functions. A bound for a special composition, or one with an additional dependence on the input length, does not automatically supply that universal relation.

cards.answer_criterion: Establish one polynomial bound valid for every finite total Boolean communication problem, or prove that no universal polynomial bound holds. Promise problems and restricted subclasses do not suffice.
cards.definitions: X and Y are arbitrary finite sets. Cost is the worst-case total number of communicated bits or qubits, and error at most \(1/3\) is required on every input pair. Public random bits and prior entanglement, respectively, are not charged as communication.

importance.reason: A general classical-versus-quantum comparison across all total communication problems, with a sharp distinction from promise-problem separations.

sentences: A halfspace is the sign of a weighted sum of input bits and a threshold.
Its degree-zero and degree-one Fourier coefficients measure its mean and coordinate correlations.
The question asks whether their squared weight is always at least \(2/\pi\).
Majority functions approach that proposed universal constant as dimension grows.
The exact inequality is retained because a general algorithm for merely approximating the extremal constant is already known.

cards.definitions: A linear threshold function has \(f(x)=\operatorname{sign}(\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i} x_{i}- \theta )\) for some real weights \(w_{i}\) and threshold \(\theta\), with \(\operatorname{sign}(t)=1\) when \(t\ge 0\) and −1 otherwise. Constant functions are included. Under the uniform measure on \(\{- 1,1\}^{n}\), define \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum_{x} f(x)\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with empty product 1. Thus \(\hat\{f\}(\varnothing )\) is the mean and \(\hat\{f\}(\{i\})\) is the correlation with the i-th coordinate. The displayed squared coefficients are the Fourier weight in degrees zero and one. There is no bound on dimension, weights or bias, and no regularity assumption on the halfspace. The constant \(\pi\) is the usual circle constant.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the exact universal inequality or give a threshold function with a rigorous proof that its low-degree weight is strictly less than \(2/\pi\). Approximation of the extremal constant to 0.01 would not settle this universal proposition. An algorithm for approximating that constant is already known; the retained target is the source’s sharp inequality.

cards.title: Removing low-influence directions from convex sets
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a function \(\tau :(0,1)\to [0,1]\) with \(\lim _{\varepsilon \to 0^{+}}\tau (\varepsilon )=0\) such that the following holds for every \(n\ge 1\), every centrally symmetric convex Borel set \(K\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{n}\), every unit vector v and every \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\)? If \(Inf_{v}[K]\le \varepsilon\), then there exists a centrally symmetric convex Borel set \(C\subseteq v\perp\) such that \(\gamma _{n}(K \triangle  (C+\mathbb{R} v))\le \tau (\varepsilon )\). The same \(\tau\) must work in all dimensions and for all such sets and directions.
cards.why: Would make convex influence a robust measure of whether a Gaussian direction matters, strengthening the analogy between symmetric convex sets and Boolean functions with irrelevant variables.

cards.definitions: \(\gamma _{n}\) is standard Gaussian probability measure, the law of X with independent \(N(0,1)\) coordinates. Central symmetry means \(K=- K\), with symmetry about the origin. Convexity means \(tx+(1- t)y\in K\) for \(x,y\in K\) and \(t\in [0,1]\). Write \(1_{K}\) for the indicator of K. The convex influence in a Euclidean unit direction v is \(Inf_{v}[K]=(1/\sqrt{2}) E[1_{K}(X)(1- \langle v,X\rangle ^{2})]\). This is nonnegative for centrally symmetric convex K. The orthogonal subspace is \(v\perp =\{y:\langle v,y\rangle =0\}\), and \(C+\mathbb{R} v=\{y+tv:y\in C,t\in \mathbb{R}\}\) is a cylinder whose membership depends only on the projection \(x- \langle v,x\rangle v\). The symmetric difference \(K\triangle \mathrm{L}\) consists of points in exactly one of K and L, so its Gaussian measure is the probability that their membership indicators disagree. Empty sets and the whole space are permitted. No lower or upper bound away from zero or one is imposed on \(\gamma _{n}(K)\), and no bound on total influence is assumed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a single modulus \(\tau\) tending to zero that bounds the Gaussian approximation error uniformly over the stated sets, dimensions and directions, or prove that no such modulus exists. Equivalently for a negative answer, exhibit a sequence with directional influence tending to zero while its Gaussian distance from every symmetric convex cylinder in that direction stays bounded below by a positive constant. A dimension-dependent modulus or a cylinder in some other direction does not suffice.

cards.title: Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every real \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), does there exist an integer \(k\ge 3\) such that no deterministic algorithm decides k-SAT on n variables and input length L in time $O(2^{(1-\varepsilon)n}L^c)$ for any fixed constant c? Here k is fixed independently of n and L. This is the deterministic Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis \((\mathrm{SETH})\).
cards.definitions: A k-SAT input is an explicitly encoded conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most k literals \(x_{i}\) or \(\neg x_{i}\). Variables are relabeled consecutively and n counts the distinct variables actually present; L counts the full binary formula encoding, including literal indices and delimiters. The decision is exact satisfiability, with no promise about clause density, the number of satisfying assignments, or how the formula was generated. Empty clauses make the input unsatisfiable, and the empty conjunction is satisfiable. Running time is worst-case deterministic Turing-machine time. For a fixed k, the algorithm, polynomial exponent, and hidden constant may depend on k and \(\varepsilon\), but not on the individual formula. Define \(s_{k}=\inf\){\(\alpha \ge 0 : k-\mathrm{SAT}\) has an \(O(2^{\alpha n}\mathrm{L}^{c})\)-time deterministic algorithm for some constant c}. SETH equivalently asserts \(\lim _{k}\to \infty s_{k}=1\); monotonicity follows because k-SAT is a restriction of \((k+1)-\mathrm{SAT}\). Polynomial factors are retained explicitly so reading the input is allowed even when clauses are repeated. No advice, oracle, random bits, or quantum computation is allowed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: SETH is one of the main assumptions used to explain why specific polynomial running-time exponents resist improvement. Settling it would test the foundation of a broad network of tight conditional bounds in strings, graphs, data structures, and exact exponential-time algorithms.

importance.reason: A principal organizing hypothesis of fine-grained complexity, connecting exact SAT complexity to tight running-time barriers across many algorithmic areas.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi study the optimal exponential rates for k-SAT and their growth with clause width, using critical clauses and sparsification.
SETH-based reductions extend to numerous problems in polynomial time. Vassilevska Williams surveys the reductions, hypotheses, and resulting equivalence and hardness questions.
The parameterized-algorithms textbook gives explicit deterministic definitions of ETH and SETH and separately discusses their randomized analogues.

Jiang and Cai report randomized \(O*(1.307031578^{n})\) time for general 3-SAT and \(O*(1.306969598^{n})\) for Unique-3-SAT by refining the analysis of PPSZ. These are preprint bounds for fixed width, not a constant saving valid for every k.

cards.status_note: The cited primary sources state SETH as an open hypothesis. Research through 10 September 2026 found no deterministic all-width constant-saving refutation or unrestricted proof. Bounds for a fixed width, random instances, restricted solvers, or unique satisfiability are not recorded as resolutions.

context_blocks.text: Exhaustive search tries all \(2^{n}\) assignments and checks the formula each time. Restricting clause width supports much faster algorithms, particularly for small k. SETH accommodates these speedups: it says that no positive constant saving in the exponent survives uniformly across arbitrarily large fixed widths. It does not assert that 3-SAT needs essentially \(2^{n}\) time.

The order of quantifiers separates this statement from several nearby claims. A \(2^{0.9n}\)-time algorithm for every fixed k would refute SETH even if the polynomial factors and implementations depended on k. A family of bounds \(2^{(1- 1/k)n}\) would be compatible with it. A fast algorithm for unrestricted CNF-SAT would also refute it, but the failure of such an unrestricted algorithm is not the definition being used here.

ETH asks for a positive optimal exponential rate already at width three; SETH additionally asks that the rates approach one as width grows. Sparsification relates bounded-width formulas to bounded-density formulas and helps transfer these hypotheses through reductions. It does not make the two hypotheses equivalent. Proving either would go beyond \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), which by itself allows intermediate running times such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\).

Fine-grained reductions turn this hypothesis into precise conditional barriers for familiar polynomial-time problems, including Orthogonal Vectors, edit distance, and graph-distance questions. The reduction must preserve the intended exponential saving, not merely be polynomial-time as in an NP-hardness reduction. When a reduction or resulting algorithm uses randomness, the corresponding randomized hypothesis must be tracked separately.

Recent work continues to sharpen small-width algorithms. Jiang and Cai’s July 2026 preprint reports a slightly improved randomized PPSZ bound for general 3-SAT, distinguished from its better bound under a unique-solution promise. Both the fixed width and use of randomness keep this improvement outside the deterministic, all-width saving required to refute the present statement.

cards.title: Truly subcubic APSP
cards.formal: Is there a constant $\varepsilon>0$ and a uniform randomized algorithm that, for every n-vertex directed graph with real edge weights and no negative-weight cycle, outputs all exact shortest-path distances in $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ worst-case time with probability at least \(2/3\)? Use a comparison-addition real RAM: adding, subtracting, and comparing stored real values costs \(O(1)\), and standard arithmetic and bit operations on \(O(\log  n)\)-bit index words cost \(O(1)\). Unreachable distances must be reported as infinity. Arbitrary real-number encodings or unit-cost floor operations are unavailable.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: I include this because exact distances are a basic graph primitive, and this particular exponent question organizes many conditional lower bounds. A resolution would identify either a common algorithmic improvement across equivalent problems or a precise limitation of what those reductions can accomplish.
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its adjacency matrix, with a special symbol for absent edges. Output contains one distance for every ordered pair, including zero self-distances. Negative-cycle detection outside the promise is not required. Space and preprocessing are included in the algorithm’s ordinary running time. The probability guarantee applies to the complete output matrix on each fixed input. This is a classical sequential model; quantum and parallel work/depth bounds are separate targets.

progress.text: Vassilevska Williams and Williams establish truly subcubic equivalences between APSP and several path, matrix, and weighted-triangle tasks.
Williams gives a randomized real-RAM algorithm with time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$, demonstrating a substantial subpolynomial saving while leaving a fixed exponent improvement unresolved.

Akmal and Fischer solve the node-weighted zero-triangle problem in matrix-multiplication time; their introduction explicitly distinguishes it from the edge-weighted variant governed by the APSP hypothesis.

cards.status_note: Reviewed 10 September 2026. The target is a fixed exponent saving for arbitrary real edge weights; the 2026 node-weighted triangle result does not supply it.

context_blocks.text: Single-source shortest paths produce one row of a distance matrix. All-pairs shortest paths ask for every row, including the effects of intermediate vertices shared by many shortest routes. Running a source algorithm repeatedly is useful, but does not explain how much computation those rows can share.

For example, a path from u to v can be much cheaper than their direct edge even when it visits many intermediate vertices. Restricting attention to one-hop or two-hop routes changes the problem. Negative edges are allowed here, but negative cycles are excluded so that every reachable distance has a finite optimum.

Matrix formulations expose the shared work: combining two path segments uses a minimum over sums, rather than the ordinary sum of products of ring multiplication. Fast algorithms for ordinary matrix multiplication therefore do not automatically give the required bound for arbitrary weighted distances. Subcubic equivalences connect the problem to several other path and matrix tasks.

The distinction between subcubic and truly subcubic is quantitative. Dividing cubic time by a very large subpolynomial factor still leaves an exponent tending to three. The target asks for a fixed positive exponent saving. The 2026 progress on node-weighted triangles does not settle the edge-weighted problem underlying this hypothesis.

cards.title: Orthogonal Vectors Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is it true that for every \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\) there is a fixed integer \(c\ge 1\) for which no uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm decides bichromatic Orthogonal Vectors on two lists of n vectors in \(\{0,1\}^{d}\), with \(d=\lceil c \log _{2} n\rceil\), in worst-case time \(O(n^{2- \varepsilon})\) and with error probability at most \(1/3\) on every input?
cards.definitions: Here \(n\ge 2\) and the two input lists A and B each have length n; repeated vectors are allowed. The answer is YES exactly when some \(a\in A\) and \(b\in B\) satisfy \(\sum_{j=1}^{d} a_{j} b_{j}=0\) as an integer sum, equivalently their supports are disjoint. This is not an inner product over the field with two elements. Inputs are explicitly supplied as packed binary vectors. Computation uses a uniform classical RAM with words of \(\Theta (\log (n+d))\) bits, ordinary constant-time word arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, comparisons, memory access and generation of a random word. Each program uses a fixed word-length constant; arbitrary-precision unit-cost operations, nonuniform advice and free preprocessing tables are excluded. Reading, preprocessing and all subsequent computation count in the time bound. For fixed \(\varepsilon\) and c, hidden time constants and the program may depend on these parameters, but not on n. There is no promise on vector weights, overlap or input distribution. Randomness is internal to the algorithm; correctness must hold for every pair of lists.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated lower-bound proposition, or refute it by exhibiting one fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) such that for every fixed integer \(c\ge 1\) an algorithm \(A_{c}\) meets the \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) time and error bounds. This quantifier order matters: the algorithms and constants may depend on c, but the exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) must work for every c. Giving a different positive saving \(\varepsilon _{c}\) that tends to zero with c, shaving logarithmic factors from quadratic time, or proving lower bounds only for restricted circuit models does not settle the proposition.
cards.why: A basic disjointness problem anchors a large part of fine-grained complexity. Settling its uniform exponent barrier would reshape conditional lower bounds for strings, geometry and data structures.

importance.reason: One of the principal hypotheses organizing polynomial-time lower bounds across multiple algorithmic areas, with an elementary explicit task and precise dimension dependence.

progress.text: Abboud–Williams–Yu obtain dimension-dependent truly subquadratic algorithms via the polynomial method; the exponent saving decreases with the dimension constant.
Rohatgi develops OV-based conditional hardness for exact Earth Mover Distance, illustrating geometric consequences.
Alman–Andoni–Zhang improve average-case OV algorithms; the work appears at SOSA 2025.
Dürr–Kipouridis–Lampis–Węgrzycki present \(\widetilde{O}\)\((1.25^{d} n)\) randomized low-dimensional algorithms at ICALP, with a computer-aided \(O(1.16^{d} n)\) refinement.
Choudhury and coauthors establish the logarithmic-dimension monotone-circuit version for the negated predicate and strengthen other restricted-model lower bounds.

references.title: New and Improved Concrete Lower Bounds for Orthogonal Vectors
references.authors: Tameem Choudhury; Nutan Limaye; Karteek Sreenivasaiah; Srikanth Srinivasan
references.locator: v1, 26 July; Conjecture 1, Theorem 5 and restricted-model discussion; no unrestricted word-RAM lower bound

cards.status_note: The July 2026 primary literature explicitly states the unrestricted OV conjecture as open while proving restricted-model variants. Low-dimensional and average-case improvements do not negate its quantifier order. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: Each vector can be viewed as a subset of a universe of d coordinates. The task is to find a disjoint pair across two collections. Although checking one pair is easy, there are \(n^{2}\) possible pairs. For logarithmic dimension, packed coordinates make a single check take only a constant number of machine operations when c is fixed. The hypothesis asks whether there is an unavoidable exponent arbitrarily close to two as that fixed dimension constant grows.

The dependence on c is the main subtlety. There are already truly subquadratic algorithms for each fixed c, with a saving that can deteriorate as c increases. The polynomial-method algorithm of Abboud, Williams and Yu runs in time \(n^{2- 1/O(\log  c)}\) in the relevant large-c regime. This is consistent with the hypothesis: selecting a sufficiently large c can make that known saving smaller than any proposed universal \(\varepsilon\). The source is SODA 2015; some later bibliographies mistakenly label it 2014.

Very small dimension permits another strategy: enumerate possible coordinate patterns and aggregate the input instead of considering all pairs separately. The 2026 low-dimensional algorithms achieve a randomized bound of \(\widetilde{O}\)\((1.25^{d} n)\), with a further reported \(O(1.16^{d} n)\) bound obtained through computer-aided parameter evaluation. These improve the useful range of the pattern-based approach, but their exponential dependence on d becomes a power of n when \(d=c \log _{2} n\).

For example, substituting \(c=2\) into \(1.25^{d} n\) gives, up to constant and logarithmic factors, \(n^{1+2 \log _{2} 1.25}\), whose exponent is about 1.644. Increasing c increases this exponent. Thus an impressive subquadratic algorithm for one small logarithmic dimension does not supply one exponent saving for all logarithmic dimensions. This numerical example illustrates the quantifiers; it is not an additional algorithmic theorem.

The hypothesis is useful because disjointness can encode compatibility between partial solutions. In the standard split-and-list SAT reduction, each half-assignment produces a vector marking clauses it fails to satisfy. Two half-assignments extend to a satisfying assignment exactly when their vectors are disjoint. Sparsification controls the number of clause coordinates. For the randomized version stated here, the corresponding randomized Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a conditional justification; a deterministic-only SAT assumption must not silently be used to exclude randomized solvers.

Reductions then transfer the conjectured time barrier to problems that look quite different. Rohatgi’s Earth Mover Distance paper, the inherited source for this record, develops one such geometric application. The significance of OV is its role as a common intermediate problem: a new algorithm can overturn a collection of conditional barriers, while an unconditional proof would establish a strong lower bound for a concrete problem already known to be in polynomial time.

Restricted-model lower bounds provide evidence without establishing that unrestricted conclusion. Choudhury and coauthors prove near-quadratic monotone-circuit lower bounds for the negation of OV at logarithmic dimension. This negated predicate says every cross-pair intersects and is monotone in the input bits. Their July 2026 paper also strengthens formula and branching-program bounds. General RAM programs can use operations and intermediate representations beyond those restrictions, so these theorems do not prove the hypothesis as formulated here.

Distributional improvements are a separate frontier. Alman, Andoni and Zhang obtain faster algorithms when vector coordinates are independently sampled with a specified Bernoulli bias, including difficult parameter ranges. Such a result can explain why random instances are easier while leaving adversarial instances unresolved. The card deliberately requires correctness and the stated running time on every input rather than only on a random input distribution.

cards.title: Algebraic k-Clique Hypothesis
cards.formal: Let \(\tau (k)\) be the infimum of worst-case time exponents of randomized algorithms deciding k-Clique, as specified below, and let \(\omega\) be the arithmetic matrix-multiplication exponent over C. Is \(\liminf _{k\to \infty} \tau (k)/k=\omega /3\)?
cards.definitions: For each fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), the input is the adjacency matrix of a simple undirected graph on \(n\ge k\) labeled vertices; accept iff some k distinct vertices are pairwise adjacent. A uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, and its time bound must hold for every random tape. Set \(\tau (k)=\inf\){\(a\ge 0\): such an algorithm runs in \(O(n^{a})\) time as \(n\to \infty\)}. The program and hidden constants may depend on k, but not on n. Words have \(C_{k}\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for some fixed constant \(C_{k}\); arithmetic modulo the word range, division with remainder, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and indirect memory access cost one step, and a fresh random word costs one step. Initial memory apart from the input is zero; preprocessing counts; there is no nonuniform advice, giant-word operation or free oracle. For \(\omega\), let \(M(N)\) be the smallest number of binary +,−,× gates in a circuit over C that computes all entries of the product of two formal \(N\times N\) matrices. Arbitrary complex constants and sharing are allowed, but division and branching are not. Define \(\omega =\inf \{a:M(N)=O(N^{a})\}\). This fixes the characteristic-zero arithmetic convention, separately from the bit-based graph algorithm. The question concerns the coefficient of k in the exponent; it does not fix k proportional to n or treat the latest published numerical upper bound on \(\omega\) as its exact value.
cards.answer_criterion: The matrix-multiplication reduction gives the upper asymptotic benchmark \(\omega /3\). An affirmative answer therefore proves that, for every \(\delta >0\), there is K such that \(\tau (k)\ge (\omega /3- \delta )k\) for every fixed \(k\ge K\). A negative answer proves a strict saving in this coefficient, for example via algorithms with \(\tau (k)\le (\omega /3- \delta )k\) for arbitrarily large k and one \(\delta >0\). Saving logarithmic time factors or an additive \(o(k)\) in the exponent does not refute this leading-exponent formulation.
cards.why: A basic quantitative hardness hypothesis for graph patterns and many reductions in fine-grained complexity, precisely testing whether the matrix-multiplication exponent gives the optimal leading coefficient.

cards.status_note: Open in the stated unrestricted randomized leading-exponent form, following the inherited hypothesis and later primary sources checked through 11 September 2026. The liminf and machine conventions make the asymptotic claim explicit. Logarithmic speedups, matrix-exponent improvements and conditional lower bounds do not settle it.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, clique detection is already a polynomial-time problem: one can inspect every k-element subset. The issue is which polynomial is necessary. An exponent near k and an exponent near 0.79k differ dramatically as the fixed pattern size increases. This is why ordinary NP-hardness, which allows k to vary with the input, leaves the main quantitative question unanswered.

The arithmetic reduction groups the vertices of a candidate clique into three parts. For \(k=3r\), create auxiliary vertices representing r-cliques and join two auxiliary vertices when their represented sets are disjoint and their union is a clique. A triangle in this auxiliary graph represents a 3r-clique in the original graph. There are \(O(n^{r})\) auxiliary vertices, so matrix-based triangle detection gives the familiar leading time exponent \(\omega k/3\).

When k is not divisible by three, the groups have unequal sizes. Rectangular matrix multiplication gives more refined bounds for individual k; padding to the next multiple of three already changes the exponent by only a constant. Because this card asks for the leading coefficient as k grows, those residue-class effects do not alter the target. They would matter in a card asking for the exact exponent at a particular small k.

The inherited source states the hypothesis in the \(n^{\omega k/3- o(k)}\) form and allows both randomized and deterministic algorithms. The explicit liminf formulation records the order of limits: first study \(n\to \infty\) for each fixed k, then ask about large k. The model definitions make time, error and machine operations explicit. This avoids relying on an informal distinction between which graph algorithms count as combinatorial.

The word algebraic names the benchmark supplied by matrix multiplication. It does not restrict the algorithms against which the conjecture asserts hardness. A refuting algorithm could use arithmetic, combinatorial structure, randomization, or a combination. Likewise, \(\omega\) is an unknown mathematical constant defined by the best possible arithmetic circuits, rather than a decimal frozen at the date of an old reduction.

A better upper bound on \(\omega\) immediately improves the matrix-based clique algorithm without disproving this hypothesis. Conversely, an algorithm whose exponent beats an old numerical estimate may still be slower than the conjectured benchmark using the true \(\omega\). The distinction becomes especially relevant after small improvements in matrix multiplication: Dupont and coauthors’ August 2026 note reports \(\omega <2.371177\), improving the preceding 2.371339 bound. Its numerical certificate has not been replayed for this catalogue.

Abboud–Fischer–Shechter improve the algorithms usually called combinatorial by logarithmic factors. At fixed k, their displayed detection bound is \(n^{k}(\log  n)^{- (k+1)}(\log  \log  n)^{k+3}\). Such progress is useful, but the logarithmic factor changes an exponent by \(o(1)\) as n grows and does not establish a new leading coefficient below \(\omega /3\). Their separate hypergraph and listing results have different outputs or incidence structures.

The hypothesis supports lower bounds for tasks that do not look like clique detection. Das–Lincoln–Lynch–Munro use clique reductions for dynamic Boolean-formula evaluation and counting. A faster data structure with the relevant preprocessing and update guarantees could therefore force faster clique algorithms. This explains the inclusion of an apparently indirect dynamic-data-structure paper as the inherited reference: its computational-hypothesis section states this exact leading-exponent assumption.

Recent work strengthens the network of reductions rather than proving the hypothesis. Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß show that suitable regularity restrictions on partite graphs and hypergraphs preserve the relevant detection exponent, with parameter-dependent factors. This helps transfer conditional hardness to Boolean constraint optimization. Their result cannot be read as an unconditional lower bound for all word-RAM algorithms.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redzic’s January 2026 coverage and partial-domination results similarly give algorithms and matching bounds conditional on clique and hyperclique hypotheses. The 3-uniform hyperclique assumption concerns triples as constraints and has a different exhaustive-search benchmark; it is not the graph hypothesis in this card. Keeping the two separate prevents a strong conditional statement for one problem from being mistaken for a resolution of the other.

The fundamental question is whether all-pairs algebra can capture the optimal leading cost of enforcing every pairwise adjacency in a growing fixed pattern. An affirmative answer would justify a widely used quantitative barrier. A negative answer would identify a way to exploit the clique decision task beyond the matrix-multiplication benchmark, potentially changing many currently conditional optimality claims.

cards.title: Hyperclique Hypothesis
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of integers \(h\ge 3\) and \(k>h\) and every constant \(\varepsilon >0\), is there no classical randomized \(O(n^{k- \varepsilon})\)-time algorithm deciding whether an n-vertex h-uniform hypergraph contains a k-clique, with error at most \(1/3\) on each input?
cards.definitions: The input hypergraph \(H=([n],E)\) is simple and unweighted, with E a subset of the h-element subsets of \([n]\). It is given by a dense table containing one Boolean membership entry for each h-element subset, in a fixed computable order. A k-clique is a set \(S\subseteq [n]\) of k distinct vertices such that every h-element subset of S belongs to E. The task outputs one yes/no bit and requires neither counting nor listing cliques. Fix the classical word-RAM with \(O(\log (n+2))\)-bit words, constant-time arithmetic, bitwise operations and random access on words; the word-length constant and runtime constants may depend on the fixed \(h,k,\varepsilon\). Random bits are allowed, but quantum operations, nonuniform advice and precomputed input-dependent tables are not. All processing of the input and construction of auxiliary data are charged. The excluded algorithm must run in \(O(n^{k- \varepsilon})\) steps on every execution and answer correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) for every input. The quantifiers concern each fixed pair h,k separately, not only a limit as k tends to infinity. The card explicitly uses the bounded-error randomized version of the classical hypothesis.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated exclusion of all such algorithms, or refute it by giving one fixed pair \(h\ge 3,k>h\), one fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) and a correct algorithm with the required worst-case time and per-input success probability. A conditional confirmation must name the stronger assumption. A logarithmic-factor speedup, an algorithm for a sparse or promised subclass, or a circuit-size bound in a restricted algebraic model is not a resolution of the full claim.
cards.why: A principal fine-grained hypothesis for higher-order combinatorial interactions, supporting conditional lower bounds beyond ordinary graph clique and shortest paths.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No classical bounded-error algorithm with a fixed positive exponent saving for a covered h,k pair was found in the checked sources. The 2025 regularization and 2026 reductions use or relate the hypothesis; they do not prove it unconditionally.

context_blocks.text: A graph records pairwise compatibility. An h-uniform hypergraph records compatibility of h vertices at a time. For \(h=3\) and \(k=4, a\) positive instance contains four vertices whose four triples are all hyperedges. Knowing that every pair participates in some hyperedge is insufficient: the compatible triples must be exactly those supported on the same four vertices. This is the smallest parameter pair covered by the hypothesis.

For fixed h and k, exhaustive search takes \(O(n^{k})\) time: enumerate all k-element vertex sets and check the fixed number of required hyperedges. The problem is therefore already polynomial-time for every individual card parameter pair. The conjecture asks whether that polynomial exponent can be reduced by a positive constant. Ordinary NP-hardness when k varies would not establish such a fine-grained statement.

The graph case \(h=2\) behaves differently. Matrix multiplication gives algorithms beating the direct k-tuple search for many clique sizes. Lincoln–Vassilevska Williams–Williams explain why the corresponding higher-order operation for hypergraphs is a separate obstacle and formulate hyperclique-based lower bounds. This distinction is the reason the present hypothesis starts at \(h=3\), instead of extending a graph-clique bound mechanically to all uniformities.

Their connections to satisfiability concern optimization problems such as Max-h-SAT: find an assignment satisfying as many clauses as possible. A suitable hyperclique speedup would also improve exhaustive-search algorithms for these problems. This must be distinguished from deciding whether every clause of a fixed-width SAT instance is simultaneously satisfiable, for which exponential improvements are already known. The Max-h-SAT hypothesis is an additional assumption, not an unconditional proof.

The fixed exponent saving is essential. A running time \(n^{k}\) divided by any fixed power of log n would not contradict the card. Nor would an improvement available only when k grows with n. Conversely, an \(O(n^{3.99})\) algorithm for 4-cliques in 3-uniform hypergraphs would be enough to refute the universally quantified statement, without resolving every other h,k pair.

The dense encoding prevents an implicit promise about sparsity. Its size is \(\Theta (n^{h})\) table entries, which is below the exhaustive-search exponent because \(k>h\). Any refuting exponent saving can be reduced to a smaller positive saving so that reading this table still fits the claimed time. Thus routine conversions between explicit dense representations do not provide an artificial refutation.

The inherited paper works with k-partite hypergraphs. This is essentially equivalent for fixed k: make k copies of the vertex set and place an edge between copies in distinct parts whenever their distinct original vertices form an input hyperedge. Selecting one vertex from each part then tests the original clique condition. The vertex blowup depends only on k, preserving a positive polynomial exponent saving.

Fischer–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß go further in their ICALP 2025 regularization theorem. They transfer algorithms between general k-partite hypergraphs and a strongly regular class in which each transversal \((h- 1)\)-tuple has the same number of extensions to a hyperedge. Controlling these overlapping incidences without introducing false cliques is the substantive part of the construction. The result shows that this regularity promise does not remove the conjectured difficulty.

The same work uses regularization to classify optimization of Boolean CSPs over assignments with exactly k nonzero variables. The degree of the constraint functions separates easy linear cases, graph-clique cases and higher-degree cases with exhaustive-search lower bounds under a 3-uniform hyperclique assumption. This supplies a reason to study the hypothesis beyond the clique problem itself.

Dudek and coauthors’ STOC 2026 work gives another connection: a refutation for the 3-uniform, 4-clique case would yield a truly subquadratic algorithm for detecting four-term arithmetic progressions in an integer universe. Their paper studies verification of algebraic identities and uses this relationship for conditional lower bounds. It supplies a new consequence or conditional foundation, rather than establishing the hyperclique lower bound outright.

Fritsch–Künnemann–Redžić–Stieß’s ICALP 2026 paper studies when sparsity helps for small independent sets in hypergraphs and Boolean CSPs. Its algorithms have separate vertex-count and edge-count terms, with matching bounds under clique hypotheses. Improved running time on sparse forbidden-hyperedge inputs is compatible with the dense worst-case statement here; taking a complement can turn a sparse instance into a dense one.

The hypothesis expresses a possible computational divide between pairwise and higher-order interactions. Its value is that precise reductions turn it into concrete runtime barriers for other tasks. The proper status is a conjectural foundation for those barriers. Repeated applications and increasingly robust reductions strengthen its usefulness, while a proof or one genuine exponent-saving algorithm would be a qualitatively different result.

cards.formal: For the binary alphabet \(\Sigma =\{0,1\}\), do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon \in\)(0,1], a constant \(C>0\) and one uniform deterministic word-RAM algorithm A such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every pair \(x,y\in \Sigma ^{n}, A\) outputs the exact unit-cost edit distance \(ED(x,y)\) in at most \(C(n+1)^{2- \varepsilon}\) operations?
