cards.definitions: An edit inserts one symbol, deletes one symbol, or substitutes one symbol by the other; each operation costs 1. \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum total number of edits transforming the entire string x into the entire string y. Equal symbols can be retained at cost 0. The output is this integer, not necessarily a sequence of edits. Both strings have length n and are provided explicitly, one symbol per word. The word-RAM has \(w=\operatorname{ceil}(4 \log _{2}(n+2))\) bits per word, zero-initialized addressable memory of w-bit words, and a fixed finite program independent of n. One operation reads or writes one addressed word, branches or compares words, or applies unsigned addition, subtraction or multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer division by a nonzero word with rounding down, a bitwise Boolean operation, or a logical shift by fewer than w positions. Constants are fixed by the program, and words cannot hold arbitrarily large integers in one step. The running time includes every memory access and arithmetic operation; no oracle, advice or input-dependent precomputed table is supplied. All preprocessing is charged. The time guarantee is worst-case over inputs, with no random coins or probability of error. The constant exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) cannot tend to zero with n. The chosen binary alphabet is an explicit specialization of the imported phrase “a fixed finite alphabet”, supported by Bringmann–Künnemann’s binary-alphabet formulation; a unary alphabet would make the equal-length problem trivial.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive resolution supplies one algorithm with a proof of exact correctness for every binary input pair and a worst-case \(O(n^{2- \varepsilon})\) bound for some fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) in the specified model. A negative resolution rules out every such deterministic algorithm and every fixed positive exponent saving. A lower bound conditional on an unproved hypothesis is not an unconditional negative resolution. Faster approximation, special-case performance and logarithmic-factor savings do not meet the target.

context_blocks.title: Edits can shift an entire alignment
context_blocks.text: The strings 0101 and 1010 disagree at all four positions, but their edit distance is 2: delete the first 0 and append a 0. One edit cannot suffice, because the lengths are equal and a single substitution would leave other disagreements. Edit distance therefore measures more than the number of mismatched positions. Insertions and deletions let long portions of the two strings line up at different offsets.

context_blocks.title: What the quadratic barrier means
context_blocks.text: The classical dynamic-programming computation compares prefixes of the two strings and takes \(O(n^{2})\) time. The question concerns the best possible algorithm, not the necessity of evaluating every entry in that particular computation. A bound such as \(n^{2}/\log  n\) is smaller than \(n^{2}\) but does not give a fixed positive saving in the exponent. The target asks for \(n^{2- \varepsilon}\) with one \(\varepsilon >0\) that remains valid for arbitrarily long strings.

context_blocks.title: A precise conditional obstacle
context_blocks.text: The Strong Exponential Time Hypothesis, SETH, states that for every \(\delta >0\) there is a clause width k for which Boolean k-SAT on N variables cannot be decided deterministically in \(O(2^{(1- \delta )N} \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L}))\) time, where L is the formula length. Backurs and Indyk relate a truly subquadratic exact edit-distance algorithm to a faster satisfiability algorithm. Bringmann and Künnemann establish the conditional obstruction even for binary strings. This is strong evidence for a barrier, but SETH is an assumption. The reduction does not prove unconditionally that the requested algorithm is impossible.

context_blocks.title: Why recent approximation is different
context_blocks.text: Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 result gives a randomized \((1+\eta )\)-approximation for each fixed \(\eta >0\), with running time \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega}(1) n}\). A multiplicative approximation can return a nearby value rather than the exact minimum. Its error guarantee and its dependence on \(\eta\) cannot simply be replaced by exact correctness at no cost. Thus this progress does not supply the deterministic exact algorithm requested here.

context_blocks.title: Scope of the benchmark
context_blocks.text: The alphabet is explicitly binary, the edit costs are all one, and the guarantee is for every input pair. Results for typical strings, a bounded number of edits, weighted substitution schemes, or a supplied good alignment may have different complexity. Computing the distance is already a polynomial-time task. The unresolved issue is the finer rate within polynomial time and its connection to the exponential-time cost of satisfiability.

cards.title: Online matrix–vector multiplication conjecture
cards.formal: Given a Boolean matrix $M\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, receive vectors $v_1,\ldots,v_n\in\{0,1\}^n$ one at a time. Output each Boolean product $(Mv_t)_i=\bigvee_{j=1}^{n}(M_{ij}\wedge(v_t)_j)$ before receiving $v_{t+1}$. Is there any constant $\varepsilon>0$ and randomized algorithm with total running time $O(n^{3-\varepsilon})$ and error probability at most $1/3$? The OMv conjecture asserts that there is no such algorithm. In this formulation the total includes preprocessing of $M$.
cards.why: I include this because it is one of the central assumptions used to explain why many dynamic data structures resist fast updates and queries simultaneously. Refuting it would invalidate a large collection of conditional barriers; proving it would give a major unconditional lower bound for an explicit polynomial-time problem.
cards.definitions: The product uses OR and AND, not addition modulo two. The matrix remains fixed throughout the sequence. The word-RAM has logarithmic-size words. Success concerns the complete online computation. This is distinct from multiplying over a field, updating the matrix itself, or answering one query after an uncharged preprocessing phase.

progress.text: Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai, and Saranurak formulate OMv and derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems, including reachability and variants of connectivity.
Larsen and Williams give randomized online multiplication in total time $n^3/2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$. This improves the algorithmic baseline without refuting the conjecture.

Hu and Polak show fine-grained equivalences between Boolean OMv and several online non-Boolean products, including min-max, dominance, and equality. These broaden the supporting connections; they do not prove the conjecture.

context_blocks.text: If all vectors were available together, they would form another matrix and fast matrix multiplication could batch the work. The online requirement forbids waiting for future columns. A data structure can learn and preprocess the fixed matrix, but it must answer a sequence of queries whose later values have not yet arrived.

A small graph construction explains the relevance to dynamic algorithms. Make one vertex for each matrix column and one for each row; put a directed edge from column j to row i exactly when the matrix entry is one. Add a source with edges to the columns activated by the current query vector. The rows reachable from the source are exactly the one-entries of the answer vector. Changing the active columns turns each matrix query into a sequence of graph updates followed by reachability questions.

The conjecture is about a polynomial saving in the exponent. An improvement from $n^3$ to $n^3/\log n$ is significant but compatible with it. Even the stronger documented saving $2^{\Omega(\sqrt{\log n})}$ is only $n^{o(1)}$, so it leaves the total time in the $n^{3-o(1)}$ range.

The graph reduction gives intuition, not a universal update-time theorem by itself. To derive a particular data-structure lower bound, one must account for preprocessing, the number of updates and queries, and how the graph size relates to the matrix dimension. These are precisely the parameters handled in the original reductions.

cards.title: Min-Plus Convolution Hypothesis
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) such that, for every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computes the min-plus convolution of any two length-\(n\) integer arrays with entries in \([-n^{a},n^{a}]\) in \(O(n^{2-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time?

references.title: Necklaces, Convolutions, and \(X+Y\)
references.authors: David Bremner; Timothy M. Chan; Erik D. Demaine; Jeff Erickson; Ferran Hurtado; John Iacono; Stefan Langerman; Mihai Pătraşcu; Perouz Taslakian
references.locator: Algorithmica 69, 294–314; introduction and section 3.

importance.reason: A central fine-grained hypothesis supporting quadratic barriers in knapsack and dynamic programming.

category_assignment.reason: The fixed polynomial exponent improvement is a fine-grained complexity target.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge2\), input arrays \(A=(a_{0},\ldots,a_{n-1})\) and \(B=(b_{0},\ldots,b_{n-1})\) are explicitly listed. Output all \(2n-1\) integers \(c_{k}=\min\{a_{i}+b_{j}:0\le i,j<n,\ i+j=k\}\), for \(0\le k\le2n-2\). Inputs need not be sorted or monotone. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The exponent saving \(\varepsilon\) is common to all fixed magnitude exponents \(a\); the program, word-size constant and hidden time constant may depend on \(a\). Signed entries and exact output sums use a constant number of words.

context_blocks.text: Min-plus convolution combines two cost profiles: entry \(c_k\) is the cheapest way to split the total index \(k\) between them. For \(A=(3,1)\) and \(B=(4,2)\), the output is \((7,5,3)\). The middle entry compares two different splits, while an endpoint has only one. All output positions are required simultaneously.

The direct computation checks every pair of input entries, producing a quadratic amount of work for a linear-size output. Unlike ordinary convolution, replacing sums of products by minima of sums changes the algebraic operation. The hypothesis is a computational barrier for this exact cost-combination primitive.

The 2026 paper records an unrestricted upper bound \(n^2/2^{\Theta(\sqrt{\log n})}\), obtained from earlier results. This is an improvement over quadratic time, but its exponent saving tends to zero with input length. The requested algorithm must save a fixed positive exponent, not merely a growing subpolynomial factor.

The same paper gives \(n^{1.5+o(1)}\) deterministic time when the arrays are monotone and their values obey the specified bounded-range condition. Neither monotonicity nor that special linear range is assumed by this card. Structured convolution is therefore a restricted positive result rather than an unrestricted resolution.

The established hypothesis name predicts a negative answer to the displayed algorithm-existence question. The card fixes a precise polynomially bounded integer formulation: one exponent saving works for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), while the implementation and constants may depend on \(a\). There is no claim about arbitrary real-number inputs or bit lengths growing faster than \(O(\log n)\).

The probability guarantee is for the entire output on each fixed input. A small error probability for each entry separately would not automatically give that guarantee for the full array. Likewise, average performance over an input distribution is different from the worst-case time and per-input correctness requirements.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that some fixed \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\) permits the stated family of uniform algorithms for every fixed magnitude exponent \(a\), with worst-case time and whole-output success guarantees, or prove the logical negation in Lean. In the negation, every proposed saving \(\varepsilon\) fails for at least one fixed \(a\), allowing all permitted algorithms and their constants. Neither a conditional hardness implication nor a theorem for monotone inputs proves that negation.

cards.title: ETH versus Gap-ETH
cards.formal: Does the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis imply the deterministic Gap Exponential Time Hypothesis for sparse 3-CNF formulas?
cards.definitions: For a 3-CNF formula F with n variables, let \(\operatorname{val}(F)\) be the maximum fraction of clauses simultaneously satisfiable. The ETH convention here asserts that there is \(c>0\) for which no deterministic algorithm decides satisfiability of all 3-CNF formulas in time \(O(2^{cn} \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L}))\), where L is the binary encoding length. Gap-ETH asserts that there exist constants \(B\ge 1, \delta \in (0,1)\) and \(c' >0\) for which no deterministic algorithm in time \(O(2^{c' n} \operatorname{poly}(\mathrm{L}))\) distinguishes \(\operatorname{val}(F)=1\) from \(\operatorname{val}(F)\le 1- \delta\) on formulas with at most Bn clauses. Its inputs are promised to satisfy one of those two alternatives. Empty formulas are satisfiable. All constants are fixed independently of F; randomized versions are not asserted.

context_blocks.text: ETH concerns exact satisfiability, while Gap-ETH postulates comparable exponential hardness even when unsatisfiable inputs violate a fixed fraction of clauses. Their equivalence would unify many exact and approximation lower-bound assumptions.

Bitansky and coauthors distinguish ETH from the stronger gap hypothesis while obtaining exponential hardness for particular approximation tasks. Hardness for those tasks does not imply a gap-preserving sparse 3-CNF statement. This implication is distinct from asking whether either hypothesis is true.

cards.title: Directed unweighted APSP below \(n^{5/2}\)
cards.formal: Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) and a uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm computing the full exact all-pairs distance matrix of every unweighted directed graph on \(n\) vertices in \(O(n^{5/2-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. Every arc has length one. For each ordered pair \((u,v)\in V\times V\), output the minimum number of arcs on a directed path from \(u\) to \(v\), or infinity if no path exists; diagonal entries are zero. The output is an explicit \(n\times n\) array. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The constant \(\varepsilon\) and all other constants are independent of the graph. cards.title: Balanced dense NFA Acceptance Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is it true that, for every constant \(\varepsilon>0\), no uniform bounded-error randomized word-RAM algorithm decides acceptance of length-\(n\) binary words by the dense n-state automata defined below in \(O(n^{3-\varepsilon})\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: An instance supplies \(n\ge2\), states \(Q=\{0,\ldots,n-1\}\), a start state \(q_0\), a set \(F\subseteq Q\) of accepting states, and a transition relation \(\Delta\subseteq Q\times\{0,1\}\times Q\). There are no empty-word transitions and no multiplicities. Require \(n^2\le|\Delta|\le2n^2\); the transition relation is given as two explicit Boolean adjacency matrices. The input word is \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), supplied explicitly. Acceptance means that states \(q_0,q_1,\ldots,q_n\) exist with \((q_{i-1},x_i,q_i)\in\Delta\) and \(q_n\in F\). Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Correctness probability is at least \(2/3\) for every fixed automaton and word. The bound includes reading the automaton, and all preprocessing; no preprocessed automaton is supplied. A finite program and constants may depend on fixed \(\varepsilon\), but not on an instance. Non-combinatorial algorithms are allowed.

cards.title: Linear-size Circuit-SAT below exhaustive search
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(c\ge 1\), do \(\varepsilon _{c}>0\) and a deterministic algorithm exist deciding satisfiability of every Boolean circuit with n inputs and at most cn gates in time \(O((2- \varepsilon _{c})^{n}\cdot n^{O(1)})\)?

Integers and rational numerators and denominators are encoded in binary; L denotes the total input bit length. A polynomial bound has constants independent of the input. cards.title: P versus BPP
cards.formal: Does \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}\)? Precisely, for every language L for which a randomized Turing machine R runs in polynomial time on every input and every random tape, and satisfies $\Pr[R(x)=1_L(x)]\ge2/3$ for every binary string x, does there exist a deterministic polynomial-time Turing machine deciding L correctly on every x? The polynomial time bound of the deterministic machine may depend on R.
cards.definitions: Input length is \(n=|x|\). A polynomial-time bound means \(C(n+1)^{k}\) steps for fixed constants C,k, independent of x and of the random bits. R uses independent unbiased random bits, at most one fresh bit per computation step, and outputs a single bit. Its error may be on either yes or no inputs, but is bounded separately on each input. P consists of deterministic polynomial-time decision languages and BPP of languages meeting the randomized guarantee above. These are total decision problems, with no excluded promise inputs. No advice, oracle, quantum operations, or input distribution is allowed. The requested deterministic simulation may use a different algorithm; it need not reproduce R's random choices, preserve its precise exponent, or be generated by an effective compiler from R.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This determines whether random bits add power to efficient total decision computation. It is a central organizing question for pseudorandom generators, explicit constructions, and the connection between circuit lower bounds and algorithm design.

importance.reason: The main general derandomization question for polynomial-time decision algorithms, with broad consequences for the role of randomness and for hardness-versus-randomness techniques.

progress.text: Adleman establishes \(\mathrm{BPP}\subseteq \mathrm{P}\)/poly. Suitable fixed random advice exists for each input length, but uniform polynomial-time computation of that advice is not supplied.

Impagliazzo and Wigderson prove \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{BPP}\) if there is a Boolean function computable in time \(2^{O(n)}\) that requires circuits of size \(2^{c n}\), for some \(c>0\) and all sufficiently large n. The circuit-hardness assumption remains essential to this theorem.

Doron, Moshkovitz, Oh, and Zuckerman improve conditional pseudorandomness parameters for algorithms satisfying an insensitivity property of their correct and incorrect random tapes. This concerns finer generators for a specified algorithm class, not unconditional removal of randomness from all BPP computations.

Version 9 of a preprint by Tianrong Lin claims the opposite conclusion \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{BPP}\), along with stronger separations. This review has not verified that construction or located independent primary validation. The claimed separation is recorded without treating it as established.

context_blocks.text: Randomized decision algorithms may use randomness to avoid exceptional choices or to test a property through a small sample. Their guarantee is pointwise: even the worst input must receive the correct answer with high probability. Repeating an algorithm reduces its error but leaves it randomized. The question asks whether every such use of randomness can ultimately be replaced by a deterministic polynomial computation.

Exhaustive majority evaluation over all random tapes has a time cost exponential in their length. That is correct, but takes exponential time when the tape has polynomial length. A suitable pseudorandom generator would reduce the search to a polynomial-size set of tapes, constructed efficiently. The hard part is ensuring that this small set fools the computation on every input.

A nonuniform version of this idea already works: after error amplification, an averaging argument supplies one polynomial-length advice string that works for every input of a given length. This proves BPP is contained in P/poly. The string can depend on the input length without an efficient procedure to find it, which is exactly why that inclusion does not answer the uniform question.

Strong circuit hardness provides a conditional route to full derandomization. Impagliazzo and Wigderson show that an exponentially circuit-hard function computable in exponential time suffices. The condition is substantially more specific than merely \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). Current work also studies the amount of slowdown and the structure of the randomized algorithm, producing finer conditional results without an unconditional equality proof.

This card concerns computing one correct decision bit. Sampling a distribution, producing one of many valid witnesses, or deciding only inputs with a promise leads to related but different formulations. Keeping these tasks separate prevents a derandomization theorem for one setting from being silently substituted for another.

The saved review explains conditional routes through strong circuit lower bounds and distinguishes uniform algorithms from advice strings that merely exist for each input length.

cards.context:
Randomized decision algorithms may use randomness to avoid exceptional choices or to test a property through a small sample. Their guarantee is pointwise: even the worst input must receive the correct answer with high probability. Repeating an algorithm reduces its error but leaves it randomized. The question asks whether every such use of randomness can ultimately be replaced by a deterministic polynomial computation.

Exhaustive majority evaluation over all random tapes has a time cost exponential in their length. That is correct, but takes exponential time when the tape has polynomial length. A suitable pseudorandom generator would reduce the search to a polynomial-size set of tapes, constructed efficiently. The hard part is ensuring that this small set fools the computation on every input.

A nonuniform version of this idea already works: after error amplification, an averaging argument supplies one polynomial-length advice string that works for every input of a given length. This proves BPP is contained in P/poly. The string can depend on the input length without an efficient procedure to find it, which is exactly why that inclusion does not answer the uniform question.

Strong circuit hardness provides a conditional route to full derandomization. Impagliazzo and Wigderson show that an exponentially circuit-hard function computable in exponential time suffices. The condition is substantially more specific than merely \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). Current work also studies the amount of slowdown and the structure of the randomized algorithm, producing finer conditional results without an unconditional equality proof.

This card concerns computing one correct decision bit. Sampling a distribution, producing one of many valid witnesses, or deciding only inputs with a promise leads to related but different formulations. Keeping these tasks separate prevents a derandomization theorem for one setting from being silently substituted for another.

benchmark_focus.reason: The main general derandomization question for polynomial-time decision algorithms, with broad consequences for the role of randomness and for hardness-versus-randomness techniques.

cards.title: Optimal explicit pseudorandom generators for read-once branching programs
cards.formal: Do there exist absolute constants C,D and a uniform family of generators \(G_{n,w,p}:\{0,1\}^{s}\to \{0,1\}^{n}\), for all integers \(n,w\ge 2\) and \(p\ge 1\), with \(s\le C(\log _{2} n+\log _{2} w+p)\), such that \(\left|\Pr_{u\text{ uniform in }\{0,1\}^{s}}[B(G_{n,w,p}(u))=1]-\Pr_{z\text{ uniform in }\{0,1\}^{n}}[B(z)=1]\right|\le2^{-p}\) for every length-n, width-at-most-w ordered read-once branching program B? Require a single deterministic algorithm that, given n,w,p,u and an output position i, computes \(G_{n,w,p}(u)_{i}\) using at most \(D(\log _{2} n+\log _{2} w+p)\) work bits and time \((nw\cdot 2^{p})^{D}\).
cards.definitions: An ordered read-once branching program has layers \(V_{0},\ldots ,V_{n}\), each containing at most w states, a designated initial state in \(V_{0}\), and an accepting subset of \(V_{n}\). For each layer \(i- 1\), each state has one outgoing edge labeled 0 and one labeled 1 to \(V_{i}\). On input z, the program follows the edge labeled \(z_{i}\) at step i and accepts exactly when the final state is accepting. Different edges may merge; neither regularity nor permutation transitions are required. The order is the fixed order \(z_{1},\ldots ,z_{n}\). Programs may be arbitrary nonuniform objects, but the generator cannot inspect their descriptions. The parameters and seed are read-only inputs to the generator algorithm, and the output bit is written separately; all work space, counters and intermediate storage are counted. Seed length is a computable function of the parameters within the stated resources. Uniform seeds induce an ordinary probability distribution, without signed or externally assigned weights. Set \(\varepsilon =2^{- p}\); this dyadic formulation gives the usual \(O(\log (nw/\varepsilon ))\) target for arbitrary positive error by rounding down to a smaller dyadic tolerance.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: An optimal generator would remove randomness from logarithmic-space computation and identify how little entropy suffices to fool every small-memory streaming computation. The question joins explicit constructions, space complexity and the gap between real distributions and useful signed approximations.

importance.reason: A central constructive route to L=BPL, with optimal nonconstructive seed length known and a persistent gap for uniform space-efficient generators despite advances in restricted and weighted models.

progress.text: Nisan constructs generators using \(O(\log  n\cdot \log (nw/\varepsilon ))\) seed bits for general ordered read-once branching programs.

Hoza obtains weighted generators with additive \(\log (1/\varepsilon )\) dependence and notes deterministic simulation in space \(O(S^{3/2}/\sqrt{\log  S})\); this is not a logarithmic-seed ordinary PRG.
Cheng and Hoza show that suitable logspace hitting sets imply \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\) and analyze stronger reductions toward ordinary PRGs; the journal version appears on 20 September 2022.
Cheng and Wu publish improved weighted PRGs via weighted pseudorandom reductions.

Chen and coauthors post revision 3 of Improved Error Reduction for Weighted PRGs. The revision preserves the weighted-output distinction and attributes the alphabet/error implication to Cheng and Hoza.
Cohen, Doron and Goldgraber give an improved INW analysis for permutation programs. Arbitrary ordered programs remain outside its structural promise.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. ECCC TR26-064 revision 3 explicitly retains the optimal general PRG target and the log-squared barrier. Its new generator is weighted; the July TR26-123 result is restricted to permutation programs. This card requires one ordinary, program-independent distribution family and optimal seed length as well as optimal work space.

context_blocks.text: The program processes a long stream while remembering only its current state. Width w corresponds to about \(\log _{2} w\) bits of memory; length n is the number of random bits it can inspect. A pseudorandom generator replaces that long random stream with the deterministic expansion of a much shorter genuinely random seed. The requirement is simultaneous: the same generated distribution must fool every permitted program, even though their transition tables may be entirely different.

There is no information-theoretic obstacle to the seed-length target. After padding to w states, the number of programs is at most \(w\cdot 2^{w}\cdot w^{2nw}\). Choose a list of independent uniform n-bit strings and use a uniformly chosen list position as the seed. A concentration bound and union bound show that a list of \(O(\varepsilon ^{- 2}(nw \log  w+w))\) strings suffices to approximate every acceptance probability. Indexing that list takes \(O(\log  n+\log  w+\log (1/\varepsilon ))\) bits. The argument does not tell us how to generate its entries in the tiny workspace required here.

The computational payoff is direct. Fix an input to a bounded-error logarithmic-space randomized machine and view its evolution on random bits as a polynomial-length, polynomial-width branching program. A logarithmic seed permits enumeration of all seeds, regeneration of individual pseudorandom bits and counting accepting runs within logarithmic space. With constant error small enough to preserve the acceptance gap, this would prove \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\). The card asks for a uniform generator, which is a particular strong route to that complexity-class equality.

Nisan’s construction gives seed length \(O(\log  n\cdot \log (nw/\varepsilon ))\). For polynomial width and constant error this is \(O(\log ^{2}n)\), so reaching the target would remove an entire logarithmic factor. The difficulty is generating a universally useful sample space in little space, rather than merely showing that some sample space exists. Even considerable improvements for simpler transition structures need not survive arbitrary merging of states.

Weighted pseudorandom generators relax the distribution requirement. They approximate acceptance by a weighted sum of program evaluations, with weights that may be negative. Hoza’s RANDOM 2021 construction attains seed length \(O(\log ^{2}n+\log (1/\varepsilon ))\) for width-n, length-n programs, improving the dependence on small error. Such weighted estimates can support deterministic simulation, but negative mass cannot be sampled as an ordinary probability distribution over the generated strings.

Cheng and Wu’s SODA 2026 work improves weighted generators across width and error regimes. Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma’s May 2026 revision improves error reduction and the dependence on the input alphabet. It still constructs a weighted object. Its discussion credits Cheng and Hoza’s earlier reduction showing that sufficiently good ordinary-generator dependence on alphabet size and error would break the log-squared barrier. That implication does not turn the newly constructed weighted generator into an ordinary one.

The role of hitting sets provides another useful distinction. A hitting set ensures that an accepting string is included when the accepting fraction is sufficiently large; it does not directly approximate that fraction. Cheng and Hoza prove that sufficiently strong logspace hitting sets nevertheless imply two-sided logspace derandomization through a more involved reduction. Their results explain why a derandomization theorem need not arrive packaged as the universal probability distribution requested here.

Cohen, Doron and Goldgraber’s July 2026 paper gives an ordinary generator for permutation programs with seed \(O((\log  w+\log (1/\varepsilon ))\log  n)\), by a new analysis of the INW generator. In this subclass each symbol acts bijectively on the states between layers. The result has optimal logarithmic dependence on length when width and error are fixed, but the permutation promise excludes the arbitrary state merging allowed in this card.

cards.title: L versus BPL
cards.formal: Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{BPL}\)? Equivalently, for every language \(S\subseteq \{0,1\}\)* decided with two-sided error at most \(1/3\) by a uniform randomized Turing machine using \(O(\log (n+2))\) work space and polynomial time on inputs of length n, is there a uniform deterministic Turing machine deciding S with \(O(\log (n+2))\) work space?
cards.definitions: The machines have a finite description, a read-only two-way input tape, and a fixed finite number of work tapes over a fixed finite alphabet. Space counts all visited work-tape cells; the input tape is excluded. A randomized machine receives independent fair coin outcomes one at a time, without a freely rereadable random tape: an outcome must be stored in counted work space to be remembered. It halts with ACCEPT or REJECT on every input and every random tape within \(K(n+2)^{c}\) steps and uses at most \(K \log _{2}(n+2)\) work cells, for some constants K,c depending only on the machine. For each input x, acceptance probability is at least \(2/3\) if \(x\in S\) and at most \(1/3\) if \(x\notin S\). This is a language problem with no promise excluding intermediate-probability inputs. A deterministic decider must halt and give the correct answer on every input; any halting deterministic logarithmic-space decider has polynomially many configurations and hence polynomial running time. Both classes are uniform and have no advice. The deterministic machine and its space constant may depend on S. The equality does not demand a computable compiler transforming arbitrary machine descriptions, nor a particular pseudorandom-generator construction.

context_blocks.text: A logarithmic-space computation can maintain indices and counters while remembering only a small part of the input. Randomness lets it explore many possible choices without storing all of them. The equality asks whether this apparent extra power disappears when the required output is only a bounded-error decision about the input.

The memory convention is central. Fresh random outcomes can be read once; a machine cannot revisit an arbitrarily long random string without paying for its storage or reconstructing it. Conversely, the deterministic simulator is allowed a different constant in its logarithmic-space bound. The question concerns equality of language classes, not identical execution traces.

Saks and Zhou gave a deterministic simulation using \(O(\log ^{3/2} n)\) space. Hoza improved the bound to \(O(\log ^{3/2} n / \sqrt{\log  \log  n})\), with the expression understood asymptotically. These bounds are substantially below squared logarithmic space but remain above a constant multiple of log n.

The 2026 work of Chen, Cohen, Doron, Khaskelberg and Ta-Shma improves error reduction for weighted pseudorandom generators. Its revised account distinguishes weighted generators from ordinary generators and attributes the relevant arity/error connection to Cheng and Hoza. Those parameter improvements do not establish the equality of classes asked here.

The catalogue separately contains a concrete optimal-generator problem for read-once branching programs. Such a construction can have consequences for logarithmic-space derandomization, but the language-class equality does not prescribe that particular construction. This completed card retains the original TCS-0026 identity and Wigderson reference while making the computation and error models explicit.

cards.title: Optimal deterministic restricted-isometry matrices
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C,B,b>0\) and a deterministic algorithm which, for every pair of integers \(N\ge 2\) and \(2\le s\le N\), outputs in at most \(B N^{b}\) bit operations a rational \(m\times N\) matrix A, with \(m\le C s \ln (eN/s)\), such that \((2/3)\Vert x\Vert _{2}^{2}\le \Vert Ax\Vert _{2}^{2}\le (4/3)\Vert x\Vert _{2}^{2}\) for every real vector \(x\in \mathbb{R} ^{N}\) with at most s nonzero coordinates?
cards.definitions: The input consists of N and s in binary. The output is an explicit list of all entries of A, each encoded as a signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. Its total encoding length must also be at most \(B N^{b}\). Time is ordinary deterministic Turing-machine bit complexity, polynomial in N; randomness, advice and unit-cost exact real arithmetic are unavailable. The row count m is a positive integer chosen by the algorithm. The same constants and algorithm work for all allowed pairs N,s. The norm is Euclidean, and the displayed inequalities concern squared norms. They define restricted isometry of order s and distortion \(\delta =1/3\). The condition must hold simultaneously for every support of size at most s and every real choice of coefficients on that support. No probability over supports or signals is permitted. The natural logarithm and the factor e ensure a nonzero expression when s is close to N. The omitted case \(s=1\) is trivial and can be handled by a single row of ones.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm satisfying all the uniform dimension, encoding, time and restricted-isometry requirements, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A negative result conditional on a complexity assumption must state it. An existence proof, a construction using random bits, success for most sparse signals, or a deterministic construction with a larger asymptotic row count does not settle the stated question.
cards.why: A central gap between random existence and efficient explicit construction, with direct consequences for uniform sparse recovery and for how pseudorandomness controls exponentially many spectral constraints.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No polynomial-time deterministic construction with the required uniform optimal row bound was found in the checked sources. Optimal randomized row counts, restricted parameter regimes and coherence guarantees are recorded as partial progress.

context_blocks.text: Suppose an unknown vector has N coordinates but only s of them matter. A measurement matrix replaces the vector by m linear measurements. Sparsity allows m to be much smaller than N, but the matrix must preserve every possible sparse direction if the measuring device is to work uniformly. The question asks whether a short, guaranteed measurement design can be computed without random choices.

The restricted-isometry requirement has a concrete spectral interpretation. For every set S of at most s column indices, all eigenvalues of \(A_{S}^{T}A_{S}\) must lie between \(2/3\) and \(4/3\). Thus columns must behave almost orthogonally in every small group. Checking only individual column lengths, only pairs of columns, or a large collection of sampled test vectors leaves many of these simultaneous constraints untested.

This condition supports stable sparse recovery. If a matrix has restricted isometry of order 2t with distortion \(1/3\), then two different t-sparse signals cannot have identical measurements: their difference has at most 2t nonzero coordinates. Standard recovery theorems also give robust reconstruction by \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) minimization. The distinction between order t and order 2t is necessary; injectivity for t-sparse differences alone would not compare arbitrary t-sparse signals.

Random independent Bernoulli or Gaussian matrices attain \(m=O(s \log (eN/s))\) for fixed distortion, and matching row lower bounds make this the optimal order for \(s\ge 2\). Rao’s paper summarizes this benchmark and improves the amount of randomness needed to attain it. The unresolved resource in the card is therefore deterministic construction time, rather than whether matrices with the desired geometric property exist.

Requiring rational output does not destroy the random benchmark. For example, choose the number of rows to be a perfect square \(t^{2}\) within a constant factor of a sufficiently large target value, and use independent entries ±\(1/t\). This keeps the usual normalized Bernoulli construction while giving an exact, short binary description of every entry. The real difficulty is choosing all the signs deterministically with a proof that every sparse direction is preserved.

One basic deterministic analysis bounds the coherence \(\mu\), the largest absolute inner product between two unit columns. Gershgorin’s theorem then gives restricted-isometry constant at most \((s- 1)\mu\). When \(\mu\) is about \(1/\sqrt{m}\), this argument certifies only s on the order of \(\sqrt{m}\). This is a limitation of that sufficient-condition analysis, commonly called the square-root bottleneck, rather than an impossibility theorem for deterministic matrices.

Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova broke that bottleneck in a restricted parameter regime. Their explicit construction uses additive-combinatorial and exponential-sum estimates to control interactions beyond pairwise coherence. It is a major proof that deterministic analysis can go further, but its small exponent improvement does not reach the optimal \(s \log (eN/s)\) row count uniformly in N and s.

Rao’s construction achieves the optimal row order with \(O(s \log (N/s) \log  s)\) random bits in the sparse parameter regime discussed in the paper. Its proof extends the Hanson–Wright inequality to biased distributions. Reducing the seed length makes progress toward explicit construction, but enumerating all seeds can still take far more than polynomial time, and recognizing a successful seed is a separate issue.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

For a simple illustration, the \(m+1\) unit vertices of a regular simplex in \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}\) have small and equal pairwise inner products, yet their sum is zero. Their coefficient vector of all ones is therefore a nonzero sparse kernel vector. The example explains why an attractive frame construction must be accompanied by control over all relevant column subsets, not just a calculation of coherence.

The all-parameter formulation also matters. The identity matrix handles s comparable to N, while many explicit algebraic constructions work only along particular dimension sequences or for specified sparsity ranges. A resolution must cover the intermediate sparse regimes with one polynomial-time procedure. Likewise, statistical recovery guarantees and \(\ell\)\(_{1}\)-norm versions of restricted isometry answer different geometric questions.

Random matrices achieve this row order, but a usable deterministic construction must control every sparse support simultaneously.
Optimal explicit matrices would provide guaranteed measurement designs for compressed sensing without random setup choices.
The saved review identifies the limitations of pairwise coherence analyses and notes that reduced randomness or success on typical signals does not establish the requested all-signal guarantee.

cards.context:
Suppose an unknown vector has N coordinates but only s of them matter. A measurement matrix replaces the vector by m linear measurements. Sparsity allows m to be much smaller than N, but the matrix must preserve every possible sparse direction if the measuring device is to work uniformly. The question asks whether a short, guaranteed measurement design can be computed without random choices.

The restricted-isometry requirement has a concrete spectral interpretation. For every set S of at most s column indices, all eigenvalues of \(A_{S}^{T}A_{S}\) must lie between \(2/3\) and \(4/3\). Thus columns must behave almost orthogonally in every small group. Checking only individual column lengths, only pairs of columns, or a large collection of sampled test vectors leaves many of these simultaneous constraints untested.

This condition supports stable sparse recovery. If a matrix has restricted isometry of order 2t with distortion \(1/3\), then two different t-sparse signals cannot have identical measurements: their difference has at most 2t nonzero coordinates. Standard recovery theorems also give robust reconstruction by \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) minimization. The distinction between order t and order 2t is necessary; injectivity for t-sparse differences alone would not compare arbitrary t-sparse signals.

Random independent Bernoulli or Gaussian matrices attain \(m=O(s \log (eN/s))\) for fixed distortion, and matching row lower bounds make this the optimal order for \(s\ge 2\). Rao’s paper summarizes this benchmark and improves the amount of randomness needed to attain it. The unresolved resource in the card is therefore deterministic construction time, rather than whether matrices with the desired geometric property exist.

Requiring rational output does not destroy the random benchmark. For example, choose the number of rows to be a perfect square \(t^{2}\) within a constant factor of a sufficiently large target value, and use independent entries ±\(1/t\). This keeps the usual normalized Bernoulli construction while giving an exact, short binary description of every entry. The real difficulty is choosing all the signs deterministically with a proof that every sparse direction is preserved.

One basic deterministic analysis bounds the coherence \(\mu\), the largest absolute inner product between two unit columns. Gershgorin’s theorem then gives restricted-isometry constant at most \((s- 1)\mu\). When \(\mu\) is about \(1/\sqrt{m}\), this argument certifies only s on the order of \(\sqrt{m}\). This is a limitation of that sufficient-condition analysis, commonly called the square-root bottleneck, rather than an impossibility theorem for deterministic matrices.

Bourgain, Dilworth, Ford, Konyagin and Kutzarova broke that bottleneck in a restricted parameter regime. Their explicit construction uses additive-combinatorial and exponential-sum estimates to control interactions beyond pairwise coherence. It is a major proof that deterministic analysis can go further, but its small exponent improvement does not reach the optimal \(s \log (eN/s)\) row count uniformly in N and s.

Rao’s construction achieves the optimal row order with \(O(s \log (N/s) \log  s)\) random bits in the sparse parameter regime discussed in the paper. Its proof extends the Hanson–Wright inequality to biased distributions. Reducing the seed length makes progress toward explicit construction, but enumerating all seeds can still take far more than polynomial time, and recognizing a successful seed is a separate issue.

The inherited 2025 paper of Fickus and Lake studies highly symmetric equiangular tight frames, which minimize coherence. It analyzes their minimal dependent column sets through regular simplices and designs. Such structure is informative in both directions: a dependent set of r columns immediately prevents restricted isometry of order r with distortion less than one. Optimal pairwise geometry alone does not guarantee the higher-order property.

For a simple illustration, the \(m+1\) unit vertices of a regular simplex in \(\mathbb{R} ^{m}\) have small and equal pairwise inner products, yet their sum is zero. Their coefficient vector of all ones is therefore a nonzero sparse kernel vector. The example explains why an attractive frame construction must be accompanied by control over all relevant column subsets, not just a calculation of coherence.

The all-parameter formulation also matters. The identity matrix handles s comparable to N, while many explicit algebraic constructions work only along particular dimension sequences or for specified sparsity ranges. A resolution must cover the intermediate sparse regimes with one polynomial-time procedure. Likewise, statistical recovery guarantees and \(\ell\)\(_{1}\)-norm versions of restricted isometry answer different geometric questions.

cards.title: Two-source extraction at log n plus constant entropy
cards.formal: Do a constant C and a deterministic algorithm running in \(\operatorname{poly}(n)\) time exist that compute \(E_{n}:\{0,1\}^{n}\times \{0,1\}^{n}\to \{0,1\}\) with |\(\Pr [E_{n}(X,Y)=1]- 1/2|\le 0.01\) for every pair of independent sources X,Y of min-entropy at least \(\log _{2}n+C\)?
cards.definitions: The algorithm receives n and the two n-bit strings, and defines one function for every \(n\ge 1\). A source is any probability distribution on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\); its min-entropy is −\(\log _{2}(\max _{x} \Pr [X=x])\). Independence means the joint law is the product of the two marginal distributions. For n where the entropy threshold exceeds n there are no eligible sources. No auxiliary uniform seed, advice or distribution description is supplied. The constants and time polynomial are universal.

context_blocks.text: Two independent weak sources can contain much randomness while neither source by itself yields even one predictably unbiased bit. The target reaches the entropy threshold permitted by a random truth table with a polynomial-time evaluable function.

cards.title: FPT versus \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)
cards.formal: Do there exist a total computable function \(f:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N} , a\) constant c, and one deterministic algorithm that decides whether an n-vertex graph contains a k-clique in time at most \(f(k)(n+2)^{c}\) on every input? Equivalently, is \(\mathrm{FPT}=\mathrm{W}[1]\)?
cards.definitions: An instance is a finite simple undirected graph G on \([n]\), encoded by its adjacency matrix, and an integer k with \(0\le k\le n\), encoded in binary. A k-clique is a set of k distinct vertices for which every pair is an edge; \(k=0\) is a yes-instance. Inputs with \(k>n\) are rejected immediately, and other malformed inputs are rejected. The parameter is k, not treewidth, degree, or the size of a supplied decomposition. Running time counts deterministic Turing-machine steps on the full input. Constants and the function f may be arbitrary but must be fixed independently of n; the exponent c must also be independent of k. FPT comprises parameterized decision problems solvable in \(f(k)N^{c}\) time, where N is their input encoding length. One equivalent definition of \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) is the class of parameterized problems reducible to k-Clique by a deterministic \(f(k)N^{c}\)-time many-one reduction whose output parameter is bounded by a computable function of k alone. This is the standard parameterized reduction convention under which Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-complete. No randomness, advice, or promise about G is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This is the principal boundary question for algorithms whose exponential difficulty is confined to a small parameter. It determines the force of thousands of parameterized hardness reductions and separates efficient small-solution search from algorithms whose input-size exponent grows with the solution size.

importance.reason: The defining unresolved tractability separation of parameterized complexity, with Clique as a precise and widely used complete problem.

progress.text: Downey and Fellows develop the W-hierarchy and the completeness framework that makes parameterized Clique a canonical target for the FPT-versus-\(\mathrm{W}[1]\) question.
ETH-based reductions establish the stronger conditional obstruction to \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) Clique algorithms; the textbook develops this in its parameterized lower-bound chapters.

Bottesch studies structural and relativization evidence concerning FPT and \(\mathrm{W}[1]\), explicitly distinguishing this conjecture from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\). No unrelativized separation is proved.
Lin proves constant-factor FPT approximation of Clique \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard, transferring the same central assumption to approximate search.
Chen, Feng, Laekhanukit, and Liu give a simpler combinatorial construction for the \(k^{o(1)}\) parameterized Clique inapproximability bound.
Abboud, Fischer, and Shechter improve combinatorial fixed-k Clique running times by logarithmic factors. The Algorithmica publication of 22 May 2026 retains dependence on k in the exponent of n.

cards.status_note: Explicitly presented as the central open conjecture in Bottesch’s primary paper and the parameterized-algorithms textbook. Research through 10 September 2026 located no proof of equality or separation. Conditional lower bounds and improved fixed-k algorithms are recorded with their distinct quantifiers.

context_blocks.text: For each fixed k, exhaustive search over vertex subsets decides Clique in polynomial time. The exponent grows with k, so this observation gives a different kind of tractability: increasing the target clique size can increase the power of n in the running time. The question asks whether all dependence on k can instead be moved into one multiplicative function. For example, \(2^{2^{k}}n^{3}\) meets the requested form, while \(n^{k/10}\) does not.

The unrestricted Clique problem is NP-complete, but this alone cannot rule out fixed-parameter tractability. The permitted function f can grow much faster than any polynomial when k grows with n. If \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\) then Clique is certainly FPT; the converse implication is not known. Thus \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\) is a stronger separation conjecture than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in the direction currently proved.

Parameterized reductions keep the output parameter controlled solely by the original parameter. Since Clique is complete under these reductions, an FPT Clique algorithm would solve every \(\mathrm{W}[1]\) problem in FPT time. This is why a \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hardness proof is useful evidence against a parameterized algorithm for another problem. The evidence is conditional on the separation being true, even when the reduction theorem itself is unconditional.

The Exponential Time Hypothesis supplies a stronger quantitative barrier: it rules out \(f(k)n^{o(k)}\) algorithms for Clique. That conclusion excludes FPT, but uses an assumption that is itself open. Matrix-multiplication methods and improved combinatorial methods accelerate Clique for fixed k while leaving an exponent that grows with the parameter. Their progress does not eliminate the central gap.

Approximation has become another way to measure the reach of the conjecture. Lin proves that even fixed-factor parameterized approximation of Clique is \(\mathrm{W}[1]\)-hard. Later constructions strengthen the factor and simplify the reductions. These results enlarge the consequences of a separation; they do not prove \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\).

cards.title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is there a constant \(c>0\) such that, for every deterministic algorithm A that correctly decides every 3-CNF satisfiability instance, and every constant \(d\ge 0, A\) does not have worst-case running time \(O(2^{cn}\mathrm{L}^{d})\)? Here n is the number of variables and L is the full binary input length. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis \((\mathrm{ETH})\).
cards.definitions: A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of explicitly listed clauses, each containing at most three literals \(x_{i}\) or \(\neg x_{i}\). Satisfiability means existence of a Boolean assignment satisfying all clauses. Variables are relabeled consecutively; n counts the distinct variables actually present, and L includes all literal indices, signs, delimiters, and repetitions. An empty clause is unsatisfiable and an empty conjunction is satisfiable. Algorithms are uniform deterministic Turing machines with no advice or oracles; they must halt and answer exactly on all inputs, with no promise about density, solution count, or distribution. Define \(s_{3}=\inf\){\(\alpha \ge 0\) : some such algorithm runs in \(O(2^{\alpha n}\mathrm{L}^{d})\) for a fixed d}. ETH asserts \(s_{3}>0\). The excluded exponent c is a single constant independent of the algorithm. The polynomial exponent and hidden constant may depend on the algorithm, but not the instance. Polynomial input factors allow the complete formula to be read even if clauses are repeated many times. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.

importance.reason: A foundational quantitative hardness hypothesis underlying exact, parameterized, graph, and geometric algorithm lower bounds.

progress.text: Impagliazzo and Paturi formalize the exponential rates of k-SAT and study their relations. These rates remain conjectural lower bounds against unrestricted algorithms.
The authors’ IPEC survey describes how exact satisfiability complexity connects to parameterized complexity, circuit lower bounds, and data structures.

The parameterized-algorithms textbook states ETH as a positive infimum, develops sparsification, and derives consequences including \(\mathrm{FPT}\ne \mathrm{W}[1]\). It distinguishes randomized variants.
Liu gives a deterministic 3-SAT upper bound with base 1.32793 using branching and generalized covering codes. The saving leaves a positive exponential rate.

Aggarwal, Gupta, Morolia, and Zhang obtain new lattice approximation hardness from ETH or randomized ETH, depending on the target problem and reduction. Their ICALP paper continues to treat these as hypotheses and separates them from Gap-ETH.

cards.status_note: The cited foundational and 2026 conference sources treat ETH as an open hypothesis. Checked through 10 September 2026. This formulation is uniform, deterministic, and a positive-infimum assertion; randomized, nonuniform, gap, and stronger all-width hypotheses are distinct.

context_blocks.text: NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\) remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size \(n^{3}\), which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one \(2^{o(n)}\) algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

There are substantial deterministic improvements over trying all \(2^{n}\) assignments. Liu combines branching with derandomized local search to obtain a \(1.32793^{n}\) bound for 3-SAT, up to polynomial factors. Such an algorithm decreases an upper bound on \(s_{3}\) while leaving it positive. Empirical solver success, promises of many solutions, and bounded-occurrence restrictions do not address worst-case unrestricted formulas.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size \(n^{3}\), which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one \(2^{o(n)}\) algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

There are substantial deterministic improvements over trying all \(2^{n}\) assignments. Liu combines branching with derandomized local search to obtain a \(1.32793^{n}\) bound for 3-SAT, up to polynomial factors. Such an algorithm decreases an upper bound on \(s_{3}\) while leaving it positive. Empirical solver success, promises of many solutions, and bounded-occurrence restrictions do not address worst-case unrestricted formulas.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

cards.title: Breaking the \(2^{n}\) barrier for weighted TSP
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(\varepsilon \in (0,1), c\ge 1\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every complete undirected graph on \(n\ge 3\) labelled vertices with nonnegative binary-encoded integer edge weights of total encoding length L, outputs a minimum-weight Hamiltonian cycle with probability at least \(2/3\) in worst-case time \(O((2- \varepsilon )^{n}(n+\mathrm{L})^{c})\)?
cards.definitions: Each unordered pair of distinct vertices has one explicitly listed weight. A Hamiltonian cycle visits each vertex exactly once before returning to its first vertex, and its weight is the sum of its n edge weights. Output the cyclic list of vertex labels. The input has no metric, bounded-weight, planarity or sparsity promise. Use a random-access word RAM with \(w=B\lceil n+\log _{2}(\mathrm{L}+2)\rceil\) bits per word for one fixed sufficiently large integer B; unit-cost operations are reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division by nonzero words. Integers occupying several words incur the cost of all word operations. This word size permits addressing exponential-space subset tables; its polynomial bit-operation overhead is already permitted by the polynomial factor in \(n+\mathrm{L}\). The running-time bound includes reading weights, preprocessing, random bits and output and holds on every execution. Only independent private fair random bits are allowed; there is no quantum access, advice or oracle. The constants \(\varepsilon ,c,B\) and the implicit multiplicative constant are independent of n,L and the weights. A deterministic algorithm also qualifies. Dependence polynomial in the numerical maximum weight, rather than its binary length, does not qualify.

context_blocks.text: The exact travelling salesman problem asks for a cheapest tour through all vertices. In the general weighted setting, discovering a Hamiltonian cycle is not enough: the input is complete, so tours certainly exist, but their costs can vary greatly. The computational target is the minimum among them.

The classical subset dynamic program has a base-two dependence on the number of vertices. Stoian’s 2024 algorithm improves the familiar \(O(2^{n} n^{2})\) time by a factor \(2^{\Omega (\sqrt{\log  n})}\). Its bound retains the exponential base two and does not yield \(O*((2- \varepsilon )^{n})\) for any fixed positive \(\varepsilon\).

This distinction is substantial even though both bounds are exponential. A fixed base reduction saves an exponential factor on increasingly large instances, whereas savings in the polynomial or subexponential prefactor do not. The card asks about unrestricted classical algorithms, not about the optimality of the original dynamic-programming recurrence.

Weight encoding separates this target from several related exact questions. A method whose time is polynomial in the maximum integer weight can be very expensive when a large weight has a short binary representation. Likewise, faster algorithms for unweighted Hamiltonicity or for special weighted graph classes do not establish the general weighted guarantee.

No asserted reduction from SETH is built into the question. The desired algorithmic existence is itself the target; a conditional lower bound must state its assumption separately. The Parameterized and exact algorithms bucket is appropriate because the defining issue is the exponential dependence on n, rather than polynomial-time approximation of a tour.

cards.title: FPT approximation of twin-width
cards.formal: Do there exist total computable functions \(f,g:N\to N\) and a constant \(c\ge 1\), and one deterministic Turing machine A, such that for every finite nonempty simple graph G on n vertices and integer \(k\ge 0, A\) halts within \(f(k)(n+1)^{c}\) bit operations and either correctly reports \(tww(G)>k\) or outputs a contraction sequence of G of width at most \(g(k)\)? No order, decomposition or contraction sequence is supplied with G.
cards.definitions: The input gives n, the \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix of G, and k in binary. A contraction sequence is a sequence of partitions of \(V(G)\), starting with the singleton partition and ending with \(\{V(G)\}\), each obtained from its predecessor by merging two parts. For distinct parts X,Y, their pair is mixed if there exist both an adjacent pair \(x\in X,y\in Y\) and a nonadjacent pair \(x' \in X,y' \in Y\) in the original graph. The red degree of a part is the number of other parts with which it has a mixed pair. The sequence width is the maximum red degree over every part of every partition. Twin-width \(tww(G)\) is the minimum sequence width; a one-vertex graph has twin-width zero. The output lists the \(n- 1\) merges using integer part labels. Both f and g depend only on k, whereas c is independent of k and G. If \(tww(G)\le k\), rejection is forbidden. If \(tww(G)>k\), either a correct rejection or the stated bounded-width sequence is allowed.

cards.definitions: The input is \(n\ge1\), a target \(t\ge0\), and an explicitly listed multiset \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\) of positive integers, all in binary with delimiters; \(L\) is the bit length of that full encoding. Accept if and only if there is \(I\subseteq[n]\) with \(\sum_{i\in I}x_{i}=t\). Each index is used at most once, repetitions of values are permitted, and the empty subset is allowed. Use a uniform random-access machine with \(w=d(n+\lceil\log_{2}(L+2)\rceil)\)-bit words for fixed \(d\ge1\), large enough to address exponential memory. Unit-cost instructions are word read/write, copy, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor, comparisons, Boolean operations and shifts; shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword integers are handled through charged component operations. Input packing, preprocessing and memory initialization are charged. Random words are independent and uniform and cost one instruction each. A fixed finite program receives no advice or tables. It answers correctly with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input and the time bound holds on every random execution. Constants are independent of all input values and \(n,L\). Quantum operations and random-instance promises are absent.

context_blocks.text: Subset Sum asks whether some selection of the supplied indices adds to the target exactly. For values \((3,3,5)\), target \(6\) is attainable by taking both occurrences of \(3\); an occurrence cannot be used twice. Target zero is always attainable by the empty subset. The input multiplicities and the exact integer comparison are part of the problem.

The classical meet-in-the-middle benchmark is \(2^{n/2}\) times polynomial factors. The question asks for a smaller fixed exponential rate on every input, not an improvement in one polynomial factor. A bound such as \(2^{n/2}/n^{100}\) would still leave the requested exponent saving unresolved.

Pseudopolynomial algorithms depend on the numerical target rather than just the number of bits needed to write it. They can be excellent when the target is small, but binary input values can be exponentially large relative to their descriptions. Chan’s 2026 work improves this separate regime while explicitly retaining the worst-case exponential question.

An August 2026 preprint claims a quantum \(O^{\ast}(2^{2n/7})\) algorithm and still identifies the classical half-exponent benchmark. The star notation hides polynomial factors. The use of quantum computation is decisive: this does not supply the classical algorithm quantified over here. The new preprint proof was not independently checked.

Random instances, uniqueness promises and restrictions on the magnitude or density of the numbers can also alter exponential complexity. This target has none of those input promises and permits bounded-error classical randomness on every instance. Exponential memory is allowed and addressable in the specified RAM; a polynomial-space restriction would ask a different question.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one uniform classical randomized algorithm, constants \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\), \(c\ge1\), and a constant multiplier meet the stated \(2^{(1/2-\varepsilon)n}L^c\) time bound on every random execution and success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input, or prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The theorem must allow unrestricted binary magnitudes, repeated positive values, all targets, and the full permitted RAM model.

cards.definitions: A k-expression is a finite expression building a labeled graph using labels from \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\). It can create one isolated vertex with a chosen label; take the disjoint union of two previously constructed labeled graphs; add all edges between the vertices labeled i and those labeled j for distinct i,j; or change every label i to j. Edge insertion leaves existing edges in place without duplicating them. Relabeling changes no edges. The two operands of a disjoint union may both be arbitrary expressions, so this is ordinary clique-width, not linear clique-width. For a nonempty graph \(G, \operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the least k for which some k-expression produces a graph isomorphic to G after labels are erased. Set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The input contains \(n\ge 0\) and the \(n\times n\) symmetric zero-diagonal \(0/1\) adjacency matrix for the graph on \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). It contains no construction expression or promise about its width. \(A_{k}\) outputs YES exactly when \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\) and NO otherwise, always halting with the stated worst-case bit bound. The quantifier order is \(\forall k \exists A_{k},C_{k},c_{k} \forall G: k\) is fixed for each machine, and the polynomial exponent may depend on it. Each \(A_{k}\) is a single finite program with no advice depending on graph size; the statement imposes no effective map from k to its program and no uniform exponent.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove polynomial-time exact recognition for every fixed threshold k in the model stated, or prove that for at least one fixed k the language \(\{G:\operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\}\) has no deterministic polynomial-time decider. cards.title: Independent set algorithms from tropical circuit size
cards.formal: Do there exist one deterministic Turing machine A and constants \(C,c\ge 1\) such that for every finite simple graph G on \(n\ge 1\) vertices and nonnegative integer weight vector w, A outputs the maximum independent-set weight within \(C(\tau (G)+n+\mathrm{L}+1)^{c}\) bit operations, where L is the total binary encoding length of w and \(\tau (G)\) is the minimum size of a tropical MWIS circuit defined below? Only G and w are supplied; neither \(\tau (G)\) nor a circuit is part of the input.
cards.definitions: G is given by its \(n\times n\) adjacency matrix. The n nonnegative weights are binary integers with delimiters, all counted in L. A vertex set I is independent when no edge has both endpoints in I. \(MWIS(G,w)=\max\)_{I independent}\(\sum_{v\in I}w_{v}\), allowing \(I=\varnothing\) with weight zero. A tropical circuit for G is a finite acyclic circuit with one designated output, arbitrary fan-out, input gates labeled \(x_{v}\) or the constant 0, and binary internal gates labeled max or + with their ordinary real-number meanings. No other constants or operations are allowed. Size counts every gate, including input and constant gates. An MWIS circuit must output \(MWIS(G,x)\) for every vector \(x\in R_{\ge}0^{n}\), so its topology depends only on G. Define \(\tau (G)\) as the minimum size of such a circuit. This minimum exists because finitely many independent sets can each be summed and their maximum computed. The output algorithm may use general deterministic computation, not only tropical operations. Constants C,c are uniform over all graphs and weight vectors.

cards.title: Fixed-parameter tractability of graph isomorphism by rank-width
cards.formal: Do a computable function \(f:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}\), an absolute constant c and a deterministic algorithm exist which decide isomorphism of graphs G,H in time \(f(k)(|V(G)|+|V(H)|+2)^{c}\), where \(k=\max (\operatorname{rw}(G),\operatorname{rw}(H))\)?
cards.definitions: Graphs are finite simple undirected graphs given by adjacency matrices. Isomorphism is a vertex bijection preserving adjacency. For a graph G and \(X\subseteq V(G)\), the cut-rank is the rank over the two-element field of the adjacency submatrix with rows X and columns \(V(G)\setminus X\). A rank decomposition is a tree of maximum degree three whose leaves are bijectively labeled by \(V(G)\). Every tree edge partitions the leaves and hence defines a cut-rank; the decomposition width is the maximum of those ranks. Rank-width \(\operatorname{rw}(G)\) is the minimum width, with \(\operatorname{rw}(G)=0\) for at most one vertex. No decomposition or parameter value is supplied to the algorithm. The exponent c is independent of the rank-width.

context_blocks.text: Rank-width measures graph complexity through low-rank adjacency cuts and supports many structural algorithms. Graph isomorphism on bounded rank-width is tractable at each fixed width, but that does not by itself yield one exponent independent of the parameter.
