cards.status_note: No polynomial-time fixed \((2- \varepsilon )\) improvement found through 11 September 2026. Svensson’s factor-two hardness requires the specified possibly stronger Unique Games variant. Recent fixed-machine approximation schemes and exact unit-job algorithms have narrower scope, while July 2026 UMPS hardness imposes machine eligibility restrictions absent here. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

context_blocks.text: The target is the infimum polynomial-time approximation ratio. The factor-two algorithmic question discussed in the saved history selects one threshold in this larger numerical target.

Two basic obstructions limit how quickly dependent jobs can finish. Total work \(\mathrm{W}=\sum_{j} p_{j}\) needs at least \(\mathrm{W}/m\) time across m machines. A precedence chain must execute sequentially, so the length L of a longest weighted path is another lower bound. A schedule must manage both parallel throughput and the timely completion of jobs that unlock later work. Even with identical machines and no communication costs, these priorities can conflict.

Graham’s list scheduling follows a fixed priority order and starts available jobs whenever machines become free. A job is available once all its predecessors have finished. Its analysis gives Cmax\(\le \mathrm{W}/m+(1- 1/m)\mathrm{L}\), and hence Cmax\(\le (2- 1/m)\)OPT. The bound approaches two as the machine count grows. Therefore the fact that each individual instance has a guarantee strictly below two does not establish a fixed improvement of the universal infimum below two.

A simple example shows why choosing priorities matters. Take \(m(m- 1)\) independent unit jobs and one independent job of length m. If the long job comes last in the list, the units occupy all machines for \(m- 1\) time, and the final job finishes at \(2m- 1\). An optimal schedule starts the long job immediately and runs the unit jobs on the other \(m- 1\) machines, finishing at time m. This proves a limitation of that list order, not hardness for every algorithm: the example has no precedence edges.

Classical NP-hardness excludes approximation factors below \(4/3\) unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\), leaving room between that barrier and two. Svensson’s STOC 2010 work, published in 2011, connects the missing hardness to a different scheduling objective: minimizing total weighted completion time on one machine with precedences. Sufficiently strong hardness near factor two for that problem transfers to makespan on identical parallel machines, even with unit processing times.

Combined with Bansal and Khot’s hypothesis, the reduction gives hardness for every fixed factor below two. The hypothesis is a particular Unique Games variant with additional structure: near-perfect satisfiability on large subsets in the yes case and an expansion requirement in the no case. Svensson explicitly describes it as possibly stronger than the usual Unique Games conjecture. Thus this is substantial conditional evidence, but it should not be presented as a theorem following solely from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

There has been strong progress when the number of machines is a fixed constant and jobs have unit length. Levey–Rothvoss initiate a line of approximation schemes based on hierarchy relaxations, followed by faster bounds. Das and Wiese provide a simpler quasipolynomial scheme by guessing selected jobs and time intervals and filling the remaining positions greedily. Their paper was published at ESA 2022, despite being uploaded to arXiv in January 2025. Its fixed-machine and running-time restrictions are essential.

Nederlof, Swennenhuis and Węgrzycki advance exact algorithms for unit jobs. Their bound \((1+n/m)^{O(\sqrt{nm})}\) is subexponential when \(m=o(n)\), and they also give an exponential improvement when m is proportional to n. The work appeared at SODA 2025 and was published online in ACM Transactions on Algorithms in January 2026. Exactness is stronger than approximation, but these running times are not polynomial and the processing-time promise remains narrower than this card’s model.

Guruswami, Ren and Tang’s July 2026 preprint proves that even unit-length jobs can be hard to approximate within any constant when each job has one predetermined eligible machine. That extra restriction prevents the scheduler from freely distributing ready jobs. It is a different model, called unique-machine precedence scheduling, and its hardness transfers to certain communication-delay models. It does not contradict the factor-two guarantee available when every job may use any identical machine.

A fixed improvement below two would show that global information about the precedence graph can reliably overcome the worst interactions between chain length and machine utilization. A matching hardness theorem under a standard assumption would explain why a very old greedy guarantee remains near the limit of efficient scheduling. The question isolates that issue without combining it with heterogeneous machines, strategic reports, or communication delays.

cards.title: Constant additive error for one-dimensional bin packing
cards.formal: Do a universal integer \(C\ge 0\) and a randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist that pack every explicitly listed one-dimensional bin-packing instance into at most OPT+C unit-capacity bins with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: The input is a list of \(n\ge 1\) rational item sizes \(s_{1},\ldots ,s_{n}\in\)(0,1], each encoded as a binary numerator and positive binary denominator; L is the total encoding length. A feasible packing is a map \(b:[n]\to [k]\) with \(\sum_{i:b(i)=j}s_{i}\le 1\) for every bin j. OPT is the minimum feasible integer k. The algorithm is uniform and classical, has access to the entire input before assigning items, and must output an explicit feasible packing. For absolute constants K,d, every execution must take at most \(KL^{d}\) bit operations. Its output is always feasible, and on each fixed input it uses at most OPT+C bins with probability at least \(2/3\) over its private random bits. C,K,d are independent of n, the number of distinct sizes, OPT and coefficient precision. No capacity augmentation, splitting of items, cardinality constraint or promise on the input distribution is allowed. Repeated items are explicitly listed rather than represented by binary multiplicities. Randomization is expressly allowed; a deterministic algorithm would also resolve the question. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A basic boundary between asymptotic approximation and almost exact combinatorial optimization: can efficient packing lose only a fixed number of bins on every instance?

importance.reason: A longstanding central problem in approximation algorithms, with connections to configuration LPs, discrepancy and the computational effect of input encoding.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No universal constant-additive polynomial-time algorithm or general impossibility result was found in the checked primary sources. The logarithmic-additive guarantee and recent high-multiplicity/support results do not settle this explicitly listed, randomized formulation.

context_blocks.text: The objective is to minimize the number of identical containers needed to hold indivisible items. Each bin has a single numerical capacity constraint, so the model contains no geometric placement issue. Nevertheless, many different combinations of small and large items can fit exactly or almost exactly, and choices that look locally efficient can leave unusable capacity elsewhere. The inherited invited survey explicitly asks for an OPT+\(O(1)\) guarantee.

Additive and multiplicative errors behave differently as the optimum grows. A one-percent excess can mean thousands of unnecessary bins on a large instance; an additive constant remains fixed. Conversely, this card allows any universal constant, even a very large one. It does not ask for an additive-one algorithm or for exact optimization on small instances.

The elementary hardness example is distinguishing instances needing two bins from those needing three, through Partition. This rules out exact polynomial optimization under the usual complexity assumptions, but it does not settle constant additive approximation. With allowance \(C=1, a\) valid three-bin answer is permitted in both cases. A stronger hardness argument would need a gap that survives the particular additive allowance.

Asymptotic approximation schemes achieve a ratio approaching one, with additional losses depending on their accuracy parameter. This does not automatically give OPT+C. Choosing \(\varepsilon\) on the order of 1/OPT makes \(\varepsilon \cdot\)OPT small, but the additive term and the running time may worsen as \(\varepsilon\) shrinks. The dependence on every parameter must be controlled simultaneously; the existence of a scheme alone does not establish the desired fixed loss.

Several published bounds use the Gilmore–Gomory configuration LP. A configuration specifies a multiset of item types that fits in one bin. The LP permits fractional numbers of such bins while covering all required items. Its optimum \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}\) is a lower bound on the integral optimum. Karmarkar–Karp obtain a polynomial-time packing with \(O(\log ^{2} \operatorname{OPT})\) additive loss by combining approximate LP optimization with repeated rounding.

Hoberg–Rothvoss improve the guarantee to \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}+O(\log  \operatorname{OPT}_{f})\), and hence OPT+\(O(\log  \operatorname{OPT})\). Their Theorem 2 gives randomized expected polynomial time in the number of explicitly represented items, with the usual accounting for encoded numerical data. Packing first into intermediate containers, and then into bins, improves how rounding errors accumulate. This is the logarithmic-additive general algorithmic benchmark found in the checked literature.

A constant additive LP integrality gap is a related mathematical conjecture, but it is not identical to this card. An efficiently constructible packing within a constant of \(\operatorname{OPT}_{f}\) would suffice. A nonconstructive proof of a small gap would still need an algorithmic rounding step. Conversely, an unbounded gap for this LP would not rule out a different algorithm whose guarantee is measured against the true integral optimum.

Discrepancy results explain why several familiar approaches encounter barriers. Eisenbrand–Pálvölgyi–Rothvoß connect a restricted bin-packing relaxation to discrepancy of three permutations. Their revised paper also proves limitations for a class of algorithms based on rounding item sizes upward. Those limitations concern specified techniques, rather than all algorithms for the original packing problem.

Newman–Nikolov disprove the conjecture that three permutations always have constant discrepancy, constructing examples requiring \(\Omega (\log  n)\). This eliminates one proposed route to a constant additive bound. It does not itself provide numerical item sizes with a growing bin-packing integrality gap, and it does not show that every polynomial-time packing algorithm must lose logarithmically many bins.

Recent work also settles nearby structural questions. Jansen–Pirotton–Tutas’s ESA 2025 paper constructs bin-packing instances requiring exponentially many distinct configurations as a function of the number of item types. Its discussion records an OPT+1 algorithm whose runtime depends heavily on that parameter. Exponential support in the number of types does not contradict a polynomial algorithm in an explicit list of all items, and a parameter-dependent additive-one algorithm is not uniformly polynomial as the number of types grows.

The ICALP 2026 work of Jansen–Ohnesorge–Pirotton proves a tight ETH-based lower bound for the dependence on the number of types in a high-multiplicity exact algorithmic regime. Binary multiplicities can encode far more items than the input length. Both the compressed input model and exact optimization differ from the constant-additive, explicitly listed target here. The result should therefore not be reported as a negative answer to this question.

This problem isolates how close efficient approximation can come to an integral packing optimum. A constant-additive algorithm would show that all unavoidable combinatorial inefficiency can be confined to a bounded number of extra bins, regardless of instance size. A general impossibility theorem would establish a meaningful approximation barrier beyond the standard two-versus-three-bin hardness example.

cards.title: Minimax dimension dependence in bandit convex optimization
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors jointly in dimension d and horizon T, the information-theoretic minimax expected regret \(R*(d,T)\) for one-point adversarial bandit convex optimization with losses in \([0,1]\). Use the oblivious-adversary, exact-feedback model and worst-case normalized convex body defined below; logarithmic dependence is part of the requested rate.
cards.why: Determines the price of limited feedback in a basic model of online convex optimization.
cards.status_note: The March 2026 primary book explicitly lists the minimax dimension dependence as open. Searches through 11 September 2026 found no established matching rate for the specified unrestricted one-point model. Recent smooth-loss and two-point results do not settle it.
cards.review_note: Recovered the oblivious exact-observation model from the same author’s 2020 primary formulation; the imported proposal mentioned only one function value per round. Fixed loss range, affine domain normalization, expected minimax quantifiers and a fixed hindsight comparator. Kept the full joint rate question rather than choosing a conjectured exponent, and separated the book’s noisy and stochastic variants.

cards.definitions: Let \(d,T\ge 1\) be integers and \(B_{2}^{d}=\{x\in R^{d}:\sum_{i} x_{i}^{2}\le 1\}\). A permitted constraint set K is a compact convex subset of \(R^{d}\) satisfying \(B_{2}^{d}\subseteq K\subseteq dB_{2}^{d}\); the learner knows K,d,T in advance. This is an affine normalization of general full-dimensional convex bodies, not a smoothness condition on losses. Write \(F(K)\) for the Borel-measurable convex functions \(f:K\to [0,1]\), where convexity means \(f(\lambda x+(1- \lambda )y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1- \lambda )f(y)\) for \(x,y\in K\) and \(\lambda \in [0,1]\). No common Lipschitz, differentiability, strong-convexity or curvature bound is imposed. Before any play, an oblivious adversary fixes \(f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}\in F(K)\), possibly using knowledge of the learner’s policy but not its realized random choices. At round t the learner chooses \(X_{t}\in K\), incurs \(f_{t}(X_{t})\), and observes exactly that one real value. It receives no noise, gradient, second evaluation, whole function or future loss. A policy is a sequence of Borel probability kernels assigning a distribution on K to each observed history \((X_{1},f_{1}(X_{1}),\ldots ,X_{t- 1},f_{t- 1}(X_{t- 1}))\). This permits arbitrary randomized decision rules; computation, representation and sampling time are unrestricted, so the target is statistical rather than polynomial-time optimization. For fixed K, define \(R_{K}(T)=\inf _{\pi} \sup _{f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}} E_{\pi}[\sum_{t} f_{t}(X_{t})- \inf _{x\in K}\sum_{t} f_{t}(x)]\), with the supremum over fixed legal loss sequences and expectation only over policy randomness. Finally \(R*(d,T)=\sup _{K} R_{K}(T)\), over the normalized bodies above. The comparator is one fixed point for all rounds, chosen in hindsight. Using an infimum avoids assuming a minimizer on the boundary. Joint constant-factor precision means a stated function \(g(d,T)\) and universal constants \(a,b>0\) with a \(g(d,T)\le R*(d,T)\le b g(d,T)\) for all \(d,T\ge 1\). Constants cannot depend on the shape of K. The Borel convention ensures the displayed expectations are defined.
cards.answer_criterion: Identify a joint rate \(g(d,T)\) and prove upper and lower bounds within universal constant factors for the defined minimax value. The upper bound must hold for every allowed convex body and loss sequence with some admissible policy for that known body; the matching lower bound must hold against every policy on suitable allowed instances. Bounds for a fixed dimension with unspecified dimension-dependent constants, or bounds that hide an unresolved polynomial or logarithmic factor, do not give the full requested rate. Efficient implementation is not an additional acceptance condition.

context_blocks.title: One value does not reveal a direction
context_blocks.text: On the interval \([- 1,1]\), the convex losses \(f(x)=(1+x)/2\) and \(h(x)=(1- x)/2\) both equal \(1/2\) at \(x=0\), but their minimizing endpoints are opposite. Observing one loss value therefore need not reveal which way to move. Across rounds the loss may also change, so a value observed yesterday is not a second evaluation of today’s function.

context_blocks.title: The benchmark is one fixed decision in hindsight
context_blocks.text: Regret compares accumulated loss with the best single point that could have been used throughout the sequence. It does not compare with a different minimizer on every round. This distinction makes learning possible even when the environment changes. Randomization protects the learner against a sequence chosen before its random actions, while the adversary may still choose that sequence with knowledge of the policy.

context_blocks.title: Dimension remains a major gap
context_blocks.text: Lattimore’s 2020 theorem gives an upper bound of order \(d^{5/2}\sqrt{T}\), apart from a logarithmic factor, for exact one-point feedback. In the regime where T is sufficiently large relative to d, known lower bounds grow as \(d\sqrt{T}\). The March 2026 book explicitly retains the dimension gap. For smaller horizons, regret is always at most T because each loss lies in \([0,1]\); an asymptotic expression must respect this saturation.

context_blocks.title: Normalization and computational cost
context_blocks.text: Bounded loss values fix the scale of regret. Restricting K to a rounded affine position prevents an arbitrary choice of coordinates from introducing an extra geometric parameter. This still permits general convex losses and many domain shapes. The information-theoretic question asks what is attainable by decision rules with no computation limit. A practical algorithm can be a major advance while still having a worse dimension dependence than the best existence bound.

context_blocks.title: Which newer results change the assumptions
context_blocks.text: The July 2026 revision of Ye’s paper uses two evaluations per loss and assumes strong convexity, with carefully stated comparator guarantees. Cheng, Hatano and Takimoto’s June 2026 result allows globally budgeted perturbations but assumes a smooth convex underlying loss even when the perturbations vanish. These assumptions differ from arbitrary bounded convex functions with one exact observation. Neither establishes the minimax rate requested here.

cards.title: Matroid secretary conjecture
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C\ge 1\) such that every finite matroid M admits a randomized online selection strategy which, for every assignment of nonnegative weights to its elements, returns an independent set of expected weight at least \(\operatorname{OPT}(M,w)/C\) when the elements arrive in a uniformly random order?
cards.definitions: A matroid is a finite set E and a nonempty family \(I\subseteq 2^{E}\) closed under subsets and satisfying augmentation: if \(A,B\in I\) and |\(A|<|B|\), some \(b\in B\setminus A\) has \(A\cup \{b\}\in I\). The strategy knows E and I in advance, but not the weights. A fixed adversary assigns \(w:E\to \mathbb{R} _{\ge 0}\) before the order and strategy coins are sampled. Upon each arrival its identity and weight are revealed. The strategy must accept or reject it irrevocably before the next arrival, keeping the accepted set in I. \(\operatorname{OPT}(M,w)=\max _{S\in I}\sum _{e\in S}w(e)\). Expectation includes a uniformly random permutation of E and the strategy’s independent random coins. There is no computation or oracle-query bound; this is the competitive-existence conjecture for the full-information matroid model.

context_blocks.text: The general matroid secretary problem asks whether random arrival order is enough to recover a constant fraction of a best feasible weighted set without seeing future weights. It unifies classical secretary selection with broad independence constraints.
The random-assignment model also randomizes where weights are placed, and admits stronger results. Those results do not settle the adversarial-assignment, random-arrival model used here.

cards.why: The main unresolved competitive-ratio question for online selection under general matroid constraints.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated proposition or its logical negation, preserving the quantifiers, model and guarantees. Conditional results settle only their conditional claims. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-checked proof of the full target.

cards.title: Randomized competitiveness of k-server
cards.formal: Determine, up to universal constant factors as \(k\to \infty , R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)=\inf\){\(r\ge 1\): for every finite metric \((X,d)\) with |\(X|\ge k+1\) and every initial placement, some randomized online strategy and finite \(\beta \ge 0\) satisfy \(E[\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma )]\le r\cdot \operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )+\beta\) for every finite request sequence \(\sigma\) fixed independently of the strategy’s coins}, for integers \(k\ge 2\).
cards.definitions: There are k movable servers at points of X; repeated server locations are allowed. Each request names a point of X. Before the next request, at least one server must occupy that point. Moving a server from u to v costs \(d(u,v)\). The full finite metric and initial placement are known. \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )\) is the minimum total movement of a strategy knowing the entire sequence and starting at the same placement. The adversary is oblivious: it fixes \(\sigma\) independently of the online strategy’s random coins. The strategy uses only the prefix revealed so far. No running-time bound is imposed. The competitive factor r is uniform over metric spaces and initial placements for each fixed k. The strategy and additive \(\beta\) may depend on the metric, initial placement, k and r, but not on the future sequence or its length. The infimum is finite by deterministic competitive strategies, and need not be attained.

context_blocks.text: This quantitative target asks for the growth of the optimal competitive ratio. The earlier polylogarithmic question asks only whether that growth is bounded by some fixed power of log k.

Randomized k-server is a central test of whether an online algorithm can manage a large changing state at a cost depending mildly on the number of servers. The number of metric points must not occur in the competitive ratio.
The old \(O(\log  k)\) conjecture is false: a superlogarithmic lower bound is known. Polylogarithmic dependence on k remains a different open target. Bounds containing log|X| do not settle it.

cards.why: A surviving central problem in randomized competitive analysis, beyond the refuted logarithmic k-server conjecture.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(f(k)\) and universal constants \(0<c\le C<\infty\) with \(c f(k)\le R_{\mathrm{rand}}(k)\le C f(k)\) for all \(k\ge 2\), adjusting constants for finitely many small k if needed, and prove both inequalities in Lean. Upper bounds must hold for every finite metric and oblivious sequence in the stated model; lower bounds must apply to every eligible randomized strategy on suitable metrics. The asymptotic precision is constant-factor matching, not additive 0.01.

cards.title: Minimax rate of sequential binary calibration
cards.formal: Determine \(C(T)=\inf _{A} \sup _{B} E[\sum _{p\in \mathrm{P}_{A}}|\sum _{t:p_{t}=p}(y_{t}- p)|]\) up to universal multiplicative constants as the integer horizon T tends to infinity, in the finite-forecast sequential game below. The requested rate includes logarithmic factors.
cards.definitions: Before play, forecaster A selects a finite set \(\mathrm{P}_{A}\subseteq [0,1]\), which may depend on T. Both players know this set and T. At each time t, A selects \(p_{t}\in \mathrm{P}_{A}\) and adversary B selects \(y_{t}\in \{0,1\}\) simultaneously; neither sees the other’s current selection. Each may randomize using independent coins and the full history \((p_{s},y_{s})_{s<t}\), and after the round both selections become public. The infimum is over every such finite set and randomized forecaster, and the supremum is over all randomized adaptive adversaries. There is no computational restriction. The displayed sum measures unnormalized \(\ell\)\(_{1}\) calibration error and is finite; groups are defined by exact equality of predictions. Expectation is over both players’ coins.

context_blocks.text: Calibration asks whether forecasts agree with empirical frequencies on the rounds when each probability was announced. The minimax rate measures the unavoidable error in this requirement against an adaptive sequence of binary events.

The long-standing \(T^{2/3}\) upper bound has already been improved by a constant in the exponent. A lower bound strictly above \(\sqrt{T}\) is also known. Thus neither the old two-thirds barrier nor a square-root target is an appropriate new open question. The remaining problem is the optimal rate itself.

cards.definitions: For \(k\ge 1\) an instance environment consists of a finite set X with |\(X|\ge k+1\), uniform distance \(d(x,y)=1\) if \(x\ne y\) and 0 otherwise, positive real weights \(w_{1},\ldots ,w_{k}\), and an initial location \(c_{i}\in X\) for each labeled server i. Co-location is permitted. These data are known to the online algorithm. A finite request sequence \(\sigma \in X\)* is revealed one request at a time. Before proceeding, at least one server must occupy the requested location. Moving server i from x to y costs \(w_{i} d(x,y)\); all movements count. The algorithm may use arbitrary computation but cannot inspect future requests. \(\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )\) is the minimum cost of an offline execution with the same weights and initial locations. A real \(c\ge 1\) is universally achievable for k if, for every environment, there are a randomized online strategy A and \(b\ge 0\) such that for every finite \(\sigma , E[\operatorname{cost}_{A}(\sigma )]\le c \operatorname{OPT}(\sigma )+b\). The strategy and b may depend on the environment; b may not depend on \(\sigma\) or its length. The sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s private random choices, and expectation is over those choices. Define \(R_{w}(k)\) as the infimum of universally achievable c. It is finite by known upper bounds and need not be attained. Metric size and the ratios between server weights are unbounded independently of k. No running-time bound or bit encoding of the real weights is imposed; the target measures online movement cost.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(k)\) and constants \(a,A>0,k_{0}\) such that a \(g(k)\le R_{w}(k)\le A g(k)\) for every integer \(k\ge k_{0}\), proving both bounds in the specified randomized model. cards.title: Randomized competitive ratio of list update
cards.formal: Determine \(\rho_{\rm LU}=\inf\{r\ge1:\text{ randomized online list update is }r\text{-competitive}\}\) against an oblivious adversary in the full-cost model below. The benchmark accepts a real approximation with absolute error at most \(1/100\).
cards.definitions: For each \(n\ge1\), the input is a fixed set of \(n\) distinct items, an initial linear order \(L_0\), and any finite request sequence \(\sigma\) fixed independently of the algorithm’s randomness. Access to the item currently at position \(i\), counting from one, costs \(i\). After accessing an item, it may be moved toward the front by any distance for free. Any other swap of two adjacent items costs one. The algorithm serves each request before seeing the next. Offline OPT knows the sequence, starts in the same \(L_0\), and pays under exactly the same rules. A ratio \(r\) is achievable if, for every \(n,L_0\), an online randomized rule and a finite \(\beta\ge0\) exist such that \(\mathbb E[\operatorname{cost}_A(\sigma)]\le r\operatorname{OPT}(\sigma)+\beta\) for every \(\sigma\). The rule and \(\beta\) may depend on \(n,L_0,r\), but not on future requests; there is no computational-time constraint on choosing legal rearrangements. The infimum need not be attained. The constant is dimensionless.
cards.why: Even for an elementary self-organizing list, the optimal benefit of randomization in competitive performance is unknown.

cards.title: Planted clique conjecture
cards.formal: Is the following hardness statement true? For every fixed \(\varepsilon \in (0,1/2)\), there is no uniform classical randomized polynomial-time algorithm A whose success probability in the experiment below is at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large n, with \(k=\lfloor n^{1/2- \varepsilon}\rfloor\).
cards.definitions: Set \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}\). The null distribution \(N_{n}\) draws a simple undirected labeled graph by including each unordered pair independently with probability \(1/2\). The planted distribution \(\mathrm{P}_{n,k}\) first chooses S uniformly among all k-element subsets of \([n]\), includes all edges inside S, and includes every other edge independently with probability \(1/2\). Draw b uniformly from \(\{0,1\}\); draw G from \(N_{n}\) if \(b=0\) and \(\mathrm{P}_{n,k}\) if \(b=1\). Give A the binary integers n,k and the full adjacency matrix of G, but neither b nor S. It outputs a bit b̂. Success means \(\Pr [\hat\{b\}=b]\), averaged over b, the graph, S when present, and A’s independent random bits. Equivalently success is \((\Pr _{N}[A=0]+\Pr _{\mathrm{P}}[A=1])/2\). Polynomial time means at most \(C(n+1)^{c}\) bit operations for every input and random tape, with fixed C,c; they and A may depend on the fixed \(\varepsilon\). The forbidden guarantee is \(\exists A,C,c,N \forall n\ge N\), success\(\ge 2/3\). This is a one-graph detection problem; A may generate its own random graphs at its own computational cost. The size of S is exactly k, not an independent per-vertex planting probability. No advice, quantum computation, oracle, side information, or algorithm-family restriction is allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A foundational average-case hardness hypothesis and a central test case for statistical–computational gaps. It asks for a clean separation between the presence of information and efficient extraction of that information; reductions transfer related assumptions to sparse estimation and latent-structure learning. Proving this formulation would in particular imply \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), since a polynomial algorithm for maximum clique would distinguish the distributions.

importance.reason: A canonical computational threshold with broad consequences in average-case complexity, statistical inference, and the study of algorithmic lower-bound frameworks.

progress.text: Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov give polynomial-time recovery for \(k\ge c\sqrt{n}\) for any fixed \(c>0\), using spectral methods and boosting.

Barak, Hopkins, Kelner, Kothari, Moitra, and Potechin prove a nearly tight sum-of-squares integrality gap: degree \(d=o(\log  n)\) assigns random graphs clique value \(n^{1/2- o(1)}\). This is a restricted-model lower bound.

Gheissari, Jagannath, and Xu show that an appropriate discrete gradient descent and low-temperature local chain recover at the \(\sqrt{n}\) scale from the full-graph initialization; the final preprint version is dated 15 May 2025.
Nagda and Raghavendra derive optimal efficient distinguishing advantages conditional on a planted-clique hypothesis, in the independent-vertex planting model.

Göbel, Ruff, and Schiller give robust sum-of-squares algorithms for multiple overlapping cliques in random intersection graphs when clique size is much larger than \(\sqrt{n \log  n}\). This is progress in a related model, not below the threshold fixed here.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026; no unrestricted polynomial-time solution below \(n^{1/2- \varepsilon}\) or unconditional hardness proof was identified. The exact formulation fixes constant-success detection and exactly k planted vertices. Low-degree and sum-of-squares bounds remain scoped to their models; the optimal-advantage result is conditional.

context_blocks.text: This asks whether a planted structure can be statistically obvious yet computationally inaccessible. In the specified regime, k grows as a positive power of n, while an unplanted graph has no clique of size \(r=\lceil 3 \log _{2} n\rceil\) with probability tending to one: a union bound is at most \(n^{r}\cdot 2^{- r(r- 1)/2}\), which tends to zero. Enumerating all r-subsets therefore distinguishes the two distributions with success tending to one in quasipolynomial time \(n^{O}(\log  n)\). The obstacle is reducing that computation to polynomial time, not a lack of information in the graph.

The classical spectral algorithm of Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov recovers the hidden vertex set for every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt{n}\), with a polynomial whose exponent can depend on that constant. Recovery immediately yields detection here by checking that the reported set is a sufficiently large clique. Letting the constant shrink as \(n^{- \varepsilon}\) does not keep that analysis polynomial with a fixed exponent.

Substantial evidence comes from provable failures of general algorithmic frameworks. Barak and coauthors show that low-degree sum-of-squares relaxations assign a random graph an implausibly large clique value near \(\sqrt{n}\), despite its true largest clique having only logarithmic size. This is an unconditional limitation of that relaxation. It does not rule out every algorithm allowed in this card.

Recent positive work also illustrates why an algorithmic barrier must state its model. Gheissari, Jagannath, and Xu permit local optimization to pass through vertex sets that are not cliques, penalizing missing edges. Starting from the whole graph, their procedure reaches the planted clique at a sufficiently large constant times \(\sqrt{n}\). Restrictions to moves among actual cliques can fail even in easier regimes; those failures do not establish the unrestricted conjecture.

Nagda and Raghavendra obtain sharp bounds on efficient distinguishing advantage assuming planted-clique hardness. Their paper uses independent vertex planting, so the planted size fluctuates around its mean, and uses a different normalization of advantage. It strengthens consequences of a hypothesis in that related model. It is not an unconditional lower bound for the fixed-size experiment here.

The question isolates detection from stronger output requirements such as recovering every planted vertex. It also fixes the random background: arbitrary base graphs, geometric random graphs, and adversarially modified edges describe different experiments. Work on robust recovery of overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs continued in COLT 2026, but its distribution and signal regime do not settle this question.

category_assignment.reason: Average-case complexity and hardness

sentences: Planted clique detection distinguishes a random graph from one with a uniformly chosen clique inserted into it.
The conjecture rules out polynomial-time classical randomized detection when the planted size is \(n^{1/2- \varepsilon}\) for fixed positive \(\varepsilon\).
The graph statistically contains a signal, but the challenge is finding a computationally accessible feature that reveals it below the square-root scale.
This makes the problem a central candidate for a gap between information and computation.

The reviewed model fixes clique size exactly and asks only for detection, so recovery algorithms, different planting distributions, or lower bounds for restricted relaxations do not automatically settle it.

cards.context:
This asks whether a planted structure can be statistically obvious yet computationally inaccessible. In the specified regime, k grows as a positive power of n, while an unplanted graph has no clique of size \(r=\lceil 3 \log _{2} n\rceil\) with probability tending to one: a union bound is at most \(n^{r}\cdot 2^{- r(r- 1)/2}\), which tends to zero. Enumerating all r-subsets therefore distinguishes the two distributions with success tending to one in quasipolynomial time \(n^{O}(\log  n)\). The obstacle is reducing that computation to polynomial time, not a lack of information in the graph.

The classical spectral algorithm of Alon, Krivelevich, and Sudakov recovers the hidden vertex set for every fixed positive constant times \(\sqrt{n}\), with a polynomial whose exponent can depend on that constant. Recovery immediately yields detection here by checking that the reported set is a sufficiently large clique. Letting the constant shrink as \(n^{- \varepsilon}\) does not keep that analysis polynomial with a fixed exponent.

Substantial evidence comes from provable failures of general algorithmic frameworks. Barak and coauthors show that low-degree sum-of-squares relaxations assign a random graph an implausibly large clique value near \(\sqrt{n}\), despite its true largest clique having only logarithmic size. This is an unconditional limitation of that relaxation. It does not rule out every algorithm allowed in this card.

Recent positive work also illustrates why an algorithmic barrier must state its model. Gheissari, Jagannath, and Xu permit local optimization to pass through vertex sets that are not cliques, penalizing missing edges. Starting from the whole graph, their procedure reaches the planted clique at a sufficiently large constant times \(\sqrt{n}\). Restrictions to moves among actual cliques can fail even in easier regimes; those failures do not establish the unrestricted conjecture.

Nagda and Raghavendra obtain sharp bounds on efficient distinguishing advantage assuming planted-clique hardness. Their paper uses independent vertex planting, so the planted size fluctuates around its mean, and uses a different normalization of advantage. It strengthens consequences of a hypothesis in that related model. It is not an unconditional lower bound for the fixed-size experiment here.

The question isolates detection from stronger output requirements such as recovering every planted vertex. It also fixes the random background: arbitrary base graphs, geometric random graphs, and adversarially modified edges describe different experiments. Work on robust recovery of overlapping planted cliques in random intersection graphs continued in COLT 2026, but its distribution and signal regime do not settle this question.

benchmark_focus.reason: A canonical computational threshold with broad consequences in average-case complexity, statistical inference, and the study of algorithmic lower-bound frameworks.

cards.title: Average-case NP hardness from \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\)
cards.definitions: A sampler is one randomized Turing machine S which, given \(1^{n}\), halts within \(q(n)\) steps on every random tape for a fixed polynomial q. Its output distribution \(D_{n}\) is over finite binary strings \(x; |x|\le q(n)\), and n is the ensemble parameter, not necessarily |x|. Sampling is exact with independent unbiased coin flips, and S has no advice or oracle. An exact decider A receives \((1^{n},x)\), halts, and returns the membership bit of L correctly for every n and x. Write \(T_{A}(1^{n},x)\) for its running time. The pair \((\mathrm{L},D)\) belongs to AvgP if there exist such an \(A, \varepsilon >0, C>0\), and integer \(k\ge 1\) with $\mathbb E_{x\sim D_n}[T_A(1^n,x)^\varepsilon]\le C(n+1)^k$ for every \(n\ge 1\). The constants and A may depend on L and S but not on n. This moment definition is the robust Levin notion, not the requirement that the first moment itself be polynomial. The algorithm is deterministic and never gives a wrong answer; difficult inputs may take a long time. NP uses ordinary polynomially bounded certificates and deterministic polynomial-time verification. Both the hard language and its sampler must be fixed across all input lengths.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This asks whether worst-case intractability necessarily survives on inputs generated by a feasible process. It is the basic bridge between the standard theory of NP-completeness and distributional complexity, and a prerequisite issue in attempts to derive useful cryptographic hardness from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone.

importance.reason: One of the central missing implications in complexity theory, connecting worst-case lower bounds to feasible instance generation and the limits of algorithms on typical inputs.

progress.text: Levin develops robust average-time definitions and distributional completeness; Impagliazzo and Levin extend completeness to samplable ensembles. The survey develops the moment definition and this completeness theory.

Bogdanov and Trevisan show limitations of nonadaptive worst-case-to-average-case oracle reductions for NP. Their result is a conditional obstruction to a reduction method, not a disproof of the unrestricted implication.
Wigderson’s Open Problem 4.5 and the revised Bogdanov–Trevisan survey explicitly ask whether \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) implies average-case NP hardness.

Liu and Pass obtain a worst-case-to-average-case reduction for an exact time-bounded Kolmogorov problem under an exponential circuit-hardness derandomization assumption. The extra hypothesis is stronger and more specific than \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

cards.status_note: The original question is explicitly open in Wigderson’s book and the revised average-case survey. Current primary literature was checked through 10 September 2026; no resolution from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) alone was located. The card fixes deterministic exact AvgP and strict polynomial-time sampling, rather than conflating them with randomized heuristic hardness.

context_blocks.text: Worst-case hardness says that an algorithm has difficult inputs. It does not say that a feasible instance generator produces them with enough probability to obstruct average efficiency. The sampler is therefore part of the mathematical problem. It may depend on the language, but it cannot contain an uncomputable table selecting a hard input at every length.

A padding example shows why a fixed familiar distribution is insufficient. Encode a formula x as 0 followed by |\(x|^{2}- 1\) further zeros, a separator 1, and x. Satisfiability of these padded strings remains NP-complete under polynomial reductions. Under the uniform distribution on strings of a fixed length, valid encodings are so rare that checking the format and brute-forcing the rare valid formulas has polynomial average cost. An easy uniform distribution does not remove worst-case hardness.

Levin’s moment condition makes average efficiency stable under polynomial slowdowns. If a machine is simulated with its running time raised to a fixed power, a correspondingly smaller positive moment still suffices. This prevents the answer from depending on an incidental choice of machine representation. Exact computation with this runtime guarantee differs from a heuristic allowed to give incorrect answers on a small fraction of inputs.

Distributional completeness is already available: Impagliazzo and Levin extend the theory to polynomial-time samplable ensembles. Completeness identifies a common average-case target; it does not prove that this target is hard from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\).

There are barriers for nonadaptive oracle reductions from worst-case NP hardness to average-case NP hardness: the relevant reductions would collapse the polynomial hierarchy. Such a barrier leaves other proof mechanisms open. Recent reductions for specific time-bounded Kolmogorov problems use additional assumptions or specific forms of hardness, so they do not supply the implication on this card.

cards.title: Computational threshold for tensor PCA
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), rational \(\varepsilon\) with \(0<\varepsilon <(k- 2)/4\), and rational \(c\in (0,1)\), is the following impossibility statement true? No uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm, given the finite-precision observation of \(Y=n^{k/4- \varepsilon}v^{\otimes k}+Z\) specified below, achieves |\(\langle u,v\rangle |\ge c\) with probability at least \(2/3\) for every sufficiently large dimension n, where v is uniform on the unit sphere in \(R^{n}\) and the \(n^{k}\) ordered entries of Z are independent \(N(0,1)\) variables.
cards.definitions: The experiment draws v, Z and the algorithm’s random bits independently. For an ordered tuple \((i_{1},\ldots ,i_{k})\in \{1,\ldots ,n\}^{k}\), the signal entry is \(n^{k/4- \varepsilon}v_{i_{1}}\cdots v_{i_{k}}\). Noise is not pre-symmetrized and each entry has variance one. To give polynomial time a precise bit-model meaning, for \(n\ge 2\) set \(b=\lceil 10k \log _{2}n\rceil\) and \(Q_{b}(x)=2^{- b}\lfloor 2^{b} \max (- 2^{b},\min (x,2^{b}))\rfloor\). The input consists of n and all entries \(Q_{b}(Y_{i_{1},\ldots ,i_{k}})\), represented as signed dyadic rationals with \(O(\log  n)\) bits each. This fixed rounding convention is an explicit finite-precision version of the usual Gaussian-model question. An algorithm may depend on the fixed constants \(k, \varepsilon\) and c, but is one probabilistic Turing machine for all n, with worst-case running time polynomial in n on every input and random tape. For fixed k this is polynomial in the input size. It outputs a nonzero rational vector w, interpreted as the unit vector \(u=w/\Vert w\Vert _{2}\); zero or invalid outputs fail. Success is the event |\(\langle w,v\rangle |\ge c\Vert w\Vert _{2}\). The algorithm receives no side information about v, informative initial vector, or additional independent observations. The probability averages over the spike, noise and internal randomness. Absolute correlation makes the target invariant under the unavoidable sign ambiguity when k is even.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that for every fixed \((k,\varepsilon ,c)\) in the stated ranges, each such polynomial-time algorithm has success probability below \(2/3\) for arbitrarily large n; or refute this by giving one fixed triple and one algorithm that succeeds with probability at least \(2/3\) for all sufficiently large n. Proving failure only for low-degree polynomials, a chosen iterative method, or a different spike prior does not prove the full assertion. An improvement by logarithmic factors at \(n^{k/4}\) does not supply the fixed power saving \(n^{\varepsilon}\) requested here.
cards.why: Determine whether the canonical statistical–computational gap for a dense Gaussian tensor persists against all polynomial-time recovery algorithms.

importance.reason: A central average-case inference problem linking tensor algorithms, statistical thresholds, low-degree methods and computational hardness.

progress.text: Montanari–Richard introduce and analyze the spiked tensor model, exhibiting a gap between information-theoretic recovery and the analyzed polynomial-time methods.
Kunisky–Moore–Wein prove spherical-prior low-degree detection thresholds and odd-order reconstruction lower bounds with the predicted dependence on degree.
Wu–Zhou sharpen the analysis and stopping rule for randomly initialized power iteration; its threshold improves by a polylogarithmic factor.

cards.status_note: The May 2026 low-degree paper retains the conjectured gap for unrestricted algorithms and distinguishes spherical from independent-coordinate priors. The 2024 power-iteration and October 2025 stochastic-gradient improvements concern particular methods and do not provide a fixed-power improvement below \(n^{k/4}\). No full resolution found through 11 September 2026. The card explicitly fixes a finite-precision bit model; restricted lower bounds in the standard unrounded model are evidence, not a proof for all algorithms here.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary principal component analysis looks for a hidden direction in a noisy matrix. Tensor PCA asks the analogous question when observations have three or more indices. Here the clean signal has rank one: every entry is a product of coordinates of the same hidden unit vector. Gaussian noise obscures those products. The goal is only a constant correlation with the direction, much weaker than estimating every coordinate accurately.

For fixed tensor order, information-theoretic recovery in the standard Gaussian model becomes possible at a signal scale of order \(\sqrt{n}\). Montanari and Richard established the basic statistical-versus-computational distinction while studying tensor unfolding, power iteration and message-passing methods. Their noise normalization differs from the variance-one convention used in this card; their constant statistical threshold corresponds to order \(\sqrt{n}\) here.

Known polynomial-time methods reach signal strength around \(n^{k/4}\), up to factors that do not change this leading exponent. Wu and Zhou’s 2024 introduction records both this algorithmic scale and the conjectured gap from \(\sqrt{n}\). The interval for \(\varepsilon\) deliberately places our target strictly between them: \(\lambda /\sqrt{n}=n^{(k- 2)/4- \varepsilon}\) grows without bound. There is therefore ample statistical signal in the usual model, while efficient recovery remains unproved.

For example, at order four and \(\varepsilon =1/8\), the observation contains \(n^{4}\) noisy numbers and signal strength \(n^{7/8}\). The statistical scale is \(n^{1/2}\), and the conjectured efficient scale is n. A polynomial-time algorithm below that latter scale would have to exploit structure that current threshold evidence misses. Merely reading all \(n^{4}\) entries is allowed: the question concerns computation polynomial in the complete input, not a sublinear-access restriction.

Low-degree polynomial estimators provide one rigorous way to test proposed computational barriers. Kunisky, Moore and Wein establish the predicted degree-versus-signal tradeoff for detection with a spherical spike and derive a matching reconstruction lower bound for odd tensor orders. Their reconstruction theorem is specifically for odd orders; they explain that even orders require a sign-invariant estimand such as \(vv^{T}\) and additional work. Detection and recovery are separate tasks, and a detection lower bound should not silently be relabelled as their reconstruction theorem.

Fu and Sohn’s May 2026 preprint advances low-degree estimation bounds for tensor PCA with independent, mean-zero, variance-one spike coordinates and bounded moments. Its general-prior theorem controls estimation of fixed products of coordinates and obtains the predicted signal-versus-degree scaling within a stated degree range. Independent-coordinate priors are different from a vector conditioned to have unit norm. The result strengthens evidence for the computational gap without establishing an unrestricted polynomial-time lower bound for this card’s spherical prior.

Some recent algorithmic improvements resolve narrower conjectures. Wu and Zhou lower the threshold for randomly initialized power iteration by a polylogarithmic factor. Ding, Gu, Liu and Fang obtain improved guarantees for an overparameterized stochastic-gradient method using multiple independent observations. For even order, their stated sample-signal condition reaches the familiar \(n^{k/4}\) scale after averaging the observations. Neither result supplies the fixed-power improvement below that scale demanded here.

The rounding convention prevents an ambiguity about algorithms operating on exact Gaussian real numbers. Each coordinate is given with logarithmically many bits. Outside the clipping event, the total rounding error in Euclidean norm across the tensor is at most \(n^{k/2}2^{- b}\), an extremely small inverse power of n; clipping has vanishing probability. This is a specified computational model, rather than an assertion that every exact-real algorithm automatically transfers to it. Likewise, polynomial-estimator theorems for unrounded observations do not by themselves cover arbitrary algorithms that process rounded entries.

A resolution would clarify whether a simple, highly symmetric random model can hide statistically recoverable information from every efficient algorithm. A successful method would challenge a widely used picture of algorithmic thresholds. A full impossibility proof would require a complexity argument beyond the restricted algorithm families currently understood. Both outcomes would inform how computational hardness assumptions are formulated for inference problems.

cards.title: Computational Kesten–Stigum threshold
cards.formal: Do there exist a fixed integer \(q\ge 5\), fixed rational constants \(a>b>0\) satisfying \((a- b)^{2}<q(a+(q- 1)b), a\) constant \(\delta >0\), and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that, for every sufficiently large n, A weakly recovers the communities of the symmetric stochastic block model \(SBM(n,q,a,b)\), with expected overlap at least \(1/q+\delta\)?
cards.definitions: Generate the hidden labels \(\sigma _{1},\ldots ,\sigma _{n}\) independently and uniformly from \([q]=\{1,\ldots ,q\}\). Conditional on these labels, each unordered pair of distinct vertices is independently an edge with probability \(a/n\) if its labels agree and \(b/n\) otherwise. Thus the graph is simple and undirected; take \(n\ge a\). Equal prior probabilities make communities asymptotically balanced, but their sizes are not conditioned to equal \(n/q\). The algorithm receives this one graph and knows q,a,b; it receives no planted labels or auxiliary samples. It outputs a label vector \(\hat\{\sigma\}\in [q]^{n}\). Define \(overlap(\hat\{\sigma\},\sigma )=\max\) over permutations \(\pi\) of \([q]\) of \(n^{- 1}\sum_{i} 1\{\hat\{\sigma\}_{i}=\pi (\sigma _{i})\}\). The expectation in the question is over labels, graph edges and the algorithm’s random bits. Weak recovery means a fixed positive advantage over the limiting chance baseline \(1/q\). Running time is worst-case polynomial in n on a standard bit model, for every graph and random tape; the algorithm and polynomial exponent may depend on the fixed parameters but not on n. Put \(d=(a+(q- 1)b)/q\) and \(\theta =(a- b)/(a+(q- 1)b)\). The strict inequality is \(d\theta ^{2}<1\), below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. All three model parameters remain constant as n grows.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer must exhibit one fixed parameter choice below the threshold and prove the stated polynomial running time and nonvanishing expected overlap for all sufficiently large n. A negative answer must rule out every such algorithm at every fixed parameter choice in the formulation. Recovery with unlimited computation does not answer the question. An algorithm with q growing with n, a result only above the threshold, or a lower bound conditional on an unproved computational hypothesis is partial progress. The question does not impose an extra promise of information-theoretic recoverability: any positive algorithmic example automatically has that property.
cards.why: Determine whether the canonical local signal threshold is a true barrier for every efficient algorithm in a basic model of network inference.

importance.reason: A central, sharply parameterized computational-versus-statistical gap linking sparse random graphs, inference, message passing and average-case complexity.

progress.text: Abbe–Sandon prove efficient recovery above the Kesten–Stigum threshold for all fixed community counts; preprint 2015, revised 2016, journal publication 2018.
Banks–Moore–Neeman–Netrapalli prove information-theoretic recovery below the threshold in suitable assortative regimes with \(q\ge 11\), using a potentially exponential algorithm.
Ding–Hua–Slot–Steurer’s revised paper derives recovery lower bounds under its explicitly restricted low-degree conjecture; Theorem A.1 allows a fixed gap below the threshold.

Chin–Mossel–Sohn–Wein revise their many-community analysis, correcting the proof of Theorem 1.2. Their below-threshold algorithms require a growing community count and do not settle the fixed-q question.

context_blocks.text: Community detection asks whether the edges of a network reveal an underlying partition. Here every vertex has the same expected degree, regardless of its group. Consequently, sorting vertices by degree cannot directly identify their communities. The signal is in the pattern of connections between vertices, and each vertex has only a constant expected number of observations even as the network grows.

The target is deliberately much weaker than recovering every label. A constant-degree graph has many isolated vertices, whose memberships cannot be inferred from their incident edges. Weak recovery asks only for a fixed improvement over random guessing on average. Permuting all community names must be allowed: renaming the hidden groups changes neither the graph distribution nor the quality of an inferred partition.

The quantity \(d\theta ^{2}\) compares the growth in the number of observed neighbours with the decay of label information along an edge. In a local tree approximation, d describes branching and \(\theta\) describes how much a child’s label remembers its parent’s label. This explains why the value one is a natural boundary for algorithms based on propagation of small correlations. It does not by itself prove an impossibility result for algorithms that use the whole graph.

Abbe and Sandon prove efficient recovery above this boundary for every fixed number of communities. Their method uses an acyclic form of belief propagation and addresses the effect of cycles in the finite graph. This supplies the algorithmic side of the proposed threshold. The question asks whether a qualitatively different method can succeed strictly below it in the assortative case \(a>b\).

There really are parameters for which the graph contains useful information below the Kesten–Stigum threshold. Banks, Moore, Neeman and Netrapalli establish such regimes for at least eleven groups in the assortative model. Their recovery argument permits exponential computation, searching over sufficiently plausible partitions. Their five-group statement concerns the disassortative case, where between-group edges are more likely; that is a different parameter range from this card.

This produces a concrete computational-versus-statistical puzzle. The missing labels are not intrinsically unidentifiable everywhere below the boundary, yet known efficient methods do not recover them throughout the information-theoretically possible region. An affirmative answer to this card would refute the universal fixed-community barrier with a single parameter example. A negative answer would establish that the obstruction is computational wherever recovery is statistically possible.

Ding, Hua, Slot and Steurer give conditional evidence in 2025. In their parameterized symmetric model, a low-degree conjecture implies a strong computational lower bound for recovery below the threshold by a fixed margin. Their recovery definition uses correlation with the centred membership matrix. The result is a reduction from a conjecture about testing to recovery hardness, not an unconditional exclusion of polynomial-time algorithms. Its model and hypothesis restrictions matter when applying it to a particular choice of a,b.

The precise conjecture in that paper also matters. Its bounded test functions must have expectation bounded below under the planted distribution. The authors explain that a broader earlier version was refuted using rare events. Thus citing a generic “low-degree conjecture” without stating that a hypothesis remains unproved would erase both the conditional nature of the result and an actual correction in the underlying evidence.

A 2026 revision of work by Chin, Mossel, Sohn and Wein gives efficient recovery below the usual boundary when the number of communities grows sufficiently quickly, in particular in a regime above \(\sqrt{n}\). This is an important warning against treating the threshold as universal over every block model. Here q is fixed before n tends to infinity. Even a very large fixed q eventually lies below \(\sqrt{n}\), so the growing-community algorithm does not supply the fixed-parameter example requested.

Settling this problem would test whether a threshold suggested by local propagation describes all efficient global algorithms in a basic random graph model. A new algorithm would identify exploitable structure missed by the familiar threshold calculation. A rigorous barrier would give a particularly clean example in which unlimited inference and efficient inference have different capabilities, with the data distribution specified by only three constants.

cards.title: Polynomial-time refutation of random 3-SAT at constant density
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge 6\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm A such that A never outputs UNSAT on any satisfiable 3-CNF formula, and \(\Pr [A(F)=\mathrm{UNSAT}]\to 1\) as \(n\to \infty\) for F drawn from \(R_{3}(n,Cn)\)? The probability is over both the formula and A’s independent random bits.
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 3, R_{3}(n,m)\) is the distribution on ordered lists of m clauses obtained independently with replacement. Each clause selects a uniformly random three-element subset of \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and independently negates each of its three variables with probability \(1/2\). Each clause is their disjunction; the formula is the conjunction of the list, with duplicate clauses permitted. On every input A outputs UNSAT or UNKNOWN. Soundness is exact: for every satisfiable formula and every random tape A returns UNKNOWN. Its time is bounded by a fixed polynomial in the explicit binary input length on every input and every random tape, including adversarial formulas; variable names are binary integers and n is part of the encoding. A may use only fresh independent fair random bits and has no advice or external oracle. The constant C, the machine, and the time polynomial are chosen before n. The probability limit means that for every \(\eta >0\) there is n0 such that the probability is at least \(1- \eta\) for all \(n\ge n0\). There is no requirement to use a specified refutation proof system: a sound decision procedure certifying unsatisfiability suffices. Restricting the existential choice to integers \(C\ge 6\) loses no larger constant-density regime, since an algorithm at a smaller density can run on the corresponding prefix of the random clause list.

context_blocks.text: At a sufficiently large fixed clause density, a random 3-CNF formula is unsatisfiable with probability approaching one. That fact alone does not give a sound algorithm for a particular input: a procedure that always announces unsatisfiability would incorrectly reject satisfiable adversarial formulas. The question is whether an efficient algorithm can recognize almost all random instances while retaining exact soundness on every satisfiable instance.

The random distribution and the algorithmic quantifiers have different roles. A is constrained on all inputs, but its success guarantee applies to the stated distribution. C is an absolute constant, so success only at a density growing with n does not meet the target. Likewise, proving that short certificates exist does not automatically yield an algorithm that finds them.

Allen, O’Donnell and Witmer define refutation as a sound UNSAT-or-fail procedure and develop refutation algorithms for random constraint satisfaction problems. They distinguish this task from planted-instance detection and from strong refutation, which certifies that every assignment violates a positive fraction of constraints. These distinctions determine which hardness assumptions and consequences apply.

Feige’s random-3-SAT hypothesis is often presented in a stronger gap formulation. For example, Barak’s formulation requires soundness even on nearly satisfiable formulas. This card records the exact-satisfiability, constant-density refutation question requested in the proposal; it does not identify that formulation with every version called Feige’s hypothesis. The gap formulation is documented as related context.

Chan, d’Orsi and Xu’s 2026 work generalizes density, sum-of-squares degree and refutation-strength tradeoffs for random CSPs. Its broader predicate model is not a polynomial-time, constant-density solution of this random-3-SAT target. The question remains a distinct counterpart to the catalogue’s planted-clique detection problem.

cards.title: Infinitely-often one-way functions from average-case NP hardness
cards.formal: Does $\mathrm{DistNP}\not\subseteq\mathrm{HeurBPP}$ imply the existence of a polynomial-time computable function f with the following property? For every probabilistic polynomial-time inverter I and every constant \(c>0\), infinitely many lengths n satisfy $\Pr[|z|=n\ \land\ f(z)=f(x)]<n^{-c}$, where $x\sim U(\{0,1\}^n)$ and $z\leftarrow I(1^n,f(x))$. The probability includes inverter randomness. This card fixes the infinitely-often security convention used by the cited characterization.
cards.why: It asks whether distributional hardness alone suffices for basic cryptography: a central connection between average-case complexity and cryptographic constructions.

progress.text: The revised paper characterizes the remaining obstruction by the gap between approximation factors $\ell^{1-o(1)}$ and $O(\ell)$ for minimum-description-length agnostic learning. Here $\ell$ is advice complexity of sampling. The original April version states a different quantitative claim.

context_blocks.text: Hardness of deciding typical instances and hardness of finding preimages are different requirements. The assumption \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\) alone is weaker and belongs to a separate existing question.

An average-case decision problem asks an algorithm to classify instances drawn from a specified distribution. A one-way function creates a different experiment: sample an input, reveal its efficiently computed image, and ask an adversary to find any valid preimage. The sampling process and the form of the required answer both matter.

A reduction has to turn the first kind of difficulty into the second while preserving efficient generation and a meaningful success probability. It cannot simply use a hard yes/no question as a function and assume its inverse is hard. The question is whether some average-case hardness can exist without yielding the basic inversion obstacle on which one-way-function cryptography is built.

cards.definitions: DistNP consists of pairs \((\mathrm{L},D)\) with L in NP and \(D_{n} a\) polynomial-time samplable distribution on n-bit inputs. Such a pair is in HeurBPP if a single randomized algorithm A runs in time polynomial in n and 1/delta and, for every n and $0<\delta<1$, at least a $1-\delta$ fraction of x drawn from \(D_{n}\) have $\Pr[A(x,\delta)=L(x)]\ge2/3$. The output is a decision bit. Infinitely-often security is weaker than requiring negligible inversion probability at all sufficiently large lengths; the latter is a distinct stronger target.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication under the two explicit distributional and security definitions, or prove that average-case NP hardness can hold while every polynomial-time function fails that infinitely-often inversion guarantee. A result only about an oracle world does not settle the unrelativized implication.

importance.reason: Links average-case NP hardness to the existence of a basic cryptographic primitive; resolving it would clarify the foundations of complexity-based cryptography.

cards.title: Polynomial smoothed complexity of FLIP for Max-Cut
cards.formal: Are there absolute constants \(C,a,b>0\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\), every simple undirected graph G on n vertices, every \(\varphi \ge 1/2\) and every collection of independent edge-weight distributions supported on \([- 1,1]\) with probability densities bounded by \(\varphi\), the expected length of the longest strictly improving single-vertex-flip path is at most \(C(n+1)^{a}(1+\varphi )^{b}\)?
cards.why: A flagship unresolved explanation of why a canonical PLS local-search algorithm works efficiently on perturbed inputs.
cards.status_note: The ESA 2024 source explicitly retains the arbitrary-graph problem. Searches for subsequent work through 11 September 2026 found no resolution of this expected longest-path target. cards.definitions: The graph and one Lebesgue-measurable density \(f_{e}\) for each edge are chosen adversarially before the random weights. Each \(f_{e}\) is nonnegative, integrates to 1 on \([- 1,1]\), and is at most \(\varphi\) almost everywhere; weights \(w_{e}\) are sampled independently once from these densities and then held fixed. They may be negative and need not be identically distributed. A cut is a subset \(S\subseteq V\), with value \(\mathrm{W}_{w}(S)=\Sigma\)_{\(uv\in E\): exactly one of u,v lies in S} \(w_{uv}\). A legal step replaces S by \(S\triangle \{v\}\) for one vertex v, and requires a strictly larger cut value. Define \(\mathrm{L}(G,w)\) as the largest number of steps in any such path, maximized over all starting cuts and all choices of improving vertices after w is known; set \(\mathrm{L}=0\) if there is no step. There are finitely many cuts and strict improvement prevents revisiting one, so \(\mathrm{L}\le 2^{n}- 1\) and its expectation is well-defined. The expectation is over w alone, with the maximum over paths inside it. The resource counted is improving steps, not the bit cost of exact real arithmetic or of sampling distributions. The target concerns all graphs and all allowed densities with one common polynomial. A run ends at a single-flip local maximum, which need not maximize cut value globally.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed universal polynomial bound on \(E_{w}[\mathrm{L}(G,w)]\), or prove its logical negation by exhibiting admissible families that exceed every such polynomial. A bound for selected graph classes or for one favorable pivot rule does not establish the proposition. A rare long path or an unperturbed worst-case instance alone does not refute an expected bound under these density constraints.

context_blocks.title: What FLIP improves
context_blocks.text: The procedure repeatedly moves a vertex to the opposite side when this increases the weight crossing the cut. Different choices can produce different paths, so the question controls the longest one. This includes starting cuts and choices made after seeing the sampled weights, rather than relying on a particular implementation to avoid a bad path.

context_blocks.title: Local optimality has a different goal
context_blocks.text: Consider a four-cycle 1–2–3–4–1 with weights 0.9 on edges 12 and 34 and weights 1 on edges 23 and 41. The cut \(\{1,2\}\) has weight 2, and moving any single vertex decreases it by 0.1. Nevertheless, the alternating cut \(\{1,3\}\) has weight 3.8. Fast termination here would mean finding a state with no improving single move, without asserting that FLIP finds a global maximum.

context_blocks.title: What the smoothing parameter permits
context_blocks.text: The adversary chooses the graph and the distributions, while independent draws supply the randomness. Density bounded by \(\varphi\) prevents a distribution from putting too much probability in an arbitrarily short interval: an interval of length h has probability at most \(\varphi h\). Larger \(\varphi\) permits more concentrated weights, and the requested running-time bound may grow polynomially with \(\varphi\).

context_blocks.text: The general-graph theorem of Chen and coauthors gives \(\varphi n^{O(\sqrt{\log  n})}\) steps with high probability, uniformly over improving paths. Schwartzman proves polynomial expected length when arboricity is \(O(\log ^{1- \delta}n)\) for fixed \(\delta >0\); arboricity is the minimum number of forests needed to partition the edges. This includes sparse graph classes but not arbitrary graphs. The expectation requirement matters: a high-probability statement by itself does not bound the contribution of a long tail.

cards.definitions:
Fix an integer \(k\geq3\) and a real constant density \(\alpha\geq0\). On Boolean variables \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\), generate \(m=\lfloor\alpha n\rfloor\) ordered clauses. Each clause has \(k\) literal positions, each independently uniform among \(x_{1},\ldots,x_{n},\neg x_{1},\ldots,\neg x_{n}\). The formula is the AND of these OR clauses. Sampling is with replacement: repeated literals, tautological clauses and repeated clauses are allowed.

The algorithm receives the entire explicit formula, with variable indices in binary, together with \(n\). It must output one full assignment in \(\{0,1\}^{n}\) satisfying every clause. It may report failure otherwise. The input is sampled without conditioning on satisfiability and without planting or revealing any assignment.

A density \(\alpha\) is algorithmically attainable at width \(k\) if there is a classical randomized algorithm \(A\), with no advice depending on \(n\), such that its running time is bounded by a polynomial in the explicit input length and \(n\) on every input and random tape, and
\[\Pr_{\Phi,A}[A(\Phi)\text{ outputs a satisfying assignment of }\Phi]\longrightarrow1
\quad\text{as }n\to\infty.\]
The probability includes both the random formula and the algorithm's internal randomness. One fixed algorithm must work for all \(n\) at the chosen \(k,\alpha\). Its code, polynomial degree and constants may depend on those fixed parameters. They are not allowed to depend separately on each input length.

Let \(\alpha_{\mathrm{alg}}(k)\) be the supremum of all such densities. Attainment at the supremum is not required. First take \(n\to\infty\) at fixed \(k,\alpha\); only then consider the asymptotic behavior as \(k\to\infty\). Here \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm. This is a leading-order asymptotic question, not a request for an exact critical density at a particular small \(k\).

The target ranges over all randomized polynomial-time assignment-finding algorithms. It imposes no locality, stability, low-degree representation or restriction to a named heuristic. Deciding satisfiability without producing an assignment, satisfying only most clauses, or proving a barrier for a restricted algorithm family is a different guarantee.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed asymptotic equality, or refute it. The known algorithm gives the lower bound \(1-o_{k}(1)\) on the ratio, so the missing positive direction is the matching upper bound for all polynomial-time algorithms. A refutation must change the limiting leading-order behavior along arbitrarily large widths; an improvement confined to one fixed small width or a lower-order term does not suffice.

cards.title: Rapid mixing of Glauber dynamics with \(\Delta +2\) colours
cards.formal: Do absolute constants \(C,c>0\) exist such that, for every finite simple n-vertex graph G with maximum degree \(\Delta\) and every integer \(q\ge \Delta +2\), the single-vertex heat-bath Glauber chain on proper q-colourings has total-variation mixing time \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le Cn^{c}\)?
cards.definitions: Let \(n\ge 1\) and \(\Omega\)={\(\sigma :V(G)\to [q] : \sigma (u)\ne \sigma (v)\) for every edge uv}. Colours are labelled; unused colours are allowed. At each discrete step choose v uniformly from \(V(G)\), then choose a colour uniformly from \([q]\)\\(\{\sigma (u):u\in N(v)\}\) and assign it to v, leaving all other vertices unchanged. The current colour is among the available choices. Let P be this transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega\). Define \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)=\min \{t\in Z_{\ge 0}: \max _{\sigma \in \Omega} (1/2)\sum_{\tau \in \Omega}|\mathrm{P}^{t}(\sigma ,\tau )- \pi (\tau )|\le 1/4\}\). This counts individual vertex updates, not sweeps or bit operations. The constants C,c must be independent of \(n, \Delta , q\) and G. The initial proper colouring is arbitrary, and the graph has no girth, treewidth or randomness promise. This card fixes a uniform polynomial bound across degrees, rather than leaving the exponent’s parameter dependence implicit.
