cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The general-graph \(\Delta +2\) conjecture remains open in the checked sources. August 2026 results improve restricted-girth regimes with fixed relative slack; they do not establish the universal additive-two bound.

context_blocks.text: A proper colouring is easy to construct greedily with this many colours. Sampling one nearly uniformly is a different task: a deterministic rule can strongly favour a small part of the solution space. Glauber dynamics is an appealing candidate because every update uses only a vertex and its neighbours, yet repeated local changes must reproduce the global distribution. The inherited paper states the conjecture and proves it for particular graph classes.

The threshold \(\Delta +2\) has a concrete role. On a clique with \(\Delta +1\) vertices and exactly \(\Delta +1\) colours, every vertex sees all other colours in its neighbourhood. No vertex can change colour, so each proper colouring is a separate absorbing state. With at least \(\Delta +2\) colours, the single-vertex chain is irreducible on every graph and converges to the uniform distribution. The unresolved issue is how long this convergence takes.

Connectivity of the recolouring graph is insufficient to control that time. A walk may need to cross a narrow passage between two large collections of colourings. Even short paths between every pair do not show that a random walk finds the appropriate passages often enough. The card therefore asks for a distributional guarantee from the worst starting colouring, rather than a bound on the number of recolourings in an intelligently chosen path.

The update convention matters when comparing sources. A second standard version proposes a colour uniformly from the entire palette and rejects it if a neighbour uses it. This is the Metropolis version used in several cited papers. Its off-diagonal transition probabilities and the heat-bath probabilities differ by a factor between 1 and \(q/(q- \Delta )\). That factor is at most \(1+\Delta /2\) in the present range, so the distinction is relevant to sharp runtime statements but does not create an exponential gap between their polynomial-mixing questions.

The early general-graph milestones were Jerrum’\(s q>2\Delta\) regime and Vigoda’s improvement to roughly \(11\Delta /6\). The latter used a flip chain that interchanges two colours on a small connected bichromatic component, followed by a comparison with single-vertex dynamics. Chen and coauthors subsequently crossed the \(11/6\) threshold by a small constant improvement. The 2026 ICALP paper retains \(\Delta +2\) as a conjecture, including its Glauber-dynamics version.

Carlson–Vigoda’s October 2024 revision gives a substantial further improvement. Theorem 1.1 assumes \(\Delta \ge 125\) and \(q\ge 1.809\Delta\) and proves \(O(n \log  n)\) mixing for the flip chain. Comparison gives polynomial mixing for Glauber dynamics in that regime. Their optimal \(O(n \log  n)\) Glauber corollary has a constant depending on \(\Delta\) and q; it is stated for fixed parameters. The headline coefficient should therefore not be read as an unrestricted optimal-time theorem for all degrees.

Graph structure can bring the colour threshold much closer to the target. Heinrich proves \(n^{O(\operatorname{tw}(G)^{3})}\) mixing with \(q\ge \Delta +2\), so bounded treewidth is covered even when maximum degree is unbounded. For chordal graphs, the proved regime instead uses \(q\ge (1+\varepsilon )(\Delta +1)\) for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\). Letting treewidth grow with n, or substituting \(\varepsilon\) that shrinks with \(\Delta\), does not give the uniform statement in this card.

There was further progress during 2026. Jain–Mizgerd–Vigoda prove \(O_{\delta}(n \log  n)\) mixing for the Metropolis chain when \(q\ge (1+\delta )\Delta , \Delta\) is sufficiently large in terms of fixed \(\delta >0\), and the graph has sufficiently large girth. Their August 27 revision improves the required girth from eleven to seven. This is stronger than the original April abstract, but still excludes general graphs and does not establish additive slack of only two colours.

Chen–Liu’s August 26 preprint reaches girth at least five in the same fixed-relative-slack regime for heat-bath dynamics. Its Theorem 1 proves spectral gap \(\Omega _{\delta}(1/n)\) and mixing time \(O_{\delta}(n^{2} \log  q+n \log (1/\varepsilon ))\); the sharper \(O_{\delta}(n \log  n)\) consequence requires degree bounded in terms of \(\delta\). Both the girth restriction and the dependence on \(\delta\) matter. Taking \(\delta =2/\Delta\) is not justified by a theorem that first fixes \(\delta\) and then requires sufficiently large \(\Delta\).

The other inherited 2026 source studies an additional constraint: prescribed colour-class sizes. Such a condition changes the sample space, and a single-vertex update generally cannot preserve it. Its algorithms for equitable or mildly skewed colourings therefore address a separate sampling problem. They provide useful context for why global constraints complicate local sampling, while explicitly leaving the unconstrained \(\Delta +2\) conjecture open.

This is fundamental because it tests whether the basic local sampler remains efficient throughout the universally ergodic range. A proof would connect a simple combinatorial availability condition with global probabilistic convergence. A negative answer would identify an obstruction to efficient local sampling that survives despite spare colours at every vertex and connectivity of the entire state space.

The inherited paper states the conjecture and proves it for particular graph classes.

The threshold \(\Delta +2\) has a concrete role. On a clique with \(\Delta +1\) vertices and exactly \(\Delta +1\) colours, every vertex sees all other colours in its neighbourhood. No vertex can change colour, so each proper colouring is a separate absorbing state. With at least \(\Delta +2\) colours, the single-vertex chain is irreducible on every graph and converges to the uniform distribution. The unresolved issue is how long this convergence takes.

Connectivity of the recolouring graph is insufficient to control that time. A walk may need to cross a narrow passage between two large collections of colourings. Even short paths between every pair do not show that a random walk finds the appropriate passages often enough. The card therefore asks for a distributional guarantee from the worst starting colouring, rather than a bound on the number of recolourings in an intelligently chosen path.

The update convention matters when comparing sources. A second standard version proposes a colour uniformly from the entire palette and rejects it if a neighbour uses it. This is the Metropolis version used in several cited papers. Its off-diagonal transition probabilities and the heat-bath probabilities differ by a factor between 1 and \(q/(q- \Delta )\). That factor is at most \(1+\Delta /2\) in the present range, so the distinction is relevant to sharp runtime statements but does not create an exponential gap between their polynomial-mixing questions.

The early general-graph milestones were Jerrum’\(s q>2\Delta\) regime and Vigoda’s improvement to roughly \(11\Delta /6\). The latter used a flip chain that interchanges two colours on a small connected bichromatic component, followed by a comparison with single-vertex dynamics. Chen and coauthors subsequently crossed the \(11/6\) threshold by a small constant improvement. The 2026 ICALP paper retains \(\Delta +2\) as a conjecture, including its Glauber-dynamics version.

Carlson–Vigoda’s October 2024 revision gives a substantial further improvement. Theorem 1.1 assumes \(\Delta \ge 125\) and \(q\ge 1.809\Delta\) and proves \(O(n \log  n)\) mixing for the flip chain. Comparison gives polynomial mixing for Glauber dynamics in that regime. Their optimal \(O(n \log  n)\) Glauber corollary has a constant depending on \(\Delta\) and q; it is stated for fixed parameters. The headline coefficient should therefore not be read as an unrestricted optimal-time theorem for all degrees.

Graph structure can bring the colour threshold much closer to the target. Heinrich proves \(n^{O(\operatorname{tw}(G)^{3})}\) mixing with \(q\ge \Delta +2\), so bounded treewidth is covered even when maximum degree is unbounded. For chordal graphs, the proved regime instead uses \(q\ge (1+\varepsilon )(\Delta +1)\) for a fixed positive \(\varepsilon\). Letting treewidth grow with n, or substituting \(\varepsilon\) that shrinks with \(\Delta\), does not give the uniform statement in this card.

There was further progress during 2026. Jain–Mizgerd–Vigoda prove \(O_{\delta}(n \log  n)\) mixing for the Metropolis chain when \(q\ge (1+\delta )\Delta , \Delta\) is sufficiently large in terms of fixed \(\delta >0\), and the graph has sufficiently large girth. Their August 27 revision improves the required girth from eleven to seven. This is stronger than the original April abstract, but still excludes general graphs and does not establish additive slack of only two colours.

Chen–Liu’s August 26 preprint reaches girth at least five in the same fixed-relative-slack regime for heat-bath dynamics. Its Theorem 1 proves spectral gap \(\Omega _{\delta}(1/n)\) and mixing time \(O_{\delta}(n^{2} \log  q+n \log (1/\varepsilon ))\); the sharper \(O_{\delta}(n \log  n)\) consequence requires degree bounded in terms of \(\delta\). Both the girth restriction and the dependence on \(\delta\) matter. Taking \(\delta =2/\Delta\) is not justified by a theorem that first fixes \(\delta\) and then requires sufficiently large \(\Delta\).

The other inherited 2026 source studies an additional constraint: prescribed colour-class sizes. Such a condition changes the sample space, and a single-vertex update generally cannot preserve it. Its algorithms for equitable or mildly skewed colourings therefore address a separate sampling problem. They provide useful context for why global constraints complicate local sampling, while explicitly leaving the unconstrained \(\Delta +2\) conjecture open.

This is fundamental because it tests whether the basic local sampler remains efficient throughout the universally ergodic range. A proof would connect a simple combinatorial availability condition with global probabilistic convergence. A negative answer would identify an obstruction to efficient local sampling that survives despite spare colours at every vertex and connectivity of the entire state space.

cards.definitions: For integers \(r,s\ge1\), let \(a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{r}\) and \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{s}\). The promised nonempty set \(\Omega(a,b)\) consists of binary matrices \(M\in\{0,1\}^{r\times s}\) with row sums \(a_i\) and column sums \(b_j\). At each attempted transition independently, stay with probability \(1/2\). Otherwise choose an unordered pair of distinct rows uniformly and an unordered pair of distinct columns uniformly and independently. If their rectangle has either alternating pattern \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}1&0\\0&1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\) or \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), replace it by the other; otherwise stay. If \(r<2\) or \(s<2\), the state space is a singleton and the chain stays. Let \(P\) be the transition matrix and \(\pi\) the uniform distribution on \(\Omega(a,b)\). For an integer \(t\ge0\), define \(d(t)=\max_{M\in\Omega(a,b)}\frac12\sum_{N\in\Omega(a,b)}|P^t(M,N)-1/|\Omega(a,b)||\). Let \(t_{\rm mix}(1/4)=\min\{t\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}:d(t)\le1/4\}\), or \(+\infty\) if this set is empty. Time counts attempted transitions, including holds. The polynomial bound must use the same constants for every dimension and feasible pair of margins, without density, regularity or balance assumptions. This is a mathematical mixing-time question, with no requirement on bit complexity or implementation of a sampler.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that universal constants \(K,c>0\) bound the specified worst-case mixing time by \(K(r+s)^c\) for every nonempty binary-margin state space, or prove its logical negation in Lean: for every such pair of constants there are feasible dimensions and margins violating that bound. The theorem must concern the exact lazy chain and every starting matrix defined here.

context_blocks.text: Status update: Fu, Qin and Wang’s July 2026 revision claims a solution for this exact lazy binary-matrix chain. Theorem 2.2 gives \(t_{\mathrm{mix}}(1/4)\le \operatorname{binom}(r,2)\operatorname{binom}(s,2)(rs \ln  2+\ln  4)\), which implies a universal polynomial bound in \(r+s\). The transition probabilities and scope were compared with this card. The proof was not independently verified here, so the card records an uncertain claimed resolution.

A binary matrix can describe which species occur at which sites, or which vertices are adjacent across the two sides of a bipartite graph. Fixing its row and column sums preserves the activity of every individual row and column. Sampling uniformly from all matrices with those same margins provides a baseline for asking whether additional patterns are unusual, without confusing them with the already-fixed totals.

The elementary move preserves every margin. Replacing \([[1,0],[0,1]]\) by \([[0,1],[1,0]]\) changes where four entries lie while leaving each involved row sum and column sum unchanged. For a \(2\times 2\) matrix with all margins equal to one there are exactly two states. The chain stays or switches with equal probability, so one attempted transition already gives the uniform distribution. Larger instances may have many possible rectangles, most of which are not switchable.

Every allowed transition has the same probability as its reverse, making the uniform distribution stationary. Feasible binary matrices with the same margins are connected by switches, and the explicit probability of staying removes periodicity. These facts establish eventual convergence. Rapid mixing asks for a bound on how long the worst initial state can remain far from uniform; connectivity alone need not give a small bound.

Earlier theorems establish rapid mixing under additional structure. The unified approach handles P-stable degree-sequence families: roughly, small perturbations of the prescribed degrees do not create more than polynomially many times as many realizations. Such results cover broad families while retaining a hypothesis absent from the universal question. An efficient algorithm that merely finds one feasible realization would address a different task.

The inherited 2018 reference compares the switch chain with Curveball, which resamples relationships across a pair of rows using a larger move. Faster practical movement does not by itself prove a polynomial worst-case bound. A theorem about another transition rule must include the appropriate chain comparison before it can answer this card’s fixed-chain question.

The authors also supply a Lean formalization repository and identify its closed main theorem. This review checked that the artifact is linked by the paper and author, but did not build it or audit the correspondence of its definitions and theorem dependencies. The presence of a formalization is recorded as evidence, not as an independent machine verification performed by this catalogue.

The question is specifically the bipartite, zero-one matrix case. Integer-valued contingency tables, forbidden positions and general nonbipartite graphs have different state spaces or moves. A theorem for arbitrary feasible binary margins is broad enough here, while its consequences for those other sampling questions must be assessed separately.

sentences: A graph's cover time is the maximum, over starting vertices, of the expected time a random walk needs to visit every vertex.
The recorded question asks whether this exact quantity can be computed by a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm.
Tracking both the current vertex and the entire set already visited gives a direct approach with exponentially many possible states.
The challenge is to avoid that expansion while still accounting for dependencies between visits to different vertices.
An exact algorithm would provide more than simulation or approximate bounds, and the final card must specify the graph encoding and how the exact numerical answer is represented.

sentences: A self-avoiding walk is a lattice path that never visits the same vertex twice.
The pivot chain proposes a geometric transformation of part of such a path and accepts moves that preserve self-avoidance.
The saved textbook direction asks for rigorous convergence and mixing-time analysis of this sampling procedure.

Changing a large portion of a path in one move can explore configurations efficiently, but the self-avoidance constraint makes acceptance and global communication between configurations difficult to control.
The particular lattice, path length, pivot transformations, and desired quantitative bound remain part of the source's formulation rather than a single rate fixed by this short summary.

cards.title: FPRAS for counting perfect matchings
cards.formal: Does there exist a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme for the number \(Z(G)\) of perfect matchings in every finite undirected simple graph G? More precisely, is there one randomized algorithm A and one polynomial p such that, for every explicitly encoded graph G and rational \(0<\varepsilon <1, A\) halts within \(p(\mathrm{L},\lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil )\) bit operations and outputs a nonnegative rational Ẑ satisfying \(\Pr [(1- \varepsilon )Z(G)\le \hat\{Z\}\le (1+\varepsilon )Z(G)]\ge 3/4\), where L is the total binary input length?
cards.definitions: A matching is a set of edges with no shared endpoints. It is perfect if every vertex is incident to exactly one selected edge. \(Z(G)\) is the number of distinct such edge sets; edges and vertices are unweighted. The graph is specified by a labeled vertex set and its full edge list, without bipartiteness, density, degree, expansion or planarity promises. For an odd number of vertices \(Z(G)=0\); for the empty graph \(Z(G)=1\). The random bits are independent fair bits, all computational and output costs are counted, and the time bound holds for every random tape. When \(Z(G)=0\), require output zero with probability one; this causes no loss of generality because existence of a perfect matching can be decided deterministically in polynomial time before approximation begins. The fixed success probability \(3/4\) can be amplified to \(1- \delta\) by independent repetitions and a median, with an \(O(\log (1/\delta ))\) multiplicative overhead. The same polynomial p must work for all graphs and all requested accuracies. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A canonical unresolved problem in approximate counting, separating efficient existence testing from estimating the number of solutions. It also controls the approximability of other counting and partition-function problems through reductions.

importance.reason: The major missing generalization of the permanent FPRAS, with an established obstruction to the direct Markov-chain approach and consequences beyond matchings.

progress.text: Jerrum–Sinclair give an FPRAS for the monomer–dimer partition function, which counts matchings of all sizes. This is not an unrestricted perfect-matching FPRAS.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The general-graph question remains open in the checked primary literature. The August 2026 improvement is a permanent algorithm for bipartite graphs. Slow mixing of the particular general-graph Markov chains does not establish impossibility of all FPRAS approaches.

context_blocks.text: Finding a perfect matching and estimating how many exist are different tasks. Edmonds’ algorithm handles existence and maximum cardinality in general graphs, whereas exact counting is #P-complete even in bipartite graphs. Approximation avoids asking for every digit of a potentially exponential count, but still requires a reliable multiplicative estimate. The 2018 paper of Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes places this gap at the center of general matching-counting research.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda resolve the bipartite case through an FPRAS for the permanent of any nonnegative matrix. A square bipartite adjacency matrix records allowed pairs between two fixed vertex classes; a permutation chooses one partner for every vertex. The algorithm combines a Markov chain on perfect and near-perfect matchings with simulated annealing and weights that balance different pairs of unmatched vertices.

Applying that theorem to the ordinary adjacency matrix of a nonbipartite graph does not count its perfect matchings. For example, \(K_{4}\) has three perfect matchings, but its adjacency matrix has permanent nine: the latter also counts directed cycle-cover patterns. The corresponding general-graph quantity is a hafnian, a sum over partitions of the vertex set into unordered pairs. The distinction is combinatorial, not a matter of merely changing the matrix dimensions.

Counting all matchings is another solved neighboring problem: Jerrum and Sinclair give an FPRAS for the monomer–dimer partition function. The desired perfect matchings may form a very small fraction of that distribution. A disjoint union of k edges already has \(2^{k}\) matchings and just one perfect matching. Thus approximate uniform sampling from all matchings, followed by waiting for a perfect one, need not run in polynomial time. This example concerns that proposed reduction, not hardness of counting on the example graph.

Štefankovič, Vigoda and Wilmes show that the straightforward extension of the JSV chain encounters exponential mixing bottlenecks on general graphs; changing weights based only on the unmatched-vertex pattern does not give a universal remedy. They also use the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition to obtain algorithms for structurally restricted graphs. A factor-critical component is one whose deletion of any one vertex leaves a perfect matching. Their parameter concerns the number of ears in such a component’s ear decomposition, not simply its vertex count.

The problem matters beyond matching counts themselves. Fei, Goldberg and Lu’s 2025 journal paper classifies approximation of several two-state spin-system partition functions. Some parameter settings are linked by approximation-preserving reductions to perfect-matching counting in general graphs, and the paper explicitly retains that task as a central open question. A resolution would therefore determine tractability for related counting models as well.

On 27 August 2026, Chen, Vigoda and Yang post an improved permanent FPRAS. For an \(r\times r\) zero–one matrix their stated bound is \(O(r^{6} \varepsilon ^{- 2} \log ^{5} r \log (2/\delta ))\), improving the previous leading dependence at fixed accuracy and success probability. Their analysis controls mixing of observables describing unmatched-vertex patterns through a restricted Poincaré inequality and coupled flows. The state space remains bipartite; the new theorem does not remove the general-graph obstruction.

The central issue is whether the extra structure available in bipartite graphs is essential for efficient approximate counting. A positive result would extend one of the landmark successes of randomized counting to all graphs. A negative result would establish a striking boundary: even though perfect matching existence remains efficiently decidable on both sides, relative counting would become computationally harder once arbitrary odd-cycle structure is permitted.

cards.title: FPRAS for #BIS
cards.formal: Does there exist one probabilistic Turing algorithm A and one polynomial p such that, for every finite simple bipartite graph G and rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1), A(G,\varepsilon )\) halts within \(p(\mathrm{L},\lceil 1/\varepsilon \rceil )\) steps on every random tape and returns a nonnegative rational Ẑ with \(\Pr [(1- \varepsilon )Z(G)\le \hat\{Z\}\le (1+\varepsilon )Z(G)]\ge 3/4\)? L is the full input bit length, including \(\varepsilon ; Z(G)\) is the number of independent sets.
cards.definitions: The input lists the vertices, their bipartition U,V and all edges, with no loops or repeated edges; \(\varepsilon\) is supplied as a positive binary numerator and denominator. An independent set \(I\subseteq U\cup V\) contains no edge’s two endpoints. \(Z(G)\) counts all such subsets, including \(\varnothing\), so \(Z(G)\ge 1\) and the empty graph has \(Z=1\). The output is a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator representing \(\hat\{Z\}\ge 0\). A uses independent fair coin bits, with no advice or oracle. All input reading, computation, random-bit access and output writing count toward the bound. The success probability is separately required on every input and is over A’s coins. The same program and polynomial work for all bipartitions, degrees, graph sizes and accuracies.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Determines whether the canonical intermediate approximate-counting problem can be solved with a uniform polynomial-time randomized relative-error algorithm, with consequences for many equivalent counting and statistical-mechanics problems.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved boundary in approximate counting, with broad approximation-preserving consequences and a well-defined gap between FPRAS and hardness evidence.

progress.text: Dell, Husfeldt and Nederlof describe #BIS as the canonical approximate-counting problem of intermediate complexity and record the belief that it has no efficient approximation algorithm without being NP-hard.
Liao, Lin, Lu and Mao give an FPTAS for independent sets on almost every sufficiently regular bipartite graph, a restricted result that leaves arbitrary worst-case graphs open.
Container and spectral methods give FPRAS or FPTAS results for additional dense, regular, or expanding subclasses, without resolving general #BIS.

context_blocks.text: #BIS asks for the number of independent sets in an arbitrary bipartite graph. Exact counting is already difficult, while approximate counting places the problem in a widely studied intermediate regime: it is a canonical complete problem for the class #\(RH\Pi _{1}\) under approximation-preserving reductions, and many spin-system and combinatorial counting problems are equivalent to it. The main unresolved issue is whether this intermediate status hides a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme.

The relative-error requirement matters when the graph has few independent sets as well as when it has exponentially many. The algorithm must work for every explicitly encoded graph and every requested accuracy, with no structural promise that would make local sampling mix rapidly. A polynomial bound in |V| alone, an additive approximation, or an algorithm whose polynomial degree depends on the graph family would be a different statement.

Several restricted classes do admit efficient approximation schemes. For example, results for almost every sufficiently regular bipartite graph and for dense regular bipartite graphs exploit expansion or spectral structure. These theorems demonstrate that the target is achievable on substantial subclasses, but they do not provide a worst-case FPRAS for arbitrary bipartite inputs.

The conjectured difficulty is deliberately weaker than #P-hardness of approximation. #BIS is believed not to have an FPRAS, yet it is also believed not to be NP-hard under the usual approximation-preserving reductions. Resolving the card would therefore locate a central intermediate point between problems with known FPRASes and problems with robust hardness barriers.

The earlier catalogue pointer TCS-6225 came from a paper on independent sets in random regular bipartite graphs and preserved only a truncated source excerpt. This card states the general #BIS question explicitly and keeps the restricted-family results as progress rather than treating them as a solution.

cards.title: Deterministic FPTAS for the nonnegative permanent
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm that, for every explicitly given nonnegative rational \(n\times n\) matrix A and every rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), outputs a rational Z satisfying \((1- \varepsilon )\operatorname{per}(A)\le Z\le (1+\varepsilon )\operatorname{per}(A)\) in time polynomial in the input bit length and \(1/\varepsilon\)?
cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 1, \operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\pi \in S_{n}}\prod _{i=1}^{n} A_{i,\pi (i)}\), where \(S_{n}\) is the set of permutations of \([n]\). Each entry is represented by a nonnegative integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary. Let L be the total binary description length of A and \(\varepsilon\). There must be one fixed polynomial P such that the algorithm uses at most \(\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{L},1/\varepsilon )\) bit operations on every input. Ordinary deterministic Turing computation is intended, with output bits and arithmetic costs counted; there are no random bits, nonuniform advice, counting oracles or exact-real unit-cost operations. No density, expansion, lower-bound-on-positive-entries, bounded-degree or matrix-scaling promise is imposed. Zero entries are allowed. If \(\operatorname{per}(A)=0\), the algorithm must return \(Z=0\) exactly. This zero case is decidable in polynomial time by checking whether the bipartite support graph has a perfect matching. FPTAS means fully polynomial-time approximation scheme: the running-time exponent must be independent of \(\varepsilon\), and the error is relative to \(\operatorname{per}(A)\), not additive relative to n!, a matrix norm, or another normalization.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct such a deterministic approximation scheme or prove that none exists. A randomized FPRAS does not settle the deterministic question. An approximation within a factor depending superconstantly on n, or a scheme with running time \(n^{g(1/\varepsilon )}\), does not meet the stated guarantee. Exact #P-hardness alone is not a refutation, since using exponentially small \(\varepsilon\) is allowed to take exponential time under the FPTAS bound.
cards.why: A landmark derandomization problem: match the accuracy and efficiency of the permanent FPRAS using deterministic computation on every nonnegative rational matrix.

importance.reason: One of the central explicit tests of derandomization in approximate counting, with broad connections to matchings, sampling, convex optimization and correlation decay.

progress.text: Jerrum–Sinclair–Vigoda establish an FPRAS for arbitrary nonnegative permanents.

Kudria–Luo–Majid give a deterministic polynomial-time \(\exp (O(n(\log  \log  n)^{2}/\log  n))\) approximation and explicitly retain the FPTAS question.

cards.status_note: The 9 September 2026 primary preprint explicitly leaves a deterministic FPTAS open. Its new general subexponential-factor guarantee improves the late-August exponential-base results without yielding arbitrary relative accuracy. Checked through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: For a zero–one matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings in its bipartite support graph: rows and columns are the two vertex classes, and a permutation chooses one allowed partner for every row. With nonnegative weights it sums the products of edge weights over these matchings. Finding one perfect matching is efficient, but estimating how much total weight all perfect matchings contribute is a different task.

Unlike the determinant, the permanent has no alternating signs in its permutation sum. Nonnegativity makes multiplicative approximation meaningful even when the total is very small. It also makes zero detection easy: a positive permanent is equivalent to existence of a perfect matching using positive entries. The hard part is accurate quantitative estimation on positive instances, not distinguishing an arbitrary exponentially tiny value from zero by floating-point tolerance.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda provide a randomized fully polynomial approximation scheme for every nonnegative matrix. Their method combines weighted perfect and near-perfect matchings, sampling and simulated annealing. Thus a solution need not discover that approximate counting is possible; it must remove randomness while retaining arbitrary relative accuracy and polynomial dependence on the requested inverse accuracy.

The randomized side continues to improve. Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s August 2026 preprint reduces the reported running time for zero–one matrices to \(O(n^{6} \log ^{5} n)\) when the relative accuracy and success probability are fixed, with an extension to general nonnegative matrices. The better analysis concerns a restricted Poincaré inequality for the Markov chain. It remains a sampling-based randomized algorithm.

A major deterministic approach is the Bethe permanent, obtained from a variational optimization over doubly stochastic matrices. Anari and Rezaei prove that it lower-bounds the permanent and loses at most a factor \(2^{n/2}\). This factor is attained on block-diagonal matrices built from two-by-two all-ones blocks. The tight example limits the unmodified Bethe estimate, rather than proving that every deterministic approximation algorithm must lose that much.

In late August 2026, Anari and independently Narang and Perkins go beyond the canonical Bethe estimate. Both approaches exploit structure near the bad two-by-two blocks and achieve a factor \(c^{n}\) for some absolute \(c<\sqrt{2}\). This improves the exponential base. A fixed positive base above one, however, still gives an error factor growing exponentially with the matrix dimension.

The September 9 preprint of Kudria, Luo and Majid improves the general deterministic polynomial-time guarantee to \(\exp (O(n(\log  \log  n)^{2}/\log  n))=\exp (o(n))\). Its algorithm uses convex optimization of weighted matching sums, together with deterministic correlation-decay estimates. The theorem explicitly handles arbitrary nonnegative rational matrices in the bit model, so it applies to this card’s input class. Its approximation factor is still much larger than \(1+\varepsilon\).

sentences: The nonnegative permanent sums the weights of all perfect matchings in a bipartite graph.
The question asks for a deterministic approximation within any requested relative error, with fully polynomial running time.
Randomized approximation already achieves this guarantee, so the missing resource is derandomization without sacrificing accuracy.
The saved September review describes deterministic subexponential-factor progress but explains why that factor is still far from one plus epsilon.
Zero entries and arbitrary rational weights are allowed, making bit complexity and reliable handling of very small positive values part of the full target.

cards.context:
For a zero–one matrix, the permanent counts perfect matchings in its bipartite support graph: rows and columns are the two vertex classes, and a permutation chooses one allowed partner for every row. With nonnegative weights it sums the products of edge weights over these matchings. Finding one perfect matching is efficient, but estimating how much total weight all perfect matchings contribute is a different task.

Unlike the determinant, the permanent has no alternating signs in its permutation sum. Nonnegativity makes multiplicative approximation meaningful even when the total is very small. It also makes zero detection easy: a positive permanent is equivalent to existence of a perfect matching using positive entries. The hard part is accurate quantitative estimation on positive instances, not distinguishing an arbitrary exponentially tiny value from zero by floating-point tolerance.

Jerrum, Sinclair and Vigoda provide a randomized fully polynomial approximation scheme for every nonnegative matrix. Their method combines weighted perfect and near-perfect matchings, sampling and simulated annealing. Thus a solution need not discover that approximate counting is possible; it must remove randomness while retaining arbitrary relative accuracy and polynomial dependence on the requested inverse accuracy.

The randomized side continues to improve. Chen, Vigoda and Yang’s August 2026 preprint reduces the reported running time for zero–one matrices to \(O(n^{6} \log ^{5} n)\) when the relative accuracy and success probability are fixed, with an extension to general nonnegative matrices. The better analysis concerns a restricted Poincaré inequality for the Markov chain. It remains a sampling-based randomized algorithm.

A major deterministic approach is the Bethe permanent, obtained from a variational optimization over doubly stochastic matrices. Anari and Rezaei prove that it lower-bounds the permanent and loses at most a factor \(2^{n/2}\). This factor is attained on block-diagonal matrices built from two-by-two all-ones blocks. The tight example limits the unmodified Bethe estimate, rather than proving that every deterministic approximation algorithm must lose that much.

In late August 2026, Anari and independently Narang and Perkins go beyond the canonical Bethe estimate. Both approaches exploit structure near the bad two-by-two blocks and achieve a factor \(c^{n}\) for some absolute \(c<\sqrt{2}\). This improves the exponential base. A fixed positive base above one, however, still gives an error factor growing exponentially with the matrix dimension.

The September 9 preprint of Kudria, Luo and Majid improves the general deterministic polynomial-time guarantee to \(\exp (O(n(\log  \log  n)^{2}/\log  n))=\exp (o(n))\). Its algorithm uses convex optimization of weighted matching sums, together with deterministic correlation-decay estimates. The theorem explicitly handles arbitrary nonnegative rational matrices in the bit model, so it applies to this card’s input class. Its approximation factor is still much larger than \(1+\varepsilon\).

There is a useful amplification threshold. Make a block-diagonal matrix containing r copies of A; its permanent is \(\operatorname{per}(A)^{r}\). If a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm approximated an N by N permanent within \(\exp (O(N^{1- \gamma}))\) for one fixed \(\gamma >0\), applying it at \(N=rn\) and taking an rth root would reduce the logarithmic error to \(O(n^{1- \gamma}/r^{\gamma})\). Polynomially many copies in n and \(1/\varepsilon\) would then suffice for an FPTAS.

The September theorem’s logarithmic saving does not cross that threshold: polynomially many copies increase \(\log (rn)\) by only a constant-factor scale, leaving a large logarithmic error after root extraction. Consequently, subexponential approximation and arbitrary relative accuracy remain distinct milestones. A solution would remove one of the most prominent uses of randomness in approximate counting while clarifying how much global matching information deterministic optimization can recover.

cards.title: Output-polynomial vertex enumeration
cards.formal: Do there exist a deterministic Turing machine A and a polynomial p such that, for every rational matrix M and rational vector b with \(\mathrm{P}=\{x\in R^{d}:Mx\le b\}\) bounded, A lists each vertex of P exactly once and halts within \(p(\mathrm{L}+S)\) bit operations, where L is the binary input length and S is the total binary length of the required vertex list? The dimension d is part of the input.
cards.definitions: The input specifies integers \(m,d\ge 1, M\in Q^{m\times d}\), and \(b\in Q^{m}\). Every rational is written as a reduced signed integer numerator and positive integer denominator in binary, with delimiters; L includes this entire explicit representation. P may be empty or lower-dimensional, and redundant inequalities and degeneracy are allowed. A vertex is an extreme point: \(v\in \mathrm{P}\) such that \(v=(x+y)/2\) with \(x,y\in \mathrm{P}\) implies \(x=y=v\). Every vertex is rational. The output is a finite list in arbitrary order of these vectors, with each coordinate in the same reduced rational encoding, followed by an end marker. S includes separators and the end marker; it is determined independently of the algorithm, so padding or duplicate outputs cannot enlarge the permitted bound. The empty polytope has an empty vertex list. The bound concerns total running time, including writing the output, without a polynomial-delay or polynomial-workspace requirement. Correctness and the bound are required on the bounded-polyhedron promise; behavior outside that promise is immaterial.

context_blocks.text: A finite system of inequalities describes a convex region implicitly, while a vertex list describes its extremal feasible points explicitly. Linear programming can optimize one linear objective without producing that list. Enumerating the list asks whether the entire conversion can be performed with only polynomial overhead relative to the information that must actually be returned.

The number of vertices can be exponential in the input length, so a running-time bound polynomial in the input alone would be inappropriate. Output-polynomial time allows that unavoidable cost. It still excludes an algorithm that examines exponentially many intermediate objects when the final list is short. Degeneracy is particularly relevant because many collections of tight inequalities can describe the same vertex.

Reimers and Stougie explicitly identify total-polynomial vertex enumeration for bounded polyhedra as a longstanding open question. They obtain such an algorithm under a bounded branch-width condition. Their paper also distinguishes the general unbounded-polyhedron problem, for which output-polynomial enumeration would imply \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). That hardness statement does not resolve the bounded target here.

Dong, Fan, Xiong and Zeng study vertices of hyperplane arrangements. An arrangement includes intersections that may lie outside the feasible region selected by a system of inequalities. Consequently, an output-sensitive bound for the entire arrangement is measured against a different output and does not establish the required bound in the number of vertices of this polytope.

This card adds geometric enumeration to a category that already contains counting and hypergraph-transversal questions. Its target is the exact finite output of an algorithm in variable dimension. Neither approximate vertices nor a fast method restricted to simple polytopes meets that target.

cards.definitions: \(H=([n],E), n\ge 0\), is supplied as the explicit vertex list and a finite list of edges \(e\subseteq [n]\), each edge an increasing list of binary vertex identifiers. Repeated edges have no effect. \(\mathrm{L}(H)\) is the bit length of this input including delimiters. A transversal is a set \(T\subseteq [n]\) intersecting every \(e\in E\); it is inclusion-minimal when no proper subset has this property. Output each such T as an increasing list of its binary vertex identifiers with a delimiter, in arbitrary order; no duplicate, nonminimal or incomplete output is allowed. \(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{out}}(H)\) is the sum of the bit lengths of these records, counting one delimiter even for \(T=\varnothing\). If E is empty, the unique minimal transversal is \(\varnothing\). If E contains \(\varnothing\), there is no transversal and \(\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{out}}=0\). Time includes all computation, output and termination detection. The polynomial and algorithm are independent of n, E, edge size and output size; there is no separate delay or workspace bound, advice, oracle or randomization. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

cards.title: Fully polynomial randomized approximation of mixed discriminants
cards.formal: Does an FPRAS exist for the mixed discriminant of arbitrary rational positive semidefinite matrices?
cards.definitions: The input is an integer \(n\ge1\), symmetric matrices \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\in\mathbb Q^{n\times n}\) satisfying \(z^{\mathsf T}A_i z\ge0\) for every \(z\in\mathbb R^n\), and a rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\). Define \(D(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\) to be the coefficient of \(t_1\cdots t_n\) in \(\det(\sum_{i=1}^{n}t_iA_i)\). This fixes the normalization: for n identical identity matrices, D=n!. This D is nonnegative. An FPRAS is one uniform randomized Turing machine returning a nonnegative rational Z with \(\Pr[(1-\varepsilon)D\le Z\le(1+\varepsilon)D]\ge3/4\) on every promised input, and worst-case time polynomial in the full binary input length and \(1/\varepsilon\). Probability is over independent fair random bits. All entries and epsilon are encoded as integer numerators and positive integer denominators. Singular matrices and D=0 are included, in which case the event requires Z=0. No rank bound, commutativity, or lower bound on positive eigenvalues is promised.

context_blocks.text: For diagonal positive semidefinite inputs this coefficient is a nonnegative permanent. The general case therefore extends a central approximate-counting success to matrices without a common diagonal structure.

The mixed discriminant also controls constrained determinantal sampling. The cited works distinguish exponential multiplicative approximation from an FPRAS; the latter requires arbitrarily small relative error in polynomial time.

cards.title: #BIS-easiness of Boolean log-supermodular counting CSPs
cards.formal: For every fixed finite family F of functions \(f:\{0,1\}^{r_{f}}\to \mathbb{Q} _{\ge 0}\) satisfying \(f(x\lor y)f(x\land y)\ge f(x)f(y)\) for all x,y, is #\(\mathrm{CSP}(F)\) approximation-preserving reducible to #BIS?
cards.definitions: Arity \(r_{f}\) is a nonnegative integer fixed with \(f; \lor\) and ∧ act coordinatewise. A #\(\mathrm{CSP}(F)\) instance consists of finitely many Boolean variables and a list of constraints, each naming a function in F and an ordered tuple of variables of its arity; repeats in a tuple are permitted. Its value Z is the sum over all Boolean assignments of the product of all constraint values. Function tables are fixed nonnegative rationals, not part of the instance. #BIS counts all independent vertex sets of a finite simple bipartite graph. An approximation-preserving reduction is a randomized oracle algorithm which, on an instance I and rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), returns a relative \((1\pm \varepsilon )\) estimate of Z with probability at least \(3/4\) using time polynomial in |I| and \(1/\varepsilon\). Its oracle calls request relative approximations to #BIS with inverse tolerances polynomially bounded in |I| and \(1/\varepsilon\). Oracle failure probabilities may be reduced to an inverse polynomial by independent repetitions; the reduction’s overall correctness guarantee includes them. If \(Z=0, a\) valid relative estimate is exactly zero. Reduction polynomials may depend on the fixed family F. The oracle is an approximation oracle, not exact counting.

context_blocks.text: Exact finite-domain counting CSPs already have major dichotomy theorems. Approximate counting has a different landscape, and log-supermodularity is one of its central boundaries. This question asks whether that whole Boolean region reduces to the benchmark problem #BIS.

Some log-supermodular functions cannot be represented by the standard implication-and-unary gadgets. That algebraic obstruction does not refute an approximation-preserving reduction, which is a more general notion. The target is this computational gap, not a claim that every counting problem has an established three-way classification.

cards.title: Treewidth classification of approximate counting CSP
cards.formal: Assume that parameterized Clique has no randomized fixed-parameter algorithm with bounded error. For every fixed recursively enumerable class C of finite relational structures with a uniform bound on relation arity, are the following equivalent: (1) counting homomorphisms \(A\to B\) for \(A\in C\) and arbitrary compatible B is exactly solvable in polynomial time; (2) this problem admits a fully polynomial randomized approximation scheme; (3) it admits a fixed-parameter randomized approximation scheme with parameter \(\Vert A\Vert\); and (4) the Gaifman graphs of structures in C have bounded treewidth? The missing implication is \((3)\Rightarrow (4)\). No fan-grid containment, minor closure or other closure property is assumed for C. This is the source’s Theorem 3 with its fan-class hypothesis removed.
cards.why: Would determine whether approximation enlarges the tractable classes of structurally restricted counting CSPs, and whether treewidth remains the complete structural criterion.

cards.definitions: A finite relational signature \(\tau\) is a finite collection of relation symbols, each with a specified nonnegative integer arity. A finite \(\tau\)-structure A consists of a finite universe \(V(A)\) and, for every r-ary \(R\in \tau , a\) set \(R^{A}\subseteq V(A)\)ʳ. Input structures A and B share \(\tau\), but \(\tau\) may vary between instances. Every arity is at most a constant \(r_{C}\) fixed for the class C. Universes, symbols, arities and relation tuples are explicitly listed in a standard binary encoding; \(\Vert A\Vert\) denotes its length, and similarly for B. Nullary relations, if present, are either empty or contain the empty tuple and are checked in the same way as other relations. A homomorphism is any function \(h:V(A)\to V(B)\) such that for each relation tuple \((a_{1},\ldots ,a_{r})\in R^{A}\), the tuple \((h(a_{1}),\ldots ,h(a_{r}))\) belongs to \(R^{B}\). It need not be injective or surjective. Count all such functions, including zero when none exists. C is fixed before the input and can be enumerated by a Turing machine; a promised input has \(A\in C\), and an algorithm need not decide membership in C. The Gaifman graph \(G(A)\) has universe \(V(A)\) as vertices and joins distinct elements occurring together in some relation tuple. A tree decomposition assigns vertex bags to a tree so that every vertex is in a bag, every edge has both ends in a bag, and bags containing a given vertex form a connected subtree. Its width is the largest bag size minus one; treewidth is the minimum width, with empty graph assigned width zero here. Bounded treewidth of C means one constant w works for every \(A\in C\). It refers to A itself, not to a homomorphically equivalent core. An approximation scheme receives A,B and a rational \(0<\varepsilon <1\) and outputs an integer random variable X satisfying \(\Pr [|X- H|\le \varepsilon H]\ge 3/4\), where H is the homomorphism count. In particular it must output zero with that probability when \(H=0\). Probability is over internal fair random bits. An FPRAS uses time polynomial in \(\Vert A\Vert +\Vert B\Vert +\varepsilon ^{- 1}\); an FPTRAS uses \(f(\Vert A\Vert )\cdot (\Vert A\Vert +\Vert B\Vert +\varepsilon ^{- 1})^{a}\) for a computable f and constant a. Reading the rational accuracy encoding is included. These are worst-case time bounds, and a,f and the algorithm may depend on fixed C but not on individual input structures. The hypothesis means that no uniform randomized algorithm decides whether an N-vertex graph has a k-clique in \(g(k)N^{b}\) time for computable g and constant b, with error at most \(1/4\) on every instance. This states explicitly the randomized parameterized separation used in the source.
cards.answer_criterion: Under the stated parameterized complexity hypothesis, prove the equivalence for every eligible class C, or refute it by a recursively enumerable bounded-arity class of unbounded Gaifman treewidth with an FPTRAS for its homomorphism-counting problem. The other implications are already known. An exact-counting hardness result, a theorem only for minor-closed or fan classes, or a classification with the right-hand structure fixed does not establish the missing unrestricted implication.

cards.title: Decision versus approximate counting for fixed-width SAT
cards.formal: For every fixed clause width \(k\geq3\), do randomized decision \(k\)-SAT and randomized multiplicative approximation of \(\#k\)-SAT have the same optimal exponential running-time rate in the number of variables? With \(d_k\) and \(a_k\) defined below, the target is \(a_k=d_k\) for every fixed \(k\geq3\). This makes “close the gap” precise at the exponential-rate level, as in the later source’s fixed-width question.
cards.why: Tests whether estimating the number of satisfying assignments intrinsically requires more exponential work than finding out whether any exist. Equality would transfer the leading exponential savings in fixed-width SAT to a broader counting task.

references.title: An Approximation Algorithm for #k-SAT
references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 9; PDF page 9

cards.definitions:
An input is a Boolean CNF formula \(F\) on an explicitly declared set of \(n\) variables, with at most \(k\) literals in each clause. A literal is a variable or its negation. Let \(N(F)\) be the number of assignments to all declared variables satisfying every clause. Variables absent from clauses still contribute their two possible values. There is no promise of satisfiability or sparsity.

Decision asks whether \(N(F)>0\). Approximate counting receives a rational accuracy parameter \(0<\varepsilon<1/2\) and must output a nonnegative binary-encoded rational \(Z\) such that
\[
(1-\varepsilon)N(F)\leq Z\leq(1+\varepsilon)N(F)
\]
with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input. When \(N(F)=0\), a successful output is exactly zero. Probability is over algorithmic randomness. Decision also has success probability at least \(2/3\), allowing two-sided error.

Use ordinary classical randomized algorithms and worst-case bit-operation running time, over both inputs and random tapes. Let \(L\) be total input bit length, including the formula and, for approximate counting, the rational accuracy. Define \(d_k\) as the infimum of \(\alpha\geq0\) for which decision has time \(O(2^{\alpha n}L^C)\) for some fixed \(C\). Define \(a_k\) as the infimum of \(\alpha\geq0\) for which an approximation scheme has time \(O(2^{\alpha n}(L+\varepsilon^{-1})^C)\) for some fixed \(C\), for every admissible accuracy. The algorithm, polynomial exponent and hidden constants may depend on the fixed \(k\) and \(\alpha\), but not on the input or accuracy.

The infima need not be attained. Equality asks that every exponential decision rate can be matched for approximation with any arbitrarily small positive addition to that rate and polynomial dependence on inverse accuracy. It does not demand a single optimal algorithm at an unattained infimum, identical polynomial factors, or an effective compiler transforming all decision programs.

Already \(d_k\leq a_k\): a constant-relative-error estimate distinguishes zero from a positive count. The unresolved direction compares approximation with decision at the same fixed clause width. Taking a supremum or a limit over all widths is a different statement. A reduction whose decision queries add parity constraints or increase clause width must account for their cost before it can establish this comparison. The source uses an \(e^\varepsilon\) multiplicative convention; changing to the displayed relative-error convention only rescales accuracy by constant factors in this range.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove equality of the two defined infimum rates for every fixed integer width at least three, or prove a strict separation for at least one such width. A reduction preserving the width and adding arbitrarily small exponential overhead would suffice for equality. Improved individual upper bounds, a result only as width tends to infinity, or hardness for exact counting alone does not settle this comparison.

context_blocks.title: Approximation improved before the gap closed
context_blocks.text: Thurley obtains a randomized approximation scheme substantially faster than the exact counting bounds cited in 2012. Schmitt and Wanka later improve the three-literal upper bound to \(O(\varepsilon^{-2}1.51426^n)\). These are historical upper bounds, not claims about the optimal rates or the latest decision record.

context_blocks.title: Later reductions preserve all-width savings
context_blocks.text: Dell and Lapinskas show that a common exponential saving for decision at every constant width transfers to approximate counting with arbitrarily small loss. Their Theorem 8 therefore matches the all-width saving, but its hypothesis is stronger than having a fast algorithm at one selected width.

It also relates subexponential decision and approximation, without settling each fixed positive exponential rate.

cards.title: Hadwiger’s conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(t\ge 1\) and every finite nonempty simple undirected graph G, does \(\chi (G)\ge t\) imply that G contains \(K_{t}\) as a graph minor? Equivalently, is every \(K_{t}\)-minor-free graph \((t- 1)\)-colorable?
cards.definitions: A simple graph has no loops or parallel edges. A proper coloring assigns colors to vertices so that adjacent vertices receive different colors; \(\chi (G)\) is the minimum number of colors. \(K_{t}\) is the complete graph on t vertices. A \(K_{t}\) minor is witnessed by t pairwise disjoint nonempty vertex sets \(B_{1},\ldots ,B_{t}\) such that each induced subgraph \(G[B_{i}]\) is connected and every pair \(B_{i},B_{j}\) has at least one edge between it. These branch sets can be contracted and all unwanted vertices or edges deleted. They may have arbitrary sizes; the minor need not be induced and no parity condition is imposed. Equivalently, the Hadwiger number \(h(G)\), the largest t for which G has a \(K_{t}\) minor, must satisfy \(h(G)\ge \chi (G)\). The statement concerns existence, with no running-time requirement on finding the coloring or branch sets.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A flagship structural graph problem connecting coloring, contractions, and excluded-minor classes. A resolution would identify the exact universal coloring obstruction in every minor-closed setting; improvements also develop structural tools relevant to graph algorithms and approximation.

importance.reason: One of the central graph-theoretic conjectures, with an exact extremal target and consequences across coloring and minor structure.

progress.text: Hadwiger proposes the relation between chromatic number and complete graph minors; the current preprint restates the original assertion.

Kostochka and Thomason establish the asymptotically sharp average-degree threshold yielding \(O(t\sqrt{\log  t})\) colors; sharpness of this density method does not give a matching chromatic lower bound.
Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas prove the \(K_{6}\)-minor case using the Four-Color Theorem.
Delcourt and Postle prove \(O(t \log  \log  t)\) coloring and their reduction to small graphs. The preprint began in 2021 and the journal version appeared in 2025.
Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner, and Wigderson disprove the stronger odd-minor version, leaving ordinary Hadwiger open.

Version 2 of Liu and Luo’s preprint claims an absolute-C upper bound \(\chi (G)\le Ct \log  \log  \log  t\) for every \(K_{t}\)-minor-free graph and \(t\ge 16\) (Theorem 1.1). This does not reach \(\chi (G)\le t- 1\).

references.title: Disproof of the Odd Hadwiger Conjecture
references.authors: Marcus Kühn; Lisa Sauermann; Raphael Steiner; Yuval Wigderson
references.locator: 23 December 2025 preprint; ordinary formulation in Conjecture 1.1, odd-minor definition, and Theorem 1.3

cards.status_note: Ordinary Hadwiger remains explicitly open in the 9 September 2026 preprint; checked through 10 September 2026. The new triple-logarithmic upper bound is a preprint claim. The December 2025 disproof concerns the stronger odd-minor conjecture.

context_blocks.text: A graph can have very few large complete subgraphs and still need many colors. Hadwiger asks whether contracting connected pieces always reveals a complete graph as large as the number of colors originally needed. This would make a global obstruction to coloring visible through a precise structural certificate: disjoint connected regions linked in every pair. The complete graph \(K_{t- 1}\) shows that the proposed upper bound for \(K_{t}\)-minor-free graphs cannot be reduced.

The conjecture encompasses the Four-Color Theorem because planar graphs exclude \(K_{5}\) minors. Wagner’s structure theorem makes the \(t=5\) case equivalent to four-colorability of planar graphs. Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas extended this equivalence to \(t=6\) by proving that a minimal counterexample in that case would be apex: deleting one vertex leaves a planar graph. Thus the known exact cases extend through \(K_{6}\) minors; the first unresolved case is \(t=7\).

The earlier general approach forced clique minors from high average degree. The resulting \(O(t\sqrt{\log  t})\) degeneracy bound gives a coloring bound of the same order by repeatedly removing a low-degree vertex and coloring in reverse. That density threshold is sharp, so simply improving its numerical constant cannot yield Hadwiger’s linear target. The chromatic-number question requires using structure beyond this degree argument.

Delcourt and Postle obtain \(O(t \log  \log  t)\) colors through a reduction to coloring much smaller minor-free subgraphs, on roughly t times a polylogarithmic number of vertices. Their reduction also shows that proving a linear bound on these small graphs would imply a linear bound without a size restriction. It narrows where a genuinely new coloring argument is needed, without imposing the small-size hypothesis on the conjecture itself.

Liu and Luo’s September 2026 preprint builds on that reduction and claims \(O(t \log  \log  \log  t)\). Its proof combines contractions that reduce degeneracy with fractional colorings, which distribute weight across independent sets. Even this extra logarithm removed leaves both the \(O(t)\) weakening and the sharp coefficient in the original conjecture unresolved. The result is recorded as a new preprint claim, not as an independently verified proof.

An odd clique minor imposes additional compatibility conditions on two-colorings inside its branch trees. Kühn, Sauermann, Steiner, and Wigderson construct graphs with no odd \(K_{t}\) minor and chromatic number approximately 1.5t, disproving the odd Hadwiger conjecture. Their graphs are not counterexamples to the ordinary-minor assertion asked here: forbidding odd minors permits more graphs than forbidding all clique minors.

cards.title: Deterministic linear-time minimum spanning tree
cards.formal: Is there one deterministic comparison-based algorithm that, on every connected simple undirected graph with n vertices, m edges and arbitrary real edge weights, outputs a minimum spanning tree in \(O(m+n)\) worst-case time in the comparison RAM model below?
cards.definitions: The graph is explicitly supplied as vertex and edge records, with vertices numbered \(1,\ldots ,n\) and edges given distinct identifiers. An edge record contains its two endpoints and a weight key representing an arbitrary real number. A spanning tree is a set T of \(n- 1\) edges connecting all vertices without a cycle; it is minimum when \(\sum_{e\in T}w(e)\) is smallest among all spanning trees. For \(n=1\) the output is empty. Equal and negative weights are permitted, and any minimum tree is acceptable. Weight keys may be copied and compared, but their bit representations cannot be inspected, and arithmetic on their numerical values is unavailable. Each comparison has unit cost. Nonweight data, addresses and indices use \(O(\log (m+n+2))\)-bit words on a random-access machine, with unit-cost reads, writes, comparisons, standard word arithmetic, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts; arithmetic is restricted to these words. All ordinary operations count in the running time, not just weight comparisons. The algorithm has a fixed finite description and no input-length-dependent advice or free precomputed tables. Any tables it constructs, as well as writing the output, are charged to its time. The hidden linear-time constant must be independent of graph topology, n,m and the weights. This fixes a conventional uniform sequential comparison model. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central unresolved boundary between deterministic and randomized algorithms for a classical graph optimization problem, and a rare case where a provably optimal algorithm exists before its exact asymptotic complexity is understood.

importance.reason: A foundational graph-algorithm question about the necessity of randomness and the relationship between comparison complexity and actual computation.

progress.text: Fredman–Willard obtain deterministic linear time in a stronger integer-word model.
Karger–Klein–Tarjan obtain randomized linear time for arbitrary comparison weights.
Chazelle achieves deterministic \(O(m\alpha (m,n))\) comparison-based time.
Pettie–Ramachandran match the optimal decision-tree complexity with a uniform deterministic algorithm, without determining that complexity.
Pettie–Ramachandran develop alternative randomized MST algorithms using far fewer random bits; complete deterministic linear time remains unresolved.

cards.status_note: The deterministic linear-time comparison problem remains open in the primary-author material checked through 11 September 2026. Integer-word algorithms, high-girth results and the optimal-decision-tree theorem do not settle this formulation.

context_blocks.text: A minimum spanning tree connects a graph as cheaply as possible without redundant cycles. It is among the basic examples where a local greedy rule produces a global optimum, and it appears in network design and clustering. The optimization objective is well understood; the unsettled issue is how much computation is fundamentally needed to identify the right \(n- 1\) edges when the input already contains m edge records.

Sorting every edge is sufficient for Kruskal’s algorithm, but sorting is a stronger task than the required output. On a graph that is itself a tree, every edge belongs to the answer regardless of their relative weights. On a triangle, only the identity of a largest-weight edge is needed: discard it. Thus the familiar comparison lower bound for sorting all keys does not automatically become a lower bound for finding an MST. A faster algorithm must exploit the graph’s structure to avoid unnecessary ordering information.

The cut and cycle rules make this possible. A lightest edge across a cut can be selected safely, and a strictly heaviest edge on a cycle can be discarded. Equal weights can be handled consistently by comparing pairs consisting of the weight and the edge identifier. These rules avoid numerical arithmetic on weights, so the problem is meaningful for arbitrary real keys even though the objective is expressed as a sum.

Karger, Klein and Tarjan combine random sampling with linear-time MST verification to obtain a Las Vegas algorithm with expected \(O(m+n)\) running time. It always returns a correct tree; randomness controls the work spent on recursive filtering. The target here is a deterministic guarantee for every input, so fixing an arbitrary random seed does not inherit the expected-time theorem.

Chazelle’s deterministic algorithm achieves \(O(m\alpha (m,n))\) time, where \(\alpha\) is a slowly growing inverse-Ackermann function. Its soft-heap machinery deliberately permits a controlled set of key increases inside an auxiliary data structure while the surrounding algorithm preserves the exact MST answer. The extra factor is tiny for practical input sizes, yet unbounded asymptotically. Removing it asks for an exact structural understanding of the problem’s complexity, not merely an implementation improvement.

Pettie and Ramachandran establish a different kind of optimality: total algorithmic running time can match, within a constant factor, the optimal worst-case number of edge comparisons for MST. Their algorithm is uniform; it constructs the small optimal decision trees it needs within the time analysis. But the asymptotic size of that optimum is itself unknown. Consequently a proof that linear-size comparison decision trees always suffice would settle the algorithmic question through their theorem.

The graph family also matters. Eisenstat and coauthors show that it is enough to solve graphs with at most \(3n/2\) edges, and separately relate the general problem to graphs with any fixed lower bound on girth, the length of a shortest cycle. Their available high-girth algorithm requires a lower bound that grows with n. That difference between a fixed girth threshold and a slowly growing threshold leaves the general deterministic question open.

Changing the access model can remove the obstacle. Fredman and Willard give a deterministic linear-time algorithm using integer-word operations on the weights. That theorem can exploit their binary representation, which the real-key comparison model deliberately withholds. Similarly, an algorithm that is fast for a random graph topology has an average-instance guarantee, even if the algorithm itself is deterministic; it does not bound the work on every graph.

The remaining challenge can therefore be stated without ambiguity: retain exactness, arbitrary real-key weights and all graph topologies, and make every part of the computation linear without random choices. A negative answer would be equally significant, by establishing an intrinsic cost for deterministic comparison-based optimization that expected-time random sampling avoids.

cards.title: Erdős–Hajnal conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite undirected simple graph H with at least two vertices, does there exist a real constant \(c(H)>0\) such that every n-vertex undirected simple graph G with \(n\ge 1\) and no induced copy of H satisfies \(\max \{\alpha (G),\omega (G)\}\ge n^{c(H)}\)?
cards.definitions: An induced copy of H is an injective map \(f:V(H)\to V(G)\) such that distinct u,v are adjacent in H if and only if \(f(u),f(v)\) are adjacent in G. Thus both edges and nonedges must match. \(\alpha (G)\) is the maximum size of a set of pairwise nonadjacent vertices, and \(\omega (G)\) is the maximum size of a set of pairwise adjacent vertices. The constant \(c(H)\) may depend arbitrarily on the entire fixed graph H, but not on G or n. No density, degree, dimension or algorithmic promise is imposed on G. The claim concerns existence of a clique or independent set, without requiring a polynomial-time construction. A hereditary graph class is one closed under taking induced subgraphs; the class of H-free graphs is hereditary.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A foundational prediction that forbidding any fixed induced pattern forces polynomial-size order inside a graph. Its links to hereditary classes, neighborhood complexity and sparse/dense decompositions make it a central structural question with connections to algorithmic graph theory.

importance.reason: A major unifying conjecture for hereditary graph classes, with a sharp qualitative gap between general bounds and the target and substantial recent progress on special cases.

progress.text: Erdős–Hajnal’s Ramsey-type theorems establish \(\exp (c_{H}\sqrt{\log  n})\) and pose the polynomial target.
Bucić–Nguyen–Scott–Seymour improve the general bound by \(a \sqrt{\log  \log  n}\) factor in the exponent.
Bucić–Fox–Pham prove equivalence with polynomial Rödl and Nikiforov formulations.
The five-vertex-path theorem is published, completing the property for all forbidden graphs with at most five vertices; the preprint first appeared in December 2023.
Sun–Wang–Zeng sharpen the exponent for graphs of bounded VC-dimension, an additional restriction on the input graphs.
Tran–Nguyen post a proof for the six-vertex graph with edge set \(\{ab,bc,cd,de,af,bf,df\}\).
Huang–Ju–Zhou revise their E-graph and Bird proofs and unified sparsification framework.

context_blocks.text: Ramsey’s theorem guarantees a clique or independent set of logarithmic size in every sufficiently large graph, and random graphs show that this order of magnitude is unavoidable without further restrictions. Erdős–Hajnal predicts a dramatic change after forbidding even one fixed induced pattern: the guaranteed set should grow as a positive power of the number of vertices. The conjecture therefore asks how much global organization a single local structural exclusion forces.

For a simple example, a graph with no induced three-vertex path is a disjoint union of cliques. If it has t components, choosing one vertex from each gives an independent set of size t, while the largest component has at least \(n/t\) vertices and is a clique. One of these sets has size at least \(\sqrt{n}\). This proves the conjecture for that forbidden graph and illustrates the desired polynomial gain through a structural decomposition.

The general theorem of Erdős and Hajnal gives a lower bound \(\exp (c_{H}\sqrt{\log  n})\). Bucić, Nguyen, Scott and Seymour improve it to \(\exp (c_{H}\sqrt{\log  n\cdot \log  \log  n})\) for a positive constant depending on H. Their 2024 journal paper is the first improvement of this general bound. It is still smaller than nᵟ for every fixed \(\delta >0\) as n grows, so the extra logarithmic factor does not reach the conjectured scale.

Closure under complementation and vertex substitution lets proofs for a few building blocks settle many further forbidden graphs. Substitution replaces one vertex by a graph whose vertices all have the same neighbors outside the replacement. The remaining five-vertex building blocks were the bull, the five-cycle and the five-vertex path, together with its complement. Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s proof for the path, published in March 2026, completes all forbidden graphs on at most five vertices.

For longer fixed paths, their separate all-path theorem gives homogeneous sets of size \(2^{(\log  n)^{1- o(1)}}\). This is close to the polynomial scale in its exponent but still does not assert \(n^{c}\) for any fixed positive c. In particular, the five-vertex result should not be described as resolving the conjecture for paths of arbitrary length.

Huang, Ju and Zhou’s August 2026 revision proves two additional six-vertex cases using an extension of iterative sparsification. The E-graph is a five-vertex path with a new leaf attached to its middle vertex. The Bird starts from a triangle with leaves attached to two different triangle vertices, then extends one of those leaves by one more edge. Both contain an induced five-vertex path, so excluding either permits a larger class than excluding the path itself.

A 28 August 2026 preprint by Tran and Nguyen reports another six-vertex case, specified without a drawing by vertex set \(\{a,b,c,d,e,f\}\) and edge set \(\{ab,bc,cd,de,af,bf,df\}\). It develops the comb and sparsification framework further. This is an individual new forbidden pattern, rather than a proof for every six-vertex graph.

Another strand connects the conjecture with finding large nearly empty or nearly complete induced subgraphs. Bucić, Fox and Pham prove equivalence with polynomial quantitative versions of the Rödl and Nikiforov statements. This makes the problem relevant to structural decompositions and induced-pattern density, beyond locating a single clique or independent set.

There are also stronger quantitative results under additional hypotheses. Sun, Wang and Zeng’s July 2026 preprint gives exponent at least \((Cd)^{- d}\) for graphs of neighborhood VC-dimension at most d. This dimension bounds the size of a vertex set on which neighborhoods realize every possible subset. Such a restriction controls neighborhood complexity; arbitrary H-free graphs are not assumed to satisfy a fixed VC-dimension bound.

cards.title: Reed’s conjecture
cards.formal: Does every nonempty finite simple undirected graph G satisfy \(\chi (G)\le \lceil (\Delta (G)+1+\omega (G))/2\rceil\)?
cards.definitions: A graph is simple when it has neither loops nor parallel edges. A proper k-colouring is a map from \(V(G)\) to \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\) assigning different colours to endpoints of every edge; \(\chi (G)\) is the minimum such k. The degree of a vertex is its number of neighbours, and \(\Delta (G)\) is the maximum degree. A clique is a vertex set whose distinct vertices are all adjacent, and \(\omega (G)\) is its largest possible size. The ceiling \(\lceil x\rceil\) is the least integer at least x. The statement concerns all such graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices. For an edgeless nonempty graph, \(\chi =\omega =1\) and \(\Delta =0\). The empty graph can be included with \(\chi =\omega =\Delta =0\), without changing the question. There are no restrictions on graph size, maximum degree, forbidden subgraphs or the method used to obtain a colouring.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated inequality for every finite simple graph, or give a finite graph and a proof that its chromatic number exceeds the displayed ceiling. The target is an existence theorem, so a polynomial-time colouring algorithm is not required. An asymptotic bound with an additive error, a convex combination with clique coefficient less than \(1/2\), or a theorem restricted to sufficiently large maximum degree is partial progress unless the remaining cases are also covered.
cards.why: A central structural colouring problem with an exact, best-possible target. It asks how much the absence of a large clique must reduce the number of colours, and guides probabilistic, structural and algorithmic approaches to colouring.

importance.reason: A defining universal conjecture linking three basic graph parameters, with sharp examples and broad influence on colouring theory and its algorithmic methods.

progress.text: Reed proposes the half-average bound and proves an interpolation with some universal \(\varepsilon >0\).

De Meyer and coauthors develop a distinct Kempe-recolouring analogue with additional reconfiguration obstructions.
The revised digraph analogue retains the undirected exact inequality as Conjecture 1.1 and proves only a positive-\(\varepsilon\) generalization.
