cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The September 8 primary revision explicitly retains the exact undirected inequality as open. Small-clique estimates, sufficiently-large-degree interpolation bounds, and the recolouring and directed variants do not settle the full statement. The published 0.119 bound’s stated dependency is preserved in the context.

context_blocks.text: Two elementary bounds frame graph colouring. A clique needs a distinct colour for every vertex, so \(\chi \ge \omega\). On the other hand, greedily colouring vertices in any order uses at most \(\Delta +1\) colours: at most \(\Delta\) colours are forbidden by already coloured neighbours. Reed asks whether an upper bound halfway between these two numbers always suffices, after rounding up. This would sharply connect a local obstruction, the size of a clique, to the global task of partitioning all vertices into independent sets.

The rounding is essential even for a five-cycle. It has maximum degree two and clique number two, but it needs three colours because an odd cycle is not bipartite. The unrounded average is \(5/2\). Complete graphs also meet the proposed upper bound exactly. These examples show that the question is about a precise universal inequality, rather than merely reducing the leading constant in a loose estimate.

There is also a useful family explaining the coefficient \(1/2\). Replace each vertex of a five-cycle by a clique of size t, joining every vertex of two replacement cliques whenever their cycle vertices were adjacent. The resulting graph has 5t vertices, maximum degree \(3t- 1\) and clique number 2t. An independent set contains at most two vertices, so at least \(\lceil 5t/2\rceil\) colours are necessary. A universal bound \(\lceil (1- \varepsilon )(\Delta +1)+\varepsilon \omega \rceil\) with \(\varepsilon >1/2\) would give fewer colours for large t. Thus the conjectured interpolation coefficient cannot be increased.

Reed established a weaker universal interpolation with some fixed positive coefficient \(\varepsilon\) in place of \(1/2\). This already gives a saving proportional to the gap between maximum degree and clique number. Proving such a saving is difficult because high degree need not mean that a neighbourhood resembles a clique, and local savings must coexist across many overlapping neighbourhoods.

Hurley, de Joannis de Verclos and Kang report \(\varepsilon =0.119\) for sufficiently large maximum degree, using a refined random colouring procedure and local sparsity estimates. Their published paper explicitly records a dependency: the 0.119 calculation uses a then-unreviewed result of Delcourt and Postle. Remark 3.1 gives \(\varepsilon =0.113\) using an alternative published ingredient. The September 2026 digraph paper continues to cite the 0.119 bound. Both constants remain far below the conjectured \(1/2\).

A different advance handles graphs with much smaller cliques. Bonamy, Kelly, Nelson and Postle bound the chromatic number by \(O(\Delta \sqrt{\log  \omega /\log  \Delta})\), with related list and correspondence colouring results. For suitable relations between \(\omega\) and \(\Delta\) this is much stronger than a small fixed improvement on the greedy bound. It does not prove the desired average bound across the full range of clique sizes.

Recent related work also changes the task. The 2025 recolouring paper studies whether proper colourings can be connected by Kempe changes: swap two colours on a connected component induced by those colours. Its general conjectured interpolation coefficient is \(1/3\) because reconfiguration has obstructions beyond the existence of one colouring. Its positive results on odd-hole-free graphs therefore need to be read in that separate model.

Kawarabayashi and Picasarri-Arrieta extend the framework to directed graphs, where each colour class must induce an acyclic digraph. Their SODA 2025 work, revised in September 2026, proves a positive-\(\varepsilon\) interpolation and proposes the exact half-average analogue. Replacing each undirected edge by arcs in both directions recovers ordinary colouring, so the proposed directed statement would imply Reed’s conjecture. The directed partial theorem does not supply the missing coefficient.

cards.title: Graph isomorphism in polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist one deterministic classical algorithm that, for every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G and H given by explicit adjacency matrices, decides whether G and H are isomorphic in time polynomial in the total input length?
cards.definitions: Two graphs on equally many vertices are isomorphic if a bijection of their vertex sets preserves adjacency in both directions. The input contains the complete graph descriptions; unequal vertex counts are rejected immediately. The algorithm must be uniform, deterministic and correct on every graph pair, with no promise of bounded degree, rigidity, expansion, or random input. Polynomial time is measured in the binary input length, so the \(\Theta (n^{2})\) adjacency data may be read in full. The question concerns ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism, not quantum isomorphism, graph canonization under a different output requirement, or isomorphism of groups or tensors. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Tests whether the central equivalence problem for finite combinatorial structures can be recognized in deterministic polynomial time after the quasipolynomial barrier was broken.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved problem at the intersection of algorithms, permutation groups and complexity theory, with a precise best-known general upper bound.

context_blocks.text: Graph isomorphism asks whether two finite graphs differ only by a relabelling of their vertices. A proposed relabelling is easy to verify, so the problem lies in NP, but ruling out all relabellings can be difficult for highly symmetric graphs.

Many special cases have polynomial-time algorithms, including bounded-degree graphs and several classes with strong structural restrictions. These results do not automatically combine into an algorithm for arbitrary graphs, whose automorphism groups can have a much richer structure.

Babai’s breakthrough gives a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with running time \(\exp ((\log  n)^{O(1)})\), improving the earlier subexponential bound. Quasipolynomial time is still asymptotically larger than every fixed polynomial, so the final gap to P remains exactly the question on this card.

Graph canonization is closely related: producing a canonical labelled representative is at least as demanding as deciding isomorphism in many standard reductions, but a theorem about one output formulation must preserve the required runtime and uniformity before it answers the decision problem. Quantum graph-isomorphism relations and BQP algorithms likewise concern different computational problems.

No general polynomial-time algorithm or unconditional lower bound excluding one was found in the checked literature through 11 September 2026. The problem remains a clean benchmark for the boundary between efficiently verifiable symmetry and efficient recognition of symmetry.

The introductory discussion in Butti and Dalmau's 2021 paper also poses polynomial-time graph isomorphism. The reference places the general question in the context of fractional homomorphisms, Weisfeiler–Leman invariance and Sherali–Adams hierarchies; the saved passage does not select a separate conjecture about one hierarchy.

cards.title: Tutte’s 5-flow conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless undirected multigraph G admit an orientation of every edge and an assignment \(f:E(G)\to \{1,2,3,4\}\) such that, at each vertex, the sum of f on incoming edges equals the sum on outgoing edges as integers?
cards.definitions: A finite loopless undirected multigraph consists of a finite vertex set and a finite set of distinct edge identities, each with two different endpoints. Several edges may have the same endpoint pair. An edge is a bridge if deleting that edge increases the number of connected components. Bridgeless means there are no such edges; disconnected graphs and isolated vertices are allowed. An orientation chooses a tail and head for each edge independently. At vertex v, integer flow conservation is \(\Sigma\)_{\(e:head(e)=v\)}\(f(e)=\Sigma\)_{\(e:tail(e)=v\)}\(f(e)\), with empty sums zero. A nowhere-zero k-flow is such an orientation and assignment with values \(1,\ldots ,k- 1\). The statement is an existence assertion, not a bound on construction time, and does not impose an embedding or a vertex-degree bound.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
cards.why: Determine whether four nonzero integral flow values suffice for every graph with the necessary bridgelessness condition.

importance.reason: A defining flow-existence conjecture with consequences for graph decompositions, orientations and directed-cut packing.

context_blocks.text: A nowhere-zero flow circulates a nonzero amount through every edge without accumulating anything at a vertex. Bridges prevent such circulation, so bridgelessness is a necessary condition.

The established 6-flow theorem proves that five positive integer values suffice. Tutte asks whether the palette can always be reduced to four. The orientation is part of the witness, so negative values in a fixed orientation are represented by reversing edges.

The 2025 work exhibits a quantitative connection between flow existence and disjoint sets meeting directed cuts. This gives the conjecture an algorithmic and optimization role beyond the existence of an edge labeling.

sentences: Tutte’s conjecture asks for a nowhere-zero 5-flow in every bridgeless graph.
Each edge receives a direction and an integer from one to four.
At every vertex the incoming and outgoing totals must agree.
Parallel edges are allowed and are treated as distinct edges.
The claim would sharpen the universal 6-flow theorem and strengthen a central graph-decomposition principle.

cards.title: Almost-linear-time exact maximum matching in general graphs
cards.formal: Is there one randomized sequential algorithm that, on every explicitly represented finite simple undirected graph G with n vertices and m edges, outputs an exact maximum-cardinality matching with probability at least \(2/3\) and has expected running time \((n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}\) in the word-RAM model below?
cards.definitions: A matching \(M\subseteq E(G)\) is a set of edges no two of which share an endpoint. Its size is |M|, and \(\nu (G)=\max\){|M|:M is a matching in G}. The algorithm must output valid edge identifiers forming a matching on every terminating execution, and |\(M|=\nu (G)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on each input. It must terminate with probability one. Vertices are labelled \(1,\ldots ,n\) and the input is an adjacency-list or edge-list representation of size \(O(n+m)\); isolated vertices are included in n. Put \(N=n+m+2\). Use a random-access machine with \(\Theta (\log  N)\)-bit words, supporting constant-cost reads, writes, comparisons, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations and shifts on words, and fresh uniform random words. Intermediate larger integers require multiple words and their processing is charged. Preprocessing and output writing are included. The program is uniform, with no advice or free precomputed tables. The time statement means that this same algorithm satisfies: for every real \(\varepsilon >0\) there are constants \(C\varepsilon\) and \(N\varepsilon\) such that for every input with \(N\ge N\varepsilon\), its expected number of operations is at most \(C\varepsilon  N^{1+\varepsilon}\). The expectation is over its own random choices, not a distribution on graph inputs. No edge weights, degree restriction, bipartiteness promise, approximation slack or auxiliary communication model is assumed. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A major remaining exact graph-optimization problem beyond the almost-linear flow framework. It asks whether odd-cycle and blossom structure impose a real asymptotic cost, even when randomization is allowed.

importance.reason: A core combinatorial optimization primitive with a large gap between general graphs and the fast bipartite case, connecting augmenting paths, polyhedral methods and algebraic algorithms.

context_blocks.text: Maximum matching is a basic model of pairing compatible objects while using each object at most once. General graphs allow compatibility patterns that cannot be separated into two sides. Edmonds’ blossom method established that this optimization is polynomial-time solvable. The remaining question is how close its exact computational cost can come to the size of the graph that must be read.

Maximum and maximal have different meanings. A maximal matching merely cannot be extended by adding a single edge. On a four-vertex path, the middle edge alone is maximal, while the two outside edges form a maximum matching of size two. A greedy linear-time procedure can therefore solve maximal matching and still fail the exact task on a tiny input. The card requires the global optimum, with no allowed loss of even one matched pair.

Alternating paths explain how a nonmaximum matching can improve. Such a path alternates edges outside and inside the matching and starts and ends at unmatched vertices. Flipping its edge membership increases the matching size by one. In general graphs, odd cycles complicate the search for shortest augmenting paths; contracted structures called blossoms keep track of these possibilities. Micali and Vazirani’s classical algorithm achieves \(O(m\sqrt{n})\) time, with later work developing its proof and presentation.

Bipartite graphs have a particularly effective flow formulation. Direct each edge from the left side to the right, join a source to left vertices and right vertices to a sink, and give every edge capacity one. Integral maximum flow gives a maximum matching. Almost-linear exact flow algorithms therefore solve bipartite matching within the desired time scale. There is no supplied bipartition in the present question, and the same construction does not automatically encode odd-cycle constraints.

A triangle illustrates the polyhedral obstacle without requiring a large example. If a fractional variable of one half is placed on each edge, every vertex has total incident value one, but the total value is \(3/2\) while an integral matching has size at most one. For any odd vertex set S, an integral matching uses at most \((|S|- 1)/2\) edges entirely inside S. Handling these additional odd-set restrictions efficiently is part of what distinguishes general matching from its bipartite counterpart.

Algebraic algorithms offer another route. Mucha and Sankowski use Gaussian elimination to construct maximum matchings in randomized time governed by matrix multiplication, conventionally written \(O(n^{\omega})\) for an available exponent \(\omega >2\). This is a major improvement over combinatorial bounds on dense graphs. It still does not yield input-size almost-linear time on all sparse graphs, where a dense n-by-n matrix representation can itself exceed the input size by a large factor.

Approximation also behaves differently. Duan, Pettie and Su obtain a \((1- \delta )\)-approximation for maximum weight matching in \(O(m\delta ^{- 1} \log  \delta ^{- 1})\) time, hence linear time for fixed \(\delta\); unit weights cover cardinality. To force exact cardinality purely by rounding this guarantee, one would need \(\delta\) small enough that the possible loss is below one edge. When the optimum is \(\Theta (n)\), that requires \(\delta =O(1/n)\), so substituting it into the approximation running time loses the desired almost-linear bound.

Ansaripour, Danaei and Mehlhorn’s 2024 implementation study is useful for interpreting experiments: the observed behaviour on random graphs can be close to linear, while specially constructed inputs expose substantial differences between algorithms. Empirical speed and average graph behaviour therefore cannot establish the bound quantified over every input here. Their paper also keeps the distinction between the faster bipartite results and general matching explicit.

A June 2026 revision by Chakraborty and coauthors places construction of a general maximum matching in polynomial-time catalytic logspace. This model permits a large auxiliary tape with arbitrary initial contents, provided those contents are restored. It is progress on space and reversible use of auxiliary memory. The polynomial-time statement is not an almost-linear running-time theorem, so it does not resolve this card.

cards.title: Gyárfás–Sumner conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite nonempty tree T and every integer \(r\ge 1\), does there exist a finite integer \(B(T,r)\) such that every finite simple undirected graph G with clique number at most r and no induced subgraph isomorphic to T has chromatic number at most \(B(T,r)\)?
cards.definitions: A tree is a connected graph with no cycle. All graphs here are finite, simple and undirected. The clique number \(\omega (G)\) is the largest number of pairwise adjacent vertices, and the chromatic number \(\chi (G)\) is the least number of colours in a proper vertex colouring, in which adjacent vertices receive distinct colours. Both parameters are zero for the empty graph. For \(S\subseteq V(G)\), the induced graph \(G[S]\) retains all edges of G with both endpoints in S. Saying that G contains an induced T means there is an injective map \(\varphi :V(T)\to V(G)\) such that xy is an edge of T if and only if \(\varphi (x)\varphi (y)\) is an edge of G. Extra edges between image vertices are forbidden. The quantifier order is \(\forall T \forall r \exists B \forall G\): the integer B may depend arbitrarily on T and r, but not on |\(V(G)|\), maximum degree or any additional parameter of G. Equivalently, for each T there is a function \(f_{T}:N\to N\) with \(\chi (G)\le f_{T}(\omega (G))\) for every induced-T-free graph G. No prescribed polynomial growth, computability requirement for \(f_{T}\), or efficient colouring algorithm is part of the target. The statement concerns ordinary chromatic number, not fractional, list, oriented or domatic colouring parameters.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the stated bound for all finite trees and all fixed clique bounds, or exhibit one fixed tree T and one fixed integer r together with induced-T-free graphs \(G_{k}\) satisfying \(\omega (G_{k})\le r\) and \(\chi (G_{k})\to \infty\). A single finite graph can disprove a proposed numerical bound but cannot refute the existence of some larger bound. A bound that still grows with |\(V(G)|\), or a theorem with a different excluded object or extra host-graph promise, is not a full resolution.
cards.why: Determine whether every fixed induced tree is an unavoidable pattern in graphs whose chromatic number grows while their clique number stays bounded.

importance.reason: A central organizing conjecture for hereditary graph colouring and forbidden induced subgraphs, defining the proposed forest boundary for χ-boundedness.

Davies–Yuditsky’s journal publication proves polynomial \(\chi\)-boundedness under the additional promise of boxicity bounded by a fixed dimension.

cards.status_note: The 2025 near-linear-stable-set paper and April 2026 bounded-boxicity paper explicitly retain the general conjecture. The former yields \(n^{o(1)}\) rather than a size-independent bound; the latter restricts the host class. September 2026 results on tournament analogues concern directed parameters. No resolution of this ordinary undirected statement found through 11 September 2026.

context_blocks.text: A clique explains one elementary reason for needing many colours: its vertices must all receive different colours. But graphs can require arbitrarily many colours even when every clique has size at most two. The conjecture proposes that forbidding any one fixed induced tree eliminates this unbounded gap. Once the tree and clique bound are fixed, the same finite palette should suffice no matter how many vertices the graph has.

The induced condition is essential. A copy of a tree as an ordinary subgraph can ignore unwanted edges between its vertices. An induced copy must reproduce both adjacency and nonadjacency. Complete graphs contain every sufficiently small tree as an ordinary subgraph, while most of those trees do not occur as induced subgraphs. The difficult step in building the desired tree is therefore arranging its branches without creating extra edges among them.

Trees are the natural boundary for this kind of one-forbidden-pattern statement. High-girth graphs can have arbitrarily large chromatic number while containing no short cycles. If a fixed forbidden graph contains a cycle, choosing larger girth avoids that graph while retaining an unbounded chromatic number and a bounded clique number. The corresponding obstruction is absent for forests. This is why the conjecture is a proposed classification, rather than an arbitrary choice of forbidden shape.

There are substantial positive cases. Kierstead and Penrice proved the conjecture for every tree of radius at most two: some central vertex is within distance two of every other vertex. Paths and further tree families are also known. Scott and Seymour subsequently strengthen the radius-two result under exclusion of a fixed complete multipartite subgraph, with polynomial bounds in its part size. Such results exploit restrictions on how branches can interact.

Nguyen, Scott and Seymour’s 2023 preprint, published in 2024, obtains a copy of any fixed rooted tree under the conjecture’s high-chromatic-number hypotheses, with every path from the root induced. This controls unwanted edges along ancestor–descendant paths. It still permits edges between different branches, and those edges may prevent the whole vertex set from inducing a tree. The distinction isolates one of the remaining obstacles.

Their later work on near-linear stable sets applies to every fixed excluded forest and fixed clique bound. It proves an independent set of size \(n^{1- o(1)}\), and consequently a chromatic bound \(n^{o(1)}\), where n is the number of vertices. Thus every fixed positive power \(n^{\varepsilon}\) eventually exceeds the available upper bound. Nevertheless, a function such as log n is also \(n^{o(1)}\) and is unbounded, so subpolynomial growth does not establish the constant \(B(T,r)\) sought here.

That work also proves a bounded fractional chromatic number for multibrooms, formed by identifying the roots of several paths that have additional leaves at their far ends. Fractional colouring covers vertices by weighted independent sets and minimizes the total weight. Ordinary colouring requires an actual partition into colour classes. The paper retains the full conjecture for general multibrooms despite its stronger fractional conclusion.

Davies and Yuditsky establish the conjecture, with a polynomial bound in the clique number, for intersection graphs of axis-aligned boxes in every fixed dimension d. Their result first appeared in 2024 and was published in April 2026. Both the excluded forest and dimension are fixed parameters. Allowing the dimension to grow with the input would let the bound vary with an extra parameter, so the theorem does not cover arbitrary graphs with the uniform bound required here.

For algorithms, this conjecture identifies a structural source of bounded colouring complexity and large independent sets. It does not itself promise that a suitable colouring can be found efficiently. A proof with an effective construction would offer additional algorithmic information; a counterexample would reveal a family of sparse-clique graphs whose chromatic obstruction survives exclusion of one fixed induced tree. The size-independent existence statement is already fundamental.

cards.title: Optimal bounds in the Excluded Grid Theorem
cards.formal: For each integer \(r\ge 2\), let \(f(r)\) be the least nonnegative integer t such that every finite simple undirected graph of treewidth at least t contains the \(r\times r\) square grid as a minor. Determine the asymptotic order of \(f(r)\) up to universal constant factors, including the correct logarithmic dependence.
cards.definitions: The \(r\times r\) grid has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,r\}^{2}\), with an edge between \((i,j)\) and \((i' ,j' )\) exactly when |\(i- i' |+|j- j' |=1\). It has \(r^{2}\) vertices; r denotes side length. A graph H is a minor of G if H can be obtained by deleting vertices, deleting edges and contracting edges, after removing loops and merging parallel edges. Equivalently, a model of H consists of one nonempty connected vertex set in G for each vertex of H, all pairwise disjoint, with an edge of G joining the corresponding sets for every edge of H. Additional edges are permitted. A tree decomposition of G is a tree T with bags \(B_{t}\subseteq V(G)\), such that every vertex belongs to some bag, the endpoints of every edge belong together to some bag, and the bags containing any given vertex form a connected subtree of T. Its width is \(\max _{t} |B_{t}|- 1\); treewidth \(\operatorname{tw}(G)\) is the minimum such width. Robertson–Seymour’s Grid-Minor Theorem guarantees that \(f(r)\) is finite. The quantifier over G includes graphs of arbitrary size, degree and genus. This is an extremal existence threshold; no efficiency requirement for finding the grid model is imposed. Polylogarithmic factors mean \((\log  r)^{c}\) for a fixed constant c, and matching bounds here must resolve such factors rather than suppress them.
cards.answer_criterion: Identify an explicit asymptotic function \(h(r)\) and universal constants \(a,b>0\) such that a \(h(r)\le f(r)\le b h(r)\) for all sufficiently large r. The upper bound must force a grid minor in every graph above the stated threshold; the lower bound must give graphs of comparable treewidth that exclude it. In particular, this determines whether \(f(r)=O(r^{2}(\log  r)^{c})\) for some fixed c. Merely improving a nonmatching polynomial exponent, solving the planar-host case, or replacing minors by a different containment relation is progress rather than a complete answer.
cards.why: Determine the exact asymptotic loss when converting large treewidth into a square-grid minor, a foundational link between graph structure and algorithms.

importance.reason: A central quantitative problem in graph minor theory with direct implications for structural decompositions, routing, packing and parameterized algorithms.

progress.text: Robertson–Seymour prove that sufficiently large treewidth forces any fixed planar graph, including every square grid, as a minor.
Robertson–Seymour–Thomas strengthen quantitative bounds; logarithmic-girth expanders give the \(\Omega (r^{2} \log  r)\) obstruction.
Chekuri–Chuzhoy obtain the first polynomial relationship, with a randomized algorithm finding a grid model; STOC 2014 and JACM 2016.
Chuzhoy–Tan prove the general \(O(r^{9} \operatorname{polylog} r)\) upper bound; SODA 2019, Journal of Combinatorial Theory B 2021.
The Grid-Minor Theorem Revisited gives a qualitative product-structure strengthening, with an unspecified blow-up factor depending on the excluded planar graph.
Catching Rats in H-minor-free Graphs gives bounds linear in grid side length and polynomial in |\(V(H)|\) under additional exclusion of H; SODA 2026.

cards.status_note: The checked general bounds remain \(\Omega (r^{2} \log  r)\) and \(O(r^{9} \operatorname{polylog} r)\). The November 2025 product-structure result and SODA 2026 fixed-minor result refine different aspects and do not determine the all-graphs threshold. No matching asymptotic bounds found through 11 September 2026. The problem does not assume that either the near-quadratic or cubic conjecture is correct.

context_blocks.text: Treewidth measures how large the interacting pieces of a graph must be when organized along a tree. Many algorithms work by dynamic programming across the bags of a tree decomposition, with a strong dependence on bag size. A grid provides a canonical obstruction to small treewidth: its rows and columns create many overlapping connections that cannot be separated into very small bags. The Excluded Grid Theorem states that every graph of sufficiently large treewidth contains such an obstruction as a minor.

The unknown quantity is how much treewidth must be spent to force a grid of a given side length. The qualitative theorem only says that some finite threshold exists. A sharp quantitative bound would explain how efficiently general tangled connectivity can be organized into a planar grid. This is not a statement that the graph itself is planar, or that a grid must appear as an induced subgraph.

A vertex-count example already rules out a linear threshold. The complete graph on \(r^{2}- 1\) vertices has treewidth \(r^{2}- 2\), but cannot contain an \(r\times r\) grid minor because taking a minor cannot increase the number of vertices. Thus \(f(r)\ge r^{2}- 1\). Its many edges cannot replace the need for \(r^{2}\) disjoint nonempty branch sets in a minor model. This is why the fact that the \(r\times r\) grid itself has treewidth r does not imply a linear bound for arbitrary host graphs.

The known lower bound is stronger: \(f(r)=\Omega (r^{2} \log  r)\). Robertson, Seymour and Thomas obtain it using bounded-degree expanders of logarithmic girth. Such graphs have treewidth proportional to their number of vertices, while every cycle is long. A large grid contains quadratically many vertex-disjoint small cycles; lifting those cycles through a minor model requires quadratically many disjoint long cycles in the host. This consumes a logarithmic factor of additional vertices.

Chekuri and Chuzhoy obtain the first polynomial upper bound, replacing an enormous quantitative gap by a polynomial relationship between treewidth and grid size. Their proof is constructive: a randomized polynomial-time algorithm finds a grid model at the scale established by their theorem. This makes the result useful both as a structural guarantee and as a subroutine, although this card asks only for the optimal existence threshold.

Chuzhoy and Tan improve the general upper bound to \(O(r^{9}(\log  r)^{c})\) for an absolute constant c. Their SODA 2019 paper, published in journal form in 2021, builds on well-linked sets and paths of connected clusters. Well-linkedness supplies many disjoint connections; the challenge is arranging them into the grid’s particular pattern without losing too much width at successive stages. The lower and upper bounds still differ by a large power of r.

The same paper records competing predictions: Robertson–Seymour–Thomas conjectured that the \(r^{2} \log  r\) lower bound is tight, while Demaine and coauthors proposed a cubic threshold. Consequently, the catalogue target is the actual asymptotic order. A near-quadratic upper bound would be a major result, but should not be described as the only conjectured answer. Even \(r^{2}\) times an unspecified power of log r would leave part of the present target unresolved.

The 2025 paper The Grid-Minor Theorem Revisited strengthens the structural description of graphs excluding a fixed planar minor. It represents them inside clique blow-ups of graphs whose treewidth is controlled by the excluded graph’s treedepth. The blow-up size is an unspecified function of the excluded graph. This gives useful product structure and colouring applications, while leaving the optimal numerical threshold \(f(r)\) undetermined.

Catching Rats in H-minor-free Graphs, presented at SODA 2026, makes another substantial refinement under an extra host-graph restriction. For a fixed excluded graph H with t vertices and Euler genus g, a graph excluding both H and the \(r\times r\) grid has treewidth \(O(gr+t^{2304})\), hence \(O(t^{2}r+t^{2304})\). This is linear in r when H is fixed. General graphs in our question need not exclude any fixed H, so that additional parameter cannot be treated as a universal constant.

The threshold influences the quantitative strength of grid-based routing arguments, packing-versus-covering theorems and parameterized algorithms. Better bounds can improve how a large-treewidth case yields useful structure, or how a no-grid case bounds the state space for dynamic programming. A matching lower bound would be equally informative: it would identify an unavoidable loss in converting unrestricted graph connectivity into a planar obstruction.

cards.title: Caccetta–Häggkvist conjecture
cards.formal: For every pair of integers \(n\ge 2\) and \(1\le r\le n- 1\), does every simple loopless digraph D on n vertices with minimum outdegree at least r contain a directed cycle of length at most \(\operatorname{ceil}(n/r)\)?
cards.definitions: A simple loopless digraph has a finite vertex set V and an arc set \(A\subseteq \{(u,v)\in V\times V:u\ne v\}\); each ordered pair occurs at most once. Both \((u,v)\) and \((v,u)\) are allowed. The outdegree \(d^{+}(v)\) is |\(\{u:(v,u)\in A\}|\) and minimum outdegree is \(\min _{v\in V}d^{+}(v)\). A directed cycle of length \(\ell\)\(\ge 2\) is a sequence of pairwise distinct vertices \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{\ell}\) with \((v_{i},v_{i+1})\in A\) for every i and \(v_{\ell +1}=v_{1}\). Thus an opposite pair of arcs is a directed 2-cycle. \(\operatorname{ceil}(n/r)\) is the least integer not smaller than \(n/r\). There is no planarity, regularity, connectivity or algorithmic assumption.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation with the stated model, hypotheses and quantifier order. The proof must settle the entire target. A result conditional on an additional assumption settles only that conditional version. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof checked by a proof assistant and matching this statement.
cards.why: Determine the sharp universal relationship between a local directed-degree condition and the existence of a short directed cycle.

importance.reason: A central directed-graph conjecture expressing a simple, general degree-versus-girth principle.

cards.title: Almost-linear triangle detection
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform randomized word-RAM algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph with n vertices and m edges given by adjacency lists, decides whether a triangle exists with success probability at least \(2/3\) and worst-case running time \((n+m+2)^{1+o(1)}\)?
cards.definitions: A triangle is a set of three distinct vertices u,v,w for which all three unordered edges \(\{u,v\},\{v,w\},\{w,u\}\) are present. The input gives labelled vertices \(1,\ldots ,n\) and explicit adjacency lists; it is promised to describe a simple undirected graph, and can be disconnected or contain isolated vertices. The RAM has words of \(w=\lceil 4 \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits, random-access memory, and unit-cost word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo 2ʷ, and integer division by a nonzero word. Independent random words may be generated at unit cost. Input reading and all preprocessing count toward time. The running-time bound holds for every graph and every random tape, while correctness probability is over the algorithm’s internal randomness. The \(o(1)\) is a function tending to zero as \(n+m\) tends to infinity, for this one fixed algorithm; equivalently, for every \(\varepsilon >0\) the same algorithm eventually uses at most \((n+m+2)^{1+\varepsilon}\) operations. There is no promise on density, degree, arboricity or triangle count. Matrix multiplication and other algebraic techniques are allowed if their implementation fits this machine model. Only one yes/no answer is required.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct and analyze an algorithm meeting the stated all-input time and probability guarantees, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A deterministic \(O(n+m)\) algorithm would be an even stronger positive answer. A fixed exponent above one, an \(O(n^{2})\) bound that is only input-linear on dense graphs, output-sensitive listing, or an algorithm restricted to bounded-arboricity graphs does not settle the question. The target fixes the original draft’s “linear or at least almost-linear” alternative at the precise almost-linear threshold.
cards.why: Determine whether detecting the simplest cyclic graph pattern requires a superlinear amount of computation beyond reading the input.

importance.reason: A fundamental graph primitive and fine-grained hardness assumption with consequences for dynamic data structures, joins and string matching.

context_blocks.text: Triangle detection is among the smallest nontrivial pattern-finding tasks in a graph. The pattern has only three vertices, but a graph may contain an enormous number of possible triples. The question asks whether all the relevant combinations can be handled in essentially the time required to read the graph. It must also handle triangle-free instances, where an algorithm cannot stop upon finding a convenient local witness.

Detection is different from listing. A complete graph has \(\Theta (n^{2})\) input edges and \(\Theta (n^{3})\) triangles, so explicitly listing every triangle cannot take linear time in the input size. A yes/no answer has constant output size and faces no such output-size obstruction. Likewise, approximate counting or finding triangles in a distribution of random inputs does not supply an exact decision guarantee on every adversarial graph.

Chiba and Nishizeki give triangle listing in \(O(m\cdot a(G))\) time, apart from reading isolated vertices, where arboricity \(a(G)\) is the minimum number of forests needed to cover the graph’s edges. This gives linear time on any family of bounded arboricity, including planar graphs. General graphs can have arboricity of order \(\sqrt{m}\), so this approach has a superlinear worst-case cost. A sparse graph can still contain a dense, difficult region.

Alon, Yuster and Zwick improve the general sparse-graph bound using a degree threshold. Handle triangles touching a low-degree vertex by local enumeration, and use matrix multiplication on the smaller set of high-degree vertices. For an available square matrix-multiplication exponent \(\tau\), the resulting standard bound is \(O(n+m^{2\tau /(\tau +1)})\), roughly \(O(n+m^{1.407})\) at familiar current exponents. The optimization balances the cost of the two parts.

Even setting the matrix-multiplication exponent to two in this particular reduction leaves exponent \(4/3\) in m. Thus faster dense multiplication alone, inserted into the same degree-splitting argument, would not make the sparse algorithm almost linear. This is an observation about the upper-bound method, not a proof that a different graph algorithm cannot do better.

Abboud and Vassilevska Williams formulate a no-almost-linear triangle hypothesis and use it to derive conditional lower bounds for dynamic problems. The conjecture concerns general algorithms on logarithmic-word RAMs. Their separate combinatorial Boolean-matrix-multiplication conjecture restricts the kinds of techniques used; it should not be substituted for the unrestricted question here. Reductions transfer assumed hardness, rather than establish an unconditional superlinear lower bound.

The distinction remains useful in current work. Kumabe and Uezato’s ICALP 2026 paper reduces triangle detection to matching certain fixed regular expressions with two backreference uses. Consequently, an almost-linear algorithm for that matching task would also give an almost-linear triangle algorithm. This illustrates why a small graph pattern can govern complexity in a seemingly unrelated setting.

Search results require source checks. Dumitrescu’s March 2024 claim of faster combinatorial triangle algorithms was withdrawn three days after posting; the author states that the algorithm may fail and identifies an invalid case analysis. It is not an established improvement.

I also checked the parent-edge rule in Vega’s August 2025 linear-time proposal. Consider the path 0–1–2–3–4–5–6 plus edges 0–3, 3–6 and 0–6. A legal DFS follows the whole path. Its unique triangle is \(\{0,3,6\}\), consisting entirely of back edges. No test restricted to a DFS parent, its child and a common neighbour can find it. A local simulation and exhaustive triple check confirm this counterexample to the stated rule; this is not a test of later replacement implementations.

A separate September 2026 Aegypti revision claims \(O(n^{2})\) time via bucket reduction. That claimed bound is not almost linear for every sparse input, even if its correctness were established. I have not adjudicated its different proof. An all-density statement must keep both n and m visible: a dense-case breakthrough and an input-linear sparse algorithm are distinct achievements.

A resolution would identify whether a basic three-way adjacency condition inherently requires substantial work beyond scanning an explicit graph. A positive algorithm would affect graph-pattern routines and invalidate hardness assumptions used by many reductions. A negative result would provide a major unconditional lower bound for a simple polynomial-time graph problem on a strong, standard machine model.

cards.title: Seese’s conjecture
cards.formal: For every isomorphism-closed class C of finite simple undirected graphs, does decidability of its MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability problem imply that some constant k bounds the clique-width of every graph in C?
cards.definitions: An MSO\(_{1}\) sentence is built from vertex equality, adjacency \(E(x,y)\), membership \(x\in X\) in vertex sets, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual vertices and subsets of the vertex set. There is no built-in vertex order, edge-set quantification, parity predicate or other counting extension. For a fixed class \(C, Sat_{MSO_{1}}(C)\) consists of all finite encoded MSO\(_{1}\) sentences \(\varphi\) for which some \(G\in C\) satisfies \(\varphi\). Decidable means that one Turing machine, allowed to depend on C, halts and answers correctly for every input sentence. C itself is not an input to that machine; no complexity bound is required. By negating sentences this is equivalent to deciding the theory \(Th_{MSO_{1}}(C)\)={\(\varphi\): every \(G\in C\) satisfies \(\varphi\)}. A k-expression builds a labeled graph from single vertices with labels in \([k]\), disjoint union, relabeling every vertex of one label to another, and adding all edges between two distinct labels. The clique-width \(\operatorname{cw}(G)\) is the smallest k permitting such an expression after labels are forgotten; set \(\operatorname{cw}(\varnothing )=0\). The conclusion is \(\exists k\forall G\in C \operatorname{cw}(G)\le k\), with k depending on C. No hereditary, minor-closed, bounded-degree or finite-forbidden-subgraph assumption is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every such graph class, or give one class of unbounded clique-width together with a correct terminating algorithm for its entire MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability problem. A single finite graph cannot refute a uniform width bound for a class. Model checking on a supplied graph, or decidability with a promise about sentence size, is not the premise. Results requiring parity predicates or restricted graph classes do not prove the full statement.
cards.why: A major proposed structural necessity for logical decidability, connecting graph decompositions, finite model theory and algorithms over infinite families of finite inputs.

progress.text: Seese establishes foundational connections between decidable monadic graph theories and bounded structural width, and formulates the conjectural MSO\(_{1}\) boundary.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. Seese’s MSO\(_{1}\) decidability implication remains unresolved in the checked primary literature. The parity extension, the shrub-depth expressiveness characterization and the July 2026 2-WQO result have distinct hypotheses or conclusions.

context_blocks.text: An MSO\(_{1}\) sentence can describe a graph property by quantifying over sets of vertices. Three-colorability, for example, can be expressed by choosing three sets that partition the vertices and requiring each set to be independent. Checking such a sentence on one finite graph is always decidable by exhaustive search. The premise here is much stronger: from a sentence alone, decide whether it holds in at least one member of an entire, potentially infinite graph class.

Clique-width measures how many vertex labels are needed to construct a graph using a small repertoire of operations. Labels identify groups of vertices that receive the same future edge additions. Dense graphs can have small clique-width: a complete graph can be built with two labels by inserting one vertex, joining it to all previous vertices, and merging its label. Thus the conjectured structural restriction is not a sparsity condition.

The classical treewidth theorem provides the motivation. Seese proves structural restrictions from decidability of monadic theories, and the version allowing quantification over edge sets forces bounded treewidth. Grid-minor machinery supports that argument. The MSO\(_{1}\) conjecture replaces edge-set quantification by vertex-set quantification and asks for bounded clique-width instead. Transferring the proof requires a logical way of recovering the appropriate obstruction.

Bounded-width descriptions support decidability because graph properties can be translated into properties of construction trees. In particular, for each fixed k the full class of graphs of clique-width at most k has decidable MSO\(_{1}\) satisfiability. But the conjecture is only a necessary-condition statement for an arbitrary class C. One cannot infer that every subclass of a bounded-width class has decidable theory.

For a simple reason, such a converse would be false. Choose an undecidable set S of positive integers, and let C contain exactly the edgeless graphs whose numbers of vertices belong to S. All those graphs have clique-width one. A sentence specifying exactly n vertices would decide whether \(n\in S\) if satisfiability over C were decidable. Restricting which sizes occur can encode undecidability even when each individual graph has trivial structure.

Courcelle–Oum prove the implication after extending MSO\(_{1}\) with the predicate \(Even(X)\), saying that a vertex set has even cardinality. Their vertex-minor and isotropic-system machinery establishes bounded clique-width from decidability of this stronger logic. This strengthens the premise: a decision procedure for ordinary MSO\(_{1}\) sentences need not handle parity sentences. Therefore their theorem supplies substantial progress while leaving the exact statement here open.

Hereditary classes, which are closed under taking induced subgraphs, are a useful focus even though the card quantifies over all classes. If satisfiability is decidable on C, it is also decidable on its hereditary closure: ask whether some vertex subset induces a graph satisfying the input sentence, using a relativized MSO\(_{1}\) formula. Unbounded clique-width is preserved on passing to that larger class. Thus a proof covering all hereditary classes would suffice.

Dawar–Sankaran develop a stronger route through interpreting arbitrarily large grids. Their Theorem 3.2 reduces that stronger assertion to two settings: antichains of unbounded clique-width under induced-subgraph containment, and minimal hereditary classes of unbounded clique-width. They verify the grid interpretation for the known minimal families studied in their paper. This is a research program and collection of cases, not a completed classification of all such families.

The inherited ICALP 2025 paper by Mählmann settles a different boundary: on hereditary classes, bounded shrub-depth characterizes coincidence of first-order and monadic second-order expressive power. Its conclusion formulates a stronger conjectural relationship between clique-width and MSO dependence, explaining how parts of that conjecture would imply Seese’s. Shrub-depth and clique-width are distinct parameters, and a theorem about expressive power does not by itself decide satisfiability.

Duron–Mählmann–Toruńczyk’s July 2026 preprint proves that every hereditary 2-WQO class has bounded clique-width. Here 2-WQO means that every infinite sequence of graphs with two possible vertex labels contains an earlier graph embedding as a label-preserving induced subgraph of a later one. This resolves a related structural conjecture, but it starts from a well-quasi-ordering hypothesis. It does not turn an arbitrary MSO\(_{1}\) decision procedure into such an ordering property.

The unresolved implication asks whether decidable graph theories always have bounded constructional complexity. A proof would show that broad logical decidability cannot arise from some entirely different mechanism on classes of unbounded clique-width. A counterexample would reveal precisely such a mechanism. Either outcome would change how structural graph theory explains the limits of automated reasoning over whole families of finite structures.

cards.title: Exact directed maximum flow in \(O((m+n) \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(a\ge 1\), do there exist a constant \(k\ge 0\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{a}\) that, on every directed graph with \(n\ge 2\) vertices, m arcs, distinguished distinct vertices s,t and integer capacities in \(\{0,\ldots ,n^{a}\}\), outputs an exact maximum s–t flow with probability at least \(2/3\) in worst-case time \(O((m+n)(\log (n+2))^{k})\)?
cards.definitions: The graph is explicitly given by its labelled vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and an arc list, with no loops and at most one arc per ordered vertex pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A flow assigns an integer \(f_{e}\) to each arc, with \(0\le f_{e}\le u_{e}\) and equal incoming and outgoing sums at every vertex other than s,t. Its value is the outgoing sum at s minus the incoming sum at s; maximum refers to the largest such value. Output the m flow values, not only an approximate value. Use a word RAM with word length \(B_{a}\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed integer \(B_{a}\) large enough to store capacities, total flow and memory addresses. Unit-cost operations are random-access word reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division of nonzero divisors. Multiword computations are charged for their component operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed, with each generated word charged. All preprocessing and output are included, and the time bound holds on every random execution. There are no oracles or input-dependent advice. \(A_{a}, k, B_{a}\) and the hidden constant may depend on a, but not on the graph. The \(m+n\) convention includes explicitly listed isolated vertices.

context_blocks.text: Maximum flow is a basic model for routing through capacity constraints. A feasible solution must obey conservation at intermediate vertices, and optimality measures the largest transferable amount between two terminals. Even a graph with small integer capacities can require globally coordinated changes to a feasible routing. The question asks whether finding the exact optimum can cost only a polylogarithmic factor more than reading the graph.

Almost-linear algorithms already represent a major qualitative advance. Chen and coauthors obtained exact maximum flow and minimum-cost flow in \(m^{1+o(1)}\) time for polynomially bounded integral data. Li and Wice’s August 2026 preprint obtains an almost-linear maximum-flow bound through a different framework. Neither stated asymptotic guarantee is \(O(m \operatorname{polylog} n)\).

The distinction concerns the remaining overhead. For example, \(\exp (\sqrt{\log  n})\) is subpolynomial in n but exceeds every fixed power of log n. A running time containing that factor can be almost linear without satisfying this card. Removing the residual gap would identify a sharper computational cost for a central graph optimization primitive.

Exactness is also a substantive part of the target. A flow whose value is within a fixed relative error of optimum does not determine the optimum integer value when that value is large. Conversely, restricting capacities to polynomial magnitude means their binary encodings occupy logarithmically many bits each. The question is therefore not asking an algorithm to read arbitrarily long capacities in a graph-size-only time bound.

The primary topic is a static graph algorithm, so the current catalogue places the question in Structural graph theory and graph algorithms. Dynamic maintenance, parallel computation and strong polynomiality for unbounded-bit linear programming impose different requirements. No existing maximum-matching or dynamic-connectivity card represents this flow target.

cards.definitions: A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered two-element subsets of V; there are no loops or parallel edges. An isomorphism from G to H is a bijection \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(\{u,v\}\) is an edge of G if and only if \(\{f(u),f(v)\}\) is an edge of H. Write \([G]\) for its isomorphism class. For \(v\in V(G), G- v\) is the induced graph on \(V(G)\setminus \{v\}\): remove v and exactly the edges incident with v. Define \(D(G)\) to be the multiset \(\{[G- v]:v\in V(G)\}\), with one entry for every deleted vertex. Thus \(D(G)=D(H)\) means that for each isomorphism class K of graphs on \(n- 1\) vertices, the number of vertices v with \([G- v]=K\) equals the corresponding number for H. Each entry forgets all original vertex labels, including the identity of the deleted vertex; repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities. All graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices, are included. The question is a structural uniqueness statement and imposes no running-time requirement on an algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that equal vertex decks imply isomorphism for every \(n\ge 3\), or refute the conjecture by exhibiting two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs with \(n\ge 3\) and identical decks, with proofs of those properties.

context_blocks.text: Imagine receiving every graph obtained by deleting one vertex from an unknown graph, with the vertex labels erased in each view. Different deletions can yield identical-looking graphs, and their number of occurrences remains part of the data. The conjecture says this complete collection determines the original graph uniquely up to relabeling.

For a path on three vertices, deleting either endpoint leaves a single edge, while deleting the middle vertex leaves two isolated vertices. Its deck therefore consists of two copies of the edge and one edgeless two-vertex graph. The triangle instead has three copies of the edge. The lower limit of three vertices is necessary: an edge and an edgeless graph on two vertices both have a deck of two isolated single vertices.

Some global information survives deletion automatically. If \(n\ge 3\), every original edge appears in exactly \(n- 2\) members of the deck, so the total number of edges is the sum of the edge counts in the deck divided by \(n- 2\). Comparing each member’s edge count with that total also recovers the multiset of vertex degrees. These counts do not specify how all vertices fit together; that missing arrangement is the substance of the question.

Uniqueness has a different meaning from efficient recovery. There are finitely many graphs of a fixed order, so one can always enumerate those whose decks match the input. The conjecture says there is just one matching isomorphism class whenever the input is the deck of a graph with at least three vertices. It does not require that this enumeration be replaced by a polynomial-time algorithm.

McKay reports exhaustive verification through 13 vertices, and the 2026 revision by Heinrich and coauthors proves reconstruction for every interval graph with at least three vertices. Neither a finite range nor this particular graph class covers all finite graphs. The computations and proofs were not independently reproduced in this review.

A 2026 AI-assisted result concerns a structured bipartite incidence-deletion analogue: it retains the deleted vertex as an isolated vertex, preserves a given bipartition in isomorphisms, and assumes 2-connectivity and pairwise distinct vertex types. Its theorem is not the unrestricted vertex reconstruction conjecture.

The status record also preserves a 2024 general proof claim by O’Shea and Wilkins. Its publisher abstract was checked, but the full argument was inaccessible and is not validated here. Later specialist sources still formulate the general conjecture as open, so this review does not label it resolved.

The views forget vertex labels but retain the multiplicity of repeated isomorphism classes.
Even the edge count and degree multiset can be recovered, while the full arrangement of edges is the unresolved target in current specialist sources.
Finite computational checks and a theorem for interval graphs provide partial results.

It does not require that this enumeration be replaced by a polynomial-time algorithm.

McKay reports exhaustive verification through 13 vertices, and the 2026 revision by Heinrich and coauthors proves reconstruction for every interval graph with at least three vertices. Neither a finite range nor this particular graph class covers all finite graphs. The computations and proofs were not independently reproduced in this review.

A 2026 AI-assisted result concerns a structured bipartite incidence-deletion analogue: it retains the deleted vertex as an isolated vertex, preserves a given bipartition in isomorphisms, and assumes 2-connectivity and pairwise distinct vertex types. Its theorem is not the unrestricted vertex reconstruction conjecture.

The status record also preserves a 2024 general proof claim by O’Shea and Wilkins. Its publisher abstract was checked, but the full argument was inaccessible and is not validated here. Later specialist sources still formulate the general conjecture as open, so this review does not label it resolved.

cards.title: Berge–Fulkerson conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite loopless bridgeless cubic multigraph G have an ordered list \((M_{1},\ldots ,M_{6})\) of perfect matchings such that for every edge \(e\in E(G), |\{i\in \{1,\ldots ,6\}:e\in M_{i}\}|=2\)?
cards.definitions: Edges of a multigraph have distinct identities and may share their unordered pair of endpoints; loops are forbidden. Cubic means every vertex has degree three, counting incident edge identities with multiplicity. A bridge is an edge whose deletion increases the number of connected components, and bridgeless graphs have none. Disconnected graphs are allowed. A matching is a subset of edges no two of which share an endpoint. It is perfect if every vertex is incident with exactly one of its edges. The six matchings may repeat; membership counts positions in the list, not just distinct subsets. The conclusion requires every edge to occur exactly twice, with no omitted edge and no extra coverage. No algorithmic bound is required.

cards.title: Barnette’s conjecture
cards.formal: Is every finite simple undirected graph that is 3-connected, cubic, bipartite and planar Hamiltonian?
cards.definitions: A simple graph has neither loops nor parallel edges. It is 3-connected if it has at least four vertices and deleting any set of at most two vertices leaves a connected graph. Cubic means every vertex has degree exactly three. Bipartite means its vertices admit a partition into two sets with no edge having both endpoints in the same set. Planar means it has a drawing in the plane whose edge interiors do not intersect and contain no vertices; different edges may meet only at shared endpoints. cards.title: Seymour’s second-neighborhood conjecture
cards.formal: Does every finite nonempty oriented graph D contain a vertex v for which |\(N^{++}(v)|\ge |N^{+}(v)|\), where \(N^{+}(v)\) consists of vertices at directed distance one from v and \(N^{++}(v)\) consists of vertices at directed distance exactly two?

cards.title: Strongly polynomial near-linear negative-weight shortest paths
cards.formal: Do there exist a uniform randomized comparison-addition algorithm and constants \(C>0\), \(k\ge0\) that compute all exact distances from one specified source in every directed graph with arbitrary real arc lengths and no negative directed cycle, using at most \(C(m+n)(\log(n+2))^{k}\) operations and succeeding with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. Arc lengths may be positive, zero or negative. A path length is the sum of its arc lengths; the empty path has length zero. Output the minimum source-to-vertex path length for every vertex, or an infinity marker if unreachable. The promise excludes negative cycles anywhere in the graph. Use a uniform comparison-addition RAM. Real cells contain exact real numbers and support copying, addition, subtraction and comparison at unit cost; fixed rational program constants are allowed. Real multiplication, division, floor, bit extraction and conversion of an input-dependent real to an integer are not primitives. Integer control and address words have \(d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed constant \(d\), with unit-cost Boolean operations, shifts, comparison and arithmetic on words. Integer operations cannot inspect real encodings. A fixed finite program receives no advice or free tables. Memory accesses, control, preprocessing and output all count. Bounds are uniform over all real edge values. Randomness consists of independent uniform random words, each generated at unit cost. On every input, the whole output must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). The time bound holds for every random execution, including unsuccessful ones. The operation bound is independent of all magnitudes and numerical encoding lengths. On rational inputs, intermediate values must have bit length polynomial in the total binary input length; this is the usual additional encoding condition for strong polynomiality.

context_blocks.text: Negative lengths allow shortest paths to express costs, credits and difference constraints. They make the numerical model essential: a graph-size bound uniform over real weights is stronger than a bound depending on the number of bits in integer weights.

Bernstein, Nanongkai and Wulff-Nilsen obtained near-linear integer-weight shortest paths with a \(\log W\) dependence. Bringmann, Cassis and Fischer improve the logarithmic factors and explicitly ask whether strong polynomiality can remove that dependence.

The February 2026 preprint by Li, Li and Zhang gives \(n^{2+o(1)}\) time for real weights. This is almost linear for dense graphs, but it neither has polylogarithmic overhead nor gives the requested sparse-graph bound.
Mareš supplies the shortest-path background; the endpoint and status distinctions here come from the later research papers.

cards.why: Removing numerical scaling dependence in a nearly input-linear bound would settle a central gap in exact shortest-path computation over arbitrary real data.

cards.title: Strongly polynomial maximum flow below the \(mn\) barrier
cards.formal: Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) and a uniform randomized strongly polynomial algorithm that computes an exact maximum flow in every directed network with arbitrary nonnegative rational capacities, \(n\ge2\) vertices and \(m\ge n-1\) arcs, in \(O((mn)^{1-\varepsilon})\) worst-case arithmetic-RAM operations with success probability at least \(2/3\)?

A feasible flow assigns a value \(f_{e}\) to every arc with \(0\le f_{e}\le u_{e}\) and equal incoming and outgoing total flow at each vertex except the distinct specified source \(s\) and sink \(t\). Its value is outgoing minus incoming flow at \(s\). The required output is a feasible flow attaining the largest possible value, including every arc value. Capacities and output values are finite rationals. Use exact rational cells with unit-cost copying, addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero rational and comparison. Integer control and addresses use \(O(\log(n+m+2))\)-bit words with unit-cost arithmetic, Boolean operations and shifts; they cannot inspect rational encodings or apply floor to rationals. Fixed rational constants and a fixed finite program are allowed, with no advice or free tables. The count is independent of capacity magnitudes and binary lengths. For input bit length \(L\), every intermediate numerator and denominator and the total used bit space must be polynomially bounded in \(L\), including on unsuccessful executions. Independent fair random words are allowed. The bound holds on every execution; the entire flow must be correct with probability at least \(2/3\). cards.title: Dynamic optimality conjecture
cards.formal: Fix n ordered keys and an access sequence X. In the root-BST model, an access is served by rotations until its key is at the root; its cost is one plus the number of rotations. Let \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) minimize total cost over offline executions, allowing an optimal initial tree. Is there a universal constant C such that, for every initial splay tree \(T_{0}\) and every X, \(\mathrm{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_0)\le C(\mathrm{OPT}(X)+n)\)? The additive term allows an arbitrary initial configuration.

context_blocks.text: A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost \(\Theta (n)\), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by \(O((\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n) \log  \log  n \cdot  \log ^{2} \log  \log  n)\). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

context_blocks.title: Additional source and scope
context_blocks.text: Sublogarithmic competitiveness of splay trees is a weaker quantitative milestone on the way to constant competitiveness. It is preserved as context and is not claimed to imply dynamic optimality.

cards.why: It asks whether a simple local adjustment rule can match every legal strategy with complete knowledge of the future. The issue is fundamental to instance-sensitive data structures: success would replace a growing competitive penalty by a constant for all access patterns. A counterexample would identify a limitation of splaying that its many separate locality guarantees fail to reveal.
cards.definitions: Keys are \([n]=\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 1\), ordered by their integer values. A binary search tree has one node per key, every key in a left subtree smaller than its root and every key in a right subtree larger. A rotation on a parent-child edge exchanges those two nodes while reattaching the intermediate subtree so that the order is preserved. To splay a requested key x, repeatedly apply the following bottom-up rule until x is root. If its parent is root, rotate the edge from x to its parent (zig). Otherwise let p be its parent and g its grandparent. If x and p are both left children or both right children, first rotate p above g and then x above p (zig-zig). Otherwise rotate x above p and then x above g (zig-zag). Each access costs one plus its number of rotations. The tree after the access is the initial tree for the next access. For a finite sequence \(X\in [n]*, \operatorname{cost}_{\mathrm{splay}}(X;T_{0})\) is the sum of these costs starting from \(T_{0}\). A comparator execution may start with any tree, knows X in full, and serves each request by any finite sequence of parent-child rotations anywhere in the current tree whose final root is the requested key. Its cost is the same one-plus-rotations sum. \(\operatorname{OPT}(X)\) is the minimum cost over all such initial trees and executions; it is zero for the empty sequence. There are no insertions, deletions or additional node operations. This root-BST cost convention is the one used in the saved source, with the additive n term accounting for the initial tree.

cards.context:
A balanced search tree guarantees logarithmic time per access, but that worst-case guarantee ignores the sequence. Repeatedly accessing one key, or scanning nearby keys, can be much cheaper if the tree adapts. Dynamic optimality asks for one online rule that exploits every such pattern without being told which pattern will occur.

The benchmark is itself allowed to rotate its tree and knows all future requests. Competing with the best fixed tree only captures access frequencies; competing with a changing tree also captures temporal structure. Splaying uses only local zig, zig-zig, and zig-zag rotations after each access, with no explicit prediction of the future.

For a concrete example, consider a chain on n keys with the requested key at its bottom. The first splay can cost \(\Theta (n)\), whereas an offline comparator can put that key at the root initially. The additive n allowance accounts for this starting discrepancy. Repeating the same request then costs one per access in both trees. A large cost for one badly initialized access therefore does not refute the statement.

The July 2026 preprint bounds splay cost by \(O((\operatorname{OPT}(X)+n) \log  \log  n \cdot  \log ^{2} \log  \log  n)\). Its competitive factor depends only on the number of keys, so the result covers every access pattern; that factor nevertheless grows without bound. A constant bound would be strictly stronger. The theorem is stated asymptotically, with the finitely many small values of n absorbed into constants.

Competitiveness concerns the total cost of a sequence. It does not require every individual access to be cheap, and it does not compare against an arbitrary RAM program with a hash table. Both executions must maintain binary search trees and pay for the specified rotations. Within those rules the offline execution can depend on the complete sequence, while the splay rule reacts only to the current request and tree.

Sublogarithmic competitiveness of splay trees is a weaker quantitative milestone on the way to constant competitiveness. It is preserved as context and is not claimed to imply dynamic optimality.

cards.title: Superlogarithmic static cell-probe lower bounds
cards.formal: Does there exist a fixed integer \(k\ge 2\) and a uniformly polynomial-time computable family of Boolean functions \(F_{n}\) on an n-word database and a \(k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil\)-bit query such that its optimal deterministic static cell-probe query complexity \(t*F(n)\), with word size \(\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) bits and \(n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\) memory cells, satisfies \(t*F(n)/\log _{2} n\to \infty\) as \(n\to \infty\)?
cards.definitions: For each integer \(n\ge 2\) put \(w=\lceil 4\log _{2} n\rceil\) and \(s=n\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil ^{2}\). A database is \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{w})^{n}, a\) query is \(q\in \{0,1\}^{k\lceil \log _{2} n\rceil}\), and \(F_{n}(D,q)\in \{0,1\}\). Explicit means that a single deterministic Turing machine computes \(F_{n}(D,q)\), given \((1^{n},D,q)\), in time polynomial in n; no advice is allowed in this definition. A data structure may preprocess D by any map \(E_{n}\) into s cells of w bits each. Preprocessing time is unrestricted, and this encoding may be nonlinear and nonuniform. For each query, a deterministic adaptive decision tree reads cells, choosing the next address from the query and previously read contents, and must output \(F_{n}(D,q)\) exactly for every database. Computation between probes is free. The trees may depend on n, F and the query, but their only access to D is through \(E_{n}(D)\). Each query starts without free database-dependent private information; memory is static and read-only. Define \(t*F(n)\) as the minimum, over all such encodings and trees, of the maximum number of probes over all D and q. All memory cells count toward s. This card fixes a near-linear-space, short-query, one-bit-answer specialization of the broader static lower-bound challenge; it does not assert equivalence to every space or word-size variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that some fixed k and admissible uniform family F satisfy: for every real \(B>0\) there is N such that \(t*F(n)>B \log _{2} n\) for every \(n\ge N\). Alternatively, prove the exact negation: for every fixed k and every admissible family F, there is a finite \(B>0\) such that \(t*F(n)\le B \log _{2} n\) for arbitrarily large n. In particular, the negative answer need not establish an \(O(\log  n)\) bound for all sufficiently large n.

The STOC 2026 paper retains the broader static barrier as Open Problem 1.1.
