context_blocks.text: One edge update can force a global search even though the optimal forest changes by very little. Deleting a tree edge splits one tree into two parts; the algorithm must find the cheapest surviving edge crossing that cut, if one exists. There may be many candidate edges dispersed throughout the graph. Inserting an edge is easier to understand: it creates a cycle if its endpoints are already connected, and it replaces the largest edge on that cycle when this improves the ordered forest.

The reporting convention makes the maintained answer observable without requiring the algorithm to print all \(n- 1\) tree edges after every update. With fixed tie-breaking, the forest changes by at most one insertion and one deletion. Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen use this explicit update model in their formulation. The difficulty is finding those few changes quickly, rather than paying for a large unavoidable output.

Polylogarithmic amortized maintenance is already established. Holm, de Lichtenberg and Thorup give a deterministic \(O(\log ^{4} n)\) amortized update bound. Amortization allows occasional expensive operations as long as their cost can be charged across a sequence. The present target limits the time of each individual update, so long rebuilds and large replacement-edge searches must be spread out while keeping the current answer ready.

Later amortized refinements improve the logarithmic factors. The 2015 work of Holm, Rotenberg and Wulff-Nilsen obtains \(O(\log ^{4} n/\log  \log  n)\) using the randomized priority-queue option in its table of RAM implementations. Its deterministic implementation has a different bound. None of these variants supplies the worst-case per-update guarantee requested here.

The worst-case frontier crossed a major threshold in 2017. Nanongkai, Saranurak and Wulff-Nilsen obtain Las Vegas maintenance with subpolynomial worst-case update time with high probability. Their approach combines expander maintenance with a reduction to graphs having few edges beyond a forest. Chuzhoy and coauthors subsequently derandomize the needed expander-decomposition component and obtain deterministic \(n^{o(1)}\) worst-case updates.

Subpolynomial is still weaker than polylogarithmic. For example, \(\exp (\sqrt{\log  n})\) grows more slowly than every fixed positive power of n but faster than every fixed power of log n. Thus a statement of \(n^{o(1)}\) update time does not automatically meet this card’s bound. The 2020 deterministic theorem resolves an earlier polynomial-exponent barrier while leaving the sharper target.

The SODA 2026 connectivity result of Meierhans and Probst Gutenberg achieves expected polylogarithmic worst-case updates for maintaining an unweighted spanning forest, and also discusses conversion to high-probability time bounds. It extends to a \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximate weighted minimum spanning forest with overhead proportional to \(\log (U)/\varepsilon\) for weights in \([1,U]\). The approximation parameter is essential; this is not an exact weighted minimum-forest theorem.

For integer weights, one could force an approximation guarantee to become exact by taking \(\varepsilon\) smaller than the reciprocal of a polynomial upper bound on the optimum cost. But the displayed \(1/\varepsilon\) overhead would then become polynomial in n. The straightforward reduction therefore does not preserve polylogarithmic update time for exact optimization. It identifies a concrete gap between maintaining connectivity at a few approximate weight thresholds and identifying the exact cheapest replacement edge.

The oblivious-adversary convention means the update sequence is chosen without reacting to the data structure’s random outcomes. A solution robust to an adaptive adversary would be stronger. Even this stated convention would remove a longstanding delay barrier for a central dynamic optimization primitive, with uses in algorithms that repeatedly maintain weighted spanning structures.

cards.title: Polylogarithmic maintenance of the exact global minimum cut
cards.formal: Can a fully dynamic simple, unweighted, undirected n-vertex graph maintain its exact global minimum-cut value with expected \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) amortized update time, worst-case \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) query time and polynomial space, with high probability over every polynomial-length oblivious operation sequence?
cards.definitions: Fix vertices \([n], n\ge 2\). Start from the empty graph. A legal update inserts one absent unordered edge or deletes one present edge; there are no loops, parallel edges, weights or vertex updates. A query returns the integer \(\lambda (G)=\min \{|\{uv\in E:u\in S,v\notin S\}| : \varnothing \ne S\subsetneq [n]\}\). In particular \(\lambda (G)=0\) for a disconnected graph; no distinguished terminals are supplied. Only the value is required, not a list of vertices or edges realizing the cut. Use a uniform randomized word-RAM with \(\Theta (\log (n+2))\)-bit words, ordinary arithmetic, bit operations and random access, and count all maintenance and query work. Precisely, ask for fixed exponents b,c and an algorithm accepting any fixed constant \(a\ge 1\) as a confidence parameter. For every legal sequence with U updates and Q queries, \(U+Q\le n^{a}\), fixed independently of its random bits, it uses \(O_{a}(n^{b})\) words on every execution; expected total initialization and update work is \(O_{a}(n^{b}+U \log ^{c}(n+2))\); each query takes \(O_{a}(\log ^{c}(n+2))\) worst-case time; and all query answers are simultaneously correct with probability at least \(1- n^{- 3}\). Initial preprocessing may take \(O_{a}(n^{b})\) time, accounting for the additive term. Each operation must finish before the next is revealed. The exponents are independent of \(\lambda (G), n\) and a. This fixes an expected-amortized Monte Carlo convention explicitly; it does not demand correctness against updates chosen from the random internal state.
cards.answer_criterion: Construct a data structure satisfying the complete specification for unrestricted cut values, or prove that no such data structure exists in the stated model. Conditional lower bounds must state their assumptions. Algorithms for insertion-only sequences, approximate cut values, bounded connectivity or subpolynomial but superpolylogarithmic update time are partial progress. Hardness for weighted cuts or fixed-terminal s–t cuts alone is not a negative resolution.
cards.why: A central exact dynamic graph problem asking whether a global measure of edge connectivity can be updated as efficiently as basic connectivity, across the full range of cut values.

importance.reason: A fundamental data-structure question with a persistent gap between incremental, approximate and exact fully dynamic algorithms; common terminal-cut lower bounds do not settle it.

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. No exact fully dynamic algorithm meeting the polylogarithmic bounds at unrestricted connectivity was found in the checked primary sources. The 2026 exact \(n^{o(1)}\) result has a cut-size restriction, and the unrestricted 2026 tree-packing bound remains polynomial rather than polylogarithmic.

context_blocks.text: The global minimum cut measures the weakest separation anywhere in a network: how many edges must fail before some nonempty part separates from the rest. Maintaining this number as individual links appear and disappear is a natural extension of dynamic connectivity. Connectivity only distinguishes \(\lambda =0\) from \(\lambda \ge 1\); the present question requires the exact integer throughout its full range from zero to \(n- 1\).

A small update need not make the identity of the best cut easy to maintain. For example, two dense clusters joined by a few edges have a global cut determined by their interface, although every individual vertex can have high degree. As the interface changes, an unrelated part of the graph can become the weakest separation. Tracking vertex degrees alone therefore does not identify the optimum.

The value changes by at most one after a single edge insertion or deletion: each individual cut changes by at most one, and taking the minimum preserves that bound. This simple stability is useful, but it does not tell an algorithm whether the answer actually changed. Certifying that no alternative cut is smaller is the difficult global part of an update.

The card requests a number, allowing a polylogarithmic query bound without an output-size obstruction. Listing the edges of a large minimum cut or all vertices on one side can require linear time merely to write the answer. It also uses the ordinary global convention \(\lambda =0\) for disconnected graphs. The inherited 2026 algorithm uses minimum proper, nonzero cuts internally; those intermediate objects are not the definition of this card’s output.

Henzinger, Krinninger, Nanongkai and Saranurak’s OMv paper explicitly identifies dynamic minimum cut as an unresolved frontier for polylogarithmic updates. Its many conditional lower bounds do not automatically transfer to this task. A minimum s–t cut must separate prescribed terminals, whereas a global minimum cut may isolate a completely different region. A reduction has to preserve that freedom, not silently introduce terminal constraints.

The update model is also decisive. Goranci, Henzinger and Thorup obtained deterministic polylogarithmic amortized update time and constant query time for exact incremental minimum cut. In that setting edges are only inserted. Deletions can invalidate the compressed structural information retained during a monotone growth process, so this theorem does not settle fully dynamic maintenance.

For unrestricted cut values in simple graphs, Goranci and coauthors obtained exact fully dynamic algorithms with roughly linear-in-n randomized worst-case update time and sublinear-in-m deterministic amortized update time. Their 2024 revision corrects a runtime in the expander-decomposition analysis. This establishes substantial reuse across updates without reaching a polylogarithmic bound.

De Vos and Christiansen improve the deterministic amortized bound to \(\widetilde{O}\)\((m^{11/12})\); their final 2026 theorem gives the more detailed minimum of \(m^{11/12}, m^{11/13}n^{1/13}\), and \(n^{3/2}\), up to logarithmic factors. Their analysis uses greedy tree packings: either a packed tree crosses a minimum cut only once, or a suitable contraction exposes a minimum cut around one vertex. Both structural outcomes help reduce the candidate cuts that must be maintained.

The inherited SODA 2026 paper of El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li reaches \(n^{o(1)}\) deterministic amortized update time for exact cuts of size up to \(2^{\Theta ((\log  n)^{3/4- \eta})}\), for fixed \(0<\eta <3/4\) in the stated parameter regime. This greatly expands the previous small-cut range. It still restricts the minimum-cut value, and \(n^{o(1)}\) does not itself mean a fixed power of log n.

The same paper explains the accuracy barrier behind this restriction. Its recursive procedure controls a very small multiplicative approximation error, allowing exact recovery while the integral cut value stays below the inverse error. Making that error much smaller increases the work propagated between recursive levels. Thus simply substituting a large cut value into the theorem does not preserve its running time.

Approximation has progressed separately. El-Hayek, Henzinger and Li’s SODA 2025 algorithm maintains a \((1+o(1))\)-approximate global cut in subpolynomial amortized time without a small-cut promise. For an integer optimum \(\lambda\), rounding a multiplicative estimate to an exact answer generally needs additive error below one, hence relative error on the order of \(1/\lambda\). A fixed approximation guarantee cannot supply this for arbitrary connectivity.

The remaining question isolates two bottlenecks at once: exactness for unrestricted connectivity and polylogarithmic update cost. Randomization and amortization are allowed to make it a broad algorithmic target. A positive result would put a numerical global resilience measure close to the cost of maintaining basic connectivity, while a suitable lower bound would explain why this more detailed information requires fundamentally more work.

cards.title: Logarithmic Las Vegas dynamic connectivity
cards.formal: Does an always-correct Las Vegas word-RAM data structure maintain connectivity of an initially empty undirected simple graph on \([n]\) with \(O(\log(2+n))\) amortized expected time per edge update and \(O(\log(2+n))\) worst-case time per query, using \(O((n+m)\log^c(2+n))\) words for some fixed \(c\), where \(m\) is the current number of edges?
cards.definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. Here \(w=\lceil a\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed constant \(a\) sufficient to address the allowed space. Insert adds a missing edge; Delete removes a present edge; Connected(u,v) returns whether a path joins the two supplied vertices. Valid operations form any finite sequence fixed independently of the random bits. The expected total cost is \(O(n\log^c(2+n)+(u+q)\log(2+n))\) for \(u\) updates and \(q\) queries; the first term includes initialization from the empty graph. Every individual query must meet its worst-case bound. Every answer is correct, and all operations terminate almost surely. This asks for amortized expected updates against an oblivious adversary, not deterministic or worst-case update guarantees. The algorithm has no advance access to future updates.
cards.why: Closing the remaining iterated-logarithm gap would pin down a central dynamic graph primitive near its information-theoretic lower bounds.

context_blocks.text: The 2023 Las Vegas structure has \(O(\log n(\log\log n)^2)\) amortized expected update time and \(O(\log n/\log\log\log n)\) worst-case queries.
Polylogarithmic worst-case connectivity is a separate research direction: a larger polylogarithm per operation does not provide logarithmic amortized update time.

cards.title: Dynamic APSP with edge-linear updates
cards.formal: For every fixed positive integer c, do there exist a deterministic data structure and constants \(a,d \ge  1\) such that the following holds for all \(n \ge  2\) and $n\le m\le n^2$? Maintain a directed simple graph on a fixed set of n vertices, with at most m edges at every time and integer edge weights in \(\{1,\ldots ,n^{c}\}\), under single-edge insertions, deletions, and weight changes. Return the exact current distance from any queried vertex s to any queried vertex t in $O(\log^a n)$ worst-case time. After $O(n^d)$ preprocessing, require $O(m\log^a n)$ amortized time per update and polynomial space. Constants may depend on c, but not on n, m, the initial graph, or the operation sequence.
cards.definitions: The capacity m is supplied in advance and bounds the maximum number of live edges throughout the sequence; it is not a count of all updates. Each ordered vertex pair has at most one edge and there are no self-loops. An insertion adds an absent edge, a deletion removes a present edge, and a weight change replaces the weight of one present edge by another permitted weight. A distance query returns the minimum sum of edge weights on a directed s-to-t path, zero for \(s=t\), and a distinguished infinity value if no path exists. Only the distance is requested, not every path or the whole distance matrix. All answers must be exact for any interleaving of updates and queries. Use a word RAM with \(Theta(\log  n)\)-bit words, with a sufficiently large constant for the fixed weight exponent and polynomially bounded addresses; comparisons, arithmetic, Boolean operations, shifts, and random access cost one step. Amortization means that after preprocessing any U updates and Q queries together cost $O(U m\log^a n+Q\log^a n)$; the query bound must also hold for each query individually.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a data structure with these guarantees for every fixed polynomial weight bound, or prove that the quantified proposition is false. A conditional lower bound must state its assumption. A near-quadratic-in-n update bound only meets the target for dense graphs; a subpolynomial approximation ratio or a guarantee only for insertions does not meet the exact fully dynamic specification.
cards.why: This asks whether exact shortest-path information can be maintained at a cost reflecting the number of input edges, rather than all possible vertex pairs. It is a central dynamic-graph trade-off between update work, sparse structure, and immediate exact access to global information.

importance.reason: A broad exact dynamic-graph frontier with a major sparse-versus-dense gap. It tests whether global metric information can be maintained at input-scale update cost while preserving fast queries.

progress.text: Demetrescu and Italiano give deterministic \(O(n^{2} \log ^{3} n)\) amortized updates and constant worst-case distance queries for general directed nonnegative-weight graphs.

Henzinger asks for fully dynamic APSP with edge-linear update cost and constant query cost, both allowing polylogarithmic factors. The fixed weight, edge-update, and amortization conventions here make that direction precise.
Mao’s revised paper gives a Monte Carlo algorithm with tilde-\(O(n^{5/2})\) worst-case vertex-update time and near-quadratic space. This addresses a different update guarantee.

Kyng, Meierhans, and Zöcklein use sparsification for near-linear total processing of a bounded-length update sequence with polylogarithmic queries, but their returned distances have a subpolynomial approximation factor.

context_blocks.text: Recomputing distances from every source after each change is expensive, while postponing the work until a query can make a single query expensive. A dynamic distance oracle tries to divide this work so that both kinds of operation remain useful. A single changed edge can alter distances for quadratically many vertex pairs. That observation does not by itself rule out a fast oracle: the representation may store those changes implicitly, and the interface only asks for one pair at a time. Proving a lower bound therefore requires more than counting changed entries in a materialized distance matrix.

The classical Demetrescu–Italiano algorithm achieves \(O(n^{2} \log ^{3} n)\) amortized update time and constant distance-query time for nonnegative weights. This is already close to the proposed bound when m is quadratic in n. The substantial gap is the sparse regime, where the desired amortized update cost can be nearly a factor n smaller.

Several nearby frontiers have different guarantees. Mao’s revised 2024 result targets worst-case vertex-update time and gives a randomized bound at the \(n^{5/2}\) scale. ESA 2025 sparsification gives extremely fast dynamic approximate distances, with a growing approximation factor. Neither result establishes the exact, edge-sensitive, amortized target on this card. Fixing those distinctions is necessary when assessing progress.

cards.title: Near-linear incremental topological ordering
cards.formal: Does a uniform Las Vegas randomized algorithm maintain a topological ordering of an initially empty directed graph on \(n\) named vertices during edge insertions in expected total time \((n+m)^{1+o(1)}\), with \(O(1)\) worst-case order-comparison queries and \(O((n+m)(\log(2+n))^C)\) words of space for some constant \(C\)? Here \(m\) is the number of edges inserted so far, and every graph in the sequence is promised acyclic.
cards.definitions: A uniform sequential word RAM has a fixed finite program, word-sized registers and addressed memory cells. Unit-cost instructions are reads and writes, comparisons, branching, addition, subtraction, multiplication, integer division with nonzero divisor, Boolean bit operations and logical shifts. Arithmetic stored in one word is modulo \(2^w\); shifts by at least \(w\) yield zero. Addresses must fit the available word size. All table construction and input-dependent auxiliary memory count; there is no free advice or input-dependent oracle. Randomized programs may generate independent uniform random words. For each \(n\ge2\), vertices are \([n]\), no parallel edges or loops are inserted, and the complete finite insertion/query sequence is fixed independently of the algorithm’s random bits. Word length is \(\lceil a\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed algorithm-chosen constant \(a\) large enough for its storage addresses. After every insertion there must be a total order of all vertices with every edge directed forward. A query on \((u,v)\) returns whether \(u\) precedes \(v\) in that maintained order, with all queries between insertions referring to the same order. It is not a reachability query, and printing a fresh list of all vertices after every insertion is not required. Answers are always correct, and operations terminate almost surely. The update bound means that for every constant \(\eta>0\) there is a constant \(C_\eta\) such that expected initialization plus update time is at most \(C_\eta(n+m)^{1+\eta}\) for every prefix; \(q\) order queries add \(O(q)\) time. No predictions, special graph family or advance edge information are supplied. The target allows the full stated RAM, without an undefined restriction to combinatorial algorithms.
cards.why: Maintaining an actual vertex order remains a central gap between static graph processing and incremental graph maintenance, even as cycle detection itself has become almost linear.

context_blocks.text: The 2025 report distinguishes maintaining a topological order from cycle detection, which already has almost-linear total update time. It records the dense-graph work of Bender and coauthors and sparse-graph bounds with a polynomial overhead.

The report also poses a more specific combinatorial improvement. This card instead formalizes the broader almost-linear ordering target discussed in the researcher list. Prediction-dependent graph maintenance does not establish this guarantee for arbitrary insertion sequences.

cards.definitions: The structure initializes the empty set in constant time and space. An insertion supplies a real point not currently present and returns a stable handle. A deletion supplies the handle of a present point. A query supplies \(q\in\mathbb R^2\) and returns any present \(p\) minimizing \((p_x-q_x)^2+(p_y-q_y)^2\), or an empty marker. Ties may be resolved arbitrarily but correctly. At any instant \(n\) is the number of stored points. Use an algebraic real RAM with exact real addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a nonzero real, and comparisons, each at unit cost. A point coordinate, scalar, pointer or fixed-size record field occupies one cell. Reading, writing and following pointers cost one step; no floor, bit extraction from reals, or packing unbounded discrete information into a real is an available operation. The program is uniform and finite; there is no advice or free table construction. Each independently generated fair random bit costs one operation; sampling an arbitrary exact real number is not a primitive. All answers are exact on every terminating execution and the structure terminates almost surely. For every fixed finite legal operation sequence chosen independently of its random bits, with \(u\) updates and maximum set size \(M\), the expected total update time is \(O(u\log(M+2))\); each query separately has worst-case \(O(\log(n+2))\) time on every execution. Space holds on every execution, including retained points and temporary work. All constants are universal. This states the amortization convention using the maximum size of the sequence, without an adaptive-adversary guarantee. The space exponent \(c\) may be any fixed nonnegative integer. All logarithms are base two. The sequence and its real coordinates may depend on the program but are fixed before its random bits are sampled; the bounds impose no adaptive-adversary guarantee.

context_blocks.text: A nearest-neighbor query asks for an actual stored point minimizing Euclidean distance to the query. On a line, ordered search can inspect the predecessor and successor. In the plane, closeness depends on two coordinates together, and a nearby point in one coordinate can be far away in the other.

Deletion is a substantive operation. Removing the previously closest point can expose a different answer at many query locations, while the data structure must still answer whichever query arrives next. The target retains every allowed insertion and deletion sequence instead of assuming that the stored point set only grows.

The 2025 incremental result achieves \(O(\log n)\) queries and \(O(\log^{1+\eta}n)\) insertion time for fixed positive \(\eta\). Its query bound meets this target, but its insertion bound still has a growing factor over logarithmic time and the incremental interface does not include arbitrary deletions.

Randomness is permitted to affect work, not geometric correctness: every returned point must really minimize the squared distance, with any exact minimizer acceptable in a tie. Updates are bounded in expected total time over each fixed sequence, whereas a query must meet its time bound on every execution. These are separate promises.

The original source asks for logarithmic costs in the fully dynamic planar problem. The retained benchmark states an explicit Las Vegas variant with expected amortized updates, worst-case queries and near-linear space. Its real-arithmetic cost model does not claim a logarithmic bit complexity for arbitrary real coordinates.

Approximate-neighbor libraries, empirical query throughput and high-dimensional vector indexes address related applications but do not imply this exact two-dimensional worst-case interface. The space guarantee also counts temporary work and must hold for the current number of points.

Alternatively prove in Lean that no such representation and constants exist in the specified model. An insertion-only structure, approximate answers or a time bound retaining an unbounded extra logarithmic factor does not meet the full target.

cards.definitions: The domain D is a fixed finite set throughout a run; updates do not create or delete vertices. An element y is covered when at least one red predecessor x has an arc \(x\to y\). A covered vertex is counted once, regardless of how many red predecessors it has, and it need not itself be red. E is a binary relation, so loops are allowed; R is unary. The four update types are \(ins_{E}(u,v), del_{E}(u,v), ins_{R}(u)\), and \(del_{R}(u)\). Insertions of present tuples and deletions of absent tuples leave the input relation unchanged and are also allowed. A program chooses finitely many auxiliary relation symbols S, each of a fixed finite arity, including a distinguished zero-ary answer bit Ans. For each S and update type \(\delta\) it supplies a first-order formula \(\varphi _{S,\delta}(\bar\{p\};\bar\{z\})\), where p̄ are the changed tuple’s parameters and z̄ has the arity of S. The formula may use equality, the current input and auxiliary relations, Boolean connectives, and quantification over individual domain elements. It has no parity/counting quantifier, quantification over sets, function symbol or built-in numeric relation. After update \(\delta (\bar\{a\})\), each auxiliary relation becomes \(\{\bar\{b\}:(I,A)\models \varphi _{S,\delta}(\bar\{a\};\bar\{b\})\}\), evaluated on the old input I and old auxiliary state A. All auxiliary updates occur simultaneously, alongside the specified input change. Empty initialization makes Ans false, correctly answering the empty covered set. The program’s formulas and arities are independent of |D| and of the update history. The number and arities of auxiliary relations are unrestricted finite constants chosen by the program; thus it may use polynomially many auxiliary bits, with its own fixed polynomial exponent. DynFO measures expressibility of these updates, rather than sequential constant-time execution of a formula on a Turing machine.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer is a finite collection of first-order update formulas and a proof of correctness from empty initialization for every finite domain and every finite update sequence. A negative answer must show that every such program, allowing arbitrary fixed auxiliary arities, fails on some domain and sequence. A lower bound only for quantifier-free formulas or a fixed arity, a program requiring unrestricted initial advice, or an algorithm for a bounded-degree variant does not settle the stated DynFO question.

cards.definitions: The vertex set is \([n]\), with \(n\ge2\), and the source \(s\in[n]\) is fixed at initialization. Graphs are simple and undirected. Every present edge has an integer weight in \(\{1,\ldots,n^3\}\). An update inserts an absent edge with its weight, deletes a present edge, or changes the weight of a present edge. A query supplies \(v\in[n]\) and must return exactly the minimum sum of edge weights along an \(s\)-to-\(v\) path in the current graph, or a special infinity symbol if no path exists; the distance to \(s\) is zero. Each operation must finish before the next is supplied. The sequence may be arbitrarily long and chosen using all previous outputs; the data structure receives no future operations. It must work at every density. The subquadratic bound is in the vertex count, so it expresses a saving over rebuilding for dense graphs, not a promised saving relative to the edge count of every sparse graph. The uniform machine is a word-RAM with word length \(w=c\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\), for one fixed integer \(c\ge5\) chosen with the algorithm. Unit-cost instructions are indirect read/write of an addressed word, comparison, branching, unsigned addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), bitwise Boolean operations, shifts by fewer than \(w\) places, and integer quotient/remainder by a nonzero word. Larger integers require multiple words and charged operations. Initial input is an explicit adjacency/weight table. For fixed constants \(K,C\), initialization takes at most \(Cn^K\) operations and at most \(Cn^K\) words are stored at any time, with addresses fitting the word length. Each individual update takes at most \(Cn^{2-\delta}\) operations and each query at most \(C\), after enlarging constants for small \(n\). The program, constants and \(\delta\) are independent of \(n\), weights and the operation sequence. The machine has no randomization, nonuniform advice or unit-cost unbounded-precision arithmetic. A path certificate is not required.

cards.title: Worst-case sample complexity of trace reconstruction
cards.formal: For every fixed deletion probability \(\delta \in (0,1)\), determine, up to constant factors as \(n\to \infty , N_{\delta}(n)\): the least number of independent deletion traces that permit exact reconstruction of every unknown n-bit string with success probability at least \(2/3\), with no processing-time bound.
cards.definitions: For \(x\in \{0,1\}^{n}, a\) deletion trace is generated by independently retaining each input bit with probability \(1- \delta\) and concatenating the retained bits in their original order. Let \(\mu _{x,\delta}\) be its probability distribution on ⋃_\(\{k=0\}^{n}\{0,1\}^{k}\). Different traces use independent deletion masks. The estimator is given \(n, \delta\) and m independent samples from \(\mu _{x,\delta}\); it receives neither deletion positions nor direct access to x. Its output is an element of \(\{0,1\}^{n}\), and success means equality to the entire original string. One estimator for the given n and \(\delta\) must succeed for every x with probability at least \(2/3\) over the traces and any internal randomness. There is no restriction on processing time, storage, description length or computation between observations: this card asks an information-theoretic sample-complexity question. Formally, let \(N_{\delta}(n)\) be the smallest integer m for which such an estimator exists. The requested asymptotic constants may depend on \(\delta\), but not on n or x. The value is finite because a trace of length n reveals the entire string, and this event has positive probability \((1- \delta )^{n}\). The string is adversarially chosen and has no codebook, sparsity, separation, randomness or other structural promise. Traces are ordinary linear subsequences without cyclic shifts.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(f_{\delta}(n)\) and, for every fixed \(\delta \in (0,1)\), constants \(0<c_{\delta}\le C_{\delta}<\infty\) such that \(c_{\delta} f_{\delta}(n)\le N_{\delta}(n)\le C_{\delta} f_{\delta}(n)\) for all \(n\ge 2\), allowing finitely many small n to be absorbed into the constants. Prove both the reconstruction guarantee and the worst-case information-theoretic lower bound in Lean. The dependence on n must be determined within constant factors; deciding only whether a polynomial number of traces suffices does not necessarily determine it.
cards.why: A fundamental question about how much information random subsequences preserve: can every string be identified from polynomially many observations despite completely hidden alignment?

context_blocks.text: The target is the sample-complexity function, including its growth if it is polynomial. The older polynomial-sample question is one qualitative consequence of a determination, rather than the entire target.

The input is one unknown string, observed repeatedly through independent losses of symbols. A surviving output bit carries its value but loses its original index. Repetition gives more evidence about the same underlying string, so the question is how many damaged copies contain enough information for exact recovery in the worst case.

There is an immediate exponential upper bound: with probability \((1- \delta )^{n} a\) trace suffers no deletions and reveals the entire string. After sufficiently many samples, such a length-n trace appears with high probability. The challenge is to extract the same information from much shorter typical traces without waiting for this rare event. Their lengths are observable, so the no-deletion event is recognizable.

Lower bounds can focus on two carefully selected strings whose trace distributions are extremely close. If even this binary hypothesis test needs many samples, reconstructing an arbitrary string cannot need fewer. Chase gives a lower bound of \(\Omega (n^{3/2}/\log ^{7} n)\) for fixed deletion probability. This is a substantial obstruction to near-linear reconstruction, but it remains polynomial and is therefore consistent with the target.

Chase’s earlier general upper bound uses \(\exp (\widetilde{O} (n^{1/5}))\) traces. This substantially improved previous subexponential bounds, but left a large gap above the polynomial lower bound. The saved ICALP 2025 source accurately described that frontier at publication; it is no longer the latest general sample upper bound.

Burudgunte, Valiant and Wang’s July 2026 preprint proves a quasipolynomial sample upper bound, including every fixed positive retention probability. Its theorem bounds the number of traces by \(\exp (p^{- 7/3}(\log _{2} n)^{c})\) for an absolute constant c, where \(p=1- \delta\). The strategy uses global statistics involving polylogarithmically many trace positions. It improves the upper frontier considerably while still leaving a gap to a fixed polynomial in n.

The same paper explicitly separates sample complexity from running time. Maximum-likelihood reconstruction can reuse these traces while comparing exponentially many candidate strings, whereas distinguishing two supplied candidates can be implemented much faster. The quasipolynomial sample theorem does not provide quasipolynomial time for reconstructing an arbitrary unknown string. Since this card imposes no processing-time limit, this distinction does not weaken the sample result.

The change in statistics matters. A local statistical-query procedure learns only approximate expectations of functions inspecting a short consecutive block of trace positions. Chen and coauthors prove strong accuracy requirements for that model, nearly matching the older subexponential algorithm. Those lower bounds do not apply to unrestricted use of individual traces or to statistics involving widely separated positions. Thus the new global approach does not contradict the local-query barrier.

Structural promises can also make the problem easier. Aamand, Liu and Narayanan show that \(O(n \log  n)\) traces suffice, with polynomial processing time, when successive ones are separated by sufficiently many zeros and the deletion probability is a sufficiently small constant. Their definition requires polylogarithmic separation. The theorem cannot be applied to arbitrary dense strings or to every constant deletion probability without additional arguments.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly \(n^{5}\) is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.

Circular trace reconstruction adds an unknown cyclic shift to each observation and asks for recovery up to rotation. The 2026 circular lower bound of roughly \(n^{5}\) is consequently a theorem for a different observation model. It should not replace the linear-model lower bound in this card. Likewise, deletion-channel coding permits a chosen codebook, while the worst-case reconstruction requirement here must cover every binary string.

cards.title: Constant-factor edit-distance approximation in \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time
cards.formal: Do absolute constants \(C\ge 1, K>0\) and \(d\ge 0\) and a uniform randomized classical algorithm exist that, for every two length-n strings x,y, output an integer D satisfying \(ED(x,y)\le D\le C\cdot ED(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) in at most \(Kn(\log _{2}(n+2))^{d}\) time?
cards.definitions: Use the unit-cost Levenshtein distance: ED is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input consists of \(n\ge 1\) and two explicitly stored arrays \(x,y\in \{0,\ldots ,n^{2}+1\}^{n}\). This fixes an integer alphabet whose symbols fit in \(O(\log  n)\) bits and includes binary and fixed finite alphabets. Computation is on a word RAM with word length \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) for an absolute constant B, using random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may draw independent random bits, but has no input-dependent advice, preprocessed database or oracle. All preprocessing counts toward the bound, which must hold on every execution. Success is required separately for every input pair. Output only the distance estimate; an edit script is not required. The constants C,K,d,B are fixed independently of n and the strings. There is no promise about the distance, repetitions or input distribution, and no additive error is allowed. The word instructions are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, conditional branches, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), integer quotient/remainder with nonzero divisor, bitwise Boolean operations, and shifts of a w-bit word; shifts by at least w yield zero. The constant in word length \(w=\Theta (\log  n)\) (or \(\Theta (\log  N)\) when N is the stated input size) is fixed with the algorithm. Address arithmetic has the same cost, larger integers occupy multiple words, and no instruction performs arbitrary-precision arithmetic in one step. When randomization is allowed, a fresh independent uniform w-bit word costs one operation. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.

context_blocks.text: Insertions and deletions make alignment the central difficulty. If a symbol is inserted near the start of a string, many later positions shift, even when almost all symbols are unchanged. Comparing corresponding positions can therefore report many mismatches while a short edit sequence exists. The task is to estimate the best alignment cost without inspecting the full quadratic dynamic-programming table.

For example, deleting the first symbol of an alternating binary string and reinserting it at the end produces an equal-length string with almost every position changed, but edit distance at most two. A Hamming-distance estimate can be linear in the length on this pair. This illustrates why a simple positional comparison cannot provide a universal constant-factor approximation.

The multiplicative guarantee is deliberately strict at small distances. When \(x=y\), success requires \(D=0\). When the true distance is one, the returned value must remain bounded by the same universal C used on arbitrarily long strings. An additive error such as \(n^{0.9}\) can be acceptable for very distant strings while being arbitrarily poor on these nearby pairs. Reading both complete strings is allowed; this is not a sublinear-query problem.

Early algorithms already showed that one could gain substantial speed by allowing larger distortion. Andoni–Onak obtain a subpolynomial approximation factor \(2^{\widetilde{O} (\sqrt{\log  n})}\) in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) time, with a STOC 2009 precursor and a later journal version. Both quantities improve substantially on older polynomial approximations, but the factor still grows with input length.

Koucký–Saks obtain a constant-factor result for sufficiently distant pairs, with an additive \(n^{1- \zeta}\) term in the general guarantee. The exponent \(\zeta\) and the multiplicative constant depend on the fixed runtime parameter. Their theorem makes the missing regime explicit: the additive term cannot be absorbed into a constant times the true distance on every pair.

Andoni–Nosatzki remove that distance promise. Their Theorem 1.1 gives, for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\), an \(O(n^{1+\varepsilon})\)-time randomized algorithm with approximation \(f(1/\varepsilon )\). The manuscript notes doubly exponential dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\). Its FOCS 2020 result was revised on arXiv in July 2022 and published in SIAM Journal on Computing in August 2026. The recent publication date does not change the quantified \(n^{1+\varepsilon}\) guarantee into n times a polylogarithm.

The order of these choices is decisive. A fixed \(\varepsilon =0.01\) gives a fixed approximation factor, but \(n^{0.01}\) eventually exceeds every fixed power of log n. Choosing \(\varepsilon\) as a function of n to force the desired runtime also changes the approximation factor and the hidden constants. The theorem does not provide the single constant C required here. This is a quantitative gap within already very fast approximation algorithms, rather than a question about whether any strongly subquadratic constant approximation exists.

Mao–Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 work improves a different part of the tradeoff. For every fixed accuracy parameter \(\eta >0\), it gives a randomized \((1+\eta )\)-approximation in \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega (1)}n}\) time. The approximation can be arbitrarily close to exact, but the displayed speedup is over the quadratic scale, not down to n polylog n. It does not resolve this card’s constant-factor, much-faster-runtime target.

Backurs–Indyk’s SETH-based barrier concerns exact computation in strongly subquadratic time. It should not be applied indiscriminately to approximation: the known constant-factor algorithms already run in that regime. An impossibility result for the present question would need to preserve a multiplicative gap of the appropriate size while respecting the randomized model and the very small runtime overhead.

The card concerns ordinary strings and numerical estimation. Tree edit distance, distances between languages, weighted edit operations and quantum algorithms each change the problem. Likewise, an efficient nearest-neighbour data structure with substantial preprocessing does not immediately yield the stated two-string algorithm. These distinctions keep the target useful as a precise benchmark for the algorithmic complexity of a basic sequence metric.

A positive resolution would show that constant distortion suffices to reduce this alignment problem to essentially the cost of reading its input, up to logarithmic factors. Even a large universal approximation constant would settle that structural issue. Reducing the constant, producing an alignment, and obtaining practical implementations would remain meaningful subsequent goals.

The separate card TCS-7220 asks whether every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) permits a \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation in \(O(n^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}})\) time for some fixed \(\delta _{\varepsilon}>0\). Its near-exact guarantee does not by itself provide this card’\(s O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) runtime, while this card’s unspecified constant factor does not supply arbitrary \(1+\varepsilon\) accuracy. The user explicitly approved retaining both targets on 11 September 2026.

cards.title: Almost-linear-time \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation of edit distance
cards.formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon}\) that, on every pair of explicitly given strings of total length \(n\ge 2\), outputs an integer D with \(ED(x,y)\le D\le (1+\varepsilon )ED(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\), using worst-case time \(n^{1+o(1)}\)?
cards.definitions: \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions transforming x into y, with unit cost per edit and zero cost for an equal-symbol match. String symbols are integers in \(\{0,\ldots ,n^{2}+1\}\), stored in arrays, so binary and other fixed alphabets are included. Use a word RAM with \(w=B_{\varepsilon}\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) bits for a fixed sufficiently large integer \(B_{\varepsilon}\); unit-cost operations are random-access reads/writes, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction, multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\) and integer division by a nonzero word. Larger integers require multiple charged operations. Independent fair random bits are allowed. For each fixed \(\varepsilon\) there is one algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon}\), and for every rational \(\eta >0\) there are constants \(C_{\varepsilon ,\eta},N_{\varepsilon ,\eta}\) such that every execution on every pair of total length \(n\ge N_{\varepsilon ,\eta}\) uses at most \(C_{\varepsilon ,\eta} n^{1+\eta}\) operations. \(A_{\varepsilon}\) halts on all inputs and has a finite worst-case bound at each smaller length as well. Constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\) and \(\eta\); the algorithm may depend on \(\varepsilon\) but not on \(\eta\). All preprocessing and output are charged; no advice, preprocessing oracle or input distribution is supplied. Success is required separately for every input pair. There is no additive error or promise that ED is large. Only a numerical estimate is required, not an edit script. No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\) or effective procedure generating \(A_{\varepsilon}\) from \(\varepsilon\) is required.

context_blocks.text: Edit distance captures alignment when one sequence may have inserted or deleted symbols. The near-linear target concerns every input pair and every fixed relative tolerance. It asks whether extremely accurate estimates can be computed with an exponent approaching one, rather than merely improving on the quadratic dynamic program.

The catalogue has two related but different targets. TCS-7220 asks for a \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation in \(n^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}}\) time, with a fixed positive exponent saving for each accuracy. TCS-6624 asks for some fixed constant-factor approximation in \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time. The present target strengthens the running-time requirement of the former. Its \(n^{1+o(1)}\) guarantee does not itself promise the fixed polylogarithmic overhead of the latter.

The quantifier over runtime slack is important. For a fixed accuracy \(\varepsilon\), one algorithm must meet \(n^{1+\eta}\) bounds for every fixed \(\eta >0\) once n is large enough. A different algorithm for each \(\eta\), with uncontrolled dependence on \(\eta\), is not automatically such an algorithm. Conversely, this card does not demand a common running-time bound polynomial in inverse accuracy.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain constant-factor approximation in \(n^{1+\eta}\) time for each fixed \(\eta\). Mao and Rubinstein’s March 2026 approximation scheme moves toward arbitrarily accurate approximation, but its stated runtime is quasi-strongly subquadratic. Those advances concern different points of the accuracy–time tradeoff and do not establish the present joint target.

Purely multiplicative error also controls almost identical strings. On equal strings the successful output must be zero; an additive error term increasing with n would violate the statement. This requirement separates the question from weaker large-distance guarantees. The three cards therefore record distinct accuracy–runtime requirements, with their implications stated separately.

cards.title: Truly subquadratic \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation of edit distance
cards.formal: For every fixed rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), do there exist constants \(\delta _{\varepsilon}\in (0,1), K_{\varepsilon}>0\) and a uniform classical randomized algorithm \(A_{\varepsilon}\) such that, for every \(n\ge 1\) and every pair of length-n strings \(x,y, A_{\varepsilon}\) runs in at most \(K_{\varepsilon}(n+2)^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}}\) time and outputs an integer D satisfying \(ED(x,y)\le D\le (1+\varepsilon )ED(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\)? ED is unit-cost Levenshtein distance in the model below.
cards.definitions: \(ED(x,y)\) is the minimum number of single-symbol insertions, deletions and substitutions converting x to y; matching equal symbols costs zero. The input strings are explicitly stored arrays over \(\{0,\ldots ,n^{2}+1\}\), including binary and fixed finite alphabets. Symbols occupy \(O(\log  n)\) bits. Use a word RAM with word length \(B\lceil \log _{2}(n+2)\rceil\) for a fixed sufficiently large constant B, with random access, comparisons, Boolean operations, shifts and word arithmetic at unit cost. The algorithm may use independent random bits but no input-dependent advice, preprocessing oracle or preprocessed database. The runtime bound includes all preprocessing and holds on every execution; success is required separately on every input pair. Output a numerical distance estimate, with no additive error and no promise on the distance or input distribution. An edit script is not required. For each fixed \(\varepsilon\) the algorithm is uniform in n and the strings; its constants and exponent saving may depend on \(\varepsilon\). No polynomial dependence on \(1/\varepsilon\), common positive saving for all \(\varepsilon\), or efficient procedure generating \(A_{\varepsilon}\) is required. Rational \(\varepsilon\) suffice for every positive fixed accuracy by choosing a smaller rational parameter.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed existence statement for every fixed positive accuracy, or prove that for some fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) no randomized algorithm achieves that multiplicative guarantee in \(O(n^{2- \delta})\) time for any fixed \(\delta >0\). A result for just one constant approximation factor does not establish the universal accuracy claim. A savings factor that is subpolynomial in n, an additive approximation, or a guarantee confined to special input distributions is insufficient. A deterministic algorithm would suffice for the positive direction, but a lower bound against deterministic algorithms alone would not settle the negative direction. Any conditional lower bound must retain its explicit assumption.

context_blocks.text: Edit distance measures the cost of aligning two sequences when insertions and deletions can shift all later positions. The question asks whether a small fixed multiplicative loss permits a fixed polynomial improvement over the quadratic dynamic-programming scale on every input. Rubinstein explicitly posed this approximation-scheme question in 2018, separately from the search for a fast constant-factor approximation.

The two parameters play different roles. Choosing \(\varepsilon =0.01\) fixes a one-percent approximation tolerance; the desired \(\delta _{\varepsilon}\) must then remain positive as n grows. A runtime such as \(n^{2}/\log ^{i} n\), for fixed i, is \(n^{2- o(1)}\) and does not meet the target. The requirement permits the exponent improvement to become arbitrarily small as \(\varepsilon\) approaches zero. It therefore does not ask for an exact subquadratic algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 paper gives randomized \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation for each constant \(\varepsilon\) in \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega (1)} n}\) time. Theorem 6.1 supplies a multiplicative ED estimate with high probability. This is a substantial improvement beyond logarithmic shaving, but the established quasipolynomial speedup does not provide a fixed \(\delta _{\varepsilon}>0\). The remaining question is whether near-exact approximation can cross that fixed-exponent boundary.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain a different tradeoff: for each fixed \(\eta >0, a\) constant-factor approximation in \(n^{1+\eta}\) time. The approximation constant depends on \(\eta\) and is not guaranteed to be \(1+\varepsilon\) for an arbitrarily prescribed \(\varepsilon\). Thus a very fast coarse estimate and a slower near-exact estimate are distinct algorithmic achievements.

The existing card TCS-6624 asks for one fixed approximation factor in \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time. A positive answer here would not by itself yield that running time. Conversely, the guarantee requested in TCS-6624 does not give arbitrary \(1+\varepsilon\) accuracy. Neither displayed guarantee alone implies the other, so both cards remain separate with the user’s explicit approval.

Backurs and Indyk establish a SETH-based barrier for exact strongly subquadratic edit distance. Such an exact-computation reduction does not automatically preserve a fixed multiplicative approximation gap. In particular, the parameter \(\varepsilon\) is fixed before the input length grows; choosing \(\varepsilon\) below \(1/n\) to force exactness is outside any fixed-\(\varepsilon\) runtime guarantee.

Multiplicative accuracy also constrains close pairs. When \(ED=0 a\) successful estimate must be zero, and when \(ED=1\) and \(\varepsilon <1\) an integer successful estimate must be one. An additive term that grows with n cannot be ignored for such inputs. Weighted edits, tree edit distance and guarantees for random strings each change the problem; none is substituted for the worst-case unit-cost question here.

A resolution would locate a basic accuracy–runtime boundary for sequence comparison. It would either show that every fixed relative tolerance permits a polynomial exponent saving or identify a near-exact accuracy regime with an inherent computational obstruction. This is the scientific reason for retaining the question alongside the faster, coarser approximation target.

cards.why: Determine whether arbitrarily accurate fixed-factor approximation can break the quadratic exponent for a central sequence-alignment problem. This tests a different computational boundary from constant-factor estimation with nearly linear overhead.

importance.reason: A longstanding central accuracy–runtime question for edit distance, explicitly posed before the constant-factor breakthroughs and sharpened by the 2026 approximation scheme. Retained alongside TCS-6624 because one target asks for near-exact accuracy and the other for nearly linear overhead; their stated algorithmic guarantees do not imply one another.

The question asks whether every fixed positive \(\varepsilon\) permits a randomized \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation in \(O(n^{2- \delta _{\varepsilon}})\) time for some fixed \(\delta _{\varepsilon}>0\) on every input pair.
Mao and Rubinstein’s 2026 approximation scheme gives a quasipolynomial speedup over quadratic time without establishing that fixed exponent saving.
The numerical estimate must have purely multiplicative error even for strings with very small distance, and all preprocessing is included in the runtime.

cards.context:
Edit distance measures the cost of aligning two sequences when insertions and deletions can shift all later positions. The question asks whether a small fixed multiplicative loss permits a fixed polynomial improvement over the quadratic dynamic-programming scale on every input. Rubinstein explicitly posed this approximation-scheme question in 2018, separately from the search for a fast constant-factor approximation.

The two parameters play different roles. Choosing \(\varepsilon =0.01\) fixes a one-percent approximation tolerance; the desired \(\delta _{\varepsilon}\) must then remain positive as n grows. A runtime such as \(n^{2}/\log ^{i} n\), for fixed i, is \(n^{2- o(1)}\) and does not meet the target. The requirement permits the exponent improvement to become arbitrarily small as \(\varepsilon\) approaches zero. It therefore does not ask for an exact subquadratic algorithm.

Mao and Rubinstein’s STOC 2026 paper gives randomized \((1+\varepsilon )\)-approximation for each constant \(\varepsilon\) in \(n^{2}/2^{\log ^{\Omega (1)} n}\) time. Theorem 6.1 supplies a multiplicative ED estimate with high probability. This is a substantial improvement beyond logarithmic shaving, but the established quasipolynomial speedup does not provide a fixed \(\delta _{\varepsilon}>0\). The remaining question is whether near-exact approximation can cross that fixed-exponent boundary.

Andoni and Nosatzki obtain a different tradeoff: for each fixed \(\eta >0, a\) constant-factor approximation in \(n^{1+\eta}\) time. The approximation constant depends on \(\eta\) and is not guaranteed to be \(1+\varepsilon\) for an arbitrarily prescribed \(\varepsilon\). Thus a very fast coarse estimate and a slower near-exact estimate are distinct algorithmic achievements.

The existing card TCS-6624 asks for one fixed approximation factor in \(O(n \operatorname{polylog} n)\) time. A positive answer here would not by itself yield that running time. Conversely, the guarantee requested in TCS-6624 does not give arbitrary \(1+\varepsilon\) accuracy. Neither displayed guarantee alone implies the other, so both cards remain separate with the user’s explicit approval.

Backurs and Indyk establish a SETH-based barrier for exact strongly subquadratic edit distance. Such an exact-computation reduction does not automatically preserve a fixed multiplicative approximation gap. In particular, the parameter \(\varepsilon\) is fixed before the input length grows; choosing \(\varepsilon\) below \(1/n\) to force exactness is outside any fixed-\(\varepsilon\) runtime guarantee.

Multiplicative accuracy also constrains close pairs. When \(ED=0 a\) successful estimate must be zero, and when \(ED=1\) and \(\varepsilon <1\) an integer successful estimate must be one. An additive term that grows with n cannot be ignored for such inputs. Weighted edits, tree edit distance and guarantees for random strings each change the problem; none is substituted for the worst-case unit-cost question here.

A resolution would locate a basic accuracy–runtime boundary for sequence comparison. It would either show that every fixed relative tolerance permits a polynomial exponent saving or identify a near-exact accuracy regime with an inherent computational obstruction. This is the scientific reason for retaining the question alongside the faster, coarser approximation target.

cards.definitions: An instance gives \(k\ge2\) explicit strings over a finite alphabet \(\Sigma\), and a table \(d:(\Sigma\cup\{-\})^2\to\mathbb Q_{\ge0}\) encoded by binary numerators and denominators. The distinguished gap symbol \(-\) is not an input-string symbol. Promise \(d(a,b)=d(b,a)\), \(d(a,b)=0\) exactly when \(a=b\), and the triangle inequality for all alphabet and gap symbols. An alignment is a \(k\)-row array of equal-length strings over \(\Sigma\cup\{-\}\) such that erasing gaps from each row returns its input string, and no column consists entirely of gaps. The cost is \(\sum_{1\le i<j\le k}\sum_c d(A_{i,c},A_{j,c})\). The minimum is over all such alignments. Empty input strings are allowed, and the all-empty instance has the empty alignment and zero optimum. The output is an explicit feasible alignment with cost at most \((2-\varepsilon)\) times optimum. Time is measured on a deterministic finite-tape Turing machine in the total bit length of the explicit strings and metric table. The constant, finite program and polynomial are independent of \(k\), the alphabet, lengths and costs. The metric promise is part of the input domain; the algorithm must halt within one fixed polynomial on all input strings, with output correctness required on well-formed promised instances. Ordinary length-delimited encodings list all alphabet symbols, all strings, and all metric-table entries; empty strings still have explicit list entries. If \(N\) is the total number of input symbols, every feasible alignment has at most \(N\) columns because each column contains at least one non-gap symbol. Hence the feasible set is finite and nonempty, and the stated minimum is attained. A zero optimum requires a zero-cost output. Gap costs are charged separately per column and pair; no additional gap-opening or run-length penalty is present.

context_blocks.text: An alignment adds gaps to put all strings into common columns while preserving the order of the original symbols. The sum-of-pairs objective charges every unordered pair of rows in every column. For example, a column containing a, a and a gap contributes twice the cost of comparing a with a gap, rather than one consensus-column penalty.

Pairwise comparison and multiple alignment are different optimization tasks. Pairwise alignments chosen independently need not be realizable simultaneously in one common table of columns. The target optimizes over globally feasible tables for all supplied strings, with the number of rows part of the input.

The classical metric guarantee is \(2-2/k\) for \(k\) strings. It is below two for every fixed \(k\), but the improvement \(2/k\) tends to zero as the number of strings grows. The conjectured algorithm must improve the factor by one fixed positive amount independent of \(k\).

The supplied survey also records extensions whose improvement depends on a fixed auxiliary parameter divided by the number of strings. Such guarantees do not by themselves supply one uniform polynomial-time constant improvement for arbitrary row counts. The source distinguishes the sum-of-pairs objective from evolutionary-tree alignment.

The metric includes the gap symbol and obeys symmetry and the triangle inequality. Nonmetric scores, negative rewards, affine gap penalties, structural-contact objectives and maximization of a similarity score can have different algorithms and hardness results. They are not substituted for this minimum-cost metric problem.

Exact optimization is already difficult, but NP-hardness of exact optimization alone does not rule out a constant-factor approximation. A negative answer to the present question needs the quantified impossibility of every permitted polynomial-time algorithm; an approximation-hardness theorem conditional on a complexity assumption must retain that assumption.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of one rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), one uniform deterministic algorithm and one polynomial bit-time bound that always return a feasible alignment of cost at most \((2-\varepsilon)\operatorname{OPT}\) for every promised instance, including zero-optimum cases. Alternatively prove in Lean that no such choices exist. The improvement and polynomial must be independent of the number of strings, alphabet, lengths and rational metric entries; a fixed-number-of-strings guarantee or a conditional lower bound alone does not decide the full proposition.

cards.title: Almost-linear constant-factor approximation of LCS
cards.formal: Do there exist a universal constant \(C\ge1\) and a uniform randomized algorithm which, for every pair of explicit strings of total length \(n\ge2\) over \([0..n^2)\), returns a common subsequence of length at least \(\operatorname{LCS}(A,B)/C\) with probability at least \(2/3\), in \(n^{1+o(1)}\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: A subsequence is obtained by deleting zero or more symbols without changing the remaining order; \(\operatorname{LCS}(A,B)\) is the maximum possible length common to both strings. Empty strings are permitted. The algorithm outputs the subsequence explicitly and must always output a valid common subsequence; only the approximation guarantee may fail. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. The same finite algorithm and approximation constant work for every input size. The runtime convention means that for every real \(\eta>0\) there exist \(K_\eta,n_\eta\) such that every random execution takes at most \(K_\eta n^{1+\eta}\) steps for every \(n\ge n_\eta\). The probability is over internal randomness on each fixed input. The alphabet grows with input length; a guarantee depending on alphabet size is not a universal constant approximation.

cards.title: Text-to-pattern Hamming distances below the square-root barrier
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/2)\) and a uniform Las Vegas algorithm that computes the exact Hamming distance at every alignment of an explicit pattern of length \(m\) in an explicit text of length \(n\), for all \(n\ge2\) and \(1\le m\le n\), in \(O(nm^{1/2-\varepsilon})\) expected time?
cards.definitions: The alphabet is \([0..n^2)\), and the required output is the list \(h_i=|\{j\in[0..m):P[j]\ne T[i+j]\}|\) for \(i=0,\ldots,n-m\), in increasing alignment order. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. The algorithm must terminate almost surely and return the entire list correctly on every terminating random execution. The expectation is over its internal randomness for each fixed input, with universal constants. There is no text preprocessing supplied for free, and time includes every output entry. The target is a fixed positive saving in the power of \(m\), uniformly over both lengths.

cards.title: Linear-space k-mismatch text indexing
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge2\), does a uniform deterministic static index of every text of length \(n\ge2\) exist using \(O(n)\) words, polynomial preprocessing time, and \(O(m+(\log(n+2))^{c(k)}+\mathrm{occ})\) worst-case query time for some function \(c:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\)?
cards.definitions: The explicit text \(T\) and explicit query pattern \(P\) use alphabet \([0..n)\). A query has length \(1\le m\le n\) and reports every position \(i\in[0..n-m]\) with \(|\{j\in[0..m):T[i+j]\ne P[j]\}|\le k\), without duplicates and in any order. \(\mathrm{occ}\) is the number of these positions. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. A program may depend on fixed \(k\), but cannot depend on \(n,T,P\). Space, time and preprocessing constants may depend on \(k\). The text and all retained auxiliary information count toward linear word space, as does query workspace excluding the explicit query and streamed output. All queries are exact, and the pattern is not available during preprocessing.

cards.title: Space-query exponent curve of gapped string indexing
cards.formal: Determine \(s_{\mathrm{gap}}(\delta)\) for every real \(\delta\in[0,1]\), where \(s_{\mathrm{gap}}(\delta)\) is the infimum of \(s\ge1\) for which gapped string reporting admits static indexes with space \(O(n^{s+\eta})\) words and query time \(O(m_1+m_2+n^{\delta+\eta}(1+\mathrm{occ}))\) for every fixed rational \(\eta>0\).
cards.definitions: The explicit text \(T\) has length \(n\ge2\) over \([0..n)\). A query gives two explicit nonempty patterns \(P_1,P_2\) of lengths \(m_1,m_2\le n\), and integers \(0\le a\le b<n\). Report without duplicates all ordered pairs \((i,j)\) of valid starts for these patterns with \(a\le j-i\le b\); overlaps and \(i=j\) are allowed when consistent. The output may have any order and its true size is \(\mathrm{occ}\). For each chosen \(\delta,s,\eta\), one uniform finite randomized preprocessing/query pair and its constants handle every text size and query. Preprocessing must run in polynomial time; its degree may depend on the chosen parameters. Space and query time hold for every random outcome; every fixed input/query has correct complete output with probability at least \(2/3\), over preprocessing and query randomness. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. Stored inputs, random seeds and tables count. Query workspace is included in the space bound, apart from the query and streamed output. The infimum need not be attained. Parameters indexing the curve select uniform programs; they are not real-number advice supplied to a computation. The target is a dimensionless exponent function, not the memory size for one finite input.

cards.title: Almost-quadratic unweighted tree edit distance
cards.formal: Is there a uniform deterministic algorithm computing the exact unit-cost edit distance between two rooted ordered labeled trees with a total of \(n\ge2\) vertices in \(n^{2+o(1)}\) worst-case time?
cards.definitions: Trees are supplied by explicit ordered child lists and vertex labels in \([0..n^2)\). A fixed unlabelled super-root is attached above each input root; it may not be deleted or relabelled and is not counted in \(n\). Intermediate objects may be ordered forests below this super-root. Deleting a vertex replaces it in its parent’s ordered child list by its own ordered children. Inserting a vertex is the inverse operation, grouping a consecutive block of children, possibly empty, under one new vertex. Relabelling changes one ordinary vertex label. Each of these three operations costs one. The distance is the minimum total cost of a sequence transforming the first ordered labeled object into the second. The output is this single integer, not an edit script. Set \(L=n\). Use a uniform sequential word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_2(L+2)\rceil\), for a fixed integer \(d\ge 8\) chosen with the algorithm. A fixed finite program must handle every input size; there is no advice, precomputed lookup table or input-dependent oracle. Unit-cost operations are reads, writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and integer quotient and remainder for a nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Addresses and stored values fit words; multiword operations pay for their constituent instructions. Randomized algorithms, when explicitly permitted, may generate independent uniform random words. All initialization, preprocessing, tables and output writes are charged. A static query starts without input-dependent private state, and every retained copy of the input or auxiliary information counts toward index space. The same algorithm works for all inputs. The time condition means that for every \(\eta>0\), some constants \(K_\eta,n_\eta\) bound its time by \(K_\eta n^{2+\eta}\) whenever \(n\ge n_\eta\). All preprocessing is charged, and no randomness is permitted.

cards.title: Constant-factor approximation of the smallest grammar
cards.formal: Do there exist an absolute constant C and a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm that, for every explicit nonempty string s, outputs an acyclic context-free grammar generating exactly s whose size is at most $C g^*(s)$? There is one production per nonterminal, one designated start nonterminal, and every right-hand side is a nonempty string of terminals and nonterminals. The dependency graph on nonterminals must be acyclic. Grammar size is the sum of all right-hand-side lengths, and $g^*(s)$ is the minimum such size. The alphabet is part of the input, encoded by integer symbols in {1,...,|s|}.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of one polynomial-time algorithm with some fixed approximation constant valid for all strings, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness theorem conditional on \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\) should be reported with that assumption. Exact optimization and ratios tending to one are stronger targets than the constant-factor question.
cards.definitions: Expanding a nonterminal means repeatedly replacing it by its unique right-hand side. Acyclicity guarantees termination, and the start expansion must equal the input string with no extra strings generated. Each terminal or nonterminal occurrence on a right-hand side contributes one unit to size. Runtime is measured in the ordinary binary encoding of the explicit input, not the compressed output length. Constant C cannot depend on the alphabet size, string length, or optimal grammar size. Arbitrarily long right-hand sides are permitted; the size convention is not just the number of productions.
cards.why: This is a fundamental compression-versus-optimization question: can an efficient procedure recover a representation within a fixed factor of the best hierarchical description? It also supplies a benchmark for compressed-data algorithms, whose costs often depend on grammar size rather than on the original string length.

progress.text: Charikar and coauthors give an \(O(1+\log (|s|/g*(s)))\) approximation and rule out approximation ratios below \(8569/8568\) unless \(\mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP}\).

context_blocks.text: A grammar can share repeated pieces of a string and then share larger pieces assembled from them. For example, a sequence of doubling rules represents an exponentially long run using only a linear number of rules. This makes grammar size a useful concrete measure of repetitive structure, with a finite optimum that can in principle be found by exhaustive search.

The problem is to choose the shared pieces. Two useful repeated substrings may overlap, and a locally attractive substitution can prevent a better organization at a larger scale. A method that compresses some families extremely well can therefore still have an unbounded ratio to the best grammar on other families. The proposed guarantee must cover every input, not only average compression performance.

Known approximation guarantees depend logarithmically on the ratio between the explicit string length and its optimal grammar size. Hardness rules out sufficiently accurate approximation under \(\mathrm{P} \ne  \mathrm{NP}\), but this does not exclude a coarser universal constant. The space between these two conclusions is the question on this card.

The size measure is essential. Counting productions, binary concatenations, or all right-hand-side symbols gives related but different optimization problems. Stating the measure explicitly also avoids confusing exact binary-alphabet hardness questions with the unrestricted constant-factor approximation target.
