cards.definitions: For every integer \(n\ge 1\) the input consists of two length-n binary strings encoding integers a,b with \(0\le a,b<2^{n}\); leading zeroes are allowed. The required output is the ordinary binary representation of ab, padded to length 2n. The machine has a fixed finite program, a fixed finite tape alphabet, and a fixed finite number of one-dimensional tapes with one head per tape. Input strings and end markers occupy designated tapes initially, other tapes are blank, and the output must be written explicitly on a designated output tape. In one transition the machine reads and writes at most one cell per tape and moves each head by at most one cell. The cost is the number of transitions, including access, data movement and output. The same machine must halt correctly for every n and every input pair; its tape count and alphabet cannot grow with n. For a fixed correct machine M, let \(t_{M}(n)\) be its maximum running time over the \(2^{2n}\) pairs of n-bit strings. Bounds concern these fixed-machine functions as n tends to infinity. A matching rate \(g(n)>0\) means some correct M has \(t_{M}(n)=O(g(n))\), while every correct M has \(t_{M}(n)=\Omega (g(n))\); constants and thresholds may depend on M. A fresh hardcoded machine for each n is not allowed. No random access, unit-cost arithmetic on arbitrarily long integers, advice, oracle or quantum operations are part of the model. Changing the padded output convention to ordinary unpadded binary changes the cost by only \(O(n)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give an asymptotic rate \(g(n)\) and prove both the existence of a single correct deterministic multitape machine running in \(O(g(n))\) worst-case time and an \(\Omega (g(n))\) worst-case lower bound for every correct machine. This asks for matching bounds up to multiplicative constants, not necessarily the particular rate n log n. An upper bound without a matching universal lower bound, or a lower bound for a restricted computational model, is a partial result.

context_blocks.title: A familiar operation with an unknown limit
context_blocks.text: For example, \(11_{2}\) multiplied by \(11_{2}\) is \(1001_{2}\): the input integers are 3 and 3, and the exact product is 9. The question asks how the cost grows when each input contains millions or many more bits. The school multiplication procedure performs quadratically many elementary digit operations. That describes one procedure, not a lower bound on every possible algorithm.

context_blocks.title: Bits and data movement are charged
context_blocks.text: A machine instruction that multiplies two arbitrarily large integers in one step would make the question trivial by placing the entire task inside the instruction set. Here each tape head accesses one cell at a time. Arithmetic on long numbers and rearranging their bits therefore take time. The explicit output alone gives a linear lower bound. It does not establish the additional logarithmic factor in the best known upper bound.

context_blocks.title: What the O(n log n) theorem settles
context_blocks.text: Harvey and van der Hoeven proved that binary integer multiplication takes \(O(n \log  n)\) time in this multitape model. Their 2021 theorem settles the upper-bound conjecture associated with Schönhage and Strassen. It does not prove that all algorithms require this much time. The 2025 paper by the same authors states that even a superlinear lower bound remains unknown in the unrestricted multitape model. The gap is between a linear lower bound and an n log n upper bound.

context_blocks.title: The matrix-transposition connection
context_blocks.text: A 2025 theorem relates multiplication to moving data: transposing an \(s\times s\) binary matrix written row by row. Even a \(2\times 2\) matrix with entries a,b,c,d changes its row-order encoding from abcd to acbd. If every multitape machine needs \(\Omega (s^{2} \log  s)\) time for the general transposition task, their theorem implies \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) time for multiplication. The transposition premise is itself unproved, so this is a conditional relationship between lower bounds, not an unconditional proof of multiplication’s optimality.

context_blocks.title: Which later results concern this question
context_blocks.text: Qin’s August 2026 result bounds the width of ordered binary decision diagrams computing a middle product bit on restricted inputs. Width in that model does not bound the running time of every multitape machine. Likewise, arithmetic-operation counts and performance on typical or small inputs answer other questions. This card concerns exact products, the worst input at each length, and one fixed algorithm working at all lengths.

cards.title: Strassen’s asymptotic rank conjecture
cards.formal: For every \(n\ge 1\) and every tensor \(T\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\otimes \mathbb{C} ^{n}\otimes \mathbb{C} ^{n}\) whose three flattenings all have rank n, is \(\lim _{k\to \infty} R(T^{\otimes}k)^{1/k}=n\)?
cards.definitions: \(R(T)\) is the least r such that \(T=\sum_{i=1}^{r} a_{i}\otimes b_{i}\otimes c_{i}\) with \(a_{i},b_{i},c_{i}\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\). Each flattening views the tensor as a linear map from the dual of one factor into the tensor product of the other two. In \(T^{\otimes}k\) the first, second and third tensor factors are respectively grouped, producing a tensor with three factors \(\mathbb{C} ^{n^{k}}\). Submultiplicativity of rank makes the displayed limit equal to \(\inf _{k\ge 1} R(T^{\otimes}k)^{1/k}\). This is exact rank over \(\mathbb{C}\), not border rank, and there is no explicitness or computational requirement on T.

context_blocks.text: Matrix rank has a simple algebraic characterization, whereas tensor rank changes substantially when many independent copies are considered jointly. Strassen’s conjecture says that in the asymptotic setting the three flattening dimensions already determine the answer.

The cubic concise formulation is the target proposed in the personal list. It includes matrix-multiplication tensors, so a positive resolution would imply matrix multiplication exponent two; the reverse implication is not claimed. The 2024–2026 source studies structural properties of asymptotic rank without proving this equality.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) set \(\omega _{n}=\exp (- 2\pi i/n)\), and define \(DFT_{n}(x)_{j}=\sum_{k=0}^{n- 1}\omega _{n}^{jk}x_{k}\) for \(j=0,\ldots ,n- 1\) and \(x\in \mathbb{C} ^{n}\). This is the unnormalized cyclic DFT. A straight-line program is a finite acyclic list of scalar instructions. Each instruction either adds, subtracts or multiplies two previously available values, or multiplies one value by a fixed complex scalar. Input coordinates and any fixed complex constants are available initially. Values may be reused without limit, and all n required output coordinates must occur among the computed values. Size is the number of instructions; each complex scalar operation costs one, regardless of operand magnitude. The sequence and all constants may depend on n but not on x. Constants need not be efficiently generated or have a bounded bit representation. There is no restriction on circuit depth, reuse, storage, intermediate magnitudes or numerical conditioning. Operations are exact and must compute the required polynomial identities for every complex input. This is the standard division-free arithmetic-circuit formulation used to make the imported model precise; subtraction and multiplication by any reciprocal constant are allowed. No comparison, branching, floor, bit extraction, approximation or quantum operation is present. For this linear output map, allowing products of input-dependent intermediate values changes minimum size by at most a constant factor compared with linear circuits using only addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication, as stated in the cited circuit reference. Counting a two-input linear combination as one instruction instead of at most three also changes cost only by a constant factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the uniform lower bound for every sufficiently large power-of-two length and every program in the stated model, or refute it. Precisely, a refutation must show that for every \(c>0\) and every threshold N there is a power of two \(n\ge N\) and a program of size less than \(c n \log _{2}n\). A family using \(o(n \log  n)\) operations would suffice, but the full logical negation does not require a uniformly generated family or such a bound at every length. A lower bound requiring bounded coefficients, unitary gates, limited storage or numerical stability does not establish the target.

context_blocks.title: A fast transform reuses intermediate values
context_blocks.text: For four inputs, form \(a=x_{0}+x_{2}, b=x_{1}+x_{3}, c=x_{0}- x_{2}\) and \(d=x_{1}- x_{3}\). The four Fourier outputs are \(a+b, c- id, a- b\) and \(c+id\). Shared sums let the same work serve several output coordinates. The classical FFT extends this reuse to obtain \(O(n \log  n)\) operations; the question is whether a different unrestricted program can do asymptotically better.

context_blocks.title: Normalization should not decide this question
context_blocks.text: Dividing all outputs by \(\sqrt{n}\) gives the normalized DFT. In the unbounded-scalar model, converting either normalization to the other costs at most n extra operations, so the conjectured asymptotic lower bound is equivalent for the two. A lower-bound argument tied to one normalization may nevertheless fail for the other when its coefficients are restricted.

context_blocks.title: What the classical lower bound assumes
context_blocks.text: Morgenstern’s lower bound, recalled in both full sources, gives order n log n for the unnormalized transform when scalar magnitudes have a fixed bound. The determinant magnitude of that transform is \(n^{n/2}\), whereas the normalized matrix has determinant magnitude one. Arbitrarily large scalars invalidate the bounded per-operation growth used by that result. Thus the known theorem does not already settle this card.

context_blocks.title: Unitary and well-conditioned models
context_blocks.text: Ailon proves an n log n bound for normalized Fourier computation with two-coordinate unitary gates and no extra storage. Subsequent results relate possible speedup to numerical ill-conditioning. These are meaningful restrictions on computations; the present model permits general arithmetic, arbitrary reuse and large intermediate values, so those lower bounds have a narrower scope.

context_blocks.title: Related tasks use different cost measures
context_blocks.text: The 2026 source studies necessary divisions in Toom-Cook interpolation at integer evaluation points and division-aware costs. It does not give an unrestricted DFT operation lower bound. Counting only multiplications, approximating Fourier outputs at fixed precision, or applying a quantum Fourier transform to state amplitudes also asks a different question from computing this entire classical complex output vector.

cards.title: Cubic min-plus circuit lower bounds for shortest paths
cards.formal: For \(n \ge  2\), assign an arbitrary nonnegative real weight \(x_{ij}\) to every unordered edge \(\{i,j\}\) of the complete undirected graph on vertices 1,...,n. Define $f_n(x)=\min_{P:1\leadsto n}\sum_{e\in P}x_e$, where P ranges over simple paths. A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with input gates \(x_{ij}\) and optional constants 0 and infinity, binary gates \(\min (a,b)\) or \(a+b\), unrestricted reuse of gate outputs, and one designated output. Its topology depends on n but not on x, and it must compute \(f_{n}\) exactly for every permitted weight assignment. Let \(s(n)\) be the minimum number of binary gates in such a circuit. Is \(s(n)=Omega(n^{3})\)? Equivalently, do there exist constants \(c>0\) and n0 such that every such circuit has at least \(c n^{3}\) gates for every \(n\ge n0\)?
cards.definitions: A simple path visits no vertex twice. The two occurrences \(x_{ij}\) and \(x_{ji}\) denote the same input, because the graph is undirected. Infinity is an optional internal constant with min(a,infinity)=a and a+infinity=infinity; all input edge weights are finite and nonnegative. The circuit has no subtraction, tests with separate Boolean outputs, conditional routing, or input-dependent memory access. A min gate directly returns the smaller of its two numerical arguments. Input gates, wires, and reuse of an already computed value are free; binary arithmetic gates are counted. Circuits need not be generated uniformly by an efficient algorithm, so the proposed lower bound is nonuniform and imposes no depth restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified cubic lower bound, or refute it by proving its negation: for every \(c>0\) and every n0 there is an \(n\ge n0\) with a correct circuit using fewer than \(c n^{3}\) gates. An \(o(n^{3})\)-size circuit family for all sufficiently large n would suffice for a negative answer. A lower bound for a more restricted circuit class, for all-pairs output, or for shortest paths allowing negative input weights does not establish this statement.
cards.why: This is a basic unconditional lower-bound question for dynamic programming. A resolution would clarify whether the standard cubic relaxation computation is intrinsically necessary even for one distance when computation is restricted to minimum and addition, and would illuminate why monotone lower-bound methods struggle with paths of varying lengths.

importance.reason: A central explicit lower-bound problem for tropical circuits, linking shortest paths, pure dynamic programming, and provenance computation. The gap concerns a basic polynomial-time task rather than a specialized graph family.

progress.text: Jukna gives the \(O(n^{3}) \min\)-plus upper bound and explicitly asks for a cubic lower bound for the single-pair connectivity polynomial; his framework distinguishes nonnegative tropical evaluation from formal polynomial production.

context_blocks.text: The numerical task is elementary to state: return one shortest-path distance. The difficulty is understanding what can be done by a fixed network of minimum and addition operations. An algorithm that chooses which vertex to process next using comparisons may use information to control its future computation. This circuit model cannot turn the identity of a minimum into arbitrary control flow. Consequently, a fast implementation of a graph-search algorithm does not automatically supply a circuit of comparable size.

A concrete upper bound comes from repeated relaxation. Initialize \(d_{0}(1)=0\) and \(d_{0}(v)\)=infinity otherwise, and compute \(d_{k}(v)=\min\)(\(d_{k-1}(v), \min\) over u distinct from v of \(d_{k-1}(u)+x_{uv}\)). After n-1 layers, output \(d_{n-1}(n)\). Each layer uses \(O(n^{2})\) gates. Nonnegative weights ensure that deleting cycles cannot increase a walk’s cost, so these layers suffice for the simple-path optimum. This gives \(O(n^{3})\) gates.

Every edge can influence the answer: choose a simple source-to-target path through that edge, make its other edges cheap, and all edges outside the path expensive. Thus dependence on the quadratic number of inputs gives a quadratic lower bound, but does not charge separately for repeated reuse of intermediate computations. The missing factor n is the substantive issue.

For all-pairs shortest paths, a cubic lower bound is known in the same general min-plus framework. Its many required outputs are essential to the usual argument; requesting only the distance from 1 to n leaves room for different sharing. The database formulation places the question in absorptive semirings, where adding an unnecessary detour is absorbed. This card fixes the nonnegative tropical instance so that its allowed operations and output are unambiguous.

cards.title: Linear-size circuits for integer multiplication
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(C>0\) and \(n_{0}\ge 1\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}, a\) Boolean circuit of at most Cn gates maps every pair of n-bit unsigned integers to all 2n bits of their exact product?
cards.definitions: The circuit has input bits \(a_{0},\ldots ,a_{n- 1},b_{0},\ldots ,b_{n- 1}\), representing \(a=\sum_{i}a_{i}2^{i}\) and \(b=\sum_{i}b_{i}2^{i}\), and output bits \(c_{0},\ldots ,c_{2n- 1}\) satisfying \(\sum_{j}c_{j}2\)ʲ=ab. Gates are two-input AND and OR and one-input NOT; constants 0 and 1 are allowed. Size counts gates, excluding input nodes and output wires. Fan-out and depth are unrestricted. There is one circuit for each n, with no uniformity requirement on how these circuits are generated. Every input must be answered exactly, with no randomness. Leading zeros are permitted. Let \(M(n)\) be the minimum gate count in this model; the proposition is \(M(n)=O(n)\). Changing to any other fixed functionally complete bounded-fan-in Boolean basis changes size by only a constant factor.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the quantified linear-size upper bound, or prove its negation: for every C and every \(n_{0}\) there is \(n\ge n_{0}\) with \(M(n)>Cn\). A lower bound \(c\cdot n\) with fixed c, a lower bound for bounded depth or restricted wiring, or a limitation of a particular multiplication algorithm does not give the required negative answer. A uniform linear-bit-time algorithm would imply the upper bound, but is a stronger demand than the existence of these nonuniform circuits.

context_blocks.text: Addition admits circuits whose gate count grows linearly with the input width. Multiplication is another elementary arithmetic operation, but the corresponding linear-size bound remains unknown. Goldreich singles it out immediately after the general challenge of proving a superlinear Boolean-circuit lower bound for an explicit function.

The circuit computes every output bit, including carries and the most significant half of the product. Treating a multiplication instruction on a whole machine word as one operation would hide the work being measured. The target concerns exact Boolean computation at individual-bit granularity.

Viola’s author manuscript, carrying a 2023–2026 revision notice, explicitly retains the linear-size multiplication question in Section 4.2. It also proves that multiplication and squaring are equivalent for this linear-size threshold: multiplication gives squaring immediately, and the converse uses squares together with linear-size addition and subtraction.

A negative answer would give a superlinear lower bound for a particularly concrete, efficiently computable family of multi-output Boolean functions. It would apply even to circuits tailored separately to each input length. A positive answer would show that the familiar logarithmic overhead of fast multiplication constructions is not necessary in this circuit model.

The existing TCS-7174 asks for optimal time on a deterministic multitape Turing machine. This card asks only about nonuniform gate count. The archived Karatsuba entry TCS-5168 concerns a reversible pebbling tradeoff, and TCS-6494 asks for a particular reduction from matrix transposition; neither is this unrestricted linear-size question.

cards.title: Optimal multilinear-formula size of the permanent
cards.formal: Determine the growth of \(\log _{2} F(n)\) up to universal multiplicative constants as \(n\to \infty\), where \(F(n)\) is the minimum size of a multilinear arithmetic formula over \(\mathbb{C}\) computing \(\operatorname{perm}_{n}\). Equivalently, find a positive function \(g(n)\) and constants \(a,A>0,n_{0}\) such that \(2^{a g(n)}\le F(n)\le 2^{A g(n)}\) for every integer \(n\ge n_{0}\).
cards.definitions: The permanent is \(\operatorname{perm}_{n}(X)=\sum_{\pi \in S_{n}}\prod _{i=1}^{n} x_{i,\pi (i)}\). An arithmetic formula is a finite rooted tree with variable or complex-constant leaves and binary addition or multiplication gates, evaluated as a commutative polynomial. Every gate must compute a multilinear polynomial: every variable has degree at most one in every monomial after cancellation. The formula must agree identically with \(\operatorname{perm}_{n}\) on \(\mathbb{C} ^{n^{2}}\), not merely on Boolean inputs. Size counts all gates, including leaves. No restriction on the numerical complexity of complex constants is imposed. Let \(F(n)\) be the minimum such size; it is attained because sizes are positive integers and the defining sum of monomials is a valid finite multilinear formula. The independent variables are the \(n^{2}\) entries of the matrix; n denotes its row count. Internal computations are required to be multilinear as polynomials after cancellation, not just at the output. Sharing of subexpressions is forbidden by the tree model. The requested precision is constant factors in \(\log _{2} F(n)\), not constant factors in \(F(n)\).

context_blocks.text: Multilinear formulas give a restricted but important setting in which superpolynomial lower bounds are known for an explicit central polynomial. The exponential target asks how far that separation can be taken even after substantial algebraic structure is imposed.

Raz’s lower bound grows as \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\), which is superpolynomial but not exponential in n. The broader permanent circuit problem permits sharing subcomputations and intermediate nonmultilinear polynomials, so these are not interchangeable targets. The survey records the unresolved exponential strengthening.

context_blocks.title: The full exponent instead of one proposed endpoint
context_blocks.text: The original conjecture asks for \(F(n)\ge 2^{cn}\). The retained card asks for its actual growth on the logarithmic scale, allowing an intermediate answer. Raz’s lower bound is \(n^{\Omega (\log  n)}\); the standard inclusion-exclusion formula gives an upper bound \(2^{O(n)}\) and is multilinear at every gate because its factors use different rows. No equivalence between the new determination task and the original conjecture is asserted.

cards.why: Establish a qualitatively stronger explicit algebraic lower bound in one of the few models already admitting superpolynomial separations.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a positive function \(g(n)\) and prove the two bounds displayed in the statement for the specified formula model, with constants independent of n. Merely restating \(\log _{2} F(n)\), proving a bound for constant depth or prohibiting cancellation adds restrictions not present here. This is an asymptotic exponent target, not a pointwise 0.01 approximation. The original exponential lower-bound conjecture would give \(g(n)=n\), using the known exponential-size upper bound.

cards.title: Hilbert’s tenth problem over the rationals
cards.formal: Does there exist a Turing machine that, given any integer-coefficient polynomial \(f(X_{1},\ldots ,X_{m})\), always halts and correctly decides whether $\exists (q_1,\ldots,q_m)\in\mathbb Q^m:f(q_1,\ldots,q_m)=0$? The number of variables and polynomial degree are unrestricted parts of the finite input.
cards.definitions: Encode \(m\ge 1\) and a finite list of monomials, each with a signed binary integer coefficient and an m-tuple of nonnegative binary exponents. Repeated monomials may be combined effectively; zero polynomials are allowed. A rational solution consists of exact fractions \(q_{i}=a_{i}/b_{i}\), where \(a_{i}\in \mathbb{Z}\) and \(b_{i}\) is a positive integer, with no prescribed bound on numerators or denominators. The required algorithm is one finite deterministic program, independent of m, degree, and coefficients. It must return yes exactly when a rational zero exists and no otherwise; it may use any finite amount of time and space on each input. Malformed encodings are rejected. The task supplies no oracle, height inequalities, integrality constraints on the unknowns, or promise of a solution. Rational coefficients would give an equivalent problem by clearing coefficient denominators. A finite system \(f_{1}=\cdots =f_{r}=0\) is equivalent over \(\mathbb{Q}\) to the single equation \(f_{1}^{2}+\cdots +f_{r}^{2}=0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: This is a fundamental boundary between algorithmic arithmetic and undecidability. It asks whether exact rational polynomial constraints admit any general terminating solver, connecting computation, logical definability, and the arithmetic geometry of rational points.

importance.reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.

progress.text: The Davis–Putnam–Robinson–Matiyasevich theorem settles the integer-solution problem negatively. The rational-solution analogue remains distinct.
Koenigsmann gives a universal first-order definition of \(\mathbb{Z}\) in \(\mathbb{Q}\) and related low-quantifier undecidability results. This does not supply an existential definition.
Anscombe and coauthors survey local-global methods and explicitly identify Hilbert’s tenth problem over number fields, including \(\mathbb{Q}\), as open.
Garcia-Fritz, Pasten, and Vidaux prove undecidability after adjoining finitely many height-comparison conditions. Those extra conditions are not part of ordinary rational solvability.

Rank-stability advances imply undecidability over rings of integers of all number fields. Poonen’s account dated 3 July 2026 reviews the proof and gives an alternative Diophantine-definability argument; the domains remain rings of integers.

context_blocks.text: Rational tuples can be enumerated by increasing bounds on their numerators and denominators, and substitution into an integer polynomial is exact and computable. Thus yes-instances can already be recognized eventually. The difficulty is knowing when to stop searching and certify that no rational point exists. The question asks about computability itself, before any requirement of efficiency.

Hilbert’s original problem required integer solutions. Matiyasevich’s completion of the Davis–Putnam–Robinson program proves that version undecidable. Permitting fractions changes the problem: a polynomial can have a rational zero and no integer zero, so applying a rational solver directly to the same equation would not decide the integer problem. A reduction must encode the missing integrality restriction using only the allowed rational polynomial equations.

An existential definition of \(\mathbb{Z}\) inside \(\mathbb{Q}\) would provide such an encoding and imply undecidability. Koenigsmann instead gives a universal definition of the integers, which is a major advance in definability but uses a different quantifier form. The full first-order theory of \(\mathbb{Q}\) is already undecidable; the unresolved target concerns its existential fragment.

Recent results settle the analogous problem over the ring of integers of every number field. A ring of integers restricts denominators; it is not the whole number field. In particular the ring of integers of \(\mathbb{Q}\) is \(\mathbb{Z}\), so this breakthrough does not decide the question on this card. Poonen’s July 2026 account explains how rank stability of abelian varieties yields the required Diophantine definitions for those rings.

Other nearby formulations add conditions comparing heights of rational coordinates. Garcia-Fritz, Pasten, and Vidaux prove an undecidability result with finitely many such conditions. Their formulation includes predicates absent here, and their paper explicitly retains ordinary Hilbert’s tenth problem over \(\mathbb{Q}\) as open. This distinction matters when interpreting a result whose title refers to undecidable effectivity for rational points.

A resolution would locate a fundamental computability boundary for exact arithmetic constraints and the geometry of rational points.

cards.context:
Rational tuples can be enumerated by increasing bounds on their numerators and denominators, and substitution into an integer polynomial is exact and computable. Thus yes-instances can already be recognized eventually. The difficulty is knowing when to stop searching and certify that no rational point exists. The question asks about computability itself, before any requirement of efficiency.

Hilbert’s original problem required integer solutions. Matiyasevich’s completion of the Davis–Putnam–Robinson program proves that version undecidable. Permitting fractions changes the problem: a polynomial can have a rational zero and no integer zero, so applying a rational solver directly to the same equation would not decide the integer problem. A reduction must encode the missing integrality restriction using only the allowed rational polynomial equations.

An existential definition of \(\mathbb{Z}\) inside \(\mathbb{Q}\) would provide such an encoding and imply undecidability. Koenigsmann instead gives a universal definition of the integers, which is a major advance in definability but uses a different quantifier form. The full first-order theory of \(\mathbb{Q}\) is already undecidable; the unresolved target concerns its existential fragment. 

Recent results settle the analogous problem over the ring of integers of every number field. A ring of integers restricts denominators; it is not the whole number field. In particular the ring of integers of \(\mathbb{Q}\) is \(\mathbb{Z}\), so this breakthrough does not decide the question on this card. Poonen’s July 2026 account explains how rank stability of abelian varieties yields the required Diophantine definitions for those rings.

Other nearby formulations add conditions comparing heights of rational coordinates. Garcia-Fritz, Pasten, and Vidaux prove an undecidability result with finitely many such conditions. Their formulation includes predicates absent here, and their paper explicitly retains ordinary Hilbert’s tenth problem over \(\mathbb{Q}\) as open. This distinction matters when interpreting a result whose title refers to undecidable effectivity for rational points.

benchmark_focus.reason: A central unsolved decidability problem for an elementary, pervasive constraint language. A resolution would locate the computability boundary for rational polynomial feasibility.

cards.title: Polynomial-time, polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
cards.formal: Does there exist a constant \(C>0\) and a classical randomized algorithm A running in polynomial time such that, for every rank-n rational lattice basis B, A outputs a nonzero integer vector z satisfying \(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}\le n^{C} \lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L}(B))\) with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly encoded matrix \(B\in \mathbb{Q} ^{d\times n}, d\ge n\ge 1\), with linearly independent columns. Each rational entry is given by a binary numerator and positive binary denominator. \(\mathrm{L}(B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{n}\}\) is the lattice, and \(\lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{\Vert v\Vert _{2}:0\ne v\in \mathrm{L}\}\) is the length of a shortest nonzero vector in the Euclidean norm \(\Vert v\Vert _{2}=(\sum_{i}v_{i}^{2})^{1/2}\). Rank n, rather than ambient dimension d or coefficient magnitude, controls the approximation factor. There must be one polynomial P such that every run halts in at most \(\mathrm{P}(\mathrm{L})\) bit operations, where L is the input’s total bit length; output bits and random bits are counted. Randomness consists of independent fair bits. Require z to be a nonzero integer vector on every run, while the length guarantee may fail with probability at most \(1/3\). Both P and C are independent of all input parameters. There are no distributional, uniqueness, conditioning, ideal-lattice or basis-quality promises. A deterministic algorithm would also qualify. The one-dimensional case is exactly solvable by a basis vector. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A central algorithmic gap in lattice complexity: known polynomial-time methods give superpolynomial approximation factors, while key computational and cryptographic questions lie in the polynomial-factor regime.

importance.reason: A fundamental worst-case algorithm question at the heart of lattice reduction, with a wide gap between current methods and the target and connections to cryptographic hardness.

progress.text: LLL gives polynomial-time lattice reduction with an exponential-in-rank approximation guarantee.
Aharonov–Regev place \(O(\sqrt{n})\)-GapSVP in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\); the theorem concerns gap decision certificates.
Haviv–Regev strengthen approximation hardness to nearly polynomial factors under randomized complexity assumptions.
Bennett’s survey documents the polynomial-time upper factor \(2^{O(n \log  \log  n/\log  n)}\) and the unresolved polynomial-factor region.
Sato–Yasuda prove a polynomial bound on PotBKZ’s enumeration calls, without making unrestricted block enumeration polynomial time.
Hirahara–Ogitsuka obtain one-sided-error reductions and conditional deterministic constant-factor Euclidean NP-hardness.

context_blocks.text: A lattice basis can disguise very short vectors as cancellations between long columns. For example, \(b_{1}=(N,1)\) and \(b_{2}=(N+1,1)\) both have length about N, while \(b_{2}- b_{1}=(1,0)\) has length one. Simply selecting the shortest input column therefore has no dimension-only approximation guarantee. Basis reduction changes the representation without changing the lattice, aiming to expose short integer combinations.

The LLL algorithm solves a major version of this task in polynomial bit time: with the standard reduction parameter, it finds a nonzero vector within \(2^{(n- 1)/2}\) of the shortest length. The factor is exponential in rank, even though the running time is polynomial. This was enough to transform computational number theory and enable applications such as factoring rational polynomials, but it leaves the much stronger approximation asked for here open.

Block reduction improves the quality by solving shorter-vector problems in projected sublattices of limited rank. The best general polynomial-time guarantees summarized by Bennett have approximation factor \(2^{O(n \log  \log  n/\log  n)}\). That is smaller than the basic LLL factor but still grows faster than every fixed power of n. Larger blocks improve approximation at the cost of more expensive local computations; a polynomial number of calls to an expensive subroutine does not imply polynomial total time.

Known hardness results approach, but do not reach, the polynomial-factor regime. Haviv and Regev show that approximation within \(2^{(\log  n)^{1- \delta}}\), for fixed \(\delta >0\), cannot be polynomial time unless NP has randomized quasipolynomial-time algorithms. Stronger assumptions give further nearly polynomial factors. Every such factor must be read with its quantifiers: hardness for a smaller approximation factor concerns a more demanding task and does not eliminate the possibility of a much looser \(n^{c}\) approximation.

Decision and search also need care. GapSVP distinguishes \(\lambda _{1}\le r\) from \(\lambda _{1}>\gamma r\), with no requirement on intermediate inputs. Aharonov and Regev place the decision problem with \(\gamma =O(\sqrt{n})\) in \(\mathrm{NP}\cap \mathrm{coNP}\), using short certificates on both sides. This is strong evidence about its structural complexity and a barrier to certain NP-hardness proofs. It is not a polynomial-time search algorithm that finds a short lattice vector.

The intermediate approximation regime is central to lattice cryptography. Worst-case to average-case reductions relate particular polynomial-factor lattice problems to problems such as SIS and LWE at specified parameters. These implications have a direction: an efficient worst-case algorithm would invalidate the corresponding hardness premise, but the existence of a security reduction alone would not prove that every deployed cryptosystem is broken. The exponent, problem variant and cryptographic parameters all matter.

Sato and Yasuda’s May 2026 PotBKZ algorithm guarantees termination after a polynomial number of calls to its potential-reducing enumeration routine. This improves control of the reduction process, including a self-dual variant. It does not give a polynomial-time polynomial-factor approximation for arbitrary rank, because the cost and quality of the block enumeration must still be accounted for.

Hirahara and Ogitsuka’s August 2026 preprint improves the randomness properties of lattice hardness reductions. Under a stated exponential lower-bound assumption for nondeterministic circuits, they obtain deterministic NP-hardness reductions for every constant Euclidean approximation factor. Both qualifications matter: the derandomization is conditional, and the approximation factors are constants, rather than all polynomial factors. Their separate parameterized hardness results also use a different resource measure.

The question isolates the large gap between useful reduction algorithms and the approximation range used in fundamental hardness assumptions. Even an algorithm with a very large fixed exponent C would be a major qualitative advance; the target does not demand exact SVP or a small approximation constant.

cards.title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Do there exist constants C,c and a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, on every positive integer N given in binary, outputs its complete prime factorization with probability at least \(2/3\) and always halts within \(C(n+1)^{c}\) bit operations, where \(n=\lfloor \log _{2}N\rfloor +1\)?
cards.definitions: For \(N\ge 2\), the required output is the ordered list \((p_{1},e_{1}),\ldots ,(p_{r},e_{r})\), with distinct primes \(p_{1}<\cdots <p_{r}\), positive integer exponents \(e_{i}\), and \(N=\prod _{i}p_{i}^{e_{i}}\). All output integers are encoded in binary. The factorization of \(N=1\) is the empty list; zero and malformed encodings are outside the positive-integer domain and are rejected. The same finite probabilistic Turing machine must work for all N. Its random tape contains independent fair bits, and the success probability is over these bits separately for each fixed input. The polynomial time bound holds on every random tape. An incorrect output or a failure symbol counts as failure. There are no quantum operations, input-dependent advice, factoring or order-finding oracles, promises of a special form for N, or supplied factors of nearby integers. In particular n is the bit length of N, not its numerical value.
cards.answer_criterion: Answer yes with a proved algorithm meeting the worst-case polynomial running time and per-input success guarantee. Answer no by proving that every uniform classical randomized algorithm fails one of these requirements for some inputs, regardless of its polynomial exponent. Deterministic factoring would suffice for yes, but a deterministic lower bound alone would not suffice for no. Experiments or algorithms for a restricted class of integers do not settle the statement.
cards.why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.

importance.reason: A defining open problem of computational number theory, with broad consequences for cryptography, arithmetic algorithms, and classical-versus-quantum computation.

progress.text: Sieve methods establish powerful subexponential classical approaches. The standard general number field sieve estimate remains a heuristic expected-time analysis, as summarized in the current large-order paper.
Shor gives polynomial-time quantum algorithms for factorization and discrete logarithms. Quantum computation is outside the classical model fixed here.
Agrawal, Kayal, and Saxena prove deterministic polynomial-time primality testing. The result does not give a polynomial-time factoring algorithm.
Harvey and Hittmeir rigorously factor N in \(O(N^{1/5}(\log  N)^{16/5}/(\log  \log  N)^{3/5})\) deterministic bit operations, improving the preceding exponent-one-fifth bound by a logarithmic factor.

Harvey and Hittmeir’s revised large-order algorithm removes earlier power-of-N lower restrictions on its target order parameter. Their introduction still explicitly identifies polynomial-time integer factorization as unknown; the improved subroutine does not provide such a factoring algorithm.

context_blocks.text: Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to \(\sqrt{N}\) is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Because an output can be checked, a bounded-error polynomial-time factoring algorithm can be repeated until a valid factorization is obtained, giving an always-correct algorithm with polynomial expected time. Conversely, a polynomial expected-time always-correct algorithm can be truncated at a suitable constant multiple of its expected bound to obtain the formulation above. This equivalence concerns performance on every input; success on a sampled family of integers alone is weaker.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate \(\exp (((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(\ln  N)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  N)^{2/3})\). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of \(N^{1/5+o(1)}\) make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.

Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in a more powerful computational model; it does not establish a classical lower bound. A classical polynomial-time algorithm would undermine factoring-based cryptographic assumptions, but the absence of such an algorithm has not been proved from \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) or from the efficiency of multiplication.

cards.title: Prime-field discrete logarithms in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Is there a uniform classical randomized algorithm that, for every prime p, every generator g of the multiplicative group \(F_{p}\)*, and every \(h\in F_{p}\)*, returns the unique integer \(x\in \{0,\ldots ,p- 2\}\) satisfying \(g^{x}\equiv h\) (mod p), with probability at least \(2/3\) and worst-case running time polynomial in \(\log _{2}p\)?
cards.definitions: The input consists of ordinary binary integers \((p,g,h)\), with p prime and \(1\le g,h\le p- 1\), promised that g has multiplicative order \(p- 1\). Set \(n=\lceil \log _{2}(p+1)\rceil\); the total input length is \(\Theta (n)\). A single probabilistic Turing machine must use at most \(C(n+1)^{c}\) bit operations on every random tape, for fixed constants C,c independent of p,g,h. It may output failure on unsuccessful runs. Success probability is over its own independent fair random bits and must be at least \(2/3\) separately on every promised input. Its only input is \((p,g,h)\): no factorization of \(p- 1\), precomputed logarithm table, advice, special-form description of p, or oracle is supplied. Any preprocessing it performs counts in its runtime. The algorithm may exploit the ordinary integer encoding and all efficiently computable arithmetic modulo p; it is not restricted to generic group operations. The group is multiplication of nonzero residues, not an elliptic-curve group or the additive group. For \(p=2\) the only logarithm is \(x=0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give and prove a classical algorithm with the specified uniform polynomial worst-case time and per-instance success guarantee, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A generic-group lower bound, a fast algorithm for a restricted family of primes, a quantum algorithm, or a polynomial bound in p rather than log p does not settle the question.
cards.why: A fundamental inversion problem in computational number theory and a central candidate for separating efficient classical from quantum computation. Its resolution would clarify which arithmetic structure can overcome generic group barriers and would reshape finite-field cryptographic assumptions.

importance.reason: One of the principal unresolved number-theoretic algorithmic problems, with direct connections to cryptography, index calculus, and quantum speedups.

progress.text: Number-field-sieve methods give heuristic subexponential algorithms for prime-field discrete logarithms; their arithmetic relations go beyond the generic group model.
Shor gives quantum polynomial-time algorithms for factoring and discrete logarithms. The classical requirement in this question is essential.
Shoup proves square-root lower bounds for generic group algorithms, parameterized by the largest prime factor of the group order. These are model-restricted lower bounds.
Kleinjung and Wesolowski prove quasipolynomial expected time for fixed-characteristic finite fields. Their theorem does not give polynomial time in log p for the prime-field family.

Al Aswad, Thomé, and Pierrot develop the Discrete Logarithm Factory approach to sharing sieve computations, while continuing to describe NFS variants as the leading methods outside small characteristic.

The card keeps heuristic sieve analyses, fixed-characteristic extension fields, reusable preprocessing, and quantum algorithms separate.

context_blocks.text: Computing \(g^{x}\) mod p is efficient by repeated squaring, even when x is given in binary and is as large as \(p- 2\). The inverse problem asks which exponent produced a residue. A polynomial-time solution would remove the computational asymmetry used in finite-field discrete-logarithm cryptography. It would also solve the corresponding computational Diffie–Hellman problem by recovering an exponent, although hardness of discrete logarithms alone does not establish every stronger security assumption.

A proposed answer is easy to verify: check the exponent range and compute \(g^{x}\) mod p. Consequently a bounded-error polynomial algorithm could be repeated until a verified answer is obtained, giving expected polynomial time with no incorrect output. Conversely, a verified expected-polynomial-time solver can be truncated and repeated to obtain constant success within a polynomial budget. This makes the fixed runtime convention compatible with the usual Las Vegas formulation.

The number field sieve exploits arithmetic structure that generic group algorithms cannot see. It gathers multiplicative relations among suitably smooth objects, solves a large linear system, and reduces an individual target to the resulting logarithms. Its usual large-characteristic complexity estimates have the heuristic subexponential form \(\exp (O((\ln  p)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  p)^{2/3}))\). This grows faster than every polynomial in the bit length.

Generic lower bounds do not settle the concrete prime-field problem. Shoup proves a square-root barrier in the size of the largest prime factor of a group’s order when elements are accessed through an abstract random encoding. The present algorithm receives actual residues and can use their number-theoretic structure, as the sieve already does. A proof against the oracle model cannot simply be transferred to this richer interface.

The field regime is crucial. Kleinjung and Wesolowski give a rigorous expected-time bound \((p\cdot d)^{2\log _{2}d+O(1)}\) for discrete logarithms in \(F_{p^{d}}\). For fixed p and growing extension degree d this is quasipolynomial in the input size. For prime fields \(d=1\) and growing p, that expression is merely polynomial in p, which is exponential in its binary length. Their breakthrough therefore leaves this question open.

Later sieve work also studies how preprocessing can be shared across targets and across fields. The Discrete Logarithm Factory paper develops such improvements, especially for non-prime fields, and distinguishes the cost of a target logarithm from the cost of building reusable data. Here all preprocessing is charged to the algorithm on a single input, so a cheap online lookup after a very expensive table construction is insufficient.

Exponentiation is efficient, but reversing it requires identifying one exponent among \(p- 1\) possibilities.
A solution would remove a foundational computational asymmetry used in finite-field cryptography.

The saved review distinguishes prime fields from fixed-characteristic extension fields and explains why generic-group lower bounds do not rule out algorithms exploiting the concrete arithmetic of residues.

cards.context:
Computing \(g^{x}\) mod p is efficient by repeated squaring, even when x is given in binary and is as large as \(p- 2\). The inverse problem asks which exponent produced a residue. A polynomial-time solution would remove the computational asymmetry used in finite-field discrete-logarithm cryptography. It would also solve the corresponding computational Diffie–Hellman problem by recovering an exponent, although hardness of discrete logarithms alone does not establish every stronger security assumption.

A proposed answer is easy to verify: check the exponent range and compute \(g^{x}\) mod p. Consequently a bounded-error polynomial algorithm could be repeated until a verified answer is obtained, giving expected polynomial time with no incorrect output. Conversely, a verified expected-polynomial-time solver can be truncated and repeated to obtain constant success within a polynomial budget. This makes the fixed runtime convention compatible with the usual Las Vegas formulation.

The number field sieve exploits arithmetic structure that generic group algorithms cannot see. It gathers multiplicative relations among suitably smooth objects, solves a large linear system, and reduces an individual target to the resulting logarithms. Its usual large-characteristic complexity estimates have the heuristic subexponential form \(\exp (O((\ln  p)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  p)^{2/3}))\). This grows faster than every polynomial in the bit length.

Generic lower bounds do not settle the concrete prime-field problem. Shoup proves a square-root barrier in the size of the largest prime factor of a group’s order when elements are accessed through an abstract random encoding. The present algorithm receives actual residues and can use their number-theoretic structure, as the sieve already does. A proof against the oracle model cannot simply be transferred to this richer interface.

The field regime is crucial. Kleinjung and Wesolowski give a rigorous expected-time bound \((p\cdot d)^{2\log _{2}d+O(1)}\) for discrete logarithms in \(F_{p^{d}}\). For fixed p and growing extension degree d this is quasipolynomial in the input size. For prime fields \(d=1\) and growing p, that expression is merely polynomial in p, which is exponential in its binary length. Their breakthrough therefore leaves this question open.

Later sieve work also studies how preprocessing can be shared across targets and across fields. The Discrete Logarithm Factory paper develops such improvements, especially for non-prime fields, and distinguishes the cost of a target logarithm from the cost of building reusable data. Here all preprocessing is charged to the algorithm on a single input, so a cheap online lookup after a very expensive table construction is insufficient.

cards.title: Quantum polynomial-factor approximation of Euclidean SVP
cards.formal: Do there exist a constant \(C>0\) and a uniform quantum algorithm A with polynomial running time such that, for every rational matrix \(B\in Q^{d\times n}\) with \(d\ge n\ge 1\) and linearly independent columns, A outputs a nonzero \(z\in Z^{n}\) satisfying \(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}\le n^{C} \lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L}(B))\) with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: The full matrix, dimensions and every rational entry are given classically; rationals use signed binary numerators and positive binary denominators. Let N be the total encoding length. \(\mathrm{L}(B)=\{Bz:z\in Z^{n}\}, \lambda _{1}(\mathrm{L})=\min \{\Vert v\Vert _{2}:0\ne v\in \mathrm{L}\}\), and \(\Vert v\Vert _{2}=(\sum_{i} v_{i}^{2})^{1/2}\). Approximation depends on rank n rather than the ambient dimension d or N. Use a uniform quantum circuit computation with classical polynomial-time control, polynomially many qubits initially in computational basis states, gates \(H=2^{- 1/2}[[1,1],[1,- 1]], T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\) and CNOT, and computational-basis measurements with classical feed-forward. The classical input bits may be copied into input qubits. One polynomial \(p(N)\) bounds total classical bit operations, gate applications, measurements and output bits on every branch. Classical control and circuit generation are uniform in the input length and use no advice or oracle; a unit-cost quantum random-access oracle for the input is not supplied. The output is a binary-encoded integer coefficient vector, required to be nonzero on every branch; the norm guarantee may fail with probability at most \(1/3\). The constants C and p are independent of all inputs. There is no uniqueness, average-case, ideal-lattice, modular or conditioning promise.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: A short lattice vector may be hidden by cancellation among much longer basis columns. The task is to find an integer combination with length bounded relative to the shortest possible nonzero combination. Allowing a factor \(n^{C}\) is a substantial relaxation of exact shortest-vector search, yet remains far stronger than the guarantees of basic polynomial-time lattice reduction.

The existing TCS-6667 asks the same approximate search question for a classical randomized algorithm. TCS-7169 instead asks about a quantum algorithm for exact SVP. This card distinguishes the missing intermediate combination: quantum computation with a polynomial approximation factor. A classical solution of the matching approximation target would qualify here, but a quantum solution would not automatically give a classical one.

Regev’s worst-case to average-case reduction connects specified GapSVP and SIVP tasks to Learning With Errors. Its consequence has a direction: a suitable efficient LWE solver yields quantum algorithms for the lattice tasks in the theorem. It does not establish an unrestricted equivalence between arbitrary polynomial-factor search SVP and every LWE parameter family.

The distinction matters for interpretation of a breakthrough. An algorithm satisfying this card would substantially change our understanding of quantum lattice reduction. Its effect on a particular cryptographic assumption would still depend on the approximation exponent, the exact lattice problem and the reduction parameters. Merely naming LWE is insufficient to infer that every parameter choice has been broken.

Rank and bit length are separate variables. Increasing coefficients must not be mistaken for increasing the allowed approximation factor, and a polynomial algorithm must include the cost of reading and manipulating their binary representations. The specified gate model permits ordinary quantum computation while excluding an additional oracle resource hidden in a data-access convention.

cards.title: Exact Euclidean SVP in single-exponential time and polynomial space
cards.formal: Do absolute constants \(C,d>0\) and a randomized classical algorithm exist that, given any rational rank-n lattice basis B of bit length L, find a shortest nonzero Euclidean lattice vector with probability at least \(2/3\) using at most \(2^{Cn}\mathrm{L}^{d}\) bit operations and \(\mathrm{L}^{d}\) bits of working space?
cards.definitions: The input is \(B\in Q^{m\times n}\), with \(m\ge n\ge 1\) and linearly independent columns; each rational entry is encoded by a signed binary numerator and a positive binary denominator. L includes the matrix dimensions and all entry encodings. The lattice is \(\Lambda (B)=\{Bz:z\in Z^{n}\}\), and \(\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )=\min\)_{\(z\in Z^{n}\)\{0}}\(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}\), with the ordinary Euclidean norm in \(R^{m}\). Output a nonzero integer coordinate vector z satisfying \(\Vert Bz\Vert _{2}=\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )\); any minimizer is acceptable. The algorithm is a uniform probabilistic Turing machine with read-only input, write-only output and a stream of independent random bits. Every stored bit, including retained randomness and intermediate lattice vectors, counts toward space; external writable storage and preprocessing oracles are unavailable. The time and space limits must hold on every execution, and the success probability must hold separately for every valid input. The exponent n is lattice rank, not ambient dimension or coefficient precision. All preprocessing and precision management count. There is no promise of a unique shortest vector, a random lattice, a reduced input basis or approximation slack.
cards.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer gives an algorithm satisfying both bounds simultaneously with a proof of exact success on every lattice. A negative answer proves that every randomized polynomial-space algorithm fails some single-exponential-time requirement, or establishes an appropriate time-space lower bound excluding the stated constants. An example defeating one enumeration or sieving method is not enough. Exponential-space algorithms and polynomial-space algorithms taking \(2^{\Theta (n \log  n)}\) time leave the question open.
cards.why: A canonical time-space tradeoff question in exact algorithms: can the single-exponential speed of lattice sieving and Voronoi methods be achieved with only polynomial memory?

importance.reason: A longstanding resource boundary for exact lattice algorithms, central to enumeration versus sieving and increasingly relevant to lattice time-space hardness assumptions.

cards.status_note: Open for exact Euclidean SVP with the simultaneous worst-case time and space bounds stated here, following primary literature checked through 11 September 2026. The 2026 sheaf-based proposal discusses a memory-saving regime but does not establish the required uniform exact-success and runtime theorem. Cryptographic time-space hardness is an assumption, not an unconditional negative resolution.

context_blocks.text: The familiar exact algorithms offer two different resource profiles. Enumeration explores candidate lattice vectors while retaining a relatively small search state, but its proved worst-case time is \(n^{O(n)}\). Sieving and Voronoi methods achieve \(2^{O(n)}\) time by retaining exponentially many vectors or geometric constraints. The question asks whether one can obtain the faster asymptotic time without the exponential memory.

These time scales differ by more than a constant in the exponent: \(n^{cn}=2^{cn \log _{2}n}\). For any fixed C, the factor \(\log _{2}n\) eventually makes \(n^{cn}\) exceed \(2^{Cn}\). Conversely, this card permits a large constant C. A polynomial-memory algorithm with time \(2^{100n}\) would resolve the existence question affirmatively even if it were unusable in practice and slower than current exponential-memory algorithms at moderate ranks.

The output is exact, and the zero vector is excluded. Returning a vector whose length is within a fixed or polynomial factor of optimum solves a different task. Ties create no ambiguity: if several shortest vectors exist, any one is valid. Rational input also allows exact comparison of squared lengths, so the definition does not rely on floating-point tolerance or an unspecified geometric oracle.

The standard basis illustrates why practical performance alone says little about the general bound. For \(B=I, a\) shortest vector is immediately visible. A basis with long, strongly correlated columns may describe a lattice with much shorter integer combinations. Preprocessing can improve the basis substantially, but its own running time and memory must be charged. Supplying an already ideal basis would remove part of the problem.

Kannan’s enumeration method uses recursive preprocessing to control the search region. Hanrot–Stehlé’s analysis gives the more precise \(n^{n/(2e)+o(n)}\) time benchmark, up to polynomial input-size factors, and later work reduces preprocessing overhead. This refines the constant multiplying n log n; it does not change that scale to \(O(n)\). The bound is about the method, not an unconditional lower bound on every polynomial-space algorithm.

The inherited Micciancio–Voulgaris paper proves a different landmark: deterministic single-exponential algorithms using Voronoi-cell computations. Its March 2012 revision improves the bound to roughly \(2^{2n}\) time and \(2^{n}\) space, suppressing polynomial factors. The paper explicitly leaves single-exponential time with polynomial space as an open direction. Reading only the phrase deterministic single exponential in its title would miss the resource that remains unresolved.

Exponential memory can encode reusable relationships among many short vectors. Recomputing a discarded value may save space, but repeated recomputation can increase the running time beyond the allowed bound. A valid positive solution must control this global cost as well as the size of each local calculation. Streaming a large list through a small buffer is not sufficient if later steps require repeatedly reconstructing most of the list.

Theoretical and heuristic guarantees also need separation. Pruning an enumeration tree or keeping a smaller sieve pool may work well on tested lattices. A proof for the present question must additionally show that the retained search process reaches an exact minimizer with probability at least \(2/3\) on every input within the stated time. Successful benchmark instances cannot supply that universal guarantee.

A January 2026 paper by Koyuncu–Linker–Ozel proposes a sheaf-based sieving framework and discusses polynomial memory under coarse graining. Its §4 initially gives storage \(O((M+K)n)\) for M initial vectors and K iterations, then suggests reducing memory when most new vectors replace old ones. It does not provide a uniform proof that this replacement regime retains the exact-success guarantee and a \(2^{O(n)}\) iteration bound on every lattice. It is therefore recorded as a related proposal rather than a resolution of this precise question.

The resource gap is also used in current cryptographic research. Albrecht–Lai–Postlethwaite’s CRYPTO 2026 work derives consequences from hypothetical algorithms for hinted inhomogeneous short-integer solutions, connecting them to single-exponential algorithms with polynomial memory for broader worst-case lattice tasks. Its hardness conclusions rely on a time-space assumption; they do not prove that such algorithms are impossible.

The importance of the problem is that it isolates memory as a potential source of exponential speedups in exact geometry. A solution could change the theoretical basis for choosing between enumeration and large-pool methods. Its cryptographic consequences would still have to be assessed through the relevant reductions and concrete parameters; the existence of some \(2^{Cn}\)-time exact solver is not itself a polynomial-time attack.

cards.definitions: The lattice generated by B is \(\Lambda (B)=\{Bz:z\in \mathbb{Z} ^{d}\}; d\) is its rank and m its ambient dimension. Its first minimum \(\lambda _{1}(\Lambda )\) is the minimum Euclidean length of a nonzero lattice vector. Full column rank makes this minimum positive and attained. The output is the signed binary coefficient vector z, so lattice membership and the corresponding integer vector Bz can be recovered without a real-number encoding. Any shortest vector is acceptable, with no uniqueness promise; the zero vector is excluded. Exactness means squared length equals \(\lambda _{1}^{2}\), rather than being within a multiplicative factor greater than one. Use the standard uniform quantum circuit model: a classical polynomial-time machine generates, from \(1^{\mathrm{L}}, a\) circuit on an L-bit input register, zero-initialized ancillary qubits and output qubits, using the fixed universal gates H, T and CNOT, followed by computational-basis measurement and polynomial-time classical decoding. H is the Hadamard gate, \(T=diag(1,\exp (i\pi /4))\), and CNOT maps |\(a,b\rangle\) to |\(a,a\oplus b\rangle\). Circuit size, qubit count, input processing and output writing are polynomial in L. No advice, oracle, pre-supplied quantum state or unit-cost access to an exponentially large memory is provided. Failure is allowed on at most one third of runs for each valid input; it is not an average over randomly chosen lattices. Malformed encodings and rank-deficient matrices can be rejected classically. Integer bases are the imported target; clearing rational denominators preserves shortest vectors up to a common scale and increases encoding length only polynomially.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the algorithm with the stated worst-case polynomial cost and exact-search success on every valid basis, or prove that no such algorithm exists. Classical NP-hardness alone does not establish the negative answer for quantum computation. A polynomial-factor approximation, an algorithm for a promised special family, or an exponential-time speedup does not establish the positive answer.

context_blocks.title: The basis can hide a short vector
context_blocks.text: The vectors \((100,1)\) and \((101,1)\) are both long, but their difference is \((1,0)\). Since every nonzero integer vector has length at least one, this difference is shortest in their lattice. SVP searches all integer combinations of the supplied basis, rather than choosing its shortest column.

context_blocks.title: Exactness is a separate demand from probability
context_blocks.text: A successful run must output a genuinely shortest vector. Bounded error permits some runs to fail; it does not permit every run to return a slightly longer vector. Similarly, a quantum state encoding many candidate vectors is not the requested classical answer until a shortest coefficient vector can be extracted with the required probability.

context_blocks.title: Why classical hardness does not settle the quantum question
context_blocks.text: Micciancio proves randomized NP-hardness even for some constant-factor Euclidean approximations, hence also for exact search. A polynomial-time quantum exact solver would therefore put all NP decision problems in BQP, the class with bounded-error polynomial-time quantum algorithms. This is a complexity consequence of the reduction, not a proved impossibility: \(\mathrm{NP}\subseteq \mathrm{BQP}\) is not known to be false.

context_blocks.title: Faster exponential algorithms still leave the target open
context_blocks.text: The 2025 paper gives exact quantum algorithms with exponential dependence on rank and explicitly separates QRAM access. Hhan’s August 2026 preprint states expected classical time about \(2^{0.6039d}\) and quantum time about \(2^{0.5411d}\), up to lower-order exponential and polynomial factors; the quantum bound uses exponentially large QRAM. Kim’s concurrent sampling preprint also gives an exponential exact-SVP consequence. These recent claims were checked for scope, not independently proved. None gives polynomial time in L.

context_blocks.title: The recent coset claim has a different lattice consequence
context_blocks.text: Simon’s August 2026 DCP preprint claims polynomial-factor approximate SVP, which would not provide exact shortest vectors even if the algorithm were correct. Gupte, Ragavan and Zhandry’s response, revised on 1 September, claims a direct impossibility result for that proposed algorithm. The claim and response therefore do not supply a resolution of the exact-search problem on this card.

cards.definitions: A composite integer is an integer \(n>1\) with a divisor strictly between 1 and n. Even integers greater than 2 and perfect squares are rejected; thus a candidate here is odd and nonsquare. Write \(n- 1=2^{s} d\) with d odd. The strong base-2 test accepts if \(2^{d}\equiv 1\) (mod n), or \(2^{2^{r} d}\equiv - 1\) (mod n) for some integer \(0\le r<s\). For the Lucas test, examine \(D=5,- 7,9,- 11,13,- 15,\ldots\) in that order, namely \(D_{k}=(- 1)^{k}(2k+5)\) for \(k\ge 0\). At each step reject if \(1<\gcd (|D|,n)<n\); otherwise stop at the first D with Jacobi symbol \((D/n)=- 1\). For odd \(n=\prod p_{j}^{e_{j}}\), the Jacobi symbol \((a/n)\) is \(\prod (a/p_{j})^{e}_{j}\), where \((a/p)\) is 0 if p divides a, +1 if a is a nonzero square modulo p, and −1 otherwise. This defines the symbol without requiring factorization as an implementation. Squares were excluded because their Jacobi symbols cannot be −1; for odd nonsquares the search terminates. Set \(\mathrm{P}=1\) and \(Q=(1- D)/4\). Define integer sequences \(U_{0}=0, U_{1}=1, V_{0}=2, V_{1}=\mathrm{P}\) and, for \(j\ge 0, U_{j+2}=\mathrm{P} U_{j+1}- Q U_{j}\) and \(V_{j+2}=\mathrm{P} V_{j+1}- Q V_{j}\). Write \(n+1=2^{t} u\) with u odd. The strong Lucas test accepts if \(U_{u}\equiv 0\) (mod n), or \(V_{2^{r} u}\equiv 0\) (mod n) for some integer \(0\le r<t\). Passing means surviving the parameter search and satisfying both strong tests, with exact integer congruences. The number 2 is accepted separately but cannot answer this composite-existence question. No extra trial-division cutoff, random bases or additional congruence checks are part of the specified variant.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a composite n together with a proof of compositeness and exact verification of the parameter search and both acceptance conditions, or prove that no composite integer passes this specified variant. A finite search bound, a heuristic count of expected counterexamples or a counterexample to only one component does not settle the question.

context_blocks.title: Why combine two tests
context_blocks.text: A composite can imitate some arithmetic properties of primes. For example, \(2047=23\cdot 89\) passes the strong base-2 test because \(2^{1023}\equiv 1\) modulo 2047. It fails the strong Lucas test with \(D=5\). The question is whether a composite can evade both parts together, however large it is.

context_blocks.title: The exact variant matters
context_blocks.text: Selfridge’s Method A fixes \(\mathrm{P}=1\) and \(Q=(1- D)/4\). The main source also describes Method A*, which changes P and Q to 5 when \(D=5\), and proves equivalence of the strong Lucas outcomes for integers coprime to 10. Its proposed strengthened test adds further congruences. This card keeps the imported strong base-2 plus strong Lucas target and spells out Method A.

context_blocks.title: What exhaustive computation establishes
context_blocks.text: The 2021 paper reports that no base-2 Fermat pseudoprime below \(2^{64}\) also passes its Lucas test, giving correctness through that finite range and hence ruling out smaller counterexamples to the strong combination. It reports no known larger counterexample. Such a bound leaves the existence question over all integers unanswered.

context_blocks.title: Recent evidence has finite scope
context_blocks.text: A January 2026 preprint reports that all 200 selected composites in its experiment fail the strong Lucas test despite passing several Miller–Rabin bases. This does not establish correctness for arbitrary integers or a rigorous independence theorem for the two tests. With the specified parameters, the test’s outcome on a fixed n is deterministic; “probable prime” describes the strength of the conclusion, not random choices made here.

cards.definitions: For a positive integer m, an addition chain of length r is a finite strictly increasing sequence of positive integers \(1=a_{0}<a_{1}<\cdots <a_{r}=m\) such that, for each \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,r\}\), there exist \(j,k\in \{0,\ldots ,i- 1\}\) with \(a_{i}=a_{j}+a_{k}\). The indices j and k may coincide, and any previously produced value may be reused any number of times. The length counts the r additions, excluding the initial 1. Define \(\ell\)\((m)\) as the minimum such r; this minimum exists because \(1,2,\ldots ,m\) is an allowed chain, and \(\ell\)\((1)=0\). Only additions of two previously available numbers are allowed: subtraction, division, arbitrary preloaded constants and sums of three or more terms in one step are excluded. All additions have cost one, regardless of operand size; this is an operation-count question, not a bit-running-time bound. A star chain, also called a Brauer chain, additionally requires each step to have a representation \(a_{i}=a_{i- 1}+a_{j}\) with \(j<i\). Write \(\ell\)*\((m)\) for its minimum length. Thus \(\ell\)\((m)\le \ell *(m)\); the conjecture uses the unrestricted \(\ell\) on both sides. The integer \(2^{n}- 1\) has n ones in binary, and the quantifier includes \(n=1\).
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the inequality for every positive integer n, or give an integer n together with rigorous bounds on the two minimum lengths showing \(\ell\)\((2^{n}- 1)>n- 1+\ell (n)\). A positive proof may establish existence of the required chains without an efficient algorithm for finding a shortest chain. Equality is not required. Restricted-chain results, a finite verification range, and validity for a density-one set of integers are weaker than the universal assertion.

context_blocks.text: An addition chain is a plan for reusing intermediate powers. Once \(x^{a}\) and \(x^{b}\) have been computed, one multiplication produces \(x^{a+b}\). Starting from x, a chain for m therefore specifies a multiplication-only computation of \(x^{m}\) with one multiplication per chain step. This correspondence explains the interest in short chains; it does not include algorithms that use division or other algebraic operations.

For \(n=5\), the chain 1,2,4,5 has length three and is shortest, since two additions can reach at most four. The conjectured upper bound for \(2^{5}- 1=31\) is therefore \(5- 1+3=7\). The chain 1,2,3,6,12,24,30,31 attains that upper bound: its last two additions are \(24+6\) and \(30+1\). Exhibiting it checks this instance without claiming that every n admits an analogous optimal pattern.

The target compares the cost of building an integer n with the cost of building a much larger integer whose binary expansion is entirely ones. Its dominant term is \(n- 1\), with only \(\ell\)\((n)\) further additions allowed. Merely finding a chain of order n steps would leave the exact additive allowance unresolved.

Brauer’s theorem gives \(\ell\)*\((2^{n}- 1)\le n- 1+\ell *(n)\). In a star chain, every step must use the immediately preceding value. This proves the desired inequality whenever n has a shortest unrestricted chain that is also a star chain. In general, replacing \(\ell\)*\((n)\) by the potentially smaller \(\ell\)\((n)\) is precisely the distinction that the restricted result does not settle.

Tall’s 2024 paper proves the conjecture for an explicit infinite family of integers with seven ones in binary and \(\ell\)\((2n)=\ell (n)\), and also for their doubles. An infinite family need not cover all possible exponents; its role here is a proved special case, rather than a resolution of the universal target.

A May 2026 preprint claims that the proportion of \(n\le N\) satisfying the conjecture tends to one as N tends to infinity. Its introduction expressly distinguishes this claim from a proof for all n. Even a valid density-one theorem can leave exceptions, and this preprint’s proof has not been independently verified in this review.

There is no contradiction in a chain for \(2^{n}- 1\) being shorter than the displayed bound: the conjecture is an upper bound. Nor must a positive solution provide a fast procedure for computing \(\ell\)\((n)\). These distinctions keep an existence inequality separate from exact-length formulas and shortest-chain optimization.

sentences: An addition chain starts at one and builds its target by repeatedly adding two already available values.
Its length counts additions and corresponds to the number of multiplications in the associated repeated-power computation.
The conjecture asks whether the minimum length for \(2^{n}- 1\) is always at most \(n- 1\) plus the minimum length for n.
The analogous theorem for star chains and known infinite families leave the unrestricted universal inequality open in the checked sources.
Resolving it would explain how efficiently optimal exponentiation plans can control the cost of all-ones binary exponents.
