sentences: Factoring is a central arithmetic search problem whose complete output is a unique prime-power decomposition.
The question asks whether one can factor an n-bit number in polynomial time given oracle answers only on shorter numbers.
All queries must have fewer than n bits, not merely a smaller numerical value.
The reducer is deterministic and uniform, with polynomially many ordinary computation steps.
A positive answer would place factoring in a more structured total-search class and reveal a basic recursive property of the problem.

cards.definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two expansion of N without leading zeroes, and \(n=\lfloor \log _{2}N\rfloor +1\). The output is the list of distinct increasing primes \(q_{1}<\cdots <q_{r}\) and positive integer exponents \(e_{i}\), all in binary, with \(N=\prod _{i} q_{i}^{e_{i}}\). A prime input has the single pair \((N,1)\). The oracle returns the same unique prime-factorization representation on M. Queries may be adaptive but must all satisfy \(\lfloor \log _{2}M\rfloor +1<n\) relative to the original input length. Merely requiring \(M<N\) would be weaker and is not the target. The ordinary Turing-machine cost includes writing queries, reading answers and writing the output; supplying a correct oracle answer is the sole oracle operation. The output length of prime factorization is polynomial in n. There is no randomness, advice or nonuniform family of reducers. The reduction must work for every input, with one polynomial bound independent of its factorization.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of the uniform polynomial-time reduction or its logical negation. Factoring using smaller numerical values of the same bit length, arbitrary smaller circuits for a factoring relation, or an exponential-time recursion does not meet the stated definition. The output need not be a decimal expansion of the input; its prime-power representation is explicit.

cards.title: Capacity of the two-user Gaussian interference channel
cards.formal: Determine \(F(a,b,\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2},\lambda )=\sup _{(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(a,b,\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2})}[\lambda R_{1}+(1- \lambda )R_{2}]\) for every \(a,b\in \mathbb{R}\), finite \(\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2}\ge 0\) and \(\lambda \in [0,1]\). Here C is the capacity region of \(Y_{1},t=X_{1},t+aX_{2},t+Z_{1},t\) and \(Y_{2},t=bX_{1},t+X_{2},t+Z_{2},t\) with independent messages, average power constraints, no feedback or cooperation, and vanishing average decoding error, as defined below.
cards.definitions: For a block of n uses, messages \(M_{i}\) are independent and uniform on \(\{1,\ldots ,K_{i,n}\}\). Transmitter i applies a deterministic encoder \(f_{i,n}:\{1,\ldots ,K_{i,n}\}\to \mathbb{R} ^{n}\) depending only on its own message. Its codebook satisfies \((nK_{i,n})^{- 1}\sum _{m=1}^{K_{i,n}}\sum _{t=1}^{n} f_{i,n}(m)_{t}^{2}\le \mathrm{P}_{i}\). All \(Z_{i,t}\) are mutually independent \(N(0,1)\) random variables independent of the messages. Receiver i applies a measurable decoder \(g_{i,n}:\mathbb{R} ^{n}\to \{1,\ldots ,K_{i,n}\}\) to its own received vector. The probability that either decoded message is wrong is averaged over both messages and all noise. A nonnegative pair \((R_{1},R_{2})\) is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with this error tending to zero and \(\liminf _{n\to \infty} n^{- 1} \log _{2} K_{i,n}\ge R_{i}\) for \(i=1,2\). C is the closure of achievable pairs, measured in bits per real channel use. Gains, powers and both codebooks are known to all terminals. Arbitrary encoding across time and predetermined time sharing with power allocation are permitted; transmitters have no messages in common, output feedback, or communication between them. C is compact, convex and downward closed, so the nonnegative supporting function F uniquely determines it.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all real a,b, all finite real \(\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2}\ge 0\), and all real \(\lambda \in [0,1]\), and prove in Lean that |\(g- F(a,b,\mathrm{P}_{1},\mathrm{P}_{2},\lambda )|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve.
cards.why: A defining problem in network information theory: even two interfering sender–receiver pairs expose limits of our ability to characterize optimal communication. An exact solution would distinguish which forms of message splitting, interference decoding and power allocation are fundamentally necessary.

importance.reason: A foundational multi-user capacity frontier with a simple channel model, strong approximate results and unresolved exact tradeoffs. Recent disputed claims make the precise formulation and status record especially valuable.

progress.text: Han–Kobayashi coding and strong-interference capacity results establish core exact benchmarks; the 2013 monograph surveys the resulting capacity and sum-capacity regimes.
Etkin–Tse–Wang establish a universal constant-gap approximation to the two-user Gaussian capacity region.
Huleihel–Merhav withdraw their claimed improvement by Gaussian codeword memory; the original draft’s citation must not be treated as a valid improvement.
Nair–Ng prove invariance of the Gaussian Han–Kobayashi region under temporally correlated Gaussian extensions.
Nair–Zhao settle a conjecture about the structure of the Gaussian-signaling region for Z-interference channels; this is not a full capacity converse.
Nair–Zhao demonstrate failure of Gaussian optimality without power control and explicitly distinguish the still-conjectured full Gaussian region.
Gohari–Nair–Zhao present a combined auxiliary-receiver outer bound at the Information Theory and Applications Workshop.
Khandani’s arXiv v12 claims the full weak-interference capacity region. The latest proof is not independently validated here; status remains qualified.

cards.status_note: Status checked on 10 September 2026. Khandani arXiv:2501.14941v12 (7 September) claims capacity throughout weak interference. Nair–Zhao’s January manuscript questions parts of an earlier version and disproves a restricted Gaussian-optimality statement without power control; that is not an adjudication of v12. This review has not established the correctness of the latest claim or a complete arbitrary-parameter characterization. Established partial results are separated from the claim. The original proposal’s arXiv:1508.05726 reference was withdrawn in 2018. The 12 September 2026 edit adopts absolute 0.01 benchmark acceptance; the saved open-status evidence concerns the underlying exact question and does not independently certify openness at that tolerance.

context_blocks.text: Two independent conversations share the same medium: each receiver sees its desired signal, a scaled version of the other sender’s signal, and Gaussian noise. With only one sender, Shannon’s formula gives the rate ½ \(\log _{2}(1+\mathrm{P})\). With two senders, improving one link can make the other harder to decode. The mathematical object is therefore a two-dimensional region of feasible rate pairs. Knowing its largest total rate does not identify all tradeoffs between the users.

Han–Kobayashi coding splits each message into a part decoded by both receivers and a private part decoded only by its intended receiver. It includes treating interference as noise and decoding interference as special strategies. Time sharing can also allocate different powers to different phases while meeting the average constraints. Shang and Chen’s monograph organizes these inner bounds and the exact results in particular regimes, including the distinction between full regions and sum-rate capacity.

Strong interference is a solved benchmark. When |\(a|\ge 1\) and |\(b|\ge 1\), the capacity region consists of \(R_{1}\le\)½\(\log _{2}(1+\mathrm{P}_{1}), R_{2}\le\)½\(\log _{2}(1+\mathrm{P}_{2})\), and \(R_{1}+R_{2}\le \min\){½\(\log _{2}(1+\mathrm{P}_{1}+a^{2}\mathrm{P}_{2})\),½\(\log _{2}(1+b^{2}\mathrm{P}_{1}+\mathrm{P}_{2})\)}. Both receivers can decode both messages. With \(a=b=0\), the region is the rectangle given by the two individual bounds. These exact cases anchor the question but do not characterize arbitrary interference strengths.

Etkin, Tse and Wang show that a simple Han–Kobayashi strategy and new converse bounds locate the general region within a universal additive gap. Their celebrated one-bit theorem also gives high-signal-to-noise insights. A fixed gap can be extremely useful for system design while leaving the exact boundary unknown: it does not shrink merely because longer codes are allowed.

Recent work separates several different Gaussian-optimality questions. Nair and Zhao’s ISIT 2025 result identifies a substantial parameter range in the one-sided, or Z, channel where the optimized Gaussian-signaling region needs no multiplexing. This optimizes a particular achievable region; it does not prove that no other signaling distribution or coding strategy can do better.

Their January 2026 manuscript then shows that Gaussian distributions can be suboptimal within a single-phase Han–Kobayashi region when power control is disallowed. Its Conjecture 1 still asks whether Gaussian signaling with power control achieves full Z-channel capacity. Remark 2 reports difficulty verifying parts of an earlier Khandani proof claim. The counterexamples concern the restricted single-phase statement and do not disprove optimality after the allowed power allocation and time sharing.

cards.context:
Two independent conversations share the same medium: each receiver sees its desired signal, a scaled version of the other sender’s signal, and Gaussian noise. With only one sender, Shannon’s formula gives the rate ½ \(\log _{2}(1+\mathrm{P})\). With two senders, improving one link can make the other harder to decode. The mathematical object is therefore a two-dimensional region of feasible rate pairs. Knowing its largest total rate does not identify all tradeoffs between the users.

Han–Kobayashi coding splits each message into a part decoded by both receivers and a private part decoded only by its intended receiver. It includes treating interference as noise and decoding interference as special strategies. Time sharing can also allocate different powers to different phases while meeting the average constraints. Shang and Chen’s monograph organizes these inner bounds and the exact results in particular regimes, including the distinction between full regions and sum-rate capacity.

Strong interference is a solved benchmark. When |\(a|\ge 1\) and |\(b|\ge 1\), the capacity region consists of \(R_{1}\le\)½\(\log _{2}(1+\mathrm{P}_{1}), R_{2}\le\)½\(\log _{2}(1+\mathrm{P}_{2})\), and \(R_{1}+R_{2}\le \min\){½\(\log _{2}(1+\mathrm{P}_{1}+a^{2}\mathrm{P}_{2})\),½\(\log _{2}(1+b^{2}\mathrm{P}_{1}+\mathrm{P}_{2})\)}. Both receivers can decode both messages. With \(a=b=0\), the region is the rectangle given by the two individual bounds. These exact cases anchor the question but do not characterize arbitrary interference strengths.

Etkin, Tse and Wang show that a simple Han–Kobayashi strategy and new converse bounds locate the general region within a universal additive gap. Their celebrated one-bit theorem also gives high-signal-to-noise insights. A fixed gap can be extremely useful for system design while leaving the exact boundary unknown: it does not shrink merely because longer codes are allowed.

cards.title: Optimal asymptotic binary rate–distance tradeoff
cards.formal: Determine \(R_{2}(\delta )=\limsup _{n}\to \infty  (1/n)\log _{2} A_{2}(n,\lceil \delta n\rceil )\) for every fixed real \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\), where \(A_{2}(n,d)\) is the largest size of a binary length-n code with minimum Hamming distance at least d.
cards.definitions: A code C is any nonempty subset of \(\{0,1\}^{n}\); it need not be linear or efficiently encodable or decodable. The Hamming distance \(d_{H}(x,y)\) is the number of coordinates on which x and y differ. Require \(d_{H}(x,y)\ge d\) for every pair of distinct codewords \(x,y\in C; a\) singleton satisfies this condition vacuously. \(A_{2}(n,d)\) is the maximum of |C| over all such subsets. A code has rate \((\log _{2}|C|)/n\), measured in information bits per transmitted bit, and relative distance \(d/n\). The ceiling fixes integer rounding. The limsup permits code families on a subsequence of blocklengths; existence of a full limit is not assumed. \(\delta\) is fixed before n grows. All logarithms in this card are base two unless stated otherwise. The binary entropy function is \(h_{2}(t)=- t \log _{2}t- (1- t)\log _{2}(1- t)\), with \(0 \log _{2}0=0\). The endpoint regimes are known: \(R_{2}(0)=1\) and \(R_{2}(\delta )=0\) for \(1/2\le \delta \le 1\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all real \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\), and prove in Lean that |\(g- R_{2}(\delta )|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve. For a lower bound \(\ell\)\((\delta )\), prove that for every \(\varepsilon >0\) arbitrarily large n admit codes of rate at least \(\ell\)\((\delta )- \varepsilon\) with distance at least \(\lceil \delta n\rceil\); for an upper bound \(u(\delta )\), prove that for every \(\varepsilon >0\) all sufficiently large n admit no such code of rate greater than \(u(\delta )+\varepsilon\). The proposed g must lie within \(1/100\) of the true rate throughout the domain, and polynomial-time construction or decoding is not required.
cards.why: The basic unresolved packing limit for reliable binary information. An exact answer would identify how much redundancy is intrinsically necessary for a prescribed worst-case separation, independently of algorithmic or algebraic restrictions on the code.

context_blocks.text: A binary code represents messages by selected bit strings. Keeping codewords far apart lets a receiver distinguish them after errors, while selecting many codewords increases the amount of information carried by each transmitted block. The rate–distance function asks for the best possible compromise, allowing every conceivable code. It is therefore an information-theoretic limit that must be understood before asking how efficiently an optimal code can be built or decoded.

For a small example, the repetition code \(\{000,111\}\) has rate \(1/3\) and distance three, so it corrects one arbitrary flipped bit. The full set of eight three-bit strings has rate one and distance one, so it cannot correct even one arbitrary flip. Generally, disjoint Hamming balls of radius t around codewords are necessary and sufficient for unique correction of every pattern of at most t errors; this requires minimum distance at least \(2t+1\).

The Gilbert–Varshamov bound guarantees \(R_{2}(\delta )\ge 1- h_{2}(\delta )\). A maximal distance-d code covers the cube by balls of radius \(d- 1\), because otherwise another codeword could be inserted. Comparing the cube’s size with the volume of these balls gives the lower bound. In contrast, disjoint balls of radius roughly \(d/2\) give the elementary Hamming upper bound \(1- h_{2}(\delta /2)\). The different radii create a genuine asymptotic gap.

McEliece, Rodemich, Rumsey and Welch’s 1977 linear-programming bounds greatly sharpen the converse. The first gives \(R_{2}(\delta )\le h_{2}(1/2- \sqrt{\delta (1- \delta )})\); the second also uses constant-weight restrictions and is never weaker. The argument constrains a code’s distribution of pairwise distances through positivity relations, extracting information that a volume count loses. These were the long-standing general benchmarks, but they are no longer the strongest reported bounds after August 2026.

Alrabiah and Guruswami’s August 2026 preprint uses classical-input, quantum-output channels to prove stronger bounds for classical binary codes, including nonlinear codes. Mixed-qubit channels strictly improve the first MRRW bound, and a masked version strictly improves the second throughout \(0<\delta <1/2\). Quantum states enter the converse proof as an analytical tool; the codes whose sizes are bounded still consist of ordinary bit strings. The result narrows the gap without matching the Gilbert–Varshamov lower curve.

Barg’s September 2026 note explains the relationship between this channel argument and a concurrent Delsarte-certificate proof. For the improvement of the first bound, he shows that the two variational expressions coincide. The geometric change is to associate a moving subspace, rather than a single vector, with each codeword, allowing a stronger packing argument. This provides a further derivation and interpretation of the new bound; it does not establish the exact rate function.

Lower-bound improvements require equally careful interpretation. Jiang and Vardy improve the finite-length Gilbert bound by a factor proportional to n in the fixed-distance regime they cover. Yuan and Zhu’s January 2026 preprint gives a concise probabilistic proof of a square-root-n improvement for linear codes and extends the method to quantum codes; the classical square-root factor had predecessors. After taking \(\log _{2}\) and dividing by n, any polynomial multiplicative factor contributes only \(O(\log  n/n)\). Such refinements do not increase the leading rate exponent.

Changing the error model also changes the answer. Capacity for independent random bit flips and capacity for list decoding are not the same quantity as the largest rate at a prescribed minimum distance. This card asks about worst-case pairwise separation with unrestricted binary codes. It also does not transfer improvements for sufficiently large alphabets directly to binary codes: changing alphabet and concatenating codes changes their rate and distance parameters.

cards.title: Capacity of the general broadcast channel
cards.formal: Determine the weighted capacity \(F(\mathrm{W},\lambda )=\sup \{\lambda R_{1}+(1- \lambda )R_{2}:(R_{1},R_{2})\in C(\mathrm{W})\}\) for every finite-alphabet discrete memoryless broadcast channel W(y,z|x) with rational transition probabilities and every rational \(\lambda \in [0,1]\). \(C(\mathrm{W})\) is the capacity region for two independent private messages, vanishing average decoding error, and no feedback. Determine this function with the certified numerical accuracy specified below.
cards.definitions: The nonempty finite alphabets X,Y,Z and the full table of nonnegative rational numbers W(y,z|x), summing to one for each x, are explicitly given. Over n uses, the conditional law is \(\prod _{t=1}^{n} \mathrm{W}(y_{t},z_{t}|x_{t})\). Independent messages \(M_{1}\) and \(M_{2}\) are uniform on sets of sizes \(K_{1}\) and \(K_{2}\). One deterministic encoder, knowing both messages, sends \(x^{n}=f(M_{1},M_{2})\); receiver 1 observes only \(Y^{n}\) and estimates \(M_{1}\), while receiver 2 observes only \(Z^{n}\) and estimates \(M_{2}\). The average error is Pr[the first estimate is wrong or the second estimate is wrong], averaged over both messages and channel randomness. A rate pair is achievable if there are codes with block lengths tending to infinity, error tending to zero, and \(\liminf  (\log _{2}K_{i})/n\ge R_{i}\) for \(i=1,2\). \(C(\mathrm{W})\) is the closure of achievable nonnegative pairs. There is no common message, feedback, receiver communication, secrecy constraint, input-cost constraint or restriction on code complexity. Arbitrary dependence among a codeword’s symbols and time sharing are allowed. \(C(\mathrm{W})\) is compact, convex and downward closed; its support values for all rational \(\lambda\) determine it. Rational channel laws make the evaluation task a finite-input question.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on every rational finite-alphabet channel table W and rational \(\lambda \in [0,1]\) specified below, and prove in Lean that |\(g- F(\mathrm{W},\lambda )|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve. If supplied as an evaluation algorithm, it must terminate on every such input and return a certified value with this error, without a running-time bound. An impossibility theorem for a stronger arbitrary-accuracy evaluation task does not substitute for this fixed-accuracy answer.

It asks for the basic law governing simultaneous transmission of independent information to different receivers, with consequences for coding methods and converse techniques throughout network information theory.

That paper’s narrower Marton-suboptimality claim is identified as a preprint result; accepting it would not solve the full characterization or certified-evaluation task. context_blocks.text: A broadcast channel has one transmitter that knows both messages and two receivers with different observations. This differs from an interference channel, whose transmitters know separate messages. The difficulty is to use one sequence of transmitted symbols for two purposes simultaneously: some structure can help both receivers, while other structure must carry information tailored to only one. A capacity region records all achievable tradeoffs, not just the best sum of rates.

The two point-to-point capacities alone do not determine this tradeoff. If a noiseless binary symbol X is delivered identically to both receivers, each receiver separately has capacity one, but independent private messages must satisfy \(R_{1}+R_{2}\le 1\). If X instead consists of two bits and each receiver gets its own bit, the region is the square \(0\le R_{1},R_{2}\le 1\). Both examples have the same individual capacities and different joint possibilities.

Marton’s coding method introduces auxiliary random variables describing private and shared layers and uses correlated codebooks to coordinate their information. Its inner region is achievable, so it gives a lower bound on capacity. For important structured channel classes it is exact, but neither efficient evaluation of that inner region nor optimality on those classes determines the general answer.

Gohari and Anantharam establish finite auxiliary-cardinality bounds for Marton’s region, turning the previously unrestricted optimization into a computable finite-dimensional problem. They also show that Marton’s inner region and the Nair–El Gamal outer region differ for some channels. A gap between an achievable region and an outer bound alone does not reveal which bound is loose; it is not evidence that an intermediate numerical value is capacity.

There is already an exact multiletter perspective: applying Marton’s construction to successively larger product channels and regularizing recovers the operational capacity region. Geng, Gohari, Nair and Yu develop this approach and establish new special cases. The obstacle in the present formulation is a certified finite answer: an asymptotic union without an effective convergence guarantee does not tell us how many channel uses must be examined for a requested accuracy.

Huang, Liu and Liu’s August 2026 preprint claims strict suboptimality of the full one-letter Marton region. It first finds a ternary-input example with a fixed-input-distribution advantage for two-letter coding, supported by interval-arithmetic bounds. A separate constraint-removal construction then produces a finite unconstrained channel with \(M(\mathrm{W}\otimes \mathrm{W})>2M(\mathrm{W})\), where M is Marton’s maximum private-message sum-rate. The unconstrained example has an enlarged alphabet; the result should not be stated as an unconstrained ternary-input counterexample.

That claimed inequality means a two-use code can beat the one-letter inner bound after normalizing rates per use. It does not compute capacity: further block lengths may improve the region again, and a matching converse is still needed. The paper explicitly retains the general capacity question as open. Its numerical certificates and auxiliary construction have not been independently rerun as part of this card.

On the converse side, Gohari, Liu and Nair’s ISIT 2026 work introduces two auxiliary receivers to strengthen outer bounds. These are hypothetical observers used in the proof, not additional terminals allowed in the communication model. Their reported bounds improve the sum-rate upper bound for examples such as the binary skew-symmetric broadcast channel, while still leaving an inner/outer gap.

Finding globally optimal numerical values is also separate from deriving the correct region. Dou and coauthors develop Blahut–Arimoto-style methods for evaluating inner and outer bounds, with convergence statements tied to the optimization’s structure. Such methods help explore examples, but convergence to a local optimum or to an optimum of an unproved bound is not a capacity theorem.

cards.context:
A broadcast channel has one transmitter that knows both messages and two receivers with different observations. This differs from an interference channel, whose transmitters know separate messages. The difficulty is to use one sequence of transmitted symbols for two purposes simultaneously: some structure can help both receivers, while other structure must carry information tailored to only one. A capacity region records all achievable tradeoffs, not just the best sum of rates.

The two point-to-point capacities alone do not determine this tradeoff. If a noiseless binary symbol X is delivered identically to both receivers, each receiver separately has capacity one, but independent private messages must satisfy \(R_{1}+R_{2}\le 1\). If X instead consists of two bits and each receiver gets its own bit, the region is the square \(0\le R_{1},R_{2}\le 1\). Both examples have the same individual capacities and different joint possibilities.

Marton’s coding method introduces auxiliary random variables describing private and shared layers and uses correlated codebooks to coordinate their information. Its inner region is achievable, so it gives a lower bound on capacity. For important structured channel classes it is exact, but neither efficient evaluation of that inner region nor optimality on those classes determines the general answer.

Gohari and Anantharam establish finite auxiliary-cardinality bounds for Marton’s region, turning the previously unrestricted optimization into a computable finite-dimensional problem. They also show that Marton’s inner region and the Nair–El Gamal outer region differ for some channels. A gap between an achievable region and an outer bound alone does not reveal which bound is loose; it is not evidence that an intermediate numerical value is capacity.

There is already an exact multiletter perspective: applying Marton’s construction to successively larger product channels and regularizing recovers the operational capacity region. Geng, Gohari, Nair and Yu develop this approach and establish new special cases. The obstacle in the present formulation is a certified finite answer: an asymptotic union without an effective convergence guarantee does not tell us how many channel uses must be examined for a requested accuracy.

Huang, Liu and Liu’s August 2026 preprint claims strict suboptimality of the full one-letter Marton region. It first finds a ternary-input example with a fixed-input-distribution advantage for two-letter coding, supported by interval-arithmetic bounds. A separate constraint-removal construction then produces a finite unconstrained channel with \(M(\mathrm{W}\otimes \mathrm{W})>2M(\mathrm{W})\), where M is Marton’s maximum private-message sum-rate. The unconstrained example has an enlarged alphabet; the result should not be stated as an unconstrained ternary-input counterexample.

That claimed inequality means a two-use code can beat the one-letter inner bound after normalizing rates per use. It does not compute capacity: further block lengths may improve the region again, and a matching converse is still needed. The paper explicitly retains the general capacity question as open. Its numerical certificates and auxiliary construction have not been independently rerun as part of this card.

On the converse side, Gohari, Liu and Nair’s ISIT 2026 work introduces two auxiliary receivers to strengthen outer bounds. These are hypothetical observers used in the proof, not additional terminals allowed in the communication model. Their reported bounds improve the sum-rate upper bound for examples such as the binary skew-symmetric broadcast channel, while still leaving an inner/outer gap.

Finding globally optimal numerical values is also separate from deriving the correct region. Dou and coauthors develop Blahut–Arimoto-style methods for evaluating inner and outer bounds, with convergence statements tied to the optimization’s structure. Such methods help explore examples, but convergence to a local optimum or to an optimum of an unproved bound is not a capacity theorem.

cards.title: Li–Li conjecture
cards.formal: For every finite undirected network with positive rational edge capacities and independent unicast sessions, is the zero-error causal network-coding rate region, under the entropy-capacity convention below, equal to its fractional multicommodity-routing region?
cards.definitions: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite connected undirected graph, with capacities \(c_{e}>0\), and let \((s_{i},t_{i}), i=1,\ldots ,k\), be ordered pairs of distinct vertices. Different pairs may share endpoints. Source \(s_{i}\) initially knows its own message \(M_{i}\), uniformly distributed over a finite alphabet; the messages are mutually independent. A finite deterministic code specifies in advance a finite sequence of directed edge uses. Each transmitted symbol is a function of messages initially at its sender and symbols previously received there. Every \(t_{i}\) must recover \(M_{i}\) for every message tuple. Local computation and storage are unrestricted; nonlinear functions are permitted. Let \(X_{u\to v}\) be the whole tuple sent from u to v on edge \(\{u,v\}\), and measure Shannon entropy H in bits. For a scale \(b>0\), the code supports \(r\in R_{\ge 0}^{k}\) when \(H(M_{i})\ge b r_{i}\) for all i and \(H(X_{u\to v})+H(X_{v\to u})\le b c_{uv}\) for every edge. Define \(C(G)\) as the closure in \(R^{k}\) of all such supported rate vectors, over all finite alphabets, codes and scales. This explicitly fixes the entropy formulation used in the cited network-coding literature, with exact decoding and capacity shared between directions; it is not a definition using two independent full-capacity arcs. Define \(R(G)\) by nonnegative real path flows \(f_{i,\mathrm{P}}\), for simple \(s_{i}\)-to-\(t_{i}\) paths P, satisfying \(\sum_{\mathrm{P}} f_{i,\mathrm{P}}\ge r_{i}\) and \(\sum_{i,\mathrm{P}:e\in \mathrm{P}} f_{i,\mathrm{P}}\le c_{e}\). The target is \(C(G)=R(G)\) for every G and session list. No multicast destinations, correlated sources, initial side information about other messages, or computation of functions in place of message recovery is supplied.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove \(C(G)\subseteq R(G)\) for every specified network and session list; the reverse inclusion follows by routing and closure. Alternatively, exhibit a finite undirected instance with a coding-supported rate vector outside the closed routing polytope, together with a valid causal code and a proof of fractional-routing infeasibility. The latter can use a linear-programming dual certificate. Beating integral edge-disjoint paths, a particular routing algorithm, or a cut bound that is already larger than the routing optimum is insufficient. A multicast or directed-network advantage does not refute this unicast conjecture. A theorem about vanishing-error codes must be related explicitly to this zero-error entropy formulation.
cards.why: Asks whether computation inside an undirected network can increase the throughput of independent unicast messages, with direct connections to multicommodity flow and major computational lower bounds.

importance.reason: A central capacity conjecture whose resolution would clarify the power of network coding and influence circuit and data-structure lower bounds.

A separate session-interaction framework reduces the conjecture to a property of all irreducible cores; it does not establish that property universally. Its manuscript corrects a quantifier in the conference definition to require one common witnessing solution.

context_blocks.text: Routing treats each message as a separate commodity that consumes capacity along paths. Network coding lets an intermediate node combine messages before forwarding them. If a node knows bits x and y, it may send \(x\oplus y; a\) receiver that already knows y can recover x. Whether the necessary side information can be supplied cheaply enough to improve total throughput depends on the entire network. The conjecture says that undirected edges always let fractional routing match the best coding rate for independent one-destination messages.

Fractional routing is essential to the comparison. A message may be split among many paths, and different commodities may share an edge up to its total capacity. This is more flexible than requiring one path per message or requiring edge-disjoint paths. The rate region is described by a linear program, so an apparent coding improvement over a greedy routing choice does not establish a gap. One must beat the optimum over all fractional routings.

The capacity convention also matters. An undirected edge of capacity one has one combined budget for both directions, rather than a separate budget of one in each direction. The formal statement follows the cited entropy-based definition: the entropy of each complete directional transcript is counted, and decoding is exact. Taking the closure permits limiting rates. This states precisely which capacity notion is being compared instead of assuming that all zero-error, fixed-length and vanishing-error conventions are interchangeable.

Cut constraints provide a necessary upper bound: information needed across a partition must cross its boundary. For multiple commodities, satisfying every cut constraint need not make the demands fractionally routable. Jain, Vazirani, Yeung and Yuval study the small \(K_{3,2}\) example with four same-side sessions. Its sparsity bound is one, while its maximum concurrent routing rate is \(3/4\); their entropy inequalities show that coding also cannot exceed \(3/4\). The gap between cuts and flows therefore does not by itself give a coding advantage.

Braverman, Garg and Schvartzman show that a counterexample would have consequences well beyond one small network. Any fixed coding advantage greater than one can be amplified into a family with a gap growing as a positive power of log |V|. A general logarithmic upper bound comes from multicommodity-flow and cut relationships. Thus even a modest strict separation would open the door to much larger asymptotic gains.

The conjecture is also connected to computation rather than communication alone. Afshani, Freksen, Kamma and Larsen show that it implies an \(\Omega (n \log  n)\) lower bound for constant-degree Boolean circuits multiplying two n-bit integers. Their reduction turns a sufficiently small circuit into a forbidden network-coding advantage. This is a conditional circuit lower bound, not an already proved consequence of ordinary cut arguments.

Recent positive results remain sensitive to the session arrangement. Vamsi and Thakor’s ISIT 2025 work handles specified asymmetric demands in layered networks, including partition-symmetric demands in their Type-I bipartite family. It also studies gaps between routing constructions and information-theoretic bounds for three-layer cases. Such a gap is a reason to examine an instance more closely; it is not itself a demonstrated coding scheme outside the routing region.

An August 2026 preprint by Liu, Que, Li and Li reports new cases via graph metrics, including networks with at most five terminal locations and certain planar instances supported on at most three designated face boundaries. In the planar case, each session has both endpoints on one of those faces. Five terminal locations is not the same restriction as five sessions or five total graph vertices. The general conjecture remains explicitly open in that paper.

The strongest recent undirected separation located in this review changes the demand model. Braverman and He obtain a superconstant multicast coding advantage using locally decodable codes. Each source message there must reach a set of receivers, and the routing comparison is a Steiner-tree packing problem. Replacing those copies by independent unicast messages removes exactly the shared-message structure used by the construction, so the result does not disprove Li–Li.

cards.title: Capacity of the binary deletion channel
cards.formal: Determine the capacity function \(C(\delta )\) of the binary independent deletion channel for every fixed \(\delta \in [0,1]\), in bits per input bit.
cards.definitions: For input \(x=x_{1}\cdots x_{n}\in \{0,1\}^{n}\), retain each bit independently with probability \(1- \delta\) and output the retained subsequence in its original order. The receiver sees the subsequence and its length, but neither terminal sees the deletion locations; there are no erasure markers, substitutions, insertions, feedback or side channels. Both terminals know n and \(\delta\). A block code consists of deterministic maps \(Enc_{n}:[M_{n}]\to \{0,1\}^{n}\) and \(Dec_{n}:\bigcup _{k=0}^{n}\{0,1\}^{k}\to [M_{n}]\). Its average error is Pr[\(Dec_{n}(Y)\ne M\)], where M is uniform on \([M_{n}]\) and Y is the channel output on \(Enc_{n}(M)\). A rate R is achievable if there is a sequence of such codes with \(\liminf _{n\to \infty}(\log _{2} M_{n})/n\ge R\) and average error tending to zero. Define \(C(\delta )\) as the supremum of achievable nonnegative rates. Encoding and decoding have no computational or storage restrictions. The parameter \(\delta\) is fixed as n grows. Equivalently, Dobrushin’s coding theorem gives \(C(\delta )=\lim _{n\to \infty} C_{n}(\delta )\), where \(C_{n}(\delta )=(1/n) \max\)_{\(\mathrm{P}_{X}\) on \(\{0,1\}^{n}\)} I(X;Y), with base-two mutual information. These \(C_{n}\) are normalized per input bit; the random output length is not the normalization. The endpoints are \(C(0)=1\) and \(C(1)=0\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function g on all real \(\delta \in [0,1]\), and prove in Lean that |\(g- C(\delta )|\le 1/100\) pointwise throughout that domain, in the units stated in the definitions. The answer must establish lower and upper bounds with this uniform error guarantee. An exact determination also qualifies. A finite set of sample values, an uncertified plot, or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit does not determine the curve. No predetermined formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed. This numerical acceptance criterion does not assert exact equality with a conjectured curve.
cards.why: The simplest channel with hidden synchronization errors still lacks an exact nontrivial capacity formula. Resolving it would establish how much information is fundamentally lost through missing alignment.

context_blocks.text: A deletion removes a bit and also hides where it belonged. For example, receiving 00 after sending three bits is compatible with several input strings and deletion patterns. The output length reveals how many symbols survived, but it does not reveal their positions. This uncertainty couples the interpretation of consecutive output symbols even though the deletion decisions themselves are independent.

If the receiver were additionally given the deletion locations, the channel would become the binary erasure channel with capacity \(1- \delta\). Revealing information cannot make decoding harder, so \(C(\delta )\le 1- \delta\) is an immediate upper bound. The challenge is to quantify the further loss caused by missing alignment. Counting surviving bits alone therefore does not determine the answer.

The basic coding theorem is known. Optimizing mutual information over distributions on n-bit inputs and letting n grow gives the operational capacity. Moreover, \(C_{n}(\delta )- \log _{2}(n+1)/n\le C(\delta )\le C_{n}(\delta )\). Thus the issue is not the absence of a definition or an approximation scheme in principle. The finite optimization has \(2^{n}\) possible inputs, and its rapidly growing size obstructs useful evaluation at large block lengths.

The input bits should not automatically be assumed independent. Correlations can make runs of equal symbols easier to identify after deletions. Run-based constructions choose a distribution on run lengths and analyze how deleted runs disappear and neighboring surviving runs merge. Rubinstein and Con optimize such distributions to prove \(C(\delta )>0.1221(1- \delta )\) for every \(0<\delta <1\). This establishes a positive constant fraction of the surviving-bit rate throughout the parameter range.

Near the noiseless endpoint, a much sharper asymptotic description is available. Kanoria and Montanari prove \(C(\delta )=1+\delta  \log _{2} \delta - A_{1}\delta +A_{2}\delta ^{2}+O(\delta ^{3- \varepsilon})\) for every fixed \(\varepsilon >0\) as \(\delta\) tends to zero, with explicit constants \(A_{1}\approx 1.15416377\) and \(A_{2}\approx 1.67814594\). They also identify input distributions achieving this order. This determines several leading terms, but its remainder does not vanish identically at a fixed nonzero deletion probability.

Numerical converse bounds use finite channels in which the input and output lengths are bounded and the transition matrix is explicit. Blahut–Arimoto optimization can bound their capacities, which in turn upper-bound the unsegmented deletion channel. Pinto and Ribeiro’s 2026 implementation handles larger instances, including selected input lengths of 31, and reports \(C(\delta )\le 0.3578(1- \delta )\) for \(\delta \ge 0.64\). These are computer-assisted bounds reported by the authors; this review has not rerun their large computations.

The half-deletion point illustrates the remaining gap. Rubinstein and Con report an achievable rate above 0.104075, while the 2026 upper-bound table gives 0.1896. A universal lower bound proportional to \(1- \delta\) is useful for the whole curve, but it can be weaker than a pointwise run-length optimization. These different types of statements should therefore not be collapsed into one purported best numerical bound for every parameter.

An August 2026 preprint by Chen claims a further half-deletion lower bound above 0.11032415, using joint information from several output runs and a rational certificate. Its asserted slightly sharper upper number is conditional on a precision assumption about a previously published table. This card records the new lower bound as a preprint claim whose certificate has not been independently reproduced here, and does not present the conditional upper number as a separately established converse. Even if the new lower bound is confirmed, a substantial gap remains.

This is a transmission problem: the sender may select a codebook designed for the channel. Trace reconstruction instead starts with an arbitrary unknown string and observes repeated independently deleted copies of that same string. Adversarial deletion codes also use a different error model. Progress in either neighboring subject can be informative without giving the capacity curve with the certified accuracy required here.

Its asserted slightly sharper upper number is conditional on a precision assumption about a previously published table. This card records the new lower bound as a preprint claim whose certificate has not been independently reproduced here, and does not present the conditional upper number as a separately established converse. Even if the new lower bound is confirmed, a substantial gap remains.

This is a transmission problem: the sender may select a codebook designed for the channel. Trace reconstruction instead starts with an arbitrary unknown string and observes repeated independently deleted copies of that same string. Adversarial deletion codes also use a different error model. Progress in either neighboring subject can be informative without giving the capacity curve with the certified accuracy required here.

cards.title: Binary codes beyond the Gilbert–Varshamov bound
cards.formal: Do constants \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) and \(\eta >0\) and binary codes \(C_{n}\subseteq \{0,1\}^{n}\) for arbitrarily large n exist with minimum Hamming distance at least \(\delta n\) and \(\log _{2}|C_{n}|/n\ge 1- H_{2}(\delta )+\eta\)?
cards.definitions: A code is any nonempty subset of the binary strings of length n; linearity, explicit construction and efficient decoding are not required. Hamming distance is the number of unequal coordinates, and minimum distance is the minimum over distinct codewords. \(H_{2}(t)=- t \log _{2}t- (1- t)\log _{2}(1- t)\). The constants \(\delta\) and \(\eta\) must be chosen before n and remain fixed along an unbounded sequence of block lengths. Finite-length improvements vanishing in normalized rate do not meet the target.

context_blocks.text: The Gilbert–Varshamov bound describes a rate-distance tradeoff achievable by random binary codes. Whether an asymptotically better tradeoff exists is a fundamental question about the information lost to adversarial errors.

This is a nonconstructive existence question, independent of whether codes meeting the bound can be efficiently written down. A polynomial improvement in the number of codewords at fixed length need not yield a positive constant improvement in rate. The coding-course materials distinguish these two open challenges.

cards.title: Decidability of unconditional Shannon information inequalities
cards.formal: Does a Turing algorithm exist that, given \(n\ge 1\) and rational coefficients \((a_{S})\) for nonempty subsets \(S\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,n\}\), always halts and decides whether \(\sum_{\varnothing \ne S\subseteq [n]}a_{S} H(X_{S})\ge 0\) holds for every joint distribution of n finite-valued discrete random variables?
cards.definitions: The finite input lists n and all nonzero coefficients, each as a signed binary numerator and positive binary denominator, with its subset S encoded explicitly; omitted coefficients are zero. \(X_{S}\) is the tuple \((X_{i})_{i\in S}\). Its Shannon entropy in bits is \(H(X_{S})=- \sum_{x} p_{S}(x)\log _{2} p_{S}(x)\), with \(0\log _{2}0=0\). Each variable has a finite alphabet, but alphabet sizes are unrestricted and are not supplied as bounds in the input. Joint probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers in \([0,1]\) summing to one. No independence, conditional-independence, functional-dependence, fixed-marginal or support-size promise is imposed. The inequality is a single homogeneous linear inequality, with non-strict \(\ge 0\) and no affine constant, premise, disjunction or nonlinear entropy term. Runtime may be any computable function of the input length; polynomial time is not required. The number n varies with the input.
cards.answer_criterion: An affirmative answer supplies a total effective procedure for exact validity of every such rational inequality. A negative answer proves that this language of valid inequalities is undecidable. Finding a false input inequality or proving an individual new valid inequality answers an instance, not the meta-question. A procedure that may run forever on valid inputs, or requires a promised numerical gap, does not resolve exact decidability.

importance.reason: A foundational decision problem at the intersection of information theory, computability and database theory; it asks whether exact universal entropy reasoning can be fully automated.

cards.status_note: Open for a single unconditional homogeneous rational linear inequality over all finite-valued distributions, based on primary sources and a later-result check through 11 September 2026. Invalidity is semidecidable. Conditional undecidability, restricted set-function domains and inequality-generation algorithms do not establish undecidability or decidability of this exact problem.

context_blocks.text: For a given distribution, each subset of variables has an entropy. Collecting these numbers produces one point in a space with \(2^{n}- 1\) coordinates. The question asks whether an input linear halfspace contains every such point, across all finite alphabets and distributions. It is therefore a question about all possible information structures, rather than about estimating entropies from a dataset.

Familiar examples are easy to express in this format. Subadditivity is \(H(X_{1})+H(X_{2})- H(X_{1},X_{2})\ge 0\). Conditional mutual information is \(H(X_{1},X_{3})+H(X_{2},X_{3})- H(X_{3})- H(X_{1},X_{2},X_{3})\ge 0\). Both hold without a premise. A negative coefficient is perfectly legitimate; it is the full linear combination, rather than each individual summand, whose sign is being decided.

The standard Shannon inequalities give a finite linear-programming proof method for each n. They express nonnegative conditional entropies and conditional mutual informations, or equivalently normalized monotone submodular set functions. If a candidate follows from them, it is universally valid. But the first non-Shannon inequality of Zhang–Yeung showed in 1998 that this proof method is incomplete. Rejecting an attempted Shannon derivation therefore cannot be used as a negative answer about entropy validity.

The unrestricted alphabet quantifier is a major part of the difficulty. A computation on binary variables explores only a small portion of the permitted distributions. Increasing a guessed alphabet bound may discover new counterexamples, but an unsuccessful search at every bound examined so far provides no effective stopping criterion. A solution cannot quietly replace all finite alphabets by one fixed support limit depending on a heuristic.

There is a rigorous semidecision procedure for invalidity. If an inequality is false, it is strictly negative at some distribution with finite alphabets. Entropy is continuous on that finite probability simplex, so a sufficiently close rational distribution still violates it. Enumerate alphabet sizes and rational distributions, and compute certified entropy approximations of increasing precision. Eventually the negative value is certified. The arithmetical-hierarchy study of Abo Khamis–Kolaitis–Ngo–Suciu places validity in co-r.e.

This explains precisely what a positive solution would add: a way to halt on every valid inequality as well. A complete effective enumeration of proofs of all valid inequalities, coupled with the counterexample search, would suffice. Existing automated methods can produce many correct certificates, but no completeness theorem for all rational unconditional inequalities is supplied by the inspected sources.

Taking the topological closure of the entropic region does not change this particular validity problem. A continuous linear form nonnegative on every entropic point is nonnegative on every limit point, and the reverse implication is immediate. Thus the same unconditional linear inequalities hold for entropic and almost-entropic vectors. This observation depends on the exact logical form; it does not authorize replacing the domain inside arbitrary conditional statements.

Cheuk Ting Li’s 2023 theorem establishes undecidability for conditional information inequalities and conditional-independence implication. Those inputs include premises that must hold exactly. Merely deleting a premise changes the statement. The theorem therefore does not by itself establish undecidability of a single unconditional inequality.

Adding a fixed penalty for violating a premise need not capture its limiting behavior. Kaced–Romashchenko explicitly show essentially conditional inequalities that do not extend to unconditional linear inequalities in the proposed manner. Their results explain why this seemingly direct route from conditional to unconditional validity needs additional justification.

Hannula’s 2024 work studies useful decidable simplifications: different classes of set functions and syntactic forms connected to database bounds. Its coNP-completeness result is for normal polymatroids, a restricted semantic domain, while another polynomial-time result uses monotone functions. These are precise complexity results for different domains, not a classification of validity over all entropy vectors.

The connection to databases gives the question an algorithmic role beyond coding theory. Entropy inequalities constrain how large a relational join can be under information about its inputs and degrees. Related logical forms occur in query containment and dependency implication. Understanding which constraints admit complete reasoning procedures helps explain why some query bounds can be computed effectively while broader formulations encounter undecidability.

The 2025 exploration by László Csirmaz compares the Copy Lemma, maximum-entropy constructions and the Ahlswede–Körner method, and leaves their completeness unresolved. Előd P. Csirmaz and László Csirmaz’s 2026 paper derives two infinite collections of five-variable inequalities and computes consequences through nine generations of its construction. Its enumeration concerns that method’s extremal inequalities; even the proposed characterization of the method is not a characterization of the entire entropy region.

cards.definitions: A channel has nonempty finite alphabets \(\mathcal X_1,\mathcal X_2,\mathcal Y_1,\mathcal Y_2\) and arbitrary real probabilities \(W(y_1,y_2\mid x_1,x_2)\ge0\), summing to one over outputs for each input pair. Conditional on input sequences, an \(n\)-use output sequence has law \(\prod_{t=1}^n W(y_{1,t},y_{2,t}\mid x_{1,t},x_{2,t})\). Messages \(M_1,M_2\) are independent and uniform on \([K_{1,n}]\) and \([K_{2,n}]\), where \([K]=\{1,\ldots,K\}\) and message counts are positive integers. Encoder \(i\) is a deterministic map \([K_{i,n}]\to\mathcal X_i^n\); its decoder is a deterministic map \(\mathcal Y_i^n\to[K_{i,n}]\). Error means at least one incorrectly decoded message, averaged over both messages and channel randomness. A pair \((R_1,R_2)\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^2\) is achievable if there are codes with block lengths \(n_j\to\infty\), error tending to zero, and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2K_{i,n_j}\ge R_i\) for both users. The capacity region \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{IC}}(W)\) is the closure of these achievable pairs. The channel and both codebooks are known to all terminals. There is no common message, feedback, terminal cooperation, input cost or computational bound. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. The region is compact, convex and downward closed, so all its nonnegative upper supporting values determine it. The function is measured in weighted bits per joint channel use. Channel laws and weights are mathematical real objects; no finite-precision input or algorithmic evaluation model is imposed.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g(W,\lambda)\) on the entire stated domain and a Lean proof of \(|g(W,\lambda)-F_{\mathrm{IC}}(W,\lambda)|\le1/100\) for every channel and weight. The proof must control both sides of the error; exact determination also qualifies. The guarantee concerns the support value in bits per joint use, with the coding model unchanged. Sample values, a plot or a restatement of the defining optimization or limit are insufficient. No prescribed formula syntax or polynomial evaluation-time bound is required.

cards.title: Constant-rate binary locally decodable codes with logarithmic query complexity
cards.formal: Do there exist constants \(r\in\)(0,1], \(\delta \in (0,1/2)\) and \(A>0\) such that, for arbitrarily large message lengths k, there are an integer n with \(k\le n\le k/r\), an encoding \(C:\{0,1\}^{k}\to \{0,1\}^{n}\), and randomized local decoders \(Dec_{i}\) for \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,k\}\), satisfying the following? For every message x, every received word \(z\in \{0,1\}^{n}\) differing from \(C(x)\) in fewer than \(\delta n\) positions, and every requested index \(i, Dec_{i}\) with oracle access to z outputs \(x_{i}\) with probability at least \(2/3\) while making at most \(\lceil A \log _{2}(n+1)\rceil\) bit queries on every execution.

cards.definitions: Here k counts message bits and n counts stored codeword bits; rate is \(k/n\) and Hamming distance counts unequal coordinates. “Arbitrarily large” means that every threshold K is exceeded by an admissible k; the constants \(r, \delta\) and A must be fixed before K. The encoding is deterministic and injective. A decoder knows C, k, n and the requested index, but learns the received word only by querying named coordinates, each returning one bit. Queries may be adaptive. A randomized decoder can be represented as a probability distribution over finite binary decision trees with the stated depth bound, whose leaves output 0 or 1. Computation, description length and encoding time are unrestricted: this is the source’s existence question, without an additional requirement of efficient uniform construction. The success guarantee is separate for each triple \((x,z,i)\); it does not require one random seed to recover all bits simultaneously. The adversary may choose corruptions knowing x and C, but z is fixed before the decoder’s private randomness. There is no secret key, channel-computation bound or input-dependent auxiliary information. The decoder must return the requested bit, rather than an erasure or a list of candidates.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove existence of a family with all the stated fixed constants and guarantees, or prove its logical negation. A negative result must exclude every choice of positive constant rate, positive constant error tolerance and logarithmic-query constant for unbounded message lengths. A construction over a growing alphabet or a decoder that may fail on some requested positions under the allowed corruption guarantee does not establish the proposition.

context_blocks.title: Recover one item without reading everything
context_blocks.text: A file can be protected by adding redundant bits, yet reading the whole encoded file to retrieve one bit defeats the purpose of local access. Constant rate limits the storage overhead to one fixed factor. Constant error tolerance requires recovery even when a fixed positive fraction of the stored bits have been changed adversarially.

context_blocks.title: Why simple repetition does not suffice
context_blocks.text: Repeating every message bit three times gives constant rate and a three-query majority decoder. However, an adversary can spend just three corruptions on the requested bit’s copies. For large files this fits within any fixed positive global error budget and makes those copies look like a different message. Local redundancy alone therefore does not supply the guarantee for every requested position.

context_blocks.title: The remaining query gap
context_blocks.text: The April 2026 source records a logarithmic lower bound at constant rate, while the known binary high-rate construction uses \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  n\cdot \log  \log  n})}\) queries. A bound of this latter form is subpolynomial but still larger than logarithmic. Its large-alphabet construction reaches polylogarithmic symbol queries; one such symbol can contain many bits, so it does not give the binary result here.

context_blocks.title: Related decoding guarantees
context_blocks.text: The January 2026 HDX paper gives approximate local list decoding and low-depth list decoding. A list may contain several plausible messages, and circuit depth measures parallel stages rather than bits inspected. Those results do not supply the single requested message bit with this card’s worst-case query and success guarantees.

cards.context:
A file can be protected by adding redundant bits, yet reading the whole encoded file to retrieve one bit defeats the purpose of local access. Constant rate limits the storage overhead to one fixed factor. Constant error tolerance requires recovery even when a fixed positive fraction of the stored bits have been changed adversarially.

Repeating every message bit three times gives constant rate and a three-query majority decoder. However, an adversary can spend just three corruptions on the requested bit’s copies. For large files this fits within any fixed positive global error budget and makes those copies look like a different message. Local redundancy alone therefore does not supply the guarantee for every requested position.

The April 2026 source records a logarithmic lower bound at constant rate, while the known binary high-rate construction uses \(2^{O(\sqrt{\log  n\cdot \log  \log  n})}\) queries. A bound of this latter form is subpolynomial but still larger than logarithmic. Its large-alphabet construction reaches polylogarithmic symbol queries; one such symbol can contain many bits, so it does not give the binary result here.

The January 2026 HDX paper gives approximate local list decoding and low-depth list decoding. A list may contain several plausible messages, and circuit depth measures parallel stages rather than bits inspected. Those results do not supply the single requested message bit with this card’s worst-case query and success guarantees.

cards.definitions: The source alphabets \(\mathcal X_i\) and reproduction alphabets \(\widehat{\mathcal X}_i\), for \(i=1,2\), are nonempty finite sets. The pairs \((X_{1,t},X_{2,t})\) are independent identically distributed draws from an arbitrary real probability table \(P\) on \(\mathcal X_1\times\mathcal X_2\). Distortions are finite-valued functions \(d_i:\mathcal X_i\times\widehat{\mathcal X}_i\to\mathbb R_{\ge0}\). Write \(P_i\) for the marginal source law and \(D_{i,\min}=\sum_{x\in\mathcal X_i}P_i(x)\min_{z\in\widehat{\mathcal X}_i}d_i(x,z)\). The domain requires finite real \(D_i\ge D_{i,\min}\). An \(n\)-block code consists of deterministic encoders \(f_{i,n}:\mathcal X_i^n\to[M_{i,n}]\), where \([M]=\{1,\ldots,M\}\) and \(M_{i,n}\ge1\), and a deterministic decoder from the pair of indices to \(\widehat{\mathcal X}_1^n\times\widehat{\mathcal X}_2^n\). Each encoder sees only its own source block. For the resulting reproductions define \(\Delta_{i,n}=n^{-1}\sum_{t=1}^n\mathbb E[d_i(X_{i,t},\widehat X_{i,t})]\). A nonnegative pair is achievable if, along some \(n_j\to\infty\), codes satisfy \(\limsup_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2M_{i,n_j}\le R_i\) and \(\limsup_{j\to\infty}\Delta_{i,n_j}\le D_i\) for both sources. The region \(\mathcal R\) is the closure of achievable pairs. There is no interaction, extra side information, computational restriction or variable-length encoding; distortion is expected per-symbol distortion. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. Transmitting both source blocks and selecting minimum-distortion reproductions establishes feasibility on the stated domain; smaller distortion targets, which would give an empty region, are excluded. The region is convex and upward closed. Its nonnegative lower supporting values describe its lower rate boundary. The target is finite and nonnegative, in weighted bits per source pair. All tables are mathematical real objects, with no algorithmic representation requirement.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g\) on the whole source, distortion and weight domain above and a Lean proof of \(|g-F_{\mathrm{RD}}|\le1/100\) pointwise. This is an error bound on the weighted rate in bits per source pair; the distortion constraints remain exact. Prove both sides of the bound, or determine the function exactly. A finite sample of values or a restatement of the operational infimum or limit is insufficient. No specified formula grammar or polynomial evaluation-time requirement is imposed.

cards.definitions: \(C_{7}\) has vertex set \(\{0,\ldots ,6\}\), with distinct vertices adjacent when their difference modulo 7 is 1 or 6. For an integer \(t\ge 1\), the strong power has vertex set \(\{0,\ldots ,6\}^{t}\). Two distinct tuples are adjacent when, in every coordinate, their entries are equal or adjacent in \(C_{7}\). An independent set contains no adjacent distinct pair, and \(\alpha\) is its maximum cardinality. The capacity is measured in distinguishable symbols per channel use, rather than its logarithm in bits. It lies between 3 and 7; the supremum need not occur at a finite power. There is no computational restriction on independent sets or their construction.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a specified real number \(a\) and a Lean proof that \(|a-\Theta(C_7)|\le1/100\). cards.definitions: The channel has nonempty finite input alphabets \(\mathcal X_1,\mathcal X_2\), output alphabets \(\mathcal Y_1,\mathcal Y_2\), and a table of arbitrary real probabilities \(W(y_1,y_2\mid x_1,x_2)\ge0\), summing to one over outputs for every input pair. In an \(n\)-use code, terminal \(i\) holds a message \(M_i\) uniform on \([K_{i,n}]=\{1,\ldots,K_{i,n}\}\), with positive integer message counts and independent messages. At time \(t\), its input is \(X_{i,t}=f_{i,t}(M_i,Y_i^{t-1})\), where \(f_{i,t}\) is deterministic and \(Y_i^{t-1}=(Y_{i,1},\ldots,Y_{i,t-1})\). Given the current inputs and full past history, the current output pair has distribution \(W\). Terminal 1 estimates \(M_2\) from \((M_1,Y_1^n)\), and terminal 2 estimates \(M_1\) from \((M_2,Y_2^n)\), by deterministic decoders. Error is the probability that either estimate is wrong, averaged over messages and channel draws. A nonnegative rate pair is achievable if codes along \(n_j\to\infty\) have error tending to zero and \(\liminf_{j\to\infty}n_j^{-1}\log_2K_{i,n_j}\ge R_i\) for both terminals. Thus \(R_1\) is the rate from terminal 1 to terminal 2, and \(R_2\) is the reverse rate. The region \(\mathcal C_{\mathrm{TW}}(W)\) is the closure of achievable pairs. The law and all coding functions are public. There are no extra communication links, shared messages, input constraints or computational bounds. The received outputs provide the permitted feedback. Predetermined time sharing is allowed. The capacity region is compact, convex and downward closed, so its nonnegative upper supporting values determine it. Rates are in bits per simultaneous joint channel use, without an extra factor of two. The channel table and weight are mathematical real objects, not finite-precision algorithmic inputs.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous real-valued function \(g(W,\lambda)\) on every channel and weight above and a Lean proof of \(|g(W,\lambda)-F_{\mathrm{TW}}(W,\lambda)|\le1/100\) everywhere. A finite set of examples, an uncertified plot or a restatement of the operational optimization or limit is insufficient. No specified formula syntax or polynomial evaluation-time bound is imposed.

cards.definitions: Encode G with vertices \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}, n\ge 0\), by n and its symmetric zero-diagonal \(n\times n\) binary adjacency matrix; encode k, a and b as signed or unsigned binary integers as appropriate. For \(m\ge 1\), the strong power \(G^{\boxtimes m}\) has vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}^{m}\). Distinct tuples x,y are adjacent exactly when, for every coordinate j, either \(x_{j}=y_{j}\) or \(\{x_{j},y_{j}\}\) is an edge of G. An independent set contains no adjacent pair; \(\alpha (H)\) is its maximum cardinality, with \(\alpha\) of the graph with no vertices equal to zero. Define \(\Theta(G)=\sup_{m\ge1}\alpha(G^{\boxtimes m})^{1/m}\). For nonempty G the supremum equals the limit as \(m\to \infty\), and \(1\le \Theta (G)\le n\); set \(\Theta (G)=0\) when \(n=0\). The desired output approximates \(\Theta\) itself, not its logarithm. The same machine must work for all graphs and precision requests, with no oracle or graph-dependent advice. It may use arbitrarily much finite time and memory on each input.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer supplies a single algorithm and proves termination and the stated absolute-error bound for every valid graph and precision. A negative answer proves that no such uniform algorithm exists. Hardness of exact independent-set computation, failure of a particular approximation scheme, or failure of any finite power to attain the limit does not by itself answer this computability question.

context_blocks.title: Zero-error communication as a graph
context_blocks.text: Vertices represent symbols, and an edge means that the channel can confuse the two symbols. An independent set is therefore a collection of distinguishable messages for one use. Over several uses, messages are tuples and must be distinguishable in at least one coordinate. The strong power records exactly this possibility of confusion, while the root normalizes message counts per use.

context_blocks.title: Why longer blocks matter
context_blocks.text: A complete n-vertex graph has capacity 1, since every pair of distinct symbols can be confused. An edgeless n-vertex graph has capacity n. Between these extremes, coding across several uses can help: the five-cycle has independence number 2 but Shannon capacity \(\sqrt{5}\). For nonempty graphs, \(\log _{2}\Theta (G)\) is the corresponding zero-error rate in bits per use.

context_blocks.title: A limit needs an effective error guarantee
context_blocks.text: Every finite strong power has a finite independence number, but the definition takes a supremum over unbounded lengths. Alon and Lubetzky show that a long fixed prefix of these values can seriously underestimate the eventual capacity. This result rules out an unjustified stopping inference from apparent stabilization; it does not rule out every algorithm with a graph-dependent running time.

context_blocks.title: Recent progress and the scope of the question
context_blocks.text: The October 2025 paper explicitly retains general computability as unknown. Lavi and Sason’s January 2026 results provide exact values for special families and connected examples where no finite strong power attains capacity. Nonattainment does not preclude effective approximation: a computable real can be the limit of unequal approximants. The exact capacity of \(C_{7}\) is a separate card, and computing that one value would not settle the uniform question for all finite graphs.

cards.title: Effective classification of polynomially testable hereditary graph properties
cards.formal: Is there a total algorithm which, given a finite family F of finite simple graphs, decides whether induced-F-freeness admits a one-sided dense-model tester sampling at most \(C\cdot \varepsilon ^{- c}\) vertices, for some constants C,c depending only on F?
cards.definitions: The input to the classification algorithm is a finite list of adjacency matrices; the empty list is allowed. Let \(\mathrm{P}_{F}\) contain exactly the finite simple graphs with no induced subgraph isomorphic to any member of F. For an n-vertex graph G, define \(\operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P}_{F})\) as the minimum number of edge additions or deletions needed to obtain a graph in \(\mathrm{P}_{F}\) on the same vertex set, divided by \(n^{2}\); define the distance as +∞ when no such graph exists. For an integer s, the canonical tester chooses a uniformly random subset S of \(\min \{n,s\}\) distinct vertices, queries all adjacencies in S, and rejects exactly when \(G[S]\) contains an induced member of F. Say that F is polynomially testable if there are integers \(C,c\ge 1\) such that for every rational \(\varepsilon \in (0,1)\), every \(n\ge 1\) and every G with \(\operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P}_{F})>\varepsilon\), this tester with \(s=\lceil C\varepsilon ^{- c}\rceil\) rejects with probability at least \(2/3\). It automatically accepts every graph in \(\mathrm{P}_{F}\). The requested deterministic classification algorithm must halt on every finite F and answer YES exactly for these families. No runtime bound on that classification algorithm is imposed, and it need not output the constants C,c. Graph order n and accuracy \(\varepsilon\) are universally quantified in the property being classified; they are not additional inputs to the classification algorithm.

cards.why: Asks whether the efficient sampling regime of hereditary graph testing can be recognized from a finite description, turning a broad classification programme into a precise decidability target.

references.authors: Gaia Carenini; Cameron Seth; Yuichi Yoshida
references.locator: TR26-144, submitted 13 August and published 16 August 2026; Definition 1.3 and Theorem 1.4. Quantitative equivalence, not a decision procedure on finite forbidden lists

cards.status_note: Reviewed through 11 September 2026. The source’s finite-family structural classification remains incomplete in the checked literature. This card explicitly asks its effective decidability version. The August 2026 container theorem does not provide the required terminating classifier.

context_blocks.text: The source survey asks for a characterization of finite forbidden-induced-subgraph families whose canonical sample complexity is polynomial in inverse accuracy. To make the requested output unambiguous, this card fixes an effective classification question: can that class of finite inputs be decided at all? This additional effectiveness requirement is an editorial specification, rather than wording attributed to the survey. It distinguishes the target from an equivalent reformulation involving another unresolved infinite condition.

There are two separate computational tasks. Given a fixed family F and a particular finite graph, exact membership in \(\mathrm{P}_{F}\) can be checked by searching for its finitely many forbidden patterns. The question here concerns a statement about every possible host graph and arbitrarily small \(\varepsilon\). Finite decidability of each individual membership test does not by itself provide a decision procedure for the existence of uniform polynomial sampling bounds.

The dense-model normalization matters. Being \(\varepsilon\)-far means that a positive \(\varepsilon\) fraction of all possible vertex pairs must be changed, up to the fixed normalization factor. It does not mean that an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of the edges currently present must be removed. A sparse graph can therefore be close to a property even when many of its own edges would need modification. No bounded-degree or sparse-input model is implicit.

One-sided error gives rejection a concrete witness: the sampled vertices contain a forbidden induced graph. For an induced copy, both edges and nonedges must agree with the pattern. Thus a four-clique contains an ordinary four-cycle as a subgraph, but no induced four-cycle. Replacing induced copies with arbitrary copies changes the classification problem substantially.

The general hereditary testing theorem guarantees some sample bound depending only on \(\varepsilon\), but that bound can be much larger than every polynomial. For finite F, inspecting all pairs in a sample squares its size, which preserves the distinction between polynomial and nonpolynomial dependence. Since F is fixed during testing, exhaustive checking inside the sample also has a fixed polynomial exponent, although that exponent need not be uniform across families.

Gishboliner–Shapira prove a useful sufficient condition: a finite family containing a bipartite graph, a co-bipartite graph and a split graph is polynomially testable. Here co-bipartite means a union of two cliques, and split means a partition into a clique and an independent set; the three roles may be played by the same graph. Their necessary condition requires a bipartite and a co-bipartite member, but this is not sufficient.

The gap between these conditions is real. There are finite families containing a bipartite and a co-bipartite graph that are not polynomially testable. Conversely, split graphs themselves form a polynomially testable class, described by forbidding \(C_{4}\), its complement and \(C_{5}\), although none of those forbidden graphs is split. Thus simply promoting either known condition to an equivalence would give wrong answers on known examples.
Even a singleton family remains instructive. Alon–Fox prove polynomial testability for cographs, which are precisely graphs with no induced four-vertex path.
Induced \(C_{4}\)-freeness and its complement remain the exceptional cases identified in the 2025 survey.
Gishboliner–Shapira obtain a single-exponential sample bound for induced \(C_{4}\)-freeness; that improves substantially on regularity-based bounds but is not polynomial in \(1/\varepsilon\).

An August 2026 preprint by Carenini–Seth–Yoshida gives a new quantitative characterization using ordered containers. Roughly, property-satisfying induced subgraphs inside a graph far from the property must fit into smaller vertex sets determined by short fingerprints. Theorem 1.4 translates between tester bounds and these container parameters by explicit polynomial transformations. This is relevant new progress beyond the survey.

Its effectiveness has a specific meaning: given suitable quantitative bounds on one side, the theorem supplies bounds on the other. The container premise still ranges over all sufficiently large host graphs and all accuracy parameters. The inspected theorem does not give a terminating procedure that takes only F and decides whether polynomial container parameters exist. It therefore does not establish the effective finite-family classification asked here.

The distinction is useful independently of how the eventual classification looks. An affirmative answer would provide a finite method for recognizing when global violations must have abundant small witnesses. An undecidability theorem would show that no universal terminating rule can perform this recognition from arbitrary finite forbidden lists, even though each list defines a straightforward graph-membership problem. Either outcome would identify a fundamental limit of turning qualitative testing theorems into systematic algorithm design.
