cards.title: Polynomial testability versus distance estimation
cards.formal: For every isomorphism-invariant property P of finite simple graphs with \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) nonempty for every \(n\ge 1\), does existence of a uniform randomized tester using polynomially many queries in \(1/\varepsilon\), independently of n, imply existence of such an additive-\(\varepsilon\) distance estimator, in the dense model defined below?
cards.definitions: \(\mathrm{P}_{n}\) is a nonempty subset of graphs on \([n]\), invariant under vertex permutations. For \(n\ge 2, \operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P})=\min _{H\in \mathrm{P}_{n}}|E(G)\triangle E(H)|/\operatorname{binom}(n,2)\); for \(n=1\) it is zero. An algorithm receives n and an integer \(t\ge 2\), with \(\varepsilon =1/t\), and accesses G only by adaptive queries asking whether a specified unordered pair is an edge. A tester returns a bit, accepts each \(G\in \mathrm{P}_{n}\) with probability \(\ge 2/3\) and rejects each G with \(\operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P})\ge \varepsilon\) with probability \(\ge 2/3\); no condition is imposed between those cases. Polynomial testability means there exist one probabilistic Turing oracle machine and constants \(C,a\ge 1\) with at most \(Ct^{a}\) adjacency queries on every input and every execution. An estimator is another such uniform machine and constants \(C' ,b\ge 1\), using at most \(C' t^{b}\) queries and returning a binary-encoded rational q with \(\Pr [|q- \operatorname{dist}(G,\mathrm{P})|\le 1/t]\ge 2/3\) for every G. Computation between queries and total output length have no prescribed bound, but every execution terminates. Coins are independent fair bits; programs and constants may depend on P and cannot depend on n,t or G. Neither algorithm receives a description of P or graph-dependent advice. This asks only the polynomial-testability implication named in the title. The stronger quantitative \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon ))\) conversion in source Problem 5.4 is not asserted equivalent to it.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: Separates recognizing a robust violation from measuring its magnitude and asks whether polynomially efficient dense-graph testing automatically provides polynomial distance estimation.

importance.reason: A direct quantitative frontier between two central tasks in property testing, with a universal implication that would organize many existing polynomial-testing results.

progress.text: Fischer and Newman prove a general tester-to-estimator conversion with a large quantitative overhead, leaving the polynomial regime open.
Gishboliner, Kushnir and Shapira revisit testing versus estimation and improve general conversion bounds, but do not obtain the conjectured polynomial transformation.
Gishboliner and Shapira state Problem 5.4: decide whether \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\varepsilon )\) testability implies estimation with \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon ))\) sample complexity.

context_blocks.text: Testing asks only for a robust decision: accept graphs in the property and reject graphs that are \(\varepsilon\)-far from it. Estimation asks for the actual distance to the property, so it must distinguish every pair of nearby distance scales rather than only the two extremes used by a tester.

In the dense graph model the input has \(\Theta (n^{2})\) possible adjacency queries, yet many properties can be tested with a number of samples depending only on \(\varepsilon\). The central quantitative issue is whether this efficiency survives when the algorithm must estimate distance rather than detect a large violation.

Known reductions convert a tester into an estimator with very large overhead. The 2025 survey of polynomial property testing records an explicit open problem asking whether \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\varepsilon )\) can be replaced by \(q_{\mathrm{P}}(\operatorname{poly}(\varepsilon ))\); for polynomial testers this would yield a polynomial estimator. Existing results establish the implication only with exponential or otherwise much larger transformations in general.

Some important classes already have polynomial estimators, including selected hereditary partition properties and several induced-subgraph examples. Such positive cases show that the gap is not caused by a universal information-theoretic obstruction, but they do not give the transformation for every graph property.

The question is about query complexity in the dense model. A result in the bounded-degree model, a computational-time bound after reading the full graph, or a tester that estimates only whether the distance is above one fixed threshold addresses a different problem.

cards.definitions: The graph is a finite loopless directed graph with vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\); opposite arcs are allowed, but parallel copies of an arc are not. An oracle query specifies a vertex v, a direction IN or OUT, and an index \(i\in \{1,\ldots ,d\}\); it returns the ith neighbor in that direction or a null symbol if the slot is empty. Lists are consistent with one fixed graph and have arbitrary fixed order, so correctness must hold for every permitted ordering. Vertex labels, n,d and \(\varepsilon\) are given to the tester; it may choose any vertex label, use independent fair random bits, and adapt future queries to previous answers. Internal computation is not charged to query complexity. A directed cycle is a sequence of distinct vertices \(v_{1},\ldots ,v_{k}, k\ge 2\), with arcs \(v_{i}\to v_{i+1}\) and \(v_{k}\to v_{1}\); acyclic means no such cycle exists. Let \(\tau (G)\) be the minimum number of arcs whose deletion makes G acyclic. An input is \(\varepsilon\)-far if \(\tau (G)>\varepsilon dn\). Additions cannot remove cycles, so this agrees with the minimum-edge-edit convention for this property. The tester must accept each acyclic graph with probability at least \(2/3\) and reject each \(\varepsilon\)-far graph with probability at least \(2/3\). There is no guarantee for graphs between these cases. Q is the least integer query bound attainable on all n-vertex inputs and all random branches by a randomized query procedure with these guarantees. An upper-bound family must be generated by a uniform algorithm from n,d and the binary encoding of rational \(\varepsilon\); there is no running-time requirement beyond termination. The requested \(\Theta\) bounds concern growth in n, with constants allowed to depend on the fixed d and \(\varepsilon\). One-sided error, which must always accept acyclic inputs, is a separate restriction.
cards.answer_criterion: Give an explicit asymptotic bound \(F(n,d,\varepsilon ), a\) uniform tester using \(O(F)\) queries, and a matching \(\Omega (F)\) lower bound for the same adaptive two-sided, bidirectional model, for each fixed \(d,\varepsilon\) in the stated range. Hidden constants may depend on \(d,\varepsilon\), but no factor growing with n may be left unmatched. The source’s broad best-algorithm question is made precise here as optimal query complexity; total runtime is not the cost being classified.

cards.title: A dimension-free directed \(\mathrm{L}^{1}\) Poincaré inequality
cards.formal: Does there exist an absolute constant \(C<\infty\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge 1\) and every Lipschitz function \(f:[0,1]^{n}\to \mathbb{R} , d_{1}^{\mathrm{mono}}(f) \le  C \int _{[0,1]^{n}} (\sum_{i=1}^{n} \max \{- \partial _{i}f(x),0\}^{2})^{1/2} dx\)? Here \(d_{1}^{\mathrm{mono}}(f)\) is the \(\mathrm{L}^{1}\) distance to the coordinatewise nondecreasing functions. The same C must work for every dimension and every finite Lipschitz constant.
cards.why: Would connect local directional decreases to global distance from monotonicity with a universal constant, extending a central isoperimetric principle to real-valued functions on continuous cubes.

Lebesgue measure on \([0,1]^{n}\) has total mass one. A function \(g:[0,1]^{n}	o \mathbb{R}\) is coordinatewise nondecreasing if \(g(x)\le g(y)\) whenever \(x_{i}\le y_{i}\) for all i. Define \(d_{1}^{\mathrm{mono}}(f)=\inf _{g} \int |f(x)- g(x)|dx\), over measurable integrable coordinatewise nondecreasing g; g need not have the same Lipschitz constant as f. A function f is Lipschitz if there is a finite L with |\(f(x)- f(y)|\le \mathrm{L}\Vert x- y\Vert _{2}\) for all x,y in the cube. Its gradient exists almost everywhere; its values on the exceptional null set may be set to zero without changing any integral. The negative gradient is \(
abla ^{-}f(x)=(\max \{- \partial _{1}f(x),0\},\ldots ,\max \{- \partial _{n}f(x),0\})\). The right-hand side is \(C\cdot E[\Vert 
abla ^{-}f(X)\Vert _{2}]\) for a uniform point X in the cube. It is not \(C\cdot (E[\Vert 
abla ^{-}f(X)\Vert _{2}^{2}])^{1/2}\). No boundary condition, mean-zero assumption or fixed bound on the range of f is imposed.

A bound whose constant grows with n, or a bound using the \(\mathrm{L}^{2}\) norm of the gradient over the cube, is insufficient.

cards.definitions: An input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\) is available through queries to individual coordinates. Its distance to the known property \(\mathcal P\) is \(n^{-1}\min_{y\in\mathcal P}|\{i:x_i\ne y_i\}|\). A tester accepts every member with probability at least \(2/3\) and rejects every input at distance strictly greater than \(\varepsilon\) with probability at least \(2/3\); other inputs have no correctness requirement. Under the source convention, \(j\) rounds of adaptivity mean \(j+1\) batches \(Q_0,\ldots,Q_j\). All coordinates in one batch are chosen before their answers are revealed. The coordinates and size of every later batch may depend on all earlier answers; empty batches are permitted. A randomized tester is a finite probability distribution over deterministic batch-query trees, each of which returns a bit on every input. Probabilities may be arbitrary real numbers; this is the nonuniform query-complexity model, without a computational or randomness-generation cost. Each selected tree’s total queries are bounded on every input, and cost is their worst case over the support and inputs. Let \(q_j(n,\mathcal P,\varepsilon)\) be the least such bound among all valid testers. Reading every coordinate shows \(q_j\le n\). The tester may depend arbitrarily on the fixed property, length and proximity parameter; no uniform synthesis from a property description is requested. Querying a coordinate already read gives no additional information and can be omitted. The same property, distance and error convention occur on both sides of \(F\). The source’s complete nonadaptive simulation shows \(F(q,k,\ell)\le2^q-1\), so the supremum is finite; since all values are integers, it is a maximum. The desired precision is a positive function \(g(q,k,\ell)\) and one absolute \(C\ge1\) with \(C^{-1}g\le F\le Cg\) for every admissible triple. The comparison constant must not depend on a parameter or on a hidden property.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply an unambiguous positive comparison function and a Lean proof of both universal constant-factor bounds on the full parameter domain. The upper bound must cover adaptive batch sizes, and the lower bound must be witnessed by permitted properties and proximity parameters. A bound only for deleting one round, fixed-size batches or a selected regime does not determine this tradeoff. Numerical 0.01 error is not the precision for this asymptotic-complexity target.

context_blocks.text: VC dimension characterizes nonprivate learning. Finite Littlestone dimension $\mathrm{LD}$ characterizes the existence of private learning but does not determine its optimal quantitative cost.

A sample-complexity characterization should tell us how many labelled examples are necessary from the structure of the hypothesis class, rather than from a particular learning algorithm. Two classes can have the same ordinary capacity measure while differing in how difficult it is to hide the influence of an individual training example.

The quantitative issue matters even after learnability is settled. Knowing that some finite sample size works does not distinguish a useful bound from an enormous one. The proposed relation asks whether the extra price of privacy can be controlled by ordinary statistical complexity together with a very slowly growing function of online-learning complexity.

cards.definitions: A concept class is a finite set of functions from a domain X to \(\{0,1\}\). \(\operatorname{VC}(C)\) is the largest size of a subset of X on which all binary labelings occur. \(LD(C)\) is the greatest depth of a complete binary tree labeled by domain points such that every root-to-leaf edge-label sequence is realized by a concept. The function log-star counts base-two logarithms needed to reach at most one. A learner may output a hypothesis outside C. Privacy requires $\Pr[A(S)\in E]\le e\Pr[A(S\prime)\in E]+1/(100m^2)$ whenever the two m-record samples differ by replacement of one record. Here X is finite, distributions on X are arbitrary probability vectors, and a learner is a probability kernel from length-m labeled samples to the finite set \(\{0,1\}^{X}\) of hypotheses. The sample size m is a positive integer chosen for C before the target and distribution. For every target \(h\in C\) and distribution D on X, with probability at least \(9/10\) over m independent draws \(x_{i}\) from D and learner randomness, the returned hypothesis has D-probability of disagreement with h at most \(1/10\). Privacy holds for all labeled samples, including unrealizable ones, and all subsets E of the hypothesis set. The same kernel and m work for all D,h. This finite-domain convention retains the finite-class target: points in an arbitrary domain with the same label vector \((h(x))_{h\in C}\) can be identified, giving at most \(2^{|}C|\) cells and preserving both dimensions. A learner on those cells lifts to the original domain. No running-time or computable-representation requirement is imposed.

cards.definitions: For an integer \(T\ge 2, a\) mechanism is a family of Borel probability distributions \(M_{x}\) on \(\mathbb{R} ^{T}\), one for each binary stream \(x\in \{0,1\}^{T}\). Its output \(Y_{t}\) is released immediately after observing \(x_{t}\). Causality means that whenever x and \(x'\) have the same first t bits, the marginal distributions of \((Y_{1},\ldots ,Y_{t})\) under \(M_{x}\) and \(M_{x}'\) are equal. The horizon T is known before the first output. Streams are fixed inputs, not adaptively chosen in response to outputs. Neighbors differ in exactly one bit, and pure privacy requires \(M_{x}(S)\le \exp (1/2)M_{x}' (S)\) for every pair of neighbors and every Borel \(S\subseteq \mathbb{R} ^{T}\). This protects the entire joint transcript, with no additive failure allowance. There is no restriction on computation, memory, real precision, output integrality or monotonicity; internal randomness may be correlated across times. A different family of probability distributions may be chosen for each T. The maximum over streams is outside the expectation; the maximum over time is inside it. The infimum is used without assuming attainment. \(E(T)\) is finite, for example because a data-independent all-zero transcript has error at most T. All logarithms in asymptotic comparisons may use any fixed base greater than one.

context_blocks.text: Continual counting publishes a running total as events arrive. For the stream \((1,0,1,1)\), the exact outputs are \((1,1,2,3)\). Changing its second bit gives \((1,1,1,1)\) and exact outputs \((1,2,3,4)\): one protected event changes several releases. Privacy must therefore hold for the whole visible transcript. Separate guarantees for isolated timestamps do not establish the stated joint guarantee.

The causal requirement forbids using future events to improve earlier releases. It also concerns their joint distribution, not merely the marginal law of each single output; otherwise correlations among old outputs could reveal future data. The offline query-release problem may inspect the complete database before producing any answer and consequently asks for a different capability.

The order of maximum and expectation is central. Imagine an error vector that equals one at a single uniformly random timestamp and zero elsewhere. Its expected maximum is one, but the largest expected absolute error at any predetermined timestamp is only \(1/T\). This example concerns error criteria, not a proposed private mechanism. Squared-error bounds and average-over-time bounds also cannot be substituted without checking the conversion.

For the fixed privacy budget here, the July 2026 Bairaktari–Larsen result gives the lower benchmark \(\Omega (\log ^{3/2}T)\), while the best upper bound summarized in their Table 1 is \(O(\log ^{2}T)\). The binary-tree mechanism aggregates intervals and reuses their noisy counts across prefixes. The paper closes the dependence on T for approximate privacy at fixed parameters, but its pure-privacy row retains the square-root-of-logarithm gap.

Arkhipov and Kalinin improve constants for mean and maximum per-coordinate squared error using matrix mechanisms. Those criteria take expectations before choosing the worst coordinate, or average squared errors. Improving them is useful, but does not by itself determine the expected largest absolute error of the entire transcript.

Bhowmik and Hasan’s August revision claims tight squared-error order for arbitrary real factorizations within Laplace matrix mechanisms. It explicitly excludes expected maxima and unrestricted non-matrix mechanisms. Thus even accepting its claimed theorem would not settle this card’s minimax quantity.

Lin, Mirrokni and Woodruff independently give a near-optimal lower bound for a prefix-matrix factorization cost. Its quantification is over factorizations, while this card allows every causal private output distribution. The distinction remains essential when reading a result advertised as optimal for a class of mechanisms.

A matching order for \(E(T)\) would identify the unavoidable worst-time accuracy cost of a basic continually released statistic under pure privacy. The target is a minimax information bound: it does not additionally ask for an efficient implementation or restrict the form of a candidate mechanism.

cards.answer_criterion: Determine an asymptotic rate \(g(T)\) and prove constants \(c,C>0\) and \(T_{0}\) such that \(c g(T)\le E(T)\le C g(T)\) for every \(T\ge T_{0}\). The upper guarantee must be achievable by permitted causal pure-private mechanisms, and the lower guarantee must cover all such mechanisms. Constants may not depend on T. The expected maximum absolute-error criterion must be the same on both sides.

cards.title: Polynomial-time private release of all marginals
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer \(C\ge 1, a\) function \(\alpha :N_{\ge 2}\to [0,1]\) with \(\lim _{d\to \infty}\alpha (d)=0, a\) uniform randomized mechanism M and a uniform deterministic evaluator E, such that for every \(d\ge 2\) and every database \(D\in (\{0,1\}^{d})^{n}\) with \(n=d^{C}, M\) runs in time polynomial in n,d, satisfies \((1,1/(100n^{2}))\)-differential privacy under replacement of one row, and outputs a finite synopsis S for which, with probability at least \(2/3, E(S,q)\) approximates \(q(D)\) within \(\alpha (d)\) simultaneously for every marginal query q?
cards.definitions: A marginal query is a pair \((J,a)\), where \(J\subseteq \{1,\ldots ,d\}\) and \(a\in \{0,1\}^{J}\), and \(q_{J,a}(D)=|\){\(i\in \{1,\ldots ,n\}:D_{ij}=a_{j}\) for all \(j\in J\)}|/n. The empty J query has value one. Queries of every order up to d are included. The database is an explicitly stored ordered n-by-d bit matrix; neighbouring databases have the same dimensions and differ in exactly one row. Differential privacy means that for every ordered pair of neighbours \(D,D'\) and every set O of output strings, \(\Pr [M(D)\in O]\le e\cdot \Pr [M(D' )\in O]+1/(100n^{2})\). M uses independent fair random bits and has one worst-case polynomial bound \(p(n+d)\) on bit operations, output length and random bits. Its output is a finite binary string S. E receives d,S,J,a, has a worst-case bound given by one polynomial in d+|S| and outputs a binary-encoded rational number. E has no access to D, private state of M or an additional oracle. Both algorithms are ordinary classical Turing machines, with no nonuniform advice. The accuracy event is simultaneous over all queries and its probability is over M’s randomness alone, separately for every D. S need not encode a synthetic database or a consistent probability distribution. \(C,\alpha ,p,M,E\) and the evaluator’s polynomial are fixed before d,D are chosen. No algorithm to compute \(\alpha\) and no prescribed rate of its convergence are required.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: A marginal measures the fraction of records matching a pattern on selected coordinates. Low-order marginals describe small groups of attributes, while all marginals permit every such pattern. The family contains exponentially many queries even though one query has a short description. A synopsis is therefore an efficiently evaluable representation, rather than a literal list of exponentially many answers.

Privacy and accuracy quantify different objects. The privacy guarantee compares the complete output distributions after changing one person’s row. Accuracy concerns all queries simultaneously on each fixed database. Once a successful synopsis has been released, its deterministic evaluation reveals no additional access to the original records. An algorithm answering only a prespecified small batch is not automatically an algorithm for this target.

Vadhan’s Open Problem 7.8 asks about polynomial-time private estimation of all higher-order marginals with vanishing error using only polynomially many rows in the dimension. The present card fixes approximate-DP parameters, replacement adjacency and a noninteractive evaluable synopsis. These choices state one concrete version of the proposal; they are not asserted to be equivalent to every interactive or fixed-order formulation.

Chandrasekaran, Thaler, Ullman and Wan give subexponential-time private algorithms for marginal queries on small databases. Their result illustrates useful progress between exponential and polynomial cost. The constant-accuracy, per-query statement in that paper does not provide the polynomial-time, vanishing-error synopsis required here.

Requiring synthetic records would impose an extra restriction. The benchmark permits any binary synopsis with an efficient evaluator, because hardness of synthetic-data generation need not rule out other ways of answering queries. The existing TCS-0506 concerns private PAC sample complexity, while TCS-6040 asks about strong approximation of coverage functions. Neither asks this computational query-release question.

cards.title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
cards.formal: For every pair of fixed finite relational structures A,B of the same finite signature, with a homomorphism \(A\to B\), is the decision promise problem of distinguishing \(I\to A\) from I↛B either solvable in deterministic polynomial time or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions?
cards.definitions: A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols R with fixed positive arities \(a_{R}\). A structure A consists of a finite nonempty domain and, for each R, a relation \(R^{A}\subseteq A^{a_{R}}\). A homomorphism \(h:I\to A\) is a map on domains such that \((v_{1},\ldots ,v_{a})\in R^{I}\) implies \((h(v_{1}),\ldots ,h(v_{a}))\in R^{A}\) for every R and tuple. The templates A,B and their relations are fixed for each computational problem. Only I varies; its domain and relation tuples are explicitly listed in binary, of total length L. The algorithm must accept all I admitting a homomorphism to A and reject all I admitting no homomorphism to B. On \(I\to B\) but I↛A, either answer is allowed. \(A\to B\) makes the yes and no sets disjoint. Polynomial time means one deterministic algorithm for the fixed pair, halting on every input in \(O(\mathrm{L}^{c})\), with c and hidden constants allowed to depend on A,B. NP-hardness means a deterministic polynomial-time map from 3-SAT formulas \(\varphi\) to structures \(I_{\varphi}\) such that satisfiable \(\varphi\) yield \(I_{\varphi}\to A\) and unsatisfiable \(\varphi\) yield \(I_{\varphi}\)↛B. The question is about deciding the promise, not producing a B-valued assignment. No uniform algorithm for classifying templates is required. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: The main classification question for constraint satisfaction with promises, encompassing approximate colouring and many local relaxation tasks. A resolution would determine whether finite constraint languages force a sharp tractability boundary even when their exact and relaxed solutions differ.

importance.reason: A broad structural question extending the finite CSP dichotomy into approximation and promise problems, with connections to algebra, topology, and optimization.

Barto exhibits a polynomial-time finite-domain PCSP that cannot be sandwiched through a tractable finite-domain CSP unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

cards.status_note: Open classification question in the cited survey, with relevant partial results checked through 10 September 2026. The card asks for an unconditional decision dichotomy over all fixed finite template pairs; it does not assume decision/search equivalence or a complete algebraic classification.

context_blocks.text: Ordinary constraint satisfaction asks whether a collection of local requirements can all hold simultaneously. Promise CSPs keep two versions of each requirement: the input is guaranteed to admit a solution satisfying the stronger version, while the relaxed task uses the weaker one. For graph colouring, \(A=K_{k}\) and \(B=K_{c}\) with \(k\le c\) produces the decision task of distinguishing k-colourable graphs from graphs that are not c-colourable. Graphs in between impose no decision requirement.

When \(A=B\), the promise disappears. Bulatov and Zhuk independently proved in 2017 that every finite-template CSP is either in P or NP-complete. The present question asks whether a comparable exclusion of intermediate complexity survives arbitrary finite promises. It does not follow merely by applying the classical theorem to A and B separately: the relaxed task can be easier than either endpoint CSP.

A concrete tractable example promises that each listed triple of Boolean variables can have exactly one 1 and asks only for a not-all-equal assignment. Solve the equations \(x+y+z=1\) over the integers, then map positive values to 1 and nonpositive values to 0. No such triple can become all zero or all one. Barto proves that this tractability cannot be explained by sandwiching the pair through a tractable finite-domain CSP, unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\). Finite templates can therefore need an infinite intermediate domain in this natural algorithmic framework.

The algebraic approach studies operations that combine several A-solutions coordinatewise into one B-solution. These polymorphisms capture useful structure for algorithms and reductions, but their input and output domains can differ, preventing the direct use of all the composition arguments available in ordinary CSP. The survey emphasizes that a full dichotomy was not yet backed by enough evidence to be asserted as a settled consensus conjecture; this card poses it as a precise open question.

Important subclasses are classified. Brakensiek and Guruswami obtain a dichotomy for symmetric Boolean promise CSPs allowing negations, with tractable cases going beyond a direct reuse of Schaefer’s classical Boolean CSP classification. That theorem does not classify all Boolean templates or all finite domains.

The 2026 work of Banakh, Barsukov, and Nakajima expands the logical viewpoint by relating Promise MMSNP to finite-domain PCSPs. It also classifies a family defined by forbidden monochromatic cliques under the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture. Both the restricted family and the additional assumption matter: this is not an unconditional classification of every finite template pair.

cards.title: Bodirsky–Pinsker conjecture
cards.formal: For every countable finitely bounded homogeneous structure A over a finite relational signature, and every finite-signature first-order reduct B of A, is \(\mathrm{CSP}(B)\) either decidable in deterministic polynomial time or NP-complete under polynomial-time many-one reductions?
cards.definitions: A relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols with fixed finite arities. A is homogeneous if every isomorphism between two finite induced substructures extends to an automorphism of A. It is finitely bounded if there is a finite set F of finite structures in its signature such that a finite structure embeds into A exactly when none of the structures in F embeds into it; embeddings preserve both relations and their complements. Countable allows finite or countably infinite domains. B has the same domain as A, with finitely many relations each definable by a first-order formula over A without parameters; it may forget original relations and introduce definable ones. For each fixed B, an input to \(\mathrm{CSP}(B)\) is an explicitly encoded finite structure I in B’s signature. Accept exactly when there is a map h from the domain of I to that of B preserving every relation tuple. Equivalently, a finite conjunction of atomic B-constraints must have a satisfying assignment. h need not be injective. A, B and their defining formulas are fixed, not part of the input; running times are measured in the finite instance’s bit length. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: The main tractability-classification conjecture for well-behaved infinite-domain CSPs. It links algorithm design, universal algebra and model theory, and would extend the finite-domain dichotomy to substantially richer constraint languages.

importance.reason: A central unifying conjecture about the boundary of polynomial-time constraint solving, with broad logical scope and active links to promise CSPs.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The latest checked primary papers explicitly retain the general dichotomy as open. The July \(FO/\mathrm{L}\)-hard classification has both a different complexity boundary and an expansion hypothesis; the August interpretability result does not settle tractability.

context_blocks.text: The finite-domain CSP dichotomy, proved independently by Bulatov and Zhuk in 2017, says that fixing a finite collection of relations on a finite domain leaves no intermediate complexity between polynomial time and NP-completeness. The infinite-domain conjecture asks whether this organizing principle survives when variables can take rational values, positions in a countable graph, or other infinitely many possibilities, provided the template has a finite structural description.

The restrictions explain why the question is computationally meaningful. Homogeneity means that finite patterns completely determine their symmetry type. Finite boundedness gives a finite list of forbidden patterns for checking whether a proposed finite configuration can occur. For a fixed reduct, one can guess a partition of the variables representing equal values and the finite relational pattern on those values, then check the constraints and forbidden patterns. The signature and forbidden sizes are constants, so this yields polynomial-size NP certificates despite the infinite domain.

For a concrete example, the ordered rational numbers \((\mathbb{Q} ;<)\) are homogeneous and finitely bounded. Constraints consisting only of strict inequalities are feasible exactly when their directed inequality graph is acyclic. Adding the definable ternary relation “y lies strictly between x and z” gives the classical NP-complete Betweenness problem. Thus the same domain can support both tractable and hard constraint languages; the choice of allowed relations is decisive.

A central method studies polymorphisms: operations which, applied coordinatewise to several satisfying tuples of any relation, produce another satisfying tuple. Such operations record ways of combining solutions and can prevent standard hardness gadgets. Barto and Pinsker identify a particular algebraic identity that characterizes the absence of the relevant hardness construction for model-complete cores. The missing general step is turning the tractable-side algebraic structure into polynomial-time algorithms. The bare \(\mathrm{P}/\mathrm{NP}\)-complete dichotomy asked here is weaker than proving that full algebraic classification.

Pinsker, Rydval, Schöbi, Spiess and Winkler’s May 2026 revision shows that the conjecture can be reduced to templates without algebraicity: fixing finitely many elements does not force any additional element into a finite orbit. Their construction replaces domain elements by infinite families while preserving the relevant constraint complexity. They also connect tractable infinite-domain templates to finite-domain promise CSPs through intermediate structures. These are reductions in the scope of the conjecture, rather than a general tractability algorithm.

Dorochko and Wrona’s July 2026 revision proves a different dichotomy: for first-order expansions of finitely bounded homogeneous model-complete cores, the CSP is first-order definable or hard for deterministic logarithmic space under first-order reductions. An expansion retains all original relations; this hypothesis does not cover arbitrary reducts. Moreover, L-hard problems can still be in P, so the result separates a much lower boundary and leaves the P versus NP-complete question open.

Feller and Pinsker’s August 2026 revision develops effective tools for comparing templates. In particular, a model-complete core is computable when the structure has a finitely bounded Ramsey expansion, an additional structural hypothesis. Their decidability results concern interpretability and equivalent algebraic presentations, not a complete algorithmic classification of all templates in this card.

A resolution would say whether a finite description by symmetric local patterns rules out intermediate NP complexity across a large family of logical and combinatorial problems. The difficulty is to find algorithms that exploit this description uniformly within each fixed template, without assuming that the infinitely many possible values can simply be replaced by one fixed finite domain.

cards.title: Constant-colour polynomial-time colouring of 3-colourable graphs
cards.formal: Is there a fixed integer \(C\ge 3\) and a uniform randomized polynomial-time algorithm that, on every finite simple undirected graph G promised to be 3-colourable, outputs a proper vertex colouring using at most C colours with probability at least \(2/3\)?
cards.definitions: The input is an explicitly given graph \(G=([n],E), n\ge 1\), with no loops or parallel edges, encoded by its adjacency matrix. A proper k-colouring is a map \(c:[n]\to [k]\) such that \(c(u)\ne c(v)\) for every \(\{u,v\}\in E\). The promise is existence of a proper 3-colouring; such a colouring is not supplied. There must be one C, one randomized Turing machine A, and fixed constants K,d such that A uses at most \(K(n+1)^{d}\) bit operations on every graph and every random tape. On each promised input, the probability, over independent unbiased internal random bits, of outputting a proper C-colouring is at least \(2/3\). Invalid outputs can be replaced by a failure symbol after checking all edges. No correctness requirement is imposed on non-3-colourable inputs, but the time bound still applies. The algorithm may colour such an input whenever it can; it need not recognize the promise. C is independent of n, degree, density and the input graph. No planarity, bounded-degree, expansion, forbidden-subgraph, random-input or supplied-decomposition promise is available. Randomization is explicitly permitted in this version of the inherited question; a deterministic algorithm would be a stronger positive result. The algorithm must colour every vertex and avoid every monochromatic edge on a successful run.
cards.answer_criterion: Give such an algorithm for at least one fixed C, or prove that no such C and randomized polynomial-time algorithm exist. A growing colour bound, a partial colouring of most vertices, or a guarantee only on a restricted graph family is insufficient. NP-hardness of the 3-versus-C promise for every fixed C would establish the usual complexity-theoretic obstruction; excluding randomized algorithms from that obstruction additionally uses \(\mathrm{NP}\ne \mathrm{RP}\). Hardness for \(C=5\) alone leaves all larger constants unresolved. Conditional hardness results must keep their assumptions explicit.
cards.why: A defining promise-CSP problem: determine whether relaxing an NP-hard colouring task to any fixed larger palette permits efficient construction of a valid solution.

importance.reason: The paradigmatic approximate graph-colouring question, central to promise CSPs and to the gap between algorithmic relaxations and hardness with perfect completeness.

progress.text: Barto–Bulín–Krokhin–Opršal establish the NP-hardness of five-colouring three-colourable graphs; the full work appears in JACM in 2021.
Guruswami–Sandeep derive hardness for every fixed output palette from a d-to-1 conjecture with perfect completeness.
Kawarabayashi–Thorup–Yoneda obtain \(\widetilde{O}\)\((n^{0.19747})\) colours using improved combinatorial progress combined with SDP methods.
Bansal–Huang–Lee improve the general polynomial-time upper bound to \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours through a new SDP-based analysis.
The revised Dawar–Molnár full version proves an all-constant obstruction for fixed-point logic with counting; it does not establish unrestricted computational hardness.

cards.status_note: No constant-colour algorithm or unrestricted all-constant hardness resolution found through 11 September 2026. The February 2026 primary paper retains the gap between five-colour NP-hardness and a growing \(O(n^{0.19539})\) algorithmic bound. The March logic result is restricted to fixed-point logic with counting. This card explicitly allows bounded-error randomized algorithms.

context_blocks.text: The input comes with a guarantee that three colours suffice, but not with the partition into three independent sets. Allowing more colours is a relaxation of the output requirements. The question asks whether some fixed amount of this relaxation makes the problem efficiently solvable on every promised input. A mechanism for choosing 100 colours would qualify just as a mechanism for choosing six colours would; the constant need not be close to three.

This promise matters. Strong inapproximability results for the chromatic number on unrestricted graphs can use instances whose chromatic number grows with the graph size. They do not automatically establish hardness when the yes-instances must have chromatic number at most three. Conversely, an algorithm for planar graphs would use a structural assumption missing here. Three-colourable graphs can be dense and can have high-degree vertices.

The problem is a basic example of promise constraint satisfaction. An edge asks its two endpoints to receive different labels. The promise says the constraints have a solution over a three-element domain; the algorithm is allowed to use a larger fixed domain. In graph-homomorphism language, an input maps to \(K_{3}\) and the output must provide a map to \(K_{C}\). The associated decision promise distinguishes graphs mapping to \(K_{3}\) from graphs not mapping to \(K_{C}\).

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal prove NP-hardness of finding a five-colouring of a three-colourable graph, as part of a broader algebraic framework. This is far stronger than hardness of finding the promised three-colouring, yet it excludes only particular small output domains under standard complexity assumptions. It does not rule out a successful algorithm using six, 100 or any other larger fixed number of colours.

A useful elementary observation is that the neighbours of any vertex in a three-colourable graph induce a bipartite graph: the vertex’s own colour cannot appear among its neighbours. Thus one can efficiently colour a large neighbourhood using two fresh colours. When all remaining degrees are small, greedy colouring is effective. Balancing these two procedures already gives an \(O(\sqrt{n})\)-colour algorithm. The challenge is to extract much more global information than this local observation provides.

Modern algorithms combine combinatorial reductions with semidefinite relaxations. The relaxation assigns vectors that mimic the separation of colours, and rounding extracts independent sets or other useful progress. Kawarabayashi, Thorup and Yoneda’s STOC 2024 work strengthens the combinatorial side and obtains \(\widetilde{O}\)\((n^{0.19747})\) colours after combining it with the SDP approach. The suppressed factors are polylogarithmic in n.

Bansal, Huang and Lee’s February 2026 preprint improves the SDP analysis using third-level neighbourhoods and a new vector \(5/2\)-colouring construction. Combined with the combinatorial component, its theorem gives \(O(n^{0.19539})\) colours. A vector \(5/2\)-colouring is a geometric relaxation, not an ordinary assignment using a fractional number of colours. The exponent improvement is real progress, while the final number of actual colours still grows with n.

Hardness evidence also goes beyond five colours under additional assumptions. Guruswami and Sandeep show that a fixed d-to-1 Label Cover conjecture implies hardness for every constant output palette. Their premise requires perfectly satisfiable yes-instances. Replacing perfect completeness by near-perfect completeness changes what the reduction guarantees, so established results about almost-satisfiable games cannot simply be substituted into this argument.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.

Dawar and Molnár’s full version, revised in March 2026, proves that fixed-point logic with counting cannot separate three-colourable graphs from graphs requiring more than any fixed number of colours. This is an unconditional obstruction for that logic on unordered structures, not for all polynomial-time algorithms on explicitly encoded graphs. The card sits at the intersection of approximation algorithms, algebraic reductions and limits of relaxation methods: a resolution would tell us how much a fixed expansion of the solution domain can help.

cards.title: Search-to-decision equivalence for finite promise CSPs
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures A and B with the same finite signature and \(A\to B\), does polynomial-time solvability of the decision promise \(\mathrm{CSP}(A,B)\) imply polynomial-time solvability of its search version? Decision must accept X whenever \(X\to A\) and reject X whenever X↛B. Search, on every X promised to satisfy \(X\to A\), must output an explicit homomorphism \(X\to B\).
cards.definitions: A finite relational signature is a finite list of relation symbols with fixed positive integer arities. A structure A consists of a finite nonempty domain and one relation \(R^{A}\subseteq A^{r}\) for each r-ary symbol R; B and the input X have relations with the same symbols and arities. A homomorphism \(h:X\to B\) is a map on domains such that \((x_{1},\ldots ,x_{r})\in R^{X}\) implies \((h(x_{1}),\ldots ,h(x_{r}))\in R^{B}\) for every symbol and tuple. Write \(X\to B\) when some such map exists. A and B are constants defining the computational problem, and are not part of each input. The input explicitly lists X’s vertices and relation tuples; its encoding length is N. Both algorithms are deterministic Turing machines with running time polynomial in N on all inputs; their constants and exponents may depend on A and B. The decision algorithm may answer either way when X↛A but \(X\to B\). The search algorithm receives no homomorphism to A, only the promise that one exists. It must output the image of every vertex and satisfy every B-relation on promised inputs; outside that promise it may output anything or a failure symbol, but must still halt within its polynomial bound. The quantifiers are \(\forall (A,B)\): (\(\exists\) polynomial-time decider D)⇒(\(\exists\) polynomial-time search algorithm S). No uniform procedure that discovers D or S from arbitrary templates, and no requirement to use D as a black-box oracle, is included.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the implication for every fixed finite template pair, or identify one fixed pair with a polynomial-time decision algorithm and prove that its promised search problem has no polynomial-time algorithm. An impossibility for one rounding scheme, an undecidable problem with the template as part of the input, or hardness on instances lacking \(X\to A\) does not refute the statement. A conditional separation is relevant progress but must retain its complexity assumption.
cards.why: Determine whether every efficiently decidable finite promise constraint problem also has an efficient way to construct its promised weaker solution.

cards.status_note: Explicitly open in §10 of Larrauri’s revised full paper, dated 25 May 2026. Its rounding hardness uses a weaker input promise than \(X\to A\), and its meta-problem undecidability varies the template. The revision corrects earlier overbroad interpretations. No full resolution found through 11 September 2026; this card asks the per-template tractability implication, not a stronger uniform black-box reduction theorem.

context_blocks.text: A promise CSP separates the conditions known to be satisfiable from the conditions a solution must meet. The structure A describes the stronger requirements; B describes the weaker ones. The fixed homomorphism \(A\to B\) ensures that an A-solution can always be converted into a B-solution if it is known. The difficulty is that the input supplies only the existence promise, without the stronger solution itself.

Graph colouring is a concrete example. Take A to be the complete graph on three vertices and B the complete graph on six vertices. Search asks for an actual six-colouring of a graph known to be three-colourable. Decision merely separates three-colourable graphs from graphs that are not six-colourable. On graphs whose chromatic number is four, five or six, the decider may say anything. That unconstrained region is a central obstacle to turning its answers into a colouring.

Search immediately gives decision: run the search algorithm and check the proposed B-homomorphism. Every A-satisfiable input yields a valid output, while a graph or structure with no B-homomorphism can never pass verification. The all-input polynomial running-time requirement makes this argument valid even when the search promise fails. The unknown direction is whether a decider can always be made constructive.

For ordinary finite CSPs, where \(A=B\), polynomial-time decision and search are equivalent. With a genuine promise, a step-by-step fixing procedure has an extra difficulty. After committing a variable to a B-value, the residual instance may still have a B-solution but cease to have an A-solution. The original decision guarantee then no longer certifies which remaining choices are safe. Adding arbitrary pinning constraints can also change the fixed constraint language.

Some positive cases are immediate. If there is a fixed finite structure C with \(A\to C\to B\) and a polynomial-time solver for \(\mathrm{CSP}(C)\), solve in C and compose with the fixed map \(C\to B\). This includes the cases where \(\mathrm{CSP}(A)\) or \(\mathrm{CSP}(B)\) is tractable. But the general PCSP framework admits tractable examples that are not explained by an intermediate tractable finite CSP, assuming \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\), so this method does not cover the whole question.

There are also elementary constructive relaxations. Suppose Boolean variables occur in triples, with a promise of an assignment having exactly one 1 in every triple, and the goal is merely to make each triple nonconstant. Solve the integer linear system \(x+y+z=1\) for the listed triples, allowing arbitrary integers. The promise makes it feasible. Map positive integers to 1 and nonpositive integers to 0. No equation can have all three integers positive, or all three nonpositive, so this map satisfies every weaker triple. This illustrates a rounding rule whose correctness can be checked directly.

Larrauri’s FOCS 2025 work proves that finding a B-solution on every instance accepted by BLP, AIP or their combination can encode any chosen TFNP problem through a suitable fixed template. TFNP consists of polynomially verifiable search problems whose solutions are guaranteed to exist. The accepted instances need not satisfy \(X\to A\). Thus the rounding task can be harder than the promised search task. The May 2026 revision explicitly corrects earlier overbroad claims and keeps the general implication open.

The same work proves undecidability of several algorithmic meta-problems, where A and B are supplied as input and one asks whether a relaxation solves their PCSP. This concerns recognizing an entire family of templates. Our question permits a different fixed algorithm for each fixed template, so undecidability of that recognition task is logically compatible with a positive answer here.

Recent constructive progress also occurs under explicit algebraic hypotheses. The SODA 2026 robust-satisfiability paper gives algorithms for Boolean PCSPs with majority polymorphisms when the stronger constraints are almost satisfiable, along with matching conditional tradeoffs in several settings. Such results identify useful rounding structure, but do not provide a transformation for an arbitrary tractable decision template.

The issue is fundamental because a feasibility guarantee is often only the beginning of an algorithmic application: one needs the assignment, colouring or schedule. A positive theorem would justify moving between classification of decision problems and construction of solutions throughout finite PCSPs. A negative theorem would reveal a precise local-constraint problem where efficient recognition of the promised gap conceals a harder search task.

cards.title: Hardness of 6-coloring 3-colorable graphs
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic polynomial-time many-one reduction R from Boolean 3-SAT to finite simple undirected graphs such that, for every 3-CNF formula F, satisfiability of F implies \(\chi (R(F))\le 3\) and unsatisfiability of F implies \(\chi (R(F))>6\)?
cards.definitions: A 3-CNF formula is a conjunction of clauses containing at most three literals, each literal being a Boolean variable or its negation; the formula and variable indices have a standard explicit finite binary encoding. R is a uniform deterministic multitape Turing machine that outputs a graph as a labelled vertex set \(\{1,\ldots ,n\}\) and a list of unordered pairs of distinct vertices, with no repeated edges. Its total running time and output length are bounded by one polynomial in the formula’s encoding length. A proper k-colouring assigns one of \(\{1,\ldots ,k\}\) to each vertex so that endpoints of every edge receive different colours. \(\chi (G)\) is the least such k, with \(\chi\) of the empty graph taken to be zero. The promise decision problem, also denoted \(PCSP(K_{3},K_{6})\), has yes-instances \(\chi \le 3\) and no-instances \(\chi >6\); graphs with \(\chi =4,5,6\) are outside the promise. \(K_{k}\) is the loopless complete graph on k vertices. No colouring or satisfiability witness is supplied as input. The reduction must satisfy the two implications unconditionally, without a Unique Games or Label Cover hardness hypothesis. Because 3-SAT is NP-complete, this reduction is precisely the usual deterministic many-one NP-hardness target for the promise problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or its logical negation, with all definitions, promises, resource bounds and quantifiers as stated. A conditional result establishes only the explicitly conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete proof-assistant-verified proof of the full target.

context_blocks.text: The input promise says that three colours suffice, but it does not reveal the three colour classes. Allowing a larger palette relaxes the output condition. The associated gap decision task distinguishes such promised yes-instances from graphs that cannot be coloured even with six colours. This isolates a small finite-template promise CSP with a particularly clear combinatorial meaning.

Barto, Bulín, Krokhin and Opršal establish hardness for colouring k-colourable graphs with \(2k- 1\) colours, including the 3-versus-5 case. The 3-versus-6 question remains explicitly posed in subsequent work. Increasing the permitted palette weakens the output requirement, so hardness at five colours does not imply hardness at six.

TCS-6637 asks whether some fixed constant C admits a polynomial-time colouring algorithm for every 3-colourable graph. A negative result for six colours alone does not exclude algorithms using seven, one hundred or another fixed palette. Conversely, an algorithm with a growing number of colours does not settle even the six-colour search problem. The new card is a precise frontier case, rather than a duplicate of the quantifier over arbitrary constants.

The decision and search tasks should also be kept distinct. A polynomial-time six-colouring algorithm on 3-colourable inputs would decide the gap by checking its output: on a graph requiring more than six colours, no valid output exists. This implication explains the algorithmic relevance of the decision hardness target without redefining NP-hardness as a blanket statement about every search reduction.

The six-colour case has value beyond its small numerical parameters. It tests how far promise relaxation can preserve intractability after the classical CSP dichotomy, and it provides a fixed finite object on which algebraic and combinatorial limitations can be stated. Its specialist home remains Constraint satisfaction under the catalogue’s graph-category expansion.

cards.title: Exact exponential-time equivalence for nonnegative Boolean Max-CSP
cards.formal: Does the following extension of the source’s degree-based classification hold? For every fixed finite Boolean constraint language \(\Gamma\) that is neither 0-valid, 1-valid, nor 2-monotone, let \(d=\deg (\Gamma )\). For every fixed real \(\alpha >1\), if Max \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma ,N,c)\) has an exact deterministic algorithm running in \(\alpha ^{n}n^{O(1)}\) time for every fixed constant \(c\ge 1\), must Max d-CNF-SAT with nonnegative integer weights of total weight at most \(n^{c}\) also have an exact deterministic \(\alpha ^{n}n^{O(1)}\)-time algorithm for every fixed \(c\ge 1\)? The same base \(\alpha\) is required. Algorithms and polynomial factors may depend on \(\Gamma ,\alpha ,c\). This formulates the conclusion’s speedup question as extending Theorem 6.2 to all NP-hard nonnegative-weight languages; tractable languages are explicitly excluded.
cards.why: Would show whether the algebraic degree of a Boolean constraint language determines its exact exponential-time complexity even when every constraint has the usual nonnegative weight.
cards.status_note: Checked the conference statement against the March 2024 version of record, including the exact-base quantifiers, all-c convention and tractability dichotomy. Subsequent searches through 12 September 2026 did not locate a general resolution. The displayed statement is the NP-hard-language extension of the source’s Theorem 6.2; this editorial interpretation of the shorter conclusion is explicit. Search is not exhaustive.

references.authors: Jansen, Bart M. P.; Włodarczyk, Michał

cards.definitions: A Boolean predicate f of arity r is a map \(\{0,1\}\)ʳ→\(\{0,1\}\). A language \(\Gamma\) is a fixed finite set of such predicates, not part of an input instance. An instance \(\Phi\) has variables \(x_{1},\ldots ,x_{n}\) and weighted applications \((f,(i_{1},\ldots ,i_{r}),w)\), where \(f\in \Gamma\), each \(i_{j}\in [n]\) and w is a nonnegative integer. Indices may repeat. Arguments are variables themselves: constants and negated literals are available only if the corresponding predicate can already be expressed by a member of \(\Gamma\) with variable arguments. The value \(\Phi (x)\) is the sum of weights whose predicate applications evaluate to 1. Max \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma ,N,c)\) asks whether \(\max _{x\in \{0,1\}^{n}}\Phi (x)\ge t\) for an input integer t, under the promise that total weight is at most \(n^{c}\). Weights, indices and t use binary encoding; duplicate applications can be combined and zero-weight applications discarded. Trivial thresholds outside the possible objective range are handled during input reading. Polynomial-time normalization is included; equivalently the runtime has an additional input-reading term for a redundantly listed representation. The normalized input has polynomial length for fixed \(\Gamma ,c\). The algorithm must answer every promised instance correctly, and n denotes variables, not clauses, total weight or bit length. For each f there is a unique multilinear real polynomial \(\mathrm{P}_{f}\) agreeing with f on its Boolean cube. Its degree is the largest number of variables in a monomial with nonzero coefficient; \(\deg (\Gamma )=\max _{f\in \Gamma}\deg (\mathrm{P}_{f})\). This is neither maximum predicate arity nor polynomial degree over \(F_{2}\). Constants can be removed with a threshold adjustment. Disregarding constant predicates, a language is 0-valid if every predicate accepts its all-zero input, and 1-valid if every predicate accepts its all-one input. It is 2-monotone if each predicate has a DNF representation with at most two terms, one consisting only of positive variables and one only of negated variables. The excluded three cases are the source’s polynomial-time cases for nonnegative weights; the remaining cases are NP-hard and have \(d\ge 2\). Max d-CNF-SAT is the same threshold maximization problem for disjunctions of at most d literals, with both signs of variables allowed, and nonnegative integer clause weights. Equivalently one may use the source’s d-ary clause language and repeated variables. All complexity statements are worst-case exact running times in an ordinary discrete computation model, up to polynomial factors. The premise is quantified over every fixed polynomial weight bound c; a result for only one small weight range does not supply that premise.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the displayed implication for every eligible fixed language \(\Gamma\) and every \(\alpha >1\), retaining the same exponential base and the all-c weight convention, or refute it by a language and a rigorously established failure of that implication. A theorem comparing only whether both problems are NP-hard, or comparing compression sizes or exponential rates after a constant-factor increase in variable count, does not establish the stated base-preserving classification.

context_blocks.title: Degree already classifies the signed-weight model
context_blocks.text: Theorem 6.2 places all degree-d signed-weight languages in the same exact exponential-base class as weighted Max d-CNF-SAT. The forward implication from Max d-CNF-SAT algorithms also covers its nonnegative-weight restrictions.

context_blocks.title: Two closure conditions settle special nonnegative cases
context_blocks.text: The same theorem covers nonnegative languages closed under predicate-output negation, \(f\mapsto 1- f\), or under substitution of literals for arguments. An arbitrary NP-hard language need not have either closure.

context_blocks.title: Preserving variables is essential
context_blocks.text: The source’s additive reductions introduce only \(O(1)\) variables, so \(\alpha ^{n+O(1)}\) preserves \(\alpha\). Its general conversion to nonnegative weights can instead introduce a linear number of variables. That suffices for transferring a polynomial compression exponent but can change an exponential base.

references.locator: Unresolved-question passage on page 8; PDF page 8

cards.definitions: A crisp language is a finite set \(\Gamma\) of relations \(R\subseteq D\)ʳ of possibly different finite arities on a finite nonempty explicitly listed domain D. Each relation is given by its arity and a list of its allowed tuples; unlisted tuples are forbidden. This is equivalent to a cost function with value 0 on allowed tuples and +∞ elsewhere. The input size N includes D, relation delimiters, arities and the binary encodings of all listed entries. There is no fixed bound on |D| or arity imposed outside the input. An m-ary operation \(g:D^{m}\to D\) preserves an r-ary relation R if, for every m tuples \(a^{1},\ldots ,a^{m}\in R\), the coordinatewise tuple \((g(a^{1}_{1},\ldots ,a^{m}_{1}),\ldots ,g(a^{1}_{r},\ldots ,a^{m}_{r}))\) lies in R. A polymorphism of \(\Gamma\) preserves every relation in \(\Gamma\). The language is a core if every unary polymorphism \(u:D\to D\) is bijective; for a finite relational structure such a map is an automorphism. Core status is promised rather than something the requested algorithm must verify. An idempotent Siggers polymorphism is a four-ary operation \(s:D^{4}\to D\) that preserves every relation and satisfies \(s(x,x,x,x)=x\) for all \(x\in D\) and \(s(r,a,r,e)=s(a,r,e,a)\) for every \(r,a,e\in D\). On a core, existence of a Siggers operation without the idempotence identity is equivalent to existence of an idempotent one. An ordinary \(\mathrm{CSP}(\Gamma )\) instance has variables and constraints requiring selected variable tuples to belong to relations of \(\Gamma\); it asks for a satisfying assignment from D. In the source’s terminology, solvable means satisfying the dichotomy’s polymorphism criterion. Such languages have polynomial-time CSP algorithms when \(\Gamma\) is fixed; failure of the criterion gives NP-hardness. The present target tests that algebraic criterion and does not assume \(\mathrm{P}\ne \mathrm{NP}\) in order to define its yes/no answers. The requested machine must halt in \(N^{O(1)}\) time on all inputs and be correct on every input satisfying the core promise. Its behavior on non-core inputs is unrestricted. The task only asks to decide existence, not to output the operation table, although a four-ary table has |\(D|^{4}\) entries and gives a polynomial-size, polynomially checkable existence certificate.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a deterministic algorithm with one polynomial running-time bound in N that accepts exactly the promised core languages having such a polymorphism, or prove that no such algorithm exists. A hardness statement requires the core promise to be respected. Testing whether the input is a core, classifying languages without that promise, or solving CSP instances for one fixed tractable template does not settle this meta-decision problem.

cards.title: Word equations with linear length constraints
cards.formal: Is there a Turing machine that halts on every finite input consisting of a system of word equations \(U_{i}=V_{i}\) and a system of integer linear equalities and inequalities on the variable lengths, and answers YES exactly when a simultaneous solution exists in the free monoid \(\Sigma\)*? The alphabet, equations, variables, and arithmetic coefficients are part of the input, with the conventions below.
cards.definitions: \(\Sigma\) is a finite nonempty alphabet of constant symbols and \(X=\{X_{1},\ldots ,X_{k}\}\) is a disjoint finite set of variables. Each \(U_{i},V_{i}\) is an explicitly written finite word over \(\Sigma \cup X\); repeated occurrences of a variable must receive the same substitution. A solution assigns a finite word \(\sigma (X_{j})\in \Sigma\)* to each variable and extends by concatenation while fixing every letter of \(\Sigma\). The empty word is allowed. Every substituted equality \(\sigma (U_{i})=\sigma (V_{i})\) must hold as a literal equality of words. The additional constraints are a finite conjunction of atoms \(\sum _{j} a_{j}|\sigma (X_{j})|\le b\) or \(\sum _{j} a_{j}|\sigma (X_{j})|=b\), where all coefficients and constants are signed binary integers. Length is the number of alphabet symbols. There is no product of two variable lengths, letter-frequency counter, regular-expression predicate, string-to-integer conversion, or universal quantifier. The requested decider need not run in polynomial, elementary, or any specified computable time bound, but must terminate on satisfiable and unsatisfiable inputs alike. Nonempty-substitution requirements can be imposed using |\(\sigma (X_{j})|\ge 1\). In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
cards.why: A fundamental boundary for reasoning about concatenation and numerical size simultaneously. It governs whether a complete terminating solver can exist for a basic fragment of string constraints used in verification, while connecting free-monoid equations, arithmetic and reachability.

importance.reason: A longstanding decidability question at the intersection of formal languages, number-theoretic constraints and automated verification; even unrestricted termination is unknown, before asking for efficient algorithms.

progress.text: Makanin establishes decidability of plain word equations. Adding linear length constraints remains outside that theorem; the distinction is reviewed by Ciobanu.
Ciobanu’s survey explicitly separates the open length-constraint problem from undecidable letter-count and Parikh-image extensions.

Day and Konefal’s RP 2025 paper appears online, giving decidability for quadratic equations with at most two unknowns and semilinear constraints on solution lengths. The proceedings carry a 2026 copyright year.
Version 3 of Barros, Cadilhac, and Pérez claims NEXP-hardness for the nonerasing positive-Boolean formulation. Only its arithmetic-with-divisibility problem is asserted NEXP-complete.

cards.status_note: Checked through 10 September 2026. The IJCAR 2026 primary source explicitly leaves general word-equation satisfiability with length constraints open. The two-variable quadratic theorem is a restricted case, and the July NEXP-hardness claim is a lower bound rather than a decidability result. This card fixes existential satisfiability with concatenation and integer linear length constraints only.

context_blocks.text: The two ingredients are individually manageable: plain word equations are decidable by Makanin’s theorem, and integer linear arithmetic is decidable. Their combination is difficult because string equality constrains how letters align, while arithmetic constrains the lengths of pieces across those alignments. A decision procedure for either component does not automatically decide their interaction. Ciobanu’s survey identifies this specific combination as a major remaining question.

Taking lengths gives useful necessary conditions, but can lose decisive information. For distinct letters a and b, the equation \(Xa=bX\) yields the harmless length identity |\(X|+1=1+|X|\). Nevertheless, it has no finite-word solution. If X is nonempty its first letter must be b, and cancelling that b leaves the same equation for a shorter word; eventually one obtains the false equality \(a=b\). This example shows why satisfying the induced linear equations alone cannot certify a word solution.

There is an elementary way to recognize every YES instance eventually: enumerate all tuples of finite words and test the equations and length constraints. If a solution exists, this search reaches it. For a NO instance, however, there is no prescribed point at which enumeration can stop. A computable bound on the size of some solution to every satisfiable input would therefore be sufficient for decidability. The existence of large witnesses by itself does not establish undecidability.

Several nearby theories have a different status. Constraints on the numbers of individual letters, or on the full vector of letter counts, can make word-equation satisfiability undecidable. Those predicates carry information beyond total length. Similarly, results with alternating quantifiers concern a stronger logical language. Importing either kind of undecidability theorem into this purely existential length-only question would change the problem.

Day and Konefal prove decidability for quadratic word equations in at most two unknowns, using a connection with matrix-semigroup reachability. Quadratic means each unknown has at most two occurrences across the equation. The two-unknown restriction is essential to the result stated in their RP 2025 paper. Its abstract also explains that sets of possible solution-length vectors need not be semilinear, so representing every such set by ordinary Presburger arithmetic cannot simply be assumed.

Przybocki and Barrett’s IJCAR 2026 work analyzes when extended Nielsen transformations terminate. These transformations reason about prefixes of variable values while tracking partial length information. Their cut graph records dependencies between occurrences, giving a sufficient termination criterion and a partial converse. This advances a procedure used in string solvers, but neither guarantees termination for every input nor decides the unrestricted problem.

Barros, Cadilhac, and Pérez’s July 2026 preprint claims NEXP-hardness for nonerasing satisfiability of positive Boolean combinations of word equations and Presburger length constraints, already over two letters. This strengthens the PP-hardness stated in its first version. Its NEXP-completeness theorem is for arithmetic with divisibility, not for unrestricted word equations with lengths. Positive Boolean formulas can be expanded into finitely many conjunctions for purposes of decidability, but that expansion need not be polynomial. The result therefore records a substantial complexity barrier without establishing a general decider or undecidability.

cards.title: Decidability of unification in the basic modal logic K
cards.formal: Is there a deterministic Turing machine that halts on every finite modal formula \(\varphi\) and decides whether there exists a substitution \(\sigma\) for its propositional variables such that \(\sigma (\varphi )\) is valid on every Kripke frame?
cards.why: Determines whether automated reasoning can decide the existence of a validity-making substitution in the basic normal modal logic, despite the decidability of checking each individual instance and the poorly behaved structure of its unifiers.
cards.status_note: Checked through 11 September 2026. No decision procedure or undecidability theorem for this exact basic-K problem was located. Beklemishev’s 2025 introduction explicitly states it as open. Nullary unification type, undecidability with extra modalities and 2025 decidability for K5 extensions do not settle it.
cards.review_note: Developed from the source proposal after checking the exact modal language and distinctions among validity, unifiability, unification type and stronger logics.

cards.definitions: Formulas are finite expressions generated by variables \(p_{i} (i\in \mathbb{N} ), \perp\), negation, conjunction and the unary operator □; other Boolean connectives and ◇ are abbreviations. Variable indices use binary notation and formulas are supplied as fully written syntax trees. A substitution assigns a finite formula to each variable occurring in \(\varphi\), may use new propositional variables, and extends simultaneously through the connectives and □; it does not substitute recursively inside its newly inserted formulas. There are no distinguished parameters that must remain unchanged. A frame is a nonempty set W with an arbitrary relation \(R\subseteq \mathrm{W}\times \mathrm{W}\), finite or infinite. A valuation assigns a subset of W to every variable. Satisfaction uses the usual truth tables, ⊥ is false everywhere, and \(w\models\)□\(\psi\) iff \(v\models \psi\) for all v with wRv. Validity means satisfaction at every world in every frame with every valuation. This is the basic normal modal logic K, with no reflexivity, transitivity or seriality requirement on R. The substitution is existentially quantified without a length bound. Only its existence is decided; no running-time bound or output unifier is required. Malformed formula encodings are rejected.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a total decision procedure correct for every finite formula in the stated language, or prove that no such Turing machine exists. The unbounded substitution and arbitrary-frame semantics must remain those of parameter-free, single-modality K.

upgraded_from.title: Decidability of unification in the basic modal logic K

references.title: Research reference · www.mathnet.ru

context_blocks.text: A modal formula talks about truth at a world and at worlds accessible from it. Unification asks whether its variables can be replaced by formulas so that the result becomes valid on every frame. This is a global requirement on one syntactic replacement, shared across all worlds and models. Choosing a satisfying assignment in one model is a different and weaker task.

For example, □p is unifiable: replacing p by ⊤ makes it valid. In contrast, ◇p is satisfiable in a model with an accessible world where p holds, but has no unifier in K. At a world with no successors, ◇\(\psi\) is false for every replacement \(\psi\). Such dead ends are allowed by K’s unrestricted frame semantics. These examples distinguish satisfiability from the existence of a valid substitution instance.

For any proposed finite substitution, validity of the resulting K formula is decidable. Enumerating all finite substitutions therefore eventually finds a witness whenever one exists. The unresolved part is a procedure that also halts and answers no on every nonunifiable formula. A search that works only for positive instances does not give the requested decider. There is no time bound in this question.

Jeřábek’s theorem that K has nullary unification type concerns the organization of all unifiers, not their nonexistence. For the formula \(p\to\)□p, unifiers exist, including \(p\mapsto \top\), but they lack a complete irredundant family under the usual instantiation order. In that order, a unifier is more general when other unifiers arise by further substitution, modulo equivalence in K. The theorem blocks a particularly well-behaved classification of witnesses; it does not prove undecidability of whether any witness exists.

The choice of logic changes the problem. Wolter and Zakharyaschev prove undecidability after adding a universal modality, which can state that a formula holds at every world of a model. That extra operator is absent here. Their other negative results also add modalities and nominals. A decidable validity problem can thus coexist with undecidable unification, but those extension results do not settle basic K.

Positive results for stronger frame conditions likewise require care. Gougeon’s 2025 work computes most general unifiers for extensions of K5, including versions with fixed parameters. K5 imposes a Euclidean condition on accessibility: two successors of one world must be accessible from one another in the appropriate direction. K does not impose that condition. Beklemishev’s 2025 paper explicitly separates the open K case from solved transitive logics.

A resolution would locate a basic limit of automated substitution reasoning: can the simplest normal modal logic recognize when an expression can be made universally valid? The target concerns only existence. Constructing every unifier, deciding admissibility of arbitrary inference rules, or finding a most general unifier asks additional questions.
